No day passes on earth without ordinary men and women doing extraordinary things—speaking words of courage, enduring sorrows of noble depth. Yet most of these quiet heroes, thinkers, and martyrs remain unknown, their names lost to time until the day when greatness is measured not by power or title, but by virtue and heart. Some, though recorded in history’s ledgers, sleep forgotten: their lives buried beneath dry facts and cold chronicles. The average reader cannot feel them—these stories are not alive; they are like hailstones that strike and vanish, leaving no trace upon the soul. And so they are not understood, for summaries are not stories, just as skeletons are not bodies.

It is here, then, that fiction may serve a purpose—not merely to entertain, but to interpret.

There exists an ancient, musty chronicle written in stiff Latin, each sentence packed with truth. In one chapter lies the tale of two people who lived quietly, died unheralded, and now rest nameless in stone, as if frozen in time. They were neither kings nor saints, yet their story holds a truth worth remembering. If I can bring them to life—reveal what lies beneath those harsh lines—I believe you will see them differently. You will give them, if only for a moment, a place in your heart.

It was the middle of the fifteenth century. Louis XI ruled France, Edward IV sat uneasily on England’s throne, and Philip “the Good,” Duke of Burgundy, held sway over Holland with cunning and force. He had seized the lands of his cousin Jacqueline, broken her spirit, and now ruled without challenge. It is here, in this quiet corner of Europe, that our story begins.

In the small town of Tergou lived Elias and Catherine, a modest couple whose lives revolved around cloth, silk, brown holland, and especially curried leather—a sturdy material prized by common folk, able to last twenty years and even dull a knife. In an age when steel was freely drawn at dinner tables, such durability was no small virtue.

They were well-off enough, and might have lived free from care—if not for nine children. Each child had been welcomed with joy, a blessing from heaven, a source of delight for parents who saw them as little treasures meant to brighten their days. But as the years passed and the children grew, so too did the weight of responsibility. The olive branches of childhood had become strong saplings, and the parents, aging, began to wonder: *Who will feed them all when we are gone?*

This thought troubled them deeply. Though Dutch families were known for their wisdom and foresight, Elias and Catherine felt the burden more than most. Their table, once full of laughter and chatter, now seemed crowded with futures they could not predict. When the great loaf came round, seeming to vanish before it reached each person, they would exchange glances and whisper, “Who will find bread for them all?”

The younger children, still innocent, believed food came naturally, like sunrise. But the older ones—especially the boys—began to think. Some pondered wisely; others, less so. One evening, Elias said, “Kate, the children grow so fast—the table will soon be too small.”

“We cannot afford it, Eli,” Catherine replied—not answering his words, but his worry, as women often do.

Their fears took another form: pride. As free burghers, they could not bear the thought of any of their blood sinking into obscurity after their deaths. So they saved. With frugality and sacrifice, they fed all the mouths and dressed all the bodies, and still managed to set aside a modest hoard. As it grew, so did their quiet joy—not the miser’s greed, but the peace of knowing they had prepared.

One day, Richart, nineteen and thoughtful, approached his mother. With calm composure, he asked her to speak to his father about sending him to Amsterdam to apprentice under a merchant. “It is the path I wish to follow,” he said. “Merchants are wealthy. I am good with numbers. Please, Mother, speak for me. I shall always be in your debt.”

Catherine gasped. “Leave Tergou?”

“What is one street to me more than another? If I can leave the people, I can leave the stones.”

“Leave your poor father, now that he is no longer young?”

“If I can leave you, I can leave him.”

“Leave your brothers and sisters, who love you so?”

“There are enough in the house without me.”

“What do you mean, Richart? Who is more dear than you?” She stepped closer, her voice trembling. “Wait—have I spoken sharply? Have I been unkind?”

“No, Mother,” Richart said gravely, a tear in his eye. “It is simply this: there will be one mouth less to feed.”

And then she knew. She saw her first fledgling testing the wind. Richart had a steady will—she knew he would not change his mind.

He left. His journey cost every penny of their savings except one gold crown. But he never needed another farthing. Two years later, Jacob, his brother, followed. After dinner—eleven o’clock—Jacob walked out, and at supper, Elias whispered, “Sit wider, dears.” Catherine, who had promised not to grieve, suddenly said, “Ah! The table will soon be too big for the children—and you thought it would be too small.” Then she covered her face with her apron and wept.

“It is best they go,” she sobbed. “That is the cruel part.”

“Nay, nay!” Elias said sharply. “Our children are good. All are dear. Do not listen to her. What God takes seems better than what He leaves—that is to say, men are ungrateful, and women foolish.”

“And I say Richart and Jacob were the flower of the flock,” Catherine insisted.

The coffer was empty again. But they gathered like ants. There was no stock market in those days—only dice and cards for speculation. Elias believed in slow, sure gain. “A penny saved is a penny gained,” he said. Everything not needed went into the coffer—steel-banded, key-locked. They denied themselves even small luxuries, then smiled at each other, perhaps happier than if they’d indulged. In three years, they saved enough to set up their fourth son as a master tailor and their eldest daughter as a robe-maker—both in Tergou. Their trade would support them. But the coffer was drained. This time, even the shop bled a little.

Still, two remained unable to earn: Giles, a dwarf, half-stupid, half-malicious, feared by dogs and shunned by women, yet fiercely defended by his mother; and Little Catherine, frail and crippled, who moved only with crutches. She endured pain with quiet grace, her marble face softened by violet eyes and long lashes, never complaining. Then there were two unwilling: Sybrandt, youngest, who loved play more than work; and Cornelis, eldest, who waited patiently for dead men’s shoes.

Tired and disheartened, Elias and Catherine often asked, “What will become of them when we are gone?” But after saying it many times, the clouds lifted. They still said it—but now with a smile. “But thanks to St. Bavon and all the saints—there’s Gerard.”

Young Gerard had long been apart. He was destined for the Church. In those days, the Church could always provide for its own—by hook or by crook. But hopes were low: his family had no influence, and Gerard himself was frivolous, wrapped in books and penmanship. He carried a tinder-box and brimstone matches, begged candle ends from neighbors, and lit them late into the night—even at eight in winter, when the burgomaster was already asleep.

At home, his quirks were tolerated. But the monks of a nearby convent encouraged them. They taught him calligraphy—until one day, during a lesson, they realized he was teaching them. They laughed gently. He blushed. He had suspected it himself, but dared not admit it.

Then an elderly monk said, “My son, why do you not color your writing? A scroll is bare without borders of fruit, leaves, and rich arabesques. Why not paint the holy figures that adorn each chapter? Let the colors soothe the eye, and the saints lift the heart.”

Gerard stammered, “I’ve tried illuminating—but I failed.”

The monk nodded. “Then try again.”

Soon after, a new mentor arrived—an old woman named Margaret, sister of the famous Van Eyck brothers. She left Flanders and returned to her homeland, buying a small house near Tergou. She heard of Gerard and saw his work. Delighted, she sent her servant, Reicht Heynes, to invite him.

Their meeting changed everything. At first, Margaret overwhelmed Gerard with drawings and paintings—some by her own hand—so beautiful they seemed beyond reach. But her kindness kept his spirit alive. She and Reicht drew him out, discovering the real reason he avoided illumination: he couldn’t afford the costly pigments—gold, ultramarine, vermilion. He was afraid to ask his mother.

Then Margaret gave him a brush, vellum, and paints. He nearly worshipped her. As he left, Reicht ran after him with a candle and two quarters. He kissed her hand.

But more than the materials, it was the understanding that mattered. For in that age, art was not divided from craft, and artists sought each other out. Like early Christians, they found kinship in shared passion.

With Margaret’s guidance and the monks’ trust, Gerard flourished. His confidence grew. He still lagged at meals when caught in the midst of an initial G, but once seated, he sparkled—his wit sharp, his humor bold. He brought laughter to the table, quoting ancient jests unknown to his family.

To repay the monks, he copied two of their finest manuscripts: the life of their founder and Terence’s comedies—on fine vellum, at their expense.

Meanwhile, the mighty Prince Philip “the Good” ruled with flair. Duke of Burgundy, Count of Flanders, Lord of Friesland—he was a man of many passions. He fought bravely, lied skillfully, hunted fiercely, and loved jewels, fine clothes, and beautiful women. He adored paintings—so much so that he ennobled Jan Van Eyck. He also loved giants, dwarfs, and Turks. The latter he brought from Istanbul with promises, then baptized them by force, letting them pray to Mahound while laughing inwardly at their ignorance.

He kept lions in cages, leopards trained to hunt, and delighted in anything rare—except simple virtue. But he had two virtues: generosity to the poor, and genuine patronage of the arts.

Now he announced a contest: prizes for the finest works in orfevrerie, painting, glasswork, illumination, and calligraphy. Towns were to send entries from the poor, at public expense.

When the bellman rang through Tergou, a thousand voices stirred—one heart beat wildly: Gerard’s.

He told his family timidly he would enter two categories. They stared—speechless. Then a roar erupted from the floor. Giles, the dwarf, split open with laughter, his voice thundering like a bassoon. Nature had made him small, but gifted him with the loudest voice ever heard.

Gerard flushed. Others tittered. White Catherine looked up, her cheeks pink. “Why laugh?” she said softly. “Because he is our brother, you think he cannot succeed? Yes, Gerard—try. Many say you are skilled. Mother and I will pray to the Virgin to guide your hand.”

“Thank you, little Kate,” Gerard said. “You pray, and mother buy me vellum and colors.”

“How much?” she asked.

“Two gold crowns.”

“Two crowns!” Catherine shrieked. “When a bushel of rye costs a groat! Spend a month’s food on vanity? The lightning of Heaven would strike me—my children would starve!”

“Oh, Mother,” sighed Little Catherine, pleading.

“It’s hopeless, Kate,” Gerard said sadly. “I’ll have to give it up—or ask Dame Van Eyck. She would give it, but I’m ashamed to take from her again.”

“That’s none of her business,” Catherine snapped. “She has no right to come between me and my son.” And she stormed out.

But Little Catherine smiled. Soon, Catherine returned—calm, tender—with two gold pieces in her hand.

“There,” she said. “You won’t need to ask anyone.”

Gerard hesitated. “One crown will do, Mother. I’ll send my copy of Terence—it’s on fine vellum. I only need six sheets for borders, gold, and colors.”

“Never tyne the ship for lack of tar, Gerard,” she said. “But I’ll keep it in my pocket. Taking from the box feels like drawing blood from my heart. You’ll need it.”

And indeed, when the day came, Gerard longed to go to Rotterdam—to see the Duke, to see the works of others, to learn from defeat. The crown came out easily.

He was soon to be a priest. It seemed fair that he should enjoy the world a little before renouncing it forever.

The night before departure, Margaret Van Eyck asked him to deliver a letter—to Princess Marie, at the Stadthouse in Rotterdam.

On the morning of the prize-giving, Gerard set off in his holiday clothes: a silver-grey doublet, a sleeveless jerkin over it, tight buckskin hose laced to his waist, pointed shoes secured with straps, and flowing hair tied back. On his back, pinned between his shoulders, was his hat—held in place by a purple ribbon knotted across his chest, given him by Little Catherine. From his belt hung his leather wallet.

Near Rotterdam, he grew tired. Then he saw an old man sitting by the roadside, pale and weak, supported by a young woman whose face was full of concern. The townsfolk passed without notice. But Gerard, trained in observation by his art, read their story in their clothes.

The old man wore a fur-trimmed gown and velvet cap—signs of rank—but the purse at his belt was thin, the fur worn, the gown faded. The girl wore plain russet cloth, yet her neck was draped in snow-white lawn, edged with gold embroidery. Her head-dress was new: a silver net with spangles, framing glossy auburn hair rolled into waves. Her eyes held sorrow.

Gerard passed, then stopped. He turned back, bashful.

“Father,” he said, “you seem weary.”

“I am,” the old man replied. “Faint from hunger.”

The girl glanced at him—ashamed. “It was my fault,” she murmured. “I underestimated the distance. I let him start too late.”

“No,” the old man said gently. “It is not the distance. It is hunger.”

She put her arms around his neck, whispering, “Father—a stranger. A young man.”

But it was too late. Gerard, with quiet kindness, began gathering sticks. Then he opened his wallet, pulled out bread and an iron flask, lit a match, then a candle-end, then the fire. He placed the flask on the flames, then lay down—taking a long drink.

As he rose, he saw her face soften. She watched him with a shy smile.

He laughed. “Mind the pot—don’t let it spill. Use the cleft stick to hold it steady.” Then he ran toward a cornfield.

And so, with a heart full of hope and a step lightened by compassion, Gerard continued his journey—toward a future he could not yet foresee.

“The soup is hot,” Gerard said.

“But how shall we bring it to our lips?” the elder man asked, his voice heavy with weariness.

“Father,” Margaret replied softly, a glint in her eye, “the young man has brought us straws.”

“Ay, ay!” the old man murmured. “But my bones are stiff, and this fire burns too fiercely for one such as I to kneel over with these short reeds. St. John the Baptist, but the lad is clever!”

Even as he spoke, Gerard acted. In an instant, he untied the knot at his chest, removed his hat, placed a stone into each corner of it, then wrapped his hand in the tail of his jerkin and swiftly lifted the flask from the flames. He wedged it securely between the stones and set the hat before the old man with a cheerful grin. The man trembled as he slipped the rye-straw pipe into his mouth and drew in a long breath.

Lo and behold—his pale, drawn face began to glow. A warmth spread across his features until he seemed reborn. As he exhaled:

“Hippocrates and Galen!” he exclaimed. “This is *soupe au vin*—the restorative of all restoratives! Blessed be the nation that devised it, the woman who made it, and the youth who brought it to those on the brink of fainting! Have a sip, my dear, while I tell our young host the history and virtues of this divine concoction. This elixir was unknown to the ancients—we find no trace of it in their medical treatises or in the popular tales that recount their remedies. Even Hector, in the *Iliad*, if memory serves—”

(Margaret: “Alas, he’s off again.”)

—was offered wine by one of the ladies in the poem, yet refused, saying he was about to enter battle and could not afford to weaken himself. But had the *soupe au vin* existed in Troy, he surely would have added in hexameter verse, *‘But a soupe au vin, madam, I will taste, and gratefully.’* Not only would that have been proper courtesy—a trait no true commander lacks—but failing to do so would have marked him as shallow and unprepared, unfit to lead men into war. Soldiers going to battle need sustenance and strength, as history proves: foolish generals who sent hungry troops against well-fed enemies were defeated time and again, even by smaller forces. The Romans lost a great battle in northern Italy to Hannibal, the Carthaginian, solely because they neglected this truth. Now, this celestial brew invigorates the limbs and lifts the spirit in a single draught; had Hector drunk it just before combat, aided by Phoebus, Venus, and the blessed saints, the Greeks might well have suffered defeat. Observe how weak and weary I was but moments ago—now, after this heavenly cordial, I am bold as Achilles and strong as an eagle.”

“Oh, father, now? An eagle, indeed?”

“Girl, I defy you and all the world. Ready as a steed in full foam to gallop from here to Rotterdam, strong enough to face life’s trials—even poverty and age, which philosophers call the *summum malum*. Nonsense! Unless a man’s life has been wasted—though, by the way, most lives are. Now, let us speak of modern times!”

“Father! Dear father!”

“Fear me not, child; I’ll be brief—unreasonably, even unseasonably brief. The *soupe au vin* does not appear in modern medicine, but this only confirms what we already know: for centuries, physicians have been fools, peddling chicken broth and gold decoctions, praising the weakest meat and the least reactive metal. Mountebanks! Fools! Murderers! Since no wisdom comes from them, let us turn to chronicles. First, we find Duguesclin, a French knight, preparing to fight the English—who ruled half France at the time and struck hard by sea and land—drank not one, but three *soupes au vin* in honor of the Holy Trinity. Then he charged the enemy and, as expected, slew many and drove the rest into the sea. Yet he was merely the first in a long line of noble warriors who, through this sacred tonic, were sustained, strengthened, and comforted.”

“Dear father,” Margaret pleaded, holding the hat gently in both hands, “do add yourself to that honored company before the soup cools.”

The old man smiled, and once more inserted the straw.

This spared them the modern examples—and gave Gerard a chance to tell Margaret how proud her mother would be that her soup had helped a learned man.

“Ay,” she said, “but she’d be displeased to see her son give all and take nothing. Why did you bring only two straws?”

“Fair mistress,” he answered, “I hoped you would allow me to share your straw. There were only two.”

Margaret smiled and blushed. “Never beg when you may command,” she said. “The straw is not mine—it belongs to you. You cut it in that field.”

“I cut it, and thus it was mine. But then your lips touched it—and so it became yours.”

“Did it? Then I lend it to you. There—now it is yours again. Your lips have touched it.”

“No,” he said, “it belongs to us both now. Let us divide it.”

“By all means—you have a knife.”

“No,” he said, “I won’t cut it—that would be ill luck. I’ll bite it. There—I keep my half. Yours, I doubt, you’ll burn once home.”

“You don’t know me,” she replied. “I waste nothing. I’ll likely make it into a hairpin—or something.”

Her words surprised Gerard, not with anger, but with renewed resolve. He fell silent.

With bread and soup finished, the old scholar prepared to continue his journey. But Gerard, though clever, could not retie his ribbon as Catherine had done. Margaret watched him for a moment, then offered help—girls at her age delight in being coy and kind, playful and tender by turns, and she sensed she had put him off balance. She bowed her head, its crown of auburn hair gleaming like molten copper beneath silver strands, and with delicate fingers, she worked the stubborn ribbon into place. Soft touches shaped it, gentle strokes smoothed it. A sudden thrill passed through the innocent youth, and visions of a new world—of feeling, of tenderness—opened before him.

And Margaret, unaware, prolonged the moment. It is not natural for women to rush through matters of the toilet. When at last her fingers subdued the ends, she still felt uneasy—so, with a motion unique to her sex, she pressed her palm gently against the center of the knot, making it convex, as if whispering, *Now be good and stay.* The kiss was given to the ribbon—but the heart of the wearer leapt to meet it.

“There,” she said, stepping back to admire her work. Then, lifting her eyes to seek simple approval, she met a gaze so intense, so full of devotion, that she lowered her lashes and flushed deeply. A trembling seized her, and she retreated, cheeks burning, taking her father’s arm on the other side. Gerard, ashamed of having startled her, took the remaining arm. And so the two walked downcast and aware, supporting the old man in silence.

They entered Rotterdam through the Schiedamze Poort. Since Gerard knew nothing of the city, Peter directed him to the Hooch Straet, where the Stadthouse stood. He himself was going with Margaret to his cousin’s house in the Ooster-Waagen Straet. Almost at the gate, their paths diverged. They exchanged a friendly farewell, and Gerard disappeared into the bustling town.

A profound loneliness settled upon him, despite the crowded streets. He regretted, too late, that out of shyness he had not asked who they were or where they lived.

“Beshrew my modesty!” he muttered. “Their speech and bearing were above their station, and something whispered they wished to remain unknown. I shall never see her again. Oh, weary world, I hate you and your ways. To think I must meet beauty, goodness, and learning—three pearls beyond price—and never see them again!”

Lost in sorrow, he wandered aimlessly, letting his feet carry him. Soon, he found himself among a crowd moving in one direction. He joined them, reasoning they must be heading toward the Stadthouse. Before long, the noisy throng emerged not onto the Stadthouse, but onto a wide meadow beside the Maas River. There, the source of the gathering became clear: games of every sort were underway—wrestling, the game of palm, the quintain, legerdemain, archery, tumbling—women as well as men performing with great skill, much to the delight of the audience. A trained bear stood on his head, marched upright, and bowed gravely to his master. A hare beat a drum, and a rooster strutted on tiny stilts, disdainful and proud.

Gerard laughed now and then, but the festive scene could not truly cheer him—his heart was elsewhere. Hearing a young man say the Duke had been there but had gone to the Stadthouse to entertain burgomasters, aldermen, prize competitors, and their guests, Gerard suddenly remembered he was hungry—and would love to dine with a prince. He left the riverside and, this time, found the Hooch Straet. It led quickly to the Stadthouse.

But when he arrived, he was turned away—at one door, then another—until he reached the grand courtyard gate. It was guarded by soldiers and overseen by a pompous major-domo, resplendent in an embroidered collar and a golden chain, clutching a white staff tipped with gold. A crowd gathered before him, pleading in vain. They came forward like waves, only to retreat as quickly. Gerard struggled to approach, and when he stood four heads from the gate, he saw something that made his heart leap: Peter, with Margaret on his arm, begging humbly for entry.

“My cousin the alderman is not at home—they say he’s here.”

“What does that matter to me, old man?”

“If you won’t let us in to him, at least take this leaf from my tablet. See, I’ve written his name—he will come out to us.”

“For what do you take me? I deliver no messages. I guard the gate.”

Then, in a thunderous voice, he roared:

“No strangers enter—only competitors and their parties!”

“Come, old man,” someone shouted, “you’ve had your answer. Make way.”

Margaret turned halfway, her voice pleading:

“Good people, we’ve come from far, and my father is old. My cousin has a new servant who does not know us—and refuses to let us sit in his own house.”

The crowd laughed harshly. Margaret flinched as if struck. At that moment, a hand closed around hers—strong, warm, magnetic. It felt like soul meeting soul. She turned sharply—and it was Gerard. A small cry escaped her, half joy, half appeal. She began to whimper softly.

They had jostled her, frightened her. Her cousin’s carelessness—failing even to inform his servant of their arrival—was cruel. And the servant’s caution, though wise, was deeply humiliating to her father and herself. And now, in that moment of distress, this kind hand and face appeared. *Hinc illae lacrimae.*

“All is well now,” a coarse humorist remarked. “She’s found her sweetheart.”

“Haw! haw! haw!” the crowd jeered.

She dropped Gerard’s hand instantly and turned, eyes flashing through her tears:

“I have no sweetheart, you rude men. But I am friendless in your crude town, and this is a friend—one who knows, what you do not, how to treat the aged and the weak.”

Silence fell. They had been thoughtless, and now felt the sting of her rebuke, though sharp, it was just. The quiet allowed Gerard to speak to the porter.

“I am a competitor, sir.”

“What is your name?” the man asked, suspicious.

“Gerard, son of Elias.”

The janitor checked a parchment slip:

“Gerard Eliassoen may enter.”

“With my companions—these two?”

“No. They came before you. They are not your party.”

“What matters? They are my friends. Without them, I go not in.”

“Stay without, then.”

“That I will not.”

“That we shall see.”

“We will—and swiftly.” With that, Gerard raised his voice—deep, powerful, commanding—and echoed through the street:

“Are you mad?” the porter cried.

“Hush, hush!”

“Hush! Murder! The Dukes are there! I’m dead!” the janitor shrieked, trembling.

Then, trying to drown Gerard’s voice, he bellowed with all his might:

“OPEN THE GATE, YE KNAVES! WAY THERE FOR GERARD ELIASSOEN AND HIS COMPANY! (The fiends go with him!)”

The gate swung open as if by magic. Eight soldiers lowered their pikes, forming an arch. Under it, the trio marched in triumph. The moment they passed, the pikes clashed shut—nearly pinning a citizen who tried to squeeze through.

Beyond the gate, a few steps revealed a scene of Eastern splendor. The courtyard was filled with tables piled high with rich meats and adorned with glittering plate. Guests in colorful garments sat beneath a canopy of fresh branches tied with golden, silver, and blue silken cords. Fruits of every hue—some real, others crafted from gold, silver, and wax—hung like jewels among the green leaves of plane and lime trees. The Duke’s minstrels played lutes at intervals, and a fountain sprayed red Burgundy in six jets that danced and collided in midair. The evening sun pierced the wine streams, turning them into molten rubies, casting crimson light on fair faces, snowy beards, velvet, satin, jeweled hilts, glowing gold, gleaming silver, and sparkling glass. Gerard and his friends stood transfixed, spellbound.

Then a whisper passed: “Salute the Duke! Salute the Duke!”

They looked up—and there, under the dais, was their sovereign, waving kindly. The men bowed low. Margaret curtsied with grace and depth. The Duke waved again, pointing them out to a group of valets. Seven of them rushed forward, seated the trio at a table, and placed fifteen colorful soups in little silver bowls, and as many wines in crystal vases.

“Nay, father,” Margaret said, recovering from the whirlwind, “let us not eat until we thank our good friend.”

“Girl, he is our guardian angel.”

Gerard buried his face in his hands.

“Tell me when you’ve finished,” he said, “and I’ll return to supper. I am hungry. But I know which of us three is happiest to meet again.”

“Me?” she asked.

“No. Guess again.”

“Father?”

“No.”

“Then I have no guess,” she said, laughing lightly. “Ah!”

The soup vanished in a flurry of fourteen hands. Fish arrived in a dozen forms—lobster patties mixed with almonds, almond-and-cream cakes, and countless *brouets*, known today as rissoles. Next came a wild boar—its scent divine. Yet why did Margaret recoil with two cries of horror and pinch Gerard?

Because the Duke’s chef had been too clever. He had restored the animal’s hair and bristles with burnt sugar and edible pigments. The tusks remained intact, giving the beast a winning smile. Two eyes of colored sugar glowed in its head—bright, bloodshot, menacing—watching every move of knife and spoon.

St. Argus! What eyes!

And I need Granville or Tenniel to paint the scene: two gilded valets placing the monster before the guests with smiling, self-satisfied reverence; old Peter clasping his hands in holy awe; Margaret wheeling round, eyes wide with terror, hand on Gerard’s shoulder, squealing and pinching; Gerard’s face lit with foolish delight at being pinched; the grizzly brute glaring sulkily; guests grinning from ear to ear.

“What’s the matter?” the Duke called, hearing the outcry. Seven servants rushed to report. He laughed.

“Give her the beef-stuffing, then. Bring me Sir Boar.”

Generous monarch! The beef-stuffing was his private dish. On such occasions, a whole ox was roasted and reserved for the poor. But the wise and charitable king discovered that skewering venison, lamb, poultry, etc., into the ox’s cavity cooked them to perfection—retaining their juices and absorbing the ox’s rich flavor. These he called his beef-stuffing—and now, at his word, seven servants plunged silver tridents into the steaming flesh, spearing a kid, a cygnet, and a flock of wildfowl. They soon smoked before Gerard and his companions. Peter’s face, sad at losing the savage hog, brightened and shone.

Afterward came twenty different tarts of fruit and herbs, and finally, confectionery on a colossal scale—sugar cathedrals with gilt bas-reliefs, castles with moats and ditches, elephants, camels, toads, knights jousting, kings and princesses watching trumpeters blow—all eating, veins filled with sweet nectar. Works of art meant to be destroyed. The guests shattered a bastion, crushed a crusader and his horse, cracked a bishop in cope and crosier, as casually as one breaks a caraway candy. They sipped hippocras, spiced drinks, Greek and Corsican wines, while turbaned, jeweled, gilt Turkish boys knelt, offering golden troughs of rose and orange water to cool and perfume their hands.

But long before this feast reached its end, appetite had fled. Gerard suddenly remembered he carried a letter for Princess Marie. In a low tone, he asked a servant if he could deliver it. The man bowed deeply: “I cannot deliver it myself, but I will give it at once to one of the Princess’s attendants—several are here.”

It may be recalled that Peter and Margaret came not to dine, but to find their cousin. Well, the old man ate heartily, and—exhausted—fell asleep, forgetting all about him. Margaret did not remind him. We shall learn why.

Meanwhile, their cousin sat just behind them, unnoticed—until Margaret turned and screamed at the boar. But he said nothing. Municipal pride held him back. Margaret wore plain clothes; Peter looked threadbare. So the alderman decided:

“It will be time to welcome them when the sun sets and the guests disperse. Then I will take my poor relations home—no one need know.”

Half the courses passed Gerard and Margaret unnoticed. They were not great eaters, and now their minds feasted on sweeter thoughts—thoughts that always dull the appetite.

Margaret leaned back, eyes half-closed, murmuring to Gerard: “What a lovely scene—the warm sun, the green shade, the rich dresses, the music of the lutes, the cool song of the fountain, all faces joyful and bright. And it is all thanks to you.”

Gerard said nothing—only his eyes moved.

“Now, speak not,” she sighed. “Let me listen to the fountain. What are you competing for?”

He told her.

“Very well. You will win at least one prize.”

“Which? Which? Have you seen my work?”

“I? No. But you will win.”

“How can you be sure?”

“Because you were so kind to my father.”

Gerard smiled at her logic, hung his head at her praise, and remained silent.

“Speak not,” she murmured. “They say this is a world of sin and misery. Can that be? What is your opinion?”

“No,” Gerard said. “That’s just an old song. A byword our elders repeat by habit. It’s not true.”

“How can you know? You’re but a child,” she said, with thoughtful dignity.

“Look around! And then—thought I had lost you forever. And now you are here. And the minstrels are about to play again. Sin and misery? Nonsense!”

The lutes burst forth. The courtyard rang with delicate harmony.

“What do you admire most of all these wonders, Gerard?”

“You know my name? How?”

“White magic. I am a—witch.”

“Angels are never witches. But I can’t understand—”

“Foolish boy! Was it not shouted loud enough at the gate to deafen one?”

“So it was. Where is my head? What do I admire most? If you will lean a little more this way, I’ll tell you.”

“This way?”

“Yes—so the light falls upon you. There. I see many fair things here, fairer than I ever dreamed. But the fairest of all, to my eye, is your lovely hair, framed in silver, kissed by the setting sun. It reminds me of what the Vulgate calls beautiful—*an apple of gold in a network of silver*. And oh, how I regret I did not know you before I sent in my efforts at illuminating! I could illuminate so much better now. I could do everything better. Look—now the sun is full upon it. It shines like an aureole. So did Our Lady look—and none since her—until today.”

“Oh, fie! It is wicked to speak so. Compare a poor, plain girl like me with the Queen of Heaven? Oh, Gerard! I thought you were a good young man.”

Margaret seemed genuinely shocked.

Gerard tried to explain. “I am no worse than any other. But how can I help having eyes—and a heart, Margaret?”

“Gerard!”

“Be not angry now!”

“Now? Is it likely?”

“I love you.”

“Oh, for shame! You must not say that to me,” she said, flushing violently.

“I cannot help it. I love you. I love you.”

A grave, white-haired seneschal approached their table and inquired with polite formality whether Gerard Eliassoen was among them. When Gerard affirmed it, the man said, “The Princess Marie desires to speak with you, young sir. I am to escort you to her presence.”

At once, every face within earshot turned sharply, drawn by curiosity and envy toward the young man summoned by a princess. Gerard rose at once to comply.

“I wager we shall not see you again,” Margaret said calmly, though a faint blush touched her cheeks.

“That you will,” he replied, then leaned close and whispered, “This is my good princess—but you are my queen.”

Aloud, he added, “Wait for me, I pray you. I shall return shortly.”

“Ay, ay!” Peter muttered, suddenly rousing himself as if from a dream.

Once Gerard had departed, the two who had seemed so plain in dress—yet were now linked to one summoned by royalty—became the center of attention. The eyes of all nearby followed them, and William Johnson stepped forward, feigning surprise. “And to think,” he said, “I stood right behind you, and you did not see me!”

“Nay, cousin Johnson,” Margaret replied coolly, “I saw you long ago.”

“You saw me—and spoke not?” he asked, wounded.

“Cousin,” she replied, “it was your duty to welcome us to Rotterdam, as it is ours to welcome you to Sevenbergen. Your servant refused us a seat in your house.”

“The fool!” Johnson muttered.

“And I wanted to see if ‘like maid, like master’ held true,” Margaret added, “for there is truth in old sayings.”

Johnson flushed deeply. He sensed her sharpness and suspected her intent. In that moment, he chose wisdom over words. He insisted they come home with him at once, and he would show them whether they were truly welcome in Rotterdam or not.

“Who doubts it, cousin? Who doubts it?” the scholar chimed in.

Margaret thanked him graciously but hesitated. “I would like to hear the minstrels again,” she said.

After about a quarter of an hour, Johnson returned to the matter. “See,” he said, “many guests have already left.”

Then came her true reason: “It would be ill-mannered to abandon our friend. He does not know where we are staying in this large city, and we’ve already parted once.”

“Oh!” Johnson exclaimed. “Then let us fix that. My young man—ahem! I mean my secretary—shall remain here and wait. He shall bring Gerard to my house. He shall lodge with me, and nowhere else.”

“We would not wish to be such a burden,” Margaret said.

“Nay, nay,” Johnson insisted. “You shall see whether you are welcome—or not. You, your friends, even your friends’ friends, if need be. And I shall learn what the Princess has to say to him.”

Margaret felt a sudden warmth at the thought of Gerard staying under the same roof as she. But then a flicker of unease crossed her mind. “But what if your young man should be careless, go off playing, and Gerard miss him?”

“He go play?” Johnson laughed. “Leave the spot I set him in? Ho! Stand forth, Hans Cloterman!”

A figure clad in black serge and dark violet hose rose slowly, took two deliberate steps, and stood before them without moving a muscle—solemn, precise, the very image of disciplined propriety.

At the sight of him, Margaret, whose heart was light, could barely suppress a smile. Yet she leaned close to Johnson and whispered, “I would stake my hand in fire on his loyalty. We are at your command, cousin, when you have given him his orders.”

Hans was instructed to remain at the table and await Gerard’s return, then guide him to Ooster-Waagen Straet. He obeyed not with words, but by silently taking the seat indicated.

Margaret, Peter, and William Johnson then departed together.

“And indeed,” Margaret said gently, “it is time you were abed, father, after all your travel.” That had been her intention all along.

Hans Cloterman sat waiting—calm, unflinching, businesslike. Minutes passed, yet no impatience stirred in him. Johnson had done him justice when he mocked the idea of his secretary abandoning post for sport or youthful folly. As Gerard delayed, the patient Hans—now free from his employer’s watchful eye—used the time wisely. He drank wine solemnly, silently, at measured intervals: goblets of strong Corsican wine, which he consumed with quiet dignity.

The wine was potent, but so was Cloterman’s head. An hour passed before the model secretary began to feel the notion that Creation expected him to drink a toast—to all good fellows, and especially to the Duke of Burgundy present.

With that thought, he filled the ninth bumper and rose with careful slowness, as if balancing a sacred object. Once upright, he toppled sideways onto the grass, goblet still in hand, spilling wine across several ankles—whose owners jumped back in alarm—yet not a muscle in his long, grave face shifted. Even in total loss of reason, he retained his composure, stiffness, and infallibility.

Meanwhile, the seneschal led Gerard through winding corridors to the pavilion’s door, where young noblemen in embroidered silks and plumed hats sat guard, playing cards by torchlight. A whisper passed between them, and one reluctantly rose, stared at Gerard with haughty surprise, and entered the pavilion.

He soon returned, beckoning Gerard forward. Through a few passages, they arrived in an antechamber where three more young gentlemen sat—feathered, furred, and adorned like elaborate tapestries—deep in the noble art of dice.

“You can’t see the Princess,” one declared. “It is too late.”

Another added, “She passed this way moments ago with her nurse. She’s gone to bed, doll and all. Deuce—ace again!”

Gerard prepared to leave.

The seneschal smiled skeptically. “The young man is here by the Countess’s order. Kindly conduct him to her ladies.”

A magnificent Adonis rose, looking affronted, and led Gerard into a room where eleven ladies sat or lounged, chattering like magpies. Two, more industrious than the rest, played cat’s-cradle with fingers as nimble as their tongues.

At the sight of a stranger, all voices ceased abruptly—like machinery tripped by a single lever—and all eyes turned to Gerard as if guided by the same string. He had already been uneasy; now this sudden scrutiny unnerved him. His gaze dropped to the floor.

The ladies, finding a creature they could intimidate, giggled with delight.

Then a duenna stepped forward and said sternly, “Mesdames!”

Instantly, they fell silent—abashed as if a modesty string had been pulled.

The duenna took Gerard by the arm and marched him forward in silence. His heart sank. Halfway through the hall, he almost turned and fled.

“What must princes be,” he thought, “when their courtiers are so cold? Doubtless they inherit their manner from those they serve.”

His thoughts were interrupted when the duenna led him into a room where three ladies sat sewing, and a small girl tuned a lute.

The ladies wore rich but tasteful garments. The duenna approached the woman hemming a kerchief and whispered a few words.

She turned to Gerard with a gentle smile and gestured for him to approach. She did not rise, but laid aside her work. Her simple motion carried grace and ease.

She began at once. “Margaret Van Eyck is an old friend of mine, sir. I am delighted to receive a letter from her hand, and grateful to you for delivering it safely.”

“Sir, I thank you a thousand times,” said the young lady.

“I am glad you feel indebted to her, sweetheart,” the Countess said. “Our friend asks us to do you a favor in return.”

“I will do anything on earth for him,” the girl replied fervently.

“Anything on earth is nothing in the world,” the Countess murmured quietly.

“Well, then,” the girl said, “what would you have me do, sir?”

Gerard now understood the rank of the company he was in.

“My sovereign demoiselle,” he said softly, voice trembling slightly, “where there is no effort, there needs no reward.”

“But we must obey mamma. All the world must obey.”

“That is true,” the Countess replied. “Then, our demoiselle, reward me—if you will—by letting me hear the song you were about to sing when I interrupted you.”

“What! You love music, sir?” the girl asked.

“I adore it.”

She glanced at her mother, who nodded with a smile.

Then she took up her lute and sang a popular romaunt of the day. Though only twelve, she was well trained and diligent. Her small hand swept the strings with courage and precision, striking arpeggios clear and bright as stars. But the true magic was her voice—not loud, but round, pure, full, and ringing like a bell.

She sang with modest eloquence, unburdened by affectation. Too young for theatrics or sentiment, she poured out emotion naturally—everything flowed. Her little mouth seemed the mouth of Nature itself.

The song, too, was as pure as her voice—no false divisions, no whining slurs, no overwrought cadences or empty flourishes. No trite embellishments to drown melody or meaning. It was honest, simple, and radiant.

As the tender melody poured from her young throat, Gerard’s eyes filled with tears.

The Countess watched him closely. Most praised the princess loudly, but not with the depth of feeling in his gaze. When the song ended and the last note faded, she asked demurely, “Was he content?”

Gerard started. The spoken word broke the spell and brought him back to reality.

“Oh, madam!” he cried, “Surely it is thus that cherubs and seraphs sing—charming the saints in heaven!”

“I am somewhat of your opinion, my young friend,” the Countess said, moved. She gazed at her daughter with love and quiet pride—a look said to be granted only to the brief-lived when beholding the brief-lived.

She continued: “My dear friend has asked me to assist you. It is the first favor she has honored us with—and therefore sacred. You are in holy orders, sir?”

Gerard bowed.

“I fear you are not a priest—you look too young.”

“Oh no, madam,” he replied. “I am not even a sub-deacon. I am merely a lector. Next month I shall become an exorcist, and soon after, an acolyte.”

“Well, Monsieur Gerard,” the Countess said, “with your talents, you may pass quickly through the lower ranks. And I beg you to do so—for the day after you celebrate your first mass, I shall appoint you to a benefice.”

“Oh, madam!” he exclaimed.

“And, Marie, remember—I make this promise in your name as well as my own.”

“Fear not, mamma,” the princess said. “I shall not forget. But if he follows my advice, he will be Bishop of Liege. The Bishop of Liege is a beautiful bishop. Do you not remember him, mamma, when we visited Liege? He was braver than grandpapa himself. He wore a high crown, split down the middle, studded with jewels so brilliant! His gown was stiff with gold, his mantle adorned with pictures—above all, his gloves! They were embroidered with jewels, scented with the sweetest perfume. I smelled them all the time he blessed me. Dear old man—he will surely die soon, as most old people do. Then, sir, you may be bishop—and wear—”

“Gently, Marie, gently,” the Countess interjected. “Bishoprics are for older gentlemen. This is a young man.”

“Mamma! He is not so very young.”

“Not compared to you, Marie, eh?”

“He is of good birth, dear mamma. And I am certain he is good enough for a bishop.”

“Alas, mademoiselle,” Gerard said, “you are mistaken.”

“I know not that, Monsieur Gerard,” the Countess said, “but I am puzzled how you can judge so boldly.”

“Alas, mamma,” the princess said, “you have not looked at his face.”

She raised her eyebrows, as if amused by her mother’s simplicity.

“I beg your pardon,” the Countess said, “I have. Well, sir, if I cannot go quite so fast as my daughter, attribute it to my age, not to lack of interest in your welfare. A benefice will be a good beginning. And I must ensure it is near—what is the name of your place?”

“Tergou, madam.”

“A priest gives up much,” the Countess continued, “often, I fear, he learns too late how much.” Her gaze rested on Gerard with quiet pity—half-surprised that he would surrender his sex, all the joys of love and family, for a life of service. “At least you shall be near your friends. Do you have a mother?”

“Yes, madam, thanks be to God!”

“Good. You shall have a church near Tergou. She will thank me.”

Now, sir, we must not keep you longer from those who claim your company more than we do. Duchess, please send a page to guide him to the banquet hall—the way is difficult to find.”

Gerard bowed low to the Countess and the princess, then backed toward the door.

“I hope it will be a nice benefice,” the princess said with a pretty smile as he left. Then, shaking her head with solemn warning, “But you had better have been Bishop of Liege.”

Gerard followed his new guide, heart warm with gratitude. But before reaching the hall, a chill settled over him.

A quiet soul unaccustomed to extremes finds it hard to hold two emotions at once. While with the Countess, joy had overwhelmed him—the unexpected promise, the honor it would bring to his family. But now, passion reasserted itself.

What! Give up Margaret? Her soft hand still felt in his, her deep eyes burned in his heart. Resign her, and all the world of love she had opened to him today?

The reversal was so powerful he resolved instantly to say nothing at home about the benefice.

“The Countess is kind,” he thought. “She has many ways to help a young man. She will not force me to become a priest when she learns I love a woman. One might almost think she knows it—she looked at me strangely and said, ‘A priest gives up much, too much.’ Perhaps she will give me a position at court.”

With that comforting thought, his spirits lifted. Now at the banqueting hall’s entrance, he thanked his guide and hurried toward Margaret—eyes alight with joy.

He reached the table—she was gone. Peter was gone too. No one remained. Only a soberly dressed citizen lay unconscious beneath the table, being lifted away by others.

Gerard did not recognize the importance of this drunken man. He was searching for “Beauty” and ignored the “Beast.”

He ran wildly around the hall, now nearly empty. She was not there.

He left the palace. Outside, a crowd gathered before two newly lit fan-lights over the gate.

He asked urgently if anyone had seen an old man in a gown and a lovely girl pass by.

They laughed. “We were staring at these new lights—turning night into day. We didn’t care about old men and young wenches. Common sights.”

From another group, he learned a Mystery play was being performed nearby, drawing all of Rotterdam.

Hope flared. He went to see it.

The play featured divine beings—too sacred to name—descending clumsily from heaven to debate with cardinal virtues, the nine Muses, and the seven deadly sins—all portrayed in human form, indistinguishable from one another.

To enliven the scene, the Prince of the Power of the Air appeared, tormented by a mischievous imp who struck him with a bladder. Each thwack sent the crowd into laughter.

When the Vices had delivered their obscenities and the Virtues their platitudes, the celestial figures retreated one by one to heaven—on a single cloud, operated by two artisans with a winch, visible to all.

Then the bottomless pit opened, blazing in the center. The carpenters and Virtues pushed the Vices inside, and the Virtues, Beelzebub, and the imp danced merrily around the infernal flames to the tune of fife and tabor.

This play, written by the Bishop of Ghent to spread religious feeling through sensation, was typical of clerical theater in its time. But eventually, the laity took over—and the stage, I’m told, became profane.

Margaret was nowhere in the crowd. Gerard could not enjoy the performance. He left mid-act, during a celebrated exchange where Justice out-quibbled Satan.

He wandered through the streets, unable to find her. At last, exhausted, he found a hostelry and slept until dawn.

All day, heavy and sorrowful, he searched—never finding her or her father, never gaining a clue.

He began to believe she had changed her mind—or worse, deceived him.

Anguish turned to irritation. More fortune fell upon him—and he almost resented it.

On the third day, after retracing every street once more, he said aloud, “She is not in the town. I shall never see her again. I will go home.”

He started for Tergou—royal favor promised, fifteen golden angels in his purse, a golden medal on his chest, and a heart as heavy as lead.

It was nearing four in the afternoon. Eli sat in his shop, while his eldest and youngest sons were away from home. Catherine and her frail daughter had been anxious all day about Gerard, and now they’d walked a short way down the road, hoping against hope to catch sight of him returning. In the quiet sitting-room, only Giles remained—alone with the furniture, and with himself.

Let me describe this room, as it stood then: plain, but clean, and full of character. The Dutch people had long been known for their ingenuity and industry. They claimed to have invented printing (with wooden type), oil painting, banking, gardening, and even liberty. But above all, years before this tale began, they had perfected cleanliness. While English nobles trod through floors covered in stale rushes, littered with bones, spoiled food, spittle, dogs, eggs, and every sort of filth, this humble hosier’s house in Tergou had floors of polished Dutch tiles—so bright and often washed that one could eat off them without fear.

There was one large window, its central stone crosswork thick and bold, rising like a true cross in the eyes of those who looked upon it. It stood out in relief, and during prayers, the family would turn their gaze toward it as if it were a sacred symbol. The glass panes were small, shaped like diamonds, and joined together with strips of lead—a style still seen today in country cottages.

The chairs were rough and simple, save for one armchair, whose back rose straight up at a right angle to the seat, so tall that the head of anyone seated in it barely reached the top. It was carved from oak, with a design at its peak. Beside it stood a copper pail, shaped like a woman's waist, filled with holy water, and next to it a tiny hand broom used to sprinkle blessings across the room. A long, narrow oak table dominated the space—and perched on its edge, clinging by his teeth, was Giles, the dwarf.

Nature, it seemed, had not meant to make Giles small out of spite. She had formed his head and torso with care—but then, distracted, she left the rest to chance. The result was a human wedge, an inverted cone. His upper body was massive, his lower limbs thin and stunted. He might well have quoted Horace: *“Amphora coepit institui; currente rota cur urceus exit?”* —“A jar was begun to be made; why did a jug come out?” His center of gravity was far from his physical center. If cut in half, the upper part would outweigh three times the lower. Yet this very imbalance gave him astonishing strength. His arms, powerful and unburdened by weight, allowed him to climb vertical poles like a squirrel or hang from a tree branch by one hand, suspended like a cherry on its stem. Had he possessed the suction power of a lizard’s feet, he might have walked across ceilings.

And yet, this miniature athlete had a peculiar passion: gripping the dinner table with both hands and swinging from it. And when he reached the height of joy? He’d clamp his jaws around the edge, release his hands, and hang there, trembling with delight, held fast by his great white teeth.

But such pleasures rarely last. Little Kate caught him mid-swing, and froze in horror. She was her mother’s daughter—her heart lay with order and propriety, not with the antics of a twelve-month-old gymnast.

“Oh, Giles! How can you? Mother is coming!” she cried.

“Go tell her, little tattletale,” growled Giles, refusing to let go. “You’re the one who causes all the trouble.”

“Am I?” she asked calmly. “That’s news to me.”

“The biggest mischief-maker in Tergou,” he snarled, resuming his grip.

“Oh, indeed?” she replied dryly.

The remark landed like a dart. Giles didn’t flinch. Instead, Kate sat down quietly and began to cry.

At that moment, her mother entered. Giles dropped instantly beneath the table, glaring up from the shadows.

“What’s going on now?” the woman demanded sharply.

Her eyes swept from Kate to the hidden figure under the table. Seeing his position and the guilty look on his face, she raised a hand as if to strike.

“Nay, mother,” said Kate softly. “It was only a foolish word. I wouldn’t have minded at another time—but I was tired, and worried about Gerard, you know.”

“Let no one worry over me,” whispered a weak voice at the door.

Gerard stumbled in—pale, dusty, exhausted. Hands shot up in surprise and delight, mingling with concern and joy. He collapsed into the nearest chair, spent from his journey.

He had raced through Rotterdam like a hunted animal, fleeing after Margaret, then endured a long, grueling ride home. The effort had worn him down completely. But youth is resilient. Soon, he revived—and became the focus of everyone’s attention.

They clamored to hear about the prizes first. Then Gerard told them how he’d been allowed to view all the competitors’ works laid out in a vast hall before the judges delivered their verdicts.

“Oh, mother! Oh, Kate!” he exclaimed. “When I saw the goldsmiths’ pieces—I nearly fell to my knees. I thought all the goldsmiths in the world couldn’t have produced so much gold, silver, jewels, and artistry. Truly, all crafts are divine.”

To please the women, he described the reliquaries, feretories, chalices, croziers, crosses, pyxes, monstrances—the sacred treasures—and then the goblets, hanaps, watches, clocks, chains, brooches—each piece dazzling in its detail. Their mouths watered at the thought.

“But when I came to the illuminated manuscripts from Ghent and Bruges,” he continued, “my heart sank. Mine looked like dirt beside theirs. For a moment, I almost wept. But I prayed for a better spirit, and soon I could admire them—thank God for such beauty, and for the patient artisans who created them. I forgot all about black-and-white work.”

Then, the next day, when all other prizes had been awarded, they came to the writing competition.

“And whose name do you think was called first?” he asked.

“Yours,” Kate guessed.

The others laughed at her.

“You may laugh,” Gerard said, “but it was true. Gerard Eliassoen of Tergou—that was the name the herald shouted. I stood stunned. They pushed me forward. Everything swam before my eyes. I found myself kneeling on a cushion at the Duke’s feet. He spoke to me, but I was too flustered to reply. Then he placed his hand at his side—not to draw a sword and behead me, but to give me a gold medal. Here it is.”

A cry erupted—almost a scuffle.

“And then,” he added, “he gave me fifteen golden angels. I’d seen one before, but never held one. Here they are.”

“Oh, Gerard! Oh, Gerard!”

“One for you, our eldest son,” he said, handing out coins. “One for you, Sybrandt. One for you, Little Mischief. Two for you, Little Lily—because God has afflicted you. One for myself—to buy colors and vellum. And nine for her who nursed us all and risked two crowns on poor Gerard’s hand.”

The gold brought out their true natures. Cornelis and Sybrandt grabbed their coins, eyes gleaming with greed—and envy, especially toward Kate, who received two. Giles snatched his and rolled it across the floor, chasing it like a child. Kate set aside her crutches, sat down, and stretched her arms toward Gerard with a gesture of pure love.

The mother, overwhelmed at first by the shower of gold landing in her apron, finally cried out: “Stop kissing him, Kate—he’s my son, not yours. Ah, Gerard! My boy! I’ve not loved you as you deserved.”

Gerard knelt beside her. She embraced him tightly, weeping with joy and pride upon his neck.

“Good lad! Good lad!” the hosier said, emotion in his voice. “I must go tell the neighbors. Lend me the medal, Gerard—I’ll show it to my friend Peter Buyskens. He always boasts about how his son Jorian won a tin mug at the archery butts.”

“Ay, go,” said Gerard. “And show him one of the angels. Tell him there are fourteen more just like it. But mind—you bring it back!”

“Stay a minute, father,” Gerard said, flushing with joy. “There’s better news.”

“Better than this?” someone gasped.

Gerard smiled. Then he told them of his meeting with the Countess—and the house rang with jubilation.

“Now, God bless the good lady—and bless the dame Van Eyck! A benefice? Our son? My cares are ended. Eli, my dear friend and master—we can die happy whenever our time comes. This dear boy will carry on for us. None of these children shall want a home or a friend.”

From that moment, Gerard was seen as the pillar of the family. He was not merely a son—he was special. Always right, always worthy. Nothing was too good for him.

Cornelis and Sybrandt grew more jealous with each passing day. They longed for the day he would leave for his benefice—when the favorite would be gone, and the priest’s purse would be open to them. Secretly, Gerard encouraged their hopes.

The wound love had dealt him throbbed less and less. His success, the affection of his parents, and the admiration of the village lifted his spirit. He began to resent Margaret’s coldness more fiercely. Yet she still held power over him—enough to make him wary of all women. For that reason, he now desired ordination more than ever.

He already knew the Vulgate better than most priests, studied church rubrics and doctrine with monks, and when the bishop visited, he applied to be admitted as an exorcist—the third step in holy orders.

The bishop questioned him—and ordained him immediately.

Gerard knelt. After a brief prayer, the bishop handed him a small manuscript filled with exorcisms.

“Take this, Gerard,” he said, “and have power to lay hands on the possessed—whether baptized or catechumens.”

Gerard accepted it reverently, and returned home bearing the Church’s authority to cast out demons.

As he stepped from the church, he met little Kate on her crutches.

“Oh, Gerard!” she said. “Who do you think sent for you? The burgomaster himself!”

“Ghysbrecht Van Swieten!” Gerard frowned. “What does he want?”

“I don’t know,” she replied. “But he seems urgent. You’re to go to his house at once.”

“Well,” Gerard said, “he is the burgomaster—I’ll go. But I don’t like it. Kate, I’ve seen him look at me… not like a friend. No matter. Such looks warn the wise. To be sure—he knows.”

“Knows what, Gerard?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing?”

“Kate, I’ll go.”

Ghysbrecht Van Swieten was a man of cunning, and he approached the young novice not with direct accusation, but with a subtle feint. “The town records,” he began, “are written in cramped hand, and the ink has faded with time.” He offered Gerard the task of copying them into a clearer form—a duty that would take months. Gerard asked what he would be paid. Ghysbrecht named a sum barely enough to cover parchment, ink, and quills.

“But burgomaster,” Gerard replied, “what of my labor? This is no mere scribbling—it is skilled work, and a year’s worth of it.”

“Your labor?” Ghysbrecht scoffed. “Is marking parchment truly labor? It requires little sweat, I should think.”

“It is labor,” Gerard insisted, “and skilled at that. Such craft is valued more than brute toil, whether it sweats or not. And then there is my time.”

“Your time?” Ghysbrecht laughed. “What is time to a man of twenty-two?”

Then, fixing his gaze sharply upon the youth, he pressed on: “Say rather, you are idle. You are in love. Your body may be here among these chanting monks, but your heart is with Peter Brandt and his red-haired girl.”

“I know no Peter Brandt,” Gerard said flatly.

That denial only deepened Ghysbrecht’s suspicion. The boy had been playing his part well—too well. “You lie!” he burst out. “Did I not find you standing beside her on the road to Rotterdam?”

“Ahh!” Gerard murmured, though he said nothing more.

“Ahh!” Ghysbrecht echoed. “And you were seen at Sevenbergen just the other day.”

“Was I?” Gerard asked quietly.

“Ahh—and at Peter’s house.”

“At Sevenbergen?” Gerard repeated.

“Ay,” Ghysbrecht declared. “At Sevenbergen.”

It was a gambit—what today might be called a bluff—deliberately cast as fact to provoke a reaction. But the result startled even the crafty burgomaster. Gerard leapt to his feet, trembling, his eyes alight with sudden agitation.

“Burgomaster,” he said, voice shaking, “I have not set foot in Sevenbergen in three years. I do not know the names of those you claim to have seen me with, nor where they lived. But since you care so little for my time—though it is precious to me—I bid you good day.”

And with that, he turned and fled from the room, his eyes blazing.

Ghysbrecht rose in fury—but then sat back down, his expression darkening. “He does not fear me,” he muttered. “He knows something—perhaps all.”

Without delay, he summoned his trusted servant and nearly dragged him to the window. “See that man?” he hissed. “Go! Follow him—but keep hidden. He is young, yet seasoned in deceit. Watch him all day. Report every step he takes, every place he goes.”

Night fell before the servant returned.

“Well?” Ghysbrecht demanded, voice sharp with anticipation. “Well?”

“Master,” the servant reported, “the young man left you and went straight to Sevenbergen.”

Ghysbrecht groaned aloud.

“To the house of Peter the Magician.”

“Look into your own heart and write!” cried Herr Cant, and the earth’s cuckoos echoed his words. Look into the Rhine where it is deepest, or the Thames where it is thickest, and paint what lies beneath. Lower a bucket into a well of self-deception—what rises must be truth, mustn’t it? Yet no son of Adam ever truly reads his own heart, except through the lens of years spent studying others’ souls. Even then, with borrowed wisdom and reflected light, one can only decipher, not fluently read.

Halfway to Sevenbergen, Gerard paused and turned inward, asking his heart why he was going. Without hesitation, it answered: “We go out of curiosity—to know why she cast us aside, to show her our hearts remain unbroken, that we are content with our honors and future benefice, and that we need neither her nor any woman of her fickle kind.”

He soon found Peter Brandt’s cottage. At the doorway sat a girl, stitching quietly, while a broad-shouldered man leaned on a longbow, speaking to her. Gerard felt an unexpected pang at the sight. But the man proved to be over fifty—an old soldier whom Gerard remembered from the archery butts, renowned for strength and precision. A moment later, the youth stood before them.

Margaret looked up, dropped her needle, gasped softly, and flushed pale and red in turn. Then, as if catching herself, she grew colder than before, more aloof than if she had never shown such emotion.

“What! Is it you, Master Gerard? What brings you here?”

“I passed by and saw you,” he said, “so I thought I’d greet you and inquire after your father.”

“He is well. He’ll be here shortly.”

“Then I may as well wait.”

“As you wish. Good Martin, go to the village and tell my father a friend has come.”

“And not yours?”

“My father’s friends are mine.”

“That may be doubted,” Gerard replied. “It wasn’t like a true friend to promise to wait—and then vanish the moment my back was turned. Cruel Margaret, you little know how I searched for you. Without you, nothing brought joy.”

“Idle talk,” she said sharply. “If you truly wanted my father—or me—you would have returned. That day, I had a bed ready for you at my cousin’s. He would have welcomed you warmly. And who knows—I might have done so too. I was in a generous mood. You’ll never find me in such a frame again—not you, nor any young man, I swear.”

“Margaret,” he insisted, “I came back the moment the Countess released me—but you were gone.”

“No,” she said, “or you would have seen Hans Cloterman at our table. We left him to bring you.”

“I saw no one—only a drunken man who had just fallen.”

“At our table? How was he dressed?”

“I paid little heed—he wore dull-colored clothes.”

At this, Margaret’s face softened slowly. Then, feigning skepticism, she questioned him closely—each inquiry sharp and probing. Gerard answered every one with honesty. Gradually, the clouds lifted. They understood how the misunderstanding had arisen.

And then—like a tide turning—came a surge of tenderness, all the deeper because they had wronged each other. Confessions followed, mutual and heartfelt. Neither had been happy since their parting. Neither could imagine happiness without this reunion.

Gerard noticed a manuscript Vulgate open on the table and reached for it eagerly—books of such rarity were his passion. But before he could touch it, two white hands pressed flat against the page, and a flushed face leaned over them.

“Take away your hands, Margaret,” he said gently, “so I may see where you’ve been reading. I’ll read the same passage at home—so our souls may meet in sacred words.”

“You will not?” she challenged.

“Then I must kiss them away.”

And he kissed those hands again and again, until shame forced them to withdraw. The book lay open now at: *“An apple of gold in a network of silver.”*

“There,” she said, smiling faintly, “I’d searched for this verse for ages—just found it moments ago—and now caught!” With a hint of contradiction, she pointed it out with her slender finger.

“Ay,” he said, “but today it’s hidden under that great cap.”

“It’s a becoming cap, some say.”

“Perhaps. But what it hides is beautiful.”

“It is not—it’s hideous.”

“But it was beautiful in Rotterdam.”

“Ay,” she whispered, “everything was beautiful that day.”

Then Peter arrived, greeted Gerard warmly, and invited him to stay for supper. Margaret vanished briefly, returning with her hair veiled in silver netting. She glanced at Gerard—half teasing, half shy—then moved gracefully about them, setting the meal with radiant cheerfulness.

As evening cooled, Gerard coaxed her outside. She hesitated, but came. He urged her toward the road to Tergou; she declined, yet followed. There, hand in hand, they walked back and forth, the world forgotten. When it was time for him to leave, they vowed never again to quarrel or misunderstand. Their promise was sealed with a long, loving kiss—and Gerard returned home as if borne on wings.

From that night onward, Gerard spent most evenings with Margaret. Their bond deepened steadily, until the hours they shared became the only hours they truly lived. The rest were mere endurance.

At first, all went smoothly. Obstacles existed, but seemed distant, small—lost in the glow of hope, youth, and love. The passions of others threatened by this attachment gave no warning signs, no smoke to signal the fire beneath. True love flowed calm and clear—until it drew these two hearts into its current forever.

And then—

A bright morning broke over Tergou, and with it came a spectacle unlike any other. Velvet cloaks shimmered in the sunlight, feathers fluttered on hats and headdresses, and the clatter of hooves echoed through the narrow streets as the French ambassador made his way toward the nearby forest for a day of hunting. His procession was grand—accompanied not only by his own entourage but also by several servants lent by the Duke of Burgundy, whose presence added both dignity and splendor to the occasion.

At the head of the cavalcade rode the Duke’s tumbler—a man of grave demeanor and solemn bearing who moved with such stately composure that even the noblemen beside him seemed frivolous by comparison. Yet every now and then, when respect threatened to grow too heavy, he would suddenly tumble from his horse with absurd clumsiness, rolling across the ground in a way that provoked laughter even from the ambassador himself. Then, with equal flair, he’d climb back up by grasping the tail of his steed like some clumsy acrobat, completing his act with a grin that never failed to amuse.

Toward the rear of the procession came an even more remarkable sight: the Duke’s leopard. A huntsman, mounted upon a massive Flemish horse of enormous strength and size, carried a long wooden box strapped securely to his body. Upon this box sat a sleek, golden-spotted leopard, crouched low and alert. She was chained to her rider, and though she appeared calm, her eyes held a wildness that kept the crowd at a respectful distance.

The townsfolk gathered at windows and balconies, drawn by curiosity. Some leaned forward, eager to touch her glossy fur or pull gently at her tail. But the huntsman roared a warning so sharp it silenced them all: “Beware! At Antwerp, one man dared throw dust at her—and the Duke turned him into dust.” He paused, letting the tale sink in. “I speak truth. The good Duke threw him into a dungeon beneath the earth. Rats stripped his flesh from bone in a single night. Justice done, for disturbing the poor beast.”

A murmur of fear passed through the crowd. No one dared approach again.

But just as tension settled, another figure emerged—the Duke’s giant, a Hungarian towering seven feet four inches tall. He brought up the rear, walking with slow, deliberate steps, his voice a high, fluty squeak that belied his immense frame. Proud and unaware of his oddity, he noticed Giles perched atop a balcony and stopped abruptly.

“Hallo, brother!” he chirped, stretching out a hand the size of a mutton leg. “I nearly missed you!”

“You’re plain enough to see,” bellowed Giles, his deep voice cutting through the air like thunder.

“Come sit on my shoulder,” squeaked the giant, grinning. “It’ll be fun!”

“If I do,” thundered Giles, “I’ll punch your ears off!”

The giant chuckled, delighted by the defiance. Encouraged by the laughter from the crowd, he pressed further, teasing the dwarf. But no one realized they were laughing not at wit, but at the sheer absurdity of two voices—one tiny and shrill, the other huge and roaring—clashing like mismatched instruments.

Then, suddenly, Giles lost control. In a fury born of pride and unshakable courage, he leapt from the balcony, landed squarely on the giant’s neck, seized his hair with one hand, and began pounding his head with the other.

The giant laughed at first—but the force of the blows soon turned that laughter into cries of pain. “He! he! Ah! ha! hallo! Oh! Holy saints! Help me! I can’t breathe! I’ll crush this imp—no, I’ll split your skull against—”

And with a wild cry, he ran backward, crashing into the balcony.

Giles, seeing danger, grabbed the railing with both hands and swung himself over just as the giant’s head struck the wood with a sickening crack.

The crowd erupted in cheers. They had witnessed something extraordinary—a small man standing up to a mountain, and winning.

The giant, furious, snatched two nearby men and slammed them together like stones. Catherine screamed and threw her apron over Giles, shielding him from view. Then, still fuming, the giant stomped away after the procession.

No one knew it then, but this moment would echo far beyond the day.

Its immediate effect, however, was joyful. The people of Tergou now looked upon Giles with new respect. When he went about begging parchment for his brother Gerard, they listened more kindly. It had become a kind of trade—Giles collected scraps of paper freely, and Gerard gave him copper coins in return.

That afternoon, Catherine and her daughter Kate sat together, talking softly of their beloved son Gerard—his kindness, his priesthood, the future he promised for their family. Their fortune had come in the form they most desired: not just a benefice, but a holy man within their own home.

“He will marry Cornelis and Sybrandt,” Catherine said. “They may wed now, if they wish. And Gerard will care for us when we are gone.”

“And we can confess to him,” Kate added, “instead of to strangers.”

“Ay,” nodded her mother. “And he can bless us with the sacred oil when our time comes.”

“Oh, mother,” Kate whispered, “not for many years. Please don’t speak of that. It makes me sad. I hope I go before you.”

She smiled then, feeling light and free. “I’m not in pain anymore. It feels strange—so bright and happy. Mother… can you keep a secret?”

“Better than anyone,” Catherine replied, her eyes alight with curiosity.

“Then I’ll show you something beautiful. You’ve never seen anything like it. But Gerard must never know—he’s hiding it, covering it up, sometimes taking it away altogether.”

Kate took her crutches and moved slowly to the corner of the room. She returned with a cloth wrapped tightly around something. She unfolded it carefully.

There, painted with astonishing life and grace, was the Virgin Mary—her face serene, her eyes lifted to heaven as if belonging there, her golden hair flowing loosely over her shoulders, crowned with a tiara of stars and jewels.

Catherine gasped. “It is herself,” she breathed. “The Queen of Heaven. I have never seen her so real.”

“And her eyes,” Kate murmured, “as if they belong to the sky. Her hair—like fire.”

“And to think,” Catherine said, tears in her eyes, “we have a son who can bring the saints back to life on wood.”

“He is a saint himself,” Kate said softly. “Too good for this world. He paints the blessed because he belongs with them.”

Just as they began to admire the image anew, a strange voice cut through the silence.

At the door stood Ghysbrecht Van Swieten—the burgomaster, a man who had not entered their home in ten years.

Both women froze. Their faces told the story before words could form.

“The burgomaster!” they said together, their tone filled with shock.

Ghysbrecht cleared his throat. “Yes. The last time I came here, it was not in friendship. Men follow their interests. Mine and Eli’s were at odds. But today—I come on your behalf, not mine.”

Catherine and Kate exchanged a glance—of suspicion, of disbelief. They knew him well.

“It’s about your son Gerard.”

“Ay,” Catherine snapped. “You want him to work for the town for nothing. We know.”

“No,” Ghysbrecht said sharply. “I come to warn you. Your son has fallen into bad company.”

“Now Heaven forbid!” Catherine cried. “Speak plainly, man. Don’t torment a mother. Speak quickly—before you lie.”

Ghysbrecht paled. Anger mixed with shame. “Then hear it. Your son Gerard is not fit to be a priest. He spends all his time with Margaret—Peter Brandt’s red-haired girl. He loves her like a cow loves its calf.”

Mother and daughter burst into laughter.

Ghysbrecht stared. “What? You knew?”

“Take this news to those who don’t know my son,” Catherine said coldly. “Women mean nothing to him.”

“Other women, perhaps,” Ghysbrecht retorted. “But this one—she’s the apple of his eye. My servant has seen them together—holding hands, gazing into each other’s eyes like fools in love. Come, woman—don’t waste my time. Tell me now—will you stop them?”

“I am ill at ease,” Catherine whispered. “I remember being young. My heart turns sick. Kate—what if it’s true?”

“No!” Kate cried, her voice rising. “Gerard might love a woman—every young man does—but if he did, he’d tell us. He wouldn’t deceive us. You wicked man! No, mother—look at me! Gerard is too pure for earthly love. His heart is for Our Lady and the saints. Look—see this picture! If he loved a mortal, could he paint the Queen of Heaven like this?” She held it up, radiant with conviction.

The burgomaster stared, dumbfounded. “Why—it is herself,” he gasped.

“It is!” Kate insisted. “And you admire it? Then forgive me for fearing you.”

“Am I in a madhouse?” Ghysbrecht muttered. “You show me a portrait of a girl, say he painted it, and that proves he doesn’t love her? Painters always paint their sweethearts!”

“A girl?” Kate exclaimed, horrified. “This is the Blessed Virgin!”

“No,” Ghysbrecht insisted. “It’s Margaret Brandt.”

“Blind fool!” Kate cried. “Look at her crown!”

“Silly child,” he snapped. “See her red hair! Would the Virgin wear red hair? She chose colors ten thousand years before creation!”

At that moment, Peter Buyskens, their neighbor, peeked through the doorway.

“What’s going on?” he whispered. “I can hear you across the street.”

“Here’s the burgomaster accusing Gerard,” Catherine said.

“Stop!” Ghysbrecht interrupted. “Peter Buyskens has come just in time. He knows them both. They cast spells on him.”

“What?” Peter asked, confused.

“They bewitched him,” Ghysbrecht said. “They cured him of colic with unholy magic. Now, Peter—look at the picture. Who is it?”

“Well,” Peter said slowly, “you know as well as I do. But why put a crown on her? I never saw her wearing one.”

“Curse you!” Ghysbrecht shouted. “Can’t you just name the wench?”

“I’d do more to please you than that,” Peter replied calmly. “If it isn’t as natural as life.”

“Curse him!” Ghysbrecht growled.

“Oh, sir,” little Kate said, “tell us—does this face belong to a living woman? To Margaret Brandt?”

“A mirror couldn’t be truer,” Peter said.

“But is it her?” Kate pressed.

“Who else should it be?”

“Why couldn’t you say so at once?” Ghysbrecht snapped.

“I did,” Peter shot back. “As plain as I could.”

They argued fiercely, oblivious to the fact that Catherine and Kate had covered their faces with their aprons and were rocking back and forth in silent anguish.

Then Elias entered from the shop, stopping short at the scene.

Catherine, though her face was hidden, recognized his footsteps.

“That’s my poor man,” she sobbed. “Tell him, Peter Buyskens—I cannot.”

Elias turned pale. The burgomaster’s presence, after years of silence, combined with his wife’s distress, sent a chill through him.
