“Richart! Jacob!” he gasped.

“No,” the burgomaster said. “It’s closer to home. No one is dead or dying, old friend.”

“God bless you,” Elias breathed, relief washing over him. “Ah—something has lifted from my chest. Now—what is it?”

Ghysbrecht repeated the accusation and showed the painting.

“Is that all?” Elias asked, calmer now. “What are you shouting about? It’s troubling—yes—but not deadly. Boys will be boys. He’ll grow out of it. It’s skin-deep.”

But when Ghysbrecht added that Margaret was a decent girl, and that such closeness likely meant marriage had been discussed, Elias’s face darkened.

“Marriage?” he said sternly. “That shall never happen. I’ll stop it—by force, if need be. Like old John Koestein did.”

“And what did he do?” Catherine asked, lifting her apron.

The burgomaster answered: “He locked young Albert Koestein in the Stadthouse prison until he submitted. Forty-eight hours—bread and water—cooled his hot blood. ‘Tell my father I am his humble servant,’ he said. ‘Let me out into the sun—sun is worth all the wenches in the world.’”

“Oh, the cruelty of men,” Catherine sighed.

“Nay,” Ghysbrecht said. “It’s the law. If a father says, ‘Lock up my son,’ the burgomaster must obey. It would be chaos if fathers couldn’t protect their children.”

“Well,” Elias said, “it won’t come to that. My son has never disobeyed me. He never will. Where is he, Kate?”

“I don’t know, father.”

“I do,” Ghysbrecht said. “He’s at Sevenbergen. My servant met him on the road.”

Supper passed in silence.

Night fell. Still no Gerard.

Eight o’clock came. Still no sign.

Elias sent everyone to bed, except Catherine.

“You and I will walk abroad,” he said. “Talk over this new trouble.”

“Abroad at this hour?” she asked. “Whither?”

“To Sevenbergen.”

“No hasty words, father,” Catherine pleaded. “Poor Gerard—he never wronged you before.”

“Fear me not,” Elias said. “But it must end. I don’t trust tomorrow with today’s duty.”

They walked hand in hand—strange, perhaps, to modern readers, but in those times, couples walked side by side, not arm in arm. The night was clear and warm, the air soft with memory.

“It’s been many years since we walked so late,” Catherine said softly.

“Ay, sweetheart,” Elias replied. “More than we’ll see again. (I wonder—will he ever come?)”

“Not since our courting days,” she said.

“No. You were a buxom lass then.”

“And you were a comely lad,” she smiled. “I suppose Gerard is with her now—just as you were with me. Nature is strong. It changes nothing across generations.”

“Nay,” Elias muttered. “I hope he’s left her. Or we’ll be here all night.”

“Eli,” Catherine said gently.

“Yes, Kate?”

“I’ve been happy with you, despite all our trials—much happier, I think, than if I had become a nun. Will you not speak harshly to the child? One can be firm without being cruel.”

“Surely,” he said.

“Have you been happy with me, my poor Eli?”

“You know I have,” he said. “Friends I’ve known, but none like thee. Kiss me, wife.”

“A heart to share joy and sorrow is a great comfort,” she said. “Isn’t it, Eli?”

“It is,” he replied. “‘It doth joy double, and halveth trouble.’ That’s how I’ve found it, sweetheart.”

And just then, a voice sang in the moonlight.

“Ah—here comes the young fool.”

Catherine trembled, clutching her husband’s hand.

The moon was bright, but they stood in shadow. Gerard didn’t see them.

He came singing, his face glowing in the silver light.

While the burgomaster was exposing Gerard at Tergou, Margaret faced her own trial in Sevenbergen. It was a quiet sorrow, born of a woman’s daily care, yet deeper than most could fathom. She came to Martin Wittenhaagen, the old soldier, her eyes brimming with tears.

“Martin,” she said, “there is nothing in the house. Gerard is coming home, and he never thinks to eat before he reaches us. When his work is done, he comes straight to me—poor soul—and often he arrives weak from hunger. And now, I have nothing to set before my servant who loves me so dearly.”

Martin scratched his head, puzzled. “What can I do?”

“It is Thursday—the day you go hunting,” she replied. “I counted on you today.”

“Nay,” he said, “I may not hunt when the Duke or his friends are out. You know that well enough.” He paused, then added, “I am no scholar.” With that, he pulled from his pouch a parchment sealed with a grand wax stamp. It bore the mark of Philip, Duke of Burgundy, and granted Martin Wittenhaagen, one of his archers, a yearly stipend of four merks and a licence to shoot three arrows once a week—on Thursdays only—in any of the Duke’s forests in Holland. But there were strict conditions: he might not hunt a seven-year-old buck or a doe carrying young; nor might he enter the woods if the Duke or his companions were afield. To do so risked forfeiture of salary, fine, and even death.

Margaret sighed. “Then what shall I do?”

“Come, cheer up, mistress,” Martin said, his voice firm. “For your sake, I’ll take the risk. I’ve done it for others less worthy than your little finger. It’s not such a great danger. I’ll just slip into the edge of the forest. Odds are they’ll drive a hare or fawn within range.”

“If you go,” she said, “you must promise not to go far, and not to be seen. Better Gerard goes supperless than harm come to you, faithful Martin.”

He gave his word. Then, taking his bow and three arrows, he crept into the wood—not more than a furlong away. The distant sound of horns echoed through the trees, signaling the chase. All the game was stirring.

“Soon,” thought Martin, “I shall fill the pot, and no one will be the wiser.”

He took position behind a thick oak that overlooked an open glade. His bow—a fearsome English yew, six feet two inches long and proportionately strong—was strung with care. Martin, broad-shouldered and powerful, had drawn such bows since childhood. He could pull a three-foot arrow back to his ear, and when released, the shaft flew like lightning, the string singing as clear as a harp. This weapon had laid low many a man in the wars between the Hoecks and Cabbeljaws. In those days, battles were not shrouded in smoke; men saw their enemies clearly, and fewer bullets meant more precise kills.

A hare bounded across the clearing, then stopped, ears pricked upward in a perfect V. Martin raised his bow. The arrow left the string with a sharp twang—but he’d been too hasty. The shaft struck the ground beside the hare, slid beneath her belly, and vanished into the grass. She leapt three feet straight up and fled.

“Bungler!” Martin muttered. A true marksman would never blame the prey.

He no sooner fitted another arrow than a wood-pigeon landed on the very branch above him. “Aha!” he thought. “You’re small, but dainty.” This time he took his time. He drew slowly, released smoothly, and watched the arrow pierce the bird—feathers flying like dust. But instead of falling, the pigeon fluttered away, wounded but alive. It rose above the trees, flew fifty yards, and died unseen among the branches.

“Luck is against me,” Martin muttered, disheartened.

But he readied a third arrow, scanning the glade. Suddenly, a rustling behind him made him turn. Too late—he saw a noble deer cross the open space, but could not draw his bow. He slammed his weapon down in frustration.

Then, swift as shadow, a long-spotted animal darted past—its belly brushing the earth. Martin froze. It was the Duke’s leopard.

“The hunters won’t be far,” he said. “And I must not be seen. Gerard will go supperless tonight.”

He plunged into the woods, following the trail of buck and leopard—his usual path home. But soon he heard something strange: violent rustling, heavy trampling ahead. He hurried forward.

There, in the dim light, the leopard was atop the buck, tearing at its flesh with teeth and claws. The deer ran in a frantic circle, blood streaming from its hide.

Martin made a desperate decision. He drew his arrow to the head and loosed it. The shaft buried itself deep in the buck’s side. Though the leopard clung to its back, the deer bounded high and fell dead.

The leopard continued feeding, unaware. Martin hoped it would gorge itself and leave. He waited. Then, stepping forward, he placed a hand on the buck’s leg.

The leopard snarled—a sound like thunder in the stillness—and stopped sucking. She turned her fierce gaze upon him.

Martin knew a tale: wild beasts cannot endure the human eye. So he stood tall, fixed his stare upon her. The leopard met his gaze, unblinking, furious.

Still he held her look. Slowly, she charged—yelling, eyes blazing, jaws wide. Martin barely caught her by the throat before her teeth reached his face. One claw ripped his shoulder; the other, aimed at his cheek, snagged in the leather hood he wore over his head.

He fought to keep her mouth from his face, gripping her throat with iron hands. She tore at his shoulder—like blunt reaping hooks grinding through flesh. The pain was terrible. But instead of breaking his spirit, it fired his rage. He gnashed his teeth, squeezing harder. Their eyes burned into each other—his nearly as wild as hers.

She struggled wildly, dragging his hood over his face, blinding him. Her claw tore free, leaving a wound. Yet he held fast.

Then—her tail, raised high, began to fall.

“Aha!” Martin shouted, tightening his grip. Soon, her body lost strength. He held her until all motion ceased. Then he threw her to the ground, gasping, and removed his cowl.

The leopard lay silent, tongue lolling, paw bloody. For the first time, fear seized Martin.

“I am a dead man,” he whispered. “I have slain the Duke’s leopard.”

He quickly gathered leaves and covered her body. Then he shouldered the buck and staggered home, leaving a trail of blood—his own and the deer’s.

He burst into Peter’s house, a figure of horror—bleeding, stained with gore—and flung the carcass down.

“There,” he said. “No questions. Just broil me a steak. I’m faint.”

Margaret did not see his wound. She thought the blood was all from the deer. She rushed to the fire, while the soldier bound his own injury. Soon, Gerard joined them, and they sat down to a feast of broiled venison.

They laughed and talked, merry under the influence of Schiedam wine that Gerard had brought. Martin, warmed by drink, told them how he’d killed the deer—though he left out the leopard. They all laughed at the tale.

Then—silence.

Margaret’s face went pale. Her eyes locked onto the window, trembling. She pointed, unable to speak.

At the glass, crouched in the twilight, was a dark shape—eyes like green fire.

It was the leopard.

They stood frozen, transfixed by those glowing eyes. Then, from the woods, came a single deep bay.

Martin trembled. “They’ve lost her. They’ve sent muzzled hounds. They’ll find her here. And the venison. Good-bye, friends. Martin Wittenhaagen ends here.”

Gerard grabbed his bow and handed it to the soldier. “Be a man,” he cried. “Shoot her. Throw her into the woods before they arrive. Who will know?”

More hounds barked—closer now.

“Curse her!” Martin roared. “I spared her once. Now she dies—or I do—or both.” He raised his bow, drew the arrow to his ear.

“Nay! Nay!” cried Margaret, seizing the arrow.

It snapped in half. The pieces fell to either side of the bow.

At once, the air filled with the baying of dogs—they were hot on the scent.

“What have you done, wench?” Martin cried. “You’ve put the halter around my neck.”

“No!” she shouted. “I’ve saved you! Stand back from the window—both of you! Your knife—quick!”

She tore the long-pointed blade from his belt and darted from the room.

Now the house was surrounded—dogs barking, men shouting. The leopard remained motionless, her eyes still burning in the dusk.

Margaret sliced a large chunk of venison and dashed to the window, hurling it out into the darkness. Instantly, green eyes flared to life in the shadows—feral, hungry—and lunged forward with a snarl. The sound of tearing flesh and crunching bone echoed through the night. Then, from nearby, a hound bayed so loudly it shook the very walls of the house. The three at the window recoiled as one.

The leopard, startled by the noise, darted away with her prize, slipping silently toward the woods. No sooner had she vanished than horses thundered past the window, men shouting, dogs barking—chasing her full cry into the forest. Martin and his companions exchanged relieved glances. The beast was swift; they knew she would not be caught within miles of their home. They clasped hands in silent triumph.

Margaret seized the moment, her voice breaking as she whispered a small cry. Gerard leaned close and kissed the tears from her cheeks.

Back to the table they went. Gerard raised his cup in toast. “Woman’s wit,” he declared, “is stronger than man’s strength.”
“Aye,” replied Margaret, “when those she loves are in danger. But not otherwise.”

That evening, Gerard lingered longer than usual beside her. He left for home later than ever before, his heart swelling with pride and joy. Yet just beyond the edge of the trees, under the cover of shadow, two figures blocked his path.

It was his father and mother.

So late? What could bring them here? A cold dread settled over him. He stopped, staring at them. They stood rigid, silent, like statues carved from stone.

He stammered out a question.
“Why ask?” said his father. “You know why we’re here.”

“Oh, Gerard!” murmured his mother, her voice thick with sorrow and love.

Gerard’s heart sank. He could not speak.

Then, seeing his distress, his father softened. “Do not hang your head. You are not the first young fool to fall for a red cheek and blue eyes.”

“Nay, nay!” cried Catherine. “It was witchcraft! Peter the Magician is well known for such tricks.”

“Come now, Sir Priest,” resumed the father, “you must not meddle with womenfolk. But give us your word—you will go no more to Sevenbergen—and this ends. We won’t press you too hard for one fault.”

“I cannot promise that, father.”

“Not promise? You young hypocrite!”

“Nay, father, do not misjudge me. I lacked courage to tell you what I knew would wound you. And I am grateful to whoever warned you. It lifts a weight from my soul. Yes, father—I love Margaret. Call me not a priest, for I shall never be one. I would die first.”

“That we shall see, young man,” said his father, stiffening. “Come, do not gainsay me. You’ll learn what it means to defy your father.”

Gerard said nothing. The three walked home in silence, broken only by a few deep sighs from Catherine.

From that hour, peace fled the little house at Tergou.

The next day, Gerard was summoned before the whole family. Every voice rose against him—except little Kate’s and the dwarf’s, who seemed to follow her instinctively, though he did not know why. Cornelis and Sybrandt were especially harsh, bitterer even than their father.

Gerard, overwhelmed by so many enemies, looked pleadingly at his sister. Her eyes glistened with unshed tears at the cruel words once aimed at the boy who had been everyone’s favorite. But she turned away. “Dear, dear Gerard,” she whispered, “pray to Heaven to cure you of this folly.”

“What?” he asked, broken-hearted. “Are you against me too?”

And with a heavy sigh, he rose and left the house, walking straight to Sevenbergen.

At first, disputes born of love and duty are often innocent—both sides may be right at the start. That is when a calm, wise friend becomes a gift from heaven. But the longer the rift endures, the deeper it grows, fed by human error and temper. Neither side escapes blame. In time, both become wrong.

In this quarrel, Elias was angry, Cornelis and Sybrandt spiteful. But Gerard, with a broader mind, saw both sides where others saw only one. He struggled with doubt, not rage. He was unhappy, not furious. And he was alone—no one to confide in.

Margaret Van Eyck had once comforted him in hardship, but now he dared not share his pain with her. She was strong-willed, proud. If he told her how his family tormented him, she might choose loyalty over love—and leave him. And yet, her own story was well known. As a young woman, she had refused many suitors, choosing art instead—knowing how marriage and motherhood would drain a painter’s spirit. How could he confess that he rejected the church and the benefice she had secured for him—because he loved something she once sacrificed?

At this point, Gerard began to falter.

But on the other side stood Catherine, the elder. Though kind-hearted, she was untrained in patience or strategy. She could neither act quietly nor plan wisely. Yet she served both sides: sometimes she provoked Gerard, which stirred his resolve; at other times, she turned on her own kin, creating chaos.

One afternoon, during a gathering, Cornelis sneered, “Our Gerard marrying Margaret Brandt? Why, it’s hunger marrying thirst.”

“And what about you?” shot back Catherine. “Gerard can paint, write—what can *you* do to support a wife, lazy loon? Nothing but wait for your father’s shoes. Oh, I see why you and Sybrandt oppose this match. You fear he’ll come begging for our fortune. Even if he does, and we give it, it’s not yours to lose. Perhaps it never will be.”

Gerard smiled faintly, and found new strength. His rivals, momentarily stunned, fell silent.

But after more than half a year of tension, the crisis came.

His father called him before the family and announced: “I have ordered the burgomaster to imprison you in the Stadthouse rather than let you marry Margaret.”

Gerard paled—but held his tongue.

His father continued: “And before the year ends, you shall be a priest—whether you like it or not.”

“Is that so?” Gerard burst out. “Then hear me all. By God and St. Bavon, I swear I will never be a priest while Margaret lives. If force must decide this, then let it be force. Father—try your strength. But know this: the day the burgomaster comes for me, I leave Tergou—forever. I leave Holland, I leave your house, where it seems I’ve been valued not for myself, but for what I can yield.”

With that, he stormed from the room, white with fury and despair.

“There!” exclaimed Catherine. “That’s what happens when you push youth too hard. Men are crueler than tigers—even to their own blood. May Heaven forbid he should ever leave us, married or single.”

As Gerard stepped outside, pale and breathless, he met Reicht Heynes. She bore a message: Margaret Van Eyck wished to see him.

He found the old lady seated like a judge, stern and still.

She wasted no time. “Why haven longer visited me?”

Before he could answer, she added, sharply, “I thought we were friends, young sir.”

Gerard looked stricken.

“It is because you never told her you loved her,” said Reicht softly, pitying his confusion.

“Silence, wench!” snapped the old woman. “Why should he tell us his affairs? We are not his friends. We have not earned his trust.”

“Oh, madam,” said Gerard, trembling, “I dared not tell you my folly.”

“What folly? Is it folly to love?”

“I am told so every day.”

“You need not have feared telling my mistress. She is always kind to true lovers.”

“Madam—Reicht—I was afraid because I heard…”

“Well, you were told—?”

“That in your youth you scorned love, chose art above all.”

“I did, boy. And what has become of it? Look at me—a barren tree, while the women of my youth stand with children at their feet and grandchildren beside them. I gave up the joys of wifehood and motherhood—for my brothers. They are gone. For my art. It nearly left me too. I still have the knowledge—but what good is it when the hand trembles? No, Gerard. I see you as my son. You are good, handsome, a painter—though not like some I’ve known. I will not let you waste your youth as I did mine. You shall marry Margaret. I have inquired—she is a good daughter. Reicht has told me all. But you may tell me freely.”

Poor Gerard was overjoyed. At last, someone allowed him to speak of Margaret openly—to one who understood the depth of his love.

Soon, two pairs of eyes were wet with tears. When Gerard saw that, a third joined them.

Women possess a courage unlike any man’s. Not the same courage, no—nor should it be. We would lose our dominance if it were. Theirs is a vicarious courage. They never enter a bullfight—but watch it without flinching, while men quake with anxiety. They send men to war with iron hearts. As a witty saying goes: “Les femmes sont très braves avec la peur d’autrui.”

This trait now helped Gerard.

Margaret and Reicht agreed: a man must take the bull by the horns. He must marry Margaret at once. The elders would relent in time. Delay only worsened matters—for all, especially him.

“See how pale and thin they’ve made him,” said Reicht.

“Indeed, Master Gerard,” she added. “It makes one sad to see a young man so worn. When I met him today, I almost wept. He’s changed so much.”

“And I’ll wager the others keep their color—ah, Reicht? Such as it is.”

“Oh, I see no difference.”

“Of course not. We painters are glass—they are stone. We cannot endure the constant worry of small minds. It’s not good for mankind that we should be exposed to it. To create a masterpiece is hard enough—without gnats and flies stinging us to death.”

Though furious at his father’s threats, Gerard listened to these voices urging rebellion. But he remained unconvinced.

“I do not fear my father’s violence,” he said. “But I fear his anger. When it comes to the point, he wouldn’t imprison me. I’d marry Margaret tomorrow if that were my only fear. But he would disown me. I’d take her from her father, and give her a poor husband—burdened by his parents’ curse. Madam—I sometimes think, if I could marry her secretly, and flee to a land where artists are better paid… After a year or two, when the storm passed, I could return with money and say, ‘We don’t seek your wealth—we only ask to be loved again, as we’ve always loved you.’ But alas—I’m told this is the dream of an inexperienced youth.”

The old lady’s eyes sparkled. “It is not a dream—it is common sense. The question is, do you have the courage to act on it?”

“There is a land, Gerard,” she continued, “where fortune awaits you now. Here, art freezes. There, it flourishes—more than in any age or land.”

“Italy!” Gerard breathed.

“Italy!” she confirmed. “Where painters are honored as princes, and scribes earn three hundred crowns for copying a single manuscript. Did you know the Pope himself writes to every kingdom, seeking skilled hands to copy the priceless manuscripts pouring in from Constantinople—where learning flees the Turkish invaders?”

“I did not know,” said Gerard. “But Italy—the queen of arts—has been my dream since childhood. Oh, madam! But the journey… we are so poor.”

“If you have the heart to go,” she said, “I will find the means. I know where to lay my hands on ten golden angels. They will take you to Rome—and the girl with you, if she truly loves you.”

They talked until midnight.

After that day, Gerard regained his strength. He carried a secret talisman—invincible against the insults and scolding that flew around him at home.

Besides the money, Margaret Van Eyck gave him wisdom.

“Listen,” she said, “I will teach you secrets learned from masters now gone—secrets the Italians themselves do not know. What I tell you here, you shall sell in Florence.”

She pointed to her brother Jan’s paintings. “Time fades most works—but his colors remain bright as the day they left the brush. Why? Because he worked slowly, deliberately. He ground his own pigments. He prepared his panels—again and again—sometimes a year before painting. Most painters rush. Bad painters are always in a hurry.”

Above all, she warned: “Use little oil. Never boil it. Boiling melts impurities into its core—impure oil kills color. Pour your oil into a bottle with water. In a day or two, the water turns muddy—that’s muck from the oil. Carefully pour it off, add fresh water. Repeat. When you think it’s clear—you’re mistaken.”

She called Reicht. “Bring me that.”

Reicht returned with a glass trough, sealed tightly.

“Now,” said Margaret, “after washing in the bottle, put the oil into this trough with water. Place it in the sun. You’ll soon see the water cloud again. But beware—don’t overdo it. The sun may turn your oil to varnish. When it’s as clear as crystal, not too rich, drain it carefully, cork it tight.”

“Grind your own pigments,” she insisted. “Use this oil, and your colors shall live.”

Hubert used sand or salt to speed clarity. But Jan said, “Water does it best—give water time.”

Jan Van Eyck was never in a hurry. And so the world will not forget him in a hurry.

She gave him other secrets—too many to list now. Gerard received them like a divine inheritance. Some things, though dull on paper, shine when taught by passion.

Thus armed with gold and knowledge, Gerard resolved: he would marry Margaret and flee to Italy.

Only one thing remained: to tell Margaret, and quietly publish the banns.

He arrived in Sevenbergen earlier than usual.

First, he spoke to Margaret. He told her of Dame Van Eyck’s kindness, of his decision, and asked for her help.

She refused outright.

“No, Gerard,” she said. “We’ve never spoken of your family. But marriage—”

She paused. Then: “I believe your father bears me no ill will—only the same as another. Peter Buyskens told me so. But as long as he insists you become a priest—well, I could not marry you, Gerard, however much I love you.”

He pleaded in vain. He could make her cry—but not change her mind.

Then Gerard grew impatient, unjust.

“Very well!” he shouted. “Then you are on their side. You’ll drive me to become a priest. This must end one way or another. My parents hate me in truth—but my lover loves me only in jest!”

And with that bitter cry, he stormed home, leaving Margaret weeping.

When a man misbehaves, the effect on a loving woman is strange: she feels pity.

To many men, this seems illogical. But the fault lies in our understanding. The logic is too swift for us.

She thinks: “How unhappy, how distressed, how poor he must be to act so! Poor thing.”

Margaret was filled with this tender pity—when, to her astonishment, less than an hour later, Gerard returned, running, his face twisted with grief and rage, clutching torn pieces of a painting.

“There, Margaret!” he gasped. “Look! See! The villains! They’ve cut your portrait to shreds!”

She stared. Indeed, some cruel hand had slashed the painting into five jagged pieces.

She was gentle—but not cold. Her face flushed crimson.

“Who did it?”

“I don’t know. I couldn’t ask. I’d hate the hand that did it—forever.”

“My poor Margaret! Butchers! Ruffians! Six months’ work—destroyed. Nothing left. Look—they’ve hacked through your face—the sweet face everyone loves.”

“Oh, heartless, merciless vipers!”

“Never mind, Gerard,” she said, panting. “Since this is how they treat you for my sake—Ye rob him of my portrait, do ye? Well then—he shall have the face itself, such as it is.”

“Oh, Margaret!”

“Yes, Gerard. Since they are so cruel, I will be kinder. Forgive me for refusing you. I will be your wife—tomorrow, if you wish.”

Gerard kissed her hands, then her lips. Overwhelmed with joy, he raced to fetch Peter and Martin.

They came, and witnessed the betrothal—a solemn rite in those days, lasting more than a century before being abolished.

The banns of marriage were to be proclaimed three times, as they are even today—but in those days, they were usually read on weekdays, and the young couple had little trouble persuading the curate to complete all three readings within a single day. He was new to the parish, and their earnest looks spoke more eloquently than words ever could. On Monday morning, the banns were announced at matins and again at vespers—and to their great relief, no one from Tergou was present in the church.

The next morning, both Gerard and Margaret arrived at the church, hearts pounding with anxiety. But just as the curate prepared to speak, a stranger rose abruptly and declared the banns invalid—on the grounds that neither party had reached the age of consent, and that parental permission had not been granted.

Outside the church, trembling and nearly overcome with despair, they whispered urgently to one another. Before they could decide what to do, the man who had blocked their union approached them. With a sly smile, he confessed he regretted interfering—he truly wished the young lovers well. But, he added, his livelihood depended entirely upon such interruptions. “A crown,” he said, “and I’ll undo it all. Tell the curate I was misinformed. The matter will be settled.”

“A crown?” Gerard exclaimed. “I’ll give you a golden angel for that.” The man agreed instantly and went with Gerard to the curate, claiming he had made a grave error—one corrected by seeing the couple in person. The curate, satisfied, consented to marry them the following day at ten o’clock. The man returned home with Gerard’s golden angel.

But this clever rogue was also a fool. He drank the coin at a tavern in Tergou, near a green where men practiced archery and other pastimes. There, half-drunk, he boasted of his exploit. And who should overhear him but Sybrandt, a notorious ne’er-do-well and frequent visitor to the place.

Sybrandt rushed home to tell his father—but the man was absent, having gone to Rotterdam to purchase cloth. Instead, Sybrandt signaled his elder brother, who stepped outside. These two were Gerard’s black sheep—the reckless, idle sons of a once-honest family. Idleness breeds vice; waiting for an inheritance breeds cruelty. Their thoughts revolved around nothing but the wealth they believed awaited them after their parents’ deaths. While their parents’ frugality stemmed from love and hard work, in these brothers it had twisted into greed—a root of endless crime.

Together, they decided not to inform their mother—her feelings were too unpredictable. Instead, they would go directly to the burgomaster. They sensed his opposition to the match, though they did not know why. Ghysbrecht Van Swieten saw through them immediately, but played along. He listened gravely, then assumed an air of authority. “Since your father is away,” he said, “the duty falls upon me, as father of the town. I know your father’s mind. Leave everything to me. And above all—do not tell a woman a word of this. Not even one in your own house. Chattering tongues ruin the wisest plans.”

He dismissed them with a faint air of superiority—ashamed of their company.

When they returned home, they found Gerard seated on a low stool beside their mother’s knee. She was gently stroking his hair, speaking kindly, promising to stand by him and no longer oppose his love. Her change of heart was rooted in her nature. It was she who, in a fit of anger, had torn Margaret’s portrait to pieces. She had watched Gerard turn pale, motionless, clutching the fragments until tears blurred his vision. Then remorse struck her—she wept in secret, yet dared not confess. “I’ll say nothing,” she told herself, “but I’ll make it up to him.” Her heart softened. Her harshness died. She was turning toward Gerard when the brothers burst in.

Gerard knew nothing of the reason for her sudden kindness. In fact, her tenderness only deepened his shame—he had suspected her of betraying him. Now he kissed her again and again, and retired to bed, joyful as a prince, believing his mother had finally become his mother once more—at the very moment his fate hung in the balance.

The next morning, at ten o’clock, Gerard and Margaret stood together in the church at Sevenbergen. He glowed with joy; she blushed with emotion. Peter and Martin Wittenhaagen were there—no others. Secrecy was essential. Margaret had refused to leave for Italy. She could not abandon her father—he was too learned, too helpless. But they had agreed to flee to Flanders for a few weeks, until the storm passed in Tergou.

The curate did not keep them waiting long—though it felt like an eternity. Then he stepped forward, calling them to the altar. They walked hand in hand, the happiest pair in Holland. The curate opened his book—then, before he could utter a word, a harsh voice cried: “Forbear!”

The constables of Tergou surged down the aisle and seized Gerard in the name of the law. Martin’s knife flashed out instantly.

“Hold!” shouted the priest. “Draw your weapon in a church? And you, who interrupt this holy sacrament—what madness is this?”

“There is no impiety, father,” replied the burgomaster’s servant respectfully. “This youth seeks to marry against his father’s will. His father has requested our burgomaster to act under the law. Let him deny it if he can.”

“Is this true, young man?” the curate asked.

Gerard bowed his head.

“We take him to Rotterdam,” the servant declared, “to await the Duke’s judgment.”

Margaret let out a cry of despair. The two lovers, so radiant moments before, now clung to each other, sobbing helplessly. Even the officers of the law hesitated—ashamed. One, kind-hearted, stepped forward under pretense of separating them, and whispered: “Rotterdam? That’s a lie. We’re taking him to the Stadthouse.”

They led Gerard away on horseback, heading toward Rotterdam. After several stops and devious turns, they turned back toward Tergou. Just outside the town, a crude canvas-covered cart waited. Gerard was placed inside and, by dusk, secretly delivered to the prison of the Stadthouse.

He was taken up many flights of stairs and thrown into a small room lit only by a narrow window with a vertical iron bar. The only furniture was a massive oak chest. Imprisonment in that age was often a death sentence. Cold, isolation, starvation, torture—sometimes poison—were its companions. Gerard felt himself in the hands of an enemy.

“Oh, the look that man gave me on the road to Rotterdam,” he murmured. “There’s more here than my father’s wrath. I fear I shall never see daylight again.”

He knelt and prayed. Then, rising, he lunged for the iron bar, gripping it tightly. Pressing his knees against the wall, he managed to peer outside.

For just a moment—yet enough. He saw Martin Wittenhaagen’s back. Martin sat quietly by the brook near the Stadthouse, fishing.

Gerard whistled sharply.

Martin turned instantly—his eyes sharp, alert. He saw Gerard, made a signal, then picked up his bow and line and slipped away.

Gerard watched him go—relief flooding through him. The sight of his friend was comfort enough. Yet he wished Martin had stayed.

As the soldier vanished, Gerard pulled with all his strength—wrenching the rusted iron bar from the stone, held only by corroded nails. At that moment, the door creaked open. Ghysbrecht Van Swieten entered silently.

The burgomaster’s gaze fell upon the broken bar, then swept to the window—so high above the ground. He said nothing.

He brought a brown loaf and a pitcher of water, set them on the chest, and left in silence.

Gerard’s first impulse was to strike him with the bar and flee. But the burgomaster caught the flash in his eye and coughed softly. Instantly, three armed men appeared at the door.

“My orders,” the burgomaster said coldly, “are to hold you here until you swear to abandon Margaret Brandt and return to the Church, to which you have belonged since birth.”

“Death sooner,” Gerard replied.

“With all my heart,” the burgomaster answered, and withdrew.

Martin raced to Sevenbergen. There he found Margaret—pale, agitated, but resolute. She had just finished a letter to Countess Charolois, appealing against the injustice and treachery of Ghysbrecht.

“Courage!” Martin called as he entered. “I’ve found him. He’s in the haunted tower—the very top. I know the place. Many a man has gone up there… and come down feet first.”

He described how he had looked up and seen Gerard’s face at a narrow slit in the wall.

“Oh, Martin! How did he look?”

“What do you mean? He looked like Gerard Eliassoen.”

“But was he pale?”

“A little.”

“Anxious? Like one doomed?”

“No, no—bright as a pewter pot.”

“You mock me. Wait—then it must have been at sight of you. He counts on us. Oh, what shall we do? Martin, good friend, take this letter to Rotterdam at once.”

Martin reached for the letter.

Peter had been silent, but watching closely—more attentive than usual.

“Put not your trust in princes,” he said.

“Alas! What else have we to trust in?” Margaret sighed.

“Knowledge.”

“Father, your learning won’t help us now.”

“How do you know? Wit has overcome iron bars before.”

“Ay, father—but nature is stronger than wit, and nature is against us. Think of the height! No ladder in Holland could reach him.”

“I need no ladder. I need only a gold crown.”

“Nay, I have money. Nine angels. Gerard gave them to me to keep. But what use are they? The burgomaster won’t be bribed.”

“What use? Give me one crown, and the young man shall sup with us tonight.”

Peter spoke with such confidence that Margaret felt a flicker of hope. But Martin’s eyes lingered on him with gentle mockery.

“It passes the powers of man’s invention,” she breathed.

“Invention!” Peter snapped. “A fig for invention. Everything that can be said or done has already been said and done. Let me tell you of a Florentine knight shut in a tower higher than Gerard’s. His faithful squire stood below and freed him—with no machine but the bow in your hand, Martin, and some trinkets I’ll buy for a crown.”

Martin stared at his bow, turning it slowly. Still, he remained unconvinced.

Then Peter recounted the tale—the squire’s clever plan. Simple, yet brilliant. So simple, in fact, that now they wondered how they could have thought it impossible.

The letter never reached Rotterdam. They trusted Peter’s wisdom—and their own courage.

It was nine o’clock on a clear moonlit night. Gerard senior was still in Rotterdam. The rest of the household slept.

A figure stood beside Giles’s bed. Pale, glowing in the moonlight. With a sound halfway between a yell and a snarl, the gymnast rolled off his bed and under it in one fluid motion.

A soft voice followed: “Why, Giles, are you afraid of me?”

Giles peeked out cautiously—and saw it was his sister Kate.

She pressed a finger to her lips. “Hush! Lest Cornelis or Sybrandt hear us.”

Giles climbed back with a single gymnastic leap.

Kate revealed she had overheard Cornelis and Sybrandt mention Gerard’s name. Anxious about his absence, she had listened at their door—and learned a terrible truth: Gerard was imprisoned in the haunted tower of the Stadthouse. By their father’s order. But that couldn’t be—Gerard’s father was in Rotterdam. There must be treachery.

She begged Giles to accompany her to the tower—to speak to Gerard, to tell him their father was away and would surely release him upon return.

“Dear Giles, I’d go alone—but I’m afraid of the spirits said to haunt the tower. But with you, I’ll not fear.”

“Nor I with you,” Giles replied. “I don’t believe in spirits. I’ve never seen one. The closest thing I’ve seen was you, Kate, after all.”

Within half an hour, Giles and Kate slipped out of the house. She made him carry a lantern—though the night was bright.

“The lantern gives me courage against the evil spirits,” she said.

The first night in prison is the hardest—especially when loneliness adds to the horror. Even today, many commit suicide within the first twenty-four hours of solitary confinement. Perhaps that is why modern jailers avoid watching during that critical time.

As the sun sank, Gerard’s spirit sank with it. Hope faded with the light. He was weak from hunger—he dared not eat the food Ghysbrecht had brought. Hunger breaks men.

He sat on the chest, arms and head drooping—utterly despondent.

Suddenly, something struck the wall behind him sharply, then rattled at his feet. An arrow—white feathered.

A chill ran through him. Assassination from outside?

He crouched. No more came.

Crawling forward, he picked up the arrow. No head. A cry of hope escaped him—could it be a friendly hand?

He examined it carefully. A soft substance attached. Using his tinder-box, he struck a light.

Two things revealed themselves—filling his heart with joy, though vague.

A skein of silk tied to the shaft—and words written on the arrow:

*Well beloved, make fast the silk to thy knife and lower to us: but hold thine end fast: then count an hundred and draw up.*

Gerard grabbed the chest and dragged it to the window—using superhuman strength. Moments ago, he could not have moved it.

Standing on the chest, he looked down. Figures at the base of the tower—blurred, like one giant shadow.

He waved his bonnet.

Then he untied the silk, fastened one end to his knife, and lowered it until it stopped drawing.

He counted a hundred.

Then pulled.

The silk grew heavier.

At last, a knot. Attached—thick whipcord.

What could it mean?

Then, from below, Margaret’s voice rose—low, clear:
“Draw up, Gerard, till you see liberty.”

He drew the whipcord upward—then another knot. A thicker cord replaced it.

He began pulling. The weight increased. Sweat poured down his face.

Then it dawned on him.

He pulled harder—until the rope emerged from the shadows below, coiling like a serpent.

A shout of joy burst from him.

More pulls—and a strong new rope touched his hand.

He hauled it in, threaded it through the chest handles, and knotted it firmly.

Then paused—breathing heavily, gathering courage.

First, test the chest.

He jumped—hard.

On the third jump, the side burst open. Parchments tumbled out.

Startled, he realized the chest hadn’t broken—it had opened. He had likely triggered a hidden spring.

Still, doubt crept in. He reinforced it—fastening the iron bar across the rope and window with a thin cord.

Now, he mounted the chest, put his foot through the window, and sat half in, half out, one hand gripping the inner rope.

In the silence, he heard his own heartbeat.

The free air touched his face—giving him the courage to risk what all must lose one day—liberty.

Many dangers lay ahead. The greatest—stepping onto the rope outside.

He reflected.

Finally, he positioned himself like a swimmer—body in, legs out.

Holding the inner rope with both hands, he felt with his feet for the outer rope.

Found it.

Tucked it between his palms.

Prayed briefly.

Then, calmly, placed his left hand on the sill and wriggled out.

He grasped the iron bar—hung suspended by one hand—while his left searched for the rope at his knees.

Too tight against the wall.

But he gripped it.

Let go of the bar.

Seized the rope with his right.

His body dropped a yard.

A stifled cry came from below.

Gerard hung in midair.

He clenched his teeth, squeezed the rope with his feet, gripped it with his hands—and descended slowly, hand below hand.

Rough stones passed beneath him.

Moss clung to one.

He looked up—the moon shone into his window.

Looked down—figures below seemed miles away.

Dizziness threatened.

So he fixed his eyes on the wall.

Down—down—down.

The rope burned his hands.

Another glance upward—the window was far away.

Now he dared look down.

Thirty feet below—Margaret and Martin, hands raised, ready to catch him.

Their eyes and teeth gleamed in the moonlight.

Mouths open—breathing hard.

“Take care, Gerard! Look not down!”

“Fear me not!” he called joyfully—and focused on the wall—descending faster.

In seconds, his feet touched their hands.

They seized him before he reached the ground.

All three embraced—silent, trembling.

“Hush! Away in silence, dear one.”

They crept along the shadow of the wall.

But suddenly—light shot from a corner of the building, blazing across their path like fire.

Whispers. Footsteps.

“Back!” hissed Martin. “Keep in the shade.”

They retreated—passed the dangling rope—raced toward a small projecting tower.

Just as they rounded it, the light flickered past, vanishing into the distance.

“A lantern!” Martin groaned. “They’re after us.”

“Give me my knife,” whispered Gerard. “I’ll never be taken alive.”

“No!” Margaret murmured. “Is there no way out?”

“None! None!” Martin said. “But I carry six lives at my shoulder.”

He strung his bow—fitted an arrow.

“In war, never wait to be struck. I’ll kill one or two before they know where death comes from.”

He motioned them to silence—drew his bow—ready to loose the arrow the moment a target appeared.

Gerard and Margaret held their breath.

A wild hope stirred in Gerard—perhaps the watcher was the burgomaster himself.

But the bow wavered—shook violently.

The soldier staggered back—knees knocking, face white.

He dropped his arrow—clutched Gerard’s shoulder.

“Let me feel flesh and blood,” he gasped. “The haunted tower! The haunted tower!”

His terror spread.

They gasped—not spoken.

“Hush!” he cried. “It will hear you up the wall! It is going up the wall! Its head is on fire. Up the wall, as mortal creatures walk on grass. If you know a prayer, say it—for hell is loose tonight.”

“I have power to exorcise spirits,” Gerard said, trembling. “I will venture forth.”

“Go alone,” Martin said. “I have looked on it once—and lived.”

The cold grip of fear had settled deep within Gerard’s chest since the burgomaster’s venomous glance and his unjust imprisonment. He believed now, without doubt, that Ghysbrecht was his sworn enemy—deadly, relentless, and cruel. As he crept around the shadowed corner of the ancient tower, he expected not a ghost, but a trap: some dark scheme laid by a man bent on his destruction. Escape from the prison had been impossible to conceal, and he knew full well that if anyone had seen him slip away, they would be watching.

But as he stepped forward into the open, a soft hand slipped into his—warm, steady, and unafraid. It was Margaret, standing beside him, her presence calm in the face of danger.

No sooner had they glimpsed the tower than their breath caught in their throats. Halfway up its stone face, a creature with a blazing head—like a monstrous glowworm—was slowly climbing the wall. Its body was black, barely visible except for the fiery outline it cast, and it stretched nearly four feet long. Below, at the base of the tower, stood a pale figure wrapped in white, perfectly still, like a statue carved from moonlight.

Gerard and Margaret froze, hearts pounding. “The rope! The rope!” Gerard whispered, voice trembling. “It’s climbing the rope!”

As they watched, the glowing creature vanished into the window of the cell where Gerard had been held. But its light spilled through the bars, painting the interior in crimson and casting a hellish glow upon the stones.

The white figure remained motionless beneath.

There is a strange twist to terror: once the first shock passes, a wild impulse often takes hold—a desire to rush toward the horror, to confront it, even to throw oneself at it. Like a bird drawn to a serpent’s gaze, the mind becomes entranced. This was what seized Margaret. She gently pulled her hand from Gerard’s, stood stunned for a moment—and then, with a cry torn from her soul, darted forward toward the spectre.

Gerard, unaware of this instinct, thought only that the devil was dragging her into damnation. He dropped to his knees, hands clasped, and began to shout: “Exorcizo vos! In nomine beatae Mariae, exorcizo vos!” His voice cracked with terror, yet relief surged through him when he heard a faint, terrified whimper from the apparition.

Hell, it seemed, had weaknesses too.

He redoubled his prayers. And soon, the ghastly shape knelt before Margaret, pleading for mercy, its voice broken and small.

Not long after, Kate and Giles arrived at the tower, breathless from their haste. They stared in astonishment at the scene: a new rope hanging down from the prisoner’s window, swaying gently in the wind.

“Ah,” said Giles, practical as ever, “I see it now. Gerard has escaped. Up I go to check.”

“No, Giles, no!” cried Kate, eyes wide with alarm. “This is glamour! A trick of the devil! That rope is a snare—cast to lure you to your death. He knows our hearts, our desires. You love climbing—so he offers you a rope. But how could Gerard get such a thing? How could he fasten it so high? It defies nature! Holy saints protect us—evil walks abroad tonight!”

“Nonsense,” said Giles, grinning. “The way to hell is down. This rope goes up. And I’ve never had the luck to climb one so long. Might be years before I find another ready-made. Better to die happy than never know joy.” With a joyful leap, he sprang onto the rope like a cat pouncing on a table with fish. His arms swung strong, his legs light as feathers, and he climbed faster than Gerard had descended.

Kate tied a lantern around his neck. “Light frightens evil spirits,” she murmured.

And so, with the glow of the lantern illuminating his path, Giles became a living torch, ascending the night air like a firefly made flesh.

Kate watched, trembling. Then, suddenly, a woman burst forth from the very wall itself—flying toward her with speed beyond mortal limits.

Kate gasped, unable to speak. Her tongue felt glued to her palate. She dropped her crutches and sank to her knees, covering her face. “Take my body,” she moaned, “but spare my soul!”

Then came a voice—panting, astonished—“Why, it’s a woman!”

Kate looked up, shaking. “It’s a woman!”

Margaret laughed weakly. “You scared me half to death!”

“I’m scared enough myself,” Kate sobbed. “Oh, oh, oh!”

“This is strange,” Margaret said. “But the fiery-headed thing—where is it?”

“It was with you,” Kate replied, “and yet you’re harmless. Why are you here?”

“And why are you?” asked Margaret.

“Perhaps we’re both seeking the same thing?” she smiled. “Ah—your brother’s sister, Kate!”

“And you’re Margaret Brandt.”

“Yes.”

“Then all the better. You love him. You’re here. So Giles was right—Gerard is free.”

Gerard stepped forward, confirming it.

But before any words could follow, a terrible sound tore through the silence—a voice from the grave, echoing like a tomb come alive: “PARCHMENT!—PARCHMENT!—PARCHMENT!”

With each repetition, the cry grew louder, more unearthly.

They looked up—and there was Giles, hands full of scrolls, face lit with a diabolical glee. The lantern at his neck turned him into a glowing demon, his features twisted in infernal triumph.

At the word, he hurled the parchments downward. They fell like wounded birds—some tumbling, others fluttering, spinning slowly through the air, drifting to earth in silent circles.

Before they landed, the sepulchral roar echoed again: “Parchment! Parchment!”

Another shower rained down. Then another. Soon the grass was blanketed in white.

Finally, the fire-headed figure slid down the rope like a falling star, landing with a thud. Without a word, it turned to Gerard and said, business-like: “We should settle payment for these documents. Right away.”

“Hush,” Gerard said sharply. “You speak too loudly. Gather them up. We must go somewhere safer.”

“Will you come home with me, Gerard?” little Kate asked softly.

“I have no home,” he replied.

“You shall not say that,” she insisted. “After all this wrong, you’ll be welcome at my father’s house.”

“Father?” Gerard said, voice hardening. “I have no father. He who was my father is now my jailer. I escaped his grasp. I will never return under his roof.”

“It wasn’t your father,” Kate said gently. “It was an enemy. I overheard Cornelis and Sybrandt plotting—”

But Gerard would not be comforted. “Cornelis and Sybrandt have shown me their teeth long enough. But they could do nothing without authority. My father gave it. He gave the burgomaster power to touch me—though I am a free citizen of Tergou. So let it be. I was his son. Now I am his prisoner. He has played his part. I shall play mine. Farewell, Tergou. I was born here. I lived honestly. I was imprisoned. While there is another town in the world, I will never set foot here again.”

“Oh, Gerard!” Kate whispered.

Margaret leaned close. “Do not oppose him now. Let his anger cool.”

Kate turned quickly. “May I look at your face?”

She studied Margaret closely—and nodded. “It is a fair face. Not one of ill intent.”

“Fear me not,” Margaret said softly. “I cannot be happy without your love—as well as Gerard’s.”

Kate wept. “These words bring comfort. I never dreamed I’d come to love you so. My heart is willing—but my body cannot embrace.”

Without hesitation, Margaret moved gently around her and kissed her tenderly.

“Often he spoke of you,” she said. “Often I longed for this.”

“You too, Gerard,” Kate whispered. “Kiss me before you leave. My heart weighs heavy at parting.”

Gerard kissed her, and she limped away on her crutches, the last sound they heard a quiet, patient sigh.

Tears filled Margaret’s eyes, but Gerard saw nothing. He was already turning toward Sevenbergen.

As they walked, Giles nudged Gerard with his bundle of parchments and held out a crooked hand.

Margaret shook her head. “Why take what isn’t ours?”

“Spoil an enemy however you can,” Gerard said.

“But they might use this as an excuse for more violence.”

“How?” Gerard replied. “Think you I’ll stay in Tergou after this? The burgomaster stole my freedom. If I could, I’d take his life for it. But I can’t—so I take what comes to hand.”

He handed Giles a few coins. The boy cheered and shuffled after Kate.

Soon Martin joined them, and together they walked into the night, leaving behind the haunted tower, the ghosts, and the city that had betrayed them.

Ghysbrecht Van Swieten carried the key to Gerard’s prison in his pouch. He waited until ten o’clock before making his visit, muttering to himself, “A little hunger does no harm—it breaks their spirit.” At precisely ten, he crept up the stairs with a loaf and a pitcher, followed by his loyal servant, well armed and silent. Ghysbrecht paused at the door and listened. Not a sound came from within. A cold smile curled his lips. “By now, he must be as broken as Albert Koestein was,” he thought.

He turned the key and pushed the door open.

No Gerard.

Ghysbrecht froze. Though his face was hidden, his body stiffened in a way that spoke of shock—then, slowly, he sank forward, trembling so violently that the servant behind him sensed something was dreadfully wrong. He crept closer, peering over his master’s shoulder.

The cell was empty. The iron bar lay on the floor. And there, hanging loosely from the ceiling, was the rope.

The servant gasped. “Master! What in heaven’s name—?”

But Ghysbrecht ignored him. Instead, he dropped to his knees before the wooden chest that had held the town records, his hands flying over its surface as if he could not believe what he saw. His fingers trembled, probing every seam, every corner, as though afraid his eyes deceived him.

The servant stared, bewildered. “Master, what is it? Why do you stare into that empty box? The boy isn’t here. See—look at this! He pulled out the bar and—”

“GONE! GONE! GONE!” Ghysbrecht shrieked, his voice cracking with panic.

“Gone? What is gone, Holy saints?” the servant cried. “You’re struck mad!”

“STOP THIEF!” roared Ghysbrecht, whirling around and seizing his servant by the collar. “Do you stand there like a fool while your master is robbed? Run! Fly! I’ll give a hundred crowns to whoever brings me back what’s missing!”

He released the man, then fell back against the chest, his strength failing him. “Oh, fool! Fool! To leave it in the same room with him! But none ever found the secret spring before… only he could. It was meant to be. It is meant to be. Lost! Lost!”

His voice trailed off into a whisper, worn down by age and despair. He slumped onto the chest, muttering over and over: “Lost… lost…”

“What is lost, master?” the servant asked gently.

“House… lands… good name…” Ghysbrecht groaned, wringing his hands. “All gone.”

“WHAT?” the servant exclaimed, his voice sharp with sudden interest.

That word—sharp, urgent—struck Ghysbrecht like a spark. He straightened slightly, his cunning returning. “I’ve lost the town records,” he stammered, glancing sideways at his servant like a fox caught near a henhouse.

“Oh, is that all?” the servant said, relieved.

“Is it not enough? What will the burghers say? What will the burgomaster do?” Ghysbrecht snapped, then suddenly raised his voice again. “A hundred crowns to whoever recovers them—every single one! If even one is missing, I give nothing!”

“It’s a bargain, master,” the servant replied, already pulling a purse from his belt. “The hundred crowns are in my pouch. See—you know where Gerard Eliassoen is, and there, I warrant, are those sheepskins you value so highly.”

“That’s true,” Ghysbrecht nodded, catching the drift. “That’s true, good Dierich—faithful Dierich. Every last piece, mind you. All.”

“Master,” Dierich said, “I’ll take the constables to Gerard’s house and arrest him for theft.”

“Theft? Yes, yes—good idea. Very good. It *is* theft. I forgot. So now that he’s a thief, we’ll throw him into the dungeons below—the ones with the toads and rats. Dierich, that boy must never see daylight again. It’s his own fault—he meddled where he shouldn’t. Quick, quick! Before he has time to talk, you understand—time to talk!”

Within half an hour, Dierich Brower and four constables burst into the hosier’s house, demanding young Gerard from the terrified Catherine.

“Alas! What has he done now?” she sobbed. “That boy will break my heart.”

“Nay, dame,” Dierich said smoothly, “only a prank of youth. He’s taken some parchment skins, likely in jest. But the burgomaster is responsible for their safety, so he’s worried. As for the boy, he’ll probably get off with a scolding.”

Catherine believed him instantly. But her daughter, Kate, watched with narrowed eyes. Her suspicion deepened when Dierich’s face darkened at the news that Gerard was not home—not even the night before.

“Come along then,” he growled. “We’re wasting time.”

He added fiercely, “I’ll find him if he’s above ground.”

Affection sharpens perception—and sometimes turns the innocent into the most shrewd opponent. As Dierich stepped toward the door, Kate gave him a signal. He paused, motioning his men onward, and waited outside.

She joined him. “Hush,” she whispered. “Mother doesn’t know. Gerard has left Tergou.”

“How?” Dierich demanded.

“I saw him last night.”

“Where?” he pressed.

“At the foot of the haunted tower.”

“How did he get the rope?”

“I don’t know. But I know this—my brother bade me farewell there. He’s many leagues away by now. You know the town never deserved him. When they imprisoned him, he swore never to return. Let the burgomaster be satisfied. He has jailed him, driven him from his birthplace, from his homeland. What need now to ruin us and rob us of our honor?”

At another time, such words might have made sense. But Dierich was too humiliated by Gerard’s escape and the loss of his reward.

“What need had he to steal?” he retorted bitterly.

“Gerard didn’t steal,” Kate said calmly. “He took them to spite the burgomaster who stole his freedom. But he’ll answer to the Duke for it—he shall. As for those parchments you care so much about, look in the nearest brook or pigsty. You’ll likely find them there.”

“Think you so, mistress?” Dierich hissed, eyes flashing. “Think you so? Perhaps you know it’s true.”

“This I know,” Kate said quietly, “that Gerard is too noble to steal, and too wise to burden himself with rubbish on a journey.”

“Then good day to you,” Dierich snapped, turning sharply. “The sheepskin you despise, I value more than any skin in Tergou.”

And with that, he stormed off—pursuing a false trail.

Kate returned inside and pulled Giles aside.

“Giles,” she whispered, “my heart misgives me. Do not tell a soul what I say. I told Dierich Gerard is beyond Holland—but I fear he’s not a league from Tergou.”

“Where is he, then?” Giles asked.

“Where should he be but with the woman he loves? But if so, he must not linger. These are deep, dark, wicked men hunting him. Giles—I see it in Dierch’s eye. It makes me tremble. Oh, why can’t I fly to Sevenbergen and warn him? Why am I not strong and swift like other girls? God forgive me for fretting at His will—but never have I known what it means to be weak, lame, useless. But you—you are strong, dear Giles,” she added coaxingly.

“Yes, I am strong,” Perpusillus thundered. Then, catching her meaning, he sulked, “but I hate walking.”

“Alas, alas! Who will help me if you won’t?” she pleaded. “Dear Giles, do you not love Gerard?”

“Yes,” he said gruffly, “he’s the best of the lot. I’ll go to Sevenbergen on Peter Buyskens’ mule. Ask him—he won’t lend her to me.”

Kate protested. The whole town would follow. Everyone would know where he was going—and Gerard would be in greater danger than before.

Giles countered: “I’ll ride out the opposite way. I won’t turn the mule toward Sevenbergen until I’ve shaken the curious.”

Satisfied, Kate agreed. She borrowed the mule and gave Giles a short, urgent message. She made him repeat it over and over until he could recite it perfectly.

Giles set off on the mule, his face grim. Kate stood at the window, watching him disappear into the distance. Then, alone, she knelt on the floor and prayed—long, earnestly—for her brother’s safety.

Gerard and Margaret rode to Sevenbergen with light hearts, the fresh air of freedom filling their lungs after their narrow escape. The joy of liberty, however, soon gave way to heavier thoughts. Gerard was still a fugitive—a man hunted by law and vengeance—and though they had fled together, they could not stay together. He must leave, at least for a time, if he were to avoid capture and the gallows.

Margaret’s heart sank at the thought of parting. She longed for him to remain close, safe beside her in the quiet village where no one knew his name or crime. Yet when she heard of Italy—of the cities where artists were honored, where skill was rewarded—she felt a strange hope stir within her. Gerard spoke of it as destiny: that there, he would earn wealth and standing, and finally win the right to marry her without shame or fear.

He had told her everything—the words the demoiselle Van Eyck had whispered to him, how the gold coins were meant only for a journey across the sea. “It is not just my fate,” he said, “but ours. In Italy, I shall be seen for what I am—a craftsman, an artist.” And so, though her eyes filled with tears, she nodded. It was not for herself she consented, but for him—for the future he might build beyond this backward land.

They sat together through the long evening, hands clasped, speaking in hushed tones. At times they dreamed aloud of Venice, Florence, Rome—cities of marble and music, where men like Gerard would be celebrated. Then, without warning, Margaret would weep, and Gerard, young and tender-hearted as she, would fall silent, his voice breaking into sobs. They asked each other again and again: *What have we done? Why does every soul seem set against us?*

Night deepened, but neither could bring themselves to speak of departure. Time stretched on, soft and cruel. Perhaps they would never part—had it not been for Giles.

At about three in the afternoon, he arrived, riding hard from afar, his face grim, his breath ragged. He had taken a wide path to avoid detection. As soon as he saw them, he leapt from his horse and shouted, “Brother Gerard! Kate sends word—run for your life! They accuse you of theft. You’ve given them cause. Do not try to explain. Justice is not found in Tergou. Those parchments you took—they are merely a cover. But she has seen death in their eyes. A price is on your head. Fly! For Margaret’s sake, for all who love you—do not delay!”

The words struck like lightning. Gerard and Margaret stared at each other, pale and stunned. Then Giles, who until now had spoken only what Catherine had commanded, added quietly, “All the constables came to our house looking for you. So did Dirk Brower. Kate knows these men. Listen to her counsel, Gerard. Fly.”

“Oh, yes!” Margaret cried, clutching at his sleeve. “Go now—this very instant! Oh, those parchments—why did I let you take them? My mind warned me!”

“Hush,” Gerard said, though his own voice trembled. “They’re only a blind. Giles says so. Still—I will not leave before I hide what belongs to no one but the earth. That old villain shall never see them again.”

With a final thanks to Giles, he bade him farewell. “Tell Kate I’m gone,” he said. “I’ll be far away before you reach home.” Then he called for Martin.

Martin came quickly, bow in hand. Gerard told him of the danger, and begged him to go toward Tergou and watch the road. “If you see Dirk Brower or any of his men,” he said, “shoot an arrow into the oak tree in our garden. That will be the signal. Then I’ll run into the forest and meet you at the weird hunter’s spring. You’ll guide me through.”

Martin nodded. “Aye,” he said. “And if I hear footsteps, I’ll make sure you know.”

Relieved by this plan, Gerard turned to Margaret. While she stood trembling by the window, watching the oak tree, fearing every rustle of wind or leaf, he dug a deep hole behind the cottage. One by one, he placed the parchments inside—ancient charters, records of the burgh, deeds of land. Among them lay a private contract between Floris Brandt, father of Peter, and Ghysbrecht.

“This is yours as much as his,” Gerard murmured. “Let me read it.”

“No!” Margaret gasped. “Not now! Every second you waste fills me with dread. Look—raindrops already fall. The sky darkens.”

He obeyed, but slipped the deed into his chest, beneath his shirt. Then he covered the hole with dirt and stamped it down firmly.

As he worked, a flash lit the heavens, followed by a distant rumble of thunder. Moments later, rain fell in sheets.

They ran inside, followed by Martin. “The road is clear,” he reported. “And a storm is coming.”

True enough, the thunder grew louder, crashing overhead. Lightning split the sky like a whip, and the rain poured down in torrents. Margaret buried her face in her hands, unable to bear the sight. Gerard shut the rough shutter and lit a candle.

Together, they sat in silence, holding each other’s hands. The storm gave them a few more hours—precious, stolen moments. The sun set unnoticed. Thunder rolled on. Rain lashed the roof. Supper was brought, but neither touched it. The thought that this might be their last meal together choked their throats.

The storm eased slightly. Peter went to bed. But Gerard would leave at dawn. Neither dared sleep.

Martin stayed a while, carefully fitting a new string to his bow—a task he performed with great care. Beside him, the lovers whispered their griefs and their love.

Suddenly, Martin raised a hand. “Be still,” he hissed.

They listened. Nothing.

Then—faintly—a footstep cracked the dry leaves in the garden behind the house. Soft, deliberate. Trying to be silent.

To anyone unafraid, it meant nothing. To them, it was a blade at the throat.

Martin nocked an arrow. With a swift motion, he blew out the candle.

At once, another sound—more than one step—crept near the front door. Not quite silent, but cautious, creeping forward. Then—stillness.

Their blood turned cold.

“Oh, Kate! Oh, Kate!” Margaret sobbed. “You told him to flee instantly. Why did I hold him back? Why did I let him stay?”

“Hush, girl,” Martin whispered, fierce and low.

Then—a heavy knock.

On the door.

And on the hearts within.

The back door burst open with a violent crash, as if summoned by some hidden signal. The house was suddenly surrounded—trapped. In that moment of shock, Margaret found a flicker of composure. She whispered urgently, “Say he was here—but is gone.” Then, gripping Gerard’s arm, she nearly dragged him up the rough wooden steps leading to her father’s bedroom. Her own room lay just beyond.

Outside, the pounding on the door echoed again.
“Who knocks at this hour?” Martin called out, his voice steady despite the fear gnawing at his gut.
“Open, and you will see!” came the reply.
“I open not to thieves,” Martin answered. “Honest men are all abed now.”
“Open to the law, Martin Wittenhaagen, or you shall rue it!”

“That’s Dirk Brower’s voice,” Martin muttered under his breath. “What brings him so far from Tergou?”

“Open, and you will know!”

Slowly, deliberately, Martin drew the bolt. The door swung inward, and Dierich Brower stepped through, followed by four others. One man lingered behind at the back door, waiting for the signal.

“Now, Martin,” Dierich demanded, “where is Gerard Eliassoen?”

Gerard Eliassoen? Why, he was here but now!” Martin replied, feigning surprise.

“Was here?” Dierich’s face darkened. “And where is he now?”

“They say he has gone to Italy,” Martin said, shrugging. “Why, what is to do?”

“No matter,” Dierich growled. “When did he go? Tell me not that he left in such a storm as this!”

“There’s a coil about Gerard Eliassoen,” Martin remarked, dismissive and calm. He lit the candle and sat himself by the fire, coolly winding fine silk around his bowstring—the spot where the arrow’s nick wore it thin.

“I’ll tell you,” he continued, voice light. “You know his brother Giles? A little misbegotten imp, all head and arms? Well, he came galloping over on Peter Buyskens’s mule, bellowing something—I was too far off to hear the words, only the noise. Anyway, he startled Gerard. As soon as he was gone, there was crying and kissing, and then Gerard vanished. They say he’s gone to Italy—mayhap you know where that is, for I don’t.”

Dierich’s expression sank further still. There was no flaw in the tale. A cleverer man might have woven too many lies and raised suspicion. But Martin had done exactly what he was told—told one falsehood, and nothing more. He had not invented a single word beyond necessity.

“Mates,” Dierich said, turning to his companions, “I doubt he speaks truth. I told the burgomaster how it would be. He met the dwarf galloping Peter Buyskens’s mule from Sevenbergen. ‘They’ve sent that imp to Gerard,’ he said. ‘Then Gerard must be at Sevenbergen.’”

“Ah, master!” Dierich continued, addressing himself now to the air, “It’s too late now. We should have thought of Sevenbergen before, instead of wasting our time hunting every corner of Tergou for those cursed parchments we’ll never find until we find the man who took them. If he was at Sevenbergen—and they sent the dwarf to warn him—we’re too late. He’s leagues away by now.”

He spat. “Confound that chalk-faced girl! She’s outwitted us bearded men. I told the burgomaster, but he wouldn’t listen. A wet jerkin apiece—that’s all we’ll get from this job.”

Martin grinned faintly, watching Dierich closely.

“However,” Dierich added, “to satisfy the burgomaster, we’ll search the house.”

At once, Martin’s face turned grave. The change did not escape Dierich. He paused, then said: “Two of you watch outside—one on each side of the house. No one must leap from the upper windows. The rest come with me.” He took the candle and climbed the stairs, followed by three of his men.

Martin was left alone.

He hung his head. Everything had gone so well at first. And now—this fatal turn. But then, like a spark in darkness, an idea flared. Gerard must be either in Peter’s room or Margaret’s—both low enough to jump from. If Gerard tried to escape, he’d leap out. Dierich had left a guard below—but what then? For half a minute, Gerard and he would be two against one. In that brief span, anything could happen.

Martin slipped the back door open slightly and waited, eyes fixed on the dim light spilling into Peter’s room.

“Curse the fool,” he muttered, “is he going to let them take him like a girl?”

The light moved into Margaret’s room. Still—no window opened. Had Gerard planned to flee, he would not have waited until the men were inside. Martin saw that instantly. He left the door and crept to the foot of the stairs, listening.

He began to think Gerard had escaped while the men were searching. The longer the silence lasted, the stronger the belief grew. But then—suddenly, rudely—it shattered.

Faint cries came from the inner chamber—Margaret’s room.

“They’ve taken him,” Martin groaned. “They’ve got him.”

A new terror seized him. If Gerard were taken, his life would be forfeit. And if harm came to Gerard, Margaret’s heart would break. He looked wildly around, like a beast cornered and desperate. In a flash, he made a decision—terribly fitting for the iron age and the soldier driven to the edge.

He stepped to each door in turn, mimicking Dierich’s voice sharply: “Watch the window!”

Then he quietly closed and bolted both doors. He picked up his bow and six arrows—fitted one to the string, stowed the rest in his quiver. His knife he placed on a chair behind him, hilt toward him.

There he stood, at the foot of the stairs, ready. Calm. Resolute. Determined to kill these four men—or die trying.

Two he could dispatch with arrows before they reached him. Then, Gerard and he would fight hand-to-hand with the remaining pair. He had seen men freeze in panic when attacked suddenly. If Dierich and his men hesitated even a second, he could shoot three instead of two—and then the odds would shift.

He did not wait long. Heavy footsteps echoed in Margaret’s room, drawing closer. The candlelight approached. Voices rose.

Martin’s heart pounded—not from fear, but from the weight of what was coming. Men walking into death, perhaps into his own. Four against two, in a space no larger than ten feet square. Gerard might be bound—helpless. Yet this man, who once trembled at the sight of a Giles-o’-lanthorn, did not falter now. He stood braced, body tensed, eyes blazing—ready to give life or take it.

Desperate stakes. To win meant exile—for life. To lose meant death, right there on that floor.

Dierich and his men found Peter asleep in his bed. They ransacked his cupboards, slashed their knives through the stuffed alligator nailed to the wall, searched beneath the bed. The room was large, full of hiding places—yet no sign of Gerard.

Then they moved to Margaret’s room.

Even at first glance, it discouraged them. Small, bare, without a cupboard. Only a large fireplace and chimney. Dierich’s eye fell upon them immediately.

There, on a chest barely a foot high, lay the beauty of Sevenbergen—sleeping, uncovered, wrapped only in snowy white sheets. Her linen was pure as snow. She looked like a lily fallen into a mud puddle.

She stirred, sat up, wide-eyed with shock. Seeing the men, she began to cry softly, pleading for mercy.

Her voice pierced Dierich’s pride.

“This is a to-do,” he muttered, uneasy. “We’re not going to hurt you, my pretty maid. Lie still. Shut your eyes. Think of your wedding night, while I look up this chimney to see if Master Gerard is hiding there.”

“Gerard—in my room?” she gasped.

“Why not?” Dierich pressed. “They say you and he—”

“Cruel!” she cried. “You know they’ve driven him away from me—driven him from his home! This is a lie! You are thieves! Wicked men! You are not of Sevenbergen, or you would know Margaret Brandt better than to search for her lover in this room—of all rooms in the world! Oh, brave! Four great hulking men, armed to the teeth, to insult one poor honest girl! The women in your own homes must be naught, or you would respect them enough to spare a girl of good character!”

“There!” Dierich snapped, turning abruptly. “Come away, before we hear worse.”

He didn’t look up the chimney. “He’s not there. Plaster can mend what a cudgel breaks—but a woman’s tongue is a double-edged dagger. And a girl is a woman with her mother’s milk still in her.”

He backed out quickly. “I told the burgomaster how it would be.”

Where is the woman who cannot play a part when love demands it? Where is she who will not rise to the occasion, and act with grace and courage, to save the man she holds most dear? In moments like these, even the simplest of women find strength within them—nature itself steps in to teach her how to deceive even the wisest of men.

No sooner had the men left the room than Margaret slipped from her bed, still clad in her skirt, petticoat, stockings, and nightdress. She moved silently to the long chest where she had lain, lifted its lid—along with the blankets and coverings—and set it against the wall. Then, on silent feet, she glided to the door and listened. The footsteps faded through her father’s chamber and down the stairs. All was quiet.

But this chest held a secret known only to her and Gerard. A section of the floorboard had once been broken, and when Gerard was called upon to repair it, he lacked materials. So he cleverly cut away a portion just large enough to fit the chest beneath the boards, using the wood to mend the rest of the floor. As a result, the chest rested on the rafters a full foot below the surface, making it twice as deep as it appeared.

Margaret knelt, her heart pounding, and gave thanks to Heaven. Then she crept back to the chest, leaned over it, and whispered softly, “Gerard!”

No answer.

She spoke again, a little louder: “Gerard, it’s safe—thank God! You may come up now—but be careful!”

Still no reply.

Her hand trembled as she placed it on his shoulder. “Gerard!”

Nothing.

“Oh, what has happened?” she cried, her voice breaking. Her hands flew over his face, his chest, searching for breath, for life. She gripped his shoulders, shook him, lifted him—but he slipped from her grasp like a weightless thing, falling back without resistance, as though he were no longer flesh and blood.

A cold dread seized her. The lid had been closed. She had lain upon it. The men had been in the room for some time. With a strength born of desperation, she tore him from the chest, cradling him in her arms. She carried him to the window, flung it open wide, and laid him out into the cool night air. Moonlight bathed his pale form. His face was gray as ash. His body limp. Lifeless.

She pressed her fingers to his heart. It did not beat. Not a flicker. Horror struck her like lightning. He was dead. She had suffocated him with her own weight.

The mind cannot instantly accept such a horror—so sudden, so terrible. Just minutes ago, Gerard had been alive, hidden beneath her. How could he now be gone?

She called to him, pleading with every name of love she could summon—names never spoken before, too tender for words. She kissed his lips, stroked his hair, begged him to speak, to look at her, to show that he still lived. But there was no response. No sign. Only silence.

Then, trembling uncontrollably, she began to whisper to his ashen face—words both foolish and heartbreaking. “Oh, Gerard… I’m so sorry you’re dead. I’m so sorry I killed you. Forgive me for not letting them take you—it would have been better than this. Oh, Gerard… I’m so, so sorry.”

Suddenly, madness took hold. “No! No! This can’t be true—or there is no God! It’s monstrous! How can my Gerard be dead? How could I have killed him? I love him. Oh, God, You know how I love him! He doesn’t know. I never told him. If he knew my heart, he’d speak to me—he wouldn’t stay so deaf to poor Margaret. This must be a trick—to make me scream and betray him. But no—I love him too much for that. I’ll choke first!”

And with that, she clutched her own throat, fighting the urge to cry out in terror and despair. “If only he’d say one word… Oh, Gerard! Don’t die without speaking. Have mercy on me—scold me, curse me, but speak! If you’re angry, scold me! I deserve it—the fool who killed the man she loved more than herself. Ah! I am a murderess—the worst in all the world! Help! Help! I’ve murdered him! Ah! Ah! Ah! Ah! Ah!”

She tore at her hair, shrieking again and again—wild, piercing cries that echoed through the night like a death knell. They reached the ears of Dierich Brower and his men, who sprang to their feet, staring at one another in alarm.

Martin Wittenhaagen stood at the bottom of the stairs, bow drawn to the ear, knife ready in his belt, his face tense with alertness. He was startled when the men returned without Gerard—his eyes widened, his breath caught. He lowered his weapon slowly, staring at them in stunned silence.
