They, in turn, were equally taken aback by the sight of him—armed and poised as if expecting an attack. “Why, mates,” one muttered, “was the old man aiming at us?”

“Nonsense,” Martin replied, regaining his usual stoicism. “I was merely testing my new string. There—let me unstring it, if you like.”

“Hmph,” Dierich grumbled, eyeing him warily. “There’s more going on under that calm face than I can fathom. Light a fire, and let us dry our clothes before we go any further.”

A roaring blaze soon crackled in the hearth. The men gathered close, their damp garments steaming in the warmth, their long hair curling slightly from the heat. Then—suddenly—the sound of piercing shrieks echoed from Margaret’s chamber.

Every man jumped to his feet. One snatched up the candle and bolted up the stairs to the bedrooms. Martin rose swiftly, confusion flashing across his features. Fear gripped him—not just for Margaret, but for what this man might discover. He lunged forward, trying to block the way.

Dierich reacted instantly, wrapping his arms around Martin from behind. “Hold him!” he shouted.

The others surged upon Martin. A fierce struggle erupted—limbs tangled, bodies rolling across the floor, Martin at the center, resisting with all his strength. After minutes of desperate fighting, they overpowered him. With a rope meant for Gerard, they bound him tightly, hands and feet secured.

Martin groaned deeply, his chest heaving. He saw too late that the man had reached Margaret’s room during the fight—and now he was helpless.

“Ah, grind your teeth, old rogue,” Dierich panted, wiping sweat from his brow. “You won’t be using them again.”

“It’s my belief,” another said, breathing hard, “that none of us were safe so long as that old fellow could move.”

“And I’ll wager,” added a third, “that Gerard isn’t far behind.”

“No such luck,” Dierich snapped. “But—listen! Jorian Ketel’s been gone too long. Someone ought to check on him.”

A rough laugh broke out among them, barely fading when heavy footsteps pounded overhead.

“Oh, here he comes at last!” someone called. “Well, Jorian—what’s happening up there?”

Jorian Ketel hurried straight to Margaret’s chamber, his heart pounding with urgency. What he found there froze him in place—his breath caught, his candle trembling in his hand. There, pale as death and utterly still, lay the man he had been searching for, his head cradled in Margaret’s lap. She knelt beside him, motionless, her eyes wide yet blank, unseeing and unmoved by anything but the lifeless face she held so close. Her whole being seemed turned to stone, consumed by grief.

Jorian stood stunned. “Where was he all this time?” he murmured, but she did not hear. He stepped forward, his gaze falling on the empty chest—then it struck him. The truth unfolded slowly, like a terrible revelation. The girl’s silence, her stillness—it was agony made visible. A deep pity stirred within him.

“This is a sorry sight,” he said softly. “A black night’s work—all for a few furs! He should have come with us. But now…” He paused, then added, “She won’t answer me. Poor wench.” He hesitated, then reached for a small round mirror, no larger than his palm. Carefully, he placed it near Gerard’s mouth and nostrils, holding it steady. When he pulled it away, the glass was dimmed—not from dust, but from breath.

“There is life in him!” Jorian whispered to himself.

The words—though barely spoken—reached Margaret like thunder. Her body jerked, her eyes snapped open, and in an instant, she rose, flung her arms around Jorian’s neck, and clung to him with desperate strength. “Oh, bless the tongue that tells me so!” she gasped, squeezing him again and again, her voice raw with emotion.

“Now, now,” Jorian said gently, pushing her back. “Let us warm him. Come—lay him down.” Together, they lifted Gerard and settled him upon the bedclothes. Then Jorian drew out a flask from his belt, poured two full handfuls of Schiedamze—the sharp, fiery spirit—and dashed it sharply into Gerard’s face. The strong liquor stung the air, and though at first nothing stirred, then—faintly—a sigh escaped the young man’s lips.

That sound—so soft, so fragile—rang like music in the quiet room. Margaret leapt toward him, but stopped herself, trembling, afraid to touch him, afraid she might undo what had just begun.

“That’s right,” Jorian said firmly. “Leave him be. Don’t smother him like you did me. Let him rest. He’ll come around. He’s not an old man.”

Gerard sighed again, deeper this time. A faint blush crept across his lips. Jorian turned to leave, but before he could reach the door, he felt hands grip his legs. It was Margaret—kneeling, clinging to him like a serpent coiled about a tree.

“You won’t tell,” she pleaded, pressing her face against his hand. “You saved his life. You can’t take it back now. You wouldn’t destroy your own good deed?”

“No, no,” Jorian said, shaking his head. “I’ve done you both kindness before. I told you where to go in the church. And Dierich Brower? What does he matter to me? I’d see him hanged before I’d speak a word. But—” He paused, eyes narrowing. “Tell me—where are the parchments? A hundred crowns are offered for them. That would help my Joan and the children.”

Margaret looked up, her eyes brightening. “They shall have those hundred crowns.”

“What? Are they in the house?” Jorian asked, eager.

“No,” she replied. “But I know where they are. By God and St. Bavon, I swear you shall have them tomorrow. Come when you wish—but come alone.”

“Good,” said Jorian. “And I swear I’ll keep this secret. May my bones rot if I betray the boy.” He turned and slipped away quickly, knowing that lingering too long might draw suspicion.

Left behind, Margaret knelt beside Gerard, her body quivering with prayer and relief. She whispered words to God, begging for strength, for mercy, for life—for her beloved.

Later, when Dierich Brower asked what had happened, Jorian shrugged. “We frightened the girl half out of her mind. She had some sort of fit.”

“We should send someone to treat her,” suggested another.

“Oh, yes,” Jorian said lightly. “And scare her into the churchyard. Her father’s a doctor—I’ve already sent for him. Let’s look at the fire instead.”

His casual tone put everyone at ease. Soon enough, the group agreed that the kitchen of the “Three Kings” was warmer than Peter’s house, and they left—after freeing Martin, who had been tied up.

At the door, Dierich muttered, “See, mate? I told you we’d be too late. And we were.”

So, in one terrible night, Gerard had brushed both prison and death. Yet he escaped—not through clever hiding or quick wit, but because of a sudden spark of compassion in the heart of one of his captors. Jorian Ketel, reckless and hardened, had shown mercy—not from duty, nor from love, but from a mix of pity and greed. Such are human motives: tangled, unpredictable, often contradictory. Our best-laid plans fail; our most careful schemes collapse under the weight of chance and feeling.

Those who live sheltered lives, untouched by great joy or great sorrow, may be the wisest and happiest. But to such readers, I cannot convey what filled Margaret and Gerard in that hour. Even to those who have known deep joy and deep pain, my words fall short.

To sit and watch a loved face return from death’s edge—to see color return to the cheeks, warmth to the eyes, voice to the lips—that was Margaret’s bliss. To awaken from darkness and find oneself cradled in the arms of the one he adored, hearing her whisper sweet words, feeling her tears and kisses—this was Gerard’s miracle.

He had never truly understood how deeply she loved him—until now. He thanked his enemies, for their cruelty had brought him to this moment.

They clasped each other tightly, their arms wrapped like vines. Trouble, danger—these were forgotten, far behind them. They called each other husband and wife. Was it not true? Had they not stood together before the altar? Had not the Church blessed their union and cursed any who would tear them apart?

Yet even innocence has its perils. No longer threatened by prison or death, they now faced a greater danger: their own hearts. Their love, once tempered by fear, now burned too brightly. They were young, inexperienced, and now—safe—too easily carried away.

Tomorrow, they must part. But that mattered little now. They had seen death, and lived. All else seemed light as air. While there is life, there is hope; while there is hope, there is joy.

The future shone bright, the present was paradise. Hours passed like dreams, sweet and golden. Alas, their innocence still wandered into peril—not from men or laws, but from the very depths of their own souls.

Ghysbrecht Van Swieten lay awake all night, consumed by unease. The storm raged outside, and though he feared thunder and lightning more than any man in Sevenbergen, he would have joined the search party had it not been for his dread of the sky’s fury. But when the tempest finally quieted, he rose without delay, slipped down the stairs, saddled his mule, and rode swiftly to the “Three Kings” inn.

There, he found his men sprawled in exhaustion—some slumped over chairs, others curled on tables, a few lying flat on the floor. He stormed into their midst, shaking them awake with sharp commands. They muttered apologies and recounted their fruitless efforts, praising themselves loudly for their diligence.

“Fools!” Ghysbrecht bellowed. “To let you go without me! I swear my life that he was there all along. Did you look under the girl’s bed?”

“No,” one replied. “There wasn’t room for a man.”

“How do you know?” Ghysbrecht snapped. “If you didn’t look, how could you be certain? You should have searched every inch—under the bed, inside it, tested each panel with your knives. Come now—up with you! I’ll show you how to hunt properly.”

Dierich Brower stirred slowly, rubbing his eyes. “If you find him,” he grumbled, “then call me a horse and not a man.”

Within moments, Peter’s house was encircled once more. Ghysbrecht left his mule with Jorian Ketel and, flanked by Dierich and the others, entered the dwelling. It was silent, empty—no sign of life, not even Peter himself. They climbed the stairs, scanning each corner, until suddenly one of the men gasped and pointed through Peter’s open window.

The others turned—and there, just beyond the fields, walking calmly side by side with Margaret and Martin, stood the fugitive they had sought.

Ghysbrecht roared with triumph, darting down the stairs and leaping onto his mule. With a cry, he spurred forward, and the entire party gave chase across the open land.

Gerard, shaken by the peril of the night before, rose before dawn and awoke Martin. The old soldier stirred with surprise—hadn’t he thought Gerard had slipped away through the window? When asked how best to flee the country and escape capture, Martin offered only one safe route. “I’ll guide you through the great forest to a bridle-path I know,” he said. “It will lead you quickly to an inn where they’ll lend you a swift horse. Then a single day’s ride will carry you beyond the borders of Holland. But we must go now—before the villagers rise.”

Peter’s house stood just a furlong and a half from the edge of the woods. They set out at once: Martin with his bow and three arrows—Thursday being the day of the week when such arms were lawful—and Gerard with nothing but a sturdy oak staff that Peter had given him for the journey. Margaret gathered up her kirtle and farthingale, for the ground was wet and muddy. Peter walked with them as far as the hedge of his garden, and there, with more emotion than he usually showed in passing moments, he gave the young man his blessing.

The sun crested the horizon as they crossed the stony field toward the forest. Halfway across, Margaret, glancing back nervously, suddenly screamed and broke into a run toward the trees, shrieking all the while. Behind them, Ghysbrecht and his men were closing fast.

Resistance was madness. Martin and Gerard followed Margaret’s lead. The pursuers gained ground, but Martin kept shouting, “Only win the wood! Only win the wood!” Their head start gave them hope—the great trees seemed to stretch their branches like welcoming arms, their leaves forming a sheltering screen.

But a new danger emerged. The fiery burgomaster flung himself onto his mule, spurred it into a gallop, and charged not only his own men but the fugitives directly. His aim was to cut them off. He rode in a wide arc and reached the edge of the wood just ahead of Gerard. The others could escape—he cared not.

Margaret screamed and clutched at Gerard in terror, but he shook her off without hesitation. In his fury, Ghysbrecht forgot that hunted beasts sometimes turn on their hunters—and two men, driven by hatred, can each desire death for the same enemy.

Instead of dodging, as the burgomaster expected, Gerard lunged forward with a wild cry, swinging the oak staff with all his strength. It struck Ghysbrecht’s face with a terrible crack. The burgomaster collapsed beneath his mule’s tail, kicking wildly, blood streaming down his face, his collar splattered with gore.

In the next breath, the three were inside the forest. A cry of horror and rage erupted from Ghysbrecht’s men—proof that the fight had just begun.

“Why run?” panted Gerard. “You have your bow, and I have this,” he said, raising the bloody staff.

“Boy!” roared Martin. “The gallows! Follow me!”

They fled deeper into the woods. Soon came the sound of baying—a pack of hounds unleashed upon their trail. The pursuers had entered the forest and saw the fugitives darting between the trees.

Margaret gasped and stumbled. Gerard clenched his teeth, gripping his staff tightly. Moments later, they reached a thick hazel coppice. Martin plunged into it, pushing aside the young saplings as if they were wheat. Within fifty yards, they found four blind paths. Martin chose one.

“Bend low,” he ordered.

They crept forward, half-crawling, sliding along the narrow trails. Soon, another tangle of winding paths crossed theirs. They took one. It seemed to loop back—but then turned, leading them into a dense pine grove where the ground was firm and hard beneath their feet.

Here, no paths existed. Young fir trees grew so closely together that visibility was limited to mere yards. After walking some distance, Martin sat down. Having long since learned to dismiss danger once it passed, he pulled bread and ham from his wallet and began eating calmly.

The younger pair stared at him in disbelief.

“What?” he said, seeing their expressions. “All Sevenbergen couldn’t find you here. You’ll lose your purse, Gerard, long before Italy. Is that how you carry treasure?”

Gerard looked down—and there, caught in the chain of his wallet buckle, was a large triangular purse. “This isn’t mine,” he said. “What could be in it?”

He tried to free it, but the passage through the coppice had tangled it irreparably. “It seems unwilling to leave,” he muttered, finally cutting it loose with his knife.

Inside, the purse held silver coins of every size—but its bulk came mostly from folded brown paper. A sudden understanding lit Gerard’s eyes.

“Ah! It must be that old thief’s purse—and stuffed with paper to fool people!”

They puzzled over how it came to be on Gerard’s belt. At last, they realized: it had been tied to Ghysbrecht’s saddlebow. As Gerard charged, he had torn it away—killing his foe and stealing his goods in one motion.

Gerard smiled. “A fine feat!” he declared. “Spoil taken in battle from an enemy—lawfully won.”

But Margaret trembled. “Throw it away, Gerard—or give it back to Martin. They already call you a thief. I cannot bear it.”

“Throw it away? Give it back? Not a stiver!” Gerard insisted. “This is plunder won in combat. Isn’t it, Martin?”

“Of course,” Martin replied. “Send him back the paper—that you may. But the purse or the coin? That would be sin.”

“Oh, Gerard,” she whispered, “you are going far. We need Heaven’s favor. How can we hope for grace if we keep what is not ours?”

Gerard saw it differently. “Heaven gives it to me by miracle. I shall cherish it.” He smiled. “Like the Israelites, we took from Egypt and were blessed.”

“Then take your own way,” Margaret murmured. “You are wiser than I. You are my husband… is it for me to argue?”

Her words—so humble, so tender—surprised Martin briefly. Later, he would recall them with less astonishment.

Gerard kissed her gently, grateful for her submission, and they continued hand in hand, Martin leading them deeper into the vast forest. With each step, they felt safer. Few townspeople dared venture so far into the trackless wilderness.

Yet soon, Gerard’s conscience stirred. “Martin,” he said, “I wish I hadn’t struck quite so hard.”

“Whom? Oh, let that pass. He got what he deserved.”

“I saw his grey hairs—when my staff fell. I fear I shall not forget them.”

Martin grunted. “Who spares a badger for grey hairs? The older an enemy, the craftier. And the craftier, the better reason to end him.”

“Killing? Killing, Martin? Don’t speak of it!” Gerard shuddered.

“You’re mistaken if you think you didn’t,” Martin said cheerfully. “Now, Heaven forbid—but the old rogue’s skull cracked like a walnut. Aha!”

“Heaven and the saints forbid!” Gerard cried.

“He rolled off his mule like a stone shot from a cart,” Martin grinned. “I said to myself, ‘One wiped out.’”

Gerard dropped to his knees and began praying for his enemy’s life.

Martin lost patience. “Here’s nonsense! You who claim learning—don’t you know a wise man never strikes unless to kill? And why fuss about killing an old man? If it were a young one—full of wine, women, and plunder—then perhaps. But an old fellow near the grave? Why not push him in? He must go—today or tomorrow. What better fate for a greybeard? If ever I live as long as Ghysbrecht did, and must ride a mule instead of my own legs, with a back like this”—he tapped his bow—“instead of this”—he tapped the string—“I’d thank any young man who knocked me on the head, just as you did that old shopkeeper. Malison on his memory!”

“Oh, culpa mea! Culpa mea!” Gerard cried, smiting his chest.

“Look!” Martin sneered at Margaret. “Still a priest at heart. When he’s not in a rage, he’s St. Paul—what a milksop!”

“Tush, Martin!” Margaret reproached him softly. Then she wrapped her arms around Gerard and comforted him with the quiet wisdom and warmth only a woman could offer.

“Sweetheart,” she murmured, “you did not go out of your way to harm him. He hunted you to death. You fled. He pursued. Then you struck—but only once, in self-defense, with what you had. Malice would have drawn a knife or struck again. Men have been hit many times with staves and lived. If he fell, it was by his own malice, not yours—and by God’s will.”

“Bless you, Margaret,” Gerard breathed. “Bless you for thinking so.”

“Yes, beloved,” she said, “but if you’ve killed that wicked man, we must flee faster. Oh, let us go.”

“No, Margaret,” Gerard replied. “I fear not man’s vengeance—thanks to Martin and these thick woods. But I fear Him whose eye sees through the forest and reads the heart. If I struck only in defense—well. But if in hate—He may send the avenger of blood after me—to Italy, or to the ends of the earth.”

“Hush!” Martin snapped. “I can’t hear for your talk.”

“What is it?” Gerard asked.

“Do you hear nothing, Margaret? My ears grow old.”

She listened—and then heard it: a single, clear tone, deep and resonant, like a bell struck once in the stillness. She told Martin.

“Nay, I heard it,” he said.

“So did I,” Gerard added. “It was beautiful. Ah! There it is again. How sweet it blends with the air. It’s far off. Is it ahead?”

“No, no!” Martin corrected. “The echoes here confuse a stranger. It comes from the pine grove.”

“The one we passed?”

“Of course.”

“Martin, is this nothing?” Gerard asked, noticing the old soldier’s pale face.

“Wonderful,” Martin said, with a sickly sneer. “He asks if it’s anything. Come, on! Let us reach a better place.”

“A better place—for what?”

“To stand at bay, Gerard,” Martin said gravely. “And die like soldiers—killing three for one.”

“What’s that sound?” Gerard asked.

“It is the avenger of blood.”

“Oh, Martin, save him!” Margaret cried. “Oh, Heaven, be merciful! What new peril is this?”

“Girl,” Martin said flatly, “it’s a bloodhound.”

The courage of ordinary men, like their talents, is confined to narrow limits. Push them just an inch beyond that, and they falter. Martin’s courage was unshakable within its bounds. He had faced danger many times in his rough life—dangers he knew well—and met them with a grim resolve, almost without fear. But never before had he been hunted by a bloodhound, nor had he seen such relentless instinct defeated by human wit. Now, the unknown combined with a sense of the uncanny to shake his spirit. After walking only a few steps, he leaned heavily on his bow, and strength and hope drained from him.

Gerard, who saw the peril as distant and therefore less immediate, urged him forward. “What good will it do?” Martin said wearily. “If we escape the wood, we die cheaply. But here, close at hand, I know a place where we may die dearly.”

“Alas, good Martin,” Gerard replied, “do not despair so soon. There must be some way out.”

“Oh, Martin!” Margaret pleaded, her voice trembling. “What if we split up? Only Gerard’s life is forfeit. Can’t we draw the pursuit upon us two and let him go free?”

“Girl,” Martin said harshly, “you don’t understand the nature of a bloodhound. It does not track one man or another—it tracks blood. I swear by my life they’ve led it to where Ghysbrecht fell. From the dead man’s blood, it will follow straight to the man who shed it. That cursed hound will find him, even if Gerard ran through an army or swam the Meuse.”

He sank again upon his bow, head bowed, defeated.

Then came the hound’s deep, resonant bay—a sound more melodious than any horn ever blew in Crete, Sparta, or Thessaly. Yet beauty could be deadly. The boa-constrictor’s eye, lovely though it is, holds a spell over its prey. No crown holds a gem so rich: a ruby glowing with emerald light, ever shifting. And yet the deer who sees it freezes, helpless, awaiting death. So too did this sweet, mellow cry strike Martin—fascinating, paralyzing, draining his will.

Gerard was no better. Martin’s words had struck him hard. He had struck down a man, spilled his blood—and now, through that very blood, the four-footed avenger of justice pursued him. Was this not divine judgment?

While the men faltered, Margaret’s mind raced. Her beloved was in danger. “Give me your knife,” she said to Martin.

He handed it to her. “But what use will it be in your hands?”

She stepped behind Gerard and, swiftly, drew the blade across her arm. Blood welled freely. She stooped, smearing her hose and shoes with it, letting the stream run while she worked—so quietly, so cleverly, that neither man noticed. Then she seized Gerard’s arm.

“Come,” she said firmly, “be a man! Let this end. Take us to a thick place where numbers won’t help our enemies.”

“I’m going,” Martin muttered, sullenly. “Hurry means nothing—we can’t outrun the hound, and the spot is near.” He turned left and led the way, like a man marching to execution.

Soon they reached a dense hazel thicket—just like the one that had sheltered them earlier. “Here,” Martin said, “it’s barely a furlong wide, but it will serve.”

“What are we to do?”

“Get through it, wait on the other side. When they come straggling through, shoot three, knock two down, and the rest will kill us.”

“That’s all you can think of?” Gerard asked.

“That’s all.”

“Then, Martin Wittenhaagen,” Gerard said, “I take the lead. You’ve lost your wits. Come—can you obey a younger man than I?”

“Oh, yes, Martin,” Margaret cried, “don’t defy Gerard! He knows more than his years.”

Martin grumbled but gave in. “Do as I do,” Gerard said, and drawing his great knife, cut low hazel shoots at every step, twisting them upright behind him among the standing branches. Martin followed suit, but with dull resignation.

As they struggled through most of the coppice, the hound’s bay grew closer—less musical, deeper, fiercer. Margaret trembled. Martin dropped to his stomach and listened.

“I hear horse’s hooves.”

“No,” Gerard said. “It’s a mule. That cursed Ghysbrecht is still alive—no other would pursue me so fiercely.”

“Never strike your enemy unless you mean to kill him,” Martin muttered.

“I’ll hit harder this time—if Heaven gives me the chance,” Gerard said.

At last they emerged into open woodland. Trees stood far apart, offering no escape. And now, mingled with the hound’s cry, came a chorus of voices—hooping, shouting.

“The whole village is after us,” Martin said.

“I care not,” Gerard replied. “Listen—Martin, I’ve made the path easy for the dog, but rough for the men. We’ll face them one at a time. The hound will reach us first. As soon as it comes out, we kill it.”

“The hound? There are more than one.”

“I hear only one.”

“Ay,” Martin said, “one barks, the others run silent. But if the lead hound loses the scent, another will give tongue. There will be at least two—perhaps devils in dog-skins.”

“Then we kill two instead of one. The moment they’re dead, back into the coppice and retreat.”

“That’s a good thought, Gerard,” Martin said, lifting his spirits.

“Hush—the men are in the wood.”

Gerard whispered orders. “You, stand by the edge of the coppice, in the ditch—with your bow. I’ll go to that oak tree, hide behind it. The dogs will follow me. As they emerge, shoot as many as you can. The rest I’ll brain when they round the tree.”

Martin’s eyes lit with fire. They took their positions.

The shouts drew nearer. Rustling leaves, snapping twigs. Then, once—twice—the hound gave a single, chilling bay. The moment felt endless. Every breath was a battle. Death approached, heralded by that mournful cry.

A trembling hand touched Gerard’s shoulder. He jumped—tense, coiled like a spring.

“Martin says—if we must part, make for the high ash-tree we came in by.”

“Yes! Yes! But go back—please, for Heaven’s sake—don’t come here, out in the open!”

She turned to run toward Martin—but before she could reach him, a massive hound burst from the thicket, standing tall for a moment. Margaret cowered. But the beast ignored her. To it, scent was sight. It lowered its nose, then—suddenly, with a terrible roar—lunged straight at Gerard’s tree. A moment later, it lay dead, impaled by an arrow that sang from Martin’s bow.

At once, another hound appeared, sniffing the corpse. Gerard charged. But before he could swing his cudgel, a flash of white lightning struck—his own weapon, flung like a dart. The hound collapsed, wounded but not dead, howling in agony.

Gerard had no time to finish it—the coppice rustled violently, alive with movement. He pointed wildly at Martin, signaling to retreat, then darted right, crawling into the thickets just as three men burst out.

These were ahead of the others; the rest followed at intervals. Gerard crept back on all fours. Instinct guided Martin and Margaret to do the same—along their line of flight. Within yards, pursuers and fugitives passed each other, unseen.

A cry rang out—then chaos: voices rising, swelling as more arrived. The hunters, stunned by surprise, wasted precious moments. The hunted used every second.

“I hear no more hounds,” Martin whispered to Margaret, regaining his composure.

Now it was her turn to tremble. “Oh, why did we leave Gerard? They’ll kill him—and I’m not there!”

“Nay, nay!” Martin insisted. “No man among them has the wit to catch him. You told him to meet us at the ash-tree?”

“And so I did. Bless you, Martin, for remembering. To the ash-tree!”

“Ay—but quieter.”

They were nearly at the edge when suddenly—behind them—came hooping and hallooing. The men had confirmed the fugitives were in the coppice and were turning back.

“Doesn’t matter,” Martin whispered, calm again. “We’ll have time to clear it and vanish, running hard. Ah!”

He dropped abruptly. Just as he neared the brushwood’s edge, his eye caught a figure: Ghysbrecht Van Swieten, seated on his mule. A bloody bandage crossed his nose—broken bridge, but his eyes burned with sharp suspicion. He had heard them rustle. He was waiting.

Martin swore under his breath. Slowly, carefully, he strung his bow, fitted the last arrow. Margaret pressed her hands to her face, silent. She knew this man must die—or Gerard would.

The bow rose. The arrow drew taut. At that instant, a swift figure leaped onto Ghysbrecht from behind—like a hawk striking a pigeon. A kerchief flew over the burgomaster’s head. In a flash, his face was muffled, and he was thrown from the mule, crashing to the ground, groaning in terror. Gerard landed beside him.

“Hist, Martin! Martin!” Gerard called.

They emerged—Martin gaping. “Now fly! Fly! While they’re all tangled in the thicket—we’re saved!”

Just as safety seemed within grasp, fate intervened. Margaret, who had held firm until now, began to weaken—her wound bleeding, her strength fading.

“Oh, my beloved,” she gasped, “fly! Leave me—I am faint.”

“No! No!” Gerard shouted. “Death together, or safety. Ah—the mule! Mount her—you, and I’ll run by your side.”

In a heartbeat, Martin was on the mule. Gerard lifted the swooning girl into his arms and placed her on the saddle, taking Martin’s bow.

“Help! Treason! Murder! Murder!” Ghysbrecht shrieked, rising on his heels.

“Silence, cur!” Gerard roared, crushing him down by the throat like a serpent.

“Now—have you got her steady? Then fly! For our lives! For our lives!”

But even as Martin kicked the mule into motion, scattering flints beneath its hooves, and even as Gerard pulled his foot from Ghysbrecht’s throat to run—Dierich Brower and five men, returning for orders and hearing the cries, burst roaring from the coppice—upon them.

Words are the common outlet for human thought, but there are feelings so raw and overwhelming that they burst forth not in speech, but in sounds—simple, powerful, unbidden. At such moments, man seems to shed his humanity, becoming little more than a creature of instinct; for even animals, when gripped by passion, cry out without language. Such was the scene now: the sudden roar of triumph from the hunters as they burst from the thicket, and the sharp, piercing cry of fear from those they chased—each sound stripped bare of reason, born of pure instinct.

The pursuers lunged forward, hands grasping at empty air—barely two feet behind the fleeing figures. For a heartbeat, confusion seized them, like beasts who miss their prey. Dierich and his men staggered, stunned by the nearness of failure. Then, with weapons raised, they surged after Gerard and the mule, certain of catching them. This was no new contest; they had raced before, and known each other’s pace. Earlier that day, in open ground, they had clearly gained on the trio. Now, at last, it was a true race—decided only by speed.

A hundred yards vanished in an instant. Yet still, ten yards remained between hunter and hunted. Dierich frowned. Something had changed since morning. The reason lay in the way three people run together: the pace is set by the slowest. From Peter’s house to the edge of the forest, Gerard had matched Margaret’s stride. But now he ran his own. The mule was swift—capable of outrunning them all. And beyond that, youth and a life untouched by vice were lending him strength. With each step, daylight crept between the fugitives and their pursuers.

Then Dierich made a desperate surge—gaining two yards. But within seconds, Gerard reclaimed them, effortlessly, silently. The hunters began to curse. Martin heard, and his face brightened. “Courage, Gerard! Courage, brave lad! They’re breaking apart!”

And so they were. Dierich, leading the chase, was now followed by one man, while another fell far behind. As they climbed a long, gentle rise, the advantage of youth, grit, and clean living grew stronger. By the time Gerard reached the crest, Dierich’s forty years pressed upon him like lead weights. “Our cake is dough,” he gasped. “Take him dead if you can’t take him alive.” He stopped running, and began to follow on foot.

Jorian Ketel lagged next, then another, until one by one, the hunters faltered. Only one kept going—steady as a bloodhound, though slowly losing ground. His name, if memory serves, was Eric Wouverman.

Together, they reached a second rise—shorter, but much steeper. “Hand on mane!” shouted Martin. Gerard obeyed. The mule, sensing the climb, leaned into the effort, helping him ascend faster than he had run before.

At the sight of this, Dierich’s man lost heart. Eighty yards behind Gerard, and well ahead of his nearest companion, he halted abruptly. Following orders, he drew his crossbow, took careful aim, and as the trio disappeared over the hilltop, loosed the bolt. It whistled through the air—and struck home.

A cry of horror rose from the group. Then, as if struck by lightning, they collapsed—mule and all—into the earth below.

The effect was immediate and astonishing, so sudden that even the marksman stood stunned for a moment. Then, recovering himself, he called to his companions, urging them to join in the pursuit, and began to climb the hill. But before he had reached halfway, a figure emerged from the trees—Martin Wittenhaagen, bow drawn and arrow nocked. Eric Wouverman, seeing him, darted behind a nearby tree, pressing himself flat against the bark, trying to vanish into the shadow. Martin’s skill with the longbow was legendary, and the dead dog lying at their feet was proof enough of his deadly precision.

Wouverman peered cautiously around the trunk. The tip of the arrow still trembled, aimed directly at him. He could see its gleam in the sunlight. He dared not stir. Minutes passed as he waited, breath held, heart pounding. At last, his comrades arrived in force, shouting and panting from the climb.

Then, with a mocking laugh, Martin disappeared into the woods. Moments later, the sound of hooves echoed—the mule carrying him away at a brisk pace.

All the hunters surged forward, scrambling up the slope. From the high ground, they saw the narrow glade stretching ahead, seemingly endless. Far off, tiny figures raced along—Gerard and Margaret, fleeing at breakneck speed. They looked like insects on the horizon. Behind them, Martin galloped full tilt, riding low over the saddle, every muscle taut with effort.

The hunters were both outwitted and outrun.

To understand Martin’s actions, one must look beyond mere chance. Coincidences often deceive, just as we might once have seen a hare stumble over a thornbush the instant a gun fired, only to watch it leap away unharmed. So too, the burgomaster’s mule stepped into a rabbit hole at nearly the same moment the crossbow bolt whistled harmlessly overhead. She faltered, then collapsed, throwing both riders to the ground.

Gerard caught Margaret in his arms, but her weight and momentum pulled him down with her. And there, scattered across the earth, lay the players in this unfolding drama.

The mule rose quickly, trembling but unharmed. Martin was the first to stand. Glancing about, he saw only one pursuer closing in. Instantly, he seized the opportunity. He made the young lovers flee on foot while he confronted the enemy—just as described.

Now, he rode after his companions, catching up only after a long, grueling chase. Without hesitation, he lifted Gerard and Margaret onto the mule, then ran beside it until exhaustion claimed him. Then he handed the reins to one of them, took his turn to ride, and so they rotated—always keeping one fresh runner at the front.

In this way, their pace never slackened. Long before the hunters slowed, every trace of the fugitives had vanished into the forest. Not a sound, not a footprint remained.

Dierich and his men returned disheartened, left to tend to their fallen leader and the useless hound whose keen senses had failed them.

Life and liberty, when unchallenged, are rarely valued—why? Because they are assumed. But when threatened, their worth becomes clear. So too with sunlight: men do not admire it at midday, when it burns brightest, but in the evening, when it glows like molten topaz beneath the shade of ancient elms. Then, though weaker, its beauty is revealed by contrast with the gathering dusk.

So it was with Gerard and Margaret. Though every rustle of a leaf made them start, they moved through the forest now with hearts full of joy and quiet gratitude, gliding among the trees in peace, the silence deep and profound. Yet in their minds still echoed the barking dogs and the harsh voices that had pursued them so cruelly.

But soon Gerard noticed dark stains on Margaret’s ankles. “Martin! Martin!” he cried, his voice breaking. “Help! She’s been wounded—the crossbow!”

“No, no,” she said gently, smiling to calm him. “I’m not hurt. Not at all.”

“But what is this?” he demanded, trembling. “What in Heaven’s name is it?”

“Scold me not, then,” she whispered, her cheeks flushing. “Did I ever scold you?”

“No, dear Gerard,” he replied softly. “Well, then—Martin said the dogs were following blood. So I thought… if I could just have a little blood on my shoes, they might follow me instead, and leave you free.”

She paused, her voice low and tender. “So I scratched my arm with Martin’s knife—forgive me! Whose else could I take? Yours, Gerard? No. You would never let me. Please forgive me?”

He stared at her, choked with emotion. “Let me see it first,” he said hoarsely.

She held out her arm. He gasped. “There—it’s nothing,” she said, trying to laugh lightly.

“A scratch?” he repeated, his voice thick. “I call it a cut—a deep, terrible wound.”

He shuddered as he looked at the small but bleeding gash. “She might have used her bodkin,” muttered the soldier.

“Milksop!” he grumbled. “One who flinches at a scratch and a few drops of blood.”

“No,” Gerard said fiercely. “I could stand a sea of blood—but not hers. Oh, Margaret—how could you be so cruel?”

She smiled, her eyes shining with love. “Foolish Gerard,” she murmured, “to make such a fuss over nothing.” And she wrapped her arm around his neck, drawing him close. “As if I wouldn’t give every drop of blood in my heart for you—let alone a few from my arm.”

And there, under the weight of their shared danger, she wept upon his shoulder—not from pain, but from pity and devotion. He wept with her.

“And I must leave her,” he sobbed. “We two who love so deeply—one in Holland, one in Italy. Ah me! ah me!”

Margaret wept again, but quietly, silently. Instinct, never wrong, guided her. To speak her thoughts now would only deepen his sorrow. So she stayed silent, her tears falling unseen.

Suddenly they stepped onto a well-worn path. Martin stopped.

“This is the bridle-road I told you of,” he said, hanging his head. “And beyond lies the hostelry.”

Gerard and Margaret exchanged frightened glances.

“Come here, Martin,” Gerard whispered, pulling the soldier aside.

When they were apart, he spoke in broken tones: “Good Martin—watch over her for me. She is my wife. I leave her behind. Here—take this gold. It was meant for my journey. I cannot ask her to take it—she would refuse. But you will, won’t you? Oh, Heaven—this is all I can do? Money? But poverty is a curse. You’ll not let her want, will you? The burgomaster’s silver is enough for me.”

“You’re a good lad, Gerard,” Martin said, his voice rough with feeling. “No want, no harm shall come to her. I care more for her little finger than for all the world. And even if she were nothing to me, I’d protect her for your sake. Go with a brave heart. God go with you.”

He gripped Gerard’s hand tightly, then turned away, unable to look further.

After a pause, Martin stepped forward to return to Margaret—but Gerard stopped him.

“No, good Martin,” he said. “Please stay here, behind the thicket. Turn your face away while I—oh, Martin! Martin!”

This way, Gerard spared himself the agony of being watched as he parted from the woman he loved—and Martin spared himself the sight of their farewell.

He did not see them kneel together beneath the trees, renewing their vows before Heaven, broken only by violence. He did not see them cling to each other like drowning souls, unable to let go, pulling apart and returning, again and again, as if life itself depended on holding fast.

But he heard the sobs—Gerard’s deep, ragged cries, and Margaret’s soft, piteous moans.

Then came a sudden cry, and footsteps pounded across the road.

Martin rose, and there was Gerard running wildly, hands clasped above his head in prayer. Behind him, Margaret stumbled back toward him, arms outstretched, face pale as death, eyes fixed on nothing. He caught her in his arms and whispered comfort into her ear—but she could not hear. Only at the sound of his voice did she moan and clutch him tighter, trembling uncontrollably.

He lifted her onto the mule, wrapped his arm around her, and carried her slowly home. Her body, once strong and supple like a boy’s, now felt limp and powerless. She did not cry. She did not speak.

At the edge of the wood, he helped her down and told her to walk to her father’s house. She obeyed without protest.

Martin returned to Rotterdam. Sevenbergen was too hot for him.

Gerard, torn from the one he loved, moved like a man in a dream. At the little inn, he hired a horse and a guide, and rode swiftly toward the German frontier. But everything was mechanical. His senses dulled. Trees, houses, people passed by as if seen through a veil. His companions spoke twice—but he did not answer.

Only once did he burst out, savagely: “Shall we never be out of this hateful country?”

After many hours, they reached the crest of a steep hill. A small brook ran below.

“Halt!” the guide called, pointing across the valley. “There—Germany.”

“Where?” Gerard asked.

“On the other side of the stream. No need to ride down.”

Gerard dismounted without a word. From his belt, he drew the burgomaster’s purse. As he opened it, the guide muttered, half sulky: “You’ll soon be out of this hateful land. Maybe the one you’re going to likes you no better. But anyway—if it’s a church you’ve robbed, they can’t touch you once you cross that stream.”

Words that, at another time, would have earned a rebuke or a blow—now fell on Gerard like wind through empty air.

He paid the boy in silence and walked down the hill alone.

The brook sparkled, clear and cold, murmuring over smooth pebbles that glittered beneath the water. He sat beside it, staring blankly. Then he drank from it. Then he dipped his hands and feet into the icy flow. It stirred him.

He rose, took a run, and leaped across into Germany.

As soon as his foot touched the new soil, he turned sharply and looked back.

“Farewell, ungrateful land!” he shouted. “If it weren’t for her, I’d leave you forever—my kin, my mother, my childhood friends, my native town. Farewell, fatherland—welcome, wide world! Omne solum fortis patria.”

With those words on his lips, he suddenly sank, weak in limbs and spirit, and sat down on the foreign ground, sobbing bitterly.

After some time, he rose, wiped the tears from his eyes like a man, and stepped forward—without looking back, without hesitation—into the vast unknown.

Love and grief filled his soul so completely that fear had no place. Compared to parting from Margaret, walking alone to Italy in that harsh age seemed scarcely a burden.

All nations meet in a convent. Thanks to the monks and his own hunger for knowledge, Gerard could speak most tongues needed on his journey.

“I shall reach Rome soon,” he said to himself. “The sooner, the better.”

After walking a long league, he came to a crossroads—four paths winding through the countryside, confusing even seasoned travelers. He pulled out a small sun-dial Peter had given him, set it in the autumn light, and followed its shadow with sureness, heading south—like a young swallow flying alone, yet unlike the swallow, without any companion.

And so he went—into the world, into exile, into the future.

Not far along the road, Gerard came upon a small group. Two men in sober attire leaned casually against a horse, engaged in quiet conversation. The rider, dressed in a silk doublet and bright green jerkin and hose—both of English cloth, glossy as a mole’s back—lay flat on his stomach in the afternoon sun, looking like a giant lizard. His velvet cloak, flaming yellow, was carefully draped over the horse’s back.

“Is anything wrong?” Gerard asked.

“Not that I know of,” replied one of the servants.

“But your master lies like a dead man. Aren’t you ashamed to let him sprawl on the ground?”

“Go on,” said the servant. “The bare earth is the best cure for his condition. If you wake up from bed after drinking, you get a headache; but if you rise from hard ground, you leap up like a lark in spring. Eh, Ulric?”

“He speaks truth, young man,” Ulric added warmly.

“Then is the gentleman drunk?”

The servants burst into deep laughter at the simplicity of the question. But suddenly Ulric stopped, studying Gerard closely. “Who are you, and where were you born, that you don’t know the Count is always drunk at this hour?” And Gerard found himself under suspicion.

“I am a stranger,” he replied, “but honest and eager for knowledge. That is why I ask questions—not out of prying.”

“If you’re honest,” Ulric said shrewdly, “then give us trinkgeld for the wisdom we’ve shared.”

Gerard looked puzzled, but with a steady face, answered, “Trinkgeld you shall have—what my lean purse can spare—if you tell me why you took the man’s cloak and laid it on the horse.”

Inspired by the prospect of payment, two explanations sprang forth at once. One claimed that if the Count woke up (which, being a seasoned drinker, he often did instantly) and saw his horse sweating in the cold while a cloak lay unused nearby, he would fly into a rage—and perhaps lash out. The other, more elaborate theory, held that a horse, a poor creature drinking only water, needed warming and care; but a man, filled with good beer, carried enough inner heat to keep warm without a cloak, which was thus nothing but idle vanity.

Each speaker clung to his idea, and both had clearly imbibed a few drops of the same liquor that had befuddled their master. Their voices rose until the green-clad noble began to growl instead of snore. They didn’t notice.

Soon, the debate turned toward a topic certain to spark passion in that age. Hans, holding the bridle in one hand, struck Ulric sharply with the other. Ulric retaliated with interest, his free hand unencumbered. They went at each other, hammering over the horse’s mane, striking each other and jabbing the poor animal until it reared back and stepped heavily on the green lord’s protruding limb. He leapt up howling, one hand clutching his pain, the other gripping his hilt. The servants, startled, released the horse. It galloped off, whinnying, the men chasing after it in panic, and the noble behind them, cursing wildly, sword drawn, body bouncing from hedge to hedge as he zigzagged down the narrow lane.

Gerard turned his back and walked calmly southward, glad to have saved the four tin farthings he’d prepared for trinkgeld—but too heavy-hearted even to smile at their drunken folly.

The sun was nearly set, and Gerard, who had long hoped in vain to find an inn, felt increasingly uneasy. To make matters worse, dark clouds gathered overhead.

He quickened his pace, almost to a run.

It was useless. Rain fell in torrents, drenching the bewildered traveler and seeming to extinguish the sun itself—its fading rays no match for this sudden storm.

Gerard trudged on, soaked and shivering, in an unknown land. “Fool,” he muttered, “to leave Margaret.”

Darkness thickened.

He entered a vast forest. Massive branches arched across the narrow path, and the lost wanderer stumbled through what seemed an endless, ink-black cave with a rough floor, tripping again and again.

Onward, onward, with trembling limbs, empty stomach, and failing courage—until wolves rose from their dens and howled all around the woods.

His hair stood on end, but he gripped his cudgel tightly, ready to defend himself to the last.

There was no wind. His sharp ears caught light footsteps pattering over fallen leaves, and low branches rustling as unseen creatures slipped past.

Then, in the sea of darkness, a fiery star appeared close to the ground. He hailed it like a saint. “CANDLE! A CANDLE!” he shouted, trying to run. But the rugged terrain soon halted him. The light was farther than he thought. Yet finally, deep in the heart of the forest, he found a house—lit candles inside, voices loud and clear. He looked up for a signboard. There was none.

“Not an inn after all,” he sighed. “No matter. What Christian would turn a dog out into this wood tonight?” With that, he approached the door leading to the voices. He opened it slowly, peering in timidly—then pulled his head back abruptly as if struck, retreating into the rain and night.

He had glimpsed a large, low room dominated by a massive round stove, rising to the ceiling. Around it hung wet clothes—some on lines, others draped over wooden frames. These garments, soaked with the day’s rain and stained with life’s grime, lined with what another traveler might call “rammish clowns,” gave off thick vapors and indescribable odors in steaming clouds.

In one corner sat a traveling family, large and noisy—adding their own peculiar, sour smell of neglected children. Garlic filled the air between. All this, combined with closed windows, intense heat from the central furnace, and the breath of at least forty people, created a stifling atmosphere.

They had just finished supper.

Gerard, like most artists, had sensitive senses. The overpowering smells sent a wave of dismay through him. But the rain lashed him outside, and the light and warmth drew him in.

He couldn’t force himself through the thick perfumes at once, but returned again and again, like a moth drawn to flame. Eventually, he realized the odors didn: mix entirely—no fiend stirred them together. Family odor dominated two corners; stewed rustic ruled the center; garlic reigned near the window. By quick analysis, he found garlic occupied the smallest space in the air, while the scent of damp clothing spread farthest—a stench as if ancient goats or ancestors of foxes had been dragged through a river and dried by Nebuchadnezzar.

So Gerard crept into a corner near the door. Though the main odors were somewhat isolated, heat and moisture still circulated, making the walls drip. The novice felt a cold snake coil around his legs, his head grow heavy as lead, then a choking sensation, followed by a sweet drowsiness—almost death.

He was close to fainting, but regained consciousness with a deep sense of disgust and defeat. He decided to return to Holland at first light. This resolve lifted his spirits slightly. Still faint from hunger, he asked one of the garlic-smelling men if this wasn’t, after all, an inn.

“Where do you come from, that you don’t know ‘The Star of the Forest’?” came the reply.

“I’m a stranger. In my country, inns always have a sign.”

“Your land must be odd! Why need a sign for a public house—a place every soul knows?”

Gerard, too tired for argument, changed the subject. “Where can I find the landlord?”

This fresh display of ignorance raised the native’s contempt beyond words. He pointed to a middle-aged woman seated on the opposite side of the stove, then turned to his companions, announcing they had an outlandish creature among them. At once, the loud voices ceased, one by one, as the news spread. Every eye turned silently, like a zoological audience, watching Gerard’s every move.

The landlady sat on a chair slightly higher than the rest, between two bundles. From the first—a huge heap of feathers and wings—she plucked downy plumes, pulling others from quills, filling the second bundle and littering the floor ankle-deep. Her work contributed a stuffy, malarial haze, which might have mattered in a fine room, but meant nothing here.

Gerard asked her if he could have something to eat.

She opened her eyes in astonishment. “Supper ended over an hour ago.”

“But I didn’t eat, good woman.”

“Is that my fault? You were welcome to your share.”

“But I arrived late and was lost—against my will.”

“What concern is that of mine? Everyone knows ‘The Star of the Forest’ sups from six to eight. Come before six, you eat well; before eight, you eat as Heaven pleases; after eight, you get a clean bed and a stirrup cup—or a horn of cow’s milk—at dawn.”

Gerard stared blankly. “May I go to bed, then?” he asked sulkily. “It’s no good sitting wet and fasting. The proverb says, ‘He sups who sleeps.’”

“The beds haven’t arrived yet,” she replied. “You’ll sleep when the others do. Inns aren’t built for one.”

Gerard was stunned. “The beds weren’t here? What in Heaven’s name did she mean?” But he dared not ask—every word he’d spoken had amazed the crowd, and their silent, judging eyes watched him. He leaned against the wall and sighed deeply.

A ripple of titters ran through the watchful company.

“So this is Germany,” Gerard thought. “And Germany is a great country compared to Holland. Small nations for me.”

He consoled himself by remembering it would be his last night in the land—his first and final.

His thoughts were interrupted by an elbow jabbed into his ribs. He turned sharply on his assailant, who pointed across the room. Gerard looked and saw a woman in the corner beckoning. He approached cautiously, surprised and uncertain—so much so that to an observer, her finger seemed to pull him forward with a string.

When he reached her, she said in a strong, cheerful voice, “Hold the child.” In a moment, she dropped the baby into his arms.

He froze, hands turning to lead, horror spreading across his face.

At this expression, the sharp-eyed assembly laughed loudly and long.

“Don’t mind them,” she said cheerfully. “They know no better—how should they, born and bred in a wood?” She rummaged through her clothes with two searching hands—one of which Gerard had freed. Soon she pulled out a small tin plate and a dried pudding, then resumed the child with one arm and offered the food with the other, keeping a thumb on the pudding to prevent it from slipping.

“Put it in the stove,” she said. “You’re too young to lie down fasting.”

Gerard thanked her warmly. On his way to the stove, he glanced at the landlady. “May I, good dame?” he asked pleadingly.

“Why not?” she replied.

The question was clearly another surprise—though less shocking than the rest.

At the stove, he found the oven blocked by “the rammish clowns.” They wouldn’t move. He hesitated. The landlady noticed, calmly put down her work, and came over, pushing aside a few hircine figures with the impassive air of a housewife rearranging furniture. “Turn about is fair play,” she said. “You’ve been dry ten minutes now.”

Her practiced eye saw the truth: Gorgonii had finished stewing and begun baking. Deprived of the stove, they retreated—all except one, who stood like a table where she’d placed him. Gerard baked his pudding and, reaching the stove, burst into steam.

The door flew open, and a bundle of straw shot in.

It was thrown by a hind with a pitchfork. Another followed, then another, until the room resembled a clean farmyard. These were arranged in layers around the stove like arena seats. In moments, everyone lay on their backs.

The beds had arrived.

Gerard removed his pudding and found it delicious. As he ate, the woman who had given it to him—now in bed—beckoned again. He went to her side. “She’s waiting for you,” she whispered. Gerard returned to the stove and finished his sausage, casting nervous glances at the landlady, seated silently amid the sleeping crowd. After eating, he approached her. “Thank you kindly, good woman, for waiting.”

“You’re welcome,” she said calmly, neither overawed nor dismissive. Then she began gathering feathers. Gerard stopped her. “No, that’s my task,” he said, kneeling and collecting them with fervor. She watched quietly.

“I don’t know where you come from,” she said, still cautious. Then, more warmly, “But you’ve been well brought up—you had a good mother, I’ll wager.”

At the door, she prayed for the entire company and vanished. Gerard curled up in the very corner—the guests lay around the sacred stove in order of arrival.

This position was a blessing, placing him on the edge of the stench and heat, rather than in its midst.

Just as he drifted off, a noise awakened him. There stood the hind, shaking and waking each guest in turn, asking if it was he who had picked up the mistress’s feathers.

“It was I,” Gerard called.

“Oh, it was you?” the man said, striding over. “She told me to say, ‘One good turn deserves another.’ Here’s your nightcap,” and he thrust a large oaken mug under Gerard’s nose.

“I thank her, and bless her,” Gerard said, raising it—then grimaced. The beer was muddy, with a strange, medicinal taste unfamiliar to the Hollander.

“Trinke aus!” the hind shouted reproachfully.

“Enough is as good as a feast,” Gerard replied, Jesuitically.

The hind looked pityingly at the stranger who left liquor in his mug. “Ich brings euch,” he said, and drained it to the bottom.

Gerard turned his face to the wall, pulled up handfuls of clean straw, bored holes with his finger, and made a scabbard for his nose. Soon, all were asleep—men, maids, wives, children—snoring in a dozen keys like an orchestra tuning up. Gerard’s body rested on straw in Germany, while his spirit wandered to Sevenbergen.

When he awoke the next morning, nearly all his fellow travelers had gone. A few waited for dinner at nine—it was now six. He paid the landlady two pfenning—about half a penny—and the hind demanded trinkgeld. Receiving more than usual, and seeing Gerard eye a foaming milk-pail he’d just fetched from the cow, he hoisted it to his lips. “Drink your fill, man,” he said. When Gerard offered to pay, the man replied in broad patois that a man could drink a skinful of milk or a breakfast of air without touching his purse.

At the door, Gerard found his benefactress from the night before and her husband, a large, sturdy artisan.

He thanked her and, in the spirit of the time, offered a creutzer for her pudding.

She gently pushed his hand away. “What do you take me for?” she asked, blushing faintly. “We’re travelers, strangers like you—bound to feel for those in similar straits.”

Gerard blushed and stammered apologies.

Her husband grinned, superior to both.

“Give the vixen a kiss for her pudding, and call it quits,” he said, with an air of impartial judgment, like Jove himself.

Gerard obeyed, kissed her cheek, and said, “God bless you both, good people.”

“And God speed you, young man!” they replied. And so they parted—never to meet again in this world.

The sun had just risen. Raindrops on the leaves glittered like diamonds. The air was fresh and invigorating. Gerard headed south, forgetting his resolution of the night before.

He walked eight leagues that day and, in the afternoon, came upon a massive building with a grand arched gateway and a smaller postern beside it.

“A monastery!” he exclaimed joyfully. “I’ll go no further—I might fare worse.” He knocked at the postern, explained his journey, and was immediately admitted to the guest chamber—a large, lofty room where travelers were fed and lodged free by monastic charity.

Soon, the bell rang for vespers. Gerard entered the church and heard a service sung so beautifully, it seemed the choir of heaven. But one thing was missing—Margaret was not there to hear it with him. This made him sigh bitterly, even in rapture.

At supper, plain but wholesome food and good beer—brewed in the convent—were served. Early that evening, they were shown to a large dormitory. Since the number was modest, each had a truckle bed and sheepskins with fleece intact for coverings. Before this, a monk, struck by Gerard’s youth and appearance, questioned him and quickly uncovered his plans and feelings. When he learned Gerard was raised in a convent and traveling alone to Rome, he became a person of interest. The next morning, they showed him the monastery, invited him to dine in the refectory, gave him a route marked on parchment, and the prior presented him with a silver guilden to aid his journey. He advised Gerard to join the first honest company he met—“and not face alone the manifold perils of the way.”

“Perils?” Gerard thought to himself.

That evening, he reached a small, scattered town with one inn. It had no sign, but now more familiar with local customs, he recognized it by the coats of arms on its walls—tokens left by distinguished visitors over the years. It looked more like a mausoleum than a hotel. Nothing moved or sounded within or without. Gerard hammered on the great oak door—no answer. He shouted—no reply. After a while, he shouted louder. Finally, a small round window, or hole in the wall, opened. A man’s head emerged cautiously, like a tortoise from its shell, and stared at Gerard stolidly—without a word.

“Is this an inn?” Gerard asked, with a hidden sneer.

The head seemed to ponder. Then it nodded—slowly.

“Can I have lodging here?”

Again, the head considered, then nodded—sullenly, as if burdened by trivial questions.

“How do I get in, if you please?”

At this, the head vanished, as if the question had driven it back. A hand appeared, pointed around the corner of the building, and slammed the window shut.

Gerard followed the direction and, after some search, found a small, low door on the side of the structure. The main entrance, it seemed, was used only to keep out thieves and customers—except once or twice a year, when a duke or count arrived in pomp with his colorful entourage.

Gerard passed through the outer gate and soon found the stove—the public room named for its centerpiece. He sat near the oven, where only a few live embers burned, spreading a mild, comforting warmth.

After waiting patiently, he asked a grim old man with a long white beard—who solemnly entered, turned the hourglass, and left—when supper would be served.

The old man counted the guests on his fingers. “When I see three times as many here as now.”

Gerard groaned.

The old man frowned. “Inns aren’t built for one,” he said. “If you can’t wait, find another lodging.”

Gerard sighed.

The old man frowned again.

Eventually, guests trickled in—until eighty people of various sorts gathered. To Gerard, the place became a chamber of horrors: mothers comparing ringworms, men scraping mud from their shoes with knives and leaving it on the floor, combing their long hair—often including inmates—and performing their toilette with dry rubs. Water was brought in ewers. Gerard seized one—but at the sight of the liquid, lost his temper. “Wash your water first,” he snapped at the waiter, “then a man may wash his hands.”

“An’ it doesn’t please you, seek another inn!”

Gerard said nothing, but quietly asked an old traveler how far it was to the next inn.

“About four leagues.”

Then Gerard understood the old man’s grim humor.

The worthy returned with an armload of wood, counted the guests, and added a log for every six—making the room hotter as more heat was added. Poor Gerard noticed the flaw in logic but kept silent, fearing his feet might carry his brain four leagues farther that night.

As perspiration and suffocation mounted, they brought in tablecloths—oh, so brown, so dirty, so coarse—they looked like sacks worn out in farming or scraps from a ship’s mainsail. The Hollander, who had never seen such linen—even in dreams—let out a faint cry.

“What’s wrong?” a traveler asked. Gerard pointed sadly to the filthy cloth. The other stared, uncomprehending.

A Burgundian soldier with a crossbow at his back leaned over Gerard’s shoulder, saw the issue, and roared with laughter. The room echoed. Then he slapped Gerard on the back. “Courage! Le diable est mort.”

Gerard stared—he doubted both the news and its relevance. But the tone was hearty, and though the soldier’s beard was formidable, his face was gay and kind. Gerard smiled, then after a pause said dryly, “Il a bien faite avec l’eau et linge du pays on allait le noircir à ne se reconnaître plus.”

“Tiens, tiens!” the soldier exclaimed. “V’la qui parle le Français peu s’en faut.” He sat beside Gerard and began talking eagerly of war, women, and plunder, sprinkling his speech with curious oaths. Gerard edged away, more or less.

Then the grim servant returned, counting the guests on his fingers like Abraham tallying sheep. He left, then returned with a wooden trencher and spoon for each.

And so the night wore on.

Denys grabbed Gerard just as he began to fall, slowing his descent—though it’s doubtful that alone would have spared him from a broken neck or shattered limb. His true savior was the dying bear beneath whom his head and shoulders landed. Denys wrenched him free. It was unnecessary. The beast still breathed, her limbs trembling, but she was no longer dangerous. Soon, her breath ceased entirely. Denys propped Gerard up against her soft, lifeless body and fanned him gently. Gradually, Gerard regained consciousness—but confused, and when he felt the bear beside him, he rolled away in terror, screaming.

“Courage,” Denys called. “The devil is dead.”

“Is it truly gone? Completely?” Gerard asked, hiding behind a tree. His courage had been fleeting, and now a chill gripped him—one that had plagued him for some time.

“Behold,” said Denys, pulling the bear’s ear playfully, then opening its jaws and thrusting his head inside, mocking it with crude gestures. Midway through this, Gerard vomited violently.

Denys laughed.

“What now?” he asked. “And why tumble from your perch just when we’d won the day?”

“I fainted, I suppose.”

“But why?”

When no answer came, Denys continued, “Green girls faint at a glance, but they choose their moment and place. What woman ever fainted while climbing a tree?”

“She splashed her foul blood all over me. I think the smell overwhelmed me! Ugh—I loathe blood.”

“I believe you mean it.”

“Look what a mess she made of me!”

“But not with your own blood. I pity any foe who tries to satisfy you.”

“You needn’t boast, Maitre Denys. I saw you under the tree—your shirt was stained.”

“Let us be clear,” said Denys, flushing. “It’s natural to tremble for a friend.”

Gerard responded by throwing his arms around Denys’s neck in silence.

“Look here,” said the soldier, touched by this burst of youthful emotion, “have you ever seen anything so like a woman? I love thee, little milksop—go on. Good heavens! Now he’s on his knees. What new whim is this?”

“Oh, Denys,” said Gerard, “should we not give thanks to Him who saved our lives against such odds?” And he knelt and prayed aloud. Soon, Denys knelt beside him, hands folded across his chest in the manner of his countrymen, face long and solemn. When they rose, Gerard’s expression was radiant.

“Good Denys,” he said, “Heaven will reward your piety.”

“Ah, bah!” replied the Frenchman. “I did it out of politeness—to please you, little one. C’est égal—it was well-prayed, orderly, and edified me thoroughly. A bishop could scarcely have done better. Now that our evening song is sung, and the saints are on our side—marchons!”

Before they took two steps, Denys stopped. “By-the-by—the cub!”

“Oh, no, no!” cried Gerard.

“You’re right. It’s too late. We’ve wasted enough time climbing trees, falling off them, fainting, vomiting, praying. The brute is heavy to carry. And now I recall—we’ll have Papa after it next. Bears make such a fuss over lost cubs. Wait—what’s this? You’re wounded! You’re wounded!”

“Not I.”

“He is wounded—wretched that I am!”

“Be calm, Denys. I feel no pain. I’m unharmed.”

“You? You only feel when someone else suffers,” Denys exclaimed, deeply moved. He dropped to his knees and examined Gerard’s leg with glistening eyes.

“Quick! Before it stiffens!” he urged, helping him forward.

“Who’s making the fuss now?” Gerard asked calmly.

Denys didn’t reply directly.

“Note well,” he said, “that I have a bad heart. You were brave enough to save my life, yet I mocked you—a novice in war. Wasn’t I once a novice myself? Then you fainted from a wound, and I thought you swooned from fear, calling you a milksop. In short, I have a sharp tongue and a cruel heart.”

“Denys!”

“Plait-il?”

“You lie.”

“You’re kind to say so, little one—and I’m eternally grateful,” muttered Denys, humbled.

They walked only a short distance before the muscles in Gerard’s injured leg contracted and hardened. Soon, he could barely lift his foot, doing so only with agony.

At last, he could endure no more.

“Let me lie down and die,” he groaned. “This is unbearable.”

Denys reminded him it was afternoon, and the nights were cold. Hunger and cold were poor companions. To lose heart now, when a great man was clearly dead, would be unreasonable. So Gerard leaned on his axe and limped on—until suddenly, he collapsed helplessly into the road.

Denys pulled him aside into the woods. To Gerard’s surprise, he handed him his crossbow and bolts, instructing him strictly to stay still. If anyone approached and refused to leave, he should shoot them dead at twenty paces. “Honest men walk the path; rogues in the woods—only fools parley with them.” With that, Denys snatched Gerard’s axe and ran—not toward Dusseldorf, but back along the road they’d come.

Gerard lay in pain, smarting. Rome, which had seemed so near at the start, now felt impossibly distant—though he was two hundred miles closer. But soon his thoughts turned to Sevenbergen. How sweet it would be to hold Margaret’s hand and tell her all he’d endured for her! Just thinking of her eased his suffering. Amidst pain and nerve-jarring irritation, he lay resigned, even smiling faintly.

He had lain there over two hours when sudden shouts broke the silence. Then something struck a nearby tree and quivered in the bark.

He looked. An arrow.

He leapt to his feet. More missiles clattered among the branches. The forest echoed with battle cries. Their origin was unclear—sound traveled strangely in these vast woods, disorienting strangers. Yet the noise seemed to fill the air. Then came the thunderous galloping of hooves, louder shouts, shrieks, groans, and strange, terrifying sounds—like furious thunderclaps, roaring and fading into crackling echoes. Red flames flickered between the trees, and clouds of sulfurous smoke drifted overhead. Then—silence.

Gerard stood in awe. “What will become of Denys?” he cried. “Oh, why did you leave me? Oh, Denys, my friend—my friend!”

Just before sunset, Denys returned, nearly crushed beneath a furry bundle. It was the bear’s hide.

Gerard greeted him with joy so intense it stunned him.

“I thought I’d never see you again, dear Denys. Were you in the battle?”

“No. What battle?”

“The bloody clash of men—or devils—that raged in the wood moments ago,” Gerard said, describing it vividly, more fully than I have.

Denys patted him gently.

“Well,” he said, “you’re a fine artist. Fever stirs the imagination. Once, I lay in a cart-shed with a cracked skull and saw two armies fight for an hour on eight square feet. I described it faithfully to my comrade—though not so colorfully as you, lacking book learning.”

“What? You don’t believe me? I heard arrows whiz overhead, heard shouts, and—”

“May the foul fiends take me if I believe a word of it.”

Gerard took his arm and pointed to a nearby tree.

“Why, it looks like—no, it *is*—a broad arrow, as I live!” He stepped close and looked up.

“It came from the battle. I heard it. I saw it.”

“An English arrow.”

“How do you know?”

“By its length. English archers draw their bows to the ear, others only to the breast. Hence their shafts are three feet long—and this one is exactly that, damn them! Well, if this isn’t illusion, then there was a skirmish. And if there was a battle in such a ridiculous place, then it’s none of my concern—my Duke has no quarrel here. Let’s sleep,” said the professional. He gathered leaves and made a bed for Gerard, placing his axe beside him. Then he lay down, hand on his arbalest, and draped the bear-skin over them, fur inward. They were soon warm as toast, fast asleep.

But long before dawn, Gerard woke Denys.

“What shall I do, Denys? I’m dying of hunger!”

“Do? Why, go back to sleep at once: qui dort dine.”

“But I tell you, I’m too hungry to sleep,” Gerard snapped.

“Then let’s march,” Denys replied, indulgent as a father.

After a brief fit of yawns, Denys bundled up several bears’ ears, rolling them in a strip of skin cut for the purpose. Together, they set off.

Gerard leaned on his axe, supported by Denys on the other side, hobbling along, sighing.

“I hate pain,” he muttered bitterly.

“Therein you show wisdom,” Denys replied smoothly.

It was a clear starlit night. Soon, the moon rose, revealing the edge of the wood not far ahead—a welcome sight, since Dusseldorf was only a short league beyond.

At the forest’s edge, they encountered something so mysterious they paused to study it before approaching. Two white pillars stood apart, and between them stood many figures resembling human forms.

“I won’t go farther until I know what this is,” Gerard whispered, agitated. “Are they statues of saints, meant for prayer? Or live robbers waiting to ambush honest travelers? No—they can’t be alive, for they stand on nothing I see. Oh, Denys, let’s turn back till morning—this is no mortal sight!”

Denys halted, peering intently. “They are men,” he said finally.

Gerard wanted to retreat even more.

“But men who will never harm us, nor we them. Don’t look at their feet—look where they stand!”

“Where, in God’s name?”

“Look above their heads,” Denys said gravely.

Following his direction, Gerard soon saw the dark outline of a wooden beam stretching between the pillars. As they approached, tiptoeing carefully, dark cords appeared in the moonlight—each hanging from the beam to a corpse, taut as wire.

As they passed beneath this grim monument of crime and vengeance, a light breeze stirred the bodies, making them sway and creak. Gerard shuddered at the ghastly greeting. So absorbed were they by the gallows that only now did they notice the fire below and the living figure huddled over it. His axe lay beside him, blade glowing red in the flames. He slept.

Gerard jumped, but Denys merely whispered, “Courage, comrade—there’s a fire.”

“Aye, but there’s a man at it.”

“There will soon be three,” Denys said, adding wood to the blaze. The cautious Gerard seized the man’s axe and sat firmly upon it, gripping his own, examining the sleeper. Nothing marked him outwardly. He wore common folk’s clothes and a three-cornered hat known as a Brunswicker—stiff enough to deflect a sword strike, with a thick brass band. Its weight had pressed his ears flat, like those of a fancy rabbit today. Still, such hats were common. What was odd was a man guarding a loaded gallows. For what purpose?

Denys, though curious, showed no sign. He pulled out two bears’ ears, skewered them, and began roasting them. “This will be eating coined money,” he said. “The burgomaster of Dusseldorf offered us a rix-dollar for these ears as proof of the beasts’ deaths. Better a lean purse than a hollow stomach.”

“Unfortunate man!” Gerard exclaimed. “Could you eat here?”

“Where the fire burns, meat must roast. Where it roasts, it must be eaten—nothing travels worse than roasted meat.”

“Eat then, Denys—if you can! But I’m cold and sick. There’s no room for hunger after what I’ve seen,” he shuddered over the fire. “Oh, how they creak! And who is this man? What a coarse fellow!”

Denys studied him like a connoisseur appraising art, then delivered his verdict. “I’d say he’s from the dregs of that gang—these up there (pointing casually) were the cream, and so led themselves into danger.”

“At that rate, why not knock him out before he wakes?” Gerard fidgeted.

Denys opened his eyes with mock surprise. “For one who claims to be a milksop, you have a quick hand. Why stun one when two can handle him? Tush—he wakes. Listen now to what he says, and tell me.”

No sooner were the words spoken than the watcher opened his eyes. Seeing the fire lit and two strangers watching him closely, he stared, forcing himself to appear calm—though a visible tremor ran through him. He quickly regained composure and grumbled, “Good morrow.” But at that instant, he noticed his axe was missing—and saw Gerard sitting on it, his own weapon ready. He lost his nerve instantly. Denys smiled grimly at the scene.

“Good morrow!” Gerard said quietly, eyeing him.

The watcher, now uneasy, said, “You’re using my fire.”

“But you’re welcome,” he added, voice faltering.

Denys whispered to Gerard. The watcher watched them sideways.

“My comrade says, since we share your fire, you’ll share his food.”

“So be it,” the man said warmly. “I have half a kid hanging on a bush nearby—I’ll fetch it.” He rose cheerfully, preparing to leave.

Denys raised his crossbow and aimed at his head. The man fell to his knees.

Denys lowered the weapon and gestured him back. He rose slowly, unsteadily—like a puppet whose strings have been cut—and retreated, sickened, like a mouse released only to be caught again.

“Sit down, friend,” Denys said grimly, in French.

The man obeyed, though he understood no French.

“Tell him the fire isn’t big enough for more than one. He’ll grasp my meaning.”

Gerard translated. The man grinned—ever since Denys spoke, he’d seemed relieved. “I didn’t know you were strangers,” he said to Gerard.

Denys cut a piece of bear’s ear and offered it gracefully to the man he’d just aimed at.

He accepted calmly, drew bread from his pouch, and shared it with both. Then, he winked and plunged his hand into the leaf pile (Gerard tightened his grip on his axe, ready to strike) and pulled out a leather bottle holding two gallons. He drank deeply, then offered it to Gerard. Gerard passed it untouched to Denys.

“Mort de ma vie!” the soldier cried. “Rhenish wine—and fit for an archbishop’s throat! Here’s to you, noble fellow—may you live short and merry! Come, Gerard, drink! Drink! Pshaw, ignore them—they ignore you. Still, if I hung over such a cask of Rhenish and three men sat beneath drinking it without offering me a drop, I’d soon join them.”

“Denys! Denys!”

“My spirit would sever the rope, and down I’d come—body among you, hand on the bottle, one eye winking, the other open.”

Gerard jumped up, screaming, fingers over his ears, running away—until he saw the watcher’s axe. The real threat brought him back. He sat again, hand on the axe, fingers still covering his ears.

“Courage, l’ami, le diable est mort!” Denys shouted cheerfully, offering Gerard a piece of bear’s ear, pressing it under his nose. Gerard turned away in disgust.

“Wine!” he gasped. “Heaven knows I need it, with such company as you and—”

He took a long draught. The wine warmed his veins, strengthened his heart—but couldn’t stop his shivers whenever wind blew. Denys and the other feasted recklessly, passing the bottle endlessly, toasting beneath the creaking gallows and its silent tenants.

“Ask him how they ended up here,” Denys said, mouth full, pointing upward without looking.

The question translated, the watcher replied: treason—diabolical treason and priest-craft. Drunk, he gave a lengthy, dull account. These men, now dangling so pitifully, were strong, honest souls who lived by their wits in the forest. Their independence angered many, and attacks were frequent—but always thwarted by the Virgin, their saints, and their own skill. Yesterday, merchants arrived on mules from Dusseldorf.
