The honest men let them advance a league, then attacked to force them to surrender ill-gotten gains. But the merchants were soldiers—of multiple nations, hired by the Archbishop of Cologne. Underneath their robes were haubergeons, weapons at hand. The honest men fought bravely, pressing hard—until horsemen, hidden for hours, charged. Armed with deadly engines, they fired leaden bullets, killing many and breaking the rest’s spirits. Captured, the victors—maliciously—had already tied ropes around their waists and swiftly hanged them, including the dead, for dramatic effect. “That one at the end was the captain. He never felt the rope—he was riddled with arrows and bullets before they could seize him: a worthy man, as ever shouted ‘Stand and deliver!’—though perhaps a bit hasty. That one in the buff jerkin was the lieutenant—fine soul, hanged alive. This one here—I never liked him—(not that one; that’s Conrad, my bosom friend)—I mean this one overhead in chicken-toed shoes—you were always spreading lies, thief, causing trouble. You know you were. And I, sir, prefer living in a coppice with honest men rather than a forest full of backbiters. Strangers, I drink to you.” He went down the line, naming each with the bottle-neck like a showman, giving neat but false descriptions—his eye for character nonexistent.

“Enough talk!” Denys barked. “Marchons! Give me his axe. Tell him he must help us.”

The man’s face fell, but seeing Denys’s gaze, he submitted. Gerard objected. “Y pensez-vous? To touch a thief makes my flesh crawl.”

“Childishness! All trades must survive. Besides, I have reasons. Don’t be wiser than your elder.”

“No. But if I must lean on him, I’ll keep my hand in my chest, clutching my knife.”

“A peculiar way to walk—but suit yourself.”

So the trio walked—strange, mixed: tenderness and suspicion intertwined. I wish I could draw them—I wouldn’t trust the pen.

The watchtower’s light at Dusseldorf became visible as they cleared the woods, lifting Gerard’s spirits. After an hour’s march, the black silhouette of the tower and buildings emerged. Their companion stopped, gloomy. “You might as well kill me now as take me closer to Dusseldorf’s gates.”

When Denys heard this, he said simply, “Let him go. His neck is in danger if he goes further with us.” Gerard agreed—his horror of criminals didn’t incline him to aid the law. Yet at this time, no private citizen in Europe meddled with criminals except in self-defense—except England, which, though backward in some things, was centuries ahead in this.

With freedom restored, the man asked for his axe. It was given. To their surprise, he lingered. Was he to get nothing for walking so far with them?

“Here are two batzen, friend.”

“Add the wine—the good Rhenish?”

“Did you pay for it?”

“Yes—the risk to my life.”

“Hmm. What say you, Denys?”

“I say it was worth its weight in gold. Here, lad—silver groshen, one for every acorn on that gallows tree—and one more for you, who’ll likely hang there someday.”

He took the coins, but still lingered.

“Well? What now?” Gerard snapped, thinking him shamefully overpaid. “Seeking our bones?”

“No, good sirs. You’ve seen how perilous my life is. You’re true men—your prayers matter. Give me a small prayer, if you please. I know none.”

Gerard’s temper flared. Since his wound, irritability surged. But he bit his lip. “There go two words to that bargain. First—tell me: is it true what people say about you Rhenish thieves—that you murder innocent travelers as well as rob them?”

The man answered sulkily, “We you call thieves aren’t to blame. The fault lies with the law.”

“Gramercy! So it’s the law’s fault that evil men break it?”

“I don’t mean that. But the law here kills an honest man for stealing. What follows? He feels pity, but is discouraged—pity brings no mercy, only greater danger. Cut a purse, and your life is forfeit. So he cuts the throat too—to save his own neck. Dead men tell no tales. Pray then for the poor soul driven by bloody laws to kill or be slaughtered. If there were less gibbeting on highways, there’d be fewer throats slit in dark woods, masters.”

“Fewer words would have served,” Gerard replied coldly. “I asked a question. I am answered.” Suddenly, he removed his hat—

“Obsecro Deum omnipotentem, ut, qua cruce jam pendent isti quindecim latrones fures et homicidae, in ea homicida fur et latro tu pependeris quam citissime, pro publica salute, in honorem justi Dei cui sit gloria, in aeternum, Amen.”

“And so, good day.”

The greedy outlaw was satisfied. “Latin,” he muttered. “More than I bargained for.” Indeed it was.

He returned to his work, mind at ease. The friends walked in silence, reflecting on the events of the past hours.

At last, Gerard said thoughtfully, “That she-bear saved our lives—by God’s will.”

The afternoon sun slanted through the window, casting long shadows across the room where Gerard lay. He was no longer dizzy, but his mind wandered restlessly, clouded by feverish thoughts. One such fancy led him to ask Denys for a lemon to suck—something rare and exotic in these northern lands.

Denys, once a rough soldier now softened into something like a guardian, rose quickly. “Don’t worry,” he said with a grin. “Lemons shall be yours before the pot boils.” And off he went, searching every shop in town, only to return long after Gerard had grown impatient.

But it was not Denys who entered when the door finally opened.

A figure stepped in with quiet dignity—an old man draped in a long, sober gown trimmed with rich fur, wearing cherry-red hose and pointed shoes. A sword hung at his side in a morocco scabbard. Around his neck, a stiff ruff, starched and shaped by hidden wooden supports, stood rigid like armor. On his head sat a four-cornered cap lined with fur, and from his chin and chest flowed a majestic white beard. The boy behind him carried a basket filled with bottles, bandages, and surgical tools, none of them hidden from view.

Gerard recognized the man at once—not because of the sword, but because this was the full dress of a physician. And indeed, the doctor approached the bedside softly, speaking low: “How fares thee, my son?”

Gerard answered gently that his wound no longer hurt much, though his throat felt dry and his head heavy.

“A wound!” the doctor murmured, surprised. “They did not tell me of that. Let me see.” He leaned over, inspecting the injury. “Ah, yes—a clean bite. The dog must have had strong teeth.”

“Not a dog,” Gerard corrected. “A bear.”

“A bear?” the doctor replied, sternly. “Young man, think before you speak. It is unwise to mock the man of science who brings years of study and grey hairs to heal you. No bear’s jaw could make such a small wound. I say it was a dog—and not even a large one, but one of those little, vicious curs that run wild, biting men’s legs and bringing them low… if not for us learned men, who stop their mischief with knife and cautery.”

“But sir,” Gerard said slowly, “I did not say it was the bear’s jaw. I said *a bear*. It was his paw.”

“And why did you not tell me so at once?”

“Because you kept insisting it was a dog.”

“Never hide anything from your leech,” the doctor declared, more intent on lecturing than listening. “Well, it is a serious matter. All animal claws—tigers, panthers, badgers, cats, bears—and even human nails, especially children’s, carry deadly poison. You would have been better off bitten by a cur than scratched by a bear. Still, we shall apply a strong poultice to your leg. In the meantime, keep the body cool. Stick out your tongue—good! Fever. Now let me feel your pulse—yes, fever. I prescribe bloodletting. Immediately.”

“Bloodletting?” Gerard asked, frowning. “That means letting blood? Well, if it will cure me, then let it be done. I won’t lie here idle.”

The doctor nodded gravely. “Flebotomy is infallible, especially in your case.”

“Hans,” he called, “fetch the instruments. I’ll entertain our patient while you wait.”

And so began his lecture.

In sickness, he explained, the blood grows hot, corrupted, and poisonous. By removing some of this tainted fluid, nature is forced to produce fresh, pure blood in its place. Thus, bleeding serves both as cooling and cleansing—a remedy for all diseases, since all diseases are fevers, despite what empirics may claim.

“But remember,” he added warmly, “bleeding alone is not enough. Any barber can open a vein—though not all can close it again. The true art lies in knowing which vein to open for which illness. Recently, a man came to me with earache. I bled him in the right thigh, and his pain vanished. Alas, he died soon after. Another suffered toothache; I bled him behind the ear, and he was relieved instantly. He too is dead now. Our bailiff had rheumatism; I bled him between thumb and forefinger. Soon he returned, complaining of headache and ringing in the ears, holding out his hand over the basin. I smiled at his folly and bled him instead in the left ankle, against his will. His head became light as a nut.”

He paused, then shifted course, as scholars often do.

“Know this, young man: two great schools of medicine now divide Europe. The Arabian tradition—rooted in Avicenna, Rhazes, Albucazis—revived by Chauliac and Lanfranc. And the Greek school—championed today by Bessarion, Platinus, Marsilii Ficinus—but whose ancient masters were the oracles of healing: Phoebus, Chiron, Aesculapius, his sons Podalinus and Machaon, Pythagoras, Democritus, Praxagoras—who discovered arteries—and Dioctes, ‘who first gave meaning to urine.’ All taught orally. Then came Hippocrates, eighteenth in line from Aesculapius, whose writings we still possess. To him we owe the concept of vital principle. He invented the bandage, performed thoracentesis, and dissected animals—though never humans, due to pagan superstition.”

“Surely,” Gerard ventured, “God gave us our bodies, not Aristotle or any Greek.”

“Child!” the doctor snapped. “Of course God created the body. But Aristotle gave it a name. And young men always talk too much. Next came Galen, who studied in Alexandria, the center of learning. Disgusted with quadrupeds, he turned to apes, closer to man, and bled them mercilessly. Then Theophilus revealed nerves, lacteal vessels, and the pia mater.”

Gerard grew uneasy. “I cannot stay silent while you say mortal men gave names to parts Adam received directly from God.”

“Is there such stubbornness?” the doctor cried, flushing. “Who truly gives a thing to man—the one who hides it in darkness, or the scholar who reveals it? Knowledge is your only true possession. Are you convinced?”

“I am silenced,” Gerard admitted.

“Good,” the doctor said. “For noisy patients are hard to treat—especially when fevered. Now, Eristratus gave us cerebral nerves and milk vessels. He also invented lithotomy. Then came another—I forget his name. Then Ammonius, author of lithotrity. And here comes Hans with the basin—now silence!”

He turned to the boy. “Blow the charcoal, boy. Hand me the basin. Good.”

As the preparations continued, Denys returned, lemons in hand, and stopped short in surprise.

“What’s going on?” he asked, raising an eyebrow.

Gerard flushed slightly. “The doctor is about to bleed me and cauterize the wound.”

“Oh, indeed,” Denys said. “And what’s the boy doing with the coals?”

“To cauterize the vein once opened,” the doctor replied. “It’s the only safe way. Avicenna suggests tying the vein, but he says nothing how—nor does he know himself, nor any of Ishmael’s spawn. I trust no such tricks. Remember this: whatever an Arab or Arabist claims is true, must be false.”

“Oh,” Denys said, understanding now. “So you’re going to burn living flesh with red-hot iron? Have you ever held your little finger in a candle for ten seconds? This will last minutes. Do you not fear purgatory? Must you taste hell before death?”

“I hadn’t thought of that,” Gerard said quietly. “The doctor spoke of cautery, not burning. They sound different, though they mean the same.”

“Fool!” Denys scoffed. “That’s their trick—to confuse plain men with dark words until the flesh screams the truth. I’ve seen soldiers wounded in battle. These doctors cry, ‘Fever! Blood him!’ and burn the wick at the other end too. They bleed the already bled. Then fever fades into weakness. The man needs every drop of blood to live. But these prickers and burners care only for what’s before them. They drain the very blood the wound spared him to fight the weakness. And so he dies—exhausted. Hundreds I’ve seen die this way—strong men. Yet if they’re wounded where no doctor can reach, they live. I know this. Had I lived through that Brabant field without surgery? Only by luck—frost sealed my wounds. A surgeon would have pierced me once more, drained my last drop, and taken my soul with it. Seeing them thus reckless with bleeding soldiers, I trust them not. What kills a veteran can surely kill a weak civilian.”

“That sounds reasonable,” Gerard sighed. “But no need to shout. I’m not deaf.”

“Reasonable? Very common sense indeed,” the doctor snapped. “This is a soldier—a brute whose job is to kill, not heal.” He added in French, “Woe to you, ignorant man, if you interfere between a physician and his patient. Woe to you, misguided youth, if you listen to a butcher of blood.”

“Much obliged,” Denys said, mocking politeness. “But I’m a true man. I do draw blood, though not worth mentioning here. For every life I take, you take a hundred. For every spoonful I draw, you spill a tub. The world is fooled by appearances. We soldiers carry long swords and create two enemies for every one we kill. But you smooth-gowned men, with soft words and bare lancets—you are the ones who thin mankind.”

“A sickroom is no place for jesting,” the doctor thundered.

“No,” Gerard muttered, peevishly. “Nor for shouting.”

“Come, young man,” the doctor said, softer now. “Be reasonable. Each man should be trusted in his own craft. I have spent my life in this art. I studied at Montpellier—the finest school in France, and therefore Europe. There I learned Dririmancy, Scatomancy, Pathology, Therapeusis, and above all, Anatomy. At last, we disciples of Hippocrates and Galen had opportunities those ancients never dreamed of. Farewell, quadrupeds and apes, paganism and Islam. We bought corpses from churchwardens, shook gallows, undid sextons’ work under cover of night, driven by love of science and humanity. Paris sent orders to wink—and they did. Gods of Olympus, how they winked! Even the king helped—twice a year he sent a condemned criminal alive, saying, ‘Treat him as science demands. Dissect him if needed.’”

“By Herod’s liver and Nero’s bowels,” Denys roared, “he’ll make me blush for the land that bore me if he praises it any further!”

Gerard squeaked and covered his ears. Then, suddenly, he shouted back just as loudly: “You roaring, blaspheming bull of Basan—hold your tongue!”

Denys looked contrite.

“Tush,” the doctor said, waving a hand dismissively. “We rarely dissected the living—only in part. Mostly, we inoculated criminals with diseases of the time—choosing the most interesting.”

“That means the worst,” Denys whispered.

“We watched them through every stage until death.”

“Meaning the poor rogue died,” Denys whispered again.

“And now,” the doctor continued, “who deserves your trust more—the honest soldier with youth, ignorance, and prejudice—or a greybeard burdened with centuries of wisdom?”

“That is,” Denys interrupted, “will you believe a jackdaw in a long gown who heard from a starling who heard from a jay-pie who heard from a magpie who heard from a popinjay—or will you believe me, a man with nothing to gain, who sees with eyes, not ears, and has seen that fevered, bled men die, while fevered, unbled men live?”

“Who sent for this bloodsucker?” Denys demanded. “Was it you?”

“No,” Gerard said. “I thought you had.”

“No,” the doctor corrected. “The landlord told me someone was ill. I thought, ‘A stranger in need of my art,’ and came at once.”

“It was a Christian act,” Gerard said.

“A bloodhound’s act,” Denys sneered. “Do you not know landlords conspire with citizens who pay them fees for each victim? Whatever you pay this man for stealing your blood, the landlord takes a third for betraying you. And when your blood flows down the stairs, he smells it and sends to his undertaker—gets his third from that too. If he waited till the doctor left, the doctor might hire the undertaker first—and then he’d get the black thirds. Say I speak truth, old Rouge et Noir? Dites!”

“Denys,” Gerard said, “who taught you to distrust men?”

“My eyes,” Denys replied. “Eyes that see what men do, not what they say. I’ve seen it across many lands.”

The doctor used this moment wisely. “I too have eyes. I don’t rely on tradition alone, but on what I’ve seen and done. I’ve healed as many with bleeding as that Arabist has killed by neglect. Yesterday, I cured a man threatened with leprosy—bled him at the tip of the nose. Last year, a quartan ague—bled his forefinger. Our rival lost his memory. I restored it with a lance—bled him behind the ear. I bled a dull boy, and now he’s the only one in his family who knows his right hand from his left. When the plague struck, not the fake kind empyrics invent every six years, but the real Byzantine pest, I bled an alderman freely and cauterized the buboes—saved him. While our chirurgeon, a dangerous Arabist, caught it and died, calling on Rhazes, Avicenna, and Mahound—who, had they come, would have perished as he did.”

“Oh, my ears,” Gerard groaned.

“And am I so fallen that one of your presence rejects my art and listens to a crude soldier—so backward even in his own trade that he uses an arbalest, a worn-out invention German children shoot at pigeons with, mocked by German soldiers since arquebuses came?”

“You foul-mouthed charlatan,” Denys spat. “The arbalest is wielded by taller men than ever wore Rhenish hose. Even now, it kills more than your stinking arquebus, just as your lancet kills more than all our weapons combined. Go to! He was no fool who first called you ‘leeches.’ Sang-sues! Va!”

Gerard groaned again. “By the holy virgin, I wish you were both at Jericho, bellowing.”

“Thank you, comrade,” Denys said. “Then I’ll bark no more. But if need be, I’ll bite. If he pricks you with his lance, my sword-hilt knocks against his ribs. I’ve said it.”

Denys folded his arms, pale and grim.

Gerard sighed. “Now, since this is about me, let me speak.”

“Let the young man choose life or death,” the doctor said.

Gerard spoke with calm, gentle clarity—unlike either man.

“I doubt not you both mean well. But you assassinate me between you. Calmness and quiet are everything to me. Yet you are like two dogs growling over a bone. And truly, I would be bone, if this noise continues.”

Silence fell—broken only by Gerard’s soft voice as he gazed upward.

“First, venerable sir, thank you for coming—whether from kindness or trade. All trades must live.

“Your learning seems vast, and your age vouches for your experience.

“You say you’ve bled many, and many lived. I believe you.

“You say others you bled died. I believe you too.

“Denys knows less than you, but he knows what he sees. He does not guess. I’ve seen this myself. He says fevered, bled men mostly die—fevered, unbled men live. I must believe him.

“So here, all is doubt.

“But this is certain: if I am bled, I must pay you—and endure the agony of a hot iron, though I am no felon.

“To pay money and suffer for a doubtful cure—I will never do.

“Next to ease, peace is a treasure—especially in a sickroom. But it seems men cannot discuss medicine without anger and raised voices. Therefore, sir, I will try sleep. Denys, go outside and look upon the women of the town. I will not keep you from those who can afford blood and gold for flebotomy and cautery.”

The doctor’s temper flared. He had mastered it during the argument, but now it broke free. The noblest course was silence—he knew it—and so he rose, walked to the door, followed by his boy and basket.

But at the door, he choked. Swelled. Burst.

He whirled around, mouth open, forcing the boy and basket to dart sideways—*de minimis non curat Medicina*, even in rage.

“Ah! You reject my skill, scorn my art! My revenge shall be to leave you to yourself. Lost idiot—take your last look at me and the sun. Your blood be on your head!” And he stormed out.

But at the door, he turned again, tail twitching like a cat’s.

“In twelve hours, you’ll enter the second stage of fever. Your head will split. Your carotids will thump. Aha! And if a pin drops, you’ll jump to the ceiling. Then send for me—and I’ll not come.”

He departed. But at the handle, fury seized him. He spun back, pale-faced, boy trembling, basket swaying.

“Next—CRAMPS of the STOMACH. Aha!

“Then—BILIOUS VOMIT. Aha!

“And after that—nothing can save you. Not even I. And if I could, I would not. Farewell!”

Even Denys paled. But Gerard merely clenched his teeth in rage and gripped his bolster tightly.

This lit the fire anew. The insulted elder returned from the threshold, whisking train in tow.

“And after that—MADNESS!

“And after that—BLACK VOMIT!

“And then—CONVULSIONS!

“And then—THAT CESSATION OF ALL VITAL FUNCTIONS THE VULGAR CALL 'DEATH,' for which thank your own Satanic folly and insolence. Farewell.”

He left. He returned. He roared: “And think not to be buried in a Christian churchyard! The bailiff is my friend. I shall tell him how and why you died: *felo de se!* *Felo de se!* Farewell!”

Gerard sprang up, somehow lifted by fury, and seeing him move, the furious orator charged forward, fist raised, ready to unleash some final threat—lost to history.

But as he came, bolster flew—hurled by Gerard like a missile—striking the doctor square in the face. He crashed down, the boy’s head cracked beneath him, and the doctor tumbled into the basket, wedged upside-down, crushing phials one after another. The boy, lighter, scattered far, landing in a squat, howling.

The doctor’s face twisted in horror. He shrieked—a sound louder and more unearthly than any before—and kicked wildly, struggling to escape.

He was sitting on the hot coals.

They had singed his robe. Now they bit his flesh.

Struggling in vain, he rolled sideways with the basket—then came a great hissing. Gerard rushed forward, wrenching the basket off with effort. The doctor lay face down, groaning, his robe beautifully painted with various poisons—some green, some blue, some purple—by the very medicines he’d brought.

Gerard and Denys helped him up.

“Courage, man,” Gerard said. “It’s but cautery. Balm of Gilead—why, you recommended it just now to my comrade.”

The worthy physician returned home, his face grimacing with pain, and told his housekeeper he was suffering from “a bad burn.” Those were the precise words. For in matters of phlogiston as in matters of morality, we often scorch others’ fingers while our own are left blistered. His housekeeper, a woman of old-fashioned remedies, applied a poultice as mild as milk. He endured it without complaint—like a lamb beneath her care—his sole concern being the healing of his patient. Meanwhile, he drafted a bill for broken vials and took swift steps to have the travelers arrested. Before a magistrate, he swore under oath that the strangers, owing him money, intended to flee the town at once. Alas, it was not his lucky day. His honest effort to lie was thwarted by an unforeseen truth: he had spoken the truth—and in an affidavit.

When the officers arrived at “The Silver Lion,” they found the guests had vanished. They hastened down to the riverbank, gathered intelligence from the locals, and set off upriver in hot pursuit.

This narrow escape owed itself entirely to Denys’s quick thinking. After a burst of laughter—so hearty it seemed a tonic—he repeated his favorite phrase three times, then turned serious. “Dusseldorf is no place for us,” he declared. “That old man left unnaturally quiet for someone so talkative. We’re strangers here; the bailiff is his friend. In five minutes, we’ll be locked in a dungeon for assaulting a local dignitary. Are you strong enough to limp to the river? It’s close by. Once there, you can lie down in a boat instead of a bed. What difference does it make?”

“What difference, Denys?” Gerard replied, already stirred. “None at all—except that it favors the boat. I long for Rome; Rome leads me to Sevenbergen. And when we reach it, we shall lie in a boat—but on the Rhine, the famous Rhine, cool and refreshing. I feel its breeze already. Just seeing it will cure my little hop-'o-my-thumb fever. Away! Away!”

Seeing his friend so eager, Denys quickly settled with the landlord and they rushed toward the river. To their dismay, they learned the public ferry had departed half an hour earlier, and no other vessel would leave that afternoon. But after many questions and a growing crowd, they secured a private boat from an old man and his two sons.

A bystander mocked them. “The current is too strong for three oars.”

“Then my comrade and I will help row,” said the invalid.

“No need,” replied the old man. “Bless your silly heart—*he owns the other boat.*”

A strong wind blew from behind. The boatmen raised a broad sail and rowed with vigor, sending the craft skimming along at a brisk pace.

“Are you feeling better, lad, from the river air?” Denys asked.

“Much better. Though truth be told, the doctor did me good.”

“The doctor? You refused every one of his cures.”

“No, but—I know you’ll say I’m mad—but knocking that old fool down… somehow… it soothed me.”

“Amiable dove!” Denys laughed. “How your character unfolds each day, like a rosebud. I misjudged you at first.”

“Do not mistake me, Denys. I could have borne his idle threats—though his voice pierced my ears. But he was an infidel, or near enough. Such men I’ve been taught to despise. Did he not imply we owed our very insides to men with long Greek names, rather than to Him, whose name is but a syllable, yet whose hand rests over all the earth? Pagan!”

“So you knocked him down—like a good Christian,” Denys teased.

“Now, Denys, do not jest. Do not take the side of a villain. Had it been a thunderbolt from Heaven, he would have met his due. Yet he only received a poor blow from this weak arm.”

“What weak arm?” Denys asked, eyes twinkling.

“I’ve lived among arms, and by Samson’s strength, I’ve never seen one more like a catapult. That bolster wrapped around his nose, the ends kissed behind his head, and his forehead rang—had he been Goliath or Caesar, he’d have fallen. St. Denys protect me from such feeble foes as you—and above all, from your weak arms—you diabolical young hypocrite.”

The river wound through many bends, sometimes shifting the wind to their side. Then all moved to the weather side to prevent the boat from leaning too far—except a child of about five, the boatman’s grandson and his pet. The boy had slipped aboard just as they cast off. So light he was, he didn’t affect the balance, and thus remained untouched by the laws of navigation.

They sailed cheerfully onward, unaware that a whole posse of constables, armed with the bailiff’s writ, pursued them closely. Their hunters were gaining ground, for if the wind was strong, so was the current.

Then Gerard suddenly realized their course was not toward Burgundy. “Oh, Denys,” he said, alarmed, “this isn’t your way.”

“I know,” Denys replied calmly. “But what can I do? I cannot leave you until the fever leaves you—and it hasn’t. You grow red and pale by turns. I’ve watched you. I must go on to Cologne, I fear, and then cross country.”

“Thank Heaven!” Gerard exclaimed joyfully. Then, with a touch of self-deception, he added, “It would be a sin to be so near Cologne and not see it. Oh, man, it’s a vast, ancient city—just as I’ve dreamed of, though never seen. Me miserable, what cruel fortune brings me here now? Well, Denys,” he continued, less warmly, “it’s old enough to have been founded by a Roman lady in the first century, sacked by Attila the Hun, and later damaged by Norman Lothaire. It has a church for every week of the year—plus countless chapels and convents. Above all, the great minster, still unfinished, where lie the Three Kings who brought gifts to Christ: Melchior with gold, Gaspar with frankincense, and Balthazar, the black king, with myrrh. Over their bones stands the shrine—a wonder of the world—of ever-shining brass brighter than gold, adorned with finely wrought images, inlaid with intricate designs and rich colors. Two broad stripes run across it, studded with jewels so large and rare, each could crown a king or ransom a prince. On top stand the three kings, skillfully crafted—two in solid silver, gilded, bare-headed; the third, of Ethiopian ebony, wearing a golden crown. In the center, the Blessed Virgin, made of virgin silver, holds Christ in her arms. At the corners, golden branches hold four wax tapers burning night and day. Holy eyes have tended that flame for ages, and holy eyes shall guard it forever. I tell you, Denys, the oldest songs, the oldest Flemish and German legends, speak of those flames burning—yes, they shall light the earth to its grave.”

“And St. Ursel’s Church,” Gerard went on, “where lies a British saint. Her bones rest there, along with eleven thousand virgins who died for the faith—slain by Moorish barbarians on October 23, 238. Their bones are piled in vaults, many skulls displayed in the church. St. Ursel’s skull is encased in thin gold and placed on the high altar—shown only to humble Christians on solemn days.”

“Eleven thousand virgins!” Denys cried. “What tiny babies German men must have been in those days. I wish all their bones might turn to flesh again, and their skulls to sweet faces—should we pass through the gates. ‘Tis likely some of them are tired of their state by now.”

“Tush, Denys!” Gerard rebuked. “Why must you, being good, always seem evil? If your wishing-cap is on, pray that we meet the least of all those wise virgins in the next life—and for that, let us honor their holy dust in this one.”

“And then there’s the church of the Maccabees,” Gerard continued, “and the cauldron where they and their mother Solomona were boiled by a wicked king for refusing to eat pork.”

“Oh, peremptory king! And pig-headed Maccabees!” Denys chuckled. “I’d gladly eat bacon with my pork rather than swap places with my meat at the fire.”

“What vile words!” Gerard snapped. “It was their faith.”

“Nay, bridle your temper. Tell me—besides churches—are there nothing else in this city you praise? For I prefer Sir Knight to Sir Priest.”

“Ay, marry,” Gerard said. “There’s an university nearly a hundred years old. A marketplace no fairer in the world, with houses at the corners as grand as palaces. A magnificent senate-house covered in statues, and at the front stands a figure of stout Herman Gryn—a soldier like yourself, lad.”

“Ay! Tell me of him! What deed earned him his place?”

“A rare one. He slew a lion in fair combat, with only his cloak and short sword. He thrust the cloak into the beast’s mouth and cut its spine in two. There stands his effigy—and the lion’s—to prove it. Such a feat has been done by only three others: Samson, Lysimachus of Macedon, and Benaiah, captain of David’s host.”

“Marry! Three tall fellows. I’d like to sup with them tonight.”

“So would not I,” Gerard replied dryly.

“But tell me,” Denys said, surprised, “when were you in Cologne?”

“Never—but in spirit. I converse with the monks along the way. They tell me all things old and new.”

“Ay, ay,” Denys grinned. “Have I not seen your nose peeking beneath their cowls? When you speak of things unseen, your words are small, the thing great. But your words match or surpass the thing. You’re a fine painter with your tongue—I’ve said it. And as a saint, ready with hand, steel, or bolster—as any sinner alive. Now, shall I tell you what draws me to Cologne?”

“Ay, Denys.”

“You—only you. Not a dead saint, but my living friend, my true comrade. You alone draw Denys of Burgundy to Cologne.”

Gerard lowered his head.

At that moment, one of the younger boatmen asked sharply, “What’s wrong with ‘little turnip-face’?”

The child—thus nicknamed—had just stepped aft, solemn as a judge, then burst into sudden tears.

He was subjected to a barrage of questions—some gentle, some sharp. Had he hurt himself? Eaten too much? Been frightened? Cold? Sick? An idiot?

To each, he replied with equal fervor: *Oh! oh! oh!*—in English, or *Hi! hi! hi!*—in French. So fixed are fiction’s phonetics.

“Who knows what ails the pestilent brat?” snarled the young boatman. “Rather look this way and tell me whom those men are following!”

The old man and his son glanced over and saw four men walking along the east bank. At once, they stopped rowing and huddled in the stern, whispering and glancing between passengers and pursuers.

They might have done better to ponder the mystery of the turnip-faced child. I beg pardon—by my age, I mean the profound mind of fearless infancy.

“If it’s as I suspect,” whispered one youth, “why not give them a fright? Let’s head for the west bank.”

The old man objected fiercely. “Run into trouble for strangers? Are you mad? No. Rather, let’s cross to the east side—keep the strong arm with us! That’s my counsel. What say you, Werter?”

“I say, please yourselves.”

What age and youth could not decide, the wind settled impartially. A squall struck, and the boat leaned violently. The men scrambled to windward to steady it—only to see, horror-struck, a ditch of water rushing from stem to stern. Then, in an instant, they saw nothing—only felt the cold, rushing Rhine.

“Turnip-face” had pulled the plug.

The officers untied the cords from their waists. Gerard could swim like a duck—but even the best swimmer, flung from a capsized boat, must sink before he can rise. Dark water bubbled over his head. Then he surfaced, dazed and deaf for a moment. Next, he saw the black hull upside down, figures clinging to it. He shook his head like a dog, and instinctively swam toward it. But just before reaching it, he heard a voice behind him—low, but filled with deep anguish—cry, “Adieu, comrade, adieu!”

He turned—and there was Denys, sinking, sinking, weighed down by his heavy arbalest. Pale, eyes wide, staring desperately at his dear friend.

Gerard screamed—a cry of love and terror—and lunged forward, cutting through the water wildly. But the next moment, Denys was gone beneath the waves.

Then Gerard followed.

The officers tied a rope and threw the end into the churning water.

In life, good and evil often balance each other in ways both subtle and profound. The very steel bow strapped to the back of the arbalestrier had nearly drowned him—yet it was that same weapon, held aloft by his own hands, that now saved him. Gerard seized the bow with one hand, and with the other slipped between the bow and its cord, securing a firm grip. In an instant, Denys was hauled upward with such force that half his body broke the surface of the river.

“Don’t touch me! Don’t touch me!” Gerard shouted, trembling at the thought of a fatal mistake.

“Pas si bete,” Denys gasped, choking on water.

Seeing the kind of man he faced, Gerard’s fear melted into calm confidence. “On your back,” he commanded sharply. Seizing the crossbow, he pushed forward, aiding the motion. “Hand on my shoulder! Slap the water with the other—no, downward, like this. Do nothing but what I say.”

He grabbed hold of Denys’s long hair, twisted it tightly, and clamped the end between his teeth. With the strength of youth and the sinews of his neck, he kept the soldier’s head above water, striking out powerfully against the current. For a moment, Gerard hesitated—should he swim toward the west bank or the east? He didn’t know how vital that choice would be. Then, seeing the western shore slightly nearer, he turned toward it, abandoning the safer path to jail for a daring detour—one that would become legend.

The current pulled them sideways, and after swimming nearly a hundred yards, Denys murmured uneasily, “How much farther?”

“Courage,” Gerard mumbled. “Whatever a duck knows, a Dutchman knows. You’re as safe as if you were in bed.”

Then, to their surprise, they found themselves wading through shallow water and stepped ashore.

Once on solid ground, they stared at each other from head to toe, as though their eyes could consume the other’s soul. Then, instinctively, they threw their arms around one another’s necks, breathing heavily, hearts too full for words. At that sacred moment, life felt sweeter than heaven—especially for the exiled lover who had just rescued his friend.

Oh, what poet has ever reached the height of such joy? To save a life—especially the life of one you love. Such moments are worth living for, yes, even three score years and ten.

After a while, they calmed down, took each other’s hands, and walked along the riverbank side by side, like lovers lost in bliss, caring little where they went.

Meanwhile, the boatmen had managed to right their craft—the once concave vessel now convex—and all were safely aboard. Herr Turnip-face, the self-styled “Inverter of Things,” stood calmly in the center, seemingly unshaken by the chaos. He greeted them when they fell into the Rhine, and greeted them again when they emerged.

“Shall we wait until they fix the boat?” asked Gerard.

“No,” replied Denys. “Our fare is paid. We owe them nothing. Let us go—quickly.”

Denys agreed, noting they could walk all the way to Cologne along the riverbank.

“I’m not going to Cologne,” said Gerard quietly.

“What? Then where?”

“To Burgundy.”

“To Burgundy? Ah, no—that’s too good to be true.”

“It is true, and sensible besides. What does it matter how I reach Rome?”

“Nay, nay—you only say that to please me. This change is too sudden. And do not think me so cruel as to believe you without hesitation. Did I not see your eyes light up at the wonders of Cologne—the churches, the statues, the relics?”

“How dull you are, Denys. That was when we were meant to share them together. Churches? I’ll see plenty, wherever I go. The bones of saints and martyrs—alas, the world is full of them. But a friend like you—where else on earth can I find another? No, I will not turn you from the road to your home, nor from the woman who waits for you. Nor will I take myself from you by leaving. Since I pulled you from the Rhine, I love you more than ever. You are my pearl—I fished you out, and I must keep you. So do not argue. Or you’ll bring back my fever. Instead, cry courage and lead on—hey for Burgundy!”

Denys leapt with joy. “Courage! Va pour la Bourgogne! Oh, soyez tranquille! Cette fois il est bien decidément mort, ce coquin-là.”

And they turned their backs on the Rhine.

As soon as their decision became clear, a commotion erupted across the river among those who had watched the scene unfold. Before the friends had taken many steps, a voice called out from the opposite bank: “HALT!”

Gerard turned and saw one of the four men holding a badge of office and a parchment scroll. His heart sank—he was a dutiful citizen, used to obeying authority, especially when it summoned him back to Düsseldorf under the law.

But Denys felt no such scruples. He was French, and scorned foreign lands, laws, customs, and people alike. A soldier, he viewed the situation militarily: superior force ahead, a river between, their rear open. Retreat was simple. He saw the boat still drifting midstream and knew no ferry lay closer than Düsseldorf.

“I shall make a quick retreat to that hill,” he declared. “Then, out of sight, we’ll march swiftly.”

They walked off leisurely.

“Halt! In the bailiff’s name!” came a cry from the shore.

Denys turned, snapped his fingers mockingly at the bailiff, and continued.

“Halt! In the archbishop’s name!”

Again, he snapped his fingers and moved on.

“Halt! In the emperor’s name!”

A third time, he flicked his fingers at the emperor himself and kept walking.

Gerard watched this display with quiet dismay. Once they passed the hilltop, he said, “Now there’s only one course—we must run to Burgundy instead of walking.”

And he began to run, covering nearly a league before stopping.

Denys was breathless. “What on earth happened to your fever?”

“I begin to miss it terribly,” Gerard replied dryly.

“I dropped it in the Rhine, I suppose,” Denys answered.

Soon they reached a small village. There, Denys bought a loaf of bread and a large bottle of Rhenish wine.

“We must sleep somewhere hidden,” he said. “If we stay at an inn, they’ll arrest us in our beds.”

It was sound judgment. In that age, the web of law enforcement was tight, especially for common folk. Though public cooperation was scarce—particularly on the Continent—inns were closely monitored. Innkeepers were held partly responsible for their guests’ actions, sometimes even more than for their safety.

Both men were glad when night fell. And when, after a long journey beneath the stars (the moon, if memory serves, rising only near dawn), they reached a large barn attached to a distant house, they felt relief.

The barn had recently been used for threshing barley. One pile of straw rose almost as high as the untouched corn on the other side.

“Here are two royal beds,” said Denys. “Which shall we choose—the mow or the straw?”

“The straw for me,” Gerard replied.

They sat on the heap, ate their bread, drank their wine, and then Denys covered Gerard with straw, piling it high and leaving only a small opening for air.

“Water kills fevered men,” he muttered. “I’ll make warm water on him, anyway.”

Gerard smiled faintly. “These few drops from the Rhine won’t chill me. I feel hot enough to parch a kennel—or boil a cloud, if I were in one.”

With that, he drifted into unconsciousness.

Denys stayed awake for a time, listening. Then he heard it—the thunder of hooves coming from Düsseldorf. The wooden barn trembled as riders galloped past, their shouts echoing with a sound familiar in the 15th century, yet strange today—like the war-whoop of a Native American warrior.

Denys shivered where he lay. But Gerard slept on, undisturbed.

The troop passed, and the noise faded into silence. The soldier drew a deep breath, whistled softly, closed his eyes—and slept like a top.

At dawn, Denys sat up and reached out to wake Gerard. His hand touched the young man’s forehead—and found it drenched in sweat.

As a nurse, Denys refrained from waking him. “It’s ill to disturb sleep or sweat in a sick man,” he said. “I know that well, though I’ve never minced an ape or a gallows-bird.”

After waiting an hour, hunger overcame him. He turned over and, in self-defense, fell asleep again—a trick he’d learned from years of hardship.

At noon, he awoke to find Gerard sitting upright, surrounded by smoke rising from the straw like a dung heap. Heat versus moisture.

Gerard called him “a lazy loon.”

Denys grinned silently.

They set out again. The first thing Denys did was return the crossbow to Gerard and climb a tall tree beside the road.

“Coast clear to the next village,” he announced, and they continued.

As they neared the settlement, Denys stopped suddenly and asked, “How do you feel?”

“What? Can’t you see? I feel as if Rome were no farther than that hamlet.”

“But your body—your skin?”

“Neither hot nor cold. Yesterday it was hot one moment, cold the next. But this cursed leg—it won’t leave me alone.”

“Le grand malheur!” Denys sighed. “Many of my comrades faced no such trouble.”

“Oh, here it goes again—itching terribly.”

“Unhappy youth,” Denys said solemnly, “the sum of your troubles is this: your fever is gone, and your wound is healing.”

“And so,” he added gently, “I shall tell you something I might have kept silent.”

“What is it?” Gerard asked, eyes bright with curiosity.

“Oh!”

Gerard stood stunned by the sudden news, his face flushing and fading in rapid succession. Then, with a surge of anger, he clenched his jaw, teeth gritted tight. Men of true spirit, like the wild boar, may flee when faced with overwhelming strength—perhaps because they are not fools—but if pursued too closely, too persistently, until driven to desperation, they will wheel about and charge with furious rage, trampling all who stand in their way. Gerard, too, braced himself for battle. But no sooner had he steeled his resolve than his expression faltered, and he whispered, brokenly, “And my axe is in Rhine.”

They conferred in silence, torn between caution and necessity. Prudence urged them to avoid the village altogether; hunger demanded food. In the end, hunger spoke loudest, though prudence offered the most compelling argument. They decided upon a course: cross the open fields.

At a haystack near the road, they stopped and took two bundles of hay without asking. They laid them in a dry ditch, hidden from sight but tangled in nettles. One by one, they slipped out, gathered turnips from nearby fields, and returned to eat them in secret as they retreated through the twilight. They continued this way, nibbling at their meager harvest, until the sun sank below the horizon.

Then, shivering and drenched, they emerged into the storm—rain lashing down, darkness swallowing all, wind howling like a pack of wolves. They could neither see nor hear, nor be seen or heard. For all they knew, they passed within arm’s reach of their enemies, unseen as phantoms drifting through the night. The terror of the tempest—the blackness, the fury of the gale—drowned out all thought of pursuit. It felt as though they were carving their path through solid darkness, blind and desperate.

When the moon finally broke through the clouds, they were many miles beyond Dusseldorf. Yet still they walked on, weary but unyielding. Soon, they came upon a massive stone building, its towers rising stark against the sky.

“Courage!” Denys called out, his voice catching with relief. “I believe I know this place. Yes—it is. We are within the diocese of Juliers. Cologne holds no sway here.”

In that instant, they stepped inside the convent walls—and found safety.

Gerard met a monk who had built the great sundial in the prior’s garden, a water-drawing wheel, and a winnowing machine for grain—always at work on some clever device. He had crafted several psalteries and two dulcimers, and now was fashioning a set of regalles, a small organ for the choir. Gerard could play the psaltery a little, but the monk played it with such grace and skill that he made Gerard feel like a mere beginner. The monk also illuminated manuscripts beautifully, though his handwriting did not match Gerard’s elegance.

As they compared their talents—each with genuine warmth and sincerity, as men of their time did when learning reflected true passion—young and old quickly grew close, like brothers. The monk pressed Gerard to stay the night. Gerard consulted Denys, who nodded reluctantly, shrugging as if to say, “What can we do?”

Gerard told the monk where he was headed and recounted their recent adventures, softening the tale of the bolstered man. “Alack!” said the old monk, “I’ve traveled far in my day, but never once was I troubled.” He warned Gerard to avoid inns—they were full of rogues and rowdies, places where one’s soul might suffer even if the body escaped unharmed. Instead, he advised lodging in peaceful monasteries each night. Then, suddenly sharp-eyed and intense, he asked, “How long has it been since you were shriven?”

Gerard flushed and murmured, “Better than a fortnight.”

“And thou an exorcist! No wonder perils have found thee,” the monk replied. “Come—thou must be absolved at once.”

“Yes, father,” said Gerard humbly, “with all my heart,” and began to kneel, hands clasped. But the monk stopped him sharply.

“Not to me! Not to me! I am as worldly as any man alive. My soul is wrapped up in these wooden pipes and leather stops—things that will perish, along with those whose minds are fixed upon such vanities.”

“Dear father,” Gerard said gently, “these instruments serve the Church. Surely that sanctifies the labor?”

“That,” the monk said, wagging a finger with half-playful warning, “is exactly what the devil has been whispering into my ear. He reminds me how Solomon built a house for the Lord with fine hangings—and that was counted good, not sinful. Oh, he quotes Scripture well!”

“But I am no simpleton,” he declared, turning abruptly toward empty air as if addressing a hidden presence, “no fool who thinks toys are holy. This one project done—vigils, fasts, prayers: standing, lying on the chapel floor, even in a tub of cold water. Nothing frightens the devil more than seeing monks pray while soaked to the chin. For *corpus domat aqua*—the body loves water.”

He winked at Gerard. “Now go confess your little sins—youthful, secular, pardonable—and leave me to mine, sweet as honey, and to be atoned for in kind.”

Gerard bowed, but couldn’t help asking, “Where may I find a confessor more holy and merciful?”

“In each cell here,” the monk replied simply. “Go to Brother Anselm—there.”

Gerard walked down the corridor, following the direction. The doors stood close together, and he seemed to misjudge. Just as he raised his hand to knock, he heard a hushed cry from his friend: “Nay! nay! nay!”

He turned. There stood the monk at his own door, agitated, pacing back and forth, clapping his hands like a sawyer. Gerard thought the cell he’d approached must house a beast—or worse, the very figure whose presence had been so plainly announced in the monastery.

He looked back questioningly, then moved to the next door. Instantly, the monk nodded rapidly, his face softening into relief, and vanished inside. He took out his hourglass, flipped it over, and returned to his work on the regalles. Again and again he glanced up, muttering, “Well-a-day, how swift the sands run when a man is bent on earthly things.”

Brother Anselm was a venerable monk, with a broad head and a face radiating both dignity and kindness. As Gerard confessed, answering the gentle yet probing questions, he found himself thinking, “Here is a face—I wonder if I may draw it after this?” And in that moment, his thoughts wandered, and he forgot a few sins.

But this time he did not downplay the incident with the bolster, nor did he minimize the pagan nature of the man involved.

The penance was simple: enter the church, prostrate himself before the altar, kiss its lowest step three times, then kneel and recite three Our Fathers and one Credo. “When done, return to me immediately.”

Gerard completed his task and returned to find Brother Anselm spreading plaster on his leg.

“After the soul, the body,” the monk said. “Know that I am the surgeon here, lacking a better. This is to cool your wound—not burn it. The saints forbid.”

During the treatment, Anselm, naturally intrigued by the Dusseldorf episode, sided with Denys on the matter of bleeding.

“We Dominicans rarely bleed patients anymore. Lay doctors say it’s due to cowardice or incompetence. But truthfully, we’ve long seen that simples—herbs—can cure most ills that can be cured at all. They don’t kill when used wisely; other remedies strike like thunderbolts. And remember: the Vulgate says plainly, ‘The blood is the life of a man.’ In medicine, law, or theology, to think oneself wiser than God is folly. Besides, simples are powerful. A small creature bitten by a venomous snake finds a herb strong enough to counteract the poison—stronger, faster than any human sickness. We learn from her wisdom and our traditions, still seeking the gifts God has scattered across the earth—some to feed, others to heal. Only in dire cases do we mix heavenly and earthly virtue. We steep relics—hair or bone of a saint—in the remedy, and miracles follow.”

“Do you truly believe it’s the relic?” Gerard asked. “Peter a Floris, a learned physician and no pagan, denies it.”

“What does Peter a Floris know? And what do I know? I cannot claim we command the saints, or force them to lend their power. But I see that patients, drinking such remedies in faith, often improve—as if by charm. Faith in the receiver plays a great part. And so it always has. A woman healed by touching Christ’s garment—had she not touched it, she would not have been healed. Had she worn it without faith, it would have meant nothing. But let us not probe too deeply. All around us calls for faith. Have patience. One day we shall understand. Meanwhile, as your confessor, I strictly forbid you, on your soul’s health, to heed learned laymen on matters of religion. Arrogance is their downfall—it shuts heaven’s door in their own faces. Remember: I speak of *learned* laymen. Unlearned ones have often taught me humility—may they teach you too.”

Your wound is cared for. In three days, it will be only a scar. God speed you, and may the saints make you as good and happy as you are thoughtful and kind.”

Gerard wished he need not leave just yet—he was to dine in the refectory. But Brother Anselm said, with a faint regret, that he would not leave his cell this week—he was in penance. With gentle hands, he lifted Gerard’s head and kissed his brow. Before the door closed, he was already back to his devotions.

Gerard left, chilled by the loneliness of monastic life, saddened. “Alas,” he thought, “this kind face I shall never see again. That voice—gone from my ears, from my heart, forever. There is only meeting and parting in this sorrowful world. Well-a-day, well-a-day!”

His melancholy was broken by a young monk who led him to the refectory. There, several monks sat at a table, and Denys stood stiff as a poker, being questioned about the towns ahead. The friars pooled their knowledge, charting a route and marking every religious house along the way. They handed Gerard the map.

Then came supper. Afterward, the old monk guided Gerard to his cell. They talked eagerly, and the friar finally revealed the reason for his earlier pantomime.

“You nearly fell into Brother Jerome’s hands. That was his cell.”

“Is Brother Jerome a wicked man?” Gerard asked.

“A wicked man?” the friar crossed himself. “A saint—an anchorite, the very pillar of this house! He would have sent you barefoot to Loretto. Ah, I forgot—you’re bound for Italy. He’d have sent you to Canterbury or Compostella instead. But Jerome was born old and cloaked. Anselm and I were boys once—wicked beyond imagining” (Gerard looked skeptical). “That keeps us humble, and makes us lenient toward youth and hot blood.”

At Gerard’s request, the monk played one last melody on the psaltery—a heavenly strain that calmed the troubled spirit and soothed the weary heart. Then came rest.

I have described this day in full—not because it was extraordinary, but because it stands as a symbol of many such days that followed. For the travelers, worn and weather-beaten, found that life, like the road, is not evenly filled with drama. Great events come in clusters, separated by stretches of quiet. Perhaps they draw each other through unseen links. But there is more—life itself is an intermittent fever.

All storytellers, whether of history or fiction, must either skip these quiet intervals or risk dragging the narrative. Yet this practice gives readers a false sense of proportion—one I wish to avoid here. So I ask your understanding: though no vivid adventure followed for a long while, one journey succeeded another. One monastery after another welcomed them freely—kindly, sometimes warmly—feeding and sheltering them without charge. Though their only enemies were winter and harsh weather—challenges not to be underestimated—they marched across vast distances, covering more ground than I have detailed.

And so, Gerard—bronzed and travel-stained from head to foot—and Denys, whose shoes were in tatters, feet swollen and sore, drew near the Burgundian frontier.

Gerard was nearly as eager for the promised land of Burgundy as Denys himself. The soldier never tired of singing its praises, and at every minor irritation he would remind Gerard how much better things were done in that refined region. Above all, he dwelled on the promise of clean linens at the inns—something Gerard had longed for since leaving home. “I ask no more,” the Hollander would say, with a weary sigh. “To think I’ve not lain in a bare bed once since I left my house! When I see their linen, instead of taking off my clothes, it’s my eyes and nose I’d gladly shut away.”

Denys carried his affection for his homeland so far that he walked twenty leagues in shoes that had burst apart rather than buy new ones from a German merchant—whose rudeness, delays, and general ill-manners made him seem less a trader than an enemy. At sunset, the two travelers found themselves equally distant from a small town and a monastery, though the latter lay off the main road. Denys insisted on the inn; Gerard, on the convent. In the end, Denys gave in—but only after extracting a promise that once they reached Burgundy, they would always choose inns over monasteries. Gerard agreed readily, for his map of religious houses ended here.

They turned aside from the path.

Now, Gerard asked with quiet surprise why this sudden distaste for places that had often fed and sheltered them without charge. Denys hesitated at first, clearing his throat and shifting his weight, but then his pent-up grievances erupted.

“It’s not sudden,” he said at last. “It’s been there all along—a deep-rooted horror I’ve kept quiet out of politeness. But now, since we’re near the end, I’ll speak plainly. I saw they’d put powder in your drink,” he added, “so I held my tongue. But now, being the last, why not let it all out? Know this: I’ve felt like a fish out of water in every one of those great stone prisons. You vanish straightaway with some old monk, and I’m left to endure my purgatory alone.”

“Forgive me,” said Gerard softly. “I’ve been selfish.”

“Aye, aye,” replied Denys, “I forgive you, little one. It’s not your fault—you’re not the first fool to be priest-rid and monk-hit. But I’ll never forgive *them* for my misery.”

Then, as if recalling a trial before Henry VIII’s commissioners, he launched into his indictment.

These gloomy towers were all built alike. Inns varied, but monasteries offered nothing but repetition. A great gate, a smaller one, a flight of steps, and then a shadowy cloister. There, the dortour—the sleeping hall. Elsewhere, the cold, vast refectory, where silence was enforced—or at least whispers. “And who can eat in silence?” he demanded. “Who wants to sit mute while his belly grumbles? Or worse—when tinkle, tinkle, tinkle goes the bell, and you must rise for church, even if your soul is too numb for prayer. I am not a pig at worship, I tell you.”

“And then,” he continued, “you’re supposed to go to bed with your eyes open. By the time you manage to close them, some restless spirit has pulled the rope again—tinkle, tinkle—and now you must recite a prayer in the dark, whether you know one or not. If they heard the prayers I mutter when they wake me up like that—well, they’d have cause to shudder!”

He paused, then added: “You fall asleep again, get a few hours’ rest—then it’s tinkle, tinkle again, for matins.”

“And the only clapper you truly love,” Gerard interjected half-jokingly, “is a woman’s.”

“Because there’s music in that—even when she scolds,” came the firm reply.

“And then,” Denys went on, “the endless checks. I touch the salt cellar with my finger—‘Have you no knife?’ they cry. I wipe my knife on the cloth to save time—‘Wipe it dirty on the bread, and clean upon the cloth!’ Oh, petty souls! These tiny, priggish rules chill good fellowship like icicles melting from straw roofs.”

“I hold cleanliness no pedantry,” said Gerard firmly. “You should learn better manners once and for all.”

“Nay,” retorted Denys. “It’s they who lack manners. They silence a man at every word.”

“At every other word,” Gerard corrected, “only when it’s obscene or blasphemous.”

“Exaggerator!” Denys snapped. “Why, at the very last of these dungeons, I found poor travelers huddled round a monk, chilled and silent as criminals waiting for execution. To cheer them, I shouted, ‘Courage, tout le monde, le dia—’”

“Connu! What happened?” Gerard interrupted.

“Well,” said Denys, “‘Blaspheme not!’ said the fellow. ‘Plait-il,’ I replied. Doesn’t he wheel about and snap at me in a kind of Alsatian French, turning every P into a B. I could barely keep from laughing in his face.”

“Being yourself unable to speak ten words of his language without error,” Gerard pointed out.

“True,” Denys admitted. “But everyone ought to speak French. What use are so many tongues, except to draw a wall between men’s hearts?”

“But what did he say?” Gerard pressed.

“What matters what a fool says?” Denys countered.

“Oh, not all a fool’s words are folly,” Gerard replied. “Or I wouldn’t listen to you.”

“Well,” Denys said, “he said, ‘Those who begin by flouting the Devil’s name will end by doing the same to all the names in heaven.’ I said, ‘Father, I am a soldier—this is merely my “consigne,” my watchword.’ He asked, ‘Oh, so it’s just a custom?’ I didn’t understand the old fox, thinking to clear myself, so I said, ‘Yes, it was.’ Then he said, ‘Ah, that’s ten times worse. It will bring him down on you one day. He still comes where his name is often called.’”

“And yet,” Gerard observed, “he showed no gratitude for news neither his missals nor breviary had ever revealed.”

“No,” Denys agreed. “Then he told me soldiers usually commit the crimes others are broken on the wheel for—murder, rape, pillage.”

“And is that not true?” Gerard asked.

“True or not,” Denys replied cautiously, “it was ill mannered.”

“And so,” Gerard persisted, “this courteous host says, ‘Since you are enemies of mankind, why make enemies of good spirits too, by shouting the names of evil ones?’ And a lot more nonsense.”

“Well,” Gerard said gently, “whether you heed his advice or not, why blame someone for raising his voice to save your soul?”

“How can his voice save my soul,” Denys shot back, “when he keeps turning his P’s into B’s?”

Gerard was stunned. Before he could recover from this thunderbolt of Gallicism, Denys charged ahead, declaring all monks hypocrites.

“Look at them,” he declared. “They slink about, unable to meet a man’s eye like honest folk.”

“Nay,” Gerard said eagerly, “that modest glance downward is part of their discipline—it’s *custodia oculorum*.”

“Cursed toads eating hoc hac horum?” Denys scoffed. “No such thing. That’s how a cutpurse looks. Can’t meet a true man’s eye. Doff the cowl—monk; behold, a thief. Don the cowl—thief; lo, a monk. Tell me, how can they ever look God Almighty in the face, when they can’t even face a man here below?”

Ah, here it is—black as ink! Into the well we go, comrade. Misericorde—there goes the tinkle already. ’Tis the best tinkle of all—for dinner. Wait, listen! I knew it: the wolf in my stomach cried ‘Amen!’”

He confirmed this with two hearty oaths and marched into the convent like a triumphant gamecock, convinced he had won the argument. He did not suspect how deeply he had offended Gerard—with his crude mockery, his vulgar comparisons, and above all, his irreverent tone. Yet Gerard said nothing. Not a word.

In the refectory, where Gerard sat among the monks, conversation turned to the sudden death of the brother who had been entrusted with copying the monastery’s charter and rule. Gerard, hearing this, hesitated only a moment before offering his own services. He spoke softly, not out of pride but from a quiet desire to give something in return for the kindness he’d received during his travels. “Not for hire, my lords,” he said, “but for love—for a small token of gratitude for the many nights your order has sheltered a poor wanderer.”

A monk smiled, pleased by the gesture, yet added gently that the late brother had been an exceptional scribe—so skilled that only another master could continue his work. At once, Gerard drew from his wallet a piece of vellum, its back cleaned and inscribed with careful script as a sample of his hand. The monk stared, then quickly rose and hurried toward the high table, bowing low as he passed the fifth and tenth steps, presenting the vellum to the prior with eager words.

Instantly, a dozen eyes turned to it. A murmur spread through the hall. Then, without warning, the prior pointed—not at the writing, but at Gerard. The monk returned, beaming like a man who had just won a crown, bearing a savory crustade ryal—a rich game pie spiced and glazed—and a silver cup filled with pimentum, a sweetened wine.

Gerard took the cup, bowed deeply first to the distant prior, then to his companions, and drank. As he passed the cup around, the entire table erupted in cheer. “Brother,” they called, “you are no stranger to cloistered ways—confess it!”

He admitted it, thanking Heaven for the truth. Had he not been raised in such a place, he would have stood as awkward and ignorant as Sybrandt and Cornelis beside him. But now he was recognized, and welcomed.

“Yet how did you know?” he asked, puzzled.

“You drank from the cup with both hands,” two monks answered together, nodding as if revealing a sacred secret.

For some time, laughter had been rising from a table near the far end of the hall. Then came a burst so loud and prolonged that even the prior sent the sub-prior himself down to silence them—threatening penance upon every monk present. Gerard flushed with shame, for beneath the uproar he had heard the word “courage!” and the bold voice of Denys of Burgundy.

Soon after, Gerard was given feu Werter’s cell—furnished with wax lights, a tilting frame for writing, and all the tools of a calligrapher. But the task was too great for one night. He turned to Denys, wondering how to ask him to stay longer. To his surprise, Denys replied with unexpected grace: “A day’s rest will do us both good. Write, and I’ll pass the hours as I may.”

When the work was done, the monks praised it highly. They agreed that the monastery’s records had gained more than they had lost with Werter’s passing. The sub-prior pressed a rix-dollar into Gerard’s hand, along with brushes and pigments from the abbey’s ample stores.

As Gerard prepared to leave, his heart warmed. This was a sign—the kind of omen he needed. For it was by the pen he hoped to rebuild his life and reclaim his beloved.

“Come, Denys,” he said cheerfully, showing off his gifts. “See what these good men have given me. Try now to be fairer to them. I confess—I felt my friendship chill when I heard you call them ‘hypocrites.’”

Denys paused, then said, “I recant.”

“Thank you! Thank you, good Denys!”

“I was a scurrilous vagabond,” he admitted.

“Nay, say not so,” Gerard protested.

“But we soldiers are blunt and quick to judge,” Denys continued. “I speak plainly: I lie to myself. And I offer full esteem to those I misunderstood. It is unjust to defame thousands for the sins of a few.”

Now Gerard nodded. “You’ve thought on what I said?”

“Nay—it was their own doing,” Denys replied.

Gerard smiled, pleased to be proved right. Then, with interest, he listened as Denys began to tell how he had changed his mind.

“Well,” said Denys, “on the first day at dinner, a young monk next to me opened his mouth—and laughed. Not a dry chuckle, but a full, musical sound. ‘Ah,’ I said, ‘at last I’ve found a man, not a shorn ape.’ So I slapped his back and gave him my consigne—my salute. ‘Heaven forbid!’ he replied. I stared. The lad looked as solemn as Solomon. A better mime you never saw—even at a Mystery play.

‘I see war sharpens neither wit nor spirit,’ he said. ‘What are the clergy for? To fight the foul fiend. And what are monks for? “The fiend being dead, the friars are sped.” You may plough up the convents—we shall have nothing left to do but become soldiers… and bring him back to life.’”

At this, the whole table roared. “Well,” said Denys, “I told him, ‘You’re the monk for me.’ And he replied, ‘And you’re the crossbowman for me. I’ll wager you could tell tales that’d make our hair stand on end.’ ‘Excusez!’ I said. ‘The barber has taken care of that.’ And there—I had the laugh.”

“What dreadful jesting!” Gerard murmured.

Denys grinned. “Truth be told, I’ve seen funnier tricks with less noise.”

But he went on. “It was a great thing to rid myself of that old prejudice. ‘So,’ I said, ‘I can give you the chaire de poule—if that pleases you.’ ‘We shall see,’ they cried—and a signal passed round.”

Then he recounted, laughing still, how he had been led to a private cell instead of the dormitory, forbidden to sleep, and given a book filled with pictures of monks chasing women. Later, barefoot and wide-eyed, he was brought to the parlour, where a feast fit for a duke awaited him—twelve jovial friars, roaring louder than any troop he’d met in war or peace.

They drank, they joked, they played cards with a deck where Saint Theresa and Saint Catherine, bedecked in gold, were the queens; black, white, grey, and crutched friars were the knaves. Rosaries were staked, and curses flew when someone lost.

Near midnight, a monk slipped out—but not alone. Others followed, watching as he crept into the garden, pulled a rope-ladder from the ivy, and climbed the ten-foot wall. Almost instantly, a russet kirtle appeared from outside—then, in the moonlight, a pair embracing. “Mew!” Denys cried.

The monks joined in. The lay visitor shrieked. Only Abelard remained calm. “What?” he called. “Are ye there, ye jealous miauling knaves? You’ll caterwaul to a tune tomorrow night. I’ll dress each one of you in a fardingale.”

That threat, absurd as it was, made Denys stay—by Gerard’s request.

Gerard groaned.

Meantime, unable to silence such a bold monk, and seeing the demoiselle begin to whimper, they danced in a circle, caterwauling, then blessed the two lovers at the wall, and carried the drunk and the weeping back to their cells.

“And so shut up in measureless content,” Denys concluded.

Gerard was horrified. “Such wretches! Corrupters of youth! Perverters of innocence! Were it not for you, Denys—who have been taught no better—oh, that God might strike down every one of them! Impious, abominable hypocrites!”

“Hypocrites?” Denys echoed, startled. “That was my word before I knew them. And you stood against me. Nay—they are sinners. All good fellows are. But by St. Denis’ skull, they are not hypocrites. They are jolly, roaring blades.”

“Denys,” Gerard said, grave now, “you little know the danger you ran that night. That church—where you feasted—is haunted. I heard it from an elder monk. The dead walk there. Their light feet have been heard patter across the stones.”

“Misericorde!” whispered Denys.

“Aye,” Gerard continued, lowering his voice. “Celestial sounds have come from the crypt beneath the chapel—the very vault you turned into a tavern. Voices of the departed have held unearthly communion. Music has been heard—notes struck by no mortal hand, chords rung by no mortal finger—echoing faintly among the dead.”

Denys looked pale. “Ugh! If I’d known, mules and ropes could not have dragged me there. And so…”—he sighed—“I missed a merry time.”

Whether they might have discussed the spirits further, none can say. For at that moment, a bearded brother rode up on a mule, waving a piece of vellum. It was the deed between Ghysbrecht and Floris Brandt.

Gerard paled—then laughed, relieved. He had nearly lost it. To Denys’s amusement, he not only gave the brother a coin, but kissed the mule’s nose.

“I’ll read it to you,” he said, “even if it’s twice as ill-written. And—to make sure I never lose it”—he sat down, took out needle and thread, and sewed the vellum to his doublet with delicate skill. His thoughts fled to Sevenbergen.

They reached their destination. Denys, in high spirits, doffed his hat to every woman, who curtsied and smiled. He fired his consigne at most men—some stared, some grinned, some both. Finally, he delivered Gerard to one of the promised Burgundian inns.

“It’s a small one,” he said, “but I know it well. Les Trois Poissons.”

“But what does it say?” he asked, pointing to a long inscription painted across the front in huge letters.

“Oh,” said Denys, reading carefully, “‘Ici on loge à pied et à cheval.’” He looked proud of himself.

Gerard looked—and read aloud:

“ON NE LOGE CEANS À CRÉDIT; CE BONHOMME EST MORT, LES MAUVAIS PAIEURS L'ONT TUE.”

They met the innkeeper in the hall.

“Welcome, gentlemen,” he said, doffing his cap with a deep bow.

“We are not in Germany,” Gerard remarked lightly.

In the common room, they found the hostess—a sturdy woman of forty—curtsying and smiling warmly. “Please, sit down, sir,” she said to Gerard, dusting two chairs with her apron, though they were already clean.

“Thank you, good woman,” Gerard replied. “Well,” he mused inwardly, “this is a courteous people indeed: ‘the trouble of sitting down’? I shall endure it with patience—and then come the labor of eating, the effort of digestion, and finally, by Hercules, the struggle of falling asleep.”

“Why, Denys, what are you doing? Ordering supper for only two?”

“Why not?”

“Can we dine without waiting for forty more? Burgundy forever!”

“Aha! Courage, camarade. Le dia—”

“C’est convenu.”

The Salic Law seemed to have no hold here. In this French inn, women ruled—wimple and kirtle held sway, while doublets and hose were few and faint in their presence. The landlord wandered aimlessly, perpetually removing his hat out of habit; the women passed him by, brushing him aside as one might a twig in a thicket.

A maid brought in supper, followed by the mistress, hands empty.

“Dig in, my lords,” she said cheerfully. “You’ve but one enemy here—and he lies beneath your knife.” (I suspect this was a stock phrase.)

They began to eat. The mistress pulled her chair closer to the table, offering not just food but companionship. She chatted easily, like an old friend. But once her duty was done, she left, sending in her daughter—a lovely young woman of about twenty—who took the vacant seat. She was less broad than her mother, but gentle and bright. Learning how far Gerard had traveled, she showed quiet kindness toward him. She stayed nearly half an hour, and when she left, Gerard murmured, “Is this an inn? It feels like home.”

“Qui fit François, il fit courtois,” said Denys, swelling with pride.

“Courteous? No, Christian—welcoming us as if we were family, us wanderers, here today and gone tomorrow. Yet who deserves pity more than the weary traveler far from kin? Hola! Here comes another.”

The newcomer was the chambermaid—a woman of twenty-five, with a sharp nose, wide laughing mouth, sparkling black eyes, and a bare arm strong but not graceful.

As soon as she entered, one of the travelers made a rather bold jest at her expense. Instantly, the whole company erupted into laughter—the joke had been delivered with such speed and skill that it struck its mark before anyone could react. Like a novice fencer facing a master, the man was caught off guard. One after another tried to spar with her, but Marion planted her hands on her hips and held the room spellbound. This country girl possessed a raw, unpolished wit—coarse on paper, yet electrifying when spoken. Nature had given her much, and daily life in the inn had honed the rest.

Yet I will not try to capture her fully—only hint at her. For it was four hundred years ago, and the banter was rough. She returned every insult in kind, and though virtuous, said things without shame that no decent man today would utter even among men.

Gerard sat stunned. To him, this was almost a new species of humanity. He whispered to Denys, “Now I understand why you French say, ‘A woman’s tongue is her sword.’” At that moment, she turned on another challenger. The gallant Denys, ever the protector of the “weaker vessel,” stepped in: “Courage, ma mie, le—” etc.

She turned on him instantly. “How can he be dead so long as there’s still an archer alive?” (General laughter at his expense.)

“It is ‘washing day,’ masters,” she announced suddenly, with solemnity.

“After that? We travelers can’t strip and go bare while you wash our clothes,” grumbled an old fellow by the fire, who had kept silent during the jests but now ventured into safe territory.

“I didn’t mean you, ancient man,” Marion replied with hauteur. “But since you ask—” (she surveyed him slowly from head to toe)—“I’d wager you could take a turn in the tub, clothes and all, and come out none the worse.” (Laughter.) “But what I meant was, I thought this young lord might like his beard starched.”

Poor Gerard was next. His beard was thin and soft.

The loudest laugh came from Denys himself—his own beard was thick, stiff, and bristling. Shakespeare, though he never saw him, had nailed it perfectly:

“Full of strange oaths, and bearded like the pard.” —*As You Like It.*

Gerard bore the teasing calmly. He had little vanity. “Nay, *chambrière*,” he said with a smile, “mine is unworthy of your care. Take this fine growth instead!” He pointed to Den up.

“Oh, wait until I starch the brooms.”

While they roared over the clear jab, the mistress returned. And in the blink of an eye, the fierce Amazon transformed into a meek Madonna.

Mistresses are marvels—subjugators beyond compare. I think none like them breathe upon the earth. Housemaids, judge for yourselves. Yet it was wasted talent—she had heard everything and did not truly disapprove of the laughter.

“Ah, Marion, lass,” she said good-naturedly, “if you laid me an egg every time you cackled, *L’es Trois Poissons* would never lack an omelet.”

“Now, dame,” said Gerard, “what do we owe you?”

“For what?”

“Our supper.”

“Why hurry? Can’t you wait till you leave? Lose the guest, find the money—that’s the rule at *The Three Fish*.”

“But, dame, outside *The Three Fish*, it says—‘Ici-on ne loge—’”

“Bah! Let that flea stick on the wall. Look here,” she said, pointing to the smoky ceiling covered in scratches. These were accounts—scores—written in smoke, visible only to her and her daughter, who could climb a stool and etch lines through the grime with a knife. She explained that these marks were meant to scare off penniless guests—or used when someone refused to pay but insisted on being served. “We can’t flat-out refuse them. The law forbids it.”

“And how do you know mine isn’t such a face?”

“Out fie! Yours is the best face that’s entered *The Three Fish* this autumn.”

“And mine, dame?” asked Denys. “Do you see no deceit here?”

She studied him quietly. “Not as good as the boy’s, nor ever will be. But it’s the face of a true man. Still,” she added dryly, “if I were ten years younger, I’d as lief avoid meeting that face on a dark night far from home.”

Gerard stared. Denys laughed. “Why, dame, I’d only sip the night dew from the flower. And you needn’t subtract ten years or ten days to be worth risking a scratched face for.”

“There, our mistress,” Marion said, having just returned, “did I not tell you yesterday you could still fool them, if you chose?”

“I dare say you did—it sounds like some foolish wench’s talk.”

“Dame,” said Gerard, “this is astonishing.”

“What? Oh, no, no—it’s nothing remarkable. I’ve lived here all my life. Reading faces is the first thing a girl learns in an inn.”

Marion: “And frying eggs is second—no, lying is second. Frying eggs is third.”

Mistress: “And holding your tongue is last. Modesty? That’s never seen the light of day.”

Marion: “Alack! Speak of my tongue. But I say no more. She under whose wing I live delivers the blow. I’m undone—‘tis but a chambermaid gone. Catch what’s left!” And she staggered backward, landing squarely on the most handsome man in the room—Gerard.

“Tic! tic!” he exclaimed, annoyed. “Don’t be absurd! That’s too heavy a jest for me. Can’t you see I’m speaking to the mistress?”
