Marion regained her balance with a grimace, bounded twice across the floor, and spun into a pirouette. “There, mistress,” she declared, “I surrender. You reign supreme with the men—at least with the young ones.”

“Young man,” said the mistress, “this girl is not so silly as she seems. In reading faces and frying omelets, we are skilled. It would be hard if we failed at these arts—they are nearly all we know.”

“You don’t quite grasp me, dame,” said Gerard. “That honesty should shine from a face under your trained eye—that makes sense. But how, looking at Denys here, could you detect his one weakness—his madness, his miserable mulierosity?” Poor Gerard grew angrier the more he pondered it.

“His mule—his what?” (Crossing herself in superstitious dread at the word).

“Nay, it’s only a word I invented for him.”

“Invented? Can a child like you make words not born in Burgundy? Beware what you do! We’re overrun with them already—especially bad ones. Lord, these are troubled times. Next I expect to hear of a new thistle being invented.”

“Well then, dame, *mulierose*—meaning wrapped up, body and soul, in women. So tell me—how did you uncover the fool’s mulierosity?”

“Alas, good youth, you make a mountain of a molehill. Women are keen observers. We see more with the tail of our eye than most men can with a telescope. As I move about, my glance remains on my guests. I noticed this soldier’s eyes never left the women—my daughter, Marion, even me. All was gold to him. And there he sat, glaring—oh, you foolish, foolish man! You, however, turned to the speaker, whoever they were. That is common sense.”

Denys burst into hoarse laughter. “You’re never more wrong. This smooth-faced companion is a Turk—except for his beard. He’s sharper than any archer in the Duke’s guard. He’s more wrapped up in one Dutch girl named Margaret than I am in all of you, fair and brown.”

“Man alive, that’s just the opposite,” said the hostess. “Yours is the curse, his the cure. Cling to Margaret, my dear. I hope she’s honest.”

“She is an angel.”

“Ay, ay—they all are until better known. I’d as lief she were no more than honest. Then she’ll keep you from worse company. As for you, soldier, trouble awaits. Your eyes were never made for your soul’s good.”

“Nor your purse,” Marion interjected. “And your lips—well, they’ll sip the dew, as you call it, from many a bramble bush.”

“Enough chatter, Marion!”

“Ods bodikins, mistress—did you hire me to be one of your three fishes?” And Marion sulked for thirty seconds.

“Is that how you speak to our mistress?” the landlord asked, slipping in.

“Hold your tongue,” his wife snapped. “It’s not your place to reprimand the girl. She’s a good servant.”

“What, is the cock never to crow, while the hens run wild all day?”

“You may crow as loud as you like, my man. But the hen means to rule the roost.”

“I know a saying to match that,” Gerard offered.

“Do you? Then speak it.”

“Femme veut en toute saison, Estre dame en sa mason.”

“I’ve never heard it—but it’s as true as gospel. Ay, those who coined these sayings had eyes and tongues, and tongues and eyes. Before all the world, give me an old proverb.”

“And me a young husband,” Marion chimed in. “Now there was a chance for you all—and no one spoke. Oh! It’s too late now—I’ve changed my mind.”

“All the better for some poor fellow,” Den suggested.

Then the arrival of the young mistress—called the *petite maîtresse*—was the signal for everyone to gather round the fire, like a single happy family: travelers, host, hostess, servants forming the outer ring—all telling stories until bedtime. Gerard, in turn, told a chilling tale from his collection of saints’ lives, making them shudder delightfully. But soon he began to nod, worn out by the effort. The young mistress noticed and gave Marion a look. Marion lit a rushlight, laid a hand on Gerard’s shoulder, and led him away.

She showed him a room with two crisp white beds and invited him to choose.

“Either is paradise,” he said. “I’ll take this one. Do you know, I haven’t lain in a naked bed since I left Holland.”

“Alack! Poor soul!” she said. “Then the sooner my flax and your down—(he! he!)—meet, the better. So—*allons!*” And she presented her cheek as casually as if it were a hand for payment.

“*Allons*? What does that mean?”

“It means ‘goodnight.’ Ahem! Don’t they kiss the chambermaid in your land?”

“Not all at once.”

“What, do they make a business of it?”

“Nay, perverter of words—I mean we don’t flirt so freely with strangers.”

“They must be strangers if they don’t think you fools. Here’s a tangle. Why, all the old greasy greybeards at our inn kiss us chambermaids—faugh! And what have we poor creatures to set against it but now and then a nice young—? Alack! Time flies. Chambermaids can’t stay long in the nursery. So how is it to be?”

“If you please, arrange with my comrade for both. He is mulierose; I am not.”

“Nay, he needs a curb, not a spur. Well then—you shall sleep without paying the usual toll. And oh, it’s sweet to meet a young man who resists these ancient customs and refuses brazen hussies. You shall have your reward.”

“Thank you! But what are you doing with my bed?”

“Me? Only removing these sheets and replacing them with the pair the drunken miller slept in last night.”

“Oh, no! No! You cruel, black-hearted creature! There! There!”

“A la bonne heure! What won’t perseverance achieve? But note the stubbornness of a mad girl! I didn’t care a button. I’m sick of that game after five years. But you denied me—so I *had* to have it. I’d have walked through fire and water for it. Alas, young sir, we women are tricky beasts—poor, perverse toads. Excuse us. Keep us at arm’s length—and goodnight!”

At the door, she turned, voice and manner completely changed: “The Virgin guard thy head, and the holy Evangelists watch the bed where lies a poor young wanderer far from home! Amen!”

And the next moment, Gerard heard her dash down the stairs—then a peal of laughter from the great hall revealed her whereabouts.

“That is a character,” Gerard said profoundly, yawning at the discovery.

Within minutes, he was wrapped in cool, clean linen—refreshing after so long without. Then came warmth—and then, Sevenbergen.

The next morning, Gerard awoke, refreshed and eager to rise, but found himself trapped. His linen had vanished. This was paralysis—for the nightshirt was a modern invention. In Gerard’s time, men did not discard clean sheets lightly. They slipped into them clothed in innocence, like Adam. Out of bed, they emerged as Cain.

He complained to Denys, but at that moment the door opened and Marion swept in, carrying their freshly washed and ironed linen on her arms. She placed it on the table.

“Oh, you good girl!” Gerard exclaimed.

“Alack, have you discovered me at last?”

“Yes, indeed. Is this another custom?”

“No—unless you take them unasked. But at night, we always ask travelers: would you like washed linen? I came in, but you were both fast asleep. So I said to the little mistress, ‘La! What sense is there in waking tired men to ask if Charles the Great is dead, or whether they’d prefer dirty linen or clean—especially this one with skin like cream?’ And she said, ‘Indeed he has!’”

“That was me,” Denys remarked, sounding like a commentator.

“Guess again, and you’ll hit the mark.”

“Don’t notice her, Marion—he’s impudent. And I’m sure we can’t thank you enough for your kindness. I regret I ever refused you—anything you fancied.”

“Oh, are ye there?” said the mischievous one. “I take that to mean you’d like to brush the morning dew off, as your bashful friend calls it. Well then, excuse me—it’s customary, but not wise. I decline. Quits with you, lad.”

“Wait! Wait!” cried Denys as she fled victoriously. “I’m curious—how many of you were here last night, feasting your eyes on us?”

“It was such a satisfying feast—we weren’t half a minute over it. Who? The big mistress, the little mistress, Janet, and me—and the whole posse comitatus, tiptoeing. We usually make our rounds last thing, so we don’t get burned down. And we come in great numbers. Somehow, that makes us bolder—especially when archers are scattered about.”

“Why didn’t you tell me? I’d have stayed awake.”

“Beau sire, the saying goes: the good and the ill are all one while their lids are closed. So we said, ‘Here is one who serves God best asleep. Break not his rest.’”

“She’s amusing,” Gerard declared.

“I must be either that—or knavish.”

“How so?”

“Because *The Three Fish* pays me to be amusing. You’ll eat before you leave? Good! Then I’ll go see the meat is fit for such noble teeth.”

“Denys!”

“What is it?”

“I wish that was a great boy, going with us to keep us cheerful.”

“So do I. But I wish it was going with us as it is.”

“Heaven forbid! A fine fool you’d make of yourself.”

They broke their fast, settled their bill, and bid farewell. Then they discovered Marion had not exaggerated the “custom of the country.” The three main women kissed them warmly—and they kissed them back. The landlord kissed them—and they kissed him. The cry rang out: “Come back—soon as possible!”

“Never pass *The Three Fish*. If your purses are empty, bring yourselves. *Le sieur crédit* is not dead for you.”

And they set off again.

They reached a small town, and Denys went to buy shoes. The shopkeeper stood in the doorway, alert and attentive. He bowed deeply to Denys. The customer was quickly fitted, escorted to the street, and dismissed with graceful gestures.

The friends agreed it was Elysium to deal with such a shoemaker. “Not that my German shoes haven’t lasted well enough,” said Gerard fairly.

Outside the town was a pebbled path.

“This keeps the burghers’ feet dry when walking on Sundays with their wives and daughters,” Denys explained.

Those simple words painted “home” in Gerard’s heart. “Oh, how sweet!” he said.

“Mercy! What is this? A gibbet! And ugh—two skeletons upon it! Oh, Denys, what a dreadful sight to greet us!”

“Nay,” said Denys, “a comforting sight. For every rogue hanging there, one fewer walks free.”

A little farther on, they came to two pillars, between which stood a massive wheel studded with iron spikes. Bones and tattered cloth were tangled in the prongs.

Gerard covered his face. “To think—those scraps and bones are all that remains of a man! Of one who was what we are now.”

“Excusez! A thing that walked on two legs and stole—are we no more than that?”

“How can you know he stole? Have honest men never suffered death and torture too?”

“None of my kin ever ended up on the gibbet, I know.”

“The better their luck. Tell me—how did the saints die?”

“Hard. But not in Burgundy.”

“You massacred them wholesale at Lyons, right on Burgundy’s border. To you, the gibbet proves guilt—because you don’t read history. Alas, had you stood on Calvary that bloody day we mourn to this hour, I tremble to think you might have shouted joyfully at the gibbet built there. For the cross was but the Roman gallows, Father Martin says.”

“The blaspheming old hound!”

“Oh, fie! fie! A holy and learned man. Yes, Denys, you’d have judged those crucified by the bare light of the gibbet. ‘Drive in the nails!’ you’d have cried. ‘Drive in the spear!’ Here are three malefactors. Three *roues*. Yet of those three, one was the first Christian saint—and another was the Savior of the world, whom they gibbeted.”

Denys swore on his honor that things were handled better in Burgundy. After deep thought, he added that the horrors Gerard described had once made him curse and swear in rage when told by the village priest at Easter—“but they happened in a foreign land, a thousand years past. Mort de ma vie, let us hope it’s not true—or at least greatly exaggerated. See how tales grow as they travel!”

Then he paused, flushed with sudden anger. “Don’t you blush to play with your book-learning on your unlearned friend, throwing dust in his eyes, equating saints with these vermin?”

Then, abruptly, he smiled. “Since your heart beats for vermin, feel for the carrion crows! They’re as good vermin as these. Would you send them to bed supperless, poor pretty poppets? These are their larder. Hunger would kill them without cold cut-purses hung here and there.”

Gerard, who had remained silent, declared the subject closed—forever. “There are things,” he said, “where our hearts seem as wide apart as the poles—and our minds too. But I love you dearly all the same,” he added, with grace and tenderness.

Late afternoon brought a faint wailing sound ahead. It grew louder as they approached. Being swift walkers, they soon reached its source: a dozen pikemen, accompanied by constables, marched forward, driving a herd of animals. Over a hundred in number, mostly young, only a few elderly. The males were subdued and silent. The females screamed—loudly, continuously.

In other words, the creatures driven along at the point of law were men and women.

“Good Heaven!” cried Gerard. “So many! But surely not all these children are thieves—some are armed! What on earth is this, Denys?”

Denys advised him to ask the “bourgeois” with the badge. “This is Burgundy: here, a civil question draws a civil answer.”

Gerard approached the officer, removed his cap—a courtesy immediately returned—and said, “For Our Lady’s sake, sir, what are you doing with these poor people?”

“What concern is it of yours, my lad?” the official replied suspiciously.

“Master, I’m a stranger, and thirsty for knowledge.”

The officer looked at him, then nodded. “They are condemned criminals, sentenced to exile. Some for theft, others for violence. They will be sent beyond the borders—never to return.”

Gerard stared. “And these children?”

“Some are guilty. Others are innocent—taken with their parents. The law sees no mercy.”

Gerard fell silent. Denys placed a hand on his shoulder. “We must go on,” he said softly. “The road is long, and justice is harsh.”

And so they continued, the echoes of suffering fading behind them, the weight of human cruelty pressing upon their souls.

“Where be the true men?”
“Here be we. God bless you all! God bless you!”

A rush of movement filled the air as half a dozen strong hands reached out, gripping those of the rescued pair with rough warmth. The room blazed with torchlight, casting flickering shadows across polished breastplates and weathered faces. Archers stood tall, their bronze skins glowing in the fire’s glow, while bound thieves slumped against the walls, pale and defeated. At the center lay the lifeless form of the giant, sprawled in his own blood, unattended—his end a grim testament to the night’s violence.

Gerard moved slowly among the archers, his eyes glistening as he clasped each hand in turn. One by one, they returned the gesture with a kiss—a ritual of gratitude and camaraderie. This time, Gerard kissed them back, his voice soft but steady. Then, turning to a young archer who matched him in age and bearing, he said, “Prithee, good soldier, keep watch over me. A strange drowsiness grips me. Let no man cut my throat while I sleep—for pity’s sake.”

The archer laughed, thinking it jest. But no sooner had the words left Gerard’s lips than he sank into a deep, unbroken slumber. Denys watched, surprised—but did not disturb him. It suited his purpose well enough.

Nearby, two archers were examining the Abbot’s corpse, rolling it gently with their boots. “Which of you flung this great rogue from above like that?” one asked. “We’d fain learn the trick of your arm.”

Denys hesitated at first, puffing his cheeks in mock indignation. But then he saw Gerard asleep—and knew the moment was ripe. “Well,” he declared, stepping forward, “I ran my sword through him up to the hilt. Others swarmed around me—so I had either my blade or death. So I planted my foot on his belly, tugged with my hand, sprang with my leg—and sent him flying to his doom! He died mid-air, and his carcass rolled among you—made you jump, I warrant. But pikestaves and pillage! What matter now? These things are past. *Buvons*, comrades, *buvons*!”

The archers exchanged glances. “Easy to say *buvons* when there’s no wine,” one muttered.

“Nay,” replied Denys, “I’ll find you wine. My nose knows where to seek it. Follow me—and I’ll follow my nose. Bring a torch!”

They descended a narrow stone stairway into a low, damp cellar. The air was thick with moisture, the walls coated in crystallized saltpetre that glittered faintly in the torchlight. “Ah,” said Denys, inhaling deeply, “the sweet scent of old wine lingers here. Advance thy light.”

Then, suddenly: “Diable! What is that in the corner? A pile of rags?”

No—it was a figure, crouched in shadow, pale as ash, trembling violently.

“It is the landlord,” Denys said flatly.

One archer bellowed, “Get up, thou craven heart! The thieves are bound, and we’re dry from binding them. Show us thy wine—no bottles here!”

The landlord stammered, “Be the rascals bound? Good news… Wine? That will I, honest sirs.”

He rose shakily, joints weak, offering to lead them to the wine cellar. But Denys stepped between them. “You’re all in the dark, comrades. He’s in league with the thieves.”

“Alack, good soldier!” the landlord protested. “Me? With the accursed robbers? Is that reasonable?”

“The girl said so,” Denys replied coldly.

“The girl? What girl?” the landlord whispered. “Ah—curse her, traitress!”

Another archer spoke up. “The girl is gone to the bailiff. Let the burghers judge if he’s guilty. We caught him not in act.”

Denys paused. “One moment. Why cursed he the girl? If he’s innocent, he should bless her—as we do.”

“Alas, sir,” the landlord pleaded, “I have only my name to live by. I cursed her because you said she lied about me.”

“Humph,” said Denys. “I suspect thou art a thief—and what thief cannot lie smoothly? Hold him, comrades. A prisoner can draw wine even if his hands are bound.”

The landlord made no protest. Instead, he offered to show them where the wine was kept, adding, “But I pray ye pay for what ye drink. My rent is due these two months.”

The archers smiled grimly, seeing through his pretense. One placed a firm hand on his shoulder; another led on with the torch. They reached the threshold when Denys called sharply, “Halt!”

“What now?”

“There be bottles in this corner. Advance thy light.”

The torch-bearer approached. Denys had just removed his scabbard and was probing the heap where the landlord had crouched.

“Nay, nay!” the landlord cried. “The wine is in the next cellar. Nothing here.”

“Nothing is mighty hard,” said Denys, pulling something from the pile. It was a bone. He tossed it aside. It rattled on stone.

“There is naught here but the bones of the house,” the landlord insisted.

“Just now ‘twas nothing,” said Denys. “Now that we’ve found something, ‘tis nothing but bones. Here’s another. Look at this one, comrade. And you—come too. Bring the knave along.”

Philippe, the torch-bearer, held the bone to the flame, turning it slowly.

“Well?” Denys asked.

“Well,” Philippe said, “if this were a battlefield, I’d say it was a man’s shankbone. No more, no less. But this is no field of battle—nor churchyard. This is an inn.”

“True,” said the other archer. “Yet yon man’s face—ashen, soulless—is as good a sign as any. When the chine is missing, and the dog won’t look at you without his tail between his legs—what thief could hide such a truth? Good brothers, my mind misgives me. The deeper I dig, the more I find. Mayhap if these bones could speak, they would make true men’s flesh creep.”

“Alas, young man!” the landlord cried. “What dreadful fancies! These are bones of beeves, sheep, kids—not men or women. Holy saints preserve us!”

“Hold thy peace!” Denys snapped. “Thy words are wind. Thou hast not deceived burghers—only fools. We are soldiers who have sought our comrades and found their bones picked clean by crows. Men and women, saidst thou? Yet prithee—when spake I of women’s bones? Wouldst make a child suspect thee. Field of battle, comrade? Was not this house a battlefield but half an hour ago?”

He thrust the landlord forward, forcing him close. Then, with sudden fury, he pulled from the heap a small object and held it before the man’s eyes.

“Alas! I know not,” the landlord whimpered.

“Nor I,” Denys admitted, “but it is too like the thumb bone of a man’s hand. Mates, my flesh creeps. Churchyard? How know I this is not one?”

Drawing his sword, he began to rake the earth and broken crockery from the pile. The landlord protested again, pleading innocence.

“We poor innkeepers are sinners,” he said, “we give short measure, we water the wine—we do these things. The laws are unjust to us. But we are not assassins. How could we afford to kill our guests? May Heaven strike me dead if there be any bones here but those of meat. ’Tis the kitchen wench who throws them here. I swear by God’s holy mother, by Saint Paul, by Saint Dominic, and by Denys, my patron saint—ah!”

Denys held up a bone—silent, deadly. It was unmistakable. Not ox, not sheep, not goat. A human bone.

The liar’s mouth closed. His breath stopped. His hair stood on end like bristles. His knees gave way.

The archers dragged him upright, forcing him to stand under the torchlight. There, staring into the hollow sockets of a skull—white as his own cheek, yet colder—his lips parted, but no sound came.

“Ah,” Denys said, voice low and trembling with rage, “look upon the sockets from which thou didst pluck the eyes. Let them blast thine own—so that crows shall pick them out ere this week ends. Now, hold that while I search on. Hold it, I say—or I’ll rob the gallows myself!”

He raised his naked sword, threatening the quaking wretch until, groaning, the man took the skull and clutched it, nearly fainting. Oh! That every murderer might see himself thus—sick, terrified, holding the cold relic of his own crime, knowing his head would soon match it.

Soon, the heap was scattered. And not one, nor two, but many skulls emerged. Each discovery brought a fresh moan from the culprit.

Then Denys let out a cry—strange, sharp, coming from a man so bold. In his hand, he held a mass of long, glossy, golden hair. A woman’s hair.

At once, the archers shook the wretch violently. He whined.

“I have a sister,” Denys choked. “Her hair is just so fair and shining.”

“Jesu!” he gasped. “If it should be hers! Take my sword and dagger—keep them from my hand, lest I strike him down and wrong the gibbet.”

Then, on bended knee, he swore aloud: “Poor innocent victim—whose lovely hair this was—I swear by God, never to leave this man till I see him broken upon the wheel—for thy sake.”

He rose. “Ay,” he roared, “had he as many lives as there are hairs, I’d take them all. By God!”

And he tucked the hair into his bosom. Then, seized by fury, he grabbed the landlord by the neck, forced him to his knees, and ground his face into the bones of his victims—where they lay thickest. The assassin screamed—then whined, like a dog whose nose is pressed into the body of its prey.

“Now lend me thy bowstring, Philippe!”

He threaded it through the eye sockets of a skull and hung it round the man’s neck. Then pulled him up, kicked him fiercely into the kitchen—where the alderman had arrived with constables, already taking a deposition.

The grave magistrate stared in horror at the landlord, bleeding from a dozen scratches, wearing the ghastly crown of skulls. But Denys came panting after, and in a few fierce words explained all.

“Bind him like the rest,” said the alderman sternly. “I count him the blackest of them all.”

As the wretch begged piteously for the skull to be removed, the alderman replied: “Humph! I had not ordered such a thing to be worn by mortal man. Yet being there, I will not lift finger nor voice to take it off. Methinks it fits thee truly, thou bloody dog. ’Tis thy ensign—and hangs well above a heart so foul as thine.”

Then he turned to Denys. “Do you think we have secured the whole gang?”

“Your worship,” Denys answered, “there are seven thieves and this landlord. One we slew upstairs. One we cast down dead. The rest are bound before you.”

“Good,” said the alderman. “Go fetch the dead one from upstairs and lay him beside the one I caused to be removed.”

Suddenly, a shrill voice broke in—like a guinea-fowl peevishly squawking.

“Now, now, now—where is the hand? That is what I want to see!”

It was a petty clerk, eager for evidence.

“You’ll find it above,” someone said. “Nailed to the door-post by a crossbow bolt.”

“Good!” squeaked the clerk. He whispered to his master, “What a fine display the *pièces de conviction* will make!” And he began writing, listing them one by one:
Skulls—Bones—A woman’s hair—A thief’s hands—1 axe—2 carcasses—1 crossbow bolt.

Done, he itched to search the cellar himself—perhaps find an ear, or an earring. The alderman nodded, and the clerk snatched a torch and hurried toward the stairs—when disaster struck.

The constables ascended in single file. But the head constable, seeing the phosphorescent corpse seated by the bed, froze. Then trembled. Then howled.

In his recoil, he stumbled backward—knocking into the next man. That man, shaken by the cry and glimpsing something terrible, staggered back—unable to support the heavy head constable. The two toppled onto the third. The three carried the fourth. They tumbled into the kitchen, falling in a heap like cards laid out on a table.

The clerk, rushing forward with torch, collided with the last man—who, carrying the momentum of the pile, knocked him violently to the ground—the ace of the quint. He lay there kicking, torch still aloft, seemingly triumphant—but actually convulsed, breath and sense driven out by the blow.

“What is to do now, in Heaven’s name?” the alderman cried, leaping up in alarm.

Denys explained, and offered to accompany him.

“So be it,” said the alder man.

His men picked themselves up ruefully. He led the inspection—above and below.

As for the prisoners, their questioning was delayed until they could be confronted with the servant.

Before dawn, the thieves—alive and dead—along with every relic of crime and retribution—were swept away into the law’s net. The inn fell silent, nearly empty. Only one constable remained, and Denys—along with Gerard, still sleeping heavily.

Gerard stirred awake, his eyes blinking in the bright daylight, to find Denys seated beside him, face etched with quiet concern. “You’re still sleeping!” Denys murmured. “It’s high noon already.”

“A blessed sleep,” Gerard replied, stretching slowly. “It feels as though Heaven itself laid a veil over that dreadful night. To think we sit here now—alive, unharmed. It seems like a dream, a terrible dream I can scarcely believe was real.”

“Aye, lad,” Denys said gently, “that’s the wise way to see such things once they’re past. They fade into shadows, dreams. Eat something, and you’ll forget it all. Besides, I promised to bring you into town by noon—and take you to the alderman.”

Gerard nodded, accepting a piece of coarse rye bread soaked in red wine. He ate slowly, savoring the simple fare that broke his long fast. Then, with Denys at his side, he walked back over the site of their violent encounter. The ground bore the scars of struggle—the broken weapons, the bloodstained earth—yet no enemy remained. Still, Gerard shuddered at the memory, his nerves taut as bowstrings. As they made their way toward the town, he kept glancing through the hedges, expecting ambushes from every shadow, until at last they reached the quiet streets of the little settlement.

Denys led him to an inn called “The White Hart.” “No danger here,” he assured Gerard. “I’ve known the landlord for years. He’s a burgess, and likely to be bailiff. This is where I meant to go yesterday—but we lost time, and darkness fell upon us. And then—”

“And you saw a woman at the door,” Gerard finished, “and decided to be wiser than a Jeanneton. She told us there was nothing to fear.”

“Indeed,” Denys said, smiling faintly. “But what saved our lives if not that woman? And she risked her own to do it.”

“That is true,” Gerard said, his voice softening. “Though women mean little to me, I would give every coin in my purse to thank this poor girl, to repay her kindness. Do you not feel the same?”

“Parbleu,” Denys muttered, but there was warmth in his tone.

“But where might we find her?” Gerard asked.

“Perhaps the alderman will know,” Denys suggested. “We must speak with him first.”

The alderman greeted them with a face that held more mystery than welcome—a look both wary and unreadable. After a moment’s silence, a grim smile touched his lips, and he began questioning Gerard, recording each answer with careful precision.

When he had finished, he declared, “You must remain in town until the thieves are tried. You are required to testify—under penalty of fine or imprisonment.”

The two men exchanged stunned glances.

“However,” the alderman added, “it won’t be long. The culprits were caught red-handed.”

He paused, then continued, “And in any case, you could not leave this place this week.”

Denys blinked, taken aback. Gerard smiled—though not with humor, but with a quiet amusement at what he took to be the old man’s naivety. A provincial town in Burgundy, he thought, could hardly detain one bound for Rome and a beloved Margaret.

Then, turning to the matter closest to his heart, Gerard said, “Your worship, we cannot find our benefactress in the town.”

“Your benefactress?” the alderman repeated, puzzled.

“The good girl,” Gerard explained earnestly, “who came to you in the night and saved our lives at great peril to herself. Oh, sir, our hearts burn with gratitude—we wish only to thank her, to bless her. Where is she?”

“In prison, sir? Good heavens, for what crime?”

“Well, she is a witness—perhaps an essential one.”

“Why, Messire Bailiff,” interjected Denys, “you don’t keep all your witnesses in chains, I trust.”

The alderman, pleased to be addressed as bailiff, grew more talkative. “In matters of bloodshed, we hold fast any testimony that might help the accused escape justice. That’s why we’re still holding the women. A man may hide his guilt for weeks, but a woman—should she do her duty to the realm on Friday, she’ll betray it by Sunday, or try. If you saw that girl now, you’d find her weeping over having sent five men to the gallows. Had they been women, we might have trusted a subpoena. They despise each other—there’s sense in that. But now I recall—there were other reasons for detaining this one. Hand me those depositions, young sir.” He put on his spectacles. “Ah! Here it is in black and white. Jean Hardy—one of the thieves—confessed that… humph? Yes, here: ‘And that the girl Manon was the decoy, and her sweetheart was Georges Vipont, one of the band; hanged last month. She has been distraught ever since, openly blaming the gang for his death, saying that had they not been cowards, he would never have been caught—and it is my belief she betrayed them out of sheer spite—’”

“His belief!” Gerard exclaimed, outraged. “What weight does the opinion of a cutthroat carry, burning with revenge against the very one who delivered him to justice? And if you go by that, what value has his word? Is a thief never a liar? Is he not always lying? And here—what motive could be stronger than revenge? Oh, sir, what madness to question a convicted felon and listen to his lies as though he were a truthful man swearing under oath, hand on the Gospel!”

“Young man,” said the alderman, “restrain your passion in the presence of authority! From your tone, I see you are a stranger. Know this: in our land, we question everyone. We are not so weak as to believe we can reach the truth by closing one ear or the other.”

“And so you would listen to Satan accusing the saints?”

“Tch-tch! The law deals only with men and women, and even they cannot utter a tale entirely false, no matter how hard they try. So we leave the barn door open to every grain. Only once inside, we winnow and sift. And who told you I accepted the thief’s story wholeheartedly like clear water? Not at all. I believed only what was confirmed by stronger evidence.”

“Stronger evidence?” Gerard asked, stunned. “Who but the thieves themselves would speak against her?”

“Herself.”

“Herself, sir? Did you question her too?”

“I tell you—we question all. Here is her deposition. Can you read? Read it yourself.”

Gerard glanced at Denys and began reading aloud:

“I am from Epinal. Two years ago, I left my home because I refused the man they chose for me. My father beat me. I fled. I went into service. I left because my mistress was jealous. She said I was impertinent. Last year, I stood in the market to be hired among other girls. The landlord of ‘The Fair Star’ took me. I stayed eleven months. A young man courted me. I loved him. I discovered travelers came and never left. I told my lover. He forbade me to speak. He threatened me. I learned he was part of a band of thieves. When travelers were to be robbed, the landlord would go out and summon the gang. Then I wept and prayed for their souls. I never told. A month ago, my lover died.

“The soldier reminded me of him. He had a beard like the one I lost. I cannot say whether I would have acted if he had not had a beard. I regret telling now.”

The paper nearly slipped from Gerard’s hands. For the first time, he truly grasped the danger Manon faced. He knew the merciless law, and the cold-hearted men who enforced it. Suddenly, he dropped to his knees before the alderman. “Oh, sir! Consider the difference between those cruel men and this poor, fragile woman! Could you bear to send her to the same fate? Could you condemn us to watch her die—when, had she not risked her life for ours, we would not now be in peril? Alas, sir! Show mercy to Denys and me, if you feel none for her, poor soul. We are honest men—you would tear our hearts out if you let that gentle girl perish. What can we do? What remains but to end our lives beneath her gallows?”

The alderman, though hardened, was human. Gerard’s fervent plea startled him, then moved him. He showed it oddly—by growing irritable. “There, rise, do,” he snapped. “I doubt anyone would speak so much for me. Hey, Daniel! Fetch the town clerk.” As the clerk entered from an adjoining room, the alderman said, “Here’s a foolish lad fretting over that girl. Can we stretch a point? Suppose we allow her to testify—question her fairly?”

The town clerk was one of those “impossible” men.

“No, sir, we cannot. She was not involved in this affair. Had she been accessory, we might offer her pardon in exchange for testimony.”

Gerard interrupted, “But she did better—she prevented the crime. She offered herself as a witness by rushing here with the news.”

“Nonsense, young man—it’s a matter of law.” The alderman and clerk debated long, the one arguing, the other denying, whether she stood legally as if she had been an accomplice in the attack on the travelers. This was fortunate for Manon. The alderman, irritated by the clerk’s constant refusals, declared, “I’ll show him I can do anything I please.” He summoned Manon, secured her with the landlord of “The White Hart” as bondsman, and received five gold pieces from Denys. After coaxing, Manon promised to attend as witness. He released her—but eased his conscience by explaining his reasoning plainly.

“The town must buy a new rope for every execution and present it to the hangman—or pay him in money. In my opinion, she’s not worth that expense. But men like her late companions—those are worth it.”

Thus, Denys and Gerard led her away. Gerard danced with joy; Denys cheered her spirits by assuring her of the demise of a troublesome figure. She wept, but silently. On the way to “The White Hart,” the public recognized her. Having heard the full story from the archers—who naturally spoke warmly in her favor—they followed, shouting encouragement. Empowered by numbers, she regained courage. The landlord, seeing she would draw customers, welcomed her kindly and gave her an upper chamber. There, alone, she wept again.

Poor little heart—like a ripple, up and down, down and up, endlessly. Bidding the landlord treat her well, to keep her as a prisoner without making her feel it, the friends stepped outside. And there—before them, coming from opposite ends of the street—were two processions.

One, loud and chaotic, filled with cries and howls—the kind that reveal, at moments, the beastly kinship hidden beneath human veneer. The other, quiet and solemn, attended only by a few nuns and friars.

The condemned, bound for public exposure in the marketplace. The bones of the victims, carried to the churchyard.

They met in the narrow street, almost at the inn door. Unable to pass, the bier carrying the relics of the dead became wedged against the cart bearing the living men who had made those bones—and would soon die for it. The mob didn’t immediately grasp the irony. Then a woman cried, “Look at your work, you dogs!” The cry spread like wildfire. A terrible roar erupted. The prisoners groaned, trying to hide their faces, but couldn’t—their hands were tied. They stood there, pale, hollow-eyed, images of despair, gazing at the bier with envy—for those whose bones they had sent ahead were already beyond suffering.

Two men stood apart, watching gravely. One, Denys, gave in to curiosity and vengeance. The other, Gerard, removed his hat and walked solemnly behind the coffin, mourning those whose fate had nearly been his own. For a time, he was the only lay mourner. But as they neared the suburbs, far from the spectacle in the market, artisans laid down tools, shopkeepers left their stalls—moved by pity, by shared humanity, perhaps inspired by Gerard—and joined the procession bareheaded. They watched the remains laid to rest in holy ground, amid the prayers of the Church.

After the rites, Gerard approached the cure respectfully and offered to purchase a mass for the souls.

Gerard, son of Catherine, always considered both sides of a coin. He tried to bargain slightly below the usual price, citing the tragic circumstances. But the good cure gently deflected his cleverness and firmly brought him back to market rate.

In conversation, they found common ground. Piety and practicality are not rare bedfellows—yet rarely seen so fully embodied as in these two men. Their meeting in the spiritual marketplace sparked mutual respect, like knights recognizing worthy foes. Moreover, the cure enjoyed gossip. Learning Gerard had fought the thieves at Domfront, he invited him into his parlour to hear the tale firsthand. His heart warmed. “God has been good to you,” he said. “I thank Him with all my soul. You are a good lad.” He added dryly, “You should have told me this in the churchyard—I might have given you the mass freely. But,” he said (the temperature suddenly dropping), “it’s ill luck to break a bargain. Still, I’ll open a bottle of my old Medoc—few guests merit that.”

He fetched the wine from his cupboard, muttering to himself, “At their old tricks again!”

“Pardon me?” said Gerard.

“I said nothing. Ah, here it is.”

“No, your reverence. You spoke—‘At their old tricks!’”

“Did I? Indeed?” He smiled. Then he uncorked the wine, poured a cup for each, and placed a log on the fire—stoves being unknown in Burgundy. “So I said ‘At their old tricks,’ did I? Now, sip this fine wine, and while it lasts, story for story—I’ll tell you a little tale.”

Gerard’s eyes lit up.

“You love stories?”

“As my life.”

“Do not raise your hopes too high. It’s a mere trifle compared to your adventures.”

Once upon a time, in France, in the duchy of Burgundy, not far from this very town where we now sip old Medoc, there lived a cure. I say he lived—but barely. The parish was small, the people greedy, and they gave him no more than he could force from them. The leaner he became, the holier their prayers would be, they thought. I know not if that was their creed, but their actions gave it color.

At last, he devised a trap.

One day, the richest farmer in the village had twins to baptize. As usual, the cure was invited to the christening feast. But before baptizing them, he demanded not just the baptismal fees—but also the burial fees.

“Saints defend us, parson!” cried the mother. “Don’t talk of burying! I’ve never seen children more likely to live.”

“Nor I,” said the cure. “Praise be to God. Yet they will die, being sons of Adam, as well as of you, dame. But when they do, it will cost them nothing—the burial fees are paid and recorded in this book.”

“For all that, it will cost them something,” quipped the miller, the biggest wag and knave in the place—so big a knave, no one knew quite how large, not even the hangman.

“Miller,” said the cure, “I say no.”

“Parson,” said the miller, “I say yes. It will cost them their lives.”

A great laugh followed. Amid the mirth, the fees were paid, and the children baptized.

But when every next child in the parish had to pay burial fees or lose their place in heaven, discontent festered quietly. One fine day, they gathered secretly, sent a churchwarden to complain to the bishop—and a thunderbolt struck the poor cure. Summoned at dinner-time to the episcopal palace, he took the parish books and went trembling.

The bishop greeted him with a frown, presented the complaint. “Monseigneur,” said the cure humbly, “does the parish accuse me of many things, or only this one?”

“In truth, only this one,” said the bishop, softening slightly.

“Then, monseigneur, I admit the fact.”

“Good. That saves time. Now, your excuse—if there is one.”

“Monseigneur, I have been cure of that parish seven years. Fifty children I have baptized. Five buried. At first, I said, ‘Heaven be praised, the air of this village is healthy.’ But checking the register, I found it had always been so. Digging deeper, I learned that most born in Domfront eventually went to Aix and were hanged. This deprived not only their cure but the entire Church of funeral dues—since ‘pendards’ are buried in air, not earth. Knowing their greed, and how they grudge the Church every sou, I set a trap to prevent them from hanging. Greed against greed—some will die in their beds rather than let the Church gain those fees for nothing.”

The bishop laughed until tears ran down. He questioned the churchwarden, who confessed too many from the parish ended at Aix. “Then,” said the bishop, “I approve the act—for myself and my successors. Let it stand until they mend their ways and die in their beds.”

Next day, the ringleaders came humbly to the cure. “Parson, you were fair to us, save for this unfortunate matter. Pray, let there be no ill will over such a trifle.”

The cure replied, “My children, I would not be worthy of your pastor if I could not forgive. Go in peace—and bring me as many children as possible, so the double fees may spare your cure from starvation.”

The bishop often told the tale, keeping the cure’s memory alive—and eventually transferred him to a decent parish, where he could offer old Medoc to those worthy of it. Their names are not legion.

A light dawned in Gerard’s eyes. His face revealed it.

“Ay!” said his host. “I am that cure. Now you understand why I said ‘At their old tricks.’ I swear they’ve tricked my successor into waiving those funeral fees. You’re lucky to have escaped that parish. And so am I.”

The cure’s niece burst in. “Uncle! The weighing—la! A stranger!” And she burst out laughing.

The cure rose instantly but kept Gerard beside him. “Wet your beard once more, and come with me.”

In the church porch, they found the sexton with enormous scales and weights of all sizes. Several humble folk stood by. Soon, a woman stepped forward with a sickly child. “Be it heavy or light,” she vowed, “in the best rye meal, whatever this child weighs, I will pay to Holy Church, if he recovers. Pray, good people, for this child and for me, his mother, come here in sorrow and care!”

The child was weighed and screamed as if the scale were the font.

“Courage, dame!” cried Gerard. “This is a good sign—there’s plenty of life to fight the illness.”

“Blessed be the tongue that says so,” replied the woman. She cradled her child close and stepped aside as another woman brought her child to be weighed.

Suddenly, a loud, commanding voice rang out: “Make way! Make way for the seigneur!”

The crowd parted like waves before a noble galley. Into the porch strode the lord of the manor—dressed in rich attire: cap adorned with a feather tipped with a topaz, fur-lined jerkin, satin doublet, red hose, skates-like shoes, diamond-hilted sword in velvet scabbard, hawk on wrist—“the lord of the manor.” He flung himself into the scales as if he ruled the zodiac as well as the land. The hawk wobbled, balanced, then blinked.

While the sexton added weights, the cure whispered to Gerard, “My lord was near death. He vowed his weight in bread and cheese to the poor, with the Church taking her tenth.”

“With your permission, my lord,” Gerard said, “if you continue pressing your staff on the other scale, you’ll disturb the balance.”

His lordship grinned and removed the staff, leaning on it instead. The cure politely objected.

“Mille diables! What am I to do with it then?” the lord protested.

“Hold it out wide, my lord, clear of both scales.”

When the lord did so—falling into his own trap—the cure whispered, “Cretensis incidit in Cretensem!” meaning, “Diamond cuts diamond.” Then, with mock deference, he added, “If your lordship begrudges Heaven full weight, you might set the hawk on your servant and save a pound.”

“Gramercy for your advice, cure!” the lord said, reproachfully. “Would I deny my poor bird the benefit of Holy Church for one measly pound? I’d sooner let the devil take me and all my house than her, any day of the year.”

“Sweet is affection,” whispered the cure.

“Between a bird and a brute,” whispered Gerard.

“Tush!” the cure said, looking terrified.

The lord’s weight was recorded. Heaven, I trust, did not weigh his gratitude in the sanctuary’s balance. My unlearned reader should not suppose the man was eccentric—nor his gratitude misplaced. Men view death and past illness through different lenses. And when bargaining, they seek the sunny side—whether with man or Heaven. In this, we are unchanged from four hundred years ago—only then, we did it more naively. In that rough age, body ruled mind, and feelings took physical form. Men repented with scourges, prayed with beads, bribed saints with candles, ate fish to sanctify the soul, endured cold water to master emotion, and thanked God for health in 1 cwt. 2 stone 7 lb. 3 oz. 1 dwt. of bread and cheese.

While I preach—though rarely and poorly—the cure has been urging the lord to enter the church and decide what shall be done with his great-great-grandfather.

“Ods bodikins! Have you dug him up?”

“No, my lord—he was never buried.”

“So the old saying was true after all?”

“So true that workers today found a skeleton standing upright in the pillar they’re repairing. I sent word to you at once—but knew you’d come.”

“It is he! It is he!” the descendant exclaimed, quickening his pace. “Let us go see the old boy. This youth is a stranger, I think.”

Gerard bowed.

“Know then,” said the lord, “that my great-great-grandfather held his head high. On his deathbed, he refused to lie beneath the aisle with his ancestors, letting common folk walk over him. So, as tradition tells, he swore his son—my great-grandfather—to bury him upright in one of the church pillars.” (They entered the porch.) “‘For,’ he said, ‘NO BASE MAN SHALL PASS OVER MY STOMACH.’ Peste!” Even as he spoke, his lordship deftly parried a skull hurled at him by a boy in the aisle—bowled by a prankster who fled screaming the moment he realized what he’d done. The lord hurled the skull back furiously. The cure gasped and reached out—too late.

The cure groaned. As if summoned by mischief, a pack of children burst from hiding and clattered out of the church like a covey rising in thick woods.

“Oh! These mischievous brats,” the cure lamented. “The workmen can’t finish their task without the church swarming with them. Pray Heaven they haven’t disturbed his late lordship—no, I remember—I hid his lordship under a workman’s jerkin, and—saints defend us! The jerkin has been moved.”

The cure’s worst fears were confirmed. The rising generation of plebeians had played havoc with the proud noble. “The little ones had jockeyed for the bones,” pocketing those suited for games popular among them.

“I’ll excommunicate them!” roared the curate.

“Never mind,” said the reckless lord, stroking his hawk. “There’s enough of him left to swear by. Put him back! Put him back!”

“Surely, my lord,” the cure said, “you wish his bones laid in holy ground, masses said for his proud soul?”

The noble stroked his hawk.

“Are you there, Master Cure?” he asked. “No—this business is too old. He’s out of purgatory by now, up or down. I won’t spend a penny on him. Every dog has his day. Adieu, Messires, adieu, ancestor.” And he sauntered off, whistling to his hawk and caressing it.

The cure watched him go, rueful.

The condemned men were ordered to stand bound in the marketplace for two hours, so that anyone who recognized them—or knew of other crimes they might have committed—could come forward and testify at their trial. But throughout the entire time, no one stepped forward with any new accusation. This was not surprising, for these men were known as night predators, creatures of darkness who preyed upon weary travelers, mostly strangers passing through.

Just as the guards began to unfasten them, a piercing scream tore through the crowd. A woman pointed wildly at one of the prisoners, her eyes wide with terror—and before she could speak, she collapsed unconscious.

Instantly, people rushed around her, some to help, others out of curiosity. As she stirred and began to regain her senses, voices rose in debate.

“It was him she pointed at.”

“No, it was this one!”

“Nay,” another insisted, “it was that sullen fellow with the golden hair hanging about his neck.”

Before more could be said, the woman sprang up like a lioness defending her young. “My child! Man! Man! Give me back my child!” She seized the glossy golden locks the officers had fastened around the prisoner’s neck, tore them from his throat, and pressed them to her face, kissing them feverishly. Then, as clarity returned, she realized what the hair meant—her daughter was dead. With a heart-wrenching cry, she fell to her knees, sobbing over the lock of hair. The crowd roared in fury, surging toward the accused man as if to tear him apart. In those days, every man carried death at his belt. His life would have ended then and there, but Denys drew his sword without hesitation, shouting, “A moi, camarades!” He held the mob back, shielding the prisoner. “Who touches him dies!”

Other archers joined him, and with difficulty they kept the crowd at bay while Denys appealed to the angry throng.

“What kind of justice is this? Would you rob the wheel and give the villain an easy death?”

The mob seethed, but the steel of the archers held them at a distance. The municipal officials, seeing the danger, gathered around and formed a guard, prudently escorting the prisoners back to prison.

The crowd hooted at both the officers and the accused alike. Denys saw the prisoners safely inside, then made his way to “The White Hart,” where he expected to find Gerard.

On the way, he passed a first-floor window where two girls were working. He greeted them. They smiled. Conversation followed. Their manners were open and confident; their complexions bright and healthy.

He invited them to dinner at the inn. They hesitated. He accepted their refusal. Then they agreed. And in their pleasant company, he forgot all about poor Gerard—who, meanwhile, had been taken into custody. On the way, however, Gerard regained his wits and demanded to know by whose authority he was being arrested.

“By the vice-bailiff’s,” replied the constable.

“The vice-bailiff? Alas, what have I, a stranger, done to offend such a man? This charge of sorcery must be a cover. I am no sorcerer—I am only a poor lad far from home.”

The officer was irritated. “Show him the capias, Jacques.”

Jacques held the writ aloft, nearly a yard from Gerard’s eye, while the large constable suddenly pinned him down—both fearing he might snatch the document, which they regarded with superstitious dread.

But Gerard had no such thought. Would he have touched it with tongs? He simply leaned forward and read it. To his astonishment, he saw the name of the vice-bailiff who had signed it: the very alderman who had welcomed him just days before.

He gained courage. “There must be some mistake,” he said. “I ask to be brought before him.”

“What say you to that, Jacques?”

“Impossible. We have no orders to take him before his worship. Read the writ!”

“Nay, but good fellows,” Gerard pleaded, “what harm can it do? I’ll give each of you an ecu.”

“Jacques, what say you now?”

“Humph. I say we have no orders *not* to take him to his worship. Read the writ.”

“Then let us take him to prison—but by way of his worship.”

They agreed. They collected the silver and told Gerard they were doing him a favor. He saw they wanted gratitude as well as gold. He tried to offer it, but words failed him. Feigning was never his strength.

He entered the alderman’s presence with his heart pounding. “Sir,” he stammered, “I beg to know what I have done to displease you since I left your house with Manon and Denys?”

“Nothing that I know of,” the alder人 replied.

When shown the writ, he admitted he had signed it at dawn. “I grow old, and my memory fails me. I had forgotten your own offense—but now I recall. All is well. You are the one I committed for sorcery. Wait—before you go to gaol, you shall hear what your accuser says. Run and fetch him.”

The man could not locate the accuser at once. Impatient, the alderman turned to Gerard. “The main charge is that you set a dead body on fire with a diabolical flame—one that burned but did not consume. If true, young man, I’m sorry for you. For you will surely burn at the stake in Neufchasteau.”

“Oh, sir, let me speak with the cure!”

The alderman shook his head. “The Church is harsher than the town when it comes to sorcerers.”

“But I am innocent,” Gerard insisted, voice trembling between defiance and pleading.

“If you think so,” said the alderman, “officer, take him to the cure—but see he does not escape. Innocent, quotha?”

They found the cure in his doublet, mending a wheelbarrow. Gerard told his story and begged mercy. “They’re going to hang me for using phosphorus to defend myself against thieves!”

It was fortunate that he had already confessed everything to the cure, for now the priest had the full picture. The corporation clutched the stick by the handle; the cure, by the end. He looked solemn and said, “I must question you privately on this matter.” He led Gerard into a small room and ordered the officer to wait outside, guarding the door and ready to enter if called. The big constable stood rigid, expecting the room to vanish in a blast of brimstone.

As soon as they were alone, the cure relaxed. “Show me the trick,” he said, eager.

“I cannot unless the room is dark.”

The cure quickly shut out the light with a wooden shutter. “Now.”

“But what shall I use?” Gerard asked. “It was a dead face that made it look so terrible.”

The cure felt about the room. “Ah—here’s an image. It’s my patron saint.”

“Heaven forbid! That would be profanation.”

“Pshaw! It’ll rub off, won’t it?”

“Aye, but I’d feel guilty taking liberties with a saint,” Gerard objected.

“Fiddlestick!” said the divine.

“To be sure—by placing it on the saint, you show me it’s no Satanic art.”

“Perhaps that was why I suggested it,” the cure replied, with a subtle smile.

Encouraged, Gerard lit the eyes and nostrils of the image, making the cure jump. Then he ignited patches of hair and set the whole face glowing like a firefly.

“By Our Lady!” shouted the cure. “That’s strange—no wonder they took you for a magician. Now, come with me!”

He put on his grey gown and hat, and in moments they stood before the alderman. By his side stood the accuser—a striking figure in red hose and shoes, a black gown with blue trim, and a cocked hat.

After greeting the alderman, the cure turned to the man and said cheerfully, “So, Mangis, back at your trade again, accusing honest men? Come, your worship, this is the same old tale—two of a trade never agree. Here is Mangis, who claims to be a sorcerer, yet sells himself to Satan tonight—though Satan is too wise to buy what he can get for free. This Mangis, who pretends to be a sorcerer, but is merely a quacksalver, accuses a true lad who used a known chemical secret for self-defense—a secret familiar to me and all churchmen.”

“But he is no churchman,” objected the alderman, “to dabble in such mysteries.”

“He is more churchman than layman,” the cure replied swiftly. “Brought up in a convent, in the lesser orders. Therefore, sorcerer, withdraw your complaint.”

“That I will not, your reverence,” Mangis replied firmly. “I *am* a sorcerer—but a white one, not a black. I make no pact with Satan. On the contrary, I fight him with lawful arts. I never profane the sacraments, as black sorcerers do. I do not turn into cats or suck infants’ blood. I simply tell peasants when their livestock are possessed, when to plant rye, which days are lucky for courting or selling oxen. Above all, I detect black magicians—like that whole tribe burned at Dol last year.”

“Ay, Mangis. And what became of that famous fire your tongue lit?”

“Their ashes were scattered to the wind.”

“Ay. But the true end of your comedy is this: The parliament of Dijon has examined the case and found they were not sorcerers, but peaceful citizens. Last week, they ordered masses for their souls and expiatory plays in seven towns of Burgundy. Yet none of that can bring them back. In our land, when we slay the innocent by listening to false knaves like you, we do not blame our credulous ears—but the lying tongue that deceived them. Think, then, that at a word from me to my lord bishop, you will smell burning pine closer than any rogue has ever smelled it—and travel on a smoky cloud to the one whose heart you bear (for ‘devil’ in Latin means ‘false accuser’), and whose livery you wear.”

And the cure pointed at Mangis with his staff.

“That is true, i’fegs,” said the alderman. “For red and black are the devil’s colors.”

Mangis’s face had gone as pale as his clothes were fiery. The contrast was almost comical. He stammered, “I respect Holy Church and her will. Let him burn the churchyard and all within it for me. I withdraw my complaint.”

“Then withdraw yourself,” said the vice-bailiff.

The moment he was gone, the cure resumed his conversational tone. “Your worship,” he said courteously, “the accused received the chemical substance from Holy Church and returned it—giving it all to me.”

“Then it’s in good hands,” replied the alderman. “Young man, you are free. Let me have your prayers.”

“Doubt it not. Humph. Vice-bailiff, the town owes me four silver franks—three months overdue.”

“They shall be paid, cure—within the week.”

Thus, Church and State parted in harmony. As soon as he stepped outside, Gerard seized the priest’s hand and kissed it.

“Oh, sir! Your reverence! You’ve saved me from the fiery stake. What can I say? What can I do?”

“Nought, foolish lad. Bounty rewards itself. Though—humph—I wish I had done it without lying. It ill becomes my office to speak falsehoods.”

“Falsehood, sir?” Gerard was confused.

“Did you not hear me say you gave me the phosphorus? That little lie will cost me a fortnight’s penance.”

The cure sighed, but his eye twinkled.

“Nay, nay,” Gerard protested eagerly. “That was no lie, father. You knew the phosphorus was yours—it still is.” He thrust the bottle into the cure’s hand. “But alas, it’s too poor a gift. Will you not take something from my purse for Holy Church?” He held out his purse, eyes glistening.

“Nay,” the priest said sharply, quickly putting his hands behind him. “Not a doit. Fie! Fie! You are pauper et exul. Come daily at noon and dine with me—for my heart warms to you.” And he walked off abruptly, hands clasped behind him.

They itched.

But they itched in vain.

Where there’s a heart, there’s a Rubicon.

Gerard hurried to the inn to relieve Denys of the anxiety caused by his long absence. He found him seated comfortably, playing dice with two young women—mannered, bold, and fair of complexion.

Gerard was wounded. “N’oubliez point la Jeanneton!” he said, blushing.

“What of her?” Denys asked, rattling the dice cheerfully.

“She said, ‘Le peu que sont les femmes.’”

“Oh? And what do you say to that, mesdemoiselles?”

“We say no man speaks ill of women except those too old, too ugly, or too dull to please them.”

“Witless, quotha?” Gerard retorted loftily. “Even wise men lack folly enough to please them, nor madness enough to desire to please them. But I speak to my comrade—not to you, you brazen toads, so free with a man at first sight.”

“Preach away, comrade. Fling bywords at our heads. Know, girls, he’s a Solomon for proverbs. Methinks he was raised on them.”

“Let your friendship be a byword!” Gerard snapped. “One that melts to nothing at the sight of a farthingale.”

“Malheureux!” cried Denys. “I speak but pellets, and you answer daggers.”

“Would I could,” Gerard replied. “Adieu.”

“What a little savage!” said one of the girls.

Gerard stuck his head back in the door. “I’ve thought of a byword,” he said spitefully—

“Qui hante femmes et dez
Il mourra en pauvretez.”

“There.” And slamming the door violently, he left before they could reply.

Exhausted by his ordeal, Gerard went to the bar for bread and wine. The landlord offered only a pint bottle. Well then, he’d take it. But when he compared the contents to the size, he noticed a discrepancy. He examined the bottle closely and found the glass thin where it tapered, but unnaturally thick near the bottom.

He pointed it out at once.

The landlord answered haughtily, “I don’t make bottles. I’m not responsible for their shape.”

“That we shall see,” Gerard said. “I’ll take this pint to the vice-bailiff.”

“Nay, nay, for Heaven’s sake!” the landlord exclaimed, changing tone. “I love to please my guests. If this pint is short, we’ll charge both this and its mate three sous instead of two.”

“So be it. But I marvel that you, host of such a fine inn, should cheat so. The wine also tastes strongly of spring water.”

“Young sir,” the landlord replied, “we cut no throats here, unlike most inns. ‘The White Hart’ is no lion or bear. Whatever robbery is done here, it’s done to the poor host. How else could I survive if I dealt honestly with the few who pay?”

Gerard objected to the system entirely. Honest trade meant small profits, quick returns—neither cheating nor being cheated.

The landlord sighed. “So might one keep an inn in heaven, but not in Burgundy. When foot soldiers are quartered on me, how can I profit? Two sous per day is their pay, and they eat two sous’ worth, and drink besides. Pardoners are my friends, but palmers and pilgrims—what do I gain? A loss. Minstrels and jongleurs draw customers and claim no fee, except for liquor. Secular monks neither gain nor lose, but the black and grey friars vow poverty, not hunger—they eat like wolves and give nothing but prayers—perhaps not even those. In my father’s day, we hosted weddings. Now, the great families lend their houses, plates, mugs, spoons to any honest couple wanting to wed. The mechanics go there with their brides. They don’t come to us—we couldn’t seat them. Once, the nobles sold wine by the barrel. Now, they sell it by the galopin in the market. How can we compete? They grow it. We buy it. The coroner’s quests still bring profit—but the meat is always gone before the mouths are full.”

“You should stock better,” Gerard suggested.

“The law forbids it. We may not enter the market for the first hour. By the time we arrive, the burghers have bought all but the refuse. And we may not buy more than three bushels of meal at a time—yet market day comes only once a week. The butchers won’t kill for us unless we bribe them.”

“Courage!” Gerard said kindly. “Every trader feels the pinch somewhere.”

“Ay—but not as we do. Our shoe is trod flat on one side *and* pinches us lame. A savoir: if we fail to pay merchants for meal, meat, wine, they can throw us in prison till we pay or die. But we cannot imprison those who buy from us. A traveler’s horse we may hold for debt—but where? In our stable, eating at our expense. We may detain the traveler himself—but where? Not in gaol. In our own house—where we must feed and lodge him gratis. So fling good silver after bad? Merci, no. Let him go with a wanion. Our best customers are thieves. Would God there were more. They don’t inspect the canakin’s shape or the bill. With them, it’s lightly come, lightly go. They spend freely—knowing each carouse may be their last. But thief-takers, instead of learning from this example, rob the poor host. When noble or honest travelers arrive, the provost’s men pretend to suspect them and demand to search them. To avoid offense, the host must feed and wine them. Then come the excise—town, royal, parliamentary—swarms of them, each with a wolf in the stomach and a sponge in the gullet. Monks, friars, pilgrims, soldiers, excisemen, provost-marshals, and bad debtors—how can ‘The White Hart’ withstand them all? We cut no throats in self-defense, unlike your ‘Swans,’ ‘Roses,’ ‘Boar’s Heads.’ How can we give a pint of wine for a pint? Everything has risen so high. Not a pound of bread I sell costs me three copper deniers—twelve to the sou. Each pint of wine, bought by the tun, costs me four deniers. A sack of charcoal—two sous, gone in a day. A pair of partridges—five sous. Can you believe it? Five sous for two bones and feathers? A pair of pigeons—thirty deniers. Ruination! We may not raise prices with the market. Oh, no. I tell you, the shoe is trod flat on one side *and* pinches us dry. We may charge nothing for mustard, pepper, salt, or firewood. Do you think we get them for nothing? Candle—sou per pound. Salt—five sous per stone. Pepper—four sous per pound. Mustard—twenty deniers per pint. Raw meat—does it dwindle on the spit? No cost to me—only loss of weight? Then what do I pay my cook? But you’ll never guess. A HUNDRED SOUS A YEAR AS I AM A LIVING SINNER.

“And my waiter—thirty sous, plus perquisites. He’s richer than I. And then to be insulted as well as plundered. Last Sunday I went to church—rarely. Didn’t the cure lash hotel-keepers? He hit all trades, except the clergy—the one famed for looseness, pride, sloth. But he spared them. He beat us with a neat’s pizzle: godless this, godless that, most godless of all for opening doors during mass. But the law forces us to open at all hours for travelers from elsewhere. They can fine us if we refuse—mass or no mass. If a townsman sneaks in with them, are we to blame? They all swear they’re tired wayfarers. Can I know every face in this city? So if we obey the law, our souls suffer. If we don’t, our purses bleed—fine and lost business.”

A man speaking of himself is “a babbling brook”; of his wrongs, “a shining river.”

“Labitur et labetur in omne volubilis aevum.”

Luckily for readers, though not for the speaker, this eloquent orator was interrupted mid-sentence. Another man burst in, fresh from his own grievance—hot and furious. It was Denys, cursing and swearing, shouting he had been robbed.

“Did those hussies pass this way? Who are they? Where do they live? They’ve stolen my purse and fifteen golden pieces! Raise the hue and cry! Ah! traitresses! vipers! These inns are all guet-apens!”

“There now,” the landlord said to Gerard.

Gerard urged calm. “Tell me how it happened.”

“First one left on some pretext. Then the other went to fetch her. Neither returned. I reached for my purse—and it was empty. The ungrateful creatures—I was letting them win it slowly. But loaded dice weren’t fast enough. They had to take it all at once.”

Gerard insisted on going to the alderman and sending officers after them.

“Not I,” Denys snapped. “I hate the law. No—let it go as it came.”

Gerard refused to abandon it.

At the landlord’s suggestion, he dragged Denys to the provost-marshal. The official shook his head. “We have no clue to occasional thieves who work honestly at their needles—until some fool tempts them with easy prey, and then they strike.”

“Come away!” Denys cried. “I knew what use a bourgeois would be in a crisis.” He stormed off in rage.

“They’re clear of town by now,” Gerard said.

“Say no more if you value my friendship. I have five pieces with the bailiff, ten with Manon—luckily. Or these traitresses would have feathered their nest with my last plume. What are you gaping at? Nay, I do ill to vent my anger on you. I’ll tell you all. You’re wiser than I. What did you say at the door? Never mind. Well then—I did offer marriage to Manon.”

Gerard was stunned.

“What? You offered her what?”

“Marriage. Is that so strange to offer a girl?”

“It’s strange to offer it to a strange girl in passing.”

“Nay, I’m not such a fool as you think. I saw the corn in the chaff. I knew I couldn’t win her fairly, so I tried foul play. ‘Mademoiselle,’ I said, ‘marriage is not my habit, but struck by your qualities, I make an exception. Deign to bestow this hand on me.’”

“And she bestowed it on your ear.”

Outside the town, the road was thick with fresh tracks—paw prints of wolves that had passed in great numbers. The snow, once pristine, now bore witness to their restless passage.

“We did well to heed the old man’s warning, Denys,” Gerard said quietly.

“Ay, we did,” Denys replied. “Now I recall—I heard them last night, skittering beneath our window, howling like starving beasts in the market square. But no fat burgher tossed them a scrap from his plate. Poor vagabonds.”

Gerard smiled, but it was a distant smile, as if his thoughts were far away. They walked on in silence, each lost in their own world.

“What are you thinking so deeply about?” Denys asked at last.

“Your goodness,” Gerard answered.

Denys frowned. He could endure much nonsense, especially when it came wrapped in good humor; but sometimes—without reason—he would flare up, as if insulted by mere words.

“A civil question deserves a civil answer,” he said dryly.

“I meant no other,” Gerard insisted.

“Then why pretend you were pondering my goodness, when you know I have none beneath my skin?”

“If another had said that, I’d have told him, ‘You lie.’ But to you, I say: You see only women’s qualities, not men’s. And again, I defy your unjust anger. I *was* thinking of your goodness—last night, when you offered to marry me off to the *Tête d’Or*, or rather to the *tête de veau dorée*, and leave yourself alone.”

“Oh, are you there, lad?” Denys laughed, regaining his usual warmth. “Well, let me be honest—I didn’t mean it for goodness, but for friendship, true fellowship. No more. And truly, my young master, my conscience pricks me even now for letting you turn your back on fortune and peace. A truer friend than I might have taken your leg and crippled you—then you’d have lain healing at the *Tête d’Or* for a month, nursed by that flighty lass, and all would have been well. I had the blade ready, but remembering how you hate pain—even a scratch—my coward heart failed me at the last moment.”

He looked down, ashamed, as though confessing a failure of courage.

Gerard raised his eyebrows in surprise—this was monstrous, yet entirely characteristic of Denys. Yet the matter was never spoken of again: whether one should, out of love, cripple a friend to save him from harm. For an event intervened.

“Here comes someone behind us—riding a neighbor’s mule!” shouted Denys.

Gerard turned.

“And how do you know it’s not his own?” he asked.

“Oh, blind! Because he rides it like a madman.”

Indeed, the man came galloping wildly, eyes wide with alarm. When he reached them, he reined in so sharply the mule nearly fell, sliding between them like a four-legged table on wheels.

“You’re from the *Tête d’Or*, aren’t you?” he gasped.

They nodded.

“Which of you is the younger?”

“The one born later,” Denys replied, winking at Gerard.

“Gramercy for the news!”

“Come, divine then!”

“And shall. Your beard is full-grown, his is still green. He’s the younger. Here, youngster.” He handed Gerard a folded packet. “You left this at the *Tête d’Or*. Our mistress sends it.”

“No,” Gerard said, searching his pouch. “I don’t remember leaving anything.”

“Would you make our burgess a liar?” the man reproached. “And shall I get no *pourboire*? I came *ventre à terre*!”

“Well, you shall have your tip,” Gerard said, handing over a small coin.

“A la bonne heure!” the man cheered, beaming with joy. “The Virgin go with you! Come up, Jenny!” And he rode off, “stomach to earth,” as they say in the country.

Gerard opened the packet. It was six inches square, and inside lay another, and within that another, and so on. At the fourth layer, he threw the whole thing into the snow.

Denys pulled it out. “Now what’s this? Don’t throw things about like that.”

“I hate affectation,” Gerard muttered.

“But look—no affectation here. Only woman’s wit. Clearly, she wrapped it carefully because she wouldn’t want her servant to see what she gave a young man—perhaps a garter.”

“I wear no garters.”

“Then hers. Or a lock of hair. What’s this? A piece of raw silk, fresh from the worm. Well, of all love tokens!”

“Who ever thought she’d send me such a thing? I saw no harm in her—except her hands.”

“Stay, something hard is hidden in this soft nest. Come forth, little bird!” Denys exclaimed. “Saints and pikestaves! Look!”

It was a gold ring, set with a large amethyst—deep, glowing, pure as crystal.

“How lovely,” Gerard whispered.

“And here’s a note. Read it. I’m not so quick at reading when I don’t know what’s coming.”

Gerard took the paper. “It’s a posy—well written.”

He read aloud, blushing like a girl:

> Youth, with thee my heart is fled,
> Come back to the 'golden Hedde!'
> Wilt not? yet this token keep
> Of hir who doeth thy going weep.
> Gyf the world prove harsh and cold,
> Come back to 'the Hedde of gold.'

“The little dove,” murmured Denys.

“The great owl!” he added, shaking his head. “To risk her name like this. Thank Heaven she chose an honest lad—one who’ll never expose her folly. But oh, the absurdity! Why couldn’t she give it to *me*?”

Denys sighed and shrugged.

“To you, who are just as ripe for foolishness as she?”

Denys admitted, “That’s exactly what I was thinking.”

It seemed strange to him that a woman with eyes could pass over a man and fall for a boy. Still, he acknowledged nature’s bounty: boys were human beings too. Without such caprice, they’d be forgotten—blighted, never growing into men. Only beauty could shape a man from such raw material.

Gerard broke in, offering the ring to Denys.

He refused firmly. “No. You must return to the *Tête d’Or* right now—with the ring, and everything. Like a man. Don’t let a poor girl reach out to you in vain.”

“Her hands, you mean.”

“Her hand—with the *Tête d’Or* in it.”

When that failed, Denys tried to put the ring on Gerard’s finger.

Gerard declined. “I already wear one.”

“That sorry trinket? That’s pewter or tin. This is virgin gold—and the jewel!”

“Yes, but Margaret gave me this. I value it above rubies. I’ll never part with it—or give it a rival.” He kissed the plain metal. “Let it fear nothing.”

“I see the owl has sent her ring to a goose,” Denys said sadly.

But he finally persuaded Gerard to tuck the ring inside his bonnet.

The boy agreed readily. Certain jewels were believed to hold sovereign powers—the amethyst among the most potent talismans.

Once settled, Gerard begged Denys to drop the subject. Talking of women made him ache for Margaret, and every step farther from her felt like a wound.

“I’m not a general lover, Denys. There’s room in my heart for one sweetheart, and one friend. I’m far from my dear Margaret. And soon—just a few leagues more—I’ll lose you too. Let me drink your friendship pure while I may. Don’t dilute it with any of these silly females.”

“And you shall, honey-pot, and you shall,” Denys said kindly. “But as for me leaving you at Remiremont—don’t count on it! If I do—(three oaths) I’ll go with you to Rome. Why not? His Holiness the Pope always needs soldiers. A Burgundian is welcome in his ranks.”

At this, Gerard opened his heart.

“Denys, before I met you, I often stopped on the road—too weak to go on. My heart pulled me back. Then I’d pray to the saints, rise, and drag myself forward. But since I’ve walked with you, my courage has grown. I’ve seen the truth of the ancients: better a bright companion on the weary path than a horse-litter. Oh, brother—when I think of all we’ve done, all we’ve suffered together! You saved my life from the bear, from worse thieves. Even when I was poor, I managed to pull you from the Rhine—and from that hour, I loved you doubly. How many bonds between us! If I had my way, I’d never, never, never part with you—this side of death. Alas, God’s will be done.”

“No,” Denys roared. “My will shall be done this time. Le bon Dieu has bigger fish to fry than us. I’ll go with you to Rome. There’s my hand on it.”

“You say that? It’s impossible. Too selfish of me.”

“I tell you—it’s settled. Nothing can change me. At Remiremont, I borrow ten pieces from my uncle. We go. It’s fixed.”

They shook hands.

Then Gerard said nothing. His heart was too full. Instead, he ran twice around Denys, danced backward before him, and finally took his hand. So they walked—hand in hand, like lovers—until a company of fifty mounted soldiers rose into view on a hilltop.

“Look—the banner of Burgundy!” Denys said joyfully. “I’ll find a comrade among them.”

“How glorious it shines in the sun!” Gerard exclaimed. “And the leaders—velvet, feathers, steel breastplates like glass mirrors!”

As they drew near, Denys gasped. “Why, it’s the Bastard of Burgundy himself! Then there’s fighting afoot. A bold leader—values his life no higher than a private’s, and a soldier’s no higher than a sparrow’s. That’s the captain for me.”

“And see,” Gerard said, “even the mules—brass frontlets, fine trappings—seem proud to carry them. No wonder men long to be soldiers.”

In the midst of this admiration, the troop reached them.

“Halt!” a deep voice commanded.

They halted.

The Bastard of Burgundy glared at Denys. “How now, archer? Why face south when every loyal hand and heart hurries north?”

Denys bowed. “I’m returning home after years of service—to see my family at Remiremont.”

“Good. But not now. The duchy is troubled. Bring the dead soldier’s mule forward. Mount and ride with us to Flanders.”

“So please your highness,” Denys said firmly, “that cannot be. My home is close. I haven’t seen it in three years. Above all, I have this youth under my care. I cannot, must not leave him until I see him safely shipped for Rome.”

“Do you defy me?” the commander thundered, turning wrathful. “Are you tired of life? Let go the boy’s hand and mount—no more idle talk.”

Denys said nothing. But he held Gerard’s hand tighter, and stared back with defiance.

The Bastard roared, “Jarnac! Dismount six archers—shoot this white-livered cur dead where he stands. For an example.”

Young Count de Jarnac gave the order. Six men dismounted.

“Strip him naked,” the Bastard ordered coldly. “Put his arms on the spare mule. We may find a clown worthy to wear them.”

Denys groaned. “Am I to be shamed *and* killed?”
