“Oh, no! No! No!” cried Gerard, snapping from his shock. “He shall go with you—immediately. I’d rather lose him forever than see a hair of his head harmed. Oh, sir, my lord—give a poor boy just a minute to bid his only friend farewell! He’ll go. I swear he will.”

The leader nodded, cold and scornful. “Jarnac, stay with them. Bring him on—alive or dead. Forward!”

And he led his men away, leaving only Jarnac and six archers, one holding the spare mule.

Denys and Gerard stared at each other—haggard, silent.

What a look!

Then, in frantic haste, they spoke.

“You’re going to Holland. You know where she lives. Tell her everything. She’ll be kind—for my sake.”

“Oh, what a tale I’ll bring her! For God’s sake, go back to the *Tête d’Or*. I’m mad!”

“Hush! Let me think—have I nothing to say? My head—my head!”

“Ah! I have it. Go to Strasbourg, Gerard. The Rhine. Downstream to Rotterdam. Margaret is there. I’ll go there. I’ll tell her you’re coming. We’ll all be together.”

“My lads, hurry,” Jarnac said firmly, but gently now. “We’re wasting time.”

“Oh, sir—just one moment! One little moment!” Gerard gasped.

“Cursed be the land I was born in! Cursed be the race of man! And he who made them so!” Denys screamed.

“Hush, Denys, hush! Blaspheme not! God forgive him—he knows not what he says. Be patient. Though we meet no more on earth, let us meet in a better world—where no blasphemer may enter. To my heart, lost friend. Words are gone now.”

He opened his arms. They embraced—tight, unyielding. They kissed again and again, speechless, tears streaming down both faces.

Count Jarnac watched, amazed. But the rougher soldiers—those who knew what comrade meant—looked on with quiet pity.

Then, at Jarnac’s signal, they lifted Denys onto the mule, half-carrying him, and rode after their leader.

Gerard ran wildly after them—though the lane curved. The last he saw: Denys rocking on the mule, tearing his hair.

At that sight, something rose in Gerard’s throat—so high, so sharp—he could run no more. He gasped, leaned against a snow-covered hedge, clutching it, choking.

Thorns pierced his hand.

After a bitter struggle, he breathed again.

Now he began to feel his loss—slowly, painfully.

He staggered forward, not knowing where he went. Every few steps, he stopped. His arms dropped. His head sank. He stood still.

Then he whispered: “Can this be real? This must be a dream. Five minutes ago, we were happy—walking hand in hand, going to Rome together. We admired their banners, their helmets—oh hearts of hell!”

All nature seemed as lonely as he.

No living thing in sight.

Only white.

He, a ghost of his former self, wandered among ghostly trees, fields, hedges.

Desolate. Desolate. Desolate.

He knelt, gathered snow. “No—I do not dream. This is snow. Cold as the world’s heart. And bloody—what does that mean? Fool! It’s from my hand. I don’t remember the wound. Ah—thorns. Welcome, kind foes. I felt you not. You did not pierce my heart. You are not cruel like men.”

He rose, dragging his leaden limbs.

Then—hoofbeats. Gay voices.

He turned, hoping—perhaps the soldiers had relented, brought Denys back.

But no. A gay cavalcade approached: a nobleman in velvet and furs, his favorites, and armed retainers in buff jerkins.

They swept past.

Gerard never looked at them again. Just shadows—gay, fleeting.

Then suddenly—a harsh cry: “Stand and deliver!”

Three servants blocked his path. They had ridden back to rob him.

“How, ye false knaves,” Gerard said calmly, “would you shame your noble master? He’ll hang you from the nearest tree.”

With that, he drew his sword, backed against the hedge.

One leveled a petronel.

Another stepped forward. “Don’t be hasty! And don’t be mad! Look yonder!”

Gerard looked. A hundred yards away, the nobleman and his friends had halted—watching, too proud to dirty their hands, but eager to reap the reward.

The softer servant said, “Resistance is useless. Common thieves kill as well as steal. And it costs a mint to be a gentleman. Your master lost money last night. He’s going to visit his mistress. So he takes what he finds. Now, good youth—consider: we don’t rob for ourselves. Hand over that purse without fuss. Or we slit your throat and take it anyway.”

“This man is right,” Gerard said quietly, aloud—but to himself. “I ought not to throw away my life. Margaret would grieve. Take the poor man’s purse to the rich man’s pouch. And with it—this: tell him, I pray the Holy Trinity, each coin may burn his hand, freeze his heart, and blast his soul forever. Begone. Leave me to my sorrow.”

He flung the purse.

They rode off, muttering. His words stung them—just a little.

He staggered on, penniless now, friendless.

Until he reached the edge of a wood.

His heart could barely feel the blow. But his mind did.

What was the use?

He sat on the hard road, clawing his hair, trying to think.

Rome was impossible without money.

Denys had said: “Go to Strasbourg. Down the Rhine.”

He would obey.

But how?

Then—suddenly—the lines rang in his ears:

> Gyf the world prove harsh and cold,
> Come back to the hedde of gold.

“If I do,” he whispered, “I must go as her servant. I who am Margaret’s. I am weary. I will sleep. Dream all is as it was. Ah me—how happy we were an hour ago. We knew not how happy. There is a house—its owner well-to-do. What if I tell him my story, beg help to retrieve my purse, and reach the Rhine?”

Fool! Is he not a man—like the rest? He’d scorn me. Trample me lower.

Denys cursed the race of men.

I will not curse them. But oh—I begin to loathe them.

No. I’ll lie here till sunset. Then, in darkness, creep into his barn. Steal milk or grain—just enough to live. God, who saw the rich rob me, may forgive me.

They say it’s ill sleeping on snow. Death creeps with muffled feet and honey breath.

But what can I do? I am weary. So weary.

Is this the wood where the wolves dwell—the old man warned of?

I must trust them. They are not men.

And I am so weary.

He crawled to the roadside, stretched out on the snow, sighing deeply.

“Ah, tear not thine hair so! It breaks my heart to see thee.”

“Margaret. Never see me more. Poor Margaret.”

And the tender heart stilled.

The constant lover, the true friend of ancient mold, lay silent on the snow—threatened by cold, by beasts, by hunger, friendless, penniless, in a strange land, not halfway to Rome.

Travel, rough and rugged as it often is, holds a peculiar charm for the English mind. So too do the tales of those who have braved its hardships—whether driven by duty, desire, or mere daring. Even when the traveler bears no sacred vow of love, his journey can stir the imagination. And old friendships, like fossils unearthed from time’s soil, carry their own quiet fascination. Yet, since the heart of this story beats in Holland, it is time to return there—to the ordinary folk, the familiar scenes, and the everyday lives that have shaped human experience across the ages.

Jorian Ketel came to Peter’s house, determined to claim Margaret’s promise. But she lay ill in bed, feverish and weak. Upon hearing his purpose, Peter met him with sharp rebuke, driving him from the threshold. A few onlookers were ready to toss him into the nearest pond; both father and daughter were beloved, and the tale of their sorrow had spread through every corner of Sevenbergen. The town was inflamed with sympathy, a fervor that knows no measure. Jorian left in anger, regretting his kindness. Such remorse is not uncommon—and yet, when sincere, it carries its own weight.

Meanwhile, Dierich Brower, caught at “The Three Kings” questioning a drunken man about Martin Wittenhaagen’s whereabouts, was seized and thrown into a horsepond. He was threatened with worse if he ever returned. The outrage stirred municipal pride: the burgomaster of Sevenbergen sent a formal letter to Tergou, accusing them of overstepping their bounds and demanding that any future grievances be addressed through proper channels.

Ghysbrecht Van Swieten, though outwardly calm, seethed beneath. He replied with polite dignity, claiming he had pursued a Tergovian named Gerard—who had stolen the town records—and now fled abroad, likely carrying them with him. Thus, he turned necessity into virtue. But privately, he was consumed by dread. His spies learned nothing from the family at Tergou—they did not know where Gerard had gone. This uncertainty gnawed at him. He began to fear the boy was not far away, but lurking nearby, waiting to strike. From that moment, Ghysbrecht changed. He grew irritable, restless. His eyes darted nervously, as if expecting an unseen blow. Power had not brought peace—only deeper unease.

At Tergou, the family remained outwardly unchanged, but within, the warmth had faded. Little Kate knew her brothers, Cornelis and Sybrandt, had helped banish Gerard. Though she never spoke of it—fearing to worsen the rift—she shuddered at their sight and blushed at their false sorrow. Catherine, sharp-eyed and silent, noticed. She said nothing, but watched closely, her thoughts deepening into suspicion. The two boys, eager to share in the household’s grief, deceived their father and Giles—but not the women. Their secret satisfaction betrayed them. “That, noting all, seem nought to50 note,” they might say, but the truth lingered unspoken.

Gerard’s absence had left a hollow space at the table. His intelligent presence, once the light of the room, was missed—though none dared name it. The old hosier, wounded in pride by his son’s defiance, carried himself stiffly, refusing even to speak Gerard’s name. Yet beneath his rigid exterior, his heart strained. One thing he could not hide: his worry. “If I only knew where he is, and that he is safe,” he would sigh, “I’d care little else.” And then a long, heavy breath would follow. One cannot help thinking that if Gerard had walked through the door at that moment, there would have been tears, embraces—no reproaches, perhaps not even words.

What surprised the family most was how quickly the story became public. Within days, Gerard’s flight and the lovers’ plight were known throughout the town. Worse still, the people sided with Margaret and Gerard—against the stern parents and especially against the meddling burgomaster, who had interfered in what seemed no one’s business but their own.

“Mother,” Kate said softly, “they say Margaret is very ill—burning with fever. Her father fears for her.”

“Margaret?” Catherine asked, feigning calmness, though her voice trembled. “Which Margaret?”

“Oh, mother! How can you ask? Gerard’s Margaret.”

“Gerard’s Margaret!” Catherine cried, her voice cracking. “How dare you speak such a name here? Never mention that girl again—she has ruined my poor boy, the finest of my children. She is the reason he is not a holy priest among us, but wandering the world, while I sit broken-hearted. Do not cry, child—I speak harshly, but oh, Kate—you cannot know what a mother feels. I bear up before you all, I must swallow my fears. But at night, I dream of him—always in danger. Sometimes torn by wild beasts, sometimes bound by robbers, their knives raised above his pale face—so pale it would move a stone. Oh, when I think of that, while I sit warm and safe, perhaps he lies dead in some distant land—because of her! That name is poison to me. I tremble when I hear it.”

“I’ll never speak of her again, mother,” Kate whispered, her voice thick with pity. “I’ll do nothing to grieve you more.” And she sighed.

Yet the very woman whose name was forbidden was spoken of everywhere—with sympathy, even admiration. All of Sevenbergen pitied Margaret. Young men and maidens glanced toward her window, where the village beauty lay “dying for love”—a phrase that underestimated her strength and devotion. Gerard was not dead. She believed in his constancy. Her father was dear to her, helpless now. Had she not been weakened by illness, she would have stayed by his side, though her heart might have drooped. But the strain of emotion and physical exhaustion had brought on a fierce fever. Only youth and strong constitution saved her.

When the fever broke, she was left in a state of profound weakness—where life felt like a burden. Then, love and kindness become mortal angels, their voices soothing, their touch healing. But Margaret had no one at her side. For many days she lay alone, the hours dragging like leaden waves. Existence seemed meaningless. Gerard was gone. There was no one to live for. Often she lay still, tears silently tracing paths down her cheeks.

One day, waking from a troubled sleep, she found two women in her room. One was a servant; the other, plainly of higher station, wore fur-lined sleeves and a narrow band of silver hair peeking from her coif—a sign of age and wisdom. Both looked gentle and kind.

Margaret tried to rise, but the older woman laid a hand gently on her chest. “Lie still, sweetheart. We come not to disturb you, but to comfort you, God willing. Now, cheer up—tell us, who do you think we are?”

“I know you,” Margaret whispered, though she had never seen them. “You are Demoiselle Van Eyck, and this is Reicht Heynes. Gerard has spoken of you often—of your kindness to him. Madam, he has no friend like you near him now.” At this, she sank back, tears welling anew.

Reicht Heynes began to weep—not from sadness, but from shared feeling. The older woman scolded her gently. “Well, you’re a fine one for a sickroom!” she said, and then set about cheering Margaret with quiet humor and tender care. An old woman who has lived through sorrow knows what to say—and what to avoid. She soothed, she amused, she drew Margaret close until the young girl rested her head on her shoulder, her eyes soft with gratitude.

“Ah,” said the lady, running her fingers through Margaret’s hair, “this is hair. Come, Reicht, look at it!”

Reicht examined it, praised it sincerely. The girl, though weak, could not resist a flicker of pride. “In truth, madam, I used to think it ugly. But he praised it—ever since, I’ve almost grown vain of it. Saints forgive me. You know how foolish those are who love.”

“They are greater fools who don’t,” the old lady replied sharply.

Margaret blinked, struck by the meaning.

This was the first of many visits. Almost daily, either the demoiselle or Reicht came to the bedside. Under their care, Margaret improved swiftly. Reicht credited nourishing dishes made in Peter’s kitchen; Margaret, however, believed it was the kindness, the steady presence, the quiet reassurance that gave her reason to live again.

Martin Wittenhaagen, meanwhile, rode straight to Rotterdam, intent on confronting the source of power. The bull he sought was not beast, but man—Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, Earl of Flanders, Lord of Brabant. Arriving in Rotterdam, he learned the court was in Ghent. There he went, seeking an audience, but was turned away by lackeys and pages. Undeterred, he threw himself into the duke’s path during a hunting expedition—and, ignoring courtly etiquette, roared out: “Mercy!”

“Why, where is the peril, man?” the duke laughed, scanning the field. “Grace for an old soldier hunted down by burghers?”

Kings, though varied in nature, share one trait: they delight in affability with the low-born. These men pose no threat, no rivalry. Their blunt honesty amuses, their simplicity refreshes. Philip reined in his horse, granting Martin a rare, personal moment.

Martin reminded him of a battlefield where he had taken an arrow meant for the duke. The memory was vivid. The king smiled. “A cheerful tale indeed,” he said. “I could afford to laugh—since it wasn’t me who got hit.”

Then Martin told of Gerard’s capture in the church, his imprisonment, the escape, and the hunt that followed. Whether Martin told it better than I have, or whether the duke simply loved a good story, the result was clear: the king was spellbound. When courtiers interrupted, he swore like a street vendor and threatened, half-jokingly, to chop off the next head that blocked his tale. When Martin finished, the duke exclaimed:

“St. Luke! What sport goes on in my earldom—ay, in my own woods—and I see nothing? You base fellows have all the luck.”

He was indignant at Fortune’s favoritism.

“This was a man-hunt,” he said. “I’ve never had the chance to attend one.”

“My luck was not great,” Martin replied. “I was on the wrong side of the dogs’ noses.”

“Oh, yes—forgotten that.” The king’s mood softened.

“What would you have?” he asked.

“A free pardon, your highness—for myself and Gerard.”

“For what?”

“For breaking prison.”

“Go to—the bird will fly from the cage. 'Tis instinct. Besides, lock up a young man for loving a young woman? These burgomasters must be devoid of sense. What else?”

“For striking down the burgomaster.”

“Oh, the hunted boar turns to bay. 'Tis his right. I hold less than man who grudges it.”

“And for killing the bloodhounds.”

The duke’s expression darkened.

“'Twas their life or mine,” Martin insisted.

“Ay, but I can’t have my bloodhounds—my beautiful bloodhounds—sacrificed to…”

“No, no—those were not your dogs.”

“Whose, then?”

“The ranger’s.”

“Oh. Well, I’m sorry for him. But as I said, I won't have my old soldiers sacrificed to his hounds. You shall have your pardon.”

“And poor Gerard.”

“And poor Gerard too—for thy sake. And more—tell this burgomaster his ways displease me. This is not the role of a burgomaster, but a king. I’ll have no kings in Holland but one. Bid him be humble—or by St. Jude, I’ll hang him before his own door, as I hanged the burgomaster of… what was it? Some town in Flanders? No—Brabant. Doesn’t matter—I hanged him. I remember that.”

He beckoned his chancellor, a stout man riding like a sack, and ordered him to draw up a free pardon for Martin and Gerard. It was written, signed the next day, and Martin hurried home with it.

Margaret had risen from her bed a few days earlier, sitting pale and thoughtful by the fire when Martin burst in, waving the parchment.

“A free pardon, girl—for Gerard as well as me! Send for him back whenever you wish. Not a burgomaster on earth dares touch him!”

Her face flushed with joy. Her hands trembled as she took the scroll, read it, kissed it again and again, then flung her arms around Martin’s neck and kissed him.

When she calmed, she told him of the friendship offered by Demoiselle Van Eyck.

“And I would fain consult her about this news—but I lack strength to walk so far.”

“What need to walk?” Martin grinned. “There’s my mule.”

“My mule?” she asked, surprised.

The old soldier chuckled. “I’ve grown so used to her, I forget Ghysbrecht owns her. Tomorrow I’ll return her—but tonight, she carries you to Tergou.”

It was nearly dusk. Margaret ventured forth. By seven o’clock, she arrived at Tergou—roses blooming on her cheeks, the pardon clutched in her bosom. She startled and gladdened her new, devoted friend with her unexpected return.

Some grow old in spirit by forty, others remain young at eighty. Margaret Van Eyck’s heart was evergreen—full of warmth, life, and tenderness. She loved her namesake, the young Margaret Brandt, with a passion that felt fresh and unburdened by time. This affection was no fleeting fancy; it was rooted in deep understanding. Margaret Van Eyck had a keen eye for character, and she saw in the younger woman something rare and precious: sincerity. But beyond her own noble qualities, Margaret Brandt had an even greater ally in the artist’s heart.

Human nature.

Strange as it may seem to those who do not watch closely, our hearts often warm more quickly to those we have helped than to those who have helped us. The ancient Greeks noticed this truth long ago, but it was the British Homer who captured it most powerfully in verse:

“I heard, and thought how side by side
We two had stemmed the battle's tide
In many a well-debated field,
Where Bertram's breast was Philip's shield.
I thought on Darien's deserts pale,
Where Death bestrides the evening gale,
How o'er my friend my cloak I threw,
And fenceless faced the deadly dew.
I thought on Quariana's cliff,
Where, rescued from our foundering skiff,
Through the white breakers' wrath I bore
Exhausted Bertram to the shore:
And when his side an arrow found,
I sucked the Indian's venom'd wound.
These thoughts like torrents rushed along
To sweep away my purpose strong.”

Observe: the assassin’s hand is stayed not by kindness received, but by deeds done. Memory recalls what one has given, not what one has gained.

Margaret Van Eyck had been wonderfully kind to Margaret Brandt. She had broken her routine to visit her, nursed her through illness, soothed her fears, petted her, and healed her more effectively than any medicine could have. In return, her heart opened wide—not just to the girl’s charm, but to the gratitude she inspired. She now loved Margaret Brandt more tenderly than she had ever loved Gerard, though in truth, her original visit had been prompted only by concern for him.

When, therefore, she saw the blush rise upon Margaret’s cheeks and read the parchment that had brought it about, she gave up her own plans without hesitation.

“Sweetheart,” she said, “I once hoped he would stay in Italy five or six years, return rich, and above all, become a true master of art. But your happiness comes before all else. And I see you cannot live without him. So let us bring him home as soon as may be.”

“Oh, madam!” replied the young woman, her voice soft and trembling. “You’ve read my very soul.” She lowered her eyes and blushed deeply. “But how shall I tell him? That passes my skill. He has gone to Italy—but I know not where. Wait! He named the cities he meant to visit. Florence was one, and Rome.”

Yet even then, being wise and cautious, she feared that a letter addressed simply “My Gerard—Italy” might never reach its destination. She looked up at her friend, pleading for advice.

“You’ve come to the right place, at the right time,” said the old lady. “Hans Memling was here today—he’s going to Italy, no later than next week. ‘To improve his hand,’ he says. Not before it was needed, I assure you.”

“But how can he find Gerard?”

“Why, he knows him well, child. They’ve dined here together more than once, and were as close as hand and glove. Since their work is the same, they’ll likely travel the same roads. Sooner or later, they must meet. Now go and write a long letter—copy the pardon into it—and leave it with me. I will vouch for the messenger. Within six months, at the latest, Gerard will receive it. And when he does, he’ll kiss it, tuck it into his breast, and fly home. What are you smiling at? And why do your cheeks burn so? You’re smothering me with joy. Yes—happy days are coming for my little pearl.”

Meanwhile, Martin sat in the kitchen, the black-jack before him, while Reicht Heynes spun beside him. And oh! how she questioned him that night.

Hans Memling was an old pupil of Jan Van Eyck and his sister. Though Margaret sneered at him, he was indeed a painter—no mere artisan, but a man of talent and good heart, save for one fault: he loved the “nipperkin, canakin, and the brown bowl” far too well. This weakness kept him poor and often brought him to Margaret Van Eyck’s door—not just for food, but sometimes for a groat. Yet this dependence gave her influence over him. She knew he would never betray a trust placed in his hands.

The letter was written and entrusted to Margaret Van Eyck. The following week, Hans Memling returned from Flanders. She gave him the letter and a piece of gold toward his journey. He seemed eager to depart.

“All the better,” she said. “He’ll reach Italy the sooner.”

But as some horses race at the start and then lag after the first few steps, so did Hans’s haste fade once he reached the main inn in Tergou. There, he found two of his closest companions seated in the bay window. He entered for a farewell drink. When he offered to pay, they refused—no, he was going on a long journey; they would treat him. Everyone would treat him—the landlord included.

This generosity loosened his tongue as if wine were oil. He boasted of showing the Italians how to paint, sang of his battles with the pike, and recounted his romantic triumphs with women (not present to contradict). In short, he was “plenus rimarum erat: huc illuc diffluebat”—full of chatter, spilling out in every direction. Among his ramblings, he revealed he carried a letter for a fellow townsman—Gerard, a good fellow. “You are all good fellows,” he added, slapping Sybrandt on the back so hard it knocked the breath from his body.

Sybrandt scrambled around the table to avoid the blow, but listened closely. For the first time, he learned that Gerard had gone to Italy. Still, to test the truth, he pretended disbelief.

“My brother Gerard is never in Italy.”

“Ye lie, ye cur!” roared Hans, instantly irate, unaware that the man opposite him was the very one he had praised and struck moments before. “If he is ten times your brother, he is in Italy. What call ye this? Read that superscription!” And he flung the letter onto the table.

Sybrandt picked it up, examined it gravely, then laid it down again. “I cannot read,” he said.

But another in the group—by great fortune—could. Proud of this rare skill, he took the letter and read aloud:

“To Gerard Eliassoen, of Tergou. These by the hand of the trusty Hans Memling, with all speed.”

“'Tis excellently well writ,” said the reader, inspecting each letter.

“Ay!” Hans declared grandly. “And small wonder—it was penned by a famous hand: Margaret, sister of Jan Van Eyck. Blessed and honoured be his memory! She is an old friend of mine.”

Then Hans drifted off into forty other topics.

Sybrandt slipped away and sought out Cornelis.

They met in secret, heads bent low over the news. Italy was far. If only they could keep Gerard there?

“Keep him there? Nothing would hold him long from his Margaret.”

“Curse her!” said Sybrandt. “Why didn’t she die when she should have?”

“She die? She’d outlive the plague to torment us.” Cornelis seethed at her selfishness in not dying to ease their burdens.

The two brothers conspired, feeding each other’s malice until, at last, their corrupted hearts formed a plan: to keep Gerard in Italy forever, thus securing his share of their father’s inheritance.

But once devised, the plan stalled. Execution required cunning. Evil hesitated. Then, as if Satan himself whispered into both their ears at once, they both cried out:

They went to Ghysbrecht Van Swieten, who received them immediately—for a man under agony of uncertainty grasps eagerly at knowledge. Certainty is often painful, but suspense is unbearable.

“You have news of Gerard?” he asked, eyes restless.

They told him of the letter and Hans Memling. He listened, tense. “Who wrote it?”

“Margaret Van Eyck,” they answered, naturally assuming the content matched the handwriting.

“Are you sure?” He drew a drawer open and pulled out a document penned by Margaret during negotiations for her house. “Was it written like this?”

“Yes,” said Sybrandt boldly. “It is the same hand.”

“Good,” said Ghysbrecht, heart pounding, yet feigning indifference so convincingly that it unsettled them. They fumbled with their hats, stammered, hesitated—then slowly confessed they wanted a letter forged, one that might keep Gerard in Italy. They intended to substitute it in Hans Memling’s pouch.

As they wavered between respect and suspicion—wondering if this burgomaster was as crooked as they were—conflicting thoughts raced through Ghysbrecht’s mind. Vengeance urged him to let Gerard return and feel the law’s weight. Prudence advised keeping him a thousand miles away. But prudence also warned: why risk dirty work on uncertain grounds? Why give these rogues power to stain his name?

Finally, his conviction that Gerard possessed a secret capable of striking him to the core—combined with caution—formed his reply: “It is my duty to aid citizens who cannot write. But I will not be responsible for their matter. Tell me what I should write.”

“Something about Margaret.”

“Ay, ay! Say she is false, married to another—I’ll guarantee it.”

“No, burgomaster, no!” Sybrandt protested. “Gerard wouldn’t believe it, or only half. Then he’d come back to see. No—say she is dead.”

“Dead? At her age? Will he believe that?”

“Sooner than the other. She was nearly dead—so it’s not a full lie.”

“Humph. Do you think that will keep him?”

“We are certain,” said Cornelis. “Our Gerard will never leave Italy now he is there. It was always his dream. He’d come back for Margaret, but not for us. What does he care for us? He despises his own family—always has.”

“This would be a bitter pill,” said the old hypocrite.

“It will be for his good in the end,” replied the younger.

“What avails Famine wedding Thirst?” said Cornelis.

“And the grief you prepare so calmly?” Ghysbrecht retorted sarcastically, though he tasted his own revenge.

“Oh, a lie is not like a blow with a curtal axe. It hacks no flesh, breaks no bones.”

“A curtal axe?” Sybrandt laughed. “No, nor even like a cudgel.” And he shot a sly, poisoned glance at the burgomaster’s broken nose.

Ghysbrecht’s face darkened with fury. But it worked as intended—the old man bristled with hatred.

“Well,” he said coldly, “tell me what to write, and I must write it. But mark this: you bear the blame if anything goes wrong. Not the hand that writes, but the tongue that dictates, commits the deed.”

The brothers agreed, sneering inwardly. Ghysbrecht drew his inkhorn, placed Margaret’s sample writing before him, and began to ask about the letter’s size—when suddenly Jorian Ketel burst into the room, clearly annoyed not to find the burgomaster alone.

“You see I have business,” said Ghysbrecht.

“Ay, but this is grave. I bring good news—but not for every ear.”

The burgomaster rose and pulled Jorian aside into the deep window embrasure. The brothers heard them speak in low, urgent tones. It ended with Ghysbrecht sending Jorian to saddle his mule. Then, turning to the brothers with sudden chill, he said:

“I value household peace—but this is not to be done hastily. We will see. We will see.”

“But, burgomaster, the man will be gone. It will be too late!”

“Where is he?”

“At the hostelry, drinking.”

“Well, keep him drinking! We will see, we will see.” And he sent them away discomfited.

To understand all this, we must step back. That very morning, Margaret Brandt had met Jorian Ketel near her door. He passed her with a scowl. She remembered him.

“Stay,” she said. “Yes—it’s the good man who saved him. Oh, why haven’t you been near me since? Why haven’t you come for the parchments? Was it not true about the hundred crowns?”

Jorian snorted, but seeing her honest face, he began to suspect a mistake. He told her he had come—and how he had been turned away.

“Alas!” she said. “I knew nothing of it. I lay at death’s door.” Then she invited him to follow her into the garden, showing him where the parchments were buried. “Martin wanted to dig them up, but I stopped him. He put them there—and I said none should move them but you, who earned them so well.”

“Give me a spade!” Jorian cried. “Wait—no. He’s suspicious. Are you sure they’re still there?”

“I’ll take full blame if any hand has touched them.”

“Then keep them two hours longer, good Margaret,” said Jorian, and ran off to the Stadthouse, joyful.

The burgomaster rode toward Sevenbergen, Jorian striding beside him, promising that within an hour the missing parchments would be in his hands.

“Ah, master!” said Jorian. “Lucky it wasn’t a thief who took them.”

“Not a thief? Not a thief? What do you call him then?”

“Well, saving your presence, I call him a jackdaw. This is jackdaw’s work—if ever there was. Take the thing you least need, and hide it—that’s a jackdaw. I should know,” he added oracularly. “I was raised with a chough. He and I were born the same year, but he cut his teeth long before me. My life was a burden for years because of him. If you had a hole in your hose no bigger than a groat, in went his beak like a gimlet. For stealing, Gerard all over. What he wanted least—and what any poor Christian in the house needed most—that went first. Mother was a strong woman—so if she glanced round, away flew her thimble. Father lived by cordwaining—so at sunrise Jack stole his awl, wax, and twine. After that, make your bread how you could! One day I heard my mother tell him to his face he was enough to corrupt half-a-dozen children—and he only cocked his eye at her, then snatched the nurseling’s shoe off his foot. Now this Gerard is tarred with the same brush. The parchments mean nothing to him—like a thimble or awl to Jack. He took them out of mischief and hid them. You’d never have found them but for me.”

“I believe you’re right,” said Ghysbrecht. “I’ve vexed myself more than need.”

When they reached Peter’s gate, he grew uneasy.

“I wish it had been anywhere but here.”

Jorian reassured him.

“The girl is honest and kind,” he said. “She had nothing to do with taking them. I swear it.” He led him into the garden. “There, master—if a face can be believed, they lie there. See, the soil is loose.”

He ran for a spade stuck in the ground and began digging. Soon he uncovered a parchment. Ghysbrecht seized it, knelt, and tore it from the hole. His hands trembled, his face gleamed. He pulled out parchment after parchment. Jorian dusted them clean.

But as Ghysbrecht unearthed many, his face grew darker. When he reached the last, he pressed his hands to his temples, stunned.

“What mystery lies here?” he gasped. “Are fiends mocking me? Dig deeper! There must be another!”

Jorian drove the spade in, throwing up hard earth. In vain. And even as he dug, the burgomaster’s mood shifted.

“Treason! Treachery!” he cried. “You knew of this!”

“Knew what, master, in Heaven’s name?”

“Caitiff—you knew there was another worth twice all these!”

“That’s false!” Jorian cried, now suspicious. “It’s a trick to rob me of my hundred crowns. Oh, I know you, burgomaster!” And he nearly whimpered.

A calm voice fell on them like oil on waves.

“No, good man, it is not false—nor quite true. There was another parchment.”

“There, there, there! Where is it?”

“But,” continued Margaret quietly, “it was not a town record—so you’ve won your hundred crowns. It was a private deed between this burgomaster and my grandfather Flor—is Brandt.”

“Hush, hush!”

“Where is it, girl? That is all we want to know.”

“Have patience, and I shall tell you. Gerard read the title and said, ‘This is as much yours as the burgomaster’s.’ He set it aside, to read with me later.”

“It is in the house, then?” asked the burgomaster, regaining composure.

“No, sir,” said Margaret solemnly. “It is not.” Then, her voice faltering, “You hunted my poor Gerard so hard, so close, that you left him no time to think of anything but his life and his grief. The parchment was in his bosom. He took it with him.”

“Whither? Whither?”

“Ask me no more, sir. What right have you to question me thus? It was for your sake, good man, that I forced myself to come here, to speak to this cruel old man. For when I think of the misery he has caused me and him, the sight of him is more than I can bear.” She shuddered, then walked slowly inside, hand to her head, weeping bitterly.

Remorse, dread, avarice, fear—all tugged at Ghysbrecht’s hardened heart in one moment. He hung his head, arms limp. A coarse chuckle made him turn—there stood Martin Wittenhaagen, leaning on his bow, grinning from ear to ear.

“Ho! Arrest him! Seize him—traitor and thief!” shouted Ghysbrecht. “Dog, thou shalt pay for all!”

Martin said nothing. Calmly, he thrust the duke’s pardon under the burgomaster’s nose. Ghysbrecht stared—speechless.

Martin pressed his advantage.

“The duke and I are soldiers. He won’t let you greasy burghers trample on an old comrade. He bade me carry you a message.”

“The duke send a message to me?”

“Ay! I told him of your masterful ways—of imprisoning Gerard for loving a girl. And he said, ‘Tell him this is to be a king, not a burgomaster. I’ll have no kings in Holland but one. Bid him be more humble, or I’ll hang him at his own door.’”

(Ghysbrecht trembled—he believed the duke capable of it.)

“‘As I hanged the burgomaster of Thingembob.’ The duke couldn’t recall which of you he had hung, or where—such trifles stick not in a soldier’s memory. But he was sure he had hanged one of you for grinding poor folk. ‘And I’m the man to hang another,’ quoth the good duke.”

These insults from such a low man—coupled with his immunity, shielded by the duke—drove the choleric old man into helpless rage. He shook his fist, tried to threaten, but could not speak. Then he gave a shriek, coiled like a rattlesnake ready to strike—and spat violently onto Martin’s doublet.

The thick-skinned soldier treated it with contempt. “Here’s a venomous old toad! He knows a kick from his foot would send him to his final rest—and wants me to cheat the gallows. But I’ve slain too many men in fair fight to raise a limb against anything less than a man. And this I count no man. What is it? An old goat-skin bag full of rotten bones.”

“My mule! My mule!” screamed Ghysbrecht.

Jorian helped him up, trembling. Once mounted, he gathered unnatural strength. The figure racing to Tergou was truly terrifying—so aged and wizened the face, so white and flowing the hair, so fierce the fury that shook his bent frame as he spurred forward, yelling, “I’ll make their hearts ache. I’ll make their hearts ache. All of them. All—All—All!”

The black sheep sat disconsolate among the revelers, eyeing Hans Memling’s wallet. He had taken it off and tossed it on the table. How easily they could have switched the letters. For the first time, they regretted not learning to write like their brother.

Then Hans mentioned leaving. The brothers whispered, deciding to abandon the plan—for now. Before they could finish, Dierich Brower appeared in the doorway and winked.

They stepped outside. “Come to the burgomaster at once,” he said.

They found Ghysbrecht pale and agitated, Margaret Van Eyck’s handwriting before him. “I have written what you desired,” he said. “Now for the superscription. What were the words? Did you see?”

“We cannot read,” said Cornelis.

“Then all this labor is lost!” Ghysbrecht snapped. “Dolts!”

“But,” said Sybrandt, “I heard the words read. I remember: ‘To Gerard Eliassoen, these by the hand of the trusty Hans Memling, with all speed.’”

“Good. Now, how was it folded? How large?”

“Longer than that one, not as long as this.”

“Very well. Where is he?”

“At the hostelry.”

“Go then. Take this groat—treat him. Ask to see the letter, and substitute this. Bring me the original.”

They agreed, took the letter, and hurried to the hostelry.

They had barely left when Dierich Brower emerged from the Stadthouse, ordered to watch them until the true letter was secured. He waited outside.

He did not wait long. They returned almost immediately, heads bowed.

“Too late!” they cried. “Too late! He is gone.”

“Gone? How long?”

“Scarce five minutes. Cursed chance!”

“You must return to the burgomaster at once,” said Dierich.

“To what end?”

“No matter—come!” And he hurried them back.

Ghysbrecht Van Swieten was not a man to accept defeat.

“Well,” he said, hearing the news, “suppose he is gone. Is he mounted?”

“No.”

“Then what stops you from catching him?”

“But what use is catching him? There are no inns along the road.”

“Fools!” he snapped. “Is there no way to empty a man’s pockets but liquor and sleight of hand?”

A look passed between Ghysbrecht and Dierich—one that clarified everything. The brothers paled, their resolve crumbling.

Denys, placed at the center of his captors to prevent any desperate attempt at escape, was carried away in a storm of grief and guilt. For his sake, Gerard had abandoned the safer German route to Rome—only to be left alone, adrift in the heart of Burgundy. That thought consumed Denys most fiercely, driving him now to curse the heavens, now into a brooding silence so dark and threatening that even his guards deemed it wise to disarm him.

They intercepted their leader just beyond the town’s gates, and the entire party halted at the inn called “The Tête d’Or.” The young landlady, though occupied with the count and more deeply preoccupied with her own son, noticed Denys and asked, with some concern, what had become of his companion.

With a sudden outburst of anguish, Denys told her everything—how Gerard had been left behind, how he feared the young man would wander aimlessly, helpless and alone. “Now that he is parted from me,” he pleaded, “he may listen to my advice. Poor wretch—he cannot bear solitude.”

She tossed her head sharply. “I think I’ve already been too kind,” she said, her cheeks flushing. “You will not help?”

“No,” he snapped.

“Then,” he thundered, unleashing a torrent of curses upon her.

She turned away, tears welling in her eyes. “I’m not used to being spoken to like this,” she muttered, retreating to give orders to her servant: saddle two mules.

Denys rode northward with his escort, silent and bowed beneath the weight of sorrow, unaware that the very woman who had scorned him was now dressing herself for horseback in less than forty minutes—eager, decisive, and spurred by a purpose of her own. She set off with her servant, riding swiftly in the opposite direction.

That evening, after a long march, the bastard and his men arrived at “The White Hart.” Their entrance stirred great commotion, and it took time before Manon recognized her old acquaintance among the crowd. When she did, she showed no sign—only a faint blush, nothing more. She did not claim the bond they once shared. Already, the proud woman was beginning to look down on the past, ashamed of the low steps by which she had risen.

Denys saw her but could not smile. The inn brought back too many memories—especially of Gerard.

As night fell, the wind shifted. Manon stepped into the room and beckoned to him with a finger. He rose reluctantly, followed by his guards.

“Nay,” she whispered, “I must speak to you privately.”

She drew him aside to a corner, then lowered her voice. “Would you do me a kindness?”

He answered loudly, “No. I am not in the mood to grant favors to man or woman. If I ever do a kindness, it shall be to a dog—and not even that, if I can avoid it.”

“Oh, good archer,” she said humbly, “you once did me a kindness—you and your fair companion.”

“You did?” he replied. “Well then—for his sake—what is it?”

“I know my story,” she continued. “Once I was cast down. Now I am respected. But today, a woman mocked me—she spoke of him as if he still hung there. And so it will always be, while he remains visible. I wish him taken down. Alas!”

“With all my heart,” he said.

“And none dare I ask but you. Will you do it?”

“Not I—not even if I were free.”

At his firm refusal, Manon sighed deeply, clasping her hands together in despair.

But Denys reassured her. “There are men lower than I who would not hesitate to take such a task. It’s merely a matter of money. If you can find two angels, I’ll find two soldiers to do the work for ‘The White Hart.’”

It was not a pleasant suggestion. Yet, recalling that soldiers were transient creatures—drinking tonight, dead tomorrow—she murmured, “Send them to me. But please—tell them it’s for one who is my friend. Let them not think it’s for me. I should die of shame. Times have changed.”

Denys found two men eager to earn an angel each. He sent them out, then dismissed the matter with contempt, sinking back into thoughts of Gerard.

Manon and the soldiers soon reached an understanding. But what would they do with the body once it was removed?

“The river is near,” she whispered, “near the place.”

“Throw him in?” one soldier asked bluntly.

“No, no! Be not cruel! Could you not lay him gently… and with something heavy?”

She had clearly given it careful thought—unlike one who rarely formed ideas quickly.

Everything was settled except payment. The soldiers demanded advance gold. Manon hesitated. Did she doubt their word? Then let her come with them—or watch from afar.

“Me?” she gasped, horrified. “I would rather die than see it done.”

“But you wanted it done,” he reminded her.

“Aye,” she admitted, “for I am in sore need. Times are changed.”

She had already forgotten her earlier lesson to Denys.

An hour later, the unpleasant relic of a past life was gone—no longer a stain upon the respectable matron’s public standing, no longer casting bitter glances over the clover fields where white hinds grazed.

Manon made the landlord a decent husband and a loyal house-dog. She lived long enough to outlive all who knew her.

When the soldiers returned from carrying out their grim task with medieval simplicity—their hearts heavy—they found the market square packed with people. It had been empty just an hour before.

Conscience struck them. This was the consequence of meddling with the dead.

Yet one, bolder than the other, crept forward in the darkness, blending into a crowd. After a moment, he returned, speaking in tones of reproach that were hardly justified: “Ye born fool—it’s only a miracle.”

Letters of fire had appeared on the church wall, boldly questioning—though with a curious air of sincerity—why no mass was offered for the duke in this time of turmoil. The supernatural message had been seen by many and slowly faded from view, leaving the onlookers transfixed in stunned silence. The result was swift: the city corporation, eager not to fall behind even celestial powers in loyalty to their sovereign, hastily commissioned numerous masses. Among those who profited was our old acquaintance, the cure—a man with a particular fondness for coin. But I would not detain you over such a commonplace miracle if it were not for what followed.

Denys begged for his arms back. “Why disgrace him as well as break his heart?” he asked.
“Then swear upon the cross of thy sword,” came the reply, “that thou wilt not leave the bastard’s service until this rebellion is crushed.”
He yielded, offering three solemn oaths before reclaiming his weapons and freedom.

The troops halted at an inn called “The Three Fish.” There, Marion saw Denys and exclaimed, “I’m out of luck—how could I have expected to see you again?” Noticing his somber mood, and sensing that her jest had fallen flat, she asked gently what troubled him. He told her. She responded with quiet optimism. Gerard, she said, was too noble and well-mannered to come to harm. Women would always stand by him. And besides, things would either go well or ill for him. If well, he’d join some respectable company bound for Rome; if ill, he’d return home—perhaps even before Denys himself. “You’ve still a little fighting to do in Flanders, by all accounts,” she added, handing him his gold pieces. Though he pressed her repeatedly, she refused to accept a single one.

Denys found her argument persuasive—not only because it aligned with his own hopes, but because her honesty stirred something within him. It made him feel a little better about the world into which his dear friend had ventured alone.

Meanwhile, foot soldiers—small groups of two or three—were already making their way toward Flanders, many penniless, yet carried from town to town by bailiffs who issued orders for food and lodging at local inns. Anthony of Burgundy intercepted many of these stragglers, gathering them under his banner. Thus, he entered Flanders at the head of six hundred men.

Upon crossing the frontier, he met his brother Baldwyn, who brought reinforcements, arms, and supplies. Together they organized their forces and marched through several towns—not merely unopposed, but greeted with cheers and acclamations. Such loyalty drew sharp comments. “This rebellion of ours is a bite,” grumbled Simon, a soldier who had chosen Denys as his comrade. Denys said nothing, but silently vowed to St. Mars that he would kill Anthony of Burgundy should this uprising prove no rebellion at all.

That afternoon, they caught sight of a strongly fortified town. A whisper ran through the ranks: this place was disaffected. Yet when they approached, the great gate stood wide open, flanked by towers each guarded by a single sentinel. The advancing army, lulled into carelessness, broke formation and marched forward without caution.

Only when they were within a furlong did the drawbridge rise slowly, creaking upward until it stood vertical against the fort. At that very moment, the portcullis descended with a thunderous crash, and the towers and walls bristled with lances and crossbows. A low murmur spread through the front ranks and rippled to the rear.

“Halt!” shouted the bastard.

The order echoed down the line. They stopped.

“Herald to the gate!”

A pursuivant rode out, halting twenty yards from the gate. With herald’s flag hanging down around his bugle, he blew a summons. A tall figure in gleaming brass armor appeared above the gate. Words passed between them—too faint to hear, but their meaning clear. The herald then sounded a single sharp, menacing note and galloped back, face set with war.

The bastard rode forward to meet him. No sooner had they exchanged words than he turned in his saddle and bellowed, “Pioneers, to the van!” In moments, hedges were leveled and the army took the field, encamping just beyond arrow range. Mounted officers darted south, east, and west to nearby friendly towns, summoning catapults, palisades, mantelets, raw hides, tar-barrels, carpenters, provisions—everything needed for a siege.

One soldier, whose spirits had flagged, brightened at the clang of the portcullis. His temple flushed. When the herald returned with battle in his eyes, he understood instantly—and for the first time in days, he cried out, “Courage, tout le monde, le diable est mort!”
If the great warrior heard, how he must have grinned!

The besiegers camped a furlong from the walls, building roads, keeping pikemen ready for assault, and sending forward sappers, pioneers, catapultiers, and crossbowmen. They began filling the moat, mining beneath the walls, breaching defenses—work done under constant fire of arrows, bolts, stones, and small rocks. These engineers required “a hundred eyes,” acting with vigilance, intelligence, daring, and skill that made a siege both compelling and, to spectators, even amusing.

First, they advanced carpenters behind rolling mantelets to build a high, strong stockade right at the edge of the moat. Lives were lost, but not many—thanks to a concentrated barrage from crossbowmen, including Denys, who shot over the workers’ heads at any defender who dared show his face or peer through a loophole. Under this cover, the carpenters soon raised a solid palisade.

But the defenders anticipated this. By night, they extended wooden penthouses atop the curtain walls—structures supported by square holes near the top, allowing them to launch missiles more freely than through narrow loopholes or sloping crenelets. This gave them greater range and flexibility.

In response, the besiegers brought up mangonels and hurled massive stones at these wooden shelters, smashing them apart. Simultaneously, they constructed a triangular wooden tower as tall as the curtain wall, keeping it ready for use just outside bowshot. This tower was a terrifying sight to the defenders—such towers had taken many a town.

They began mining beneath the moat where the tower loomed, preparing for its arrival. The besiegers also mined elsewhere, aiming to collapse the square barbican. All this time, Denys remained behind his mantelet, alongside another arbalestrier, protecting the workmen and landing excellent shots. His precision earned him the attention of an unseen archer who occasionally sent a quivering shaft into his mantelet—one so close it struck within an inch of Denys’s eye slit.

“Peste!” he muttered. “You shoot well, my friend. Come forth and receive my congratulations! Shall merit such as thine hide its head?”
Then he laughed grimly. “Comrade, it’s one of those cursed Englishmen—with his half-ell shaft. I’ll not die till I’ve had a shot at London wall.”

On the side of the besieged, a figure soon drew notice: a tall knight clad in complete brass armor, carrying a long, slender lance. He directed the defenders' movements with calm authority. Whenever disaster struck the attackers, he was usually involved. My young reader may ask, “Why didn’t Denys shoot him?”

Denys did shoot him—every day. So did other crossbowmen, archers, every man who could aim. The knight was there to be shot. Yet he seemed utterly indifferent. Worse—he appeared not to know when he was hit. He walked his battlements under fire like a stout captain pacing his deck in a storm, oblivious to the raindrops falling on his woolen armor.

Eventually, the besiegers grew bitter. They refused to waste good steel on him anymore. Instead, they cursed him and his impervious coat of mail. He took the missiles like the rest.

Gunpowder has spoiled war. War has always harmed mankind’s true interests. But in ancient times, it served a purpose: it painted vividly, sang divinely, birthed epics. Now, invisible slaughter under a thick pall of smoke—what benefit is there in that? A poet might write, “Suave etiam belli certamina magna tueri,” but the sentiment is hollow, like a cuckoo’s call. You can’t *see* anything but chaos.

They managed better in the Middle Ages. This siege was modest, but it was enough for a minstrel or writer to witness and sing of it, earning an honest living. So far, the sport was justified.

It was a clear, crisp day, not quite frosty. The attackers focused their efforts on a stretch of about two hundred fifty yards—two curtains and two towers. One was the square barbican; the other, topped with a pointed roof resting on a stone machicolade, featured a row of deadly crenelets between roof and wall—like the gunports of a modern frigate, nearly closed.

The curtains bore shattered penthouses, damaged by mangonels and trebuchets. On the besiegers’ side of the moat stood what looked like a colossal arsenal—longer than broad, teeming with human ants, busy with industry, displaying the full mechanical ingenuity of the age. Winches, pulleys, cranes, capstans—all at work. Piles of stones, fascines, mantelets, tar-barrels. Horses and carts streamed in endlessly.

Yet closer inspection revealed arrows flying constantly, cranes hurling stone with reckless abandon, and among the tools, here and there, a worker or soldier lying flat—feathers protruding, blood seeping out.

At the moat’s edge opposite the wooden tower, a strong penthouse—called a “cat”—was creeping forward, slowly filling the moat with fascines and rubble. Pulled by ropes wound around pulleys and windlasses, it moved steadily.

The knight burned the first cat by tossing flaming tar-barrels onto it. So the besiegers built a steeper roof and covered it with raw hides. The tar-barrels now failed. Then the knight signaled with his spear, and a small trebuchet behind the wall began dropping stones just clear of the wall—until one pierced the cat’s roof, creating a terrible hole.

Baldwyn of Burgundy saw this and lost his temper. He ordered the great catapult battering the curtain’s woodwork to be turned and aimed slantwise at the knight.

Meanwhile, Denys and his English counterpart went to dinner. These two, ever watchful of each other, had developed a silent camaraderie, communicating through signs—especially on matters vital in peace or war. Sometimes Denys would place a piece of bread atop his mantelet; the Englishman would hang something similar by string. Or vice versa. Always, they dined together.

Now, the engineers took an extraordinary step: aiming fifty-pound stones at a single man. The catapult was a marvel—simple, elegant, effective. Imagine a fir tree cut down, mounted horizontally on uprights, unbalanced so three-quarters rested on one side. A half-ton weight fastened to the short end. The long tapering part was forced down to the ground using a winch and secured with a bolt. The stone was placed in a sling attached to the tip. The butt end rose high, struggling under the weight. The bolt was drawn—gravity took over—the short end swung down violently, the long end whipped up, and the stone flew from the sling with immense force.

This time, the stone missed the knight but crashed into the penthouse beside him, shattering roof and floor. Two figures fell through: the stone itself and a mangled body. They plunged down the high wall, down, down, into the dark waters of the moat, which closed over them, holding both stone and bone for two hundred years—until cannon disturbed the waters and civilization drained them.

“Aha! A good shot!” cried Baldwyn.

The knight retreated. The besiegers jeered. He reappeared on the barbican platform, helmet barely visible above the parapet. He seemed busy. Soon, a massive Turkish catapult emerged, elevated, and launched a twenty-pound stone two hundred forty yards into the air. It bounced, striking dirt into Lord Anthony’s eye and making him curse. The next stone killed a horse hauling arrows, knocking it dead like a rabbit and spilling the cart.

The engine then turned on the besiegers’ wooden tower—supposedly out of range. Sir Turk hurled specially shaped stones, striking it repeatedly, breaking it in places. The besiegers turned two engines on the monster, slinging smaller stones onto the barbican platform, killing two engineers. But the Turk ignored them. He flung a forty-pound stone at the great catapult, hitting near the axis and destroying it entirely. Engineers fled, yelling.

In the afternoon, Simon raced back to his mantelet after shooting at the defenders. Denys, peering through his slit, saw Simon suddenly freeze, arms outstretched, then fall face down. An arrow protruded from his back. The archer showed himself briefly, proud of his mark. It was the Englishman.

Denys, already prepared, fired. The bolt struck the archer, who staggered away wounded. But Simon never stirred. His wars were over.

“I am unlucky in my comrades,” said Denys.

The next morning, the besieged saw an unwelcome sight: the cat, now covered in mattresses and raw hides, was filling the moat. The knight bombarded it in vain, threw burning tar-barrels—useless. Then, with his own hands, he lowered a bag of burning sulphur and pitch by rope, stinking out the workmen. But Baldwyn, armored like a lobster, rushed forward, cut the rope, and the work continued.

The knight sent new engineers into the mine, undermining the area, reinforcing it with beams, and coating them thickly with grease and tar.

At dawn, the moat was filled. The wooden tower began moving on wheels toward a section of curtain already under attack by two catapults. Its approach was eerie—no visible agency, driven by internal rollers worked by leverage. On top stood a platform with the first assault party, protected by a vertical drawbridge and full armor.

The defenders attacked the tower with stones, striking often—but to no effect. It was well defended with mattresses and hides. Soon, it reached the moat’s edge.

The knight ordered the mine beneath it ignited. The Turkish engine then hurled a stone of half a hundredweight directly at the knights on the tower, sweeping two off into the plain. One writhed; the other lay motionless.

Now, the besieging catapults hurled blazing tar-barrels, setting fire to the hoards on both sides. Assailants climbed ladders behind the tower, lowering the drawbridge onto the battered curtain. Catapults fired tar-barrels, igniting adjacent works to drive defenders away.

Armored men sprang across the bridge, led by Baldwyn. The invulnerable knight and his men met them. A fierce combat erupted—figures falling headlong from the narrow bridge. But fresh attackers kept coming. The defenders were driven back.

Another minute, and the town was taken. But the mine had been timed perfectly—just as the breach occurred, the supports collapsed. The tower sank abruptly from the wall, tearing the drawbridge loose and dumping soldiers onto the dry moat.

The defenders roared and surrounded Baldwyn and his men—strangely offering quarter. While some disarmed them, others lit the turret with hand grenades. Who was busiest? The tall knight. He thrust fire-bags onto his long spear, driving them into the doomed structure once so fearsome.

To do this, he had to stand on a projecting beam of the shattered hoard, gripping a pikeman’s hand to steady himself.

This enraged Denys. He dashed from his mantelet, hoping to escape notice amid the chaos. He raised his crossbow—missed the knight completely—but his bolt struck the pikeman in the brain. The knight fell heavily from the wall, lance and all.

Denys stared, stunned. In that instant, he felt his arm grow hot, then cold—an English arrow skewering it.

No one noticed. The knight, armor glinting in the morning sun, fell headlong, turning midair, and slapped the water with a sound heard a mile away. None thought to see him again.

But he landed at the edge of the fascines, his spear lodged underwater. With great effort, he pulled himself to the side—but couldn’t climb out.

Anthony sent twelve knights with a white flag to take him prisoner. He surrendered quietly, saying nothing.

Taken to Anthony’s tent, the latter laughed at his muddy armor—then frowned. “I marvel, sir, that so good a knight should know his duty so poorly as to rebel and cause us all this trouble.”

“I am nun-nun-nun-nun-nun-no knight.”

“What then?”

“A hosier.”

“A what? Then thy armor shall be stripped off, and thou shalt be tied to a stake before the works, riddled with arrows as a warning to traitors.”

“N-n-n-n-no! Duda-duda-duda-duda-don't do that.”

“Why not?”

“Tuta-tuta-tuta-townsfolk will-h-h-h-hang t'other buba-buba-buba-buba-bastard.”

“What, whom?”

“Your bub-bub-bub-brother Baldwyn.”

“What? Have you knaves taken him?”

The warlike hosier nodded.

“Hang the fool!” Anthony snapped.

The hosier watched his eyes, then removed his helmet. From the lining, he pulled an intercepted letter from the duke—ordering Anthony to court immediately, to represent Burgundy at England’s court, to escort the English king’s sister to her bridegroom, the Earl of Charolois. A mission flattering to Anthony’s pride and appetite for pleasure. Edward the Fourth ruled the most splendid court in Europe.

The hosier saw Anthony’s longing to leave. “We’ll gega-gega-gega-give ye a thousand angels to raise the siege.”

“And Baldwyn?”

“I’ll gega-gega-gega-go and send him with the money.”

Dinner-time arrived. A flag of truce flew on both sides. The false knight and the true one dined together, reaching a peaceful understanding.

“But what is your grievance, my good friend?” asked Anthony.

“Tuta-tuta-tuta-too much taxes.”

Denys, finding the arrow in his arm, turned his back—protected by a long shield—and walked sulkily into camp. He was met by Comte de Jarnac, who had seen his brilliant shot and, learning he was wounded, handed him a handful of broad coins.

“Hast got the better of thy grief, arbalestrier, methinks.”

“My grief, yes; but not my love. As soon as this rebellion is put down, I go to Holland. There I shall meet him.”

He was closer than he knew. Relieved from duty the next day, though his wound was serious, he set out with firm resolve to rejoin his friend in Holland.

A quiet transformation had come over Margaret Brandt. She moved through her daily tasks as though walking in a dream, her movements slow and distant. If Peter spoke to her with any haste, she would start violently, her eyes wide with fear, fixed upon him as if he were a stranger. She visited her dear friend Margaret Van Eyck less often now, and when she did, she seemed uneasy, almost afraid of the warmth that once welcomed her. Where before she had accepted her old friend’s tender embraces with open affection, she now received them with trembling passivity, sometimes even flinching away.

But the most striking change was her refusal to leave her home during daylight hours. When she did go to Tergou, it was always after nightfall, and she returned before dawn. She no longer attended matins, though she had once done so regularly. Peter, who was not one to notice subtle shifts in mood or behavior, finally noticed this strange withdrawal. One evening, he asked her why she avoided going out.

“People look at me,” she whispered, her voice barely above a breath.

Later, Margaret Van Eyck, concerned for her friend, gently questioned her. A sudden flash of terror crossed Margaret’s face, followed by a flood of silent tears. She could say nothing more. The elder woman, ever kind and patient, pressed softly. “What, my dear, are you afraid to confide your sorrow to me?”

“I have no sorrow,” Margaret replied, “only one I’ve brought upon myself. I am treated far better than I deserve—especially here.”

“And yet you come so rarely?” the old lady said, puzzled.

“I come more often than I deserve,” she sighed, her voice heavy with regret.

At that moment, Reicht called from the kitchen. “Reicht is bawling for you,” Margaret Van Eyck said, turning toward the door. “Go, child—what on earth can be troubling you?”

As she walked home, the old woman mulled over the possibilities. Perhaps Margaret felt humiliated by the way Gerard’s family treated her. That thought stirred her indignation. “I shall speak plainly to them,” she decided, “at least to those among them who are women.” And so, the very next day, she wrapped herself in her cloak and hood, took Reicht with her, and made her way to the hosier’s house.

Catherine greeted her with respectful deference, her eyes glistening with gratitude. “Thank you, madam,” she said, her voice thick with emotion, “for all your kindness to Gerard.”

Encouraged, Margaret Van Eyck ventured into the subject of Margaret Brandt. But the moment her name was mentioned, Catherine’s expression changed. Her eyes hardened, her lips thinned, and her face took on the stubborn, closed-off look of someone unwilling to listen or understand. It was a mask worn only by those whose minds were set like stone. Margaret Van Eyck tried to reason with her, but her words fell on deaf ears. Frustrated, and unused to being denied, she rose abruptly and left, offering a curtsey so abrupt and incomplete it seemed more like an insult than a courtesy. Catherine returned it with a haughty tilt of the head, as if daring her to challenge her further.

Outside the gate, Margaret Van Eyck found Reicht speaking with a pale girl leaning on crutches. As she passed them, her cheeks flushed, and she lifted her chin in scornful dismissal—meant, perhaps, for the whole household. But suddenly, a small, delicate hand slipped quietly into hers. Turning, she saw two gentle, dove-like eyes filled with tears, looking up at her with both gratitude and quiet pleading.

The old woman understood instantly. Her anger vanished. She stopped, knelt down, and kissed the girl’s forehead. “I see,” she murmured. “And mind this: I leave it to you.”

Back at her own home, she told Reicht, “Today I went to a house where I saw two things—one common, one rare. I saw a foolish, stubborn woman—and I saw an angel in flesh, with a face so pure and sweet that if I had it before me now, I’d pick up my brushes again just to try and capture it.”

Kate, true to the impression formed, waited for the right moment and then told her mother what Reicht Heynes had shared—how Margaret had given her own blood to save Gerard in the forest. “See, mother,” she said softly, “how deeply she loves him.”

“Who wouldn’t love such a man?” her mother replied.

“Oh, mother,” Kate whispered, “think of it. Poor thing.”

“Ay, wench,” the mother said, “she has her own troubles, as we do. I can’t bear the sight of blood—let alone my own.”

It was a step forward. But when Kate tried to press further, she was met with silence.

About a month later, a soldier from the Dalgetty clan returned from service in Burgundy and arrived at the hosier’s house one evening. The father was away on business, but the rest of the family sat together at supper. The soldier placed a letter on the table beside Catherine and, without accepting any reward, departed for Sevenbergen.

The letter was unfolded and laid flat. Strangely enough, though none of them could read, they all recognized Gerard’s handwriting at once. “Your father must be away,” Catherine exclaimed. “Are you not ashamed? Not one of you can read your brother’s letter!”

Though the words were meaningless to them—like hieroglyphs to us—there was something in the letter they could understand. There exists a language beyond words, unbound by letters or grammar, that speaks directly to the heart. It flows across borders, crosses seas, and needs no interpreter. It is universal.

And so, when they saw the drawing Gerard had sketched between two short paragraphs—a simple image of two hands clasped together—they understood. They recognized his style in every line, every curve. In that instant, Gerard stood before them, bidding farewell.

They wept until the image blurred before their eyes. Giles murmured, “Poor Gerard,” his voice lower than anyone expected from him. Even Cornelis and Sybrandt sat in silence, their usual bravado replaced by a fleeting sense of guilt.

But how could they learn what the letter said? They were reluctant to reveal their ignorance—or their grief—to a stranger.

“The Dame Van Eyck?” Kate suggested timidly.

“And so I will,” Catherine said, her voice firming. “She has a good heart. She loves Gerard too. She’ll be glad to hear from him. I was harsh with her when she came here—but I’ll make amends. Then she’ll tell me what my poor boy writes.”

Soon she arrived at Margaret Van Eyck’s house. Reicht led her into a room where a young woman sat quietly by the stove. She rose and courteously stepped aside. “Thank you, young lady,” Catherine said. “These winter nights are cold, and your stove is a comfort.”

As she warmed her hands, Catherine studied her companion from head to foot. The young woman wore a plain wimple, but her gown was trimmed with fur—an indication of rank or wealth in those days. Yet what struck Catherine most was the honesty and gentleness in her face. She felt sure this girl would understand her pain.

“Now, what brings me here, young lady?” Catherine began. “A letter! A letter from my poor boy, far off in some wild land. And I’m ashamed to say none of us can read it. I wonder—can you?”

“Yes,” the girl answered softly.

“Can you, now? That’s a fine thing, my dear. I dare say the dame won’t be long. But every minute feels like an hour to a mother longing for news.”

“I’ll read it to you,” the girl offered.

“Bless you, my dear—bless you!” Catherine said, so eager she didn’t notice the quiet intensity with which the girl reached for the letter. She didn’t see the slight tremor in her fingers as they closed around it.

“Come then,” Catherine urged. “Read it to me. I’m dying to know.”

“The first words are: *‘To my honoured parents.’*”

“Ay!” Catherine breathed. “He always did honour us, poor soul.”

“*‘God and the saints keep you in His holy care, and bless you by night and by day. Your one harsh deed is forgotten; your years of love remembered.’*”

Catherine placed her hand over her heart and sank back into her chair, overcome by a long, shuddering sob.

“Then comes this,” the girl continued, “a sketch—*‘a long farewell.’*”

“Ay, go on,” Catherine said, wiping her eyes. “Bless you, girl—you give me sorrowful comfort. Still, it’s comfort.”

“*‘To my brothers Cornelis and Sybrandt—Be content; you will see me no more!’*”

“What does that mean?” Catherine gasped. “Ah!”

“*‘To my sister Kate—little angel of my father’s house. Be kind to her—’* Ah!”

“That is Margaret Brandt,” Catherine whispered. “His sweetheart, poor soul. I’ve not been kind to her, my dear. Forgive me, Gerard!”

“*‘—for poor Gerard’s sake, since grief to her is death to me.’*”

And then, nature, weary of holding back, gave way. The young woman collapsed from her chair, unconscious, the letter still clutched in her hand, her head resting on Catherine’s knees.

Experienced women do not panic when another woman faints, nor do they rush to assign blame beyond the body’s natural frailty—something they have seen too often to mistake for anything more profound. Catherine moved swiftly and with purpose: she laid the girl down flat on the floor, her head resting low, opened the window wide to let in fresh air, and loosened the tight folds of her dress as she lay still. Only after all this did she step to the door and call out, her voice firm and clear: “Come here, if you please.”

Margaret Van Eyck and Reicht entered at once, finding the young woman lying motionless, while Catherine stood beside her, hands clenched in quiet distress. “Oh, my poor child!” exclaimed Margaret Van Eyck. “What has happened to her?”

“Me?” Catherine replied sharply. “What could I possibly have done?”

“Nothing, madam,” said the other gently, “nothing beyond what is natural given her circumstances.”

A flush rose in Margaret Van Eyck’s cheeks. “You speak so calmly,” she said, “when it was your actions that brought her to this state.”

“That I am not,” Catherine answered bluntly, “nor any woman alive.”

“Was it not you and your husband who kept them apart? And now he has gone to Italy alone—no wife by his side. This is no mere circumstance. You’ve broken her heart between you.”

“Why, madam,” Catherine returned, “who then? In Heaven’s name! To hear you talk, one would think this were Gerard’s own sweetheart. But that cannot be. Look at this fur—five crowns an ell, and more than that in quality. Besides, this young lady is a married woman—or ought to be.”

“Of course she ought,” Margaret Van Eyck replied. “And who is to blame that she isn’t? Who stepped forward before them at the very altar?”

“God forgive whoever it was,” Catherine said gravely, “but it was not I, nor my husband.”

“Well,” the older woman conceded, her tone softening slightly, “now you’ve seen her, perhaps you won’t be so harsh toward her. Thank God, she is coming round.”

“Me bitter against her?” Catherine asked, surprised. “No, that is over. Poor soul—trouble behind her, trouble ahead. And yet I sent her, of all people, to read Gerard’s letter to me. That must have been it—she fainted from the weight of it. She is stirring now. Come, sweetheart—don’t be afraid. There’s no one here but friends.”

They helped her into a comfortable chair. As color slowly returned to her face and lips, Catherine drew Margaret Van Eyck aside. “Will she stay with you tonight?” she asked quietly.

“No, madam,” came the reply.

“I wouldn’t let her return to Sevenbergen tonight,” Catherine insisted.

“It is her choice,” Margaret Van Eyck said firmly. “She still refuses to remain.”

“But you are older than she,” Catherine pressed. “You can insist. See—she is beginning to notice.”

Then, without speaking aloud, Catherine leaned close and whispered something into the other woman’s ear—so briefly that it seemed impossible even a word could pass. Yet between two women such as these, silence could carry more meaning than words. The old lady started visibly, then whispered back, trembling: “It’s false! It’s slander! It’s monstrous! Look at her face—how could anyone accuse such a face?”

“Tut! tut! tut!” Catherine snapped. “You might as well say this is not my hand. I know it well—and I tell you plainly, it is true.”

To Margaret Van Eyck’s astonishment, Catherine then approached the girl, took her in her arms, and kissed her warmly upon the cheek. “I suffered for Gerard,” she said, “and you shed your blood for him—I heard his own words. He told me plainly I had wronged her. Yes, Gerard, my child, I held back from her; but from this hour, I will make amends. You are my daughter now.”

A second embrace sealed their sudden bond, and the impulsive woman turned away, leaving the room.

Margaret sank back into her chair, a fragile smile playing across her lips. Gerard’s mother had kissed her and called her daughter. But in the next breath, she saw her dear friend watching her with a look of deep disapproval.

“I wonder you allowed that woman to touch you,” the elder said, sternly.

“His mother,” Margaret murmured, half in reproach.

“Mother or not,” the other replied, “you would not let her near you if you knew what she whispered to me about you.”

“About me?” Margaret whispered, pale again.

“Yes—about you, whom she never saw until tonight.”

Margaret Van Eyck began to speak, choosing her words carefully, eager to share her outrage—but before she could go further, a sudden interruption silenced her.

The young woman slid from her chair onto her knees, bowing her head in anguish. With trembling voice and tear-filled eyes, she began to beg for forgiveness—not for herself, but for the pain she had caused. Her sorrow was so deep, her humility so complete, that any observer would have believed she had committed some terrible injustice, some unbearable insult, against the noble woman before her.

The small gathering at the hosier’s house sat around the table, still speaking of the recent turn of events, when their mother returned. With a sharp glance that swept across each face in the circle, she placed the letter flat upon the table. Then, without hesitation, she recited every word from memory, her finger tracing the lines as if to pretend she could read them—though her eyes betrayed no real understanding. It was a performance meant to convince both herself and those present that she had grasped the full weight of the message.

Suddenly, she raised her head, her gaze locking onto Cornelis and Sybrandt. Their eyes dropped instantly. That was all it took. The storm, long brewing beneath her silence, broke forth in a torrent of words—scathing, passionate, unrelenting. Catherine swelled like a hen ruffled by outrage, and from her mouth poured a flood of wisdom, scorn, and bitter truth, such as few men—and fewer women—could utter in one breath. Here is but a fragment of what she said, spoken in a single, continuous stream:

“I have long suspected you were the ones who fanned the flame between Gerard and your father, who stirred up that old fool Ghysbrecht. And now—here are Gerard’s own words to prove it! You’ve driven your own flesh and blood into exile, torn from his mother’s side, robbed me of my darling, the light of my life, the joy of my heart. But you are all alike—from head to foot. When you were boys together, my others brought comfort; you brought only trouble—mischievous, cunning, always needing more than half a day to keep your clothes whole. Why? Because work wears cloth, but play cuts it. A beard should bring sense—but not for you. Still the last to bed, the last to rise. And why? Because honesty goes to sleep early, and diligence wakes with the dawn. Where two lazy bones live, there are two good-for-nothings. I’ve often sat and watched you, wondering where you came from. You don’t take after your father, nor do you resemble me any more than a wasp resembles an ant. I swear you must have been switched at birth—or dropped by a cuckoo on my floor. You have neither our hands nor our hearts. Of all my children, only you ever mocked those God has afflicted. I’ve heard you laugh at Giles because he’s small, at my sweet Kate because she’s not strong as a Flanders mare. After that, rob a church if you wish—for you can be no worse in His eyes, who made both Kate and Giles, nor in mine, who suffered for them as I did for you, you pitiful, heartless, traitorous curs!

No—I will not hold back, daughter. They have filled the cup too full. It takes much to turn a mother’s heart against the sons she nursed on her knee.
