Many times I’ve turned away, pretending not to see, biting my tongue so your father would never know what I knew—he would have cast you out then and there. But now, they have filled the cup too full. Where did you get all this money? For the past month, you’ve been rolling in it. You didn’t earn it. I pray I never hear from another mouth how you came by it. It’s since that night you stayed out so late, and came home with your head swollen, Cornelis. Sloth and greed are ill-matched, my masters. Those who love gold must either sweat or steal. Well, if you stole it from someone poor, it was likely a woman—I’ll wager on it. A man would have beaten you with his bare hand. But let it be—it serves one purpose: it shows me how you’d rule our home, if ever it became yours. I’ve watched you, my boys. You spent a groat today between you. I spend scarcely a groat a week—and feed you all, good and bad. No—no more waiting for the shoes that may walk behind your coffin. This shop, this house—neither shall be yours. Gerard is our heir. Poor Gerard, whom you exiled, whom you tried to destroy. From now on, never call me mother again! But you’ve made him ten times dearer to me. My lost boy! Soon I shall see him again, hold him in my arms, set him upon my knees.

Yes—you may stare. You’re clever, but not clever enough. You cut down the stalk—but left the seed—the seed that will grow beyond you, outlive you. Margaret Brandt is quick with child, and it is Gerard’s. What is Gerard’s is mine. And I’ve prayed the saints it will be a boy—and it will be. It must. Kate, when I learned of this, my heart ached for her unborn child as if it were my own. He is our heir. He will outlive us. You will not—for a corrupt heart in a body is like a worm in a nut, swiftly bringing ruin to the flesh. So, Kate, take down Gerard’s bib and tucker from the drawer you know of. One day soon, we will carry them to Sevenbergen. We will borrow Peter Buyskens’ cart and go to comfort Gerard’s wife under her burden. She is his wife. Who is Ghysbrecht Van Swieten to stand between a couple and the altar? Can he break what God and the priest have joined? She is my daughter, and I am proud of her—as proud as I am of you, Kate. As for you—keep out of my sight for a while. You are like the black dog in my eyes.”

Cornelis and Sybrandt understood the dismissal. They slipped away, hearts heavy with guilt, shame, and hatred. They avoided her gaze as much as possible, and for many days she spoke not a word—good, bad, or indifferent—to either of them.

Liberaverat animum suum.

Catherine was a woman of quiet ways, seldom leaving home save when necessity pressed. Even then, some small mishap always seemed to follow—spilled milk, a dropped pot, or a child’s cry that broke the rhythm of her day. She felt keenly aware of this tendency, and so she delayed her planned visit to Sevenbergen from one morning to the next, watching for a lull in the household’s endless demands. But on the very afternoon when everything might have gone smoothly, Peter Buyskens’ mule—a creature of vital importance—was out of commission.

At last, one day, Eli addressed her before the whole family: “Is it true, wife, that you’ve thought of going to see Margaret Brandt?”

“Ay,” she replied, not flinching.

“Then I forbid it.”

“Oh? Do you?”

“I do.”

“And so there’s no more to be said?” she asked, her cheeks flushing with a quiet defiance.

“Not a word,” Eli answered, his voice firm.

Later, alone with her daughter Kate, Catherine spoke with sharper self-criticism than she had ever shown toward Eli.

“It was my own fault,” she confessed. “I should have gone like a cat sneaking after a robin—quiet, swift, unobserved. But no—there I go, blabbing about it as if every soul in the house must know. Like a foolish hen who cackles before laying an egg, calling all the hens to rob her of it. Next time, child, if you and I wish to do anything that might stir talk, let us do it at once, without thought or speech. Then, if we are blamed, we can say, ‘We knew nothing, we meant no harm.’ Who would have guessed such things? And yet, for two pins, I’d march straight into their midst, bold as brass.”

Kate stared, stunned by her mother’s sudden fire. “But mother, surely father will come around in time.”

“And so will Michaelmas,” Catherine retorted, “but when? And I was so set on your seeing this girl. We could have spoken together, weighed her worth. Say what they may, no one judges another rightly unless they’ve seen them with their own eyes. And were I to have fifty sons, I’d never oppose one’s choice until I’d looked upon the woman myself. Had I done so, I might have seen the truth sooner—seen Quicksands clearly—before condemning Gerard’s fancy. Life is a school, and the lesson never ends. We mend one fault, only to fall into another. We stumble here, then there, till we finally stumble into our graves—and that’s the end.”

“Mother,” Kate whispered, her voice trembling.

“What now? No good news, by the look of you. What has frightened you so?”

“A confession,” Kate murmured, barely audible.

“Ah!” Catherine smiled, proud. “A noble word—our Gerard taught you that, I’ll wager. Speak then, out with it.”

“Well,” Kate began, “sooth to say, I’ve seen her.”

“And?”

“And spoken with her too.”

“And never told me?” Catherine gasped. “After this, wonders are dust.”

“Mother,” Kate pleaded, “you were so against her. I waited—until I could speak without making you worse.”

“Ay,” Catherine sighed, half sorrowful, half bitter. “Like mother, like daughter. Cowardice is our curse. I beat the others sometimes—how else would the house hold together? But you, my dear, did I ever harshly speak to you? Did I ever scold or frown? And yet—” She stopped, sensing tears welling. “No, I won no right to weep. You had your reasons. Rise up, brave heart, and tell me all. Better late than never. First—when did you go to Sevenbergen? With your crutches? And I knew nothing?”

“I never went,” Kate insisted. “Never in my life. And though I confess I longed to see her, I never sought her.”

“There now,” Catherine said, relieved. “Did I not say it was unlike you to act without me? Come, tell me—what happened?”

So Kate began. “It came to my ears—how, I cannot say, nor will I tell—only that Gerard was imprisoned in the Stadthouse tower.”

“Ah,” Catherine breathed.

“By father’s order, they claimed.”

Catherine exhaled a sigh that was almost a moan. “Blacker than I thought.”

Giles and I went out at night to comfort him,” Kate continued. “And at the foot of the tower stood a young woman—strange to me, I swear—on the same errand.”

“Look at that now,” Catherine murmured.

“At first, we startled each other—such a place, such a name, and our heads full of devils. We turned pale under the moonlight. But then I said, ‘You are Margaret.’ ‘And you are Kate,’ she replied. Think on it!”

“Did one ever?” Catherine laughed. “It was Gerard! He’s been talking of you to her, and her to him.”

In reply, Kate gave her mother a kiss that held more meaning than words—the composite kiss: one touch, yet saying:

1. Quite correct.
2. Clever mother, for guessing so swiftly.
3. How sweet to be of one mind again, as we always have been.
4. And more.

“Now then,” Catherine said, “speak freely, child. Gerard is not here. Alas, what am I saying? Would that he were.”

“Well, mother,” Kate said softly, “she is fair, and her picture does her little wrong.”

“Eh, dear,” Catherine scoffed gently. “Young people care for looks. I care for deeds. Does she love my boy as he deserves?”

“Sevenbergen is farther from the Stadthouse than we are,” Kate said thoughtfully. “Yet she reached it before I did.”

Catherine nodded slowly.

“More than that,” Kate added, “she had already freed him before I arrived. Down from the tower, where he was captive.”

Catherine shook her head. “The tallest tower for miles! Impossible.”

“But it is true,” Kate insisted. “She brought an old man with her. Together, they sent a rope up to his window. It dangled down. Giles climbed it. When I first saw it hanging, I thought it was magic. But then—her arms around me, her chest beating against mine, her cheeks wet with tears—I knew. It wasn’t magic. It was love. For she is not like me—stronger, bolder. And even I, poor frail creature, feel sometimes I could move mountains for those I love. I love you, mother. And she loves Gerard.”

“God bless her,” Catherine whispered. “God bless her.”

“But—”

“But what, lamb?”

“Her love—can we be sure it is honest? It warms your heart, but it cools mine. Poor soul. She is not a wife, you know, mother, not truly.”

“Humph,” Catherine grunted. “They stood at the altar together.”

“Ay,” Kate said, “but they came as they left—maid and bachelor.”

“The parson said so?”

“No, I don’t know.”

“Then I’ll take no man’s word but his in such a tangled matter.” After a pause, she added, “Still, you’re right, girl. I shall go to Sevenbergen alone. I am a wife, not a slave. We are all in darkness here. She holds the clue. I must question her—alone. Not you. I’ll not bring any lily to a house with a stain, not even to a palace of gold and silver.”

The more Catherine pondered, the more she found herself drawn to Margaret. And curiosity—always a strong force—burned within her, especially in one who had little time for books. At last, on a bright afternoon after dinner, she whispered to Kate, “Keep the house from falling apart, if you can,” and dressed in her best kirtle, hood, scarlet clocked hose, and new shoes. Then she set off briskly for Sevenbergen, without troubling anyone’s mule.

When she arrived, she asked where Margaret Brandt lived. The first man she met shook his head. “Name’s strange to me.”

She walked a bit farther and asked a girl of fifteen standing at a doorway.

“Father,” the girl called into the house, “here’s another seeking the magician’s daughter.”

The man stepped out. “Peter Brandt’s cottage is just outside town, east side. You can see the chimney from here.” He pointed. “But you won’t find them. Father and daughter both left this week—bless you.”

“Say not so,” Catherine urged. “I’ve walked all the way from Tergou.”

“From Tergou? Then you must have met the soldier.”

“What soldier? Ay, I did meet a soldier.”

“Well, that soldier came looking for Margaret.”

“And wasn’t furious when he heard she was gone?” the girl chimed in. “His long beard and her cheek aren’t strangers, I warrant.”

“Hold your tongue,” Catherine snapped. “Too young to slander elders. Tell me more about this soldier, good man.”

“Nay,” the man replied, “all I know is he came seeking Margaret. I told him they’d fled under cover of night, and some say the devil carried them off—magicians, you know. He said, ‘May the devil carry you off for your ill news.’ That was my thanks. Then he said, ‘I doubt it’s a lie.’ I said, ‘If you think so, go and see.’ He did. Burst out with a string of gibberish—my wife thought curses—and rushed to the cottage. Came back singing a different tune. ‘You were right, I was wrong,’ he said, and shoved a silver coin into my hand. Show it to your wife, some of you; then she’ll believe me. I’ve been called a liar once today.”

“It needs not,” Catherine said, inspecting the coin anyway.

“And he seemed quiet, sad, didn’t he?” she asked the girl.

“That he did,” the girl replied warmly. “And, dame, he was the handsomest man I’ve ever seen. Cheeks like a rose, shining beard, eyes like sloes.”

“I saw he was well-bearded,” Catherine said. “But at my age, I don’t scan men as I once did. Still, he was civil—doffed his hat as if I were a queen, and I bowed low in return. Manners beget manners. But little did I know he was her light of love—or most likely the—Who bakes for this town?”

The man blinked, surprised by the sudden turn.

“Well, dame,” he said, “two: John Bush and Eric Donaldson. Both live in this street.”

“Then God be with you,” Catherine said, and moved on. But her step had lost its spring. She no longer tapped the ground with quick jerks and lifted her heel. She asked the bakers if Peter Brandt had left in debt. Bush said they weren’t customers. Donaldson said, “Not a stiver. His daughter paid me the very night they left. Didn’t believe they owed a copper.”

Thus Catherine gathered all she needed with ease.

“Can you tell me what sort of girl Margaret was?” she asked as she turned to leave.

“Well,” said one baker, “a bit too reserved for my taste. I like a chatty customer—when I’m not busy. But she had a good name. A dutiful daughter.”

“That’s no small praise,” Catherine said. “A fair face, they say?”

“Why, where do you come from, wife?”

“Tergou.”

“Oh. Well, judge for yourself. The boys called her ‘the beauty of Sevenbergen.’ The girls mocked it merrily, pulled her to pieces, found so many faults none could agree which was worst.”

“That is enough,” Catherine said. “I see—the bakers are no fools here, and the young women no shallower than elsewhere.”

She bought a manchet of bread—not just for sympathy (for she kept a shop), but to show her household how much better theirs was daily—and returned to Tergou, heavy-hearted.

Kate met her outside the town, eyes bright.

“Well, Kate, lass, it is a happy thing I went. I am heartbroken. Gerard has been cruelly wronged. The child is not ours. Nor shall the mother be welcome from this hour.”

“Alas, mother,” Kate said, puzzled. “I do not understand.”

“Ask no more,” Catherine said sharply. “Never mention her name to me again. That is all.”

Kate sighed humbly and they walked home together.

Inside, they found a soldier seated calmly by the hearth. The moment they entered, he rose and saluted them politely. They stood still—Kate with mild surprise, Catherine with sharp indignation.

“What brings you here?” she demanded.

“I came to seek Margaret.”

“We know no such person.”

“Surely, dame, you know her—Margaret Brandt.”

“We’ve heard of her—enough to regret it.”

“Come, dame, tell me at least where she lives.”

“I know not, and care less.”

Denys sensed the lie. He clenched his jaw. “Well, I expected this place to be enemy ground. But perhaps if you knew all, you wouldn’t be so cold.”

“I do know all,” Catherine snapped. “This morning I knew nothing.” Then, suddenly setting her hands on her hips, she raised her voice, flashing eyes blazing. “How dare you sit by *this* hearth? This very hearth—of all hearths in the world!”

“May Satan carry your hearth to the lake of fire and brimstone!” Denys shouted, fluent in Flemish. “Your servant told me to wait till you came. Else I’d never have troubled your hearth. My curse on it—and on the churlish roof that greets an innocent stranger thus!” He strode to the door, scowling.

“Oh! oh!” Catherine cried, frightened—and slightly ashamed. The fierce woman collapsed, sank into a chair, and burst into tears. Kate followed quietly, but swiftly.

A shrewd writer—now lost to us—once wrote:

She: “I feel all a woman’s weakness.”
He: “Then you are invincible.”

Denys, unknowingly, proved that truth. He stood at the door, staring ruefully at the ruin his words had wrought.

“Nay, wife,” he said, “weep not for a soldier’s rash word. I meant not all I said. Your house is yours. What claim have I to it? There—now, I’ll go.”

“What is to be done?” a deep, calm voice asked.

It was Eli. He had just come in from the shop.

“Here is a ruffian who scolded your women and made them weep,” Denys explained.

“Little Kate, what is it?” Eli asked sensibly. “Ruffians don’t usually call themselves ruffians.”

Before she could answer, Catherine cut in: “Hold your tongue, girl. Muriel told him to sit. I didn’t know. I accused him, and he was leaving, cursing us root and branch. I’ve never been so cursed in all my days—oh! oh! oh!”

“You were both to blame,” Eli said calmly. “You and he. But what the servant says, the master must stand by. We keep no open house, yet we’re not so poor we’d deny a seat to a traveler with a honest face—and, I think, a wounded man. So, end all malice. Sit down.”

“Wounded?” mother and daughter exclaimed together.

“Think you a soldier slings his arm for sport?”

“Nay,” Denys said cheerfully, “just an arrow.”

“But an arrow?” Kate whispered, horrified. “Where were our eyes, mother?”

“Nay, a trifle,” Denys said. “Which, however, I beg you to accept as excuse for my sharpness. These little wounds fret a man. Why, sweeter temper than our Gerard never breathed—yet when the bear tore a piece from his calf, he turned so hot and angry, you’d have sworn he was no son of yours, but born of Sir John Pepper and Dame Mustard. Who is this? A dwarf? Your servant, Master Giles.”

“Your servant, soldier,” roared the newcomer.

Denys started. He hadn’t expected a petard.

Denys’s words surprised his hosts—but not nearly as much as their behavior now. All three crept toward him, lips parted, eyes wide, as if he were some rare creature.

Amazement gave way to growing agitation.

“Hush!” Eli said. “Let none speak but me. Young man,” he said solemnly, “in God’s name, who are you? One who knows us though we know you not? Who speaks of our absent son—our rebellious son—whose heart we break for?”

“What, master,” Denys said, lowering his voice, “has he not written? Has he not told you of me—Denys of Burgundy?”

“He wrote—three lines. Named neither Denys nor any stranger.”

“Ay, I remember—he wrote a long letter to his sweetheart, this Margaret. She’s fled—plague take her—and now I don’t know how to find her.”

“She is not your sweetheart?”

“Who, dame? If you please.”

“Why, Margaret Brandt.”

“How can my comrade’s sweetheart be mine? I know her not from Noah’s niece. I’ve never seen her.”

“Silence, Kate,” Eli said impatiently. “Let the young man answer. How did you come to know Gerard, our son? Think of a parent’s pain. Answer me plainly, like a soldier.”

“And I will. I was discharged at Flushing, bound for Burgundy. On the German frontier, I stayed at the same inn as Gerard. I liked him. I said, ‘Be my comrade.’ He hesitated—then agreed. We walked many weary leagues together. Never truer comrades. First I altered my path to stay with him—then he his to stay with me. We spoke of Sevenbergen, Tergou, this house—countless times. We faced troubles together—but shared them, they were light. I saved his life from a bear. He saved mine in the Rhine—swims like a duck, I like a stone. Once, at an inn in Burgundy, we held a room against seven cutthroats—crippled one, killed two. Your son fought like a man, faced the strongest champion I’ve ever known, and speared him like a sucking pig. Else I would not be here. But just when all was fair, and I was to see him safely aboard ship for Rome—came that son of a—Lord Anthony of Burgundy, with his men, marching to Flanders, in revolt. They tore us apart. Took me—gave me gold, but a broad arrow in my shoulder. Left Gerard alone. At parting, though I’m a soldier, I wept—salt tears. So did he. His last words: ‘Go, comfort Margaret!’ So here I am. Mine to him: ‘Forget Rome. Head for the Rhine, downstream home.’ Now tell me—did I advise well or ill?”

“Soldier,” Eli said, “take my hand.” His lip trembled. “God bless thee. God bless thee.” That was all. But more than words.

Catherine said nothing. She darted from the room, bade Muriel bring the finest food, returned with arms full of wood, piled the fire, took out a snow-white cloth from the press, and hurried to lay it for Gerard’s friend—then suddenly sat down, strength draining from her body.

“Father!” Kate cried, her eyes sharp with love.

Denys leapt up. But Eli waved him back and splashed water sharply on Catherine’s face. Instantly, she gasped. “So sudden. My poor boy!”

Eli whispered to Denys: “Don’t notice. She thinks of him night and day.” They pretended not to see. She shook it off, laid the cloth herself—but her hands trembled, and tears slipped down her cheeks.

They could not do enough for Denys. They fed him, filled his glass again and again. Around the fire—warm with flames, red wine, and eager eyes—he told all I have related, and countless details an artist omits.

But how different the effect on the listeners! To them, the story was already alive before the first word. It was all about Gerard. The man telling it had been warm with him, fought beside him. The flesh and blood around the fire quivered—feeling every danger, every peril.

I ask you, reader, to recall all you know of Gerard’s journey with Denys. Picture it now—in your mind’s eye—told by his comrade to a father stoic outside, torn inside; to a mother and sister, all love and fear. Close the book for a moment. Try to feel it.

Then you will not be surprised when I tell you that Giles crept in and curled before the fire, gazing at Denys with reverence almost dog-like. And when the rough soldier, unaware, revealed his true heart—especially his deep affection for Gerard—Kate, timid as a bird, stole her tiny hand into his huge brown palm. It rested like a spoonful of cream spilled on a platter. Then, gently, she pinched the ball of his thumb—her Kardiometer, a measure of emotion.

Fate is just—even to rival storytellers. Denys had to pay a tax I did not. Whenever Gerard was in danger, the women’s faces paled, their throats tightened. He had to spoil his tale—break suspense—for mercy’s sake. “Now, dame, wait till you hear the end. Ma’amselle, do not blanch so. Courage! It looks ugly, but you shall hear how we prevailed. Had he failed, and I near—would I be alive?”

Meanwhile, Kate’s Kardiometer registered emotion, pinching by scale. It was not a high-pressure engine—but all is relative. Denys soon learned the tender gamut. He knew when to pause, when to stretch suspense.

Once, when he fell into the Rhine and sank, he got pinched—to his surprise and delight. “Oho!” he thought. And, like an anatomist, “experimentum in corpore vili”—he stayed under for a quarter-hour, under pressure. Even when Gerard grabbed him, he lingered, swimming to the east bank first. Then, spotting officers, he trolled them a while, treading water, before turning and swimming back across. Only then, ashamed to admit himself a pike, did he land—exhausted. The pressure released.

It was eleven o’clock—an unheard-of hour—but no one noticed. Denys still had much to tell when the door opened quietly, and in crept Cornelis and Sybrandt, looking sullen. They had drunk the last of their mysterious funds.

Catherine feared Eli would rebuke them before Denys. But he only looked sadly at them and motioned them to sit.

Denys, however, seemed unsettled. He frowned, studied them thoughtfully. Then turned to Catherine. “What say you, dame? The rest tomorrow. I’m weary. It grows late.”

“So be it,” Eli said. But when Denys rose to leave, Catherine stopped him. “And think you to sleep elsewhere? Gerard’s room has been ready for hours. The sheets—I’ll not boast—since I spun the flax and wove the web.”

“Then I’ll lie in them blindfold,” Denys replied gallantly. “Ah, dame, our poor Gerard loved fine linen. He couldn’t forgive the Germans their coarse flax. And when our countrymen erred, he’d excuse them: ‘Well, well—bonnes toiles sont en Bourgogne.’ Good lenten cloths in Burgundy. But he surpassed all in wit and cleanliness.”

The next day, Denys found a moment alone with Catherine and her daughter and told them the rest of what had happened—though he took care to excuse himself for not sharing it with Cornelis and Sybrandt. “It is not my place to speak ill of them,” he said. “They come from good stock. But Gerard does not count them among his friends in this matter—and I am Gerard’s comrade. And we soldiers have a rule: never tell the enemy anything but lies.”

Catherine sighed, but said nothing. The tale he told stirred deep sorrow within them all—a storm of grief and agitation. They wept at the thought of the friends parted so cruelly, and even now Denys could scarcely speak of it without emotion. Yet, slowly, their pain gave way to a bright hope: the joyful expectation that Gerard would return soon.

Denys shared that hope fully. But he reminded them that such confidence did not mean they should ignore Gerard’s last wishes. “Suppose he returns next week,” he said, “and Margaret is nowhere to be found—what kind of welcome will he get? What face shall I have to show him?”

Catherine, who had never before been so fond of the absent Margaret, now felt a fierce tenderness toward her. She was just as eager to find her as Denys was—to bring her back, to comfort her, to make peace before Gerard came home. But she could not agree with Denys that they should leave Sevenbergen to search for her. “She must have told someone where she was going,” she insisted. “It’s not as if they were fugitives. They owe no one a stiver here. And dear heart, Denys, you can’t hunt all of Holland for one girl.”

“Can I not?” Denys replied grimly. “We shall see.”

After a pause, he added, “We’ll divide our forces. You stay here—keep your eyes and ears open. I’ll go through every town in Holland, if need be.”

“But she won’t be far,” Catherine said. “Three people don’t travel fast or far, not like one.”

“That’s sensible,” she admitted. But she insisted he visit the demoiselle Van Eyck first. “She and Margaret were close friends. If anyone knows where she’s gone, it’s her.”

Denys was ready to go at once. So Catherine, with a quick touch of neatness, joined him. They arrived at the Van Eyck’s house, where the old lady sat in a richly furnished room. She received them graciously, and Catherine laid out their purpose.

At the mention of Margaret’s name, the tapestry slipped from the demoiselle’s hands. “Gone? Gone from Sevenbergen—and didn’t tell me? The ungrateful child.”

The visitors were stunned. “You didn’t know? When was the last time she visited?”

“Perhaps ten days ago,” the woman said. “I’d taken out my brushes after years of silence, meaning to paint her portrait. But I didn’t finish it—for reasons.”

Catherine frowned. “It’s most strange that she should leave like this—without warning, without word or reason. Just when all our hearts are warm to her! And now here is Gerard’s friend returned from the ends of the earth, bringing news and comfort from Gerard himself—and cannot find her. And Gerard himself is expected any day. What are we to do? I’m sure she didn’t leave without cause. Can you not give us a clue, my good demoiselle? Prithee, do.”

“I have none to give,” the elder woman said, slightly testy.

Then Reicht Heynes appeared in the doorway, cheeks flushed. “So you’ve been listening all along, eh?”

“What are my ears for, mistress?” Reicht retorted.

“True enough,” the demoiselle conceded. “Then throw some light on this dark matter.”

“There’s no darkness to me,” Reicht said. “And the clue? Call it a two-ply thread, and both ends are right here in this room. Oh, mistress, I wonder at you sitting there pretending.”

“Marry, come up!” the mistress snapped, her own face nearly as red as Reicht’s.

“So it was *you* who drove the foolish girl away.”

“I did my part,” Reicht said quietly. “What sort of greeting did you give her last time she came? Do you think she couldniced it, being all alone and friendless? And you said, ‘I’ve changed my mind about painting you,’ turning up your nose at her.”

“I did not turn up my nose,” the demoiselle protested. “Mine isn’t shaped like yours for looking heavenward.”

“Oh, all noses follow the heart’s bent,” Reicht said. “Poor soul. She came into the kitchen to me. ‘I am not to be painted now,’ she said—tears in her eyes. She said no more. But I knew well what she meant. I had seen you.”

“Well,” said Margaret Van Eyck, “I confess it—and I ask you to judge me, madam. These young girls do nothing on their own. They mimic their lovers’ ways. Now, your Gerard is skilled in many things, especially illuminating. Margaret is his pupil—patient and devoted. What marvel? She has a woman’s eye for color, and a lover to imitate. It’s a trick I despise: for by it, the noble art of color—free, royal, aspiring—becomes enslaved to petty crafts. It’s reduced to serving letters and books, caged like insects in gold leaf, made small to match the littleness of ink and parchment.”

“And yet,” she continued, “affection rules us all. When the poor girl brought me her thorn leaves, lilies, ivy, dewberries, ladybirds, butterfly grubs—Nature’s very scum—stuck fast in gold like wasps in honey, and her daily book showing she’d spent hundreds of hours on each page, I was furious. An immortal soul, so much labor, so much skill—wasted on trash, leaves, bugs, and barren letters! But I have feelings. I held back, dammed my better judgment, and looked kindly upon it, to see how it might be improved. I said, ‘Since Heaven has doomed us to spend our time, soul, and color on great letters and tiny beetles, rather than saints and heroes, why not present Nature as it truly is?’ I told her, ‘The grapes I see walking abroad hang in the air, not stuck in a wall. Even these insects—these creatures of Nature’s slime—do not live wedged in metal prisons like flies in glue, but crawl and hover freely, infesting the air.’”

“Ah, my dear friend,” the girl had said, “I see now where you’re going—but this ground is gold; we may not shade.”

“Who said so?” I asked.

“All teachers of this craft,” she replied. “And—Gerard himself!”

“Then let Gerard and his gang go to the devil,” I said. “Give me a brush!”

And so I chose a color false in nature, but true in relation to that glaring gold background. In five minutes, I painted a bunch of raspberries—stalk and all—so lifelike they seemed ready to fall into your mouth. A butterfly grub she’d drawn so truthfully it could turn the stoutest stomach. My lady flung her arms around my neck and cried, ‘Oh!’”

“Did she?” Denys managed to say at last.

“The little love!” he added.

Margaret Van Eyck stared, then smiled.

She went on to explain how step by step, she’d been led to promise to take up painting again—the art she’d abandoned with a sigh when her brothers died—and to paint the Madonna once more—with Margaret as model. And she revealed, almost casually, how girls became saints.

“Your hair is adorable,” she’d said.

“Why, it’s red,” Margaret replied.

“Yes,” the artist said, “but what a red! How brown! How glossy! Most hair is worthless to us painters. Yours is the artist’s very hue. But your violet eyes—earthly, yet now languid without Gerard, now fiery in hope of him—I will lift them to heaven in holy meditation. Your nose, which already turns upward (though not as piously as Reicht’s), I will soften slightly. And your chin—strong, resolute—will be weakened a bit.”

“Weakened her chin?” Catherine gasped. “Alack, what does that mean? I don’t understand.”

“It’s a resolute chin,” the demoiselle explained. “Not too strong for this world—but for a Madonna? No thank you.”

“Well, I never,” Denys muttered. “A resolute chin.”

“And now comes the rub,” the old lady continued. “When you told me she was—well, *that*—it struck me hard. I dropped my brushes. Was I really going to turn a girl who couldn’t keep her lover at bay into the Virgin Mary—at my age? I still love the poor ninny. But I adore our blessed Lady. Say you, ‘a painter mustn’t be peevish in such matters’? Well, most painters are men—and men can do anything. Their saints and virgins are no different from their mistresses. But I am not a man. I am a woman. My painting is half craft, half devotion. And so now you may read me. It was foolish, perhaps, but I couldn’t help it. Yet I regret it.”

She ended despondently, having begun in defiance.

“Well, dame,” Catherine said gently, “you must think how it would wound the poor girl’s heart—she so fond of you.”

Margaret Van Eyck only sighed.

Reicht, who had been biting her lips impatiently, turned sharply on Catherine. “Why, dame, do you think Margaret and Peter left Sevenbergen *only* because of that? Nay.”

“For what else, then?” Catherine asked.

“What else? Because Gerard’s family treats her so cruelly. Who would stay among cold-hearted folk who sent her lad to Italy—and now, with him gone, refuse to relent, refuse to come near her, even though she’s left behind?”

Reicht’s voice rose. “You said you were going to see her.”

“Oh, yes—going, and going, and going,” Reicht snapped. “You should have said less—or done more. With your words, you lifted her heart—and with your deeds, you crushed it. ‘They have never been,’ she said to me, with such a sigh. And I know how she feels—because I, too, am far from my kin. When I first came to Holland, I often cried to myself. But ten times rather would I be Reicht Heynes, with leagues between me and all my kith, than be her—surrounded by those who ought to love her, yet treat her as lonely as I.”

“Alack, Reicht,” Catherine said, “I did go yesterday—and before that. But something always came up.”

“Mistress,” Reicht said sharply, “did anything stop you from eating your dinner those days? I doubt it. And if your heart had been as kind to your own flesh and blood as it was to your flesher’s meat, nothing could have kept you from her—sitting alone, watching the road for you, her child’s child beating beneath her breast.”

Before Reicht could continue, the Van Eyck sprang from her seat. “Since you disrespect my guests, seek another place!”

“With all my heart,” Reicht said boldly.

“Nay, mistress,” Catherine interjected, “true folk speak plainly. Her tongue is a stinger.”

Tears welled in her eyes.

“But better she said it than thought it. Now it won’t rankle. And you shall not part with her. Beshrew the wench—she knows she’s a good servant and takes advantage. We poor women who keep house must pay tax for value. I once had a fine servant when I was young. Dear me, how she ground me down! In the end, by Heaven’s mercy, she married the baker—and I was my own woman again. ‘No more good servants shall come here,’ I said. ‘I’ll take fools and teach them. As soon as they learn their right hand from their left, they saucy me—then out they go, and I take another dunce.’ It’s wearisome, teaching fools one by one—but there—*I* am mistress.” She paused, then added, with a sudden twist, “And you are mistress here, I suppose.”

“No more than that stool,” the Van Eyck declared loftily. “She is neither mistress nor servant—she is *gone*. Dismissed. There’s an end of her. Did you not hear me turn the saucy baggage off?”

“Ay, ay—we all heard,” Reicht said, utterly indifferent.

“Then hear me!” Denys said solemnly.

They all turned, like dials, to fix their eyes on him.

“Ay, let us hear what the man says,” urged the hostess. “Men are fine fellows, with their great hoarse voices.”

“Mistress Reicht,” Denys began, with dignity so grand it verged on absurdity, “you are dismissed. If I may advise—since you are no longer a servant, become a mistress, a queen.”

“Easier said than done,” Reicht replied bluntly.

“Not a jot,” Denys answered. “Here is one who is a man—though only half an arbalestrier, thanks to that Englishman’s arrow. But I left a similar token in his body. That is comfort. I have twenty gold pieces” (he displayed them) “and a strong arm. In another week or so, I shall have twice as many. Marriage is not my habit—but I capitulate to virtue. You are beautiful, kind, honest, and above all—you stand by my she-comrade. Be then an arbalestriesse!”

“And what the devil is that?” Reicht asked.

“I mean—be the wife, the mistress, the queen of Denys of Burgundy here present.”

Silence fell—deep and sudden.

Then, it broke into a burst of outraged indignation.

Catherine: “Well, did you ever?”

Margaret: “Never in all my born days.”

Catherine: “Before our very faces!”

Margaret: “Of all the absurdity, and insolence of this ridiculous sex—”

Denys observed dryly, “The female to whom I spoke is silent. The others, whose eloquence is not demanded, are loud.” The voices ceased. All eyes turned to Reicht.

She glanced up at him from beneath her lashes and said, “I mean to look at any man carefully before I leap into his arms.”

Denys straightened to his full height. “Then look your fill—and leap.”

This sparked a new, unexpected development. The Van Eyck thrust out a long white finger, level with her eye, and shouted, “Stand, in the name of all the saints!”

“You are beautiful,” she cried. “You are inspired—with folly. What matters? You are inspired. I must take off your head!”

And in a flash, she was sketching him with her pencil.

“Come out, hussy!” she screamed at Reicht. “More in front of him. Keep the fool inspired and beautiful. Oh, why didn’t I have this madman for my centurion? They sent me a brute with a low forehead and a shapeless beard.”

Catherine stood, stunned, watching this pantomime. Secretly, she decided her venerable hostess had been a disguised lunatic all along—and was now revealing her true self.

Reicht, meanwhile, was miserable and cross. “I left my caldron in a precarious state,” she declared. “And duties so grave as mine leave no time to waste playing the statee and the fool.”

Her mistress replied, “It is possible to be rude and rebellious to your poor, old, affectionate, desolate mistress—without being utterly heartless and trampling on art.”

Reicht stopped. Pouted. Looked like a little basilisk at the inspired model causing her distress.

He met her gaze with unwavering admiration.

Only when the artist’s wrist cramped from disuse did the scene dissolve. By then, she had made a rough but noble sketch.

“I can work no more,” she said sadly.

“Then, mistress,” Reicht asked, “may I go to my pot?”

“Ay, ay—go to your pot! And get into it. You’ll find your soul there. Then you’ll all be together.”

“Well, but Reicht,” Catherine laughed, “she turned you off.”

“Boo, boo, boo!” Reicht scoffed. “If she wants to get rid of me, let her turn herself off and die. I’m sure she’s old enough. But take your time, mistress—if you’re not in a hurry, neither am I. When that day comes, it’ll take a man to dry my eyes. And if you’re still of the same mind then, soldier, you can say so. If not—well, it’ll be all one to Reicht Heynes.”

And she walked away.

But her words did not fall unheard. Neither Catherine nor the demoiselle could hide from themselves that this blunt, solitary girl had likely read Margaret Brandt correctly—and that she had left Sevenbergen, broken-hearted.

Catherine and Denys bid farewell to the Van Eyck, and that very afternoon, Denys set out on his quest—a wild goose chase, indeed.

His plan, like all great undertakings, was simple: he would visit a hundred towns and villages, asking in each about an old physician with a fair daughter, and an old longbow soldier. He would question burgomasters about newcomers, and stand by fountains, watching the women and girls as they drew water.

And so he went—on foot, across Holland, month after month—without finding her.

Yet, in a way, the journey was its own reward. Those who sit at home, blindfolded by pride, believe that peace and quiet are the truest joys after danger. But those who observe before they speak know that men who risk their lives constantly crave excitement between battles—they are not made for innocent tranquility.

Denys was no exception. His life had been half Sparta, half Capua—soldier and libertine, never mixed. But now, for the first time, he found himself caught between peace and duty. And he saw it as duty.

So, for months, he was a demi-Spartan—sober, vigilant, indomitable, and strangely happy, despite constant disappointment.

He flirted wildly on the road—but wasted no time on it. And during all his wanderings, he never told a single woman that “marriage was not one of his habits.”

And so we leave him—the Pilgrim of Friendship—tramping the roads of Holland, seeking not just a girl, but the honor of a vow.

Catherine sat in quiet dread, her thoughts turning like a millstone as she reckoned the time until Gerard’s return—no more than a month, perhaps just a week. How could she face him, knowing she had failed to watch over his betrothed? The weight of that failure pressed upon her chest like a stone. And then there was Margaret—what had become of her? The uncertainty gnawed at Catherine, sometimes twisting into something worse: the fear that the girl might have taken her own life.

“Oh, Kate,” she murmured, her voice thick with sorrow, “if only she hadn’t gone and done such a thing!”

“Mother,” Kate replied gently, “she wouldn’t do that. She’s not wicked.”

“Ah, my dear,” Catherine sighed, “you don’t understand how young girls can be—impulsive, reckless, without anyone to guide them. They’ll throw themselves into water for a man who, the next day, would make them forget him in an instant. I’ve seen it happen—girls jumping in one moment, screaming for help the next, as if they didn’t know their own minds. And when their bodies ache with pain—oh, no creature suffers like a woman does—then their spirits snap. That patience they carry like a shield, stronger than any other soul save perhaps a donkey, vanishes all at once. And so they leap. That’s why I say men are monsters.”

“Mother!” Kate gasped.

“Monsters, I tell you,” Catherine insisted, “for building these endless canals, tempting poor women into ruin. They know we won’t cut our throats—we hate blood, and value our skin more than our lives. Hanging gives time to change one’s mind—the nail is driven, the rope tied, and still there’s thought. But a canal? It’s like stepping into bed. Once in, the water takes care of the rest, whether you want it or not. Look at me—I’m the mother of nine, yet I confess I once stood on the edge of our own canal, ready to jump.”

“No, mother,” Kate said, shaking her head, “I won’t believe it.”

“You may,” Catherine said firmly. “It was the first year we lived together. Eli and I were young, neither of us knowing the other’s weaknesses. We quarreled, pulled apart like two stubborn oxen. I ran off, crying, to tell some idle gossip what I should never have spoken aloud—not even to saints—but there was a canal right before me. Do they take us for ducks, I wonder? Oh, how inviting it looked! I said to myself, ‘Since he has cast me out, let him see me drowned. Then he’ll change his key. He’ll weep bitterly, and I’ll look down from heaven’—though I forgot I’d be on the other side—‘and see him mourn. Oh, how sweet that would be!’ And I was already stepping forward, barefoot on the cold stones, when suddenly I stopped. I remembered my new gown—nearly finished, fine linen, embroidered at the hem. So I turned back. When I returned, Eli said nothing about my tears, nor the quarrel. Instead, he said, ‘Let yon flea stick in the wall, my lass. Not a word I heard was true—except this: “I love thee.”’ Those were his very words. I remember them well—it was our first real fight. I threw my arms around his neck and wept, thinking of the canal. And he held me just as tightly, being a young man, warm and alive. That was better than drowning, better than spoiling my wedding dress and my new shoes—old John Bush made them, and now his nephew keeps the shop. And what was my grief compared to hers?”

Kate hoped, with all her heart, that Margaret loved her father deeply enough to stay by him, especially now that he was old and frail. “He is everything to her—father, mother, protector. She couldn’t leave him.”

“Not so,” Catherine replied. “When despair strikes, a woman forgets everything—family, duty, love. The sky seems black, the world cruel. I trust more in a child not yet born than in one nearing the grave to keep her safe. For surely, when a little innocent clings to our hearts, feeding from our veins, it goes against nature to end our lives.”

“Well then,” Kate said softly, “let us hold fast to hope.”

She added that perhaps their fears were too great, that likely Margaret was safe and well. Still, she ended with a solemn plea: “Please, mother, do not name the child’s sex. It brings ill luck, everyone says. As if girls aren’t born as often as boys.”

Her words drew a sharp retort. “Do you dare threaten me with a girl?!” Catherine exclaimed. “I don’t want another daughter while I have you. What use would a girl be to me? Can I sit her on my knee and see Gerard again, as I can with a son? No. I have decided. It is settled.”

“How can it be?” Kate asked.

“In my heart,” Catherine declared. “And if I am to be disappointed at last, it shall not be because you robbed me of hope first, telling me it will not be a child at all, but only a girl.”

Margaret Brandt had always kept herself apart from the people of Sevenbergen. Her quiet dignity, her silence, and her refusal to mingle freely with others had been mistaken for pride—something she heard whispered about in hushed tones across the town. And now, as the truth of her condition began to show, she knew that those same whispers would turn into venomous tongues, eager to wound her beyond repair. The thought haunted her like a shadow: when the world could no longer deny what was plain, how would they mock her? How would they tear her down?

For weeks, she had withdrawn into the house, avoiding daylight, even on rare outings. She did not deceive herself—not in her heart or conscience. Though she knew little of legal fine points, she understood one thing clearly: a betrothal was a binding promise, as sacred as any marriage contract. It could not be broken lightly, not by either party. She knew that such unions had long been recognized by both Church and State, and that children born of such bonds were considered legitimate. But there was no document to prove hers.

Gerard had taken it. And Gerard was gone—far away, across seas and mountains, where her voice could not reach him.

She despised herself for the careless act that had left her defenseless before the world’s judgment. She had never read Horace’s words—“The more you irritate, the more you are hated”—but she lived them. With a mind sharp and clear, untouched by sentimentality, she saw exactly how the world would see her. No marriage lines in hand, only a swelling belly and a child soon to come into the world—what story could she tell that would silence the gossips? “I have my papers,” she might say, “but I cannot show them.” Would any woman believe that? Not one.

And yet, Margaret was not a woman who craved men’s approval. She cared nothing for their praise or scorn. What mattered to her was the regard of other women—the quiet, modest women of Holland, whose eyes saw deeper than mere appearances. To be judged by them as weak, reckless, unchaste—that was her true fear. And now, the slander wore a mask of truth. There was no escape from it.

She was not strong-minded in the way the modern world might expect. Though raised early to manage a household, though firm in some things, she was fragile in others—especially in matters of reputation. Like so many noblewomen of her time, she was a leaf caught in a storm, trembling at every breath of public opinion. And the storm was coming.

Her suffering was not loud, but deep—silent, constant, gnawing at her soul. Hours passed in stillness, her thoughts a torment. Even when her father spoke to her, she replied mechanically, her mind elsewhere. Then, without warning, her face would flush, her body tremble—though he said nothing to provoke it. His words meant nothing. It was the dread within that burned her cheeks red.

It reached its peak after she returned from Margaret van Eyck’s house. There, among women, her secret was discovered. The old artist, reclusive and kind, might keep silent. But Catherine—Catherine lived in the center of a busy family, surrounded by neighbors who knew everything. If she spoke, the whole town would know.

Yet, Catherine had spoken gently. That tiny spark of kindness gave Margaret hope. Perhaps she would be spared. But then came silence. No word. No comfort. And in that silence, Margaret realized: Catherine would not be her ally. Without love or loyalty to balance her instinct to gossip, she would betray her.

Then the desire to flee took root—first a whisper, then a cry, then a desperate longing. But how could she persuade her father? He was old, frail, rooted in the place where he had lived all his life. To move him would be a burden he could not bear.

There was only one path: confess to him. Better that than leave him behind, lying and ashamed. Yet, the thought of speaking to a man—even her own father—about such things filled her with horror. She wavered between flight and confession, torn by agony.

And then, one day, the unthinkable entered her mind: *End it.*

Foolish words, perhaps—but sometimes, the most foolish-sounding thoughts carry the deepest weight. One of Catherine’s fears—those wide, dark canals that ran through the city—now seemed like an invitation to peace. She stood by the water one afternoon, staring into its still, deep surface. It looked calm. Still. Unmoving. And she—so weary, so afraid—felt drawn to it. No more pain. No more shame. No more fear.

But if Gerard had not loved her—if he had not risked his life for her—she might have stepped in. As it was, she knelt beside the canal, hands clasped, heart pounding, and prayed aloud to God. “Oh, selfish wretch,” she whispered, “to leave your father! Oh, wicked wretch, to kill your child, and make poor Gerard’s suffering all in vain!” And she rose, resolved. “I will tell him. Before this sun sets.”

She rushed home, afraid her courage would vanish before she reached him.

Peter Brandt, though learned in medicine and nature, was simple in domestic matters. Since Margaret turned sixteen, she had ruled the house with quiet authority. So it was strange to see her now—hesitant, trembling, speaking in broken sentences to the man who, in household affairs, was less important than Martin Wittenhaagen or even the young girl who washed the dishes each morning.

“Father,” she said, “I must speak to you.”

“Speak on, girl,” he replied.

“Will you listen? And—and not try to excuse me?”

“We all have faults, Margaret. You no more than the rest. Fewer, unless I am blinded by love.”

“Oh, father,” she murmured, “I am a foolish girl. I meant well, but I’ve done wrong—greatly wrong. And now I must bear the shame. But I love you, and I beg you—will you forgive me, and still love your motherless daughter?”

“That you may count on,” Peter said cheerfully.

“Do not smile,” she pleaded. “If you do, I cannot speak. I will only make you sad.”

“Why, what is the matter?”

“Disgrace is coming upon this house. It stands at the door. And I—I am the cause. Turn your head away, father. I—I let Gerard take my marriage lines.”

“Is that all?” Peter asked. “It was an oversight.”

“A madwoman’s deed,” she whispered. “But worse is coming. Oh, father, turn away. Please.”

“Foolish wench,” he muttered, but obeyed.

She trembled, her face aflame, and began to stammer: “I saw Gerard as my husband—we were betrothed—and he was in great danger. I thought I had killed him. And I—oh, if you were my mother, I might find courage. You would question me. But you say nothing.”

“Why, Margaret,” he said, “what is all this? Why are your cheeks so red? You’re speaking to your father, not a stranger.”

“Why am I burning? Because—because—father, kill me! Send me to heaven! Let Martin shoot me with his arrow! Then the gossips will come and tell you why I blush today. And when I am dead, I hope you will love your girl again—for your wife’s sake.”

“Give me your hand, mistress,” Peter said, his voice firm but gentle.

She offered it, trembling. He took it, felt her pulse, and frowned.

“Alas, no,” she said. “It is my soul that burns, not my body. I cannot stay here. I will not.”

She wrung her hands, agitated.

“Be calm,” he said softly. “Do not torment yourself. You wish to leave Sevenbergen? Why not? If it troubles you so much, we can go. You are fevered, admit it.”

“What?” she cried. “You would leave without asking why? Without knowing?!”

And suddenly, she fell to her knees beside him, clutching his sleeve, then his arm, then his shoulder, pleading with tears in her eyes. “Please, father! Leave this place! Do not ask why! I cannot say it. I would rather die.”

“Who seeks your secrets, child?” he asked. “Am I not the man who has spent his life studying nature? And as for leaving Sevenbergen—what keeps me here? Respect? Gratitude? They call me quacksalver, wizard, fool. They give their thanks and honors to those who harm them. And what does it matter to me where we live? Choose your own place, as your mother did before you.”

She threw her arms around him, weeping silently. She was spared—yet in her sorrow, she almost wished she had told him everything.

After a while, Peter insisted she take a draught he brought from his cabinet. She drank it obediently, to please him. It was a calming remedy, given under a mistaken belief—but it helped. She slept deeply, and awoke refreshed. That very day, she began packing.

A week later, they left Sevenbergen, taking all their belongings to Rotterdam. They lodged above a tailor’s shop on Brede-Kirk Straet. Only one person in Tergou knew their destination: the Burgomaster. He kept the knowledge to himself. What use he would make of it, no one could guess—not even he. But time, as it often does, would reveal all.

Among strangers, Margaret Brandt found a fragile peace. And soon, an unexpected turn of fortune lifted her spirits. A prominent citizen, gravely ill and desperate, had consulted doctor after doctor—each more reckless than the last—until he lay near death. Desperate, he summoned Peter Brandt. Peter arrived to find the man bled dry, purged beyond reason, and reduced to a shadow of himself. Without hesitation, Peter threw out every bottle of medicine in the room, flung open the window, and began anew. He mixed egg yolks with strong Schiedam gin and gave it in small doses. Then came a stew of meat cooked in red wine and water, seasoned with gentle herbs that did no harm. Slowly, the man recovered—though he looked more like a ghost wrapped in linen than a living man. But he was voluble, and word of his recovery spread through the streets. Peter’s name became known, not from skill, but from luck. And so, at long last, the quiet physician who had labored in obscurity for years found fame—and money.

The old man’s pride stirred; his purse filled. Yet he spent much on rare herbs and costly remedies, determined to invest every coin in healing arts. Margaret, however, quietly set aside a portion, tucked away in a white-walled chest. The victory was sweet—but too late. Its joy proved fatal.

One evening, as she kissed him goodnight, his voice seemed thick, unsteady.

The next morning, he was found speechless, barely conscious.

Margaret, who had been her father’s devoted student for years, recognized the signs at once: a stroke. But fearing her own judgment, she sent for a doctor. One of those who had been thwarted by Peter—yet failed to kill the civic dignitary—arrived promptly. He confirmed her diagnosis with cheerfulness and immediately recommended bleeding. She refused. “He always opposed bloodletting,” she said firmly, “especially in the aged.”

Peter lived—but never again as before. His memory faltered. He could no longer prescribe with certainty. Patients waited, some demanding only him, others willing to accept another healer. Misery loomed. Margaret resolved to seek counsel and comfort from her cousin William Johnson—someone she had avoided for years, out of pride and poverty.

She found him seated in a dim room with his servant, both clearly under the influence of drink. Suppressing surprise, she greeted them politely, then explained she had come to speak of family matters. With a quiet glance toward the servant, she hinted at privacy.

But the woman misunderstood.

“Oh, you can speak before me, can’t you, my old man?” she snapped.

Margaret flushed. “I beg your pardon, mistress. I did not know my cousin had fallen into the customs of this town. Well, I shall return another time.” She rose to leave.

“I don’t know what you mean by ‘customs of the town,’” the woman retorted, rising sharply. “But this I do know: it is the duty of a faithful servant to protect her master from being devoured by his beggarly kin.”

Margaret shot back, “You’re too modest, mistress. You are no servant. Your speech betrays you. It is only when the ape climbs the tree that we see her tail plainly. No—there sits the servant, God help him! And while it stands thus, fear not that his kin will ever be so poor in spirit as to come where the likes of you may mock their charity.” With one silent, reproachful look at her cousin—so passive, so powerless—she turned and left, proud and composed. Not until she reached home did she allow herself to weep.

Now two men were dependent upon her—a pregnant girl and a newborn child yet to come.

Yet it was this very child, though helpless, who would become their greatest ally.

Nature was strong in Margaret Brandt—the same nature that drives birds to build nests, beasts to hunt, insects to prepare for winter. Stirred by instinct, she sat and thought, and thought again, how to outpace destitution. Though five gold coins remained, she saw starvation creeping closer, inevitable and cold.

When women think with the intensity of men, they often think just as wisely. Margaret rose, instructed Martin to move Peter to another room, cleaned her chamber, polished the glass globe, hung it from the ceiling, dusted the crocodile, and nailed it to the outside wall. Then, after giving Martin careful directions, she stationed him as sentinel at the door, telling all who approached that a great, ancient, learned alchemist resided within—sometimes amusing himself by curing sickness.

Patients soon arrived. They demanded to see the doctor.

“That cannot be,” Margaret replied. “He is deep in study, seeking the philosopher’s stone. Not even princes may disturb him. Tell me your symptoms, and return in two hours.”

And oh, the mysterious power of belief! When they returned, the remedy was always ready.

Sometimes, if the patient was important, she examined his face, felt his pulse and skin, listened to his story, then carried it carefully to Peter’s room. There, she recalled how her father would have treated such a case, pondered deeply, wrote a cryptic prescription in illegible script, and brought it down with reverence. “Can you read this?” she would ask.

Usually, the reply was, “I am no reader,” or, with awe, “Nay, mistress, I cannot make sense of it.”

“Then let me,” she would say. “It is sovereign. Consider yourself cured.”

If she had the ingredients, she sometimes allowed the patient to watch her mix the medicine—consulting the sacred formula with anxious care, lest science suffer in her hands. So they left, lighter in purse, heavier in faith, deceived to their hearts’ content. *Populus vult decipi.* And when they were gone, she took down two small boxes Gerard had made—labeled *Today* and *Tomorrow*. Into *Today* went the smaller coins; into *Tomorrow*, the larger ones, along with the few remaining gold pieces from Sevenbergen. Thus, she met daily needs and saved for the storm she knew was coming. She blended drugs with simples, virtue with vice. Her conscience pricked her sharply. Each night, after the day’s deception, she knelt and prayed, “Forgive me, Lord, for the sake of my child.”

But then came reports of cures. And slowly, her conscience hardened.

Martin Wittenhaagen, once a burden, now proved useful. Like many who had endured hardship, he had stiffened—not softened. Still strong, he could carry the doctor herself around Rotterdam. Instead, he carried her slops.

In this new role, he displayed soldierly traits: obedience without question, punctuality, accuracy, speed—and drunkenness.

He fell in with “good fellows”—rogues who fed him Schiedam. He rambled, bragged.

Doctor Margaret had risen high in his esteem. All this—the crocodile as banner, the dotard hidden in ambush, the disposal of waste, the receipt of coin—struck him not as science, but as strategy. In his cups, he boasted before a mixed crowd: “Me and my General—we are a biting of the burghers!”

When this tale spread through the city, Doctor Margaret received a summons from the constables. They arrested her, trembling and pleading for mercy, and brought her before the burgomaster. Standing beside him were real physicians—men in long robes and square caps—accusing her of unlawfully treating the Duke’s subjects.

At first, she could not speak. The word *Law* paralyzed her. But when questioned gently, she told the truth: she had been her father’s pupil, followed his methods, and healed many. “And it is not for myself, sirs,” she said, “but I have two helpless, honest men at home. How else can I feed them? Ah, good sirs, let a poor girl earn her bread honestly. You do not hinder men from making theirs idly and shamefully. And oh, sirs, you are husbands, fathers—surely you must see I have cause to work and provide as best I may?”

Before the words left her lips, she wished she could take them back. She placed one hand over her heart, the other across her face, hiding her tears—but not the streams that slipped beneath.

Her plea fell on deaf ears. Perhaps a female bailiff might have yielded. But not these men.

“What concern is it of ours?” the burgomaster said. “Unless you swear never to break the law again, I will remit imprisonment—but exact the fine.”

Doctor Margaret clasped her hands and vowed, with trembling sincerity, never, never, never to cure body or beast again. Released, she turned at the door and curtsied humbly, thanking them for their mercy.

To pay the fine, she must open the *Tomorrow* box—immediately. But in excess caution, she had nailed it shut, afraid even temptation might prevail. Now, she could not remove the nails. The constables grew impatient. “Let us break it for you,” they offered.

“No,” she insisted. “You’ll break it worse than I.” Taking a hammer, she struck weakly, lost strength, and wept hysterically. At last, she broke it—and a tiny cry escaped her. She paid the fine—every penny of her unlawful earnings, plus two gold coins. When they were gone, she gathered the broken fragments and remaining coins on the table. Her arms wrapped around them. Her hair, rich and loose, tumbled down. She bowed her forehead upon the wreckage and sobbed, “My love’s box is broken—and my heart with it.” She stayed there, motionless.

Martin entered. She could not lift her head. “What has happened?” she whispered. “My love’s box is broken—and so is mine.”

Martin was not sad—angry. Some traitor had betrayed her. Who had spoken? Whose stony heart had delivered her to this fate? Whoever it was, he would feel the point of his arrow. The irony of his position—delivering justice in the form of a shaft—did not occur to him.

“Idle talk! idle talk!” moaned Margaret, her brow still pressed to the table. “When you’ve killed every gossip in this town, can we eat them? Tell me how to keep us all, or hold your tongue and let the saints whisper to me.”

Martin fell silent, casting uneasy glances at his defeated General.

That evening, she rose, washed her face, tied up her hair, and ordered Martin to take down the crocodile and put out a basket instead.

“I can launder better than anyone on this street,” she said. “And you must carry it.”

“For your sake, I will,” he replied.

“Good Martin. Forgive me—I spoke harshly.”

As they spoke, a man came for advice. Margaret told him the mayor had forbidden her to sell medicine. “But,” she added, “I will gladly wash, iron, and starch your linen. I will come to your house and fetch it.”

“Are you mad, young woman?” he snapped. “I came for a doctor, not a washerwoman!” And he stormed off.

“There goes a foolish creature,” she sighed.

Soon, a woman came to describe her sick child. Margaret stopped her.

“We are forbidden to sell medicine. But I will wash, iron, and starch your linen—for you. I will come and fetch it from your house.”

“Oh, yes,” said the woman. “I have smocks and ruffs in need of cleaning. Come for them. And when you’re there, you can look at the boy.” She gave the address and the time her husband would be away—though she liked him well enough.

An introduction is an introduction. Two or three patients, denied medicine, became Doctor Margaret’s customers.

“Now, Martin, you must help. I’ll no more cats than can slay mice.”

“Mistress, the stomach is not lacking, but the headpiece—worst luck.”

“Oh, I don’t mean starching and ironing—that takes a woman, and a skilled one. But washing? A man can manage that. Why, a mule has wit enough to do it with his hoofs, if you’d drive him into the tub. Come—off with your doublet, and try.”

“I am your man,” said the brave old soldier, stripping for the task. “I’ll risk my arm in soapsuds—if you’ll risk your glory.”

“My what?”

“Your glory and honor as a—washerwoman.”

“Gramercy! If you’re man enough to bring me half-washed linen to iron, I’m woman enough to throw it back into the suds.”

So the brave girl and the brave soldier worked together, keeping the wolf from the door. More they could not do. Margaret repaired the *Tomorrow* box. As she leaned over the glue, her tears mingled with it. She cemented her exiled lover’s box with her sorrow. A smile may be allowed here—but one of pity, not mockery. Not the empty laughter of the modern fool, ridiculing sacred things. But when mended, the box stood empty.

They paid rent weekly, kept the pot boiling—but no more.

Then came a chain of events. Recommended by one to another, Margaret began washing for the mayor. One day, returning clean linen, she heard in the kitchen that the mayor’s only daughter was gravely ill, likely to die.

Poor Margaret could not resist questioning. A maid told her what symptoms she had seen—but they were vague. Yet each gossip added a detail, another a clue. Margaret collected them all.

Later, she met the mayor himself. He recognized her instantly. “Why, you’re the unlicensed doctor.”

“I was,” she replied. “Now I’m your worship’s washerwoman.”

He reddened. “That’s rather a fall.”

“Nay, I bear no malice. You might have been harder. Rather, I wish to do you a kindness. Sir, you have a sick daughter. Let me see her.”

He shook his head. “I cannot. I enforce the law on others—I may not break it myself.”

Margaret stared. “Alas, sir, I seek no reward now for curing folk. I am a washerwoman. I believe one may heal the world—if only the world will starve her in return.”

“That is just,” said the mayor. “And if you make no profit from it, there is no offense.”

“Then let me see her.”

“What good will it do? The finest doctors in Rotterdam have seen her—and helped nothing. Her illness is inscrutable. One says spleen, another liver, another blood, another stomach. Another says she is possessed. Indeed, she seems haunted—shuns company, pines alone, eats less than a sparrow. Speaks rarely, hears none. Grows thinner, paler, nearer death.”

“Sir,” said Margaret, “if you took your velvet doublet to six shops in Rotterdam and asked if it was fine, worth how much per ell—six traders would agree exactly. Why? Because they know their trade. But your doctors disagree. Why? Because they do not know theirs. Each is enamored of one ailment, sees it in every patient. Had they never seen your daughter, they would have said the same—spleen, blood, stomach, lungs, liver, madness—or possession. Let me see her. We are of the same sex. That matters much.”

Still hesitant, the mayor hesitated.

“Saints of heaven!” she cried, losing patience. “Is this how men love their own flesh and blood? Her mother would have taken me in her arms and brought me to her bedside.”

Two violet eyes flashed fire.

“Come with me,” he said hastily.

“Mistress, I have brought thee a new doctor.”

The young woman, pale and eighteen, gave a contemptuous twist of her shoulder and turned further toward the fire.

Margaret sat beside her softly. “But one who will not torment you.”

“A woman?” exclaimed the girl, surprised and scornful.

“Tell me your symptoms.”

“For what? You’ll learn nothing.”

“You’ll lose nothing.”

“Well, I have no appetite, and no heart for anything. Now cure me and go.”

“Patience. Does your food taste flat in your mouth?”

“Yes. How did you know?”

“I did not—until you told me. I think you would fare better with a little good company.”

“I doubt it. What use is their chatter to me?”

Margaret asked the father to leave. Alone, she asked practical questions. Then reflected.

“When you wake in the morning, do you tremble?”

“No. Yes. How did you know?”

“Shall I give you medicine—or merely tease you with my silly talk?”

“Which you will.”

“Then I shall tell you a story. Of two true lovers.”

“I hate stories of lovers,” said the girl. “But since you insist, it may be less nauseating than your physic.”

Margaret told the tale of Ursel and Conrad—Ursel, daughter of an old physician; Conrad, son of a hosier at Tergou. Their adventures, sorrows, hardships. She told it from a woman’s heart, in a soft, earnest voice. Gradually, it captured the girl’s attention. When she paused, her patient was disappointed.

“Nay, nay—I must hear the end. I will.”

“But I do not know it. Only God does.”

“Oh, your Ursel was a jewel,” the girl said, truly moved. “Would she were here.”

“Instead of you?”

“I do not say that.” She blushed.

“You only think it.”

“Thought is free. But if she were here, I’d give her a kiss—poor thing.”

“Then give it to me. For I am she.”

“No, no—you cannot be.”

“I am. And pray, sweet mistress, do not break your word—kiss me, with a good heart. For oh, my heart lies heavy—just as yours does.”

The young lady rose, embraced Margaret, and kissed her. “I am sorry for you,” she sighed. “You are a good soul. You have done me good—just a little.” (A gulp caught in her throat.) “Come again. Come again.”

Margaret returned. She talked, watched closely, and discovered only one topic stirred her—love. Then she said to the mayor, “I know your daughter’s trouble—and it is curable.”

“The blood?”

“No.”

“The stomach?”

“No.”

“The liver?”

“No.”

“The devil?”

“No.”

“What then?”

“Love.”

“Love? Nonsense! Impossible! She is but a child. She never leaves the house unguarded. Never has.”

“All the better. Then we need not search far.”

“I shall command her to tell me the villain’s name—how he enchanted her with magic.”

“Oh, how foolish are the wise!” said Margaret. “Would you frighten her? No—let us work by art first. If that fails, then violence and folly may follow.”

She persuaded the mayor to pay all his servants in front of his daughter—on a Saturday.

Fifteen people entered, received their wages, and left with kind words. Margaret had sat close to the girl throughout. Then she rose and stepped out. The mayor followed.

“Sir, who is that black-haired lad?”

“That is Ulrich, my clerk.”

“Well then—it is he.”

“Heavens forbid! I took him from the streets.”

“But your worship is wise. You did not take him without reason?”

“Reason? None. I liked his looks.”

“Was that not merit? He pleased the father’s eye. And now—he pleases the daughter’s. This has happened since Adam.”

“How do you know?”

“I held her hand. Lightly touched her wrist. When others came and went, it was as if dogs and cats passed through. But when Ulrich entered, her pulse leapt, her eyes shone. When he left, she sank and sighed—as if the sun had vanished from the room. Nay, burgomateur, do not look at me so. I am no witch. Only a poor girl, taught by a neglected doctor’s wisdom. This has happened thousands of years before us. Wait here. Do not spoil good work with meddling.”

She returned to her patient and asked for a lock of her hair.

“Take it,” said the girl, listlessly.

“You are like a statue of marble. How long do you intend to remain so?”

“Until I am in my grave, sweet Peggy.”

“Who knows? Maybe in ten minutes, you’ll be burning hot.”

She ran to the shop, then returned swiftly.

“Good news! He loves her—more than a little. Now—what shall we do? Marry your daughter, or bury her? There is no third way. Shame and love rend her virgin heart to pieces.”

The mayor hesitated—then chose marriage. With effort, he accompanied Margaret to his daughter. But men are slow to drink wormwood. He stood silent.

Doctor Margaret smiled. “Mistress, your lock is gone. I sold it.”

“And who was mad enough to buy such a thing?” asked the girl scornfully.

“Oh, a black-haired lad with white teeth. They call him Ulrich.”

The pale face flushed—brow and all.

“He said, ‘Oh, sweet mistress, give it to me.’ I told him whose it was. ‘No,’ I said, ‘selling is my livelihood, not giving.’ So he offered this, that—nothing less than his next quarter’s wages.”

“Cruel,” murmured the girl, barely audible.

“You are in one tale with your father. He said to me, ‘If he loves her hair so well, surely he loves the rest of her.’ And he added, ‘An honest lad. He shall have her—provided she leaves her sulks and consents.’ So—what say you, mistress? Will you marry Ulrich—or be buried in the churchyard?”

“Father! Father!”

“It is so, girl—speak your mind.”

The reader already knows how much there was to say between them. It had been a day of both sweetness and sorrow for Margaret—sweet because she had found a true friend in Denys, bitter because the news he brought left her heart heavy with grief. For the first time, she learned that Gerard was utterly alone in that distant land, cast adrift from all who loved him. She could not believe, as Denys did, that Gerard would return; if he were coming, he would have arrived long before now.

Yet Denys was a comfort—a steady presence in her solitude. He called her his “she-comrade,” and with his lively manner and endless jests, he lifted her spirits when they sank. She cherished him, teased him gently, and kept strict watch over his conduct. She refused to let him dine outside her home, forbade him from using coarse language, and scolded him lightly whenever he slipped: “It spoils you, Denys. Good lack, to hear such ugly words come from so comely a head! Forbear, or I shall be angry. So be civil.” And then, with comic dignity, Denys would straighten himself, struggling between the manners he’d once known and the roughness he’d adopted in the world, his face a mask of forced propriety.

And just as misfortune never comes alone, other visitors now sought Margaret’s company. She had written to Margaret Van Eyck, humbly acknowledging that she was no longer the favorite she once had been, and pledged to keep her distance. Yet she could not forget the kindnesses shown her in the past. In her letter, she briefly recounted the many hardships she had endured to survive, ending with a fervent plea: “I beg you, do not reveal my whereabouts—least of all to *his* people. I hate them. They drove him from me. And even after he was gone, their hearts never turned toward me as if they truly repented their cruelty.”

Margaret Van Eyck was troubled by this message. At last, she confided in Reicht, who passed it on like water through a pipe to Catherine. “Ah,” said Catherine, “and is she so bitter against us now?” “She stole our son from us,” replied the older woman, “and now she resents us for not rushing into her arms. Still, it is a blessing she lives—and no farther away than Rotterdam.”

Meanwhile, the English princess, now Countess Charolois, made a stately journey through the northern provinces of the duchy, accompanied by her stepdaughter, Marie de Bourgogne, the young heiress of Burgundy. The old Duke, most splendid prince in Christendom, outdid himself in magnificence. Knights in dazzling armor, ladies richly dressed, minstrels, jongleurs, bards, musicians, actors, and tumblers followed in their train. Every town they visited rang with music, dance, and jousting. Richart summoned all his people to Rotterdam to witness the spectacle.

After several days in the city, Denys met Catherine by chance in the street. Their greeting was warm and joyful. “Hark!” he exclaimed, “I’ve found your she-comrade at last!” He crowed with pride. But Catherine cooled his ardor. “Had you stayed quietly at Tergou, you might have found her sooner than wandering across Holland like a vagabond.” “And what good does finding her do?” she asked. “Her heart is closed to us now.” “Let that flea stick,” said Denys. “Come with me to her house.” “No,” Catherine replied firmly. “I will not go where I am certain of an unwelcome.” “Them that come unbidden sit unseated,” she added. “Then let me be the mediator,” said Denys. “I’ll bring peace between you.” He accepted the role at once, full of confidence and pomp.

He trotted off to Margaret and announced, “She-comrade, I met a friend of yours today.” “You looked into the mirror, then, and saw yourself,” she retorted. “Nay,” he insisted, “it was a woman—someone who seeks your regard. It was Catherine, Gerard’s mother.” “Oh?” said Margaret, her voice flat. “Then tell her she comes too late. Once I longed for her, but she kept aloof when I needed her most. Now we shall remain as we have been.” Denys tried to soften her resolve. He coaxed, pleaded, urged—but she remained cold and sullen. Then, losing patience, he scolded her sharply. At that, she burst into hysterics. Startled by the sudden turn, Denys faltered. Off guard, he allowed himself to be trapped into a solemn vow never again to mention the matter.

He returned to Catherine crestfallen, reporting the refusal. Catherine flared with anger and told her family what had happened. The household rose in fury. A rift opened between them, growing deeper each day. Only little Kate offered any defense of Margaret.

The very next day, another visitor arrived at Margaret’s door. She found the household in uproar: Martin buried in soap suds, Denys awkwardly ironing, and herself plaiting ruffs with a sharp eye over her charges. Into this scene stepped an old man—venerable at first glance, but upon closer view, sharp-eyed and thin-faced. “Ah!” cried Margaret, turning swiftly away and covering her face as if to hide from some dreadful sight. “Oh, that man! That man!”

“Fear me not,” said Ghysbrecht. “I come on a friend’s errand. I bring you a letter from abroad.” “Do not mock me, old man,” she whispered, turning slowly. “See,” he said, holding out a large, sealed letter. Margaret snatched it from his hands, trembling, her eyes glistening. It bore Gerard’s handwriting. “Oh, thank you, sir,” she breathed, “bless you for this—I forgive you all the harm you ever did me.” With one hand, she pressed the letter to her chest, and in silence, glided from the room.

She did not return. Ghysbrecht left, casting a dark look at Martha as he went. For hours, Margaret remained alone with her letter—alone with the words of the man she loved, carried across oceans and dangers, finally reaching her at last.

When she descended once more, she was no longer the woman who had climbed the stairs in anger and sorrow. Her eyes glistened with unshed tears, but her expression was calm, composed—her spirit quieted as if by a deep inner peace. The storm within had passed, leaving behind a stillness that seemed almost sacred.

“Denys,” she said softly, “I have received my orders. I am to read my lover’s letter aloud to his family.”

“You will not do that?” he replied, astonished.

“Ay, I will,” she answered firmly.

He stared at her, sensing a shift in her heart. “Then something in the letter has softened you toward them?”

“Not a whit, Denys—not a single thought,” she insisted. “If I hated them as poison, I would still obey Gerard. And yet, it is sweet—oh, so sweet—to obey one who is far away, powerless to command me, yet trusting me to do what is right because of love. If Gerard were here, I might resist his wishes, for I know well how much I despise his kin. But now—now, even if he asked me to walk into the sea and read his words to the sharks, I would go. So tell his mother I have his letter, and if they wish to hear it, I am ready. Let them name the hour, and I shall welcome them as best I may.”
