Denys hurried off to deliver the message. He found the family gathered around the dinner table, their faces alight with joy at the news of Gerard’s letter. He waited until the moment was right, then broke in: “And there is more. She has changed. She will read the letter herself. You may choose your own time.”

Catherine frowned. “What makes her think only she can read it? Let her send it—we’ll read it ourselves.”

“But perhaps she cannot bear to part with it,” little Kate interjected gently. “She loves him dearly.”

“And thinks we’d steal it?” Cornelis muttered darkly.

“I suspect,” he added under his breath, “that she wants to force her way into our home through this very letter.”

Denys turned on him with cold disdain. “There speaks a bitter heart,” he said sharply. “La camarade hates you all like poison. But mark this—though she loathes you, she offers to read the letter with her own voice, soft as honey. She does not ask for reward; she offers obedience. And though she bears you ill will, she yields to Gerard’s word. That is no small thing. She has a voice like music—surely such a gift deserves respect.”

The father of the house nodded slowly. “You speak truth, honest soldier. This offer merits a civil reply. Hold your tongues, women—and I shall answer her. Tell her this: I, Eli a Dierich a William a Luke, free burgher of Tergou, swear upon my honor and my ancestors’ names, that I lay aside all past grievances and thank her for this grace. Should she wish greater thanks, let her send her son’s letter by your faithful hand. I will read it to my flesh and blood, and return it to her with the same care and honesty as I have lived my life—true to my word.”

“And better than his word,” Catherine burst out. “The only man I’ve ever known who truly kept his promise.”

“Peace, wife,” Eli said quietly.

“Art a man of sense, Eli—a dirk, a chose, a chose!” Denys cried, grinning. “And bless ye, the world has turned upside down! She who once scorned us now kneels to obedience. ‘Obedience is honey,’ she says—and indeed, it is a sweetness she cannot help savoring, though she eats little of it. With her beauty, her voice, her fits of passion that scare soldiers half to death when we cross her, and her ways—chiding one moment, petting us like lambs the next—she has made two of the most devoted slaves you ever saw from two proud swashbucklers. I am the iron ruffian—my comrade washes.”

“What next?” someone asked.

“Oh, when the child comes into the world, I’ll rock the cradle,” Denys declared, “and the other fellow will wash the bibs and tucker. So now, I’ll fetch the letter at once. Will you let me stay and hear it read?”

“Else our hearts were black as coal,” Catherine replied.

Denys left, eager and hopeful. But he returned moments later, head bowed, face heavy with disappointment.

“She will not give it to anyone—not me, not you, not any living soul.”

“I knew she wouldn’t,” Cornelis said smugly.

“Whisht! Whisht!” Eli commanded. “Let Denys finish.”

“So I said, ‘But be ruled by me.’” Denys recounted. “‘Not I,’ she replied. ‘Well then,’ I pressed, ‘what of that honeyed obedience you spoke of?’”

“She looked at me and said, ‘You are a fool. Obedience to Gerard is sweet—but obedience to anyone else? Who ever said that was sweet?’”

At last, she relented slightly. “She gave me a written note—for you, mademoiselle,” Denys added, handing it over.

“For me?” little Kate whispered, blushing deeply.

Eli took the paper and read it aloud, his voice dropping low:
*“And, sweetheart, if these lines reach you safely, try my people’s hearts. Perhaps they have grown kinder, now that I am far away. If so, they will show it to you—since they may not to me. Read this letter. But I strictly forbid you to let it leave your hands. If they still turn from you, say nothing—let them believe me dead. Obey me in this. For if you dishonor my judgment, you do not love me.”*

A silence fell over the room. The words were copied in Margaret’s hand and passed around, each person studying them closely.

“Well,” Catherine said at last, “this changes things. But still—I think she should come to us, not we to her.”

“Alas, mother,” little Kate sighed, “what difference does it make?”

“Much,” Eli replied. “Tell her we are too many to go to her. Bid her come here—soon as possible.”

After Denys left, Eli admitted in a low voice, “It is a bitter pill. When that girl sets foot across my threshold, all the trouble she’s caused will rush in like a flood. But what could I do? We must hear of Gerard. I saw it in your eyes, wife—and felt it in my own heart. She is backed by our disobedient yet beloved son. So she stands stronger than we, forcing us down to the grindstone—the cunning, cruel wench. But never mind. We will hear the letter. Then let her go unblessed, as she came unwelcome.”

“Make your mind easy,” Catherine said softly. “She will not come at all.”

And in her tone, there was a quiet regret.

Shortly after, Richart arrived from Amsterdam—grave, dignified, dressed in the full robes of a burgess: gold chain, stiff ruff, fur-lined cap. He was greeted not only with affection but with respect, for he had risen above his parents in station, and such elevation was marked in medieval society as plainly as steps in a stairwell.

Admitted to the family council, he revealed his pride wounded—though not unkindly—by their willingness to receive Margaret Brandt.

“I see the temptation,” he said. “But which of us has not sometimes wished one thing and done another?”

His words cast a chill over the older generation.

Then little Kate stepped forward. “Vex not yourself, dear Richart. Mother says she will not come.”

“All the better,” he replied. “For if she does, I fear I shall return to Amsterdam at once.”

Just then, Denys appeared at the door, peering in.

“She will be here at three o’clock—by the great dial.”

They all looked at one another, silent, uncertain—caught between duty, resentment, and the fragile hope of news from a lost son.

“Nay, Richart,” Catherine said at last, “for Heaven’s sake, let not this one wretched woman turn our household into a battlefield. Has she not already stirred up enough ill will?”

“In truth, she has,” Richart replied. “Fear me not, good mother. Let her come and read the letter of the poor boy whom she has bewitched through devilish arts—and then let her go. Give me your word that you’ll show her no more than the barest courtesy, no more than is decent in our own home; and I shall say no more.” With that agreement, they waited.

She, for her part, prepared for the meeting with scarcely less hostility. When Denys brought word that they would not come to her, but expected her to come to them, her lip curled in scorn. “See how every feeling in them—however small—is greater than their love for Gerard,” she muttered. “Well, I have no such excuse. So why should I imitate the petty pride of the burgher class, the arrogance of all who are unlearned? I will go to them—for Gerard’s sake. Oh, how I loathe them!”

Thus poor, well-meaning Denys was bringing together in one house the ingredients of a storm.

Margaret dressed herself as a knight of her time might have armed himself for battle—he to parry blows, she to fend off glances: glances of contempt at her poverty, or mockery at her extravagance. Her kirtle was of English cloth, dark blue, and her farthingale and hose matched it in color but were a glossy roan, or claret shade. Not a scrap of ostentatious fur adorned her—only plain, snowy linen wristbands, and intricately plaited linen rising from the bosom of her kirtle to just below her throat, forming a square frame rather than a round collar. Her front hair still fell in two gentle waves, much like the fashion Mary Queen of Scots would later revive; but instead of a silver net—unsuitable now—her head was covered with a tiny, tight-fitting hood of dark blue cloth, edged with silver thread. Her shoes were red, yet the rich tones of her petticoat and hose prepared the eye for the contrast, highlighting her arched instep and shapely foot.

Beauty knew its purpose then as it does now.

And with all this, she kept her enemies waiting—though it was already three o’clock by the dial.

At last she set out, attended by her companion. Halfway across the courtyard, she paused and said thoughtfully, “Denys!”

“Well, she-general?”

“I must go back” (in a voice thick with emotion).

“What? Have you left something behind?”

“What?”

“My courage. Oh! oh! oh!”

“Nay, nay, be brave, she-general. I’ll be with you.”

“Aye, but will you stay close beside me when we’re there?”

Denys promised, and she resumed her walk—but cautiously.

Meanwhile, the family gathered in silence, each harboring a strange mix of emotions: mortification, curiosity, tender longing, resentment toward the woman who came to stir those feelings, yet also a secret desire to see what she looked like—what could have enchanted Gerard so utterly and caused so much turmoil.

At last, Denys returned alone and whispered, “The she-comrade is outside.”

“Bring her in,” Eli commanded. “Now, hush—all of you. No one speaks to her except me.”

They turned their eyes to the door, silent as stones.

A low murmur came from beyond—the rough voice of Denys and a soft, mellow feminine tone.

Then silence.

The door opened slowly.

There stood Margaret Brandt, dressed as described, pale but composed, lovely, her gaze fixed straight ahead.

All rose—except Kate—and remained motionless, staring.

“Be seated, mistress,” Eli said gravely, gesturing to a chair set apart for her.

She bowed her head slightly and crossed the room. As she moved, her condition was unmistakable—not only in her form, but in the quiet weariness that clung to her.

Cornelis and Sybrandt hated her for it. Richart thought it marred her beauty.

It softened the women, just a little.

She took the letter from her bosom and kissed it as if she were alone. Then she settled herself to read, with the air of one who knew she had come for this single purpose.

But as she began, she noticed they had placed her apart, like a leper. She glanced at Denys, then lowered her hand and made a swift, furtive signal for him to come near.

He obeyed instantly, stepping forward as if summoned by a command, standing guard at her shoulder like a sentinel. But his eagerness betrayed the fact that he had been ordered there—and at that, she flushed.

Then she began to read Gerard’s letter, their Gerard, to their eager ears, in a voice clear and sweet, soft yet deeply felt, as though every syllable carried the weight of her soul. It was a voice like a woman’s heart speaking directly from heaven.

“I do not doubt, my Margaret, that long before this reaches your eyes, Denys, my dearest friend, will have found you and told you of our sudden and most sorrowful parting. Therefore, I will begin at that bitter day. What happened afterward to him, poor faithful soul—I long to know, but may not. Yet I pray for him night and day, after you, dearest. There was never a truer, more loyal friend than David had in Jonathan—nor I in him. Be kind to him, for poor Gerard’s sake.”

At these words—unexpected, heartfelt—Denys leaned his head against the back of her chair and groaned aloud.

She turned quickly, found his hand, and pressed it.

So the lover and the friend held hands while the letter was read.

“I walked forward dazed, as if in a bad dream. Soon a gentleman approached on horseback, with servants following. He nearly rode over me. He pulled rein at the crest of the hill and sent his armed men back to rob me. They robbed me politely enough—taking my purse and my last copper—and rode away gaily. I wandered on, stunned, friendless, penniless.”

A collective sigh passed through the room, followed by an oath from Denys.

“Then a strange dimness came over me. I lay down to sleep in the snow. ’Twas foolish, with wolves nearby. Had I loved you as you deserve, I would have shown more strength. But oh, sweet love, the drowsiness that crept over me, numbing me, was more than nature. And so I slept. And had not God been kinder to us than I was to you or myself, I would never have awakened again—so all say. I suppose I slept an hour or two, no more. Then a hand shook me roughly. I woke to my troubles. And there stood a servant girl in holiday clothes. ‘Are you mad,’ she asked, seeming angry, ‘to sleep in the snow, beneath wolves’ noses? Are you weary of life, barely weaned?’ Then, more gently, ‘Come, now—get up like a good lad.’ So I rose. ‘Are you rich or poor?’ But I stared at her, amazed. ‘Why, it’s easy to answer,’ she said. ‘Are you rich or poor?’ Then I gave a great, loud cry. She jumped back. ‘Am I rich or poor? Had you asked me an hour ago, I would have said I am rich. But now I am poorer than any earth bears. An hour ago I was rich in a friend, rich in money, rich in hope and youth; but now the Bastard of Burgundy has taken my friend, another gentleman my purse, and I cannot go forward to Rome nor return to her I left in Holland. I am the poorest of the poor.’ ‘Alack!’ she said. ‘Yet if you’d been rich, I might have let you lie in the snow—no use to me. Then you’d soon have died as bare as you came into the world. But being poor, you are our man. Come with me.’ So I went—because she bid me, and because I cared not where I went. She took me to a fine house nearby, into a noble dining hall hung in black. A table was set with many dishes, but only one plate, one chair. ‘Fall to!’ she whispered. ‘What—alone?’ I asked. ‘Alone? And which of us, think you, would eat from the same dish with you? Are we thieves of the dead?’ Then she asked where I was born. ‘At Tergou,’ I said. She replied, ‘And when a gentleman dies in that country, do they not serve his dinner as usual until he is buried, and place a poor man at the table?’ I said no. She blushed for us. Here, they are better Christians. So I had to sit. But I had little appetite. Then this kind girl sat beside me and poured wine. I tasted it—and it cut me to the heart that Denys was not there to drink with me. He loves good wine, and good women, bad, or indifferent. The strong, rich wine curled around my sick heart. That day, for the first time, I understood why troubled men turn to drink. She made me eat from every dish. ‘It is unlucky to pass one. Nothing here is anything but her master’s daily meal.’ ‘He had a good stomach, then,’ I said. ‘Ay, lad, and a good heart. At least, so we all say now that he is dead. But while alive, I never heard a word about it.’ So I ate like a bird, nibbling at each dish. And when she saw me sigh, and nearly choke on the food, she took pity and told me to cheer up. I would sup and rest there that night. She went to the servant, and he gave me a fine bed. I told him everything and asked whether the law could recover my purse. ‘Law?’ he said. ‘There is no law for the poor in Burgundy. Why, it was the cousin of the Lady of the Manor who robbed you. He knew the wild spark. The matter must be judged before the lady—and she is young, more likely to hang you for accusing her cousin, a gentleman, a handsome man, than to make him return your goods. Inside a town, a poor man might sometimes see justice; but among the nobles—never.’ So I said, ‘I’ll remain robbed rather than seek justice and find the gallows.’ They were all kind to me the next day. The girl offered me some of her small wages to help me reach the Rhine.”

“Oh! Then he is coming home! He is coming home!” shouted Denys, breaking in.

She gently shook her head, reproving him.

“I beg your pardon, everyone,” he said stiffly.

“It was a sore temptation,” she continued, “but being a servant, my pride rebelled. ‘No, no,’ I said. She told me I was wrong. ‘It is pride misplaced. Poor folk should help one another—or who else would?’ I said if I could repay her, it would be well; but for a gift—no. I was already too indebted. Should I write a letter for her? ‘No,’ she said, ‘he is here in the house.’ Should I draw her portrait, and earn my way? ‘Can you?’ she asked. I told her I could try. Her habit would make a fine picture. So she was eager to be painted and give it to her lover. I placed her in good light, and made two sketches—one of which I send you, colored at odd moments. The other I did hastily, without care, for which may Heaven forgive me—time was short. They, poor things, knew no better, and were proud and joyful. Both kissed me after their custom—she, the servant, and he, her sweetheart—and bade me God-speed. I set off for the Rhine.”

Margaret paused and handed the colored drawing to Denys to pass around. The women examined it eagerly, drawn by the costume—different from Dutch domestic dress. Her hair was bound tightly in a linen bag, a yellow half-kerchief crossed her head from ear to ear, ending in a rectangular point down the center of her forehead, and meeting in two points over her bosom. She wore a red kirtle with long sleeves, kilted high in front, revealing a green farthingale and a large red leather purse hanging over it; red stockings, yellow leather shoes—low-quartered, square-toed, fastened with a strap buckling over the instep—a style ahead of its time, perhaps the crude ancestor of the diamond buckle.

Margaret continued:

“But oh! how I missed my Denys at every step! Often I sat down by the road and groaned. One afternoon, I stopped where two roads met, head in hand, heart heavy, thinking of you, my poor sweetheart, of my lost friend, and of the little house at Tergou—where once they all loved me, though now it has turned to hate.”

Catherine sighed. “Alas, that he should think so.”

Eli silenced her. “Hush, wife!”

“And I sighed loudly, often. And as I sighed, one came singing down the other road like a bird. ‘Ay, chirp and chirp,’ I cried bitterly. ‘You have not lost sweetheart, friend, father’s hearth, mother’s smile, or every penny in the world.’ And at last he sang so joyfully, I jumped up in anger to escape his jarring mirth. But before I fled, I looked down the path to see what could make a man so cheerful in this weary world—and lo! the singer was a humpbacked cripple, with a bloody bandage over his eye, both legs gone at the knee.”

“He! he! he! he! he!” Sybrandt cackled, laughing.

Margaret’s eyes flashed. She began to fold the letter.

“Nay, lass,” Eli said sharply, “do not heed him. Thou unmannerly cur—offer such insolence again and I’ll throw thee out.”

“Why, what is there to mock, Sybrandt?” Catherine asked more gently. “Is not our Kate afflicted? And is she not the most content of us all, singing like a thrush between her pains? But I am as bad as thou—praise God, read on, lass, and stop our chatter with something worth hearing.”

“Then I said, ‘May this be true?’ And I rebuked myself. ‘Gerard, son of Eli, dost thou well to lament thy lot, having youth and health—while here comes the wreck of nature on crutches, praising God’s goodness with a song like a thrush?’”

Catherine murmured, “There you see.”

Eli snapped, “Hush, dame, hush!”

“And whenever he saw me, he stopped singing and hobbled up, chanting, ‘Charity, for love of Heaven, sweet master, charity,’ in a whine as piteous as wind through a keyhole. ‘Alack, poor soul,’ I said, ‘charity is in my heart, but not in my purse. I am poor as thou.’ Then he disbelieved me, and to move me, rolled up his sleeve and showed a wound on his arm. ‘Poor cripple though I be,’ he said, ‘I am likely to lose this eye too—look.’ I saw and groaned for him. To excuse myself, I told him how I had been robbed of my last copper. At that, he ceased whining instantly and said, in a bold, manly voice, ‘Then I’ll take a rest. Here, youngster, pull this strap—nay, fear not!’ I pulled, and down came a sturdy pair of legs from his back; half his hump vanished, and the wound in his eye was no deeper than the bandage.”

“Oh!” exclaimed all the listeners in unison.

“Seeing my astonishment, he laughed in my face and told me I was not worth deceiving. Then he offered me his protection. ‘My face is prophetic,’ he said. ‘Of what?’ I asked. ‘Marry,’ he said, ‘that its owner will starve in this thievish land.’ Travel teaches even the young wisdom. Once I would have fled such a fraud as a pestilence; but now I listened patiently, hoping for scraps of advice. And I did well: for nature and his wandering life had filled the poor rogue with shrewdness and practical knowledge—childlike was I beside him. After examining me thoroughly, he said, ‘You did well to leave France and head for Germany. But forget Holland. Go on to Augsburg and Nuremberg—the paradise of craftsmen. Thence to Venice, if you wish. But you’ll never settle in Italy or any foreign land once you’ve tasted the great German cities. Why? Because there is but one honest country in Europe—and that is Germany. Since you are honest, and since I am a vagabond, Germany was made for us two.’ I challenged him: how could one country suit both honest men and rogues? ‘Why, thou novice,’ he said, ‘because in an honest land there are fewer rogues to bite the honest man—and more honest men for the rogue to bite.’ I was in luck, being honest, to have fallen in with a sharp, friendly rogue. ‘Be my pal,’ he said, ‘I’m going to Nuremberg—we’ll arrive with full pouches. I’ll teach you the *cul de bois*, the *cul de jatte*, how to beg, chant, patter, raise swellings, paint sores and ulcers so real they’d fool the devil.’”

I shivered and told him I’d rather die than shame myself and my family so.

“Eli,” he said, “good lad! good lad!”

“Why, what shame was there for one like me to become a beggar? Beggary was an ancient and honorable trade. What did holy monks, bishops, and kings do when they sought Heaven’s favor? Wash the feet of beggars—those favorites of the saints. ‘The saints were no fools,’ he told me. Then he held out his foot. ‘Look at that—it was washed by the greatest king alive, Louis of France, on the last Holy Thursday. And the next day, Friday, he was clapped in the stocks by the warden of a petty hamlet.’ So I said my foot should walk between such high honor and such low disgrace, on the same path of honesty, please God. Well then, since I lacked the spirit to beg, he would indulge my stubbornness. I would work under him—he the head, I the hands. And with that, he sat like a judge on a heap of dust by the roadside and questioned me strictly: ‘What can you do?’ I began to say I was strong and willing. ‘Bah!’ he said, ‘so is an ox. Say what you can do that Sir Ox cannot.’ I could write—I had won a prize for it. ‘Can you write as fast as printers?’ he jeered. ‘What else?’ I could paint. ‘That’s better.’ I nearly tore my hair to hear him say so—me, going to Rome to write. I could play the psaltery a bit. ‘That’s well. Can you tell stories?’ Ay, by the score. ‘Then,’ he said, ‘I hire you from this moment.’ ‘What for?’ I asked. ‘Nothing crooked, Sir Candour,’ he said. ‘I’ll feed you all the way and find you work—and take half your earnings, no more.’ ‘Agreed,’ I said, giving my hand. ‘Now, servant,’ he said, ‘we will dine. But you need not stand behind my chair—for two reasons: first, I have no chair; second, good fellowship pleases me more than state.’ From his wallet, he produced meat, fowl, pastry, a dozen spices wrapped in flax paper, and wine fit for a king. Never feasted I better than from this beggar’s wallet—now my master. After eating well, I was ready to go on. ‘But,’ he said, ‘servants should not press their masters too hard, especially after eating—then the body rests, and the mind turns to contemplation.’ So he lay on his back, gazing calmly at the sky, wondering if there were any beggars up there. I told him I knew of only one—Lazarus. ‘Could he do the *cul de jatte* better than I?’ he asked, looking quite jealous. I told him no—Lazarus was honest, though a beggar, fed daily on crumbs from a rich man’s table, and dogs licked his sores. ‘Servant,’ he said, ‘I see a foul fault in you—you lie without discretion. Now, the purpose of lying is to deceive. This is no better than playing with the devil’s tail. I pray Heaven you prove to paint better than you cut jokes, or I am done out of a dinner. No beggar eats crumbs—only the fat of the land. And dogs do not lick a beggar’s sores—they are made with spearwort, or ratsbane, or biting acids, which dogs—even pigs—abhor. My sores are made by my own recipe; but no dog would lick them twice. I’ve made a scurvy bargain—you’re a cheating knave, I suspect, as well as a nincompoop.’ I gave no reply to this bundle of lies, which accused heavenly truth of falsehood for not matching his tale. He rose, and we took the road. Soon we reached a place with two small inns, barely a furlong apart. ‘Halt,’ said my master. ‘Their signs are faded—so much the better. Go in, avoid the master, speak to the wife, flatter her to the heavens—except the sign—and offer to repaint it cheap.’ So I went in and told the wife I was a painter who could restore her sign cheaply. She sent me away with a rebuff. I returned to my master. He groaned. ‘You are all fingers and no tongue,’ he said. ‘I’ve made a scurvy bargain. Come and hear me patter and flatter.’ Between the inns was a high hedge. He stepped behind it a moment and returned as a respectable tradesman. We went to the other inn, and I heard him praise it so lavishly that even the wife blushed. ‘But,’ he said, ‘there is one little fault—your sign is dull and faded. Say the word, and for a silver franc, my apprentice here—the cleverest I’ve ever had—will make it shine as bright as ever.’ While she hesitated, the rogue told her he had done it for a little inn nearby, and now the inn’s face was like the starry firmament. ‘D’ye hear that, my man?’ she cried, ‘“The Three Frogs” have had their sign painted—shall “The Four Hedgehogs” be outshone?’ So I painted, and my master stood by like a lord, advising me, winking at me to ignore him, and I earned a silver franc. He took me back to ‘The Three Frogs,’ and along the way disguised me with a beard and flattered them, telling them how he had adorned ‘The Four Hedgehogs.’ Into the net jumped the three poor frogs, and I earned another silver franc. Then we went on, and he found his crutches, sent me forward, and showed his ‘cicatrices d’emprunt,’ as he called them, and all his infirmities at ‘The Four Hedgehogs,’ and got both food and money. ‘Come, share and share,’ he said. So I gave him one franc. ‘I’ve made a good bargain,’ he said. ‘You’re a master painter, but take too long.’ So I told him in honest craft, things could not be done quickly and well. ‘Then do them quickly,’ he said. And he told me my name was Bon Bec, and I might call him Cul de Jatte—because that was his trade at our first meeting. In the next town, my master, Cul de Jatte, bought me a psaltery and set himself up again by the roadside in state, like one who once judged Marsyas and Apollo, piping for vain glory. So I played a strain. ‘Indifferent well, harmonious Bon Bec,’ he said haughtily. ‘Now tune thy pipes.’ So I sang a sweet melody taught me by good monks—and singing it reminded poor Bon Bec, Gerard once, of his youth and home, bringing tears to my eyes. But looking up, my master’s face was like a child’s after a beating, or sipping the foulest medicine. ‘Zounds, stop that bellyache blether,’ he said, ‘that will never win a stiver from peasants’ purses—it’ll sour nurses’ milk and make cows jump into rivers to escape it. What, false knave, did I buy you a fine new psaltery to remind me of my end? Listen—these are the songs that gladden hearts and fill minstrels’ purses.’ And he sang a blasphemous, obscene verse so vile I stepped back, fearing lightning might ruin the new psaltery. But none came—being winter. Then I said, ‘Master, the Lord is gracious. If I held the thunder, that ribaldry would be your last, thou foul-mouthed wretch.’”

“‘Why, Bon Bec, what is to do?’ he asked. ‘I’ve made an ill bargain. Oh, perverse heart, turning from doctrine.’ So I told him to keep his breath to cool his broth—I would never shame my family with such songs. ‘Then,’ he said sulkily, ‘the first fire we light by the roadside, clap on the music box—so it will boil our pot for now; but with your,

Good people, let us peak and pine,
Cut tristful mugs, and miaul and whine
Thorough our nosen chaunts divine,

When she came to herself, her head rested on Catherine’s arm, and the honest half of the family—those she had entered like an intruder—gathered around her, speaking words of comfort in their rough, homely way. Giles roared at her, “Don’t take on like that! Gerard is alive and well—or he couldn’t have written this letter, the biggest man ever penned, and,” as he thought, “the most beautiful, moving, and smallest-written letter yet!”

“Ay, good Master Giles,” Margaret sighed faintly, “he is alive. But how can I know what has befallen him since? Oh, why did he leave Holland to wander among strangers fierce as lions? And why didn’t I drive him from me sooner than part him from his own flesh and blood? Forgive me, you who are his mother!”

She gently withdrew from Catherine’s arm and made a feeble attempt to slide off the chair onto her knees. After a brief struggle against stronger hands, she found herself cradled once more in Catherine’s embrace. Then, with trembling fingers, she handed the letter to Eli and whispered, soft but sweet, “I will trust it now from my hand. In truth, I am little fit to read further—and loth to leave my comfort.” She wound her other arm tightly around Catherine’s neck.

“Read it, Richart,” said Eli. “Thine eyes are younger than mine.”

Richart took the letter. “Well,” he said, “such writing I never saw. He writes with a needle’s point—and clear into the bargain. Why isn’t he in my counting-house in Amsterdam instead of wandering about yonder?”

“When I came to myself,” the letter began, “I was seated in the litter, my good merchant holding my hand. I babbled things I don’t remember, then shuddered in silence. He put a horn of wine to my lips.”

Catherine murmured, “Bless him! bless him!”

Eli hushed her: “Whisht!”

“And I told him what had happened. He wanted to see my leg. It was badly sprained, swollen at the ankle; all my points were broken—I could barely keep up my hose. I said, ‘Sir, I shall be a burden to you, I fear, and can make no harmony now; my poor psaltery is broken.’ And I grieved over my broken music, my companion through so many weary leagues. But he patted my cheek and told me not to fret. He raised my leg upon a pillow and tended me like a kind father.”

“January 19.—I sit all day in the litter, for we press forward with haste. At night, the good, kind merchant sends me to bed and will not let me work. Strange! Whenever I fall in with men like fiends, God sends me a good man or woman right after, lest I turn away from humanity. Oh, Margaret! How strangely mixed they are, and how old I feel compared to who I was three months ago. And lo! If good Master Fugger hasn’t gone and bought me a new psaltery!”

Catherine interrupted, “Eli, my man, if that merchant comes our way, let us buy a hundred ells of cloth from him—no haggling!”

Eli nodded firmly. “That I will, take your oath on it!”

As Richart prepared to read on, Kate glanced at her mother, blushed faintly, and pulled a piece of embroidery from beneath her apron. With her head lowered just a little more than necessary, she began to sew. Her mother, seeing this, drew out a similar piece from her pocket and joined her. Both women now revealed their secret works—baby caps, more than half finished. The sight told its own story. Horror! They were shaped and delicately stitched like tiny monks’ cowls.

“January 20.—Laid up in the litter, nearly blind, but halting to bait. Suddenly, the Lombardy plains burst upon me. Oh, Margaret! A land flowing with milk and honey—rolling slopes, noble rivers, cheerful meadows, delightful orchards, blooming gardens. Though winter, it feels warmer than beloved Holland in midsummer. It makes the wanderer’s face shine and his heart leap with joy at such kindness from the earth. Here grow vines, cedars, olives, and plenty of cattle—but only three goats for every sheep. The draught oxen wear white linen around their necks, and standing beside dark green olive trees, each one is a picture. The people, especially the women, wear delicate straw hats adorned with flowers and leaves imitated in silk, threaded with silver. Today we crossed a river in a chained ferry-boat. On either bank stood a windlass, and a single man turned it to draw our whole company across. I admired it, being a stranger. We passed some country folk. An old woman looked at a young girl, then covered her face with her hand and held out her crucifix like a knight brandishing his sword in tourney, fearing the evil eye.”

“January 25.—Safe in Venice. A place whose strange and surpassing beauty you know from mariners’ tales. Do you remember how Peter used to fill our ears with stories while we sat beneath the table, always talking of this sea-throned, peerless city—shaped like a bow, its great canal and palaces built on piles, its watery ways thronged with scores of gilded boats; and that marketplace of nations, orbis, non urbis, forum, St. Mark’s Square, his place? And his statue with priceless jewels in his eyes, and the lion at his gate? But I, lying in pain by my window, cannot yet see any of these wonders—only a dull street, fairly paved, and houses with oiled paper and linen instead of glass, which seems rude; and passers-by whose habits and gestures strike me as excessive. So, not to miss my daily comfort of whispering to you, I will turn inward and bind my sheaves of wisdom gathered by travel. For I love you so deeply that no treasure pleases me unless shared with you—and what treasure is better or lasting than knowledge? Thus I have learned, Sir Footsore, that every nation has its own wisdom and its own folly. I think, if a great king or duke walked as I have, seeing with his own eyes, he might gather the flowers and avoid the weeds of each people, and return home to set his own folk upon Wisdom’s hill.

“The Germans in the north are churlish, yet frank and honest; in the south, kindly and honest too. Their chief fault is drunkenness, carried even to contempt for sober men. They say, ‘If you can’t drink and eat, you can’t serve any master well.’ In England, the common folk drink deeply, but the respectable hold excess in disrepute. They drink a health or two out of courtesy, not gluttony, and still sweeten their wine. Their drinking is solemn—little mirth, little talk—just business, crying ‘Be joyful!’ Their best drinking game is ‘Kurlemurlehuff,’ where one touches glass, beard, table in turn, interlacing whistles and finger-snaps in such intricate order it takes Hercules to master it, yet delights the watcher. Their drunkards, by advice of German physicians, sleep with pebbles in their mouths—for just as a boiling pot must have its lid slightly open, so must these fleshy wine-pots vent their inner heat. Despite this, many die suddenly from drink; yet it’s a matter of religion to cover it up, excuse it, blame some innocent illness. Still, it’s more custom than nature, for their women join the drinkers, but only stand a moment and seem to kiss the cup—they are truly temperate in food and drink, modest and virtuous, faithful wives and friends to their husbands—far above our Holland lasses, who, when maids, ask the men the question, and when married, lord it over them. Take the wife in Tergou, near our door. One came to the house seeking her husband. She said, ‘You won’t find him—he asked my leave to go out this afternoon, and I gave it.’”

Catherine exclaimed, “True enough! True enough! That was Beck Hulse, Jonah’s wife. This is what comes of a woman marrying a boy!”

“In the south, where wine flows, the nobility drink themselves bare; not so in the north—there, beer may burst a noble’s body before melting his lands. They are quarrelsome, but it’s the liquor, not the mind; for they’re not revengeful. If they make a bad bargain drunk, they honor it when sober. They keep their windows bright and judge a man by his clothes. Whatever fruit or grain grows by the roadside, pick and eat it—the owner will say, ‘Welcome, honest man.’ But pluck a grape from the roadside, and your life is in danger—it’s eating what Heaven gave to be drunk. The French speak much fairer, though not nearly so true-hearted. Sweet words cost them nothing. They call it *payer en blanche*.”

Denys laughed. “Les coquins! Ha! ha!”

“Yet courtesy is in their hearts, yes, in their very blood. They often say, ‘Give yourself the trouble of sitting down.’ Such phrases show the direction of the wind. Also, at a public spectacle, if you wish to leave your seat without losing it, tie your napkin round the bench—no Frenchman or woman will sit there, preferring to keep it for you.”

Catherine declared, “Gramercy! That is manners. France for me!”

Denys rose and placed his hand gracefully over his breastplate.

“Yet they say things in jest that are neither courteous nor pleasant—‘Le diable t'emporte!’ ‘Allez au diable!’ and so forth. But I doubt they mean no harm—likely just habit. Moderate in drinking, they mix water with wine and sing and dance over their cups, making enchanting company. They are careful not to drink from another’s cup. In war, the English gain the upper hand in the field; but the French excel in siegecraft—witness Orleans, where they besieged their besiegers and punished them cruelly with double and triple culverines; and many other sieges this century. Above all nations, they flatter their women—and yet despise them. No. She may rule them. They often hang female criminals instead of drowning them decently, as others do. Furniture in their inns is walnut—only deal in Germany. French windows are ill-designed: the lower half is wood, opens; the upper half is glass, fixed—so servants cannot clean it. German windows are all glass, movable, shining far and wide like diamonds. In France, many humble homes are unglazed. Once I saw a Frenchman pass a church without uncovering his head—a thing I never witnessed in Holland, Germany, or Italy. At many inns, they show travelers their sheets to prove they are clean, and warm them at the fire before them—a commendable custom. They receive guests kindly, like hosts; yet mostly cheat them, sometimes even cut their throats. They plead harsh and tyrannical laws as excuse. And indeed, their law thrusts its nose into every platter, its finger into every pie. In France, gentlemen wear hats and furs indoors, and go abroad lightly clad. In Germany, they don hat and fur cloak to go out, but sit bareheaded and light-clad by the stove.

“The French do not mix men and women in assemblies, as we Hollanders do. Around their preachers, women kneel in rows, men stand behind. Their harvests are rye, flax, and wine. Three mules for every horse, and whole flocks of sheep as black as coal.

“In Germany, snails are red. I lie not. The French buy minstrels, but breed jests and make their own mirth. The Germans foster fools with ear-caps, who mimic madness to provoke laughter—a sorrow that calls for pity, not amusement. In this, I believe the lighter nation wiser than the grave German. What say you? Alas, you cannot answer me now.”

Denys leaned forward. “My foul mouth! Is that so written, Master Richart?”

Richart nodded. “Ay, in truth—see for yourself.”

Denys inspected the letter gravely. “I read it quite differently.”

“How so?” asked Richart.

“Humph! Ahem—why, just the opposite.” He added, “It’s tricky work reading these black scratches men agree to call words. And I suspect you clerks go by guess, worthy sir. My foul mouth! This is the first time I’ve heard it mentioned. Eh, mesdames?”

But the women did not seize the chance. Margaret blushed and said nothing. The others bent silently over their work, each with a smile almost hidden. Denys studied their faces long and carefully. Satisfied, he turned with a tone of injured, patient innocence and said, “Proceed, Master Richart.”

“The Italians are polished and subtle. They judge a man not by his clothes, but by his speech and gesture. Here, Sir Chough cannot pass for a falcon gentle, as I did in Germany, pranked in my noble servant’s feathers. Wisest of all nations in their remarkable temperance with food and drink. Most foolish to search strangers entering their borders and hinder them from bringing in money. They should invite it, like other nations, and let travelers take it out freely. Also, here in Venice, the ladies turn their black hair yellow by sun and art—to be wiser than Him who made them. You enter no Italian town without a bill of health, though there is no plague in Europe. This fuss is for extortion. Innkeepers cringe, fawn, cheat, and in the countryside, murder you. Yet they give clean sheets—if you pay. Delicate in eating, they abhor putting their hands in the dish; rather, they use a crust or something else. There’s even a tale of a cardinal in Rome who arms his guest’s left hand with a small bifurcated dagger to hold meat, while his knife cuts it. But I think this, too, is to be wiser than Him who made the hand so supple and strong.”

Eli nodded. “I’m with you, my lad.”

“They suffer greatly from the itch. Ointment for it—*unguento per la rogna*—is sold at every corner of Venice. From my window, I saw a urchin sell it to three noblewomen in silken trains and two velvet knights.”

Catherine remarked, “Italy, my dear, I advise you wash your body in the tub on Sundays; then you may put your hand in the plate on Thursday without offense.”

“Their bread is lovely white. Their meats they ruin by sprinkling cheese over them—O, perversity! Their salt is black—without a lie. In commerce, these Venetians are masters of land and sea, governing their territories wisely. Only one flaw I find—the same a learned friar once cast at Plato’s republic: that here women are encouraged to venal frailty and pay a tax to the State, which, not content with silk and spice and other honest goods, must trade in sin. Twenty thousand such Jezebels live in Venice and Candia, pampered and honored for drawing strangers to the city, many in princely palaces of their own. But here, I think, the wise signors of Venice forget King David’s word: ‘Except the Lord keep the city, the watchman wakes in vain.’ Also, in religion, they hang their cloth according to the wind—now with the Pope, now with the Turk—but always with the god of traders, Mammon. Can such a flower, cankered as it is, bloom forever? But since I speak of flowers, none may deny them their skill in making roses and gilliflowers bloom out of season. In summer, they nip certain budding roses and withhold water. Then in winter, they dig around these discouraged plants and insert cloves, and with great art raise sweet-scented roses, bringing them to market in January. And I first learned this art from a cow. She grazed buds in summer, and they sprouted at Yule. Women have sat in doctors’ chairs at their colleges. But the one who sat in St. Peter’s was a German. Italy also excels in artful fountains and figures moved by water, enacting life. Next to it stands Augsburg, where they harness the foul knave Smoke to good Sir Spit, and he turns stout Master Roast. But lest any place boast, two towns in Europe scorn giddy fountains and bring water tame through pipes to every citizen’s door, where he fills his vessels by turning a cock. One is London, watered for many years by pipes from Paddington, a neighboring city; the other, the fair town of Lubeck. Also, the fierce English are reported wise in driving wolves from their lands—fairly banishing those marauders into the mountains. But nowhere—in France, Germany, or Italy—is a traveler safe after sundown. I hear of no glazed house in all Venice—only oiled linen and paper; behind these barbarian eyelets, wooden shutters. Their name for a cowardly assassin is ‘a brave man,’ and for a harlot, ‘a courteous person’—as if a woman’s worst vice and a man’s worst vice were virtues. But I pray God for little Holland that an assassin may still be called an assassin, and a harlot a harlot, until Doomsday—and then let others gloss foul faults with silken names if they can!”

Eli sighed. “He should have been a priest, save your presence, my poor lass.”

“January 26.—Sweetheart, I must be brief, and tell you only part of what I’ve seen, for today my journal ends. Tonight it sails to you, but I, unhappy, not with it—tomorrow, in another ship, to Rome.

“Dear Margaret, I took a hand-litter and was carried to St. Mark’s Church. Outside, toward the marketplace, stands a noble gallery, and above it four famous horses, cast in brass by ancient Romans, seeming all in motion, ready to leap down upon the beholder at the next step. Around the church are six hundred pillars of marble, porphyry, and ophites. Inside lies a treasure greater than at St. Denis, Loretto, or Toledo. Here, a jeweled pitcher given the seigniory by a Persian king; the ducal cap blazing with jewels, crowned with a diamond and a chrysolite, each as big as an almond; two golden crowns and twelve golden stomachers studded with gems from Constantinople; a monstrous sapphire; a great diamond from a French king; a prodigious carbuncle; three unicorns’ horns. But what are these compared to the sacred relics?

“Dear Margaret, I stood and saw the brazen chest that holds the body of St. Mark the Evangelist. I saw with my own eyes and touched his ring, and his gospel written by his own hand—and all my travels seemed light. For who am I that I should see such things? Dear Margaret, his sacred body was first brought from Alexandria by merchants in 810, but not valued then. Between 829, when this church was built, and 1094, the very place where it lay was forgotten. Then holy priests fasted and prayed many days seeking light—and lo! The Evangelist’s body broke through the marble at midnight and stood before them. They fell to the earth; but in the morning, they found the crevice it had burst through, and peering within, saw him lying. Then they took and laid him in his chest beneath the altar, and carefully replaced the stone with its miraculous crack—which crack I saw, and it shall remain a monument while the world lasts. Afterward, they showed me the Virgin’s chair—of stone—and her picture, painted by St. Luke, very dark, features now scarcely visible. This image, during droughts, they carry in procession and it brings rain. I wish I had not seen it. Item: two pieces of marble stained with John the Baptist’s blood; item: a fragment of the true cross and of the pillar to which Christ was bound; item: the rock struck by Moses, still wet to this hour; also a stone Christ sat upon preaching at Tyre—but some say it is the one Jacob laid his head upon, and I agree, for our Lord never preached at Tyre. Leaving the church, they showed me the state nursery for children of those aphrodisian ladies, their favorites. In the outer wall was a broad niche—should the child be small enough to squeeze through alive, it falls into a net inside, and the state takes charge; but if too large, the mother must take it home again, where it is likely to be *mali corvi mali ovum*. Coming out, we met them carrying in a corpse, feet and face bare. I learned then this is Venetian custom—and surely no other town will ever rob them of it, nor of what follows. On a great porphyry slab in the piazza stood three ghastly heads, rotting and fouling the air, dangerous in their hot summers, likely to spawn a plague. These were traitors to the state, and a heavy price—two thousand ducats—was set on each head. Their kin killed them and brought all three to the slab, selling blood and faith alike. No state buys heads so many, nor pays so high a price for that sorry merchandise. But what I most admired was the alabaster gallows across from the Duke’s palace, erected expressly to hang him alone for the least treason to the state—and there it stands in his sight, whispering *memento mori*. I pondered, and owned these signors my masters, who allow no man—not even their sovereign—to rise above the common weal. Nearby, on a wall, workmen were finishing, by order of the seigniory, a stone effigy of a tragic and enormous act from last year—yet it looks innocent on the wall. Here two gentlefolk whisper together, swords at their sides. Four brothers conspired on either side to poison the other two, to divide their land in half instead of quarters. At a mutual banquet, two drugged the wine, two poisoned a marchpane—so effectively that the same afternoon, four ‘brave men’ lay around one table, writhing in agony, cursing each other and themselves, and perished miserably. The land, for which they lost their immortal souls, passed to another family. And why not? It could not go to a worse.

“But O, sovereign wisdom of proverbs! How truly they point to each nation’s fault.

“Quand Italie sera sans poison
Et France sans trahison
Et l'Angleterre sans guerre,
Lors sera le monde sans terre.”

Richart explained the verse to Catherine, then continued reading aloud.

Two months before the scene in Eli’s home, the people of a small coastal village between Naples and Rome gathered on the shore, their eyes fixed upon a ship battling a fierce gale that drove straight toward the land. At times, the vessel seemed to gain ground against the storm, and the watchers cheered aloud; then, as the wind and waves pressed harder, they watched with silent satisfaction—though none would admit it even to themselves—that she might not survive. For though no one delights in another’s suffering, there is a strange comfort in seeing others endure what one has escaped.

The ship, though poorly built for navigation, was perfectly made for wrecking: her towering stern caught every gust, and her lines curved like an inverted hat. To those on the beach, she appeared alive—a creature gasping for breath, fighting death with a trembling heart. But had they stood upon her deck, they would have seen not one soul, but many, each revealing their true nature in the hour of peril.

On the deck, sailors stumbled about, hauling ropes without order, cursing one moment, praying the next. Passengers huddled near the mast—some sitting, some kneeling, others lying flat—clutching the railings as the ship heaved and rolled through monstrous waves. Among them stood a young man, pale as ash but with lips tightly pressed, his face a mask of fear and pride. It was Gerard, doomed by fate to this night.

Amidst the throng, prayers rose from every corner—vows offered to gods both known and imagined. The sailors called only to one: “Queen of Heaven,” “Star of the Sea,” “Mistress of the World,” “Haven of Safety.” But among the landfolk, polytheism ran wild. An English merchant vowed gold to Our Lady of Walsingham; a Genoese promised a silver collar to Our Lady of Loretto; a Tuscan noble pledged wax candles to Ravenna’s Virgin. Each clung to their own version of salvation, swearing not on the True Cross, but on its replica in some distant city.

Then came a sudden gust—stronger than any before. The rotten shrouds snapped with a crack, and the sail tore free, flapping downwind like a blackened sheet until it vanished into the sea half a mile off. Before the helmsman could turn the ship, a wave struck her quarter, drenching all aboard and offering a chilling preview of death.

Now vows multiplied. One swore to become a Carthusian monk if St. Thomas spared him. Another promised a barefoot pilgrimage to Compostela, clad only in chain mail, if St. James would save him. Others invoked Thomas, Dominic, Denis, and above all, Catherine of Sienna. Two Neapolitan traders stood shivering. One shouted: “I vow to St. Christopher at Paris a waxen image of his own weight—if I reach land!” His companion nudged him. “Brother, take care! Even if you sold all your possessions, you couldn’t buy his weight in wax.” “Hold your tongue,” snapped the other. Then, in a whisper: “Do you think I meant it? Let me live, and I’ll give him not a single rush.”

Others lay prostrate, pleading with the sea itself: “Oh, merciful sea! Generous sea! Bountiful sea! Beautiful sea! Be gentle! Preserve us!” Some wailed with animal terror at each new plunge of the ship, now nothing more than a toy tossed by titanic waves.

Yet among the chaos sat a Roman woman of humble birth, her child at her breast. Her face was ashen, but her eyes calm. Her lips moved in silent prayer—no tears, no cries, no bargains with the gods. When the ship dipped so low that men screamed, she kissed her child. That was all. She sat still, feeding him in the jaws of death—for why should he lose joy she could give him, even as she died?

There, amid the medieval crowd, sat Antiquity. Sixteen hundred years had not dulled the blood of Rome in her veins. Instinct, perhaps forgotten by name, taught her to die with dignity.

Nearby, a giant friar stood on the poop, feet wide apart like the Colossus of Rhodes—not defying danger, but ignoring it. With a steady voice, he recited verses from the Canticles and invited passengers to confess. Some knelt, and he absolved them as though in a quiet sacristy, not a sinking ship. Gerard drew closer, drawn by instinct to strength. And indeed, the courage of heroes might have faltered beside this friar—whose composure was greater than his size.

Thus, two upheld the dignity of humanity: a woman, tender yet unbroken; a monk, steeled by faith.

With the sail gone, the sailors cut down the mast just above the deck. It fell overboard with a crash, leaving the ship lighter—but now helpless. Without canvas, she could no longer outrun the sea. Wave after wave struck her stern, each blow like a mountain falling. The captain left the helm, pale as death. “Lighten her!” he cried. “Throw everything overboard—or we sink before we strike, and lose our last chance.”

The crew obeyed. Passengers seized whatever they could find and hurled it into the sea. Soon they came upon a heavy sack. Beneath it lay an old man, sick and weak. They dragged the sack from under him—it rattled. Two men pulled it to the side. Up leapt the owner, shrieking: “Holy Moses! What do you mean? This is my fortune—silver candlesticks, plates, brooches, hanaps—everything!” “Let go, you old thief!” shouted the others. “Will you risk our lives for your stolen goods?” “Throw him in too!” someone yelled. “It’s this Jew who’s drowning us!”

They wrestled the sack away and cast it into the water. It sank. The man stared, white-haired, hair streaming in the wind, ready to leap after it—had it floated. But it disappeared forever. He staggered, tearing at his hair, cursing the sea, the ship, the heavens, and hell itself.

Then the captain pointed: “A church! Steer for it, mate—and pray to the saint it honors!”

They turned the ship. A massive wave broke the rudder, jammed it fast, and flooded the deck. Panic surged. Some turned on Gerard. “He’s the cause!” they roared. “He never prayed to a saint. He’s a pagan!”

“Alas, good friends,” Gerard stammered, teeth chattering, “I honor the saints—but now there’s no time. What good are Dominic or Thomas? Saint Peter sits nearer God’s throne. If I pray to Him, He may not have time to plead for me. I must speak directly to the Creator of sea and sky and man. Our Father in heaven, save these souls—and me! Oh, sweet Jesus, who walked on Galilee when Peter sank, who wept for Lazarus when others were dry—save poor Gerard—for Margaret’s sake!”

At that moment, sailors began loading the lifeboat. Thirty souls crowded in—men driven by self-preservation. Left behind: three bewildered, two paralyzed by terror. The paralyzed sat like wet rags; the bewildered ran back and forth, watching the boat pull away, but making no move to follow.

One remained on his knees, clutching a wooden statue of the Virgin Mary—life-sized, torn from the mast. It bobbed in the rising water as he followed it on his knees, hands clasped, water swirling around them.

And the Jew—palsied not by fear, but grief—sat cross-legged, mourning his lost bag. Whenever spray hit him, he raised a fist and cursed the Nazarenes, their gods, their ships, their waters—forever.

The Dominican friar, having confessed all, stood serene, communing with himself.

The Roman woman sat pale, drawing her child closer.

Gerard saw this—and his spirit stirred. “Look!” he said. “They’ve taken the boat—and left the woman and child to die.”

His mind worked quickly. “Wife, I’ll save you—God willing.” He searched for a plank or cask—none. Then his eye fell on the Virgin’s image. He snatched it up, heedless of the cry from its worshipper, like a child robbed of a toy. He ran aft.

“Come, wife,” he called. “I’ll lash you and the child to this. It’s rotten, but it will float.”

She looked at him—her great dark eyes full of sorrow. “Thyself?”

With quiet nobility, he answered: “I am a man—no child to care for.”

She nodded. “Ah.”

He tied the statue to her side. She trembled slightly—yet her gaze remained firm. The ship was nearly submerged. Using an oar as a lever, he slid her into the waves.

“Come,” he said. “While there’s time.”

She turned to him, eyes now wet. “Poor youth—God forgive me—my child!”

He launched her onto the surge, using the oar to keep her from smashing against the hull.

Then a strong hand gripped his shoulder. A deep voice spoke: “It is well. Now come with me.”

It was the friar.

Gerard turned. The friar took two strides and grasped the broken mast. Gerard followed, instinctively. Together, after immense effort, they hoisted the mast and carried it off.

“Throw it in,” said the friar. “And follow.”

They did. But one bewildered passenger rushed after them and jumped on one end. Gerard seized the other—the friar the middle. They drifted, the mast rising and plunging like a horse, waves lashing their faces, blinding them, threatening to knock them off.

Suddenly, ahead, a long grating sound. The ship had struck. Moments later, she lay still—and they were thrown against her with terrible force. Their companion’s head cracked against the rudder—like a coconut under a hammer. He sank instantly, leaving only a stain on the water, a clot on the wood, and a dying cry echoing in their ears as they drifted clear.

The friar murmured a short Latin prayer, then stepped forward calmly. They tumbled along—sometimes swallowed by waves, sometimes glimpsing the shore, where people waved and shouted. Between them and the shore, the woman bobbed, paddling with one arm, holding her child tight.

After a long time, the friar said quietly: “I touched the ground.”

“Impossible, father,” said Gerard. “We’re over a hundred yards out. Please—don’t leave the mast.”

“My son,” said the friar, “you speak wisely. But I have duties to Holy Church. I cannot waste time floating when I can walk. There—I felt it again. See the benefit of sandals. Again—sandy. You are shorter than I. Stay with the mast. I walk.”

He stepped off and plunged forward, arms wide, pushing through the water. Gerard followed. Each wave swept over them, but the friar stood firm, head back, mouth closed, disappearing beneath the foam, then reemerging, swimming powerfully.

At last, they neared the shore—but the current pulled them outward. Then fishermen came, linked by long spears, forming a chain. They dragged the two ashore.

The friar shook himself, gave a brief blessing, and walked on—eyes fixed forward, no glance back at the sea that had nearly claimed him. For him, the Master’s will alone determined harm or safety.

As he strode alone toward Rome, I—no servant of the Church—pause to note that we met this giant once before, narrowly escaping him. Now, I fear, we are fated to meet him again.

Gerard grasped every hand on the beach. They brought him to a fire and, with rare delicacy, left him alone to dry. Only then did he retrieve a parchment and paper from his breast, drying them carefully. When satisfied, he accepted fisherman’s clothes and returned to the shore.

What he saw was brief. The captain lingered by the wreck—not from bravery, but because he believed Castor or Pollux had come for him in fire. Yet the sea broke the ship apart, sweeping him and the poop clear—and carried him safely ashore. Gerard helped pull him from the water.

The Jewish trader landed on a fragment and, touching earth, offered a reward for his bag—drawing laughter, not pity. Two others survived on wreckage. The thirty who fled in the boat arrived—each one dead, except one who still breathed. The natives, meaning well, placed him near a hot fire—and he too passed on.

As Gerard stood by the sea, watching his former companions washed ashore, a hand gently touched his shoulder. He turned.

It was the Roman woman—glowing with gratitude. She took his hand, lifted it slowly to her lips, and kissed it—not as a beggar, but as a queen conferring honor. Then, radiant and tearful, she held up her child and made him kiss his savior.

Gerard kissed the child again and again. He loved children. But he said nothing. He was deeply moved—for she spoke not a word, only with her eyes, her cheeks, her ancient gesture. Perhaps she was right. Gratitude needs no words.

It was an ancient Roman matron thanking a modern man from the depths of her soul.

The next day, late afternoon, Gerard—twice as old as the year before, thrice as wise in human ways, no longer a boy, but a man who had fought, bled, and faced death by land and sea—arrived in Rome. Safe, at last, after all storms. *Post tot naufragia tutus.*

Gerard found modest lodgings on the west bank of the Tiber, where each morning he set out in search of work. Carrying samples of his handwriting—Latin script carefully penned—he visited every shop in Rome that might need such services. But the response was cool and dismissive. “Our letters are finer,” one merchant remarked. “Your ink is too dark,” said another. The common refrain, however, echoed with finality: “What good is this? Latin writing is scarce here now. Can you write Greek?”

“I can,” Gerard replied, “but not as well as Latin.”

“Then you’ll never earn your bread in Rome,” they declared.

Undeterred, he borrowed a beautiful Greek manuscript at great cost, returning home with a lighter purse but unshaken resolve. In just two weeks, he made remarkable progress in mastering the Greek alphabet. To make the most of his time, he worked on his hand until midday, then spent the afternoons seeking clients.

When he returned with a specimen surpassing anything they had seen, the traders were still unimpressed. “Greek and Latin alike are unsaleable,” they told him. “The city swarms with books from across Europe. You should have come last year.”

Still, Gerard refused to give up. He bought a psaltery, hoping music might bring some solace. His landlady, a woman of warm eyes and gentle manners, often spoke kindly to him. One day, she invited him to dine with her, and when he seemed subdued, she asked what weighed so heavily on his heart.

He confessed his struggles.

She listened, then offered her own insight. “Those merchants,” she said firmly, “have their own writers—paid hands who produce work for a noble’s price while receiving barely enough to survive. No wonder they treat you coldly. I think you write too well. How do I know? Because you don’t lock your door like Pietro, that sour man next door. Women are curious, and you’re open—so you must be good.”

Gerard asked for clarification.

“Because,” she explained, “your skill could ruin the work they sell. It would blind them.”

He sighed. “Ah, dear lady, you judge people harshly—yet you are so kind yourself.”

“My dear boy,” she smiled, “Romans are cunning. I am Siennese, thank the Virgin.”

“I regret leaving Augsburg,” Gerard said.

“Augsburg?” she replied, raising an eyebrow. “Is that even worth mentioning beside Rome? I’ve never heard of it.”

Yet she assured him he would succeed, despite the bookshops’ lies. “They deceive strangers without reason or shame. Everyone knows the nobility here are obsessed with writing—spending fortunes on manuscripts, turning homes and lands into parchment to store in chests. God help them through this madness, as He has others. And truthfully, there’s been less bloodshed, fewer factions tearing each other apart, since scribbling became fashionable. Take Cardinal Bassarion and the Pope himself—they both commission endless works. A dozen men like you could write for them night and day. I’ll speak to Teresa; she hears all the court gossip.”

The next day, she returned with news: five more noble patrons had fallen under the “writing spider’s” spell.

Gerard took down their names, purchased parchment, and spent days preparing samples. He left one at each door—complete with name and address—and waited.

No reply came.

Day after day passed, and hope dwindled. Unbeknownst to him, Margaret back in Rotterdam was battling hardship, feeding her dependents and arrested for healing without a license.

Gerard saw ruin ahead. He turned to music, learning canzonets by afternoon. He bought playing cards to color, and reduced his meals to one per day—a desperate move that soon brought new trouble.

In these lodgings, meals were prepared by the hostess, though guests provided the ingredients. When she discovered he was cooking for himself, she confronted him sharply. “Are you ashamed of yourself?” she demanded, making him flush with embarrassment.

But her anger softened instantly. She leaned forward, earnest. “Adversity cannot be overcome on an empty stomach. Patienza, my lad—times will change. For now, I’ll feed you freely.”

“No, hostess,” Gerard insisted. “My purse isn’t empty yet. I’d rather not cause harm by withholding what’s due.”

“You’re as mad as Pietro,” she said, “with his single bad painting.”

“How do you know it’s bad?” he asked.

“Because no one will buy it. There’s a man who has no gift. He’ll have to take up arms and carry his canvas as a shield.”

Gerard perked up. “You know Pietro?”

She nodded. “He came from Florence with money and a half-finished picture. Took one room opposite yours, furnished it neatly. When done, visitors came and offered fair prices—but he refused so proudly he made enemies. Since then, he’s taken it out again and again, always bringing it back. Last month, I saw his furniture vanish one by one. Now he wears only one suit, sleeps on a chest. I learned this by peeking through the keyhole—he locks his door whenever he leaves.”

“Does he fear we’ll steal his chest or his picture?”

“Why, no. He hides his poverty.”

“And the fool! Are all hearts so black as his? At least let us test him first.”

“Yet you speak so harshly. His fate is mine—and he’s a countryman of yours.”

“Oh, we Siennese love strangers. His case is not yours. You’re the handsomest youth ever to stay here—golden hair, bright eyes. He’s dark, sour-faced. And you know how to charm a woman; he does not. Still, I wish he wouldn’t starve in my house—it brings me ill repute. One starving man is enough. You’re far from home. I, as mistress here, shall count your meals—for me and your mother, far away. We two women will manage that. Mind your own business, being a man, and leave cooking to us, who live for little else but roasting fowl, nursing men at birth, and sweeping their grown-up cobwebs.”

“Dear lady,” Gerard said, “you often remind me of my mother.”

“All the better,” she beamed. “I’ll make you *more* like her before I’m done.”

Gerard, neither vain nor blinded by affection, saw his own sorrow mirrored in Pietro’s pride. The more he thought, the more he resolved to share what little he had. Pietro’s dignity, he believed, would repay him.

He tried to speak with him—without success. Then one day, he heard groaning from the room. He knocked. No answer. He knocked again.

A gruff voice barked: “Enter.”

He stepped in timidly.

The garret held little: a chair, a picture facing the wall, an iron basin, an easel, and a long chest upon which coiled a gaunt young man with eyes like fire. Never had Gerard seen anything so like a cobra poised to strike.

“Good Signor Pietro,” he began, “forgive me. I grow weary of solitude and intrude upon yours. I am your nearest neighbor, and perhaps your brother in misfortune. I too am an artist.”

“Are you a painter?” Pietro asked, leaping off the chest and gesturing grandly toward the bed. “Welcome, stranger. Sit.”

Gerard bowed, smiling slightly, but hesitated.

“I cannot call myself a painter,” he said. “I am a scribe, a caligrapher. I copy Greek and Latin manuscripts when I can find them.”

“And you call that art?”

“Without offense to your greater merit, Signor Pietro.”

“None at all. But to me, an artist is one who thinks—and paints his thoughts. A scribe merely traces the words of others.”

“Well said. Yet a writer may record the wisdom of ancient minds, truths beyond paint—yes, even divine thoughts, which no angel could depict. But let that pass. I am a painter too—though a poor one.”

“The better for you. They’ll buy your work in Rome.”

“But to commend myself to one of your eminence, I thought it wiser to call myself a capable writer than a clumsy painter.”

At that moment, footsteps echoed on the stairs.

“Ah!” Gerard exclaimed. “It’s the hostess. Good dame, I am here with Signor Pietro. I trust he’ll allow me to eat my dinner here.”

Pietro bowed gravely.

The landlady entered, carrying a steaming dish. She placed it silently on the chest and left.

Gerard began to eat.

But after a few bites, he paused. “I am a rude fellow, Signor Pietro. I never enjoy food alone. For the love of Heaven, let me share this ragout with you. It’s quite good, I assure you.”

Pietro fixed him with a glittering stare.

“You—a stranger—offer me your dinner?”

“Indeed. There’s more than one person can eat.”

“Very well,” Pietro said calmly, taking the dish. Then, in a sudden burst of fury, he hurled its contents out the window.

Turning, trembling with humiliation and rage, he said: “Let this teach you never to offer alms to an artist you do not know, master writer.”

Gerard flushed with anger. He fought hard not to strike the proud man. And to waste food—his mother’s milk curdled in his veins at such sacrilege.

Yet pity for Pietro’s pride, and a flicker of respect for his stubbornness, won out.

“I suppose,” Gerard said coldly, “what you did might suit a tale by Boccaccio—but it was not honest.”

“Make it good!” Pietro snapped.

“I offered you half my meal. You took it all. You had right to discard your portion—but not mine. Pride is noble, but justice is greater.”

Pietro stared. Then slowly, he reflected.

“You are right. I mistook you for a fool—so transparent was your kindness. Forgive me. And please go. You see how I am. The world has soured me. I hate mankind. I was not always so. Once more, forgive my rudeness. Farewell.”

Gerard sighed and turned toward the door.

But then—an idea struck him.

“Signor Pietro,” he said, “we Dutchmen are famed for bargaining. We are the lads ‘een eij scheeren’—to shave an egg. So for my lost dinner, I claim the right to feast my eyes upon your picture—whose face is turned to the wall.”

“Nay, nay,” Pietro cried, alarmed. “Do not ask that. I’ve already wronged you enough. I would not shed your blood.”

“Saints forbid! My blood?”

“Stranger,” Pietro muttered, “after repeated insults to my picture—my child, my soul—I vowed in anger to drive my dagger into the next who mocked it.”

“You mean to kill anyone who fails to praise it?”

“Not exactly. If you would simply look—and keep silent—I would not turn it to the wall forever. But you will talk. So I hide it. Would I were dead, buried within it!”

Gerard considered. “I accept your condition. Show me the picture. I swear I will hold my peace.”

Pietro turned the canvas, placing it in the best light the room allowed, then coiled himself once more on the chest, stiletto gleaming.

The painting showed the Virgin and Christ soaring through the air, surrounded by shadowy cherubs. Below stretched a vast landscape—forty or fifty miles wide—under a purple sky.

Gerard stood in silence. Then stepped close. Then drew back. He studied it for thirty minutes, wordless.

At last, Pietro snapped: “Well, have you nothing to say?”

Gerard blinked. “Forgive me. I forgot there were three of us. Yes—I have much to say.” And he drew his sword.

“Alas!” Pietro shrieked, leaping from the chest. “What do you mean?”

“To defend myself against your dagger,” Gerard said. “And fairly, as a Dutchman. So stand back while I deliver judgment—or I’ll pin you to the wall like a cockchafer.”

“Oh!” Pietro breathed, relieved. “I feared you’d stab my poor picture—already wounded by so many cruel tongues.”

Gerard pursued criticism under duress—sword point aimed at Pietro, eye darting to the painting.

“First, signor,” he began, “in mixing pigments and preparing oil, your Italians lag behind our Flemings. But let that pass. Though small, I can reveal secrets of the Van Eycks—secrets that would enrich your next work. Meanwhile, in this piece, I see the genius of your nation. Truly, you are sons of the sun. We have color—you have imagination. Mother of Heaven! He has poured his immortal soul onto the panel. One thing I note: this makes other pictures I once admired seem crude, earthbound. The drapery here is stiff—why not let it flow freely? The figures are airborne—why not let the cloth breathe with motion?”

“I will! I will!” Pietro cried. “I’ll do anything for those who truly see!”

“Humph. This landscape enlightens me. From now on, I scorn the tiny, cramped scenes I once praised. Here is nature’s true face—vast plains, distances marked, trees, houses, rivers shrinking in perfect gradation until vision itself dissolves. O, beautiful! And the clever rogue hangs his celestial figures above the world, untouched by earthly chaos. Saints float beneath heaven’s purple veil. Far below, Earth and her busy hives. And they let you carry this painted poem, this blooming hymn, through Rome’s streets—unsold. But I tell you, in Ghent or Bruges—even Rotterdam—they’d tear it from your hands. Yet it’s said a stranger sees clearest. Courage, Pietro Vanucci! I reverence you. Though I am a poor painter, I forgive you—for being a great one. Not forgive—thank God for you, and men like you. I bow in homage. Your picture is immortal. And you, sitting on a chest, are a king in your royal art. Viva, il maestro! Viva!”

At these words, Pietro, overwhelmed, threw himself upon Gerard’s neck.

“They called it a madman’s dream,” he sobbed.

“Madmen themselves!” shouted Gerard. “No—idiots!”

“Generous stranger! I will hate no man again—when the world holds men like you. I was a viper to throw away your dinner—a wretch, a monster!”

“Monster,” Gerard said gently, “will you sup with me now?”

“Oh, yes! Where are you going?”

“To order supper at once. We’ll have the picture as our third guest.”

“I’ll invite it while you’re gone. My poor picture—child of my heart.”

“Oh, master,” Gerard smiled, “it will watch many suppers after worms have eaten us both.”

“I hope so,” Pietro whispered.

A week had passed since the last encounter, and now the two companions sat side by side, each absorbed in their own task—but with very different hearts. Pietro moved restlessly, hurling himself into his work with sudden bursts of energy, producing astonishing strokes in moments, only to abandon it in frustration, muttering curses at his own handiwork. Then, as if driven by some inner storm, he would return to it with fierce intensity, only to fling it aside again with a groan. Meanwhile, Gerard worked steadily, quietly, his face calm, his hands sure—the steady Dutchman untouched by the tempests that raged around him.

To speak plainly, Gerard, who had never known a friend he could not guide or influence, had quietly placed his companion under his sway. Their shared labor was painting playing cards—simple enough, yet vital for survival. When finished, the proud artist took up his own picture to begin his daily rounds, seeking buyers among the city’s patrons. Gerard asked him to carry the cards along, to try selling them as well.

Pietro looked at him as though he’d just proposed stealing from a saint. But after a moment’s silence, he gave in—embracing Gerard warmly in the Italian fashion, then carefully drying the latest cards under the sun, which now shone bright and generous over Rome.

Left alone, Gerard penned a few Greek letters on parchment, then mended a small tear in his hose. His landlady found him thus, and teased him gently: “Are there no women in this house? Or have you forgotten how to speak to them?”

“Finish your work,” she said, “and come talk to Teresa—my friend I told you about. Her husband is no great man, and prides himself on knowing the powerful.”

Gerard went down. And there stood Teresa—none other than the Roman matron he had once saved from disaster. “Ah, madama!” he exclaimed. “Is it truly you? The good woman did not tell me so. And the little fair-haired boy—how fares he? Was he none the worse for that strange journey in the boat?”

“He is well,” she replied softly.

“What are you two talking about?” the landlady asked, staring between them. “And why do you tremble so, Teresa mia?”

“He saved my child’s life,” Teresa whispered, struggling to keep her composure.

“What! Your lodger? And he never said a word? You shameless creature—how can you look me in the face?”

“Do not speak harshly to him,” Teresa pleaded. Turning to her friend, she began to recount the full tale of Gerard’s courage, describing how he had risked all to save her son. As she spoke, Gerard stood red-faced, scarcely recognizing his own actions—gratitude had painted them far more noble than they were.

“And to think,” she continued, “you asked me to serve this lodger, whom I knew only through your praise. Oh, Fiammina, that was enough for me. Dear youth, in serving you, I serve myself.”

The two women then launched into a passionate discussion of the barriers artists faced—fees, commissions, petty gatekeepers who blocked access to patrons. Teresa smiled sadly at Gerard’s innocence in leaving his artwork at the doors of the great, unaccompanied by bribes or promises.

“What!” she said. “Without offering a coin to the servants? Without even giving them a share to let the signori see your wares? It might as well have been thrown into the Tiber.”

“Well-a-day,” sighed Gerard, feeling the weight of his naivety.

Then Teresa offered a solution: “Go to a city nobler, less greedy than this. La corte Romana non vuol’ pecora senza lana—Rome wants sheep with wool.” She paused, deep in thought, and promised to return the next day.

The landlady clapped her hands. “Teresa has a plan,” she declared.

Hardly had she left when Pietro returned—his face dark as thunder. Gerard exchanged a glance with the landlady, then followed the Italian upstairs, ready to offer comfort.

“Have they rejected your masterpiece again?” he asked.

“As before,” Pietro grumbled.

“Then they are fools,” said Gerard cheerfully.

“That’s not the point,” Pietro snapped.

“What *is* wrong?”

“They bought the cards!” he roared, slamming his fists against the air.

“All the better,” Gerard said, beaming.

“They flew at me for them! They pretended to be indifferent, but I saw the hunger in their eyes. I feigned ignorance, I played the fool—and lo! I pillaged them like thieves. Curse these fools!”

He threw a dozen silver coins onto the floor, stamped upon them with furious steps, danced over them with wild eyes, kicked them wildly—sending them spinning across the room.

Gerard dropped to his knees and gathered them up one by one, tucking them gently into his purse.

“You should smile at their foolishness,” he said. “And turn it to profit.”

“And I will,” Pietro muttered, still fuming. “We’ll paint a pack a day. We’ll make the whole city gamble itself into ruin—while we live like princes on its vices and blindness.”
