He paused. “There was one queen… I would have kept her back. You painted her, brother. She had hair like autumn fire, eyes like sapphires, and above all—soul.”

Gerard lowered his voice. “Pietro,” he said softly, “I painted that one from my heart.”

The Italian nodded slowly, his eyes gleaming. “You love her so much, yet leave her.”

“Yes,” Gerard said quietly. “It is because I love her so deeply that I have wandered this long, weary road.”

Their conversation was cut short by the landlady calling from below: “Come down! You’re wanted.”

Gerard descended, and there stood Teresa once more.

“Come with me, Ser Gerard,” she said.

Gerard walked beside Teresa in silence, his thoughts turning inward as artists often do—wondering what she might intend for him, rather than asking outright. And so, at last, she spoke of her own accord.

“A friend told me,” she said, “that a goldsmith’s wife is seeking a writer. Her shop is nearby—you’ll not have far to go.”

Soon they reached the woman’s door. Teresa stepped forward with quiet dignity.

“Madama,” she said, “Leonora informs me you need a scribe. I have brought you one—handsome and true, who saved my child from the sea. Pray look upon him kindly.”

The goldsmith’s wife, Olympia, obeyed in part. She fixed her gaze on Gerard’s face, drawn by its noble features, and could not easily tear her eyes away. Yet her reply was dismissive.

“No,” she said, “I have no use for a writer. Ah—now I recall! It is my neighbor Claelia, the sausage-maker, who seeks one. She told me, and I passed it on to Leonora.”

Teresa bowed slightly and withdrew without haste or complaint.

Claelia lived farther off. When they arrived, she was out. Teresa sat down calmly on the step, composed and still as a statue, her presence commanding the air around her. Gerard, unable to resist, began sketching her in secret when suddenly Claelia returned.

“Madama,” Teresa said, stepping forward, “I’ve heard from Olympia that you require a writer.” She took Gerard by the hand and led him forward. “Here is one—beautiful and brave. He rescued my child from the cruel waves. For the sake of our Lady, look upon him with favor.”

Claelia blinked. “My good lady, my fair sir,” she replied, “I have no need of a writer. But now you remind me—it was my friend Appia Claudia who asked me for one just the other day. She’s a tailor, lives in the Via Lepida.”

Teresa nodded once and turned away.

“Madama,” Gerard said gently, “this may prove wearying for you.”

She raised her eyes. “What has ever been accomplished without patience?”

She added softly, “We shall knock at every door in Rome—but you shall have justice.”

“But madama,” he insisted, “I believe we are being followed. A man trails us—sometimes near, sometimes distant.”

“I have noticed,” she said coolly, though her cheeks flushed faintly. “It is my poor Lodovico.”

She paused, then turned and beckoned with her finger. A figure approached reluctantly. When he came close, she looked him full in the face. He shifted uncomfortably.

“Lodovico mio,” she said, “know this young gentleman—of whom I have spoken to you so often. Know him and love him, for it was he who saved your wife and child.”

At those words, Lodovico’s forced smile melted into genuine emotion. He stepped forward and embraced Gerard warmly.

Yet something about his earlier stealth, his silent pursuit, made Gerard uneasy beneath the embrace.

“Shall we have your company, Ser Lodovico?” he asked.

“No, signor,” Lodovico replied. “I go not that side of the Tiber.”

“Addio, then,” Teresa said quietly.

“When shall you return home, Teresa mia?” he called after her.

“When I have finished my errand,” she answered.

They walked on in silence. Teresa now wore a solemn expression, almost sorrowful.

Appia Claudia, the tailor, proved merciful. She did not send them across the Tiber, but only a hundred yards down the street—to Lucretia, who ran the glove shop. It was she who wanted a writer, though even Appia could not say why.

Lucretia was a lively little woman, warm and welcoming. She greeted them cheerfully and confessed she needed no writer—she kept all her accounts in her head.

“It was for my confessor, Father Colonna,” she explained. “He is mad for writers.”

“I’ve heard of him,” said Teresa.

“Who hasn’t?” Lucretia laughed.

“But good dame,” Gerard interjected, “he is a friar—a man of vows. I cannot let him write without payment. He saved my child at sea.”

“Did he now?” Lucretia said, casting a kind glance at Gerard. “Well, rest easy. A Colonna never wants for money. The good father has only to speak, and princes of his blood will pour thousands into his hands. And such a confessor! The best in Rome. His mind wanders leagues away while you confess—he pays no heed. Once I tested him: I confessed I had killed my lodger’s little girl and baked her in a pie. When I finished, he woke from his dream and said, ‘My erring sister, recite three Paternosters and three Ave Marias kneeling, abstain from butter and eggs next Wednesday, and pax vobiscum!’ Then off he went, hands behind his back, as if I were nothing.”

Teresa waited patiently, then drew the conversation back. “Would you be so kind as to accompany this youth to the friar and speak for him?”

“Oh, I can’t leave my shop!” Lucretia protested. “And why should I? His door is always open to writers, painters, scholars—anyone who knows their craft. One day he refused the Duke d’Urbino because a learned Greek was with him. Their heads were so close over a parchment from Greece, you could have placed one cowl over both. Onesta told me—she comes here often to chat.”

“This is the man for you,” Teresa said firmly.

“All you need do,” Lucretia continued, “is go to his lodgings—my boy will show you—and tell Onesta you come from me. Say you are a writer, and she will take you to him. If you give the girl a piece of silver, it won’t hurt.”

“I have silver,” Teresa said warmly.

“But remember,” Lucretia warned, “if the young man claims he can do something, he must truly be able to do it—or avoid the friar like poison. He hates bunglers. Only the other day, someone brought him a poorly carved crucifix. He roared, ‘Is this how you present “Salvator Mundi,” who died in agony for you? You begrudge Him careful work? This slovenly trifle—a crucifix? Were it not a crucifix and I a holy man, I’d dust your jacket with it!’ Onesta heard every word through the keyhole. So mind!”

“Have no fear,” Teresa said proudly. “I stand by his ability. He saved my child.”

Gerard, less perceptive, did not grasp the weight of her confidence. In fact, he begged for delay.

“I would rather not see the friar today,” he said. “Would tomorrow not serve as well?”

“Here is a coward for you,” Lucretia chuckled.

“No, he is not a coward,” Teresa snapped, defending him. “He is modest.”

“I am afraid,” Gerard admitted, “of this high-born, fastidious friar. He has seen the finest writing in Italy. If you would allow me to prepare better work, I will face him tomorrow with it.”

“I consent,” Teresa said.

They walked home together. Near Gerard’s lodging stood a shop selling vellum. In the window lay a perfect white skin—pure and radiant. Gerard stared longingly, but knew he could not afford it. He hurried on.

But soon he decided where to get vellum. Parting from Teresa at his door, he rushed upstairs and took out the bond he had carried from Sevenbergen. With a sigh, he laid it on the table.

Then, with chemicals in hand, he prepared to erase the old writing. But this was his final chance to read it. Overcoming his loathing for bad handwriting, he began to decipher the deed despite its clumsy contractions.

It revealed that Ghysbrecht Van Swieten was to lend Floris Brandt money secured by land, repaying himself from the rent.

Gerard felt it would be wrong to destroy such a document. Instead, he vowed to transcribe every word at his leisure.

Descending, he resolved to buy a small piece of vellum with his half of the card-money.

At the foot of the stairs, he found the landlady and Teresa talking. Seeing him, the landlady exclaimed, “Here he is! You’re caught, donna mia. See what she bought you?”

She pulled from under her apron—the very vellum Gerard had longed for.

“Why, dame! Why, Donna Teresa!” Gerard stammered, speechless with joy and astonishment.

“Dear boy,” Teresa said, “there is no skin in all Rome like it. Did not your eyes linger on it with longing? Did you not sigh as you turned away? Could I let you want it after that?”

“What wisdom! What kindness, madama! Oh, I never thought I’d possess this. How much did you pay?”

“I forget,” she smiled. “Addio, Fiammina. Addio, Ser Gerard. Be happy, be prosperous—as you are good.”

And with that, the Roman matron glided away, leaving Gerard stunned, wondering how to repay such generosity.

The next afternoon, Gerard visited Lucretia. Her boy guided him to Fra Colonna’s lodgings. He announced himself, gave Onesta a piece of silver, and was led up.

Gerard entered with a trembling heart.

The room was vast, filled with art, antiquities, and learning—manuscripts, carvings, musical instruments—all scattered in glorious chaos. At its center sat the friar, deeply absorbed in an Arabian text.

He glanced up, annoyed by the interruption.

Onesta whispered in his ear.

“Very well,” the friar said. “Let him sit. Wait—young man, show me how you write.”

He tossed Gerard a sheet of paper and pointed to an inkhorn.

“Reverend father,” Gerard said, “my hand trembles too much now. But last night I wrote a page of Greek, with the Latin translation beside it—showing the different scripts.”

“Show it to me.”

Gerard brought it forward, heart pounding. He stood, breathless, awaiting judgment.

When it came, it struck him like thunder.

For the friar fell upon him, embracing him with a Dominican’s fervor.

Meanwhile, in Holland, an event unfolded whose consequences none could foresee—not even the reader.

A magnificent procession marched to Eli’s door—brave to the eye, noble in appearance, yet pitiable upon closer inspection. It seemed one creature—a centaur—but analysis revealed two.

The human half was dressed in finery, bedizened with gold and silver, metals that men have sold their souls to possess. But the horse was worse adorned—its ears hidden in linen sheaths tipped with silver and blue; its body swaddled in stiff, gorgeous cloths descending to the ground, save for a narrow space to mince forward; its tail concealed heaven knows how. Only its eyes gleamed through holes in the fabric, and its hooves peeped in and out like rats.

Yet this grotesque creature represented absolute power—sent from the Duke’s court, returning from a tournament. Its mission: to claim a dwarf.

“What ho!” the rider cried, as Eli emerged with his wife behind him. “Peace be with you, good people. Rejoice! I come for your dwarf.”

Eli stared, speechless.

But Catherine shrieked, “You’ve mistaken your way, good man! We have no dwarf here.”

“Nay, wife,” Eli said, “he means our Giles—he is small of stature. Why deny what cannot be denied?”

“Ay!” the rider boomed. “That is he—and speaks like a big fellow.”

“His breast is sound,” Catherine snapped. “And quick with fists, even at odds.”

“Else how would the poor thing keep his head in such a world?”

“Well said, dame. You’re as ready with your weapon as he. Likely his mother. Bring him forth, and quickly. See—they lead a stunted mule for him. The Duke needs him sorely—we’re clean out of dwarves and tiger-cats. Our last thumb-hopper tumbled down the well yesterday.”

“And think you I’ll let my darling go to such a reckless house?” Catherine cried. “Where servants leave wells open to trap innocents—like wolves?”

The official lost patience. “Beware,” he warned, voice stern. “Choose wisely: either let your abortion be fed like a bishop and clothed like a prince at court—or have all your heads cut off and borne on poles, with the bellman crying, ‘Behold the heads of hardy rebels, who, having by luck a misbegotten son, traitorously grudged him to the Duke, who is the true father of all his folk, great or small.’”

“Nay,” Eli said sadly, “do not call us rebels. We are loyal folk. But it is sudden—and the lad is our flesh and blood. He has lately shown more sense than before.”

“Threats avail not,” Catherine whimpered. “We don’t grudge him to the Duke—but truly, he cannot go. His linen is all in holes. That ends it.”

But the male mind resisted. “Think you the Duke won’t find linen—and cloth of gold besides? None are so brave, none so favored at court, as our monsters—big or small.”

How long the debate might have lasted, I know not. But it ended abruptly—by the bone of contention himself.

The dwarf stepped out of the house and declared, “If my folk are mad, I am not. I’ll go with you—this instant.”

Catherine wailed. Another child slipping from her care.

Giles, though, felt her pain. “Do not mourn, mother! It’s a blessing. I’ve grown tired of this place since Gerard left.”

“Ah, cruel Giles! Should you not say she is bereaved of Gerard? You must stay and comfort her.”

“Oh, I’m not going to Rome. Not such a fool. I’ll never go beyond Rotterdam. I’ll visit often. And if I don’t like it, who shall keep me there? Not all the dukes in Christendom.”

“Good sense lies in little bulk,” the emissary approved. “Therefore, Master Giles, kiss your parents and thank them for misbegetting you. And you—bring the mule here.”

One servant led forward the tiny mule.

Giles scorned it. “Why would you throw all into one scale? Put large with large, small with small. Besides, I hate small things. I’ll ride the highest horse here—or not at all.”

The official studied him a moment, then adopted a courteous tone. “I shall honor your will in all reasonable things. (Dismount, Eric—your horse is the highest.) And if you wish to wait an hour to bid farewell, say the word. Your pleasure shall be mine.”

Giles reflected. “Master,” he said, “if we wait a month, it will be the same. My mother is good-hearted, but her body is bigger than her spirit. We’ll part with tears—better done quickly. Bring me that horse.”

Catherine threw her apron over her face and sobbed.

The tall horse was brought. Giles tried to climb by the tail—like a rope.

“Wait!” a servant cried. “He kicks.”

“I’ll kick him,” Giles said. “Bring him beneath the window. I’ll show you how to mount a horse that kicks and refuses the tail.”

He dashed inside and reappeared at an upper window, rope in hand. He tied one end and descended swiftly—smooth as oiled lightning—landing astride the horse unperceived.

The official lifted his hands in admiration. “I have found a pearl,” he thought. “This will be a fine day’s work.”

“Come, father, mother—kiss me, bless me, and off I go.”

Eli blessed him, bidding him be honest and true, a credit to his family.

Catherine could not speak—only clung to him, sobbing. Through her tears, she saw the tear in his sleeve from climbing out the window. Without a word, she pulled out her needle and mended it—her tears falling on his arm, unnoticed—except perhaps by the unseen eyes said to fill the air.

And so the dwarf mounted the high horse and rode away, jocund and bold, the court’s butter spread thick upon his back.

Perpusillus cared little for the two women left behind, rocking and weeping by the hearth, praising his virtues, blind to his faults.

Arrived at court, he became a favorite. One strange habit electrified the palace—but due to his size, and for variety’s sake, he was indulged.

He was allowed to speak the truth.

An unpopular thing.

He made it unbearable.

He bawled it.

Happy the man who has two chain-cables: Merit, and Women. Oh, that I, like Gerard, had a 'chaine des dames' to pull up by. I would be prose laureate, or professor of the spasmodic, or something, in no time. En attendant, I will sketch the Fra Colonna.

The true revivers of ancient learning and philosophy were not scholars in the strict sense, but writers of fiction—Petrarch and Boccaccio. Their efforts did not bring them immediate fame or public acclaim; yet they planted seeds that took root in quiet soil, waiting for the sun to rise. From their time onward, Italy never lacked at least one native scholar fluent in Greek, and every learned Greek who arrived was welcomed as a brother. By the end of the fourteenth century, figures such as Poggio, Valla, and the elder Guarino had emerged. Early in the fifteenth, Florence under Cosmo de’ Medici became a haven for Platonists. Led by Gemistus Pletho, a man born in Greece, these thinkers began around 1440 to challenge Aristotle’s dominance. For few minds are broad enough to honor one great thinker without slighting another. Theodore Gaza defended Aristotle with moderation; George of Trebizond attacked him fiercely, turning his criticism toward Plato. Then Cardinal Bessarion, also a native Greek, rose in defense of Plato in his treatise *Adversus calumniatorem Platonis*. Controversy, whether wise or foolish, is a sign of life.

Born without a taste for debate in an age of fervent argument, Francesco Colonna—a young nobleman of Florence—devoted himself to the arts. At twenty, he entered the Dominican order, seeking solitude and study. He withdrew from idle chatter and political strife, from the buzz and sting of human society, to find peace with St. Dominic and the Nine Muses. An insatiable student of languages, art, sculpture, chronology, coins, and inscriptions, he grew skeptical of popular histories. He traveled extensively in the East, returning enriched with rare manuscripts and mastery of Greek, Latin, Hebrew, and Syriac.

He found his homeland transformed. Other enlightened princes had risen beyond Cosmo—Alfonso, King of Naples; Nicolas d’Este; Lionel d’Este—and above all, his old friend Thomas of Sarzana, now Pope, had given new vigor to scholarship. The Vatican library swelled to five thousand manuscripts under his patronage. He commissioned Poggio to translate Diodorus Siculus and Xenophon’s *Cyropaedia*, Valla to render Herodotus and Thucydides, Gaza to tackle Theophrastus, George of Trebizond to work on Eusebius and Plato’s dialogues. Thus, when Colonna returned, he found Plato and Aristotle in uneasy truce, while Poggio and Valla clashed over grammar and syntax, burning with philological fury.

For Colonna, this was paradise. He settled into a life of tranquil delight. Few are so fortunate as those whose talents span many fields—provided they do not need to earn their bread through them. And Fra Colonna was such a man. He spoke seven or eight languages, knew some mathematics, could write, paint, sculpt, sing, and play the lute—each skill modestly, but with genuine appreciation. His greatest gift was his ability to admire excellence in others. Such a mind deserves happiness—and he had it.

Yet wisdom often shuts out at one door. Among your acquaintances, how many have intellects deaf, blind, or dead to some great art or science? And those who are both foolish and proud parade their ignorance instead of hiding it. A passionate lover of art, Colonna remained a skeptic in faith. In every age, there are men who carry the beliefs of another—past or future. Simple-minded, his doubt was as innocent as his enthusiasm. He viewed religious rituals not with reverence, but as the ancients once saw pagan rites—mummers’ plays for the masses. Yet his mind drew a curious line: any Christian ceremony he traced back to pagan roots, he respected for its antiquity. Had he lived among the pagans, he might have mocked the same rites from his philosophical perch.

Fra Colonna admired Gerard deeply. With access to half the palaces in Rome, he praised the young artist so widely that soon nobles sought to hire him away. He told Gerard of princely offers. “But I am so happy with you, father,” Gerard protested. “Fiddlestick about being happy with me,” replied the friar. “You must not be happy—you must be a man of the world. That’s the lesson I teach the young. These Montesini can pay you three times what I can—and they shall, by Jupiter.” The friar set a high price on Gerard’s talent, which was accepted without hesitation. In those days, copying manuscripts fetched far more than authorship ever would under the printing press. Gerard earned three hundred crowns for transcribing Aristotle’s *Rhetoric*.

The powerful showered affection on their favorites—while the passion lasted. Amid the frenzy for Greek manuscripts, Gerard became a cherished pet. Nobles of both sexes fawned over him like a lapdog. It might have turned a vain man’s head, but the cautious Dutchman saw the steel beneath the velvet glove and kept his distance. Still, it was a proud day when he sat beside Fra Colonna at the table of Cardinal Bessarion.

They were near the bottom of the long table, but it mattered little—they were there. Gerard marveled at the roast pheasants served whole, feathers intact, as if freshly plucked from the woods. Chickens cooked in bottles, tender as peaches. But the true wonder was the napkins—exquisitely fine, folded into cocked hats, birds’ wings, fans—instead of lying flat. This astonished Gerard, though modern readers may have seen such things without falling backward in their chairs.

After dinner, the tables were removed, revealing another beneath, laden with sweets. The ladies rushed forward and devoured them; the men watched with wary eyes. “But, dear father,” Gerard said, “I see no bifurcal daggers—the ones they say his excellency arms the left hand with.” “Nay,” replied Colonna, “that is the invention of Cardinal Orsini—a silly tool for guests to fumble with. One man, in haste, skewered his tongue to his palate with it, I hear. O tempora, O mores! The ancients, reclining like gods at their feasts, would have scorned such absurdities.”

Once the women had finished their sugar-plums, the tables vanished again. Guests sat in a row against the wall. Two ecclesiastics entered, bowing low, each carrying a lute. They knelt before the cardinal and sang the day’s service. Then, with deep reverence, they bowed and retreated. The cardinal touched his skullcap—just as our late Iron Duke touched his hat. The company dispersed. Gerard had dined with a cardinal and one who had thrice come close to becoming pope.

But greater honor awaited. One day, the cardinal summoned him, praised his work, and took him in his coach to the Vatican. Up a private stairway led to a luxurious chamber with a grand oriel window. Inkstands, sloping writing frames, and tools of art adorned the room. The cardinal whispered to a courtier, and soon the Pope’s private secretary arrived bearing a grimy, ancient manuscript of Plutarch’s *Lives*. Soon, Gerard was alone, copying it, awestruck—yet half-joyful at the thought that the Holy Father himself would handle and read his work.

The papal inkstands gleamed outside, but within, the ink was foul. Gerard always carried his own—homemade, in a dirty little horn. He knelt and prayed for steady hands, then began.

One side of the room was dominated by a heavy curtain, split down the middle but overlapping at the edges. After a while, Gerard felt drawn to peek through it. He resisted. Then the impulse returned. Overcome, he left Plutarch, crept across the matted floor, gathered the folds with his fingers, and pressed his nose through the gap—only to meet the cold steel of a halberd. Two soldiers, fully armed, stood guard, their weapons crossed in a triangle.

Gerard pulled back swiftly—but in that moment, he heard soft voices and saw a group of people bowing before a hidden figure. He never tried again to look through the guarded curtain, though he often glanced at it. Every hour or so, an ecclesiastic would enter, glance at him, make him feel chilled, and leave.

It was gloomy, mechanical. But the next day, a richly armored gentleman burst in, glaring. “What is going on here?” he demanded. Gerard explained he was copying Plutarch, aided by the saints. The nobleman said he didn’t know the man in question. Gerard gently clarified the circumstances—time and space having deprived the ancient Greek of conversation with the modern lord. “Oh!” said the noble, “one of those dead Greeks they fuss so much over.” “Yes, signor,” replied Gerard, “one of them—who, though dead, still lives.” “I don’t understand,” said the noble, with all the dignity of ignorance. “What did he write? Love stories?” His eyes sparkled. “Merry tales, like Boccaccio?” “No, signor,” answered Gerard, “lives of heroes and sages.” “Soldiers and popes?” “Soldiers and princes.” “Will you read me one some day?” “With pleasure, signor. But what would my employers say if I stopped work?” “Never mind them,” said the noble. “Do you not know who I am? I am Jacques Bonaventura, nephew to His Holiness the Pope, and captain of his guards. I came to check on my men—I suspect they’ve been moved out for you.”

Bonaventura hurried off. But he soon returned, drawn to the quiet artist. Finding Gerard good company, he began visiting regularly, chattering idly while Gerard wrote the immortal lives.

One day, he arrived changed—moody, restless. He threw himself into a chair and muttered, “Ah, traitress! traitress!” Gerard asked what ailed him. “Traitress! traitress!” was the only reply. So Gerard resumed his work.

Then Bonaventura said, “I am melancholy. For Our Lady’s sake, read me a story from Ser Plutarcho—something to soothe my bile. Is there nothing in that Greek about lovers betrayed?”

Gerard read him the life of Alexander. The nobleman grew excited, pacing the room, embracing the reader, and swearing to shun “soft delights”—that bed of nettles—and follow glory.

Who could be happier than Gerard? His art was honored, his fees fabulous. In a year or two, he would sail home to Holland, wealthy, and settle with Margaret in Bruges, Antwerp, or beloved Augsburg—living in peace, love, and honest labor. His heart never strayed from her. In prosperity, he did not forget poor Pietro. He brought Fra Colonna to see the painting. The friar examined it closely, then embraced the artist and carried the picture to a member of the Colonna family, who paid a generous sum. Pietro descended to the first floor and lived like a gentleman. But Gerard stayed in his garret. To increase his expenses would have delayed his return to Margaret. Luxury held no appeal for the single-hearted man when love stood before him.

Jacques Bonaventura introduced Gerard to other young nobles. They liked him and tried to lure him into vice and extravagance. But Gerard humbly begged to be excused. He escaped that temptation. But a greater one lay ahead.

Fra Colonna had free access to the Pope’s library, and on occasion he would finish his work at the same hour as Gerard, walking through the city together. On these excursions, the young artist saw Rome in all its grandeur—its churches, palaces, and ancient ruins bathed in golden light, each stone whispering of empires long past. To Gerard, every street was a poem, every archway a portal into history.

But Fra Colonna, ever the scholar, tempered this awe with sober reflection. “This place,” he said, gesturing around, “is not Rome. It is the tomb of Rome.”

He pointed out how the old triumphal arches sank twenty or thirty feet beneath the modern streets, how palaces and columns lay buried under footpaths and homes. The narrow boundaries of today’s city, he noted, were dwarfed by the colossal remnants that still rose from the ground—the Temple of Peace, Monte Savello, once the Theatre of Marcellus, and Testacio, a hill formed from centuries of discarded pottery and household waste. “The women of old Rome threw their broken pots here,” he mused, “and lo—a mountain.”

“*Ex pede Herculem; ex ungue leonem*,” he quoted. “From the foot, we know the giant; from the claw, the lion.”

Gerard listened, captivated, though when the friar began to suggest that the moral greatness of pagan Rome matched its physical might, he hesitated. “Then has the world lost by Christ’s coming?” he ventured, flushing slightly—aware he was questioning his benefactor.

“Saints forbid!” replied the friar. “That would be heresy.” Yet even as he said it, he deftly sidestepped the truth with subtle language, circling toward forbidden ground like a man creeping up a spiral staircase.

They came upon a church where a crowd gathered in the porch. Inside, a demon was being exorcised. At such moments, Fra Colonna would emit a soft, sorrowful moan—one that carried more than disapproval: it spoke of pity for human credulity, for the blindness that clung to superstition even in the face of reason.

He sighed now. “Come, let us go.”

“No, father, please! I’ve never seen a devil cast out!”

Reluctantly, the friar followed Gerard inside. There, they found a man bound on his knees before the altar, a scarf tied tightly around his neck, held like a dog on a leash by the priest who conducted the rite.

Few people were present—fear had spread that the last exorcism had ended badly: “as a rabbit driven from one burrow runs to another.”

When Gerard and the friar arrived, the priest seemed satisfied with the audience. He turned to the possessed man, breviary in hand, and began to call forth the spirit.

“Come out, Ashtaroth. Oho! Not you. Come out, Belial. Come out, Tatzi. Come out, Eza. No—he trembles not. Come out, Azymoth. Come out, Feriander. Come out, Foletho. Come out, Astyma. Come out, Nebul. Aha! Found you, you serpent! At your old tricks. Let us pray!”

“Oh, Lord, we beseech You to drive the foul fiend Nebul from this Your creature—out of his hair, eyes, nose, mouth, ears, gums, teeth, shoulders, arms, legs, loins, stomach, bowels, thighs, knees, calves, feet, ankles, fingernails, toenails—and soul. Amen.”

The priest rose, turned to the crowd, and said with quiet amusement, “Gentlemen, we have here as stubborn a devil as you may see in a summer’s day.”

Then, facing the man again, he addressed him with fierce authority—sometimes speaking to the man, sometimes to the fiend. The answers came through the same mouth: denials of faith, complaints of inner torment.

It was the priest who first blurred the line between victim and villain. He struck the man hard, kicked him, spat repeatedly in his face. Then he lit a candle, held it until it burned his fingers, dropped it hastily. Next, he displayed the Host, showing the sacred body to the afflicted man. He burned another candle, more carefully this time. Then, suddenly gentle, he spoke kindly to the man in his human form, dismissed him, and received the thanks of the onlookers.

“Good father,” said Gerard, “you know their names so well. Our northern priests know little of the infernal host.”

“Ay, young man,” replied the priest. “Here we know them all—their names, their ways. This Nebul is a hard one to banish.”

He then recounted several of his own exorcisms, ending with one from the previous day: a great, hulking fiend expelled through a woman’s mouth, leaving behind nails, pins, and a tuft of hair. The demon cried out in anguish: *“It is not you who conquer me. See that stone on the windowsill. Know that the angel Gabriel once alighted there—’tis that which has undone me.”*

Fra Colonna moaned. “And you believed him?”

“Certainly! Who but an infidel would doubt such a precise revelation?”

“You believe the father of lies? That is beyond belief.”

“Oh, a liar does not always lie.”

“Yes, he does—especially when he tells an improbable tale and shows you a holy relic, arming you against the Satanic host. Fiends, if any, are not so simple. You should have answered him with antiquity: *‘I fear the Greeks even when bearing gifts.’*”

“A rogue chopped his wife’s head off on that stone,” said the friar sharply. “Take my word for it.” And he pulled Gerard away.

“Alack, father,” said Gerard, “you embarrassed the good priest.”

“By Pollux,” chuckled the friar, “I blistered him with a single touch of Socratic interrogation. What modern can resist the weapons of ancient wisdom?”

One afternoon, after finishing his work, Gerard was summoned to the Palace Cesarini by a fine lackey. He was ushered into a noble chamber where a girl sat embroidering tapestry. She rose and left, saying she would inform her mistress.

Gerard waited over an hour in the silent room, growing restless. “These nobles care nothing for a poor man’s time,” he muttered. Just as he decided to leave, the door opened, and a magnificent beauty entered, followed by two maids. It was the young Princess Cesarini.

She spoke loudly and haughtily to her attendants, but upon seeing Gerard, softened her tone. “Are you the writer, messer?”

“I am, signora.”

“Good.”

She seated herself on a high-backed chair—almost a throne—while Gerard and the maids stood.

“What is your name, young man?”

“Gerard, signora.”

“Gerard? By Bacchus, is that the name of a human being?”

“It is a Dutch name, signora. I was born in Tergou, Holland.”

“A harsh name for such a handsome youth,” she said to her maids, who nodded eagerly.

“What did I send for him for?” she asked, half-languid, half-ironic. “Ah, yes—I remember. Be seated, Ser Gerardo. Write me a letter to Ercole Orsini, my lover—at least, he says so.”

Gerard sat, took out paper and ink, and looked up expectantly.

She gazed down at him, her eyes searching. “Well, Gerardo?”

“I am ready, your excellence.”

“Write, then.”

“I await your words.”

“And who, think you, will provide them?”

“Who but your grace? It is your letter.”

“Gramercy! Do you writers not find the words? What use is your art without them? I suspect you’re an impostor.”

“No, signora. I could transcribe your speech into proper grammar and writing. But I cannot read your silence. Speak what is in your heart, and I shall put it on paper before your eyes.”

“But there is nothing in my heart. Sometimes I think I have no heart at all.”

“What is in your mind, then?”

“Nothing. Nor in my head.”

“Then why write at all?”

“Why, indeed? That is the first sensible thing either of us has said, Gerardo. Pestilence take him! Why doesn’t he write first? Then I could say ‘no’ to this and ‘yes’ to that—without headache. Is it not a lady’s part to speak first?”

“No, signora. The last.”

“Well spoken, Gerardo. Ha! ha! You shall have a gold piece for your wit. Give me my purse!” And she paid him immediately, in the fashion of the age. Money never cooled zeal. Gerard, having earned a gold coin so easily, felt compelled to help her out.

“Signorina,” he said, “these things are difficult only because people try too hard. They make them artificial. Imagine the gentleman you love—”

“I do not love him.”

“Well, then, the gentleman you do not love—seated here at this table. Dictate to me what you would say to him.”

“If he were here,” she said, “I’d say, ‘Go away.’”

Gerard, who had been preparing his pen, laid it down with a sigh.

“And when he was gone,” added Floretta, “your highness would say, ‘Come back.’”

“Likely enough, wench. Now, silence. Let me think. He begged me to write, and I promised—my honor is engaged. What lie shall I tell Gerardo to tell the fool?” She turned her head away, chin resting on her clenched hand, deep in thought.

She was so beautiful, so statuesque, so inspired—yet crafting a falsehood—that Gerard forgot everything except art. He began to sketch her profile with feverish intensity.

He was nearly finished when she turned abruptly.

“Nay, signora,” he said, a little impatient, “for Heaven’s sake, don’t move—your pose was perfect. Look, you’re almost done.”

All eyes turned to the drawing. “How lifelike! Done in a minute! Though perhaps her chin isn’t quite right.”

“Oh, a touch will fix it.”

“What a shame it’s not colored. I’m all for color. Black and white? Bah! And her skin—so fair. Take away her skin, and half her beauty vanishes.”

“Peace. Can you paint, Ser Gerardo?”

“Aye, signorina. I’m no master at oils—Pietro shines there—but in small works, I can tint you to life—if you have time to spare.”

“Call this vanity? And time? It hangs on me like lead. Send for your colors—now—this very moment—for the love of all saints!”

“Nay, signorina, I must prepare them. I could come later.”

“So be it. And you, Floretta, see that he is admitted at all hours. Alack! Leave my head! Leave my head!”

“I beg pardon, signora. I thought to prepare it at home for coloring. But I’ll leave it. Now, let us finish the letter.”

“What letter?”

“To Signor Orsini.”

“And shall I waste my time writing letters—to that empty creature, whom I regard as cold as the moon? Nay, not indifferent—I’ve just discovered my true feeling. I hate him. I despise him. Girls, I hereby forbid you to mention his name again—or I’ll whip you till blood flows. You know how I strike when angered.”

“We do. We do.”

“Then provoke me not,” she snapped, her eye flashing like a blade. Then, instantly sweet, she turned to Gerard. “Addio, il Gerardo.” And he bowed himself out of the velvet tiger’s den.

The next day, he returned to color her portrait. Soon he was commissioned to paint her full-length, then a large-scale likeness. He was granted two hours daily to draw and paint her—her beauty and vanity vast, her admirers many. Thus, Gerard found a new and profitable source of income.

Margaret seemed closer than ever.

It was Holy Thursday. No work was done. Fra Colonna and Gerard sat in a window, watching the religious processions. The number and fervor of the crowds stirred Gerard deeply—devotion had replaced earthly pleasures.

Soon the Pope appeared, majestic at the head of his cardinals, wearing a red hat, white cloak, and a red velvet capuchin, riding a white Neapolitan barb adorned with red velvet and golden tassels. Behind him rode a hundred horsemen, fully armored, lances raised, the shafts resting on their thighs. Every fifteen steps, the Pope paused briefly to bless the people, then continued.

They descended and walked through side streets to reach the portico of one of the seven churches. It was draped in black. Soon the Pope and cardinals emerged from another entrance, standing on the steps with torches, separated from the crowd by barriers. A canon read a Latin Bull, excommunicating named individuals—especially princes who denied the Church temporal power.

Gerard trembled. So did the people. But two cardinals ruined the solemnity by laughing openly throughout.

When it ended, the black cloth was removed, revealing a bright display. The Pope blessed the crowd and tossed his torch among them. Two cardinals did the same. Instantly, a brawl erupted—people fought for the torches, tearing them apart, gaining fragments at the cost of bruises, bloody noses, and burnt fingers. Then, amid the chaos, the Pope and his retinue withdrew in peace.

A cry went up. The crowd surged toward a square where a stage stood. Priests prayed, then donned red gloves. One knelt, reverently drew from a shrine a square frame resembling a mirror—and within it, a faint impression of a face.

It was the *Verum Icon*, the true image of Christ’s face taken at His agony. Received without question, it moved every heart.

People fell to their knees when the priest raised it. Tears flowed. Cries of sorrow echoed. After a while, the priest circled the platform, showing it briefly to those near—each glimpse met with fresh cries of grief.

Later, they encountered a procession of Flagellants—bare-chested men whipping themselves until blood ran down their backs, yet smiling, jesting, unaffected by pain. Bystanders offered wine; they accepted it, but rarely drank. Instead, they used it to clean the lashes, making the next blow sharper. Most were boys. A young woman pitied one fair urchin.

“Alas, dear child,” she said, “why wound your fair skin so?”

“Basta,” he laughed, “it’s for your sins I do it—not mine.”

“Hear that?” said the friar. “Show me the whip that can beat vanity from a man’s heart! The young monkey—how does he know a stranger’s sin is greater than his own?”

“Father,” said Gerard, “surely this is not pleasing to our Lord. He was merciful.”

“Our Lord?” said the friar, crossing himself. “What does He have to do with this? This custom existed in Rome six hundred years before He was born. Boys used to lash themselves during the Lupercalia. Married women even tried to get struck—believing the blows brought fertility. A foolish ritual, but interesting. It reminds us of the great heathen past. We forget too much of what we owe them.”

Next, they entered one of the seven churches to witness the Pope celebrate Mass. The ceremony was impressive—but spoiled by prelates who sat about the altar with hats on, chattering like geese.

Before the Pope took communion, an official tasted the Eucharist. Gerard was stunned. “Who is that man? What is he doing?”

“The *Preguste*,” said the friar. “He tastes the sacrament as a precaution. Poison is common here—Popes fall often.”

“But after consecration,” argued Gerard, “the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood. Poison cannot remain. The substance is gone.”

“So says Faith,” replied the friar. “But experience tells otherwise. Scores have died in Italy poisoned in the host.”

“And I tell you, father, even if both elements were laced with poison before consecration, I would take them without fear afterward.”

“So would I—but for the fine arts.”

“What mean you?”

“I would gladly leave this world, were it not for the arts. They beautify life, make it precious to the educated and thoughtful. No—so long as the Nine Muses scatter roses along my path, Apollo may inspire me with wisdom and caution. Knowing the tricks of my countrymen, I will avoid poison—whether at God’s altar or a friend’s table. For wherever I eat it, it will surely end my mortal thread. And I am writing a book—my soul in it—*The Dream of Polifilo*, the man of many arts. Do not speak of poison to me until it is finished and copied.”

Suddenly, the great bells of St. John Lateran rang in short, sharp peals. The people rushed to see the heads of St. Peter and St. Paul.

Gerard and the friar secured a good view. A heavy curtain hung across the altar. After tense silence, it was drawn back in jerks. At thirty feet high, two bearded faces appeared—lifelike, almost alive.

St. Peter had a pale, oval face, grey forked beard, crowned with a papal mitre. St. Paul was dark-skinned, thick-bearded, square-jawed, resolute.

Gerard was awestruck. The friar approved, in his own way.

“This exhibition of *imagines*—wax effigies of heroes—is an ancient custom. It inspires the common folk with virtue through powerful, invisible examples.”

“Wax images?” said Gerard. “But are they not the apostles themselves, embalmed?”

The friar sighed.

“They did not exist in 800. Roman families always displayed *imagines* at funerals—portraits of ancestors, linking past and present. I find nothing more moving or instructive. But those effigies were made during life or at death. These of Peter and Paul are pure invention.”

“Ah, but say not so, father.”

“The worst is the way they are shown—on a shelf, half in darkness, in snatches, with that mountebank trick of the drawn curtain.”

Enough. Men of today are not men of old. Let us leave these modern farces and return to the Pope’s books—there we shall find wisdom we cannot find in Rome’s streets.”

And so, once the idea took root, the friar pushed through the crowd, heedless of direction, until he reached the quiet sanctuary of the Vatican Library, among the dead and the wise.

Later, entering Gerard’s room, he found the young man in heated debate with Jacques Bonaventura. The soldier had just returned from a ceremony he found absurd—the Pope’s blessing of beasts of burden.

“It is ridiculous!” Jacques declared. “A Pope blessing donkeys?”

“Nothing a Pope does can be ridiculous,” Gerard insisted.

The argument grew intense. The friar stood silent, waiting—like the stork who eats the frog and mouse after their fight—to grind both sides in the jaws of antiquity.

Then, softly, the curtain was drawn. An old man stood there, wearing a purple skullcap, a beard like white silk, his face kind but frail.

“Happy youth,” he said, “that can heat yourselves over such matters.”

They all knelt. It was the Pope.

“Rise, my children,” he said, almost irritated. “I came not to be in state. How goes Plutarch?”

Gerard brought his manuscript, knelt, and presented it. The Pope sat; the others stood.

His Holiness examined it closely.

“Excellent,” he said.

Gerard’s heart swelled.

“Ah, this Plutarch—what art he had, Francesco. Each character stands alive on his page. Full of nature, yet unlike any other. He sees men as they are.”

Jacques Bonaventura spoke up. “Give me Signor Boccaccio.”

“An excellent storyteller, capitano,” said the Pope. “He writes exquisite Italian. But his spirit is too monotonous. Monks and nuns were not all unchaste. A few tales are diverting, but fifty paint his age falsely and sadden the heart. Moreover, he lacks skill in character. This Greek—Plutarch—is supreme. He carves men with his pen. Turn his pages, and enter a real world—of war, politics, business, love in its place. With him, men are not all chasing women. Compare this broad field to Boccaccio’s narrow garden—his little round of dishonest pleasures.”

“Your holiness,” said Jacques, “they say you wrote a novel.”

“My holiness has done more foolish things than one. When I wrote novels, I never dreamed I’d be head of the Church.”

“I search in vain for a copy to add to my library.”

The Pope smiled faintly. “You shall not find it.”

The Princess Claelia decided she wished to have a full-length portrait painted. Gerard suggested his friend Pietro Vanucci, but she refused. “We’ll see how well the Gerardo does before I give him any special favour,” she said, with a hint of challenge.

Gerard, knowing he was skilled in drawing but less confident in colouring, proposed that she pose as a Roman statue. He showed her how closely he could imitate marble on paper. She agreed at first—but hesitated when he explained that she would need to wear the ancient garments: tunic, toga, and sandals.

“Why,” she said bluntly, “I’d just as soon appear in my nightgown.”

“Oh, signorina,” Gerard replied, “you’ve never truly seen the dignity of classical dress—how free, noble, and graceful it is. And it suits you perfectly. Heaven has given you Roman features, a shapely arm, and hands worthy of antiquity. You are born for this!”

“You can flatter like the rest, then, Gerardo?” she teased. “Give me time to think. Come back on Saturday, and I’ll tell you yes or no.”

In the days that followed, the princess’s chamber became a scene of quiet preparation. The tunic and toga were carefully sewn, tried on, and adjusted—each fold examined to see if it enhanced her beauty enough to justify its anachronism.

As Gerard hurried toward their meeting, something arrested him in his tracks—a shop window. His trained eye caught sight of an open book: Lactantius. “At least it’s well written,” he thought.

But then he saw: it wasn’t handwritten. It was printed.

He groaned inwardly. “It’s over. My enemy stands at the door. The printing press has reached Rome.”

He stepped inside, pretending calmness, and asked how long printing had been in the city. The shopkeeper chuckled. “No press here, messer. That Lactantius? It came from the top of the Apennines.”

“Did the press fall from the moon?”

“No, messer,” laughed the man. “It rose from Germany. See the title page!”

Gerard took the book eagerly. The imprint read:

“Would you buy it, messer?” the seller asked. “Look at the letters—so even, so fine. Few scribes today can match them. And half the price!”

“I would gladly take it,” Gerard said sadly, “but my heart won’t let me. Know that I am a calligrapher—and these disciples of Fust chase me across the world, stealing my bread. Yet I wish them no ill.” He turned and left quickly.

“Dear Margaret,” he murmured to himself, “we must act now. We must gather our harvest while the sun shines. One month more, and a flood of type will pour down from those mountains—destroying us all who write by hand.”

He ran to the princess’s residence.

He was ushered into a room unfamiliar to him—small but opulent. A fountain played gently in the centre, and the floor was covered with panther skins, so thick no footstep could be heard. It was an antechamber to her private boudoir, one side open only to a rich tapestry curtain.

Left alone, Gerard began to grow uneasy—had he been led to the wrong place?

Then, a light step approached behind the curtain. It parted, and there stood a figure that might have inspired worship among the ancients. Not quite Venus, not quite Minerva—but a fusion of both. Nobler than Venus, softer than Jupiter’s daughter. Her attire was entirely ancient—tunic, toga, sandals—no trace of modern fashion. And her beauty—ah, that transcended time.

Gerard leapt up, every artist’s instinct aflame.

“Oh!” he breathed, staring.

That very gaze deepened her charm. A blush warmed her cheeks; her eyes sparkled; her lips curved into a smile of quiet delight.

After a moment, she spoke. “Well, Gerardo, you see I’ve made myself an antique monster for you.”

“A monster?” he replied. “I doubt Fra Colonna would kneel and worship you in such garb.”

“Nay, I care not to be adored by an old man. I’d rather be loved by a young one—by one of my own choosing.”

He pulled out his pencils, arranged his canvas, covered with sturdy paper, and began to draw. So absorbed was he that he paid no heed to his model. At last, after nearly an hour of stillness, she spoke faintly: “Gerardo, I cannot stand like this any longer—even for you.”

“Sit down and rest, Signora.”

“Thank you,” she whispered, sinking into a chair, pale and sighing.

Gerard felt alarmed. He saw he had been careless. He fetched water from the fountain and moved to splash it on her face—but she raised a delicate hand. “No. Hold it to my brow with your hand. Please, don’t throw it.”

Tentatively, he touched her forehead with his wet palm.

“Ah!” she sighed. “That revives me. Again.”

He did so again. She thanked him and rang a small bell on the table. He obeyed. A maid arrived and was sent to fetch Floretta with a large fan.

Floretta returned swiftly with the fan.

No sooner had she entered than the princess’s nostrils flared—like a bloodhorse sensing danger. “Wretch!” she snapped, rising with sudden strength. She seized Floretta’s hair with one hand and struck her sharply three times across the ears.

Floretta screamed and wept—but received no mercy.

The bare arm beneath the toga moved with startling power—like a piston—delivering heavy slaps to Floretta’s shoulders. The final blow drove her sobbing through the curtain, where her cries echoed for some time.

“Saints of heaven!” Gerard cried. “What has she done?”

“She knows well,” the princess said coldly. “It’s not the first time. The foul beast! I’ll teach her to come near me smelling of musk-cat.”

“But, signora,” Gerard protested, “it seems a small fault.”

“A small fault? No—it’s a vile one.” Then, with sudden humility, she added, “Are you angry with me for striking her, Gerar-do?”

“Signora,” he replied gently, “it ill becomes me to correct you. But surely one meant to rule others should first rule herself.”

“That is true,” she said softly. “How wise you are, for your youth.” She called another maid and handed her a purse. “Take this to Floretta. Tell her ‘the Gerardo’ pleaded for her—and so I must forgive her. There, Gerardo.”

He blushed deeply at the compliment—but, unsure how to respond, asked if he should resume painting.

“Not yet,” she said. “Beating that hussy has refreshed me. Sit awhile. Talk to me. I know you can talk—as well as you draw.”

“That would be easy,” he said.

“Then do it, Gerardo.”

He was taken aback. “But, signora, I don’t know what to say. This is sudden.”

“Say what you truly feel. Say you wish you were anywhere but here.”

“No, signora,” he answered. “But I do wish one thing.”

“And what is that?” she asked, gentle now.

“I wish I could have drawn you as you struck that girl. You were terrible—yet beautiful. Oh, what a subject for a Pythoness!”

“Ah,” she murmured, “he thinks only of art. Why fuss over my beauty, Gerardo? You are far fairer than I. More like Apollo than I am Venus. And you have lovely eyes and hair—but you don’t know what to do with them.”

“I do,” he said. “To draw you, signora.”

“Yes,” she smiled. “You see my features—but not what any Roman gallant would have seen in your place long ago. Yet surely you’ve noticed how much you mean to me, Gerardo?”

“I see your highness is always kind to me—a poor stranger.”

“No, Gerardo,” she said quietly. “I’ve often been cold, even rude. You’re too simple to see why. I feared my own heart. I feared becoming your slave. I who have always made others slaves. Ah, Gerardo, I am unhappy. Ever since you came, I’ve lived for your visits. The day you come, I am bright. The other days—listless, wishing they were past. You are unlike the Roman nobles. You make me hate them. You are ten times braver in my eyes. Wise, scholarly, never flattering or lying. I despise men who lie. Gerar-do, teach me your magic—teach me to make you as happy beside me as I am beside you.”

Her voice sank to a whisper, trembling with suppressed emotion. Her white hand slid down his arm, resting lightly on his wrist—like a bird seeking shelter, ready to flee at a word.

Gerard, innocent and devoted to Margaret and his art, had not foreseen this moment—though it had crept upon him gradually. He blushed, his heart pounding. He admired her regal beauty, but Margaret remained in his soul. Yet this was real—passionate, tender, overwhelming. How to refuse without hurting her?

He trembled.

She saw and encouraged him. “Poor Gerardo,” she murmured. “Don’t fear. No harm shall come to you under my wing. Will you not speak to me, Gerar-do mio?”

“Signora,” he stammered.

His gaze dropped—falling on her delicate hand curled around his elbow, like a vine. And suddenly, he remembered how that same arm had struck Floretta.

He flushed again.

“Alas,” she sighed. “I frighten you. Am I so terrible? Is it the Roman robe? I’ll take it off—dress as you first saw me. Remember? To write a letter to that barren knight Ercole d’Orsini. Shall I tell you? It was seeing you—your manners, your words—that made me hate him instantly. I liked him well enough before—or thought I did. Now—how many times have you been here since then? Eighteen, Gerardo. And each time dearer. When you don’t come, it’s night, not day, to Claelia. Alas—I speak for both. Cruel boy, am I not worth a word? Do you have a princess at your feet every day? Speak to me, Gerar-do.”

“Signora,” he faltered, “what can I say that wouldn’t be better left unsaid? Oh, cursed day I ever came here.”

“Ah!” she said. “Do not say that. It was the brightest day of my life—and perhaps yours too. I’ll make you admit it soon, ungrateful one.”

“Your highness,” he began, voice low and pleading.

“Call me Claelia, Gerar-do.”

“Signora,” he continued, “I am too young, too inexperienced to know how to speak to you—without seeming blind or ungrateful. But this I know: I would be both unworthy and ungrateful, and your worst enemy, if I took advantage of this madness. Surely some evil spirit has allowed you to suffer this. For it is unnatural that a princess of grace should lower herself to love a commoner.”

She slowly withdrew her hand from his wrist—yet as it passed, it lingered a moment, as if reluctant to leave.

“You fear my kinsmen’s daggers,” she said, half sad, half scornful.

“No more than I fear your women’s bodkins,” he replied proudly. “But I fear God, the saints, and my own conscience.”

“The truth, Gerardo—the truth! Hypocrisy sits poorly on you. Princesses aren’t scorned for loving God—but for loving another woman. Tell me whom you love. If she is worthy, I’ll forgive you.”

“No woman in Italy,” he swore. “Upon my soul.”

“Ah,” she said. “Then there is one elsewhere. Where?”

“In Holland. My native land.”

“Ah! Marie de Bourgoyne is fair, they say. But she is only a child.”

“Princess, the woman I love is not noble. She is like me. Nor is she as fair as you. Yet she is fair—and bound to my heart forever by virtue, by shared dangers, by griefs borne together. Forgive me—but I would not betray my Margaret for all the noblewomen in Italy.”

The princess rose abruptly—paler now, fiercer than before. Her eyes burned with fury.

“This to my face, wretched man?” she shrieked. “Was I born to be insulted as well as scorned? Beware! We nobles brook no rivals. Choose: the love of a Cesarini—or her hatred. After all I have done for you, it must be love or hate—until death. Choose now!”

He looked up at her—awe-struck. She stood tall in her toga, offering him a choice like a goddess of old. He, a mere mortal.

He sighed deeply—but said nothing.

Perhaps his silence stirred pity. Or perhaps passion ebbed, and sorrow flowed. She sank into a seat, tears rolling down her cheeks.

“Alas,” Gerard whispered. “Do not weep, sweet lady. Your tears accuse me—and I may weep too. Be yourself, my kind patron. You’ll see how much better a friend I am than I seemed.”

“I see it now,” she said. “Friend is the only word that can pass between us. I was mad. Any other man would have used my folly. You must teach me to be your friend—and nothing more.”

Gerard rejoiced. He quoted Cicero on the nobility of friendship—how it surpasses love in depth and lastingness. To prove his sincerity, he even told her of Denys and their bond.

She listened, eyes half-closed, studying him—not just his words, but his soul.

At last, she said calmly: “Leave me now, Gerardo. Come tomorrow as usual. You will find your lesson well spent.”

She held out her hand. He kissed it—and left, pondering deeply.

The next day, she received him with cold distance. She stood before him like a statue, dismissed him after a brief sitting. He felt the chill—but told himself, “She is wise.” Indeed, she was, in her way.

The following day, she sat surrounded by young nobles, all flattering her extravagantly. They treated Gerard like a dog who could perform one trick. The cavaliers mocked his work with ignorant arrogance—making his cheeks burn.

She watched him silently, half-lidded eyes noting every flicker of anger.

When they left, she shut the doors against them all.

The next day, she was alone—cold and silent. After standing for some time, she said, “You treated my company with less respect than was fitting.”

“Did I, signora?”

“Did you? You glowered at their comments—honours they paid your work.”

“I said nothing,” he replied.

“Oh, your looks speak plainly. Your face was crimson.”

“I was irritated—seeing such ignorance and malice together.”

“Now you insult me, their hostess.”

“Forgive me, signora. I meant no disrespect. I have no greater patron or friend in Rome—except one.”

“How humble you are suddenly. In truth, Ser Gerardo, you are a master of pretence. You can insult or grovel at will.”

“Grovel? To whom?”

“To me—for one. To one you once offended for a base-born girl like yourself—yet whose favour you claim.”

Gerard rose, hand to his heart. “These are harsh words. Have I truly deserved them?”

“What are words to an adventurer like you? Only cold steel terrifies you?”

“I am no duelist—but I’ve met steel with steel. And I’d rather face your kinsmen’s swords than your cruel tongue, lady. Why do you treat me so?”

“Gerar-do,” she said, “for no good reason—only because I am capricious, sharp-tongued, and curst. Because everyone admires me—except you.”

“I admire you, signora. Your friends may flatter more—but none see half your beauty. Their babble yesterday proved it. None admire you more truly, or wish you better, than I—the poor artist who cannot be your lover—but hoped to be your friend. Yet I see that cannot be—between one so high, and one so low.”

“Ay,” she said eagerly, “but it shall, Gerardo. I will not be so harsh. Tell me—where does your Margaret live? I’ll send her a gift. On that, we shall be friends.”

“She is the daughter of a physician named Peter. They live in Sevenbergen. Ah me—will I ever see it again?”

“Good. Now go.”

She dismissed him abruptly.

Poor Gerard. He had entered deep waters with this Italian princess—crafty and fiery. He resolved to finish her portrait and never return. Indeed, he regretted having begun such a task.

But his resolve wavered when the next day brought kindness.

After posing for some time, she said she was tired—and wanted his help in another way: would he teach her to draw?

He sat beside her, guiding her hand through simple lines. She learned quickly.

“I had a teacher before you, Gerar-do,” she said. “And one as handsome as you.”

She opened a drawer and pulled out several drawings—crude but full of spirit. All were of Gerard—some surprisingly accurate.

“There,” she said. “Now you see who taught me.”

“Not I, signora.”

“Who teaches us women to do all things? Love, Gerar-do. Love made me draw—because you draw. Love prints your image in my heart. My fingers touch the pen—and love supplies the lack of skill. And lo—your face lies on the paper.”

Gerard stared. “Oh, signora—you promised friendship only.”

She laughed. “How naive you are. Who believes a woman promising nonsense? Friendship? Foolish boy—no temple is built on red ashes. Between you and me, it must be love or hate.”

“Which you choose, signora,” he said firmly. “But I will neither love nor hate you. With your permission, I will leave.”

He rose.

She rose too—pale as death. “Before you go—know your fate. Outside that door wait armed men. One word from me—and they will kill you.”

“But you will not speak that word.”

“That word I will speak. And I’ll spread it abroad: that you were slain for daring to offer me brutal love. I’ll send a clever messenger to Sevenbergen—one who knows his tale. Your Margaret will hear you dead—and believe you faithless. Go to your grave like a dog. For a man you are not.”

Gerard turned white. “God have mercy on us both.”

“No,” she said. “Have mercy on her—and on yourself. She’ll never know what you do in Rome—unless I’m forced to tell her. Yield, Gerar-do mio. What does it cost to say you love me? Just feign it—handsomely. You are young. Don’t die for the sake of denying a lady the shadow of a heart. Who will weep for you? Men will laugh at your tombstone—ah!”

She screamed—because Gerard threw himself at her feet and poured out his story in one impassioned torrent: his love for Margaret, her sacrifice, his imprisonment, the bloodhounds, exile, the perils across Europe, the beasts, the attacks, the shipwreck—all for her.

The princess trembled, trying to pull away—but he clung to her robe, holding her hand, crying into it, pleading with her to consider the suffering of true lovers torn apart, and the remorse that would follow such a betrayal.

In such moments, no one resisted Gerard.

She finally broke. “You conquer me,” she sobbed. “You—or my better angel. Leave Rome!”

“I will. I will.”

“If you speak a word of my folly, it will be your last.”

“Never,” he said. “You are my benefactress again. Would I slander you?”

“Go. I’ll send you the means. I know myself—if you cross my path again, I’ll kill you. Addio. My heart is broken.”

She rang the bell. “Floretta,” she called, voice choked. “Take him safely out—through my chamber, by the side postern.”

He turned at the door. She leaned on a chair, head bowed, weeping.

He thought only of her kindness—and ran back to kiss her robe.

She did not move.

Once outside, he dashed home, thanking Heaven for his escape.

“Landlady,” he said, “someone wants to fight me. What should I do?”

“Strike first—when you have the advantage! Get behind him, then draw.”

“Alas, I lack your courage. To be serious—it’s a noble.”

“Oh, holy saints—that changes everything. Change your lodging. Stay hidden. And alter your clothes.”

She took him to her niece, who offered rooms farther away. He settled in.

With no portrait to paint, he turned to the deed of Floris Brandt—finally reading it. He understood at once: the loan had been repaid repeatedly through rents. Ghysbrecht was illegally keeping Peter Brandt from his land.

“Fool!” he exclaimed. “Why didn’t I read this before?”

He hired a horse and rode to the nearest port. A ship sailed for Amsterdam in four days.

He booked passage and paid extra to secure it.

“The land is full of cutthroats,” he said. “But the sea is fair weather. Our Dutch skippers don’t sink like these clumsy Italians.”

When he returned home, his landlady sat waiting—eyes sparkling.

“News,” she said. “You’re safe. But beware—your name is already spoken in certain circles. They say you were seen leaving the palace with a secret. And that you fled Rome.”

Gerard stirred back into awareness, only to be swallowed by despair. By the second day, fever had seized his mind, and he raged in delirium, his thoughts torn apart by pain and confusion. Near his bed lay his long auburn hair—rich as autumn flame, cut from his head like a sacrifice. The sickness advanced swiftly, one symptom following another with cruel haste. On the fifth day, the physician left him, declaring there was no hope. That same evening, as the sun dipped below the horizon, Gerard sank into a deep, unbroken sleep.

Some whispered he would wake only to die. But an old woman, once a nurse of many years’ experience, held firm in her belief. “If he sleeps twelve hours,” she said, “his youth may yet save him.” So she cleared the room, drove away all but the faithful, and stayed alone by his side. She vowed a candle to the Virgin for each hour he rested. At twelve hours, he still breathed evenly. She knelt in joy, thanking the Mother of God. Then twenty-four hours passed. Still he slept. Her certainty wavered. By the thirtieth hour, she sent for the midwife, the wise woman of the town.

“Thirty hours!” the midwife said, peering closely at him. “Shall we rouse him?”

She studied him long, then shook her head. “His breath is calm, his hand soft. I’ve seen learned doctors wake patients to examine their tongues, only to find nothing new. But we women know better—we trust nature. Sleep has never harmed a wounded mind or a broken heart.”

Forty-eight hours passed before word spread. Soon, people gathered outside, eager to glimpse the dying poet. But only two were allowed in: Fra Colonna, his friend and mentor, and the towering Fra Jerome, a man of quiet strength and unwavering faith. They took turns watching over him, silent and solemn. Colonna sat near the bed, eyes brimming with sorrow, while Jerome prayed softly, beads in hand, his face as steady as stone.

It was near the sixtieth hour when the landlady nudged Colonna gently. He turned—and saw it: Gerard’s eyes had opened, not with alarm, but with the softness of a dreamer awakening. He blinked, stared, then lifted himself slightly on his elbows. His hand went to his head—and found it bare. A shock passed through him. Then he saw Colonna, smiled faintly—then froze.

His smile shattered. His face contorted in agony so deep it seemed to tear his soul. A cry tore from his throat, raw and wild, and he turned his face to the wall, burying it in the sheets.

The landlady wept. She knew that grief—the sudden, terrible loneliness of waking to loss.

Fra Jerome recited prayers from his breviary, his voice low and soothing. Gerard curled tighter beneath the covers, trembling.

Colonna approached, voice trembling too. “My dear boy… all is not lost. Remember the Muses—they are eternal. You must give your love to them now. They will never betray you, never abandon you, as flesh and blood do.”

He spoke with tenderness, but then stepped back, overwhelmed. He could bear no more.

Fra Jerome remained. After a pause, he said, “Young man, the Muses live only in the minds of pagans and dreamers. Only the Church offers true peace—here and beyond. If the world has deceived you, if passion has torn your heart, the Church stands open. Offer your talents to her. In her arms, you will find rest. The Church is peace.”

He spoke these words gravely, then turned and left.

“Peace?” Gerard shouted, rising abruptly, his fist clenched toward the door. “Malediction upon the Church! If it weren’t for the Church, I wouldn’t lie here broken—while she lies cold, cold, cold in Holland! Oh, Margaret! My darling! My love! And I had to flee from you—just when you needed me most! Cruel! Cruel! These monsters let her die! Death comes with signs—signs they ignored, or didn’t care to see. But I saw them—I who loved her! If I had been there, I would have saved her. I would have saved her! Fool! Fool! To leave her even for a moment!”

He wept long and hard, his body wracked with sobs. Then, suddenly, rage flared again. “The Church!” he screamed. “For whose sake I was cast from her! Cursed be the Church! And cursed be the hypocrites who speak its name to my shattered heart! Accursed be this world! Ghysbrecht lives—Margaret dies! Thieves, murderers, harlots live forever. Only angels die. Curse life! Curse death! And curse whoever made them so!”

The friar heard only the roar of fury behind him. It was better so. Had he understood, he might have summoned the Inquisition without hesitation—just as he would have roasted a kid for supper.

The landlady, who had followed Colonna down the stairs, heard the shouting and returned, alarmed. She found Gerard dressing, his movements frantic.

“What good does it do to lie here?” he muttered. “Can I find what I seek?”

“Saints preserve us!” she gasped. “Are you mad again? What do you seek?”

“Oblivion.”

“Oblivion, my child? You’re too young to say such things.”

“Young or old, what else is there to live for?”

He pulled on his finest clothes, ignoring her protests.

“My dear Gerard,” she pleaded, “remember—it’s Tuesday. Not Sunday.”

“Oh,” he said dully, “Tuesday? I thought it was Saturday.”

“No, you’ve slept long. You never wear these clothes on weekdays. Think, boy.”

“I did what I did when she lived,” he replied. “Now I’ll do what I never dared. The past is gone. There lies my hair—gone with my old life. I served one Master faithfully. See my reward. Now I’ll serve another—and give him a fair trial.”

“Alas,” she whispered, turning pale, “what do you mean? What new master?”

And with those dreadful words on his lips, he stepped out into the dim light—cap tilted jauntily, feather crooked, limbs weak, face drawn and ash-white, eyes hollow, mouth twisted in defiance. A man undone, walking toward ruin with the grim resolve of one who has nothing left to lose.

A Shadow Falls on a Noble Heart

The light that had guided Gerard—his pure, unyielding love for Margaret—was extinguished. Without it, he drifted through life like a ship without a compass, adrift upon a sea of despair. He was not merely crushed by grief; he was consumed by rage at himself. All his sacrifice, his endurance, his courage, his virtue—what had they wrought? Nothing. Worse: they had cost him the one thing he held most dear. If only he had stayed home, selfish and idle, perhaps Margaret would still be alive. That thought gnawed at him day and night, a poison in his blood, fueling both his sorrow and his fury.

And so, with no anchor left to hold him, he threw himself into pleasure—not for joy, but to escape. In those times, pleasure was not mere indulgence—it was corruption. Wine flowed freely, women were sought for fleeting thrills, and gambling offered the briefest moments of oblivion. He plunged into these vices as if seeking death among enemy bullets. The money he had saved for Margaret’s future now poured into reckless excess. Soon, he became the leader of a pack of men he once despised—men who lived only for the moment, careless of consequence or conscience.

His soul grew colder as his body weakened. He resented his old landlady, who still tried to warn him with gentle words. Her concern only irritated him. Finally, he moved away, fleeing not just her advice, but the memories that haunted every corner of his former home. When he could no longer write with steady hand—when even the art that had once brought him peace failed him—he turned to painting. But even that he abandoned when his companions called. He painted no more, unless forced. Instead, he drowned himself in the filth of the world, chasing the hollow shell of forgetfulness.

I need not describe every sordid scene in which this young man now took part. But I must say plainly: he was a rake, a drunkard, a debauchee—one of the wildest and most reckless youths in Rome. To hide the sins of the good is not kindness; it is deceit. It denies hope to those who fall and wish to rise again. Gerard did not walk halfway into vice. He fell entirely. And he fell fast.

His former friends whispered about him. His old landlady told Teresa he was slipping into ruin, begging her to find where he had gone. Teresa spoke to her husband, Lodovico. “Do you remember his face?” she asked.

“Teresa,” Lodovico replied, “a man like me never forgets a face—especially a benefactor’s. But you know I rarely go out in daylight.”

She sighed. “And how long will it be so, Lodovico?”

“Until some nobleman runs me through with his sword. They won’t let a poor fellow like me take up honest work.”

Pietro Vanucci was one of those who suffered prosperity worse than poverty. After being thrown out by their landlady for staying out too late, he met Gerard in the street and greeted him warmly. Soon after, he moved into the same house. With him came Andrea—a young boy who ground his pigments, studied under him, and served as his model. Andrea was strikingly beautiful, sharp-witted, and full of spirit. Pietro claimed to cherish old memories and professed deep friendship for Gerard. But Gerard, whose heart seemed frozen, accepted the overtures with cold indifference. Their companionship was a strange alliance—two souls bound only by shared excess, yet utterly alien to each other.

Pietro was not only a libertine but half a misanthrope, openly mocking faith and morality. Together, they wandered through Rome’s pleasures, united only by their desire to escape themselves.

One day, when Gerard’s health had begun to fail and his beauty faded beneath the weight of wine and sleepless nights, Vanucci planned a grand outing. They would travel up the Tiber in a galley drawn by buffaloes—creatures Lorenzo de’ Medici had recently introduced to Florence, but still new to Rome. Vanucci insisted on this spectacle, declaring it the height of fashion. Each man was to bring a woman—handsome, or face a fine. The one bringing the most beautiful would be crowned with laurel and hailed as a public benefactor. Such was their twisted interpretation of *“Vir bonus est quis?”* —“Who is the good man?”

They gathered at the riverbank. A magnificent galley awaited, pulled by twelve massive buffaloes. The libertines and their companions arrived one by one. But Gerard was missing. They waited—first patiently, then with growing impatience. Vanucci made excuses. “He said he forgot to bring a fardingale,” he laughed. “The lad’s searching for a beauty worthy to stand beside these peerless ladies. Be patient, ladies—such a task demands time.”

At last, Gerard appeared, walking briskly with a woman at his side. From afar, one woman remarked, “She’s tall enough.” Another added, “Look at those strides!” Pietro joked, “It’s wise to hurry into good company.” But when they reached the boat, all speech died.

Gerard’s companion was breathtaking—so radiant that she dimmed the others like stars before dawn. Tall, yet graceful; straight as an arrow, yet lithe as a young panther. Her face was a flawless oval, her forehead pale, her cheeks a rich olive hue flushed with living color. Her eyes—large, dark, and framed by thick, silken lashes—seemed made to captivate hearts. Her lips were red and bold, her teeth white as ivory. The women stared in silence, their spirits crushed. The men roared with delight. One leapt onto the gunwale and knelt, shouting, “Divine! You are born of heaven!”

But the goddess, amused, kicked him gently, and another woman tugged his hair. He toppled backward, sprawling across the deck. She stepped lightly over him, ignoring him completely, and took her seat at the prow.

Vanucci sat stunned, mouth agape, like a fish gasping its last breath. The drover shouted, the ropes tightened, and the galley began to move upstream.

“What think you of our new beast, ladies?” someone asked.

“Monstrous creatures!” one woman scoffed. “Those horns make me afraid. Their nostrils are holes, not noses!”

“A gift from Florence,” another retorted. “Would you look a present cow in the nose?”

“They’re slow,” complained a lively lady. “Last time I went up the Tiber twice as fast with five mules and an ass.”

“Then we’ll fix that,” declared a gallant, jumping ashore. Drawing his sword, he charged the buffaloes despite the drivers' protests, urging them forward. They snorted, flicked their tails, but refused to quicken. The crowd laughed. Then he jabbed a massive bull, who turned instantly, impaling him with his horns and hurling him high into the air. He arced through space and landed splashing into the yellow Tiber, still clutching his sword.

The women shrieked and wrung their hands—except Gerard’s companion. She muttered something that sounded like an oath, seized the helm, and steered the boat toward him. He surfaced sputtering, grabbed the edge, and was hauled aboard dripping wet. Dazed, he looked around. “I do not understand this,” he muttered, annoyed. “One moment I am pricking African beef, the next—”

Gerard’s companion interrupted. “Disporting in your native stream.”

“Tell him nothing,” Vanucci cried. “Let him solve his own riddle.”

“Confound you all,” the man grumbled. “I might puzzle my brain till doomsday and never find it. Also—where is my sword?”

“Ask the Tiber,” she replied. “Your best course, signor, is to repeat the deed. Prick African beef until your mind sees the light. So shall you comprehend—like lawyers climbing heaven, or buffaloes ascending the Tiber.”

A knight observed that she surpassed all men in wit as she did all women in beauty. At this, Vanucci changed. He stopped staring, coiled himself like a snake, and fixed his eyes on her—twinkling, scintillating with hidden fire. But she paid him no mind. Her gaze passed over him as though he were part of the bench, not a man.

Soon, the harmony broke. Jealous of the attention Gerard’s companion drew, the other women began to whisper insults—then speak aloud. The girl, unaware of subtlety, heard and retaliated.

“You wear no natural colors,” she declared. “Look here—this is cerussa, stibium, purpurissum. I know them well—I use them every day—but not on my face, thank you.”

Vanucci nearly burst with laughter.

“And your lips are colored, your veins dyed. Your black hair—like a horse’s tail—is drugged to look like tow. Your bodies are false as your faces. Look at your padded bosoms, your wooden-heeled chopines lifting your tiny limbs. Skinny dwarfs, padded into fat giants. Ah, mesdames, it is rightly said of you: *grande—di legni; grosse—di straci; rosse—betti; bianche—di calcina.*”

The women fired back. “Vulgar toad! Why tell the men everything? Your cheeks are your own, your hair natural. But who is padded more? You look like a fire-shovel!”

“Liar,” she snapped.

“Oh, the well-educated young person! Where did you find her, Ser Gerard?”

“Hold your tongue, Marcia,” Gerard said, startled from his gloom. “Be not so insolent. The grave will close over your beauty as it has over fairer than you.”

“They started it,” Marcia protested.

“Then be the first to stop.”

“At your request, my friend.” She leaned close and whispered, “I only wanted to make you laugh. You are distraught, sad. Judge whether I care for their jokes or their admiration. Dear Signor Gerard, would I be what they think I am? You should not be so sad.”
