Gerard sighed deeply, shook his head, then gently stroked her jet-black hair—like one petting a loyal dog.

Just then, a galley drifting downstream tangled briefly with their ropes. As the river curved, they shot out into the current, and the other vessel came between them and the bank. Under a canopy sat a lady of exquisite beauty—surrounded by attendants. Gerard looked up.

It was Princess Claelia.

He blushed and withdrew his hand from Marcia’s head.

Marcia gaped. “Ah, ladies—here is a rival, if you please. Those cheeks are Nature’s own—like mine.”

“Peace, child! Peace!” Gerard said sharply.

“But she didn’t hear,” Marcia insisted. “Oh, Ser Gerard, what a lovely creature!”

Two women had been watching Marcia closely. One now approached. “Signorina, do you love almonds?”

She held a lapful.

“Yes,” Marcia replied, eyeing them hungrily. “When I can get them. But yours is not the hand to give me any.”

“You are mistaken,” the woman said, tossing two handfuls into Marcia’s lap.

Marcia instinctively pressed her knees together.

“Aha!” the woman laughed. “You’re caught, my lad. It’s a man—or a boy. A woman parts her knees to catch nuts in her apron. A man closes them, fearing they’ll fall between his hose. Confess—have you ever worn a fardingale before today?”

“Give me another handful, sweetheart, and I’ll tell you.”

“There!” the woman exclaimed. “I knew he was too handsome for a woman.”

“Ser Gerard,” Marcia said calmly, cracking an almond, “they’ve found me out.”

The libertines laughed, convinced it was impossible. But Vanucci remembered a recent argument in which they had mocked Gerard and himself for claiming that men could be as beautiful as women in an artist’s eye.

“Where are you now?” he chuckled. “This is my boy Andrea. You’ve all knelt before him. Ha! ha! But oh, my little ladies—when he lectured you, flinging your stibium, cerussa, and purpurissum back in your faces—then I nearly burst. He grinds my colours. Ha! ha! he! he! ho!”

“The little impostor! Duck him!”

“What for, signors?” Andrea cried, flushing.

The women rushed to protect him. “The dear child! How sweet his ways are!”

“Oh, what eyes and teeth!”

“And eyebrows! Hair!”

“And lashes!”

“And nose!”

“The sweetest ear in the world!”

“And what health! Touch his cheek with a pin—the blood would squirt!”

“Who would be cruel?”

“He is a rosebud washed in dew.”

They lavished affection on him, revenging themselves for the men’s admiration of Marcia.

Yet one remained apart—no longer of the crowd, though still among it. The sight of Princess Claelia had reopened his wound. Less than three months ago, he had rejected her love—a love forbidden, mad, but at least noble. How far had he fallen since then? Once, he had resisted her charms, steadfast in loyalty. Now, he blushed at her presence—though such company was his daily routine. He hung over the boat in silence, lost in thought.

From that moment, a new phase of his torment began—and deepened. Some fools try to drown sorrow in drink. But the hangover comes. The pain remains. The mind grows heavier. Gerard had done the same. To endure his loss, he needed strength—his virtue, his health, his discipline, his rest, above all, his faith. Yet he cast all aside, trusting instead to the fleeting warmth of intoxication.

The fumes passed. The pain returned—deeper, darker. Now, remorse sat upon his heart like a vulture, tearing at it. His health was broken. His money gone. Innocence fled. Margaret was gone—divided from him by a chasm wider than death.

The hot storm of despair passed. The cold, creeping despair took hold. He turned from his companions, from the world. He wandered alone. Drank alone to numb his thoughts. Lied among the ruins of ancient Rome, stony-eyed and broken, worse wrecked than the temples themselves.

And finally came the end—solitude’s final temptation. He walked alone by dark rivers at night, staring into the water, his fear fading, replaced by longing. There, peace lay—perhaps annihilation. What else remained?

Such darkness has been broken by kind words, by loving voices, by a single smile from a humble friend. Perhaps Teresa, his kind-hearted landlady, would have seen through his pain and saved him. But she did not know where he was. Nor did anyone else.

Except one.

One pair of eyes watched him—every step, every turn, every silent hour. And that eye belonged to an enemy—an enemy to the death.

In a sumptuously appointed chamber, where the floor was strewn with the hides of beasts—striped and mottled in wild patterns—a woman sat rigidly, her arms outstretched before her, fingers curled into half-fists. Her face, pale one moment and flushed the next, betrayed a storm within; her foot tapped restlessly against the polished stone. Then, softly, a curtain parted as a servant stepped forward. The lady’s brow darkened.

“Altezza,” the maid whispered, trembling, “the man has arrived.”

She nodded curtly, snatching up a small black mask from the table beside her and slipping it over her features. Instantly, her color drained away, leaving her cheeks like cold marble. The contrast between the deep shadow of the mask and her pallid skin was unsettling, almost spectral.

A man entered, bowing low, his movements stiff with deference. He was unremarkable: short hair, round head, plainly dressed but neatly so. His face offered no charm, nor any sign of malice—save for his eyes, which darted about like those of a bird caught in a trap.

After a long series of bows, he stood before her, waiting.

“They have told you why you are here?” she asked.

“Yes, Signora.”

“And did they agree on the price?”

“Yes, Signora. The full sum is promised—enough to purchase the greater vendetta. Unless, by your grace, you would settle for the lesser.”

“I do not understand,” she said.

“The first time,” he replied gently, “many do not. The lesser vendetta means only the death of the body. We wait—perhaps outside a church, or when he is unsuspecting—and strike. But the greater vendetta… that takes both body and soul. We catch him while he is still hot from sin, unrepentant, and then we end him in such a way that his soul too perishes. It was more common once, but now fewer seek it.”

“Then silence his tongue,” she said, voice tight with fury. “Let his traitorous heart cease beating. But I care nothing for his soul.”

“As you wish, Signora. The man who sent me knew nothing of him—his name, his home, or his face. From whom shall I learn these things?”

“From me.”

At this, the assassin faltered slightly, his expression shifting for the first time to one of caution. “Be careful, my lady,” he murmured. “Such details are dangerous.”

“I am not afraid,” she answered, her voice rising. “Listen well. He is young, tall, with auburn hair and deep blue eyes. His face is honest—so honest it could fool a saint. He lives in the Via Claudia, in the corner house—the glover’s shop. There are only three men there: he; a painter, short and dark; and a slim boy. The one who has wronged me is a stranger—fair-haired, taller than you.”

The bravo listened intently, every sense alert.

“That is enough,” he said at last. “Does he frequent any secret place where I might meet him?”

“My spies tell me he has lately gone to the banks of the Tiber after dusk—doubtless to meet his lover, who calls me her rival. There, kill him. Let her come and find him—dead, broken, the smooth, heartless, insolent thief.”

“Do not distress yourself, Signora,” the man said quietly. “He will betray no woman again.”

“I know not that,” she snapped. “He carries a sword and knows how to use it. He is young, bold, and strong.”

“None of that will save him.”

“Are you so certain? What weapons do you carry?”

He raised his hand, revealing a steel gauntlet. “We strike hard. We must protect ourselves. This is our hammer.”

Then, with a slow motion, he opened his doublet, showing the glint of chainmail beneath. Finally, he drew forth a slender stiletto and laid it upon the table with a flourish.

The lady shivered—not from fear, but from something deeper. She reached out, her white fingers brushing the blade. She tested its edge against her own fingertip.

“Beware, madam,” the bravo warned.

“Is it poisoned?” she asked.

“God forbid! We do not steal life with poison. We take it with steel. But this blade is freshly honed. I feared for your delicate skin.”

“She has skin as fair as mine,” she said, a fleeting tenderness crossing her face—gone in an instant. “But his heart is black as soot. Tell me—do I not act rightly in destroying a traitor who slanders me?”

“You will decide that with your confessor,” he replied. “I am merely an instrument—like this knife.”

She seemed not to hear. Her thoughts wandered elsewhere.

“Oh, how I could have loved him—truly, to the death. And now I hate him. Fool! He thinks he can toy with princes, scorn them one moment, fawn on them the next, prefer the lowest scum to nobility, and make us all laughstocks!”

She looked up sharply. “Why do you delay? Go! Revenge me!”

“It is custom,” he said, “to receive half the payment before the deed.”

“Ah—I forgot. Your revenge is bought.” She pushed a bag across the table. “Here is more than half. When the blow is struck, return for the rest.”

“You will see me soon, Signora,” he said, bowing deeply, then retreating from the room.

Left alone, the princess remained seated—masked, arms stretched forward, nails digging into the table’s surface. She sat as though carved from stone, like the mythic sphinx, or a tigress guarding her young. Yet now, with the assassin gone, a coldness crept through her veins. Doubts stirred—quiet, creeping misgivings, the first whispers of regret.

Gerard and Margaret were ahead of their time. This was the true Middle Ages: proud, passionate, cruel, generous, foolish, cunning, impulsive, without principle—and utterly ignorant. Power was the curse of such a creature. Without it, her nerves would have curbed her rage, her threats outweighed by hesitation. But power gave her hands—male hands—to wield. And so, a weak, furious woman became terrifying. In this case, she had sharpened a dagger for a man already drowning in despair.

Two days after the scene I have sought to portray, Gerard found himself wandering through one of Rome’s most squalid streets when a sudden thunderstorm swept down upon him. Seeking shelter, he stepped into a lowly hostel, its walls damp and dim with age. He called for wine, and as the rain lashed against the shutters, he drank steadily until his thoughts grew heavy and his senses dulled. Soon he was half asleep, his head resting on his hands, which lay flat upon the rough-hewn table.

The room gradually filled with guests—rough men whose voices rose in boisterous talk, their laughter echoing off the stone walls. The noise stirred Gerard from his stupor, and slowly he became aware of two figures near him, speaking in hushed tones. One wore the garb of a pardoner, his robes marked by the insignia of the Church; the other, though dressed plainly and neatly, carried himself with a certain furtiveness. His hat was pulled low over his brow, concealing his face entirely save for a thick beard—a telltale sign of one who avoided both the gaze of honest folk and the reach of justice.

They were bargaining—not over goods or coin, but over sin itself. And this was no uncommon trade in those days: forgiveness could be purchased even before the crime had been committed, sealed under what was called a celestial contract.

The man in the slouched hat grumbled about the rising cost of indulgences. “If these prices keep climbing,” he muttered, “we poor souls will be barred from heaven altogether.”

The pardoner scoffed. “Indulgences have never been cheaper for good husbandmen,” he replied.

“Who are these ‘good husbandmen’?” asked the other.

“Those who sin like sensible creatures—by the market, not by passion. But if you insist on choosing a crime the Pope has condemned, then blame yourself, not me.”

To prove that vice was within reach of nearly all except the lowest dregs of society, he unfolded a parchment and read aloud the list of sins and their corresponding prices. It was an unsettling catalogue—one too explicit to print here. To omit it would distort its meaning. Yet such records still exist in great libraries, preserved as relics of a corrupt era. Suffice it to say that the murder of a layman cost less than many offences now considered trivial by common folk.

With minor concessions exchanged, the bargain was struck. Money passed hands, and the buyer received absolution in advance—for the removal of one innocent man. The price for killing a cleric was far greater, but neither man used the word *assassination*. They spoke only of "removing" and "disposing," as if trading in livestock rather than human lives.

All of this reached Gerard’s ears, yet he did not stir. He remained motionless, his head still bowed, listening with dull awareness. Only when the two men rose and parted ways did he lift his head slightly, his eyes narrowing as they followed the retreating figure of the man in the slouched hat.

“If Margaret were alive,” he muttered beneath his breath, “I’d seize thee by the throat and strangle thee, thou base coward. But she is dead—dead—dead. Let the whole world perish; it matters not to me—so long as I die among the first.”

When he returned home, he saw a man in a slouched hat walking briskly up and down the street opposite his dwelling. “Ah,” thought Gerard, “there is that cur again.” But in his present state—numb with grief and drink—the sight meant nothing. It left no mark upon him.

Two nights after the events that had stirred their household, Pietro Vanucci and Andrea sat in quiet anticipation of Gerard’s return for supper. The hour had long passed nine, yet no sign of him. Pietro grew restless, his patience wearing thin. At last, unable to endure the silence any longer, he sent Andrea to check Gerard’s chamber—perhaps he had slipped in unnoticed.

Andrea shrugged, as if the task were futile, but obeyed. He returned moments later without Gerard, yet clutching a folded slip of paper. Though illiterate by modern standards—his mind sharp, but his letters untaught—he had learned to recognize certain names by sight. “That is for you,” he declared proudly, handing it over. “I know the name.”

Pietro snatched the note and read aloud, his voice edged with irony, though his hands trembled beneath his cloak.

“'Dear Pietro, dear Andrea, life is too great a burden.'”

“So 'tis,” Pietro muttered, though his tone belied his words. “But that’s no reason to be absent at supper-time. Supper is not a burden.”

“'Wear my habits!'”

“Said the poplar to the juniper bush,” he quipped, but his smile did not reach his eyes.

“'And thou, Andrea, mine amethyst ring; and me in both your hearts a month or two.'”

“And why, Andrea?” Pietro asked, half-jesting.

“'For my body, ere this ye read, it will lie in Tiber. Trouble not to look for it. 'Tis not worth the pains. Oh unhappy day that it was born—oh happy night that rids me of it.'”

“'Adieu! adieu!'”

“'The broken-hearted Gerard.'”

“Here is a sorry jest from the peevish rogue,” Pietro said, forcing lightness into his voice. But his pale cheeks and chattering teeth spoke otherwise.

Andrea, however, saw no joke. He burst into wails that echoed through the house. “O, miserable day! O, calamity of calamities! Gerard, my friend, my sweet patron! Help! help! He is killing himself! Oh, good people, help me save him!”

He ran from room to room, then flung open the door and rushed into the street, bareheaded, shouting to every passerby. Soon a small crowd gathered, drawn by his cries. But they hesitated. Go down to the river? No. It was not their concern. Which part? Who knew? It was dangerous after sunset—ghosts wandered the banks, they said, and misfortune followed those who ventured near.

Yet one man stood apart—a lackey who had lingered opposite the house. He stepped forward. “I will go,” he said quietly. A few young men, stirred by the urgency, joined him.

They hurried toward the Tiber, Andrea sobbing as he recounted the letter and Gerard’s recent melancholy. The lackey listened closely. He was no ordinary servant—his master was Princess Claelia, and he watched all things with a keen eye.

They walked in silence once they neared the riverbank. The spring night was still, the moon bright and clear above. The air carried the damp scent of water, and their footsteps sounded loud and ominous on the cobbles. Then, rounding a corner, they met a man.

He stopped abruptly, uncertain. He wore no hat; his hair clung to his face, glistening with moisture. His clothes were soaked, heavy with water.

“Here he is!” cried one of the youths, unfamiliar with Gerard’s features.

The man turned and fled.

They gave chase—Andrea leading, the lackey close behind. Andrea gained ground, but in an instant the fugitive darted into a narrow alley. Andrea shot past, unable to stop. The others followed, only to find themselves lost in a maze of dark streets, where every turn led deeper into confusion. The man vanished—known every inch of the way, he could now only be tracked by sound.

They returned to the spot where he’d stood and found their companions standing there, bewildered.

Pietro had told them plainly: the man was not Gerard—neither in height nor face.

“But are you sure?” they pressed. “He came from the river. Why did he run?”

Vanucci shook his head. “Friends, I believe this has nothing to do with our search. What shall we do, Andrea?”

Then the lackey spoke. “Let us follow the trail to the water’s edge. See—his steps drip all the way.”

They agreed. With little difficulty, they traced the wet path. But soon it took a strange turn. After fifty yards, the drops veered away from the river and led them to a large, shadowed gate. A monastery.

They stood before it, silent and uneasy. The building loomed like a tomb, its walls thick with secrets. Then Andrea shouted again. “Here are the drops!” he called. “And this road leads back to the river!”

They resumed their pursuit. The trail grew wetter, clearer. It wound back toward the Tiber. And there, on the bank, a bucketful of water seemed to have been emptied from the stream.

At first, they thought they’d found proof. But reflection cooled their hopes. Yes, someone had been in the river—and escaped. But it was not Gerard.

One suggested a fisherman nearby who owned nets and drags. They found him, paid him well, and begged him to cast nets below the site and drag the river above and below. Gold would be his reward if he found a body.

Then they searched the riverbanks, calling out into the calm, whispering waters. The river flowed on, indifferent, holding its mysteries tight.

Suddenly, Andrea broke from the group, racing back to the house. He returned within half an hour, breathless and broken.

“No,” he groaned, wringing his hands. “He is gone.”

“What is the hour?” asked the lackey.

“Four hours past midnight.”

“My pretty lad,” the lackey said solemnly, “say a mass for thy friend’s soul. For he is not among the living.”

Dawn broke slowly. Exhausted, Andrea and Pietro trudged home, their hearts heavy with grief. Days passed, silent as the Tiber, offering no word of Gerard’s fate.

It would have been remarkable, indeed, if men with so little to go on could have deciphered the silent message written upon the riverbank. For there, in that very place, an event had just unfolded—one so singular in its nature that it may well stand unmatched in human history, and perhaps remain so for all time. Yet it shall be told briefly, in part by me, and in part by one who took part in it.

Gerard, after writing a short farewell to Pietro and Andrea, slipped away to the river at dusk. He had resolved upon his course with a grim determination not uncommon among those who seek their own end. To ensure he would not float, he filled his pockets with every coin of silver and copper he owned. Then, prepared, he hastened to a secluded stretch of the stream, one he knew was seldom visited.

Some people—especially women—look about them to make sure they are not alone. But Gerard scanned the darkness not for companionship, but for solitude. And to his irritation, he saw a solitary figure leaning against the corner of a narrow alley. He pretended to wander off casually, but returned soon after. There stood the same man, now emerging from a side street, idling as if by chance.

“Could he be watching me? Could he know what I’m here for?” Gerard thought. “Impossible.”

He walked briskly down a few streets, made a wide turn, and came back. The man was gone. But when Gerard glanced around once more, there he was—only a few yards behind, apparently tying his shoe.

Then Gerard understood: he was being watched. At that moment, moonlight caught the glint of a steel gauntlet in the stranger’s hand. He knew at once—it was an assassin.

Yet strangely, it never occurred to him that his own life was the target. After all, he did not believe himself to have any enemies in the world.

He turned and approached the man directly. “My good friend,” he said urgently, “sell me your arm! Just one blow! See—here is everything I possess!” He thrust the coins into the other’s hands. “Oh, please! Please do one kind deed—end this hateful life for me!”

Even as he spoke, he unfastened his doublet and bared his chest.

The man stared at him, motionless.

“Why do you hesitate?” Gerard cried. “Have you no pity? Is it so hard to raise your arm and strike? Is it because I am poor and cannot pay you gold? You useless creature—you can only kill from behind, not face a man like a man. Very well—turn your head and keep silent!”

With a snarl of scorn, he fled, leaping into the river.

“Margaret!”

At the heavy splash of his body hitting the water, the assassin seemed to awaken from a trance. He raced to the bank, and with a cry unlike any other, plunged into the current after the man who had thrown himself into death.

What happened next will be told by the assassin himself.

A woman’s heart bears burdens as heavy as a man’s, though the world seldom sees them. We who write from the male perspective often sketch only the edges of her sorrow—leaving it to the woman reader to fill in the depth, the quiet agony, the silent strength that lies beneath. So too have I done here: not painted Margaret Brandt’s trials in full, but hinted at them, trusting the reader’s understanding to complete what words cannot fully convey.

And now, as the moment of her greatest trial drew near, Gerard was far away—beyond reach, beyond hope. She had little use for Eli’s sudden kindness, though he offered her comfort and shelter. Her reserve was easy enough to explain: she said she preferred solitude, that she needed privacy in this time of change. But the truth was deeper, more instinctive. There were two men in that house whose very presence chilled her blood. In their eyes she saw malice; in their glances, secrets whispered between them. She could not trust herself near them, nor endure their watchful silence. So she chose to remain at home, where she could be alone with her thoughts—and her fears.

Catherine came every day, wrapped in anticipation, her own motherly instincts overflowing. She was one of those women born to nurture, to multiply, to cradle life into being. Once the children came, they never left her side—not even when they grew strong and loud. She clucked over them like a hen, and somehow, through her care, they seemed to thrive. It was in this spirit she urged Eli to return to Tergou while she stayed behind in Rotterdam. “The poor lass has no one,” she said. “No one who knows how to help her. What good are two soldiers? They’d be better off out of doors in such a time.”

And so it was—a great comfort to Margaret. For all her fear, she found solace in Catherine’s presence, in her practical wisdom, in her unshakable faith. Yet still, her heart trembled. She would soon give birth, and Gerard was gone. The thought of dying alone, without him by her side, haunted her dreams. But life, in its strange balance, had prepared her for this moment. Poverty had taught her resilience. Her father’s frailty had forced her to rise each morning, to work, to endure. The rich, she knew, often fell prey to idle despair—but she had never known such luxury. She had always been on her feet, and now, thanks to Catherine’s steady counsel, she kept going until the end.

One evening, just as the sun dipped below the horizon, casting long shadows across the room, she lay weak and spent, but safe. Beside her, nestled close, was a small face—her child. And above them both, the heavens opened wide, not with fire or storm, but with the gentle light of new life. A peace settled over her, deep and undeniable.

“Why do you weep, sweetheart?” Catherine asked softly.

“All of a sudden,” Margaret murmured. “He is not here to see it.”

“Ah, well, lass,” Catherine replied, brushing a tear from her cheek. “He will be here before the babe is weaned. Meantime, God has been kinder to you than to any woman born. Think on it: it might have been a girl. My own Kate threatened me with one, and yet look—we have the bonniest boy in Holland, and a fine heavy one at that. Praise the saints for it!”

“Ay, mother,” Margaret whispered, her voice breaking. “I am a sorry, ungrateful wretch to weep. If only Gerard were here to see it. It seems strange—I bore him well enough to be apart from me in my pain. But oh, how hard it is that he should not share my joy. Prithee, prithee, come to me, Gerard! Dear, dear Gerard!” She stretched out her arms, feeble and pleading.

Catherine moved quickly about the room, busying herself with linens and blankets, but avoided looking directly at her daughter. Her own eyes filled with tears—she could not bear to hear her absent son named so fervently, so desperately.

Then, turning back, she found Margaret staring at her with a look neither of pain nor joy, but something deeper—something almost divine.

“Heard you nought?” Margaret asked.

“No, my lamb. What?”

“I did call upon Gerard—but now.”

“Ay, sure I heard that.”

“Well,” Margaret said, her voice hushed, “he answered me.”

“Tush, girl,” Catherine said, trying to laugh. “Say not that.”

“Mother,” Margaret insisted, “as sure as I lie here with his boy beside me—his voice came back to me. ‘Margaret!’ So. Yet methought it was not his happy voice. Perhaps it was the distance. All voices grow sad when they travel far.”

She paused, her gaze fixed on the infant, her eyes softening, glowing with a tenderness that made the room seem brighter.

“Why art not happy, sweetheart?” Catherine asked gently. “And I so happy this night?”

“Mother,” Margaret whispered, “I seem never to have felt a pain or known a care.”

And then, silence.

That very night, Gerard threw himself into the Tiber.

And at that same hour, as she heard his name spoken in her mind, he cried it aloud—into the jaws of death, into the depths of despair.

“Margaret!”

Let those who can, account for it. I cannot.

In a quiet guest chamber within the walls of a Dominican convent, a solitary figure lay spent, his body wracked by violent waves of nausea that had finally ceased, leaving him as frail and weakened as Margaret had been on that fateful night in Holland. A great fire crackled in the hearth, casting flickering shadows across the stone floor, while his clothes hung near the bed, still damp with the chill of the river. Beside him sat a massive friar, his voice resonant and steady as he read aloud from the breviary—pious prayers meant to draw the soul closer to God.

The man in the bed opened his eyes now and then, watching the monk with a dazed gaze. At other times, he closed them tightly, murmuring in pain or exhaustion. The friar knelt suddenly, his forehead touching the cold stone, and prayed long and fervently for the stranger’s recovery. Then, rising slowly, he turned to bid farewell.

“Day is breaking,” he said. “I must prepare for matins.”

“Good Father Jerome,” the sick man whispered, “before you go—how did I come here?”

“By the hand of Heaven,” the friar replied. “You cast aside God’s gift. He gave it back to you. Consider this: you have tasted the world, and found only bitterness. Now turn to the Church. The Church is peace. *Pax vobiscum.*”

And with that, he was gone.

Gerard lay back, lost in thought, his mind drifting between confusion and sorrow. He drifted into a shallow doze, only to awaken hours later to find a new presence beside him—a man dressed in plain garments, his face sharp and restless, his eyes darting about like those of a bird of prey. This was no monk, but a layman, and yet there was something familiar in his look.

“How do you feel?” the man asked, leaning forward with concern.

“Very weak,” Gerard murmured. “And… I’ve seen you before. Where?”

“None the worse for my gauntlet?” the man asked, his voice tinged with anxiety. “I had to strike you with it—or both of us would have drowned in the Tiber.”

Gerard stared. “You saved me? But how?”

“Aye,” the man said, lowering his voice. “I was near the banks of the Tiber on business—none of your concern. You came to me, begging for a dagger thrust. But even as you spoke, I recognized you. You were the nobleman who saved my wife and child at sea.”

“It’s Teresa’s husband,” Gerard breathed. “And an assassin?”

“At your service,” the man replied with a grim smile. “Well, Ser Gerard, when you flung yourself into the river and told me to stay away—I might have obeyed. Men are not my friends. Let them hang or drown, for all I care. But when you, sinking beneath the water, cried out ‘Margaret!’—my heart answered, ‘Teresa!’ How could I return home and meet her eyes if I let you die? So I plunged in—and thank God, I swim like a duck.”

He paused, then continued. “You tried to grab me, desperate to take us both down. But I swam around you and—forgive me—struck you hard on the neck with my steel glove. You passed out. I pulled you ashore against the current, barely alive, full of water. Then I carried you on my back toward my home. ‘Teresa will nurse him,’ I thought. ‘And be proud of me.’ But just beyond the monastery, a giant of a friar stopped us. He looked at you and said, ‘I know this face. It’s Gerard, the young man from Holland.’ I confirmed it. Then he said, ‘He has friends among our brothers. Leave him with us. Charity is our duty.’”

“And so,” the man added, “I agreed to visit once a day. And here you are.”

He gazed at Gerard with an odd mixture of affection and curiosity. But Gerard felt no warmth. Instead, he recoiled inwardly—as if a serpent had slithered into the room.

“Ah, you wish to sleep,” the man said quickly. “I shall leave.” And he slipped away silently, promising to return each day.

Gerard kept his eyes shut, though he was not asleep. His mind churned with thoughts. Saved from death—by a killer? Was this not the hand of Heaven itself? The same Heaven he had mocked, cursed, defied?

He shuddered at the memory of his blasphemies. He tried to pray. He could speak the words—but not mean them. “I am doomed,” he moaned. “Doomed forever.”

Then, through the wall, the organ of the convent church burst forth—rich, solemn, divine. The choir rose in song, chanting the morning liturgy. Among the voices, one stood apart—a boy’s voice, pure and sweet, soaring like an angel’s hymn. It stirred something deep within Gerard. Memories flooded back—the innocence of his youth, the peace of the cloister, untouched by sin or passion. No rage, no lust, no corruption—only stillness, clarity, grace.

“Oh,” he sighed, tears welling in his eyes. “The Church is peace. Before I left her, I knew neither sorrow nor sin.”

And he wept.

Just then, a gentle light seemed to fall upon him. He opened his eyes—and there, standing beside the bed, was Father Anselm.

The old priest had arrived at the convent only the night before. Yet Gerard recognized him instantly. “Father Anselm!” he gasped. “You healed my body in Juliers. Now heal my soul in Rome! Alas—I fear you cannot.”

Anselm sat beside him, placed a calming hand upon his brow, and spoke softly, soothingly. When he learned how Gerard had come to be there, he addressed him with kindness, but also with solemnity. He made him see the depth of his sins, urged him to repent, and reminded him of the mercy that had spared his life.

“Come, my son,” Anselm said gently. “First, cleanse your heart.”

“Ah, father,” Gerard whispered, “in Juliers I could confess. Then I was innocent. Now—now I am a monster, impious and corrupt. I dare not speak to you.”

“Why not?” Anselm asked. “Do you think I have never sinned? Oh, how deeply I have erred! Come, poor burdened soul. Pour out your grief. Hide nothing. Do not carry hidden guilt like a stone in your chest.”

And so, kneeling before the priest, Gerard confessed everything—every deed, every thought, every betrayal—sighing, groaning, broken with remorse.

“Your sins are great,” Anselm said. “But your temptation was greater still. I must consult our prior.”

He kissed Gerard’s forehead and left, to seek counsel on the proper penance.

And then—miracle of miracles—Gerard could pray. Not with forced words, but with a heart laid bare, trembling, yet open. He poured out his soul in prayer, his spirit humbled, his will surrendered.

This transformation—this profound inner shift—can be named in one word: *penitence*. He turned from the world with horror, longing only to remain within the cloister’s shelter. To him, raised in its quiet ways, it was like a wounded bird returning to its nest. He began his novitiate in silence, in prayer, in fasting, in reading sacred texts and meditating on divine truth.

Meanwhile, far from Rome, Princess Claelia received news from her spy: Gerard was dead—though the manner remained unknown. She froze, stunned. When she finally spoke, it was with bitter lamentation.

“So soon,” she murmured. “How swiftly these creatures act. They come to us in our passion, offer their daggers for gold, then carry out deeds we never imagined—until they plant the seed.”

Within hours, her grief for Gerard had curdled into hatred for the man who had killed him. Her anger burned like fever.

“Poor soul,” she whispered. “I cannot bring you back. But he—*he*—shall not live.”

She sent armed men into hiding, stationed them throughout the palace, ready to ambush Lodovico when he came for his payment. “Strike at his head,” she ordered. “He wears a secret coat of mail. If he escapes, you shall answer with your own heads.”

And so she sat, weeping for the man she had loved, while pulling the strings of vengeance—plotting the death of another, not for justice, but because he had been her tool in destroying the first.

Among the many vows Gerard had taken upon himself as a novice, one stood apart: to treat Lodovico with kindness, though in his heart he saw the man as venomous as a serpent. Yet this act of self-denial proved more powerful than he imagined. What began as a burden soon became a quiet joy—so much so that the penance ceased to feel like sacrifice at all.

At first, Lodovico’s pride was almost comical—his gaze fixed upon the very life he had once been paid to end, now preserved by his own hand. There was something absurd in the way he looked upon Gerard, as if he had earned salvation through mere survival. But even such vanity carried within it a seed of grace. For when a soul opens a door to mercy, other things follow—quietly, inevitably.

Lodovico found himself drawn to preserving life rather than taking it. Then came hesitation. Then regret. And then, slowly, something close to true repentance. Teresa, too, played her part. She warned him—again and again—that unless he abandoned his old ways, she would leave him. Her words were not gentle, but they struck deep. The nuns of the convent also lent their support, offering shelter and guidance.

Together, Lodovico and Teresa were sent by sea to Leghorn, where she had kin and friends. There, Lodovico settled into work as a porter—a humble post, far removed from the shadows of assassination. At first, he complained bitterly. "It's dull," he grumbled. "No excitement, no danger." But perhaps that dullness was the very thing he needed. Better to endure the slow grind of honest labor than to face the violent end that awaited him—the death by the Princess Claelia’s men, whom he had escaped only because fate had exiled him.

Meanwhile, the princess, thwarted in her vengeance, fell into deep sorrow. She dismissed her former confessor and sought out another—Fra Jerome, famed throughout Italy for his piety and unyielding truth. It was a stroke of divine irony that she should fall into his hands.

Fra Jerome listened to her tale without flinching. When she finished, he rose and spoke with the force of thunder. He did not spare her; he stripped away her illusions as one might shake dust from a cloak. To him, duty was above all—no prince’s anger could sway him, no title blind him.

“You are the devil,” he said, “who used your wealth to tempt a man into murder. And now, blinded by pride, you seek more blood—though none among those you wish to destroy is half as guilty as you.”

She resisted at first, offended that her confessor should speak to her so harshly. But Fra Jerome spared no effort. He threatened her with eternal damnation, tore the veil from her eyes, and left her trembling before him.

“Ah, holy father!” she cried, falling to her knees. “Have mercy on me! I am weak, lost—I see now how deceived I have been. Help me save my soul!”

“Doff your jewels,” he commanded.

“I will. I will.”

“Remove your silks and velvets. Dress as your lowest servant does. Go barefoot to Loretto—now.”

“I… I will.”

“No shoes. Only a sandal.”

“No father…”

“Wash the feet of pilgrims—both coming and going. And if any of them be holy friars, confess your sin to them, and accept their counsel.”

“Oh, holy father,” she begged, “let me wear my mask. My face is known across Italy.”

“Ay,” he replied grimly. “Beauty is often a curse. You may cover your eyes—but no more.”

She seized his hand, intent on kissing it in gratitude. But he pulled it away sharply.

“What would you do?” he snapped. “That hand touched the sacred host but an hour ago. Is it fit for a sinner like you to touch?”

“No,” she whispered. “But please—give your daughter your blessing.”

“Wait until you return from Loretto,” he said. “Then you may ask.”

And so it was. The events by the Tiber left lasting marks upon each who had passed through them. As prodigies do, they transformed lives.

Lodovico, softened by the life he had saved, turned from the dagger to the porter’s staff. The princess, humbled and broken, walked barefoot to Loretto, weeping and washing the feet of strangers—even those born beneath her. And Gerard—once brought to the convent on the brink of suicide—was now seen as a young saint among the brothers.

Eyes both loving and discerning watched over him. His probation was shortened. He was ordained priest sooner than most. Soon after, he took the solemn vows of the Dominican order and became a friar.

In dying to the world, he died also to his name. The man named Gerard vanished. In his place arose Brother Clement—a new identity, severed from all earthly ties. Here, the old life ended. And here, the monk began.

“As is the race of leaves, so is that of men.”

This year, in a quiet tailor’s house in Rotterdam, a child was born—unnoticed by the world, yet destined to leave an indelible mark upon it. At the same time, a great man fell from grace, not with a whisper, but with a thunderous crash. Philip, Duke of Burgundy, Earl of Holland, and many other titles too numerous to list, lay dying in Bruges.

In those days, sickness came swiftly to the poor and passed as quietly as it came. But for the rich, illness was a perilous trial. For every one who perished from disease, three more were lost to the remedies prescribed by doctors—whose cures often proved more deadly than the malady itself. The Duke’s illness, unnamed then, we now know as diphtheria: a wasting sickness, cruel and relentless. And though he was old, his strength had been formidable. Still, Dr. Remedy saw only one course: bloodletting.

The Duke grew cold. His limbs stiffened. The physicians stood in awe—this was no ordinary decline. Then Dr. Remedy turned to the deeper mysteries of science. “Ho!” he declared. “This is grave. Fetch me an ape at once, and place it against the Duke’s chest!”

At this command, officials of state scrambled through the streets, frantic for an ape—any ape—to counteract the human body’s supposed thirst for blood. But alas! No ape could be found. There were buffaloes, lizards, Turks, leopards—beasts enough to fill a menagerie—but none of them bore the resemblance needed.

“Why,” said one servant, “there used to be an ape here. I saw him myself standing on the gatepost.”

And indeed there had been—until the mastiff tore him apart for stealing his supper. Thus the beast fulfilled the human maxim: *Soyez de votre siècle!*—be of your age.

Despair gripped the court. Then, the seneschal cast his eyes about—and suddenly, hope flickered. “Here!” he whispered, pointing. “This may serve. It is altogether apelike—save for the doublet and hose.”

And what did he see? None other than our friend Giles, strutting proudly in cloth of gold, unaware of the chaos he was about to unleash.

“No!” snapped the chancellor, alarmed. “The Princess Marie would hang us. She favors this boy dearly.”

But Dr. Remedy, growing impatient, refused to wait. “Then flay a dog!” he ordered. “A dog is next best to an ape—only it must be of one color.”

So they seized a liver-colored hound, skinned it while still alive, and pressed its quivering flesh against the Duke’s breast. Yet it was too late. Philip the Good died—his life extinguished not by nature, but by the misguided art of medicine.

He left behind thirty-one children—only one of whom was officially legitimate. That son would inherit the throne. The good duke provided for nineteen of the others; the rest were left to fend for themselves.

According to Flemish chronicles, the deceased prince traced his lineage back to the kings of Troy, through Thierry of Aquitaine, Chilperic, Pharamond, and the ancient rulers of Franconia. But such claims were common among nobles of the age. In truth, nearly every prince of the time claimed descent from Troy. “Priam” had become, in medieval lore, a synonym for “Adam”—the first man, the root of all royal lines.

Philip’s body was carried to Burgundy and laid to rest in a grand mausoleum of black marble at Dijon. Throughout Holland, bells tolled and mourning echoed. Yet few knew—or cared—that in the same year, something far greater was born within the walls of a humble tailor’s home.

Now, centuries later, history has reversed its judgment. Men gaze upon that modest dwelling in Rotterdam, where the most significant birth of the fifteenth century took place. As for the house where the Duke died—no one knows it, nor does anyone care. Why? Because princes like Philip the Good come and go, leaving mankind no wiser, no better, no different than before.

But when, once in three hundred years, a child like Margaret’s son enters the world—then a torch is lit, kindled by fire from heaven. And across the earth, the cry rings out: *FIAT LUX*—Let there be light.

The Cloister

The Dominican Order, once the most influential religious force across Europe, was now in decline. Its rivals, the Franciscans, had gained strength and influence throughout Christendom—even in England, where the Black Friars had once held sway. In such times of shifting power, the order’s leaders grew more vigilant, seeking out gifted and devout men to send forth as missionaries and preachers, hoping to reclaim their former glory.

Among these rising figures was Clement, whose rare talents quickly drew notice—especially his command of languages. He spoke Latin with precision, Italian with grace, French with fluency, and both high and low Dutch with ease. His intellect and fervor made him a promising candidate for a mission to England, where he would serve as a spiritual ambassador to Rome.

But Jerome, who held the ear of the superior, stood in opposition.

“Clement,” he said, “still carries the milk of the world in his veins—the passions, the weaknesses of youth. Let not his new zeal or humility blind us to ancient wisdom. Try him first. Temper him. For fear one day we lean on a reed, mistaking it for a staff.”

“The counsel is sound,” replied the prior. “Take him under your wing, Jerome.”

And so Jerome, adhering to tradition, set about testing Clement’s mettle.

One afternoon, he led him into a field where young men gathered for games—a place Clement once frequented. Soon enough, Pietro Vanucci and Andrea passed by, casting a casual glance at the two friars. They did not recognize their old friend, now shaven-headed and cloaked in black.

Clement flinched slightly, then bowed his head and murmured a *Pater Noster*.

“Would you not speak with them, brother?” Jerome asked, watching closely.

“No, brother. Yet it was good to see them. They remind me of sins I can never fully repent.”

Jerome nodded, satisfied. Later, he submitted a cautious but favorable report.

Then came further trials: visits to deathbeds, where suffering clung like smoke; descent into dungeons thick with darkness, stench, and despair. Men lay there like beasts, wrapped in rags, their spirits broken. The physical toll was great, but Clement’s soul rose to meet them—offering comfort where it could still be given. He shone in those moments.

“His spirit is willing,” Jerome reported, “but his flesh is weak.”

“Good,” said Anselm. “For even if the body falters, the will remains strong.”

Yet greater tests awaited.

Let me tell it as others saw it.

One morning, Rome’s main street teemed with people, the avenues choked with heads. An execution was underway—not for a petty crime, nor against a common man. The governor of Rome had been found slain in his bed at dawn. His hand, likely raised in defense, lay severed at the wrist; his throat was cut, his temples bruised by a blunt weapon. The murder had been traced to his servant, and justice would be swift and severe.

The criminal was brought to the governor’s house and bound to its wall for half an hour—a foretaste of vengeance. Then, his left hand was chopped off, mirroring his victim’s fate. A freshly killed bird was opened and tied around the bleeding stump—why, no one knew, though some whispered it was a superstition of the physicians. Mutilated and bandaged, the man was dragged to the scaffold.

There, a young friar knelt beside him, praying earnestly—holding the crucifix close to his eyes, speaking words of mercy and salvation.

Suddenly, the executioner shoved the friar aside and struck the prisoner down with a heavy mallet, then fell upon him, slicing his throat from ear to ear.

A cry rose from the crowd.

The young friar collapsed, unconscious.

A massive monk stepped forward and carried him away like a child.

Brother Clement returned to the convent, heavy-hearted and dispirited. Before the prior, he confessed with tears.

“Courage, son Clement,” the prior said. “A Dominican is not forged in a day. You shall have another trial. And I forbid you to face it fasting.” Clement bowed in obedience.

He did not wait long. A notorious robber, a monster of cruelty, was sentenced to hang. He had murdered men not for gain, but for sport. Clement spent his final night in prison with him, walked with him to the gallows, and prayed beside him with such passion that even the hardened criminal wept and embraced him. Clement returned the embrace, though his body trembled with revulsion, holding the crucifix before the dying man’s eyes.

The rope tightened. The man died. But then, the hangman raised his hatchet and quartered the corpse on the spot.

And here, something strange happened: the people who had watched the killing with cold indifference now wailed at each blow upon the lifeless body.

Clement shuddered—but stood firm, like a rock that vibrates but does not fall.

Then, suddenly, Jerome’s voice pierced the silence.

“Brother Clement! Mount the cart. Preach to the people. Quickly! Strike while the iron is hot, while souls are ripe for salvation!”

Clement’s color rose and fell. He breathed hard. But he obeyed. With unsteady steps, he climbed onto the cart and delivered his first sermon to the first crowd he had ever faced. Oh, that sea of faces! His throat burned, his heart pounded, his voice shook.

But slowly, the moment took hold. The sight of eager, upturned faces, the fire of his own conviction—these kindled within him. He recounted the robber’s story, fresh from their time together in prison, and showed how sin climbs step by step, from folly to ruin. He thundered against bloodshed, yet moved the crowd to pity. His tremors vanished. He felt taut, like a lute strung tight, filled with an unexpected strength. He commanded the audience, sensing their pulse, shaping their emotions as a musician plays a psaltery.

Sobs and groans rose from the crowd—proof of his power.

Jerome stared, as if witnessing a spark ignite a rocket.

After a time, Clement noticed the look of astonishment on Jerome’s face—and seeing no approval, broke off abruptly and approached him.

“It was my first attempt,” he said humbly. “Your command came like a thunderbolt. Was I… did I…? Oh, correct me, guide me, Brother Jerome.”

“Humph,” Jerome muttered, uncertain. After long thought, he added grudgingly, “Give the glory to God, Brother Clement. My opinion is—you were born to preach.”

He reported this to headquarters, half-reluctantly. For though Jerome was stern and difficult, he was honest.

Another trial soon followed.

Julio Antonelli was accused of sacrilege. Three witnesses swore they saw him leave the church where candlesticks had been stolen—at the exact time. Others proved an alibi just as strongly. Neither side could be shaken. So, the law allowed a trial by water—either hot or cold.

In the hot test, the accused plunged his bare arm into boiling water fourteen inches deep and retrieved a pebble. In the cold test, he was lowered into eight feet of water.

The clergy, believing him innocent, recommended the hot trial—less fearsome for those they favored. But Antonelli lacked courage and chose the cold ordeal.

This gave Jerome another chance to test Clement.

Antonelli received communion, then was stripped naked on the banks of the Tiber, bound hand and foot to prevent thrashing that might sink him.

Gently, he was lowered into the river, floating for a moment, only his hair above water.

A roar erupted from both sides of the bank—guilty!

But then the ropes, newly wet, slipped, and he sank.

Another roar—innocent!

They left him at the bottom for over thirty seconds, then pulled him up gasping, choking, screaming for mercy.

After prayers, he was declared innocent.

Throughout, Clement prayed on the shore.

When it ended, he thanked God aloud—his voice strong, though slightly trembling.

Later, he turned to Jerome.

“Should he not be compensated?”

“For what?”

“For the pain, the terror, the suffocation. Poor soul—he lives, but has tasted death’s bitterness. Yet he did no wrong.”

“He is rewarded enough,” Jerome replied. “He is cleared of guilt.”

“But being innocent of that fault, he still drank from Death’s cup—though not to the dregs. His accusers, less innocent than he, suffer nothing.”

Jerome answered sharply:

“This world is not where men are truly punished. Woe to those who sin yet escape pain. Blessed are those who endure suffering—such pain is counted for them in heaven, yes, a hundredfold.”

Clement bowed his head.

“May your words take root in my heart, Brother Jerome.”

But the harshest trial Clement endured was unplanned.

It began when Jerome, in a rare moment of leniency, took him to visit Fra Colonna. On the table lay a freshly copied manuscript—*The Dream of Polifilo*. The author, proud and eager, pointed to a passage he called a masterpiece.

“For ages,” he declared, “fools have praised mortal women—earthly creatures, plainly marked by their origin. Sirens at windows, where Roman ladies have mastered the art of showing only one beauty—an ear, an eyelash—through a lattice, hiding all else. Magpies at doors, Capre n’i giardini, Angeli in Strada, Sante in chiesa, Diavoli in casa. Then I came—and gathered all amorous phrases from minstrels, even those Petrarch wasted on Laura, the most deceitful of all—and offered them not to mere women, but to the Nine Muses alone—worthy of divine love.”

“By which noble trick,” Jerome interjected, flipping through the pages, “you, a friar of St. Dominic, have written an obscene book.” And he slammed the manuscript down.

“Obscene? You insolent monk!” The author sprang around the table, snatched the book, locked it away, and, trembling with shame, said, “My Gerard—pshaw! Brother What’s-his-name didn’t find it obscene. *Puris omnia pura*.”

“Those who read it—may Heaven spare them—will find it what I do.”

Colonna swallowed the insult as best he could. Had he not been in his own lodgings, a nobleman and scholar, a brawl might have followed.

Instead, he shifted the topic to a beautiful chrysolite lent by Cardinal Colonna. As Clement handled it, Colonna extolled its moral virtues—just as scholars of the age revered jewels.

But Jerome refused to follow. He challenged him.

“You believe a dead stone can grant courage, chastity, immunity from poison, temperance?”

“The wisdom of centuries proves it,” Colonna replied. “Take the amethyst—look at this one. Clear, rich, flawless. This Gerard—Brother Thingemy—comes from the north, where men drink like fish, yet he is always sober. Why? Because he wears an amethyst. Where is yours, Brother? Show it to this unbeliever!”

“And that stone made him temperate?” Jerome asked, mocking.

“Certainly. The name itself means ‘not to tipple.’ Names are signs. A stone is not called *amethustos* for two thousand years without reason.”

He went on, detailing the virtues of ruby, sapphire, emerald, opal—citing grave historians.

“These are mere tales of old wives,” Jerome scoffed. “Such credulity!”

Now, credulity is a charge often hurled at believers—and it wounds deeply.

Colonna winced. Then, misreading his silence, Jerome urged him to abandon pagan lore and study the saints.

“Blot out these heathen superstitions, brother. Christianity has already erased them.”

He continued, carelessly repeating popular but loose theological claims.

Then, the wounded pride of *Polifilo* burst forth.

Colonna exploded, pouring forth a torrent of learning—some of which I can only summarize.

“The heathens blotted out? They control four-fifths of the world. What have we Christians invented without their help? Painting? Sculpture? These are heathen arts. We are dwarfs beside them. Who can carve forms as godlike as the Athenians, Licas of Libya, Dinocrates of Macedon, Scopas, Timotheus, Leochares, Briaxis, Chares, Lysippus, and the three masters of Rhodes who carved Laocoon from a single block? Who dares turn mountains into statues, as at Bagistan or Athos? Who builds a colossus in the sea, so ships sail between his legs?

“Architecture? We are children. Can we match the Parthenon, with its clusters of Doric columns? Or the Greek and Roman theatres? Or the Egyptian temples—whose portals stand a mile long, guarded by sphinxes as large as Venetian palaces? Their porphyry, polished like crystal, still gleams today, mocking our clumsy work.

“Roads? We’ve lost the art—despite having the greatest models right before us. Tombs? No Christian nation has built a monument that doesn’t make a scholar laugh. Think of the Mausoleum, the Pyramids, the tombs of the Indus and Ganges—mountains outside, mines of gems inside.

“You haven’t seen the East, Jerome, or you wouldn’t despise the heathens.”

Jerome insisted these were merely material things. True greatness lies in the soul.

“Then,” Colonna retorted, “what have we discovered in the mind? Geometry? Logic? We are pupils of Euclid and Aristotle. Writing? We didn’t invent it any more than Cadmus did. Poetry? Homer, Virgil, Horace—we’ve never matched them. Tragedy or comedy? Our mysteries and moralities—frozen personifications, dog-Latin—are pitiful compared to Greek drama, performed in marble amphitheatres before entire cities, by poets like Sophocles.

“What have we invented? Monotheism? The wise Greeks and Romans held it. Even their poets believed in one supreme power: *Zeus estin ouranos, Zeus te gy Zeus toi panta*—‘Jupiter is the sky, and Jupiter is all things.’ Lucan echoes: ‘Jupiter est quod cunque vides quo cunque moveris.’

“Their masses worshipped many gods. Ours? We haven’t invented ‘invocation of saints.’ Our saints mirror their *Daemones* and *Divi*. The heathens prayed to deified mortals to intercede with higher gods. The ignorant among them worshipped them outright. So do our common folk today—following heathen tradition.

“In scripture, there is no polytheism. We haven’t invented a new form of it. The pagans worshipped deified mortals; each had a favorite, to whom they prayed ten times for once to the Omnipotent. We do the same—praying to canonized saints ten times for once to God. Is that invention?

“Invention belongs to the East. Among the ancient vulgar, only sailors were monotheists—they worshiped Venus, calling her ‘Stella maris,’ ‘Regina caelorum.’ Among us, only sailors are monotheists—they worship Mary, ‘Star of the Sea,’ ‘Queen of Heaven.’ Is that a new religion? An old coat with a new button.

“We make images and adore them—absurd, for adoration is due only from creature to creator. Here, man is the creator. So the statues should worship him—if they had brains enough to justify a rat worshipping them. But even this abuse, though childish, is ancient. Pagans made images, knelt before them, adorned them, burned incense, lit candles, carried them in procession, made pilgrimages—just as we do today.”

Jerome interrupted impatiently.

“The most revered images in Christendom were not made by human hands—they fell from heaven.”

“Ay,” Colonna shot back, “such as the tutelary statues of Italian cities. I’ve examined nineteen. If they came from the sky, our worst sculptors must be angels. But I’m at ease—no ugly statue or bad painting ever fell from heaven to steal bread from skilled artisans.

“All this is pagan. The Trojans, with Oriental imaginations, claimed their Palladium—a wooden statue—fell from the sky. The Greeks brought it home from Troy, and soon statues rained down on every city. One such statue troubled St. Paul at Ephesus—it was Diana’s statue, said to have fallen from Jupiter. *Credat qui credere possit*.”

“What about the image of our blessed Lady, which hung in the air over Rome barely a century ago, taken by the Pope and placed in St. Peter’s?”

“I have no doubt,” Colonna said. “That’s the story of Numa’s shield, revived by theologians with a taste for fiction—but no talent. Numa’s sacred shield, the *ancile*, hung in the air over Rome until he took it down and placed it in Jupiter’s temple. Be just—accept both stories or neither.

‘Qui Bavium non odit amet tua carmina, Mavi.’

“And indeed, all our miracle statues—those that speak, nod, sweat, bleed—owe their existence to the heathens. The Athenian statues sweated before Chaeronea. Roman statues bled during Tully’s consulship—Victory at Capua, Mars at Rome, Apollo at the gates. The Palladium spoke in Vesta’s Temple. Juno at Veii nodded to go to Rome. Antony’s statue bled before Actium. Others cured diseases—like Pelichus, mocked by Lucian. The wise heathens believed in sweating marble, weeping wood, bleeding brass—as I do.

“Our holy marks—knees worn by saints, fingers pressed into stone—have heathen origins. Hercules’s footprints were shown on a rock in Scythia. Castor and Pollux left hoofprints on a rock at Regillum. A temple was built there, and the marks remained in Tully’s day. Near Venice, a stone split by St. George’s sword—except he never did it. It was a Roman who split a whetstone with a razor.

‘Qui Bavium non odit amet tua carmina, Mavi.’

“Kissing images? The Pope’s toe? That’s Eastern paganism. Egyptians learned it from Assyrians, Greeks from Egyptians, Romans from Greeks, we from Romans—whose Pontifex Maximus had his toe kissed under the Empire. Druids kissed their High Priest’s toe a thousand years before Christ. Muslims, who claim to hate paganism, kiss the Black Stone of Mecca—a pagan practice.

“The priests of Baal kissed their idols.

“Tully tells of a beautiful Hercules statue at Agrigentum, whose chin was worn smooth by kisses. The lower part of the statue we call Peter is really Jupiter. The toe is worn—but not all by Christian lips. The heathens laid theirs there first. We followed them like monkeys after their masters.

“So let us destroy the poor heathens!

“Our infant baptism is Persian—font and signing of the brow. Throwing earth on coffins and saying ‘dust to dust’ is Egyptian.

“Our incense is Oriental, Roman, pagan. Early Church Fathers feared it, died for refusing to handle it. Holy water? Pagan, and all its uses. See—this is a pagan aspersorium. Could you tell it from ours? It stood in the same place in their temples, used in worship and purification. They called it *Aqua lustralis*. Their people, like ours, believed drops could wash away sin. Their wise men, like ours, smiled or sighed at such belief.

What says Ovid of this folly, which outlived him?

You see—the heathens were not all fools. Nor are we. Not all.”

A Catherine is not a wholly welcome guest in a house not her own. She carries within her a quiet, unyielding force of order. No sooner does she step across the threshold than the hearth seems to brighten, the windows to open wider, and the very air to clear itself as if swept by invisible hands. Yet this same energy, though born of care, is relentless. It sees disorder everywhere—and corrects it without mercy. The kitchen sparkles; the furniture is rearranged; even the silence grows taut with tidiness. But such zeal knows no limits. It does not stop at pots and pans. It reaches for people.

In Margaret’s home, Catherine moved with purpose. Every chair was shifted, every table repositioned—perhaps for the better, but certainly without consultation. And when the time came for Margaret’s confinement, Catherine did not hesitate. She summoned Denys and Martin, not to help, but to remove them. When the two men, honest and gentle, asked what they could do, she smiled kindly and said, “You might go for a walk.” That was fair enough. But then she added, with a quiet edge, “If it lasts until midweek, so much the better.” Her tone made it clear: their presence was not wanted.

And so began their exile. Each morning they slipped out before dawn, returning only after dark like thieves afraid of being seen. If they were caught inside, they moved with the caution of cats on a glass-strewn wall—eyes lowered, steps light, faces drawn with tension. They lived under a silent sentence of banishment. Their mere existence seemed to grate upon Catherine’s nerves. Was it instinct that whispered: *No place for men who diminish in a house where life is growing?*

Words, too, became weapons. A woman’s tongue can pierce armor stronger than steel. Catherine used hers with subtle cruelty. She spoke lightly, yet each remark carried weight. She left no doubt that their stay was temporary, their usefulness ended.

When Margaret finally descended the stairs, she found the kitchen empty of men. Only Martin remained—old, stiff, and stubborn. He had retreated no farther than the street, but he had brought his stool with him, sat upon it, and refused to budge. Margaret saw him in the sun, but did not know he had become part of the landscape. She asked for Denys.

“Good, kind Denys,” she murmured. “He’ll be glad to see me up again.”

Catherine, wiping a bowl with unnecessary vigor, replied, “Denys has gone to his friends in Burgundy.”

“And high time,” she added, as if speaking to herself. “Hasn’t been near them in three years, by all accounts.”

“What?” Margaret gasped. “Gone without saying farewell?”

She raised her eyes—soft, tender, like violets just opened. Catherine flushed. The truth struck her: she had lied. She had not told Denys’s departure because Margaret was sleeping. But now, faced with that innocence, guilt pricked her conscience. She tossed her head and said, “Oh, you were asleep. I didn’t want to wake you.”

“Poor Denys,” Margaret whispered, and tears gathered at the corners of her eyes.

Catherine saw it—not directly, but from the corner of her eye. Without a word, she turned and hurried outside to tend to Martin. She offered him food, warmth, kindness. But Martin, old and set in his ways, shook his head.

“No, thank you, dame,” he said. “I’ve grown used to being out here. I don’t like changing. I don’t meddle with anyone, and no one meddles with me.”

“Oh, you nasty, cross old wretch!” Catherine burst out, switching in an instant from sweetness to sharpness. And she stormed back into the house.

Later, alone, she wept. Then, to soothe her conscience, she vowed to be so kind to Margaret that she would never miss the burdens of having soldiers about. Still, unease lingered. So she did what she always did when troubled: she took the baby.

From head to foot, she washed little Gerard in tepid water. Soap and water became a sacrament. In that moment, all else—the quarrels, the pride, the displaced men—faded into nothing. Heroes and their grievances dissolved like dust in the sea.

Margaret could not remain still. She hovered nearby, eager to participate, even if only in spirit. She dipped a finger into the water—not to test the temperature, but to claim a share in the act. As Catherine bathed the child, Margaret knelt opposite him, chattering softly, carefully avoiding adult speech, as though cherubs could not understand human words.

“I wish you could wash out *that*,” she said, pointing to the boy’s little finger.

“What?” Catherine asked.

“You haven’t noticed? On his finger—a mark.”

Granny looked. There, indeed, was a small brown mole.

“Eh, but this is wonderful!” she exclaimed. “Nature, my lass, you’re strong—and meddling too. Have you seen such a mark on someone else? Tell me the truth, girl!”

“On him? No, mother, not I.”

“Well then, he has. Right there. And you never noticed it. But dear heart, I forgot—you haven’t known him from child to man as I have. I’ve held him hundreds of times on my knee, just like this, and washed him from head to toe in lukewarm water.” She swelled with quiet pride. Margaret looked up, humbled, recognizing the depth of experience before her.

Catherine watched from above, thinking. She was different from other busybodies—because she sometimes thought, though not deeply. “It is strange,” she mused, “how things come full circle. Life is but a whirligig. At least, our lives as women are all cut from the same pattern. Wasn’t I once washing out *my* Gerard’s mole? ‘Oh, fie!’ I said. ‘Here’s a foul blot.’ And I scrubbed and scrubbed till he cried. Then I knew it was time to stop. And now you say to me, ‘Mother,’ you say, ‘Try to wash it out of my Gerard’s finger.’ Think on it!”

“Wash it out?” Margaret cried. “Never! For all the world, no. It’s the sweetest thing on his little body. I’ll kiss it every morning and every night until the one who first owned it returns to us. Oh, bless you, my jewel of gold and silver, for being marked like your father—to comfort me.”

And she kissed the mole, then couldn’t stop. Soon, the child was sprawled across her lap, kissed again and again, gently but fiercely, as if she feared losing him. Catherine watched, smiling. She had seen such scenes many times before.

This, then, was the rhythm of Margaret’s days for months to come. A few small events passed—worth noting, but best saved for later. One thread holds many beads.

Meanwhile, while her son’s father endured storms of soul, ending in the stillness of monastic peace, Margaret’s life unfolded in one great, simple joy—motherhood. You who know its depth, imagine her: nursing, bathing, dressing, undressing, playing, laughing with her firstborn. Then, swift as lightning, turn your gaze to Italy—where cold cloisters stand, monks moving like ghosts, eyes down, hands folded over hearts dead to earthly things. Among them walks one man—cloaked in silence, yet carrying a fire beneath. This man, filled with love and youth and longing, is the one the radiant young mother waits for.

In the valley of Grindelwald, the traveler sees on one side the towering Alps—perpendicular, icy, eternal, piercing the clouds. On the other, gentle slopes, green as emerald, dotted with cows and cottages, alive with ordinary joy. The mighty peaks are sublime, yet lifeless. The humble hills, though plain, stir the heart by contrast.

So too are the two halves of this tale. On the Italian side: adventure, passion, sin, penitence, ice, snow, and a soul soaring toward heaven. On the Dutch side: quiet, modest, domestic—yet ever green, ever living. And between these two worlds, as a path winds through Grindelwald’s ice and sunlit meadows, lies but a single page—between *the Cloister and the Hearth*.

The new pope favored the Dominican order. A message arrived from the Vatican, summoning a learned friar to teach at the University of Basle. Clement was the perfect choice—well-versed in languages and once a student under Guarini the younger. His journey to England was delayed, though not abandoned; instead, he was sent to Basle. But since he would not be needed there for three months, he was instructed to preach along the way.

He left through the northern gate, eyes lowered, his entire being wrapped in quiet devotion. If only one could paint a soul’s history as vividly as a fresco on a wall—what a living portrait this barefoot friar would have been! Within twelve short months, he had known joy and love, loss and despair, rebellion and sin, suicide and remorse, spiritual desolation, repentance, renunciation of the world, and surrender to God. Now he walked again—yet everything had changed. No longer was he hunted by danger or temptation. Even thieves and outlaws bowed before him, not to rob, but to offer stolen coin and beg for prayers.

His journey offered few dramatic scenes. Yet I know some readers who care less for spectacle than for the inner life of the soul. For them, silence can speak louder than thunder, and stillness reveal more than storm. Such moments are often the truest markers of transformation.

On the first Sunday of his travels, Clement did something he had never done before: he prayed for Margaret’s soul. Not because he doubted her salvation—no, her eternal peace meant more to him than anything on earth—but because of his own humility. When he heard of her death, his grief had burst forth in blasphemies that shocked even well-meaning hearts. But they horrified him far more than anyone else. During his novitiate, he had long wrestled with religious despair, convinced he had committed the unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit. Gradually, thanks to Anselmo’s gentle guidance, that darkness lifted. Yet deep self-loathing remained. He felt unworthy of grace himself, and how then could he dare pray for a soul so pure, so innocent compared to his own stained nature? So he had always asked others—good Anselm, another kind monk—to intercede for her. They never refused, nor did they half-heartedly fulfill the request. The older monks, especially the good ones among them, held their younger brothers with a tenderness that seemed beyond this world.

Now, after preaching in a small Italian town on Sunday morning, Clement felt an overwhelming surge of spiritual strength. That day, a warm sense of divine forgiveness washed over him. And for the first time, he prayed directly for Margaret’s soul. From that moment, it became his daily practice—the one pure thread binding his heart to earth. His family, once so close, now seemed like shadows from another life. The Church claimed all his allegiance. Yet even the Church could not fully extinguish lesser loves—only transform them.

For most of the journey, Clement felt little within him stir, except when he stood in the pulpit. Another rare spark came when he helped others.

Once, he passed a village where a young man lay in agony, bitten by a tarantula—or perhaps only imagining it. For two days, he had not slept, writhing, leaping, striking the walls. Village musicians had worsened it with their frantic tunes. Exhaustion and death loomed. Clement stopped, learned what had happened, and fetched a psaltery. He played soothing melodies, but they only made the youth moan and writhe. Then Clement noticed: the man’s lips moved, even in unconsciousness. He leaned closer and heard—whispered beneath the pain—a tune unlike any he’d ever heard, original, strange, born of madness or mind. He learned it and played it back. Instantly, the patient’s face softened. He danced lightly around the room, enchanted. When Clement’s fingers grew numb from repeating the melody, he saw the youth sink into peaceful sleep, cradled by the lullaby of his own imagination. It saved his life. Clement taught the tune to another, just in case, and continued on, his heart warmed.

Another time, he came upon a mob dragging a man through the streets. The man struggled, shouting in a language Clement didn’t recognize. He had entered the town proudly, waving a mulberry branch above his head. The villagers stared, then pounced. They dragged him before the podesta. Clement followed, but on the way, he quietly approached the prisoner and spoke to him in Italian—no reply. Then French, German, Dutch—still nothing. Finally, the man tried Latin, with a sharp accent. He said he was English, and had simply taken a branch to shield himself from the sun. “In my country,” he declared, “anyone may take what grows by the roadside. Confound these fools—I’m ready to pay. But here, all Italy rises up over a twig and leaves!”

The stubborn podesta wanted to throw him in jail. Clement stepped in, patiently explaining that silkworms—and thus mulberry trees—were sacred, protected by the sovereign, whose income depended on them. He urged that ignorance of such laws was natural for someone from a distant land where the tree might not even exist.

The Englishman, still irked, pulled out a purse and repeated his point: “This is a matter of commerce. What harm have I done? Say it, and I’ll pay at once.”

The podesta sniffed the gold. A ducat was levied—for the duke. About the value of the whole tree. He pocketed the coin.

The Englishman laughed as soon as he was free. “You’re too good for this hole of a country, father,” he said. “Come to England! That’s the only place in the world. I was a fool to leave it, wandering among mulberries and their fools. I’m a Kentish squire, educated at Cambridge. My name is Rolfe, and my estate is Betshanger. Man and house are yours. Come stay till Doomsday. We sit forty at dinner every day. One more or one less won’t be noticed. You can end your days with me and my heirs. Come now! An Englishman means what he says.” He gripped Clement’s hand firmly.

“I will visit you someday, my son,” Clement replied, “but not to burden your hospitality.”

Then the Englishman begged to be shriven. “I don’t know what will become of my soul,” he confessed. “I’ve lived like a heathen since leaving England.”

Clement consented gladly. Soon the islander knelt by the roadside, confessing sins from the past month. Impressed by his piety, Clement revealed he was indeed going to England. The man asked if it was true that the country teemed with Lollards and Wickliffites.

He flushed slightly. “There are black sheep everywhere,” he said. Then, after thought, added gravely: “Holy father, hear the truth about these heretics. None are more loyal to the Church than we English. But we are ourselves—free, independent. We love our ways, above all our own tongue. The Normans conquered our billhooks, but not our speech. They tried hard for centuries, by law and decree. Our foreign priests speak God’s word in Latin or French or Italian—like sheep bleating. Then came Wickliff and his followers, reading Scripture aloud in plain English. Who can resist that? God forgive me, I believe the English would turn deaf ears to St. Peter himself if he spoke not in the tongue their mothers planted in their hearts with kisses.”

He added quickly: “Not that I mean this for myself—I was bred at Cambridge, and good Latin words suit me well. But for the people. The key to English hearts is the mother tongue.”

“My son,” said Clement, “blessed be the hour I met you. Your words are sober and wise. But how shall I learn your English tongue? I have no book.”

“I would give you my Book of Hours, father—it’s in English and Latin side by side. But then—what would become of my soul, without my hours in a strange land?”

“Wait,” Clement said, smiling. “You are honest, and I am holy. Let us make a bargain: you pray for me every day for two months, and I’ll give you my Book of Hours. Here it is. What say you?”

His eyes sparkled with mercantile fire.

Clement gently smiled. Then he reached into his girdle and drew out a manuscript—written in Latin and Italian. “See, my son,” he said, “Heaven has provided for both our needs. Let us exchange books. And I will give you my prayers—not sell them. I do not trade in religion.”

The Englishman was delighted. “So I’ll learn Italian without risking my soul! Near is my purse, but nearer is my soul.”

He pressed money into Clement’s hands. The friar refused, saying it went against his vow to carry no more than necessary.

“Lay it out for the Church and my soul,” insisted the Englishman. “I don’t ask you to keep it—take it, you must.”

They clasped hands again. Clement kissed him on the brow, blessed him, and they parted.

About a mile later, Clement found two weary travelers resting under a great chestnut tree beside the road. A crude cart held a printing press—clumsy as a vinepress. A jaded mule was harnessed to it. And there, face to face, stood Clement and his old enemy.

As he looked at the press and the honest, blue-eyed Germans, he recalled the bitterness he once felt toward this machine. Now, he looked down kindly and whispered: “Sweynheim!”

The men jumped to their feet. “Pannartz!”

They fled into the woods.

Clement stood amazed. Then a face peered from behind a tree.

“What fear you?” he asked.

A trembling voice replied: “Say rather—how can a stranger know our names? I’ve never seen you before.”

“Oh, superstition!” Clement said. “I know you by your work—as all good craftsmen are known. Come forward, and I’ll tell you.”

They crept out cautiously, each watching the other.

“My children,” Clement said, “I saw a Lactantius in Rome—printed by Sweynheim and Pannartz, disciples of Fust.”

“Did you hear that, Pannartz? Our work has reached Rome!”

“By your hair and eyes, I knew you were Germans,” Clement said. “And the press speaks for itself. Who else could you be but Fust’s disciples?”

The men were astonished they had suspected magic.

“The good father has his wits about him,” said Pannartz.

“Ay,” said Sweynheim, “and with those wits, he could tell us how to get this tired beast to the next town.”

“And where to find money to feed it and us when we arrive.”

“I will try,” said Clement. “Free the mule from the cart and harness—leave only the halter.”

They obeyed. The animal immediately lay down and rolled on its back in the dust, like a kitten.

“This,” Clement said, “is how God teaches animals to refresh themselves. Horses do not know this art.”
