As for money, he told them a worthy Englishman had entrusted him with funds for charity. “To whom better give a stranger’s money than to strangers?” he said. “Take it. Use it to help another traveler in need. May all nations one day learn to love one another.”

Tears filled the men’s eyes. They accepted the gift with heartfelt thanks.

“It is your nation we thank—if we knew it,” one said.

“My nation is the Church.”

Clement prepared to leave, but the men begged him to wait. They had no silver or gold—but they had something else.

They took the press from the cart. While Clement fed the mule, they worked—half in shade, half in sun—setting type and pulling a quarto sheet of eight pages already prepared. They lacked enough type to print two sheets at once.

When the page emerged, Clement was stunned.

“Are these words truly fixed upon the paper?” he asked. “Will they not fly away as swiftly as they came? And you thought me a magician!”

“It is Augustine de civitate Dei,” one said.

“My sons,” Clement breathed, “you carry the wings of knowledge. Oh, never misuse this craft! Print no evil books. They would spread like locusts and devour men’s souls.”

They swore they would rather put their hands under the screw than abuse their art.

And so they parted.

In this world, there is only meeting and parting.

At a town in Tuscany, Clement met the past in a sudden, strange encounter. He joined a motley group of pilgrims—nobles and commoners, piety and vice mingled together. Such gatherings were well painted by others; I need not describe them.

Wearied and dusty, Clement sat in a corner of the inn’s barn, studying the Englishman’s Book of Hours, deciphering it by Dutch and Latin. A servant brought a bucket half-full of water and placed it at his feet. A female servant followed with towels. Then a woman approached, crossed herself, knelt silently, removed her sleeves, and motioned for him to place his feet in the water.

It was a noblewoman doing penance. She wore a narrow mask, yet it was effective. Her touch was gentle—more delicate than those born to such service.

Such acts were not uncommon. Though Clement doubted the efficacy of such contrition, he received her service calmly.

But then she sighed deeply, her head bowed low. Her sorrow seemed to crush her. He pitied her.

“Can I do anything for your soul, my daughter?” he asked softly.

She shook her head, sobbing faintly. “Nothing, holy father. Only to confess to a sinless man how vile I am. It is part of my penance.”

“Speak, my daughter.”

“Father,” she whispered, bending lower, “these hands look white—but they are stained with blood. The blood of the man I loved.”

Clement withdrew his foot.

“Ah!” she cried. “What shall I do? All holy things recoil from me.”

“Culpa mea! Culpa mea!” Clement exclaimed. “My daughter, I was moved by earthly weakness. I shall do penance. Do not judge the Church by its weakest servants. Not her foot, but her bosom is open to you. Take courage. Purge your conscience.”

She trembled, then confessed in a whisper, cringing as if afraid the Church would strike her.

“He was a stranger, base-born, but beautiful as spring, wise beyond his years. I loved him. I could not hide it. Nobles courted me. I never thought a man of humble birth would reject me. I showed him my heart—oh, shame of my sex! He drew back. Yet he admired me—innocently. He loved another, and was constant. I used a woman’s tricks. They failed. I borrowed the wickedness of men—threatened his life, lied to his lover, accused him of faithlessness.”

“Ah!” she gasped. “You shrink. Am I not a monster?”

He wept, pleaded for mercy. Then my good angel helped me—I told him to leave Rome.

“Gerard, Gerard—why didn’t you obey me? I thought he was gone. But two months later, I met him again. Never shall I forget it. I was descending the Tiber in my galley. He came up with a gay company—and at his side, a woman as beautiful as an angel, but bold and bad. She claimed me as her rival. Traitor! Hypocrite! He had exposed me to her, to all the loose tongues in Rome. In terror and rage, I hired a bravo. When he left on his bloody errand, I wavered—too late. The dagger struck. He never returned. He was dead.”

“Alas! Perhaps he was not so much to blame. No one has ever spoken ill of his name. His body is not found. Or I would kiss his wounds—and die upon them. Around his name, silence falls, as if the grave had swallowed it.”

(Clement’s eye caught her movement. He recognized her arm, her hand.)

“And oh—he was so young to die. A poor, thoughtless boy, victim of that wicked woman’s arts. She made him reveal everything. Monster of cruelty—what penance can save me? Oh, holy father, what shall I do?”

Clement’s lips moved in prayer, but he was silent. He could not see clearly.

Then she took his feet, began drying them. She rested his foot on her soft arm, pressing gently—so tenderly she seemed incapable of harming a fly. Yet her lips had just told a terrible truth.

While he prayed for wisdom, a tear fell upon his foot.

It decided him.

“My daughter,” he said, “I too have been a great sinner.”

“You, father?”

“I—quite as great a sinner as you, though not in the same way. The devil sets traps, not only snares. But penitence softened my heart. Gratitude remade it. Seeing you penitent, I hope you can be grateful to Him who has been more merciful to you than you to your fellow.”

She took his feet again, dried them carefully, wrapped one in a towel, placed the other on dry cloth, then bowed her head.

“Listen,” Clement said. “Fix your eyes on this crucifix. I will speak.”

“Yes, father. But let me finish—wet feet are uncomfortable. And you are the holiest man whose feet I have washed. I know it by your voice.”

“Woman, I am not. As for your feet, they may wait. Obey me.”

“Yes, father,” she said humbly, yet with a woman’s subtle defiance.

She bowed over the crucifix. Low, solemn tones fell upon her ear. His words stirred her body—first with sorrow, then with shock, then with awe.

“My daughter,” he began, “the man you murdered—by intent—was Gerard, a Hollander. He loved a creature no man should love but his Redeemer and His Church. Heaven punished him. A letter came to Rome. She was dead.”

“Poor Gerard! Poor Margaret!” she moaned.

Clement faltered—then regained composure.

“His weak nature broke—body and soul. He fell ill with fever. He recovered only to rebel against Heaven. He said: ‘There is no God.’”

“Poor, poor Gerard!”

“Poor Gerard? You foolish, feeble woman! No—wicked, impious Gerard. He plunged into vice, defiled his eternal jewel. Those you saw with him were his companions—but know, rash creature, that the woman you thought his lover was a boy named Andrea, dressed as a woman to mock others. What Andrea said to you, I do not know. But be sure neither he nor any layman knows your folly.”

“This Gerard—rebel against Heaven—was no traitor to you, unworthy.”

She groaned as if in physical pain. The crucifix trembled in her hands.

“Courage,” Clement said. “Comfort is near.”

“From crime he fell into despair. One night, he stood by the Tiber, resolved to kill himself. He saw someone watching him. It was a bravo.”

“Holy saints!”

“He begged the bravo to kill him. Offered all his money—to destroy body and soul. The bravo refused. Then, unsoftened even by that refusal, he threw himself into the river.”

“Ah!”

“And the assassin saved his life. You chose Lodovico, husband of Teresa—whom Gerard had saved at sea, her and her infant child.”

“He lives! He lives! He lives! I am faint.”

Clement took the crucifix from her hands, fearing it would fall. A flood of tears released her.

Then he continued calmly: “Yes, he lives—thanks to you and your wickedness, guided by an almighty and merciful hand. You are his greatest earthly benefactor.”

“Where is he? Where? Where?”

“What is that to you?”

“Only to see him alive. To beg his forgiveness on my knees. I swear I will never presume again—how could I? He knows all. Oh, shame! Father, does he know?”

“All.”

“Then I shall never meet his eye. I would sink into the earth. But I would repair my crime. I would watch his life unseen. He shall rise in the world—where I nearly cast him. The Caesare, my family, are powerful in Rome. I am near their head.”

“My daughter,” Clement said coldly, “the man you call Gerard needs nothing man can do. Saved by a miracle from double death, he has left the world and found refuge in the Church.”

“A priest?”

“A priest. A friar.”

“A friar? Then you are not his confessor? Yet you know all. That gentle voice…”

She raised her head slowly, peered through her mask.

The next moment—she gave a faint shriek and collapsed, her brow resting on his bare feet.

Clement sighed. He began to wonder if he had acted wisely with a woman so deeply stirred by passion. Yet though still young, he had already absorbed many lessons in the quiet wisdom of the Church. One such lesson was patience—knowing when to remain silent, to say nothing and do nothing, until the turmoil of the soul might settle into clarity. So he said nothing. Instead, he prayed for guidance.

All he did was gently withdraw his foot from where it rested. But the penitent clutched it at once, her arms winding tightly around it as she sobbed aloud, her body trembling beneath the weight of her sorrow. A deep flush rose up her neck and spread across her face, betraying not only shame but the fierce struggle within. She lay before him, quivering like a leaf in the wind.

“Daughter,” he said softly, “take heart. Do not torment yourself further over this Gerard, who is no more. I am Brother Clement—sent by Heaven today to comfort you, to help you save your soul. You made me your confessor; therefore, I claim your obedience.”

“Oh, yes,” she wept, her voice breaking. “Leave this pilgrimage, and return at once to Rome. Penitence far from home is little worth. The true trials are those we must face where we live—not fleeing to distant lands in search of grander sins, but enduring the daily temptations that surround us. It is easy to wash the feet of strangers when we wear masks. But how hard it is to be gentle, truly humble, with those we know and love.”

“I will never touch her again,” she vowed.

“No,” he replied, “I speak not only of servants, but of all who depend on you—kinsmen, friends, even family. This shall be your penance: each night before sleep, and each morning after matins, remember your sin and God’s mercy. Let that memory soften your heart and make you kinder to others’ faults. The world honors wealth, but seek instead the poor—not beggars, for most are neither honest nor truly destitute. Rather, find those who blush to ask for help, yet need it dearly. Give to them, and you lend to Heaven itself. Marry a good son of the Church.”

“Me?” she whispered. “I will never marry.”

“You will marry within the year,” he declared firmly. “And I command you—to wed one who fears God. For you are fragile clay. A bad match will break you. But if you choose well, through God’s grace, you may live as a pious princess—and die a saint.”

“I?” she murmured.

“You.”

He then asked her to rise and go forth to fulfill the task he had set before her. She knelt slowly, removed her veil, and looked up at him with eyes full of unspoken emotion. Then, lowering her gaze in humility, she said, “I will obey you as I would an angel. How happy I am—and yet how sad! For my heart tells me I shall never see you again. I will not leave until I have dried your feet.”

“It is unnecessary,” he said gently. “I have absolved you of this useless act.”

“But it is no burden to me,” she insisted. “Ah, you do not forgive me—if you refuse to let me tend to your feet.”

“Very well,” Clement said, yielding with quiet resignation. And inwardly he thought, *Levius quid foemina.* Yet even such frail beings, drawn to small things as stars are drawn to the sun, sometimes shine with sudden flashes of divine insight.

When she had finished drying his feet, she looked up at him again, tears glistening in her eyes, and whispered with tender compassion, “I will have masses said for her soul. May I?”

The words struck him like a soft blow. A faint blush touched his cheek, and a single tear moistened his cold blue eye. It came from one whom he had just spoken to with sternness, yet now offered such grace.

“It is a noble thought,” he replied. “Do as you wish. Such deeds often return to bless the giver like dew upon dry earth. I am your confessor, not hers. My duty is to save your soul—or else suffer the consequences. My daughter, my dear daughter, I see now angels fighting for your soul—good and evil—this very moment. Stand firm on your side. Do you remember all I have told you?”

“Remember?” she echoed. “Sweet saint, every word you spoke is carved into my heart.”

“One last thing,” he said. “Pray much to Christ, and little to His saints.”

“I will.”

“And that,” he added, “is the best counsel I can give you. So let us part on this.” He paused. “You to the place most fitting—your father’s house. I to my holy mother’s work.”

“Adieu,” she breathed, barely audible.

“Adieu,” he answered, “you whom I loved too deeply, hated too fiercely, known and honored too late. Forgiving angel, adieu—for ever.”

He heard her words, though spoken only in a sigh. “For ever?” he called out, his voice rising with sudden fervor. “Christians live for ever, and love for ever—but they never part for ever. They separate, as earth and sun do, only to meet again in greater light. We part here for life. And what is life? One line in the great story of the Church—of which we are both children. One grain in the sand of time, one drop in the ocean of eternity. Adieu—for this brief moment called ‘a life.’ We part in sorrow, we shall meet in peace. We part as mortal creatures, we shall meet as immortal spirits. We part in a world of sin and pain, we shall meet in a realm of purity and divine love, where no darkness remains, only Christ, and His saints robed in white. There—in the turn of an hourglass, in the burst of a bubble, in the passing of a cloud—we shall meet again. And sit at the feet of angels and archangels, apostles and saints, radiant with joy beyond words, bathed in the shadow of God upon His throne—FOR EVER—AND EVER—AND EVER.”

And so they parted.

The monk stood tall, his gaze lifted heavenward, burning with sacred fire. The princess walked away slowly, glancing back again and again—each look filled with awe and quiet regret. She returned home subdued, purified, transformed.

Clement reached Basel in due time, and took up his duties: teaching in the university, preaching throughout the town and surrounding villages. His life became defined by two qualities: profound study and rigorous self-denial. The reader has already glimpsed the depth of his soul. In Basel, he grew ever deeper in spiritual zeal and learning. The brothers of his order began to see in him a true heir to the saints and martyrs.

When little Gerard was almost three months old, a messenger arrived from Tergou, breathless and urgent, bearing word for Catherine. “Tell them I cannot come,” she said firmly, “and I will not. They have Kate already.” The man turned and left without another word.

Catherine resumed her thoughts aloud: “There, child, I must go. They’re all in confusion—this is the third time they’ve sent. And tomorrow he’ll come himself, dragging me home by the ear, with a flea in his ear to boot.”

She then reviewed the lessons of motherhood she had learned through years of experience, instructing Margaret on how to handle every possible emergency that might arise. She pressed money into Margaret’s hands, but Margaret refused it, bowing her head with gratitude. Catherine insisted, growing stern. Margaret offered excuses—reasonable ones—but Catherine dismissed them with quiet disdain. To her, such reserve lacked the warmth and tenderness befitting a woman.

“Come now,” she said, “speak plainly. We are parting, and who knows if we shall ever see each other again?”

“Oh, mother, do not say that!” Margaret pleaded.

“Alas, girl,” Catherine replied, “I’ve seen it too often. At every farewell, the thought comes to me. When I was your age, I never dreamed such things could happen. We believed we would live forever. So speak your heart.”

“Well then, mother—there’s something I’ve hesitated to tell you. Your Cornelis once said to me, ‘So you are come to share with us, eh, mistress?’ That was his very words. I told him I would be deeply sorry.”

“Beshrew his ill tongue! What does it matter? He’ll never know.”

“Perhaps he would, sooner or later.”

“But whether he does or not, I will accept no charity that carries a grudge. Unless I saw my child starving—Heaven alone knows what I might do. But no, mother, give me only your love. I value that above silver, and they cannot take that from me. Not a stiver shall I take from their house.”

“You are a foolish lass,” Catherine said, shaking her head. “Were it me, I’d take it just to spite him.”

“No, you wouldn’t,” Margaret replied gently. “You and I are apples from the same tree.”

Catherine smiled, yielding at last. And when the moment of parting came, both women clung to one another, tears streaming freely.

After Catherine left, the baby cried incessantly. All efforts to soothe him failed until Margaret suspected a pin caught between his clothes and skin. Upon searching, she found a gold angel pressing against his spine.

“There now, Gerard,” she whispered to the infant, “I thought granny gave in rather suddenly.”

She carefully removed the coin, wrapped it in a scrap of linen, and placed it at the bottom of her chest. Then she looked down at the child and said softly, “Observe, my dear, that I can be as resolute as granny herself.”

Catherine later told Eli of Margaret’s refusal and her stubborn pride. Eli said she was right, and Catherine wrong. Catherine tossed her head in disagreement. Eli remained silent, deep in thought.

Margaret, meanwhile, faced daily struggles. She still had two men to feed—Martin and the old man—and could no longer work as fiercely as before. Her days were filled with tending the house, caring for the child, and cooking for all. Yet she had saved a little money, and she often told her son, “Your father will return soon to help us before this runs out.” With that hope, and the joy of her boy, she passed several peaceful months.

But time wore on. No sign of Gerard. No word. And stranger still, no news at all.

Her mind began to wander, contrary to her practical nature. She would sit lost in sorrowful thoughts, sighing quietly. While her heart grew heavy, her savings dwindled.

One day, she opened the cupboard to find it empty. She looked into the faces of those who depended on her—Martin, the old man—and felt a wave of pity surge within. She knelt beside the cradle and asked the baby, “Can I let grandfather and poor Martin go hungry?” Then, without hesitation, she took out Catherine’s hidden angel.

As she unfolded the cloth, a single tear fell upon the gold—a quiet shame for having to use it.

She sent Martin to exchange it for coins. While he was gone, a Frenchman arrived with one of the dealers who had earlier offered her so little for her illuminated manuscripts. This man explained he worked for his sovereign, collecting masterpieces for a book of hours.

Margaret showed him her best pieces. He was enchanted by one—the delicate flowers, raspberries, and creeping creatures shaded by Margaret Van Eyck herself. He offered a price beyond anything she had ever imagined.

“Do not mock my need,” she said, “three mouths depend on me, and none to fill them but myself.”

“Indeed, fair mistress,” he replied, “I would not overreach. My princess commands me to seek only the finest artisans. She insists on fairness—no hard bargains. Let me satisfy you, and you satisfy me.”

The next moment, Margaret was kneeling beside the cradle, kissing little Gerard, showering four gold coins upon him again and again, speaking to him in broken Dutch: “Oh, what a kind princess—wasn’t she? We will pray for her, won’t we, my lambkin, when we are old enough?”

Martin returned furious. “They will not change it. I suspect they think I stole it.”

“I am truly grateful,” Margaret said quickly, snatching the coin back, wrapping it again, and returning it to its hiding place.

Before these unexpected funds ran out, she resumed her ironing and starching. But soon after, Martin fell ill and died after nine days. Nearly all her money went toward giving him a decent burial.

He was gone. An empty chair sat by the hearth—where he had always preferred the warmth of the fire to the sun, especially since the Busy Body had departed. Margaret refused to let anyone else sit there. Yet whenever her eyes lingered too long on the vacant seat, a tear would fall.

Now there was no one to carry her laundry home. If she did it herself, she would have to leave little Gerard with a neighbor—but she dared not trust such a treasure to mortal hands. And besides, she could not bear to be away from him for hours.

So she began seeking a boy to carry her basket on Saturdays and Mondays.

A plump, rosy-faced youth named Luke Peterson appeared—seeming fifteen, though he was eighteen. Blushing and fidgeting with his hat, he asked, “Would a man serve you better than a boy?”

Even before he spoke, Margaret had thought, *This one will do.* But she took his cue and said, “Nay, but a man might ask more than I can afford.”

“Not I,” Luke declared warmly. “Mistress Margaret, I’m your neighbor. I work as a cooper. I’ll carry your basket before or after my day’s labor, gladly. You don’t need to pay me. We’re not strangers, you know.”

“Master Luke,” she replied, “I recognize your face, but I cannot recall ever speaking to you.”

“Oh yes, you did,” he said. “One day you were trying to carry your baby and a pitcher full of water. I said, ‘Let me take the baby.’ You said, ‘No, I’ll give you the pitcher—I’ll keep the child.’ I carried the pitcher home, and you took it from me here at your door. You said, ‘I am muckle obliged to you, young man,’ in such a sweet voice—unlike how folks around here talk to a fellow.”

“I remember now,” she said softly. “And I suppose it was the least I could say.”

“Well then, Mistress Margaret,” he continued, “if you’ll say as much every time I carry your basket, I’ll bear it any number of times, no matter how far.”

“Nay, nay,” she said, blushing faintly. “I would not burden your kindness. You are young and kind-hearted. Say I offer you supper on Saturday night when you bring the linen home, and your morning meal on Monday—would that balance things?”

“As you please,” he answered, “but don’t say I asked for two meals! Such a trifle!”

With Luke’s helpful presence and the strength Heaven granted this young woman—though she bore many sorrows—the household managed for a while.

But her heart grew heavier with each passing day. Gerard’s silence stretched on—now mysterious, now terrifying. And Suspense, that cruel tormentor, began to gnaw at her soul with hot pincers, until she wept aloud: “Oh, that I could know the worst!”

One afternoon, as she sat in quiet despair, she heard heavy footsteps climbing the stairs. She started, trembling. “That is not a step I know. Bad news?”

The door opened. It was Eli, looking grave yet gentle.

Margaret stared at him, her heart pounding, unable to speak.

“Girl,” he said softly, “the skipper has returned.”

“One word,” she gasped. “Is he alive?”

“I hope so. No one has seen him dead.”

“Then they must have seen him alive?”

“No, girl,” Eli said quietly. “Neither dead nor alive has he been seen in Rome for many months. My daughter Kate believes he has gone to another city. She asked me to tell you that.”

“Ay,” Margaret murmured, darkly. “Like enough. Like enough. My poor babe!”

Eli, his voice weak, asked for a morsel to eat—he had come fasting. Margaret, touched despite her turmoil, prepared a meal, trembling and half unaware of what she did.

Before he left, he laid his hand upon her head and said, “Whether he lives or dies, I see you as my daughter. Can I do nothing for you today? Think well.”

“Ay, old man,” she whispered. “Pray for him. And for me.”

Eli sighed deeply and descended the stairs slowly, heavily.

She listened, dazed, to his footsteps fade away. Then she sank down beside the cradle, drawing little Gerard close to her breast.

“Oh, my poor fatherless boy,” she moaned. “My fatherless boy!”

Not long after, as the small household at Tergou sat down to dinner, Luke Peterson burst through the door, dust-covered and breathless. “Good people,” he gasped, “Mistress Catherine is urgently needed in Rotterdam!”

“My name is Catherine,” replied the woman at the table, her voice calm but firm. “Kate, it will be Margaret.”

“Ay, dame,” Luke panted, “she said to me, 'Good Luke, hurry to Tergou, find Eli the hosier, and beg his wife Catherine to come to me—God’s love!' I didn’t wait for daylight.”

“Holy saints!” exclaimed the wife, turning sharply to her husband. “He has come home, Kate? No—he would have told us. What could it possibly be?”

She spun one theory after another, each more frantic than the last.

“Perhaps the young man can tell us,” ventured Kate timidly.

“That I can,” Luke declared. “Why, her babe is dying. And she was so wrapped up in it!”

Catherine sprang from her seat. “What ails him?”

“I know not,” Luke answered. “But it’s been growing worse—peaking and pining these past days.”

A fleeting glance of satisfaction passed between Cornelis and Sybrandt—so quick that Catherine did not notice. Her eyes were fixed on her husband.

“Now, Eli,” she said sharply, “if you say one word against this, we’ll quarrel after all these years.”

“Who opposes you, foolish woman?” Eli retorted. “Go quarrel with your own shadow while I go borrow Peter’s mule.”

“Bless you, my good man! Bless you! You’ve never failed me yet. Now eat your dinner who can, while I prepare.” She took Luke back with her in the cart, and along the way questioned him relentlessly—now stern, now coaxing—until she had drawn every scrap of knowledge from his mind.

At the gate of the house, Margaret met her, pale and trembling, throwing her arms around her neck and gazing into her face with desperate pleading.

“Come,” Catherine said, scanning her closely, “he lives—thank God.”

She looked from the frail child to the hollow-eyed mother, then back again. “Lucky you sent for me,” she said. “The child is poisoned.”

“Poisoned? By whom?”

“By you,” Catherine replied without hesitation. “You’ve been fretting.”

“No, indeed, mother,” Margaret protested. “How can I help it?”

“Don’t tell me,” Catherine snapped. “A nursing mother must not fret. She must turn her thoughts from sorrow to the comfort in her lap. Do you not know that when a mother torments herself, the child suffers? This comes from your reading and writing—idle crafts fit for men, but they block useful knowledge from women. The child must be weaned.”

“Oh, you cruel woman!” Margaret cried, furious. “I regret sending for you. Would you rob me of the only joy left in my life? While I nurse Gerard, I forget I am the most wretched creature beneath the sun.”

“That you do not,” Catherine shot back. “Or he would not be like this.”

“Mother!” Margaret whispered, imploring.

“It is hard,” Catherine said, softening slightly. “But think: would it not be harder to look down and see his sweet little face staring up at you from a coffin?”

“Oh, Jesu!”

“And how could you face your other troubles with your heart full and your lap empty?”

“Oh, mother,” Margaret sobbed, “I consent to anything—only save my boy.”

“There, now,” Catherine said, pleased. “That’s a good girl. Trust me—I see clearer than you.”

But there was one more consent required—the baby’s—and he proved stubborn.

“There,” Margaret murmured, feigning sorrow, “he loves me too well.”

Yet Catherine was ready for both of them. As she walked through the streets, she noticed a healthy young woman sitting outside her door, cradling an infant. She approached and explained the situation. Would she nurse the failing child temporarily until arrangements were made?

The woman smiled and agreed, placing her own child in the cradle and stepping inside. She curtsied, and Catherine handed the sick babe to her.

The woman examined the child, pitied him, cooed over him, and began to nurse him as though he were her own.

Margaret, stunned by the woman’s confidence, cast a rueful glance at Catherine and broke into tears.

The nurse looked up. “What’s wrong? You told me the mother wasn’t unwilling.”

“She isn’t,” Catherine replied. “She’s just a fool. Don’t heed her. And you, Margaret—I’m ashamed of you.”

“You’re a cruel, heartless woman,” Margaret wept.

“Those who guide the weak must be firm,” Catherine replied. “And forgive me—but you are not my flesh and blood. Your son is.”

After letting the words settle, she added, “Come now—she’s giving up her own milk to save yours, and all you can do is cry in front of her. Out, fie—for shame!”

“Nay, wife,” the nurse said gently. “Thank Heaven, I have enough for both. And pray don’t blame her—perhaps life’s troubles have soured her milk.”

“And her heart too,” Catherine said coldly.

Margaret stared into her eyes—then dropped her gaze.

“I know I should be grateful,” she sobbed to the nurse, turning her head away, unable to watch another woman nurse her child. Gerard seemed to make no distinction between the two mothers.

The nurse smiled. “You’re very welcome, my poor woman. And you too, Mistress Catherine—though I don’t know you.”

“You’re from Tergou?” Catherine asked.

“All the better. But I don’t recall your face.”

“Oh, you wouldn’t. My husband and I are humble folk by you. But true Eli and his wife are known and respected in town. So I’m at your service, dame—and yours, wife—and yours, my pretty poppet—night or day.”

“There’s a woman of the right old sort,” Catherine remarked as the door closed behind her.

“I HATE her. I HATE her. I HATE her,” Margaret cried, with fierce passion.

Catherine merely laughed.

“That’s right,” she said. “Better say it than stew in silence. It’s natural. Come—here’s your bundle of comfort. Take it and hate that if you can,” and she placed the child in her lap.

“No, no,” Margaret whispered, turning her head half away—unable to turn fully. “He’s not mine now. He’s hers. I don’t know why she left him here. But it was kind of her not to take him to her house—cradle and all. Oh! oh! oh! oh! oh! oh! oh!”

“Ah,” Margaret sighed, “one comfort—he’s not dead. This gives me light: someone else has taken him from me. Like father, like son. Oh! oh! oh! oh! oh!”

Catherine felt pity and let her weep in peace.

Afterward, whenever Joan helped, Catherine would take Gerard out for fresh air. Margaret never objected—nor showed any doubt—but always returned in tears.

This quiet understanding did not last. Soon, Margaret became as eager as Catherine to wean the child. It was done. Gerard regained strength, and soon faced the next trial—teething.

But here Catherine’s wisdom proved invaluable. Amid her grief over her husband’s silence, Margaret found moments of pure joy watching her son’s tiny teeth emerge.

“Teeth, mother?” she would whisper. “I call them not teeth—but pearls of pearls.”

Each new tooth, sparkling on his red gums, was to her the greatest wonder nature had ever wrought.

Her companion shared the illusion. Had anyone claimed standing corn was equally beautiful, Margaret would have turned reproachful; Catherine would have thrown them out. So each new pearl’s arrival was greeted with a shriek of triumph by whoever discovered it first.

Catherine chatted with Joan and learned she was the wife of Jorian Ketel of Tergou—a man once servant to Ghysbrecht Van Swieten, but fallen from favor and returned to Rotterdam, his native town. His friends secured him the post of sexton, and with carpentry work, he managed fairly well.

In return, Catherine told Joan about the child she had nursed—about Margaret and Gerard, and the deep anxiety their silence caused.

“Ay,” Joan said simply, “the world is full of trouble.”

One day she said, “I believe my husband knows more about your Gerard than anyone here. But lately he’s grown tighter-lipped than ever. Drop in some evening just before sunset, and set him talking. And for Our Lady’s sake, don’t say I sent you. The only secret he ever kept from me was because I blabbed his business. And I don’t want another. Gramercy! I married a man for comfort, not to be hidden.”

Catherine visited.

Jorian was ready enough to speak of how he had aided her son—perhaps even saved his life.

But Catherine already knew that. When she pressed him on whether he suspected why her lost boy neither came nor wrote, he gave her a grim look. His wife met it with calm, stolid innocence.

His answers grew short, sullen.

“What should he know more than another?” he muttered.

After a pause, he added, “Think you the burgomaster shares his secrets with a fellow like me?”

“Oh, then the burgomaster knows something?” Catherine asked sharply.

“Likely,” he replied. “Who else should?”

“I’ll ask him.”

“I’d advise you not.”

“And tell him you say he knows.”

“That’s right, dame. Go make him my enemy. That’s what a poor fellow gets when he speaks to you women.”

From that moment, Jorian withdrew—tighter than a hedgehog, pricklier still.

His behavior filled both women with torment—fear, confusion, burning curiosity.

Ghysbrecht was Gerard’s mortal foe—had blocked his marriage, imprisoned him, hunted him down. And now, his former servant—when caught off guard—had hinted that this same enemy held the key to Gerard’s silence.

They studied every word, every glance—yet all remained dark.

Then Catherine said to Margaret, “You are young, fair. You may draw more from him than I.”

It was a reasonable guess.

Margaret went, carrying her child, and tapped timidly at Jorian’s door just before sunset.

“Come in,” a strong voice called.

She entered. Jorian sat by the fire. At sight of her, he rose, snorted, and stormed out.

“Is that for me, wife?” Margaret asked, flushing deeply.

“You must excuse him,” Joan replied, somewhat coldly. “He blames you for his poverty instead of riches. It’s about a piece of parchment. One was missing—and he got nothing from the burgomaster because of it.”

“Oh,” Margaret whispered, “Gerard took it.”

“Likely,” Joan said. “But my man says you shouldn’t have let him. You promised to keep them all safe. And truly, I blame Jorian for being angry. It’s hard for a poor man to be so near fortune and lose it through those he helped. Still, I tell him another story. ‘Folk who’ve escaped trouble,’ I say, ‘shouldn’t be too hard on those still in it. And she has enough.’ Going already? What’s the rush, mistress?”

“Oh,” Margaret said, “it’s not my place to drive the goodman from his own house.”

“Well, let me kiss the bairn before you go. He’s not to blame, poor innocent.”

So rebuffed, Margaret formed a resolution—she would not share it, not even with Catherine.

Six weeks later, Catherine returned home.

On the child’s birthday—soon after—Margaret did no work. She dressed in her Sunday clothes, cradled her boy, and went to church. There, she prayed long and fervently for Gerard’s safe return.

At that very hour, in the minster church at Basle, Father Clement celebrated a mass—and prayed for Margaret’s soul, already gone.

“A lie is not like a blow with a curtal axe,” someone once said—perhaps it was Sybrandt. And truly, that is so. A blow from a weapon may be felt, its damage measured, its reach foreseen. But a lie? It has no limits. It spreads unseen, twisting through lives like roots beneath the soil, breaking what cannot be mended, and often taking whole futures with it. In this tale, one such falsehood—uttered in cold calculation—set off consequences far beyond the minds of those who spoke it. Yet they reaped little reward for their deceit.

The brothers, who had invented the story merely to remove one rival from their father’s inheritance, saw instead their own brother Gerard rise in their mother’s heart. Not only that, but Eli, in a moment of open honesty, declared that since Gerard was presumed lost—likely dead—he had made provision in his will for little Gerard, and also for Margaret, his son’s grieving widow. At this, a look passed between the two brothers—the kind that speaks volumes without a word. It was a warning to all betrayers: even silence can carry judgment.

Cornelis, on the verge of speaking, saw his mother’s eyes upon him and held back. He could have said, “Gerard is probably alive.” But he did not.

Ghysbrecht Van Swieten, the other architect of the lie, now stood near the end of his days. His wealth was fading, his body failing, and his conscience growing louder. Though intelligent enough to know the truth, he had never been free from remorse. When he took Gerard’s letter to Margaret, he had done so not out of kindness, but as a form of penance—a bargain with himself. “I cannot give up land or money,” whispered his inner Avarice. “But I will not cause her unnecessary pain,” murmured his dwarf Conscience. So he broke the seal, found no mention of the deed, and delivered it himself—taking credit for mercy, though it was mere self-deception.

Then came the birth of Margaret’s child. It stunned him. The weight of his act shifted, becoming something more terrible than before. If his letter were believed, it would bring disgrace upon a woman whose father had saved him from plague, whose grandfather had helped him in poverty, and whose family had long loved him. These thoughts gnawed at him, especially now, when memory stirred old friendships and the body weakened. He was filled with dread—but still he dared not confess. For confession meant honesty, and honesty meant surrendering everything. To him, greed was habit; repentance, only sentiment.

It was on such a day, returning from the town hall, that he found a woman waiting in his vestibule—veiled, holding a child. Assuming she was ashamed, he addressed her with stiff authority. But then she lowered her veil—and there stood Margaret Brandt.

Her sudden presence struck him like a thunderclap. He faltered, unable to hide his alarm.

“Where is my Gerard?” she demanded, her chest rising and falling rapidly. “Is he alive?”

“For all I know,” he stammered, “he might be. I hope so—for your sake. Come into this room. The servants—”

“Not a step,” she said firmly, seizing his shoulder with both hands. “You know the secret that is tearing my heart apart. Why does Gerard not come? Why has he sent no word these many months? Answer me—or the whole town shall hear, let alone your servants. My sorrow is too deep to be mocked.”

He denied knowing anything. She replied that those who had sent her to him told her otherwise.

“You do know why he neither comes nor writes,” she insisted.

At that, Ghysbrecht turned deathly pale. But he rallied his pride. “Would you believe two rogues over a man of honor?”

“What two rogues?” she asked sharply.

He hesitated. “Said ye not—?” Then he broke off. “Here I am, a poor broken man, my memory failing. You come, and confuse me so I know not what I say.”

“Ay, sir,” she answered quietly, “your memory is shaken—or else you would not be my enemy. My father saved you from the plague when no one else would approach you. He was your friend. My grandfather Floris helped you when you were poor, and loved you, man and boy. Three generations of us you have known—and here is the fourth. This child is Peter’s grandson, and Floris’s great-grandchild. Look down on his face. See the innocence in his eyes. Think of theirs!”

“Woman,” he groaned, “you torture me.” He sank onto a bench.

But she saw her chance. Kneeling before him, she placed the child upon his knees.

“This fatherless babe is poor Margaret Brandt’s—she who has done you no harm, born of a line that loved you. Look at his face. It will move you more than any words of mine. Saints above—what have a helpless girl and her child done to erase the memory of your youth, when you were guiltless as he is now, looking up at you with pleading eyes, begging you to return his father?”

She held the child aloft, cradling him gently under her arms, smiling into the old man’s eyes.

He stared—first at the child, then at her—then rose suddenly, shrieking, “Avaunt! Ye pair of adders!”

The pain tore through him, giving his aging frame a brief surge of strength. He paced wildly, clutching his hair, wringing his hands.

“Forget those days? I forget nothing. Oh, woman, woman—sleeping or waking, I see only the faces of the dead, hear only their voices. Soon I shall join them. There, there—what is done is done. I am in hell. I am in hell.”

His voice cracked. The effort collapsed him. He staggered, and only Margaret’s arm kept him from falling. She supported him as best she could, calling for help. Servants rushed in and carried him away, half-unconscious. The last she saw was his pale, furrowed face, white as snow, hanging limply over the servant’s elbow.

“Heaven forgive me,” she whispered. “I fear I have killed the poor old man.”

And so, her search for truth brought only deeper darkness. As she reflected on every word, she became certain: Ghysbrecht *did* know something about Gerard.

“And who were the two knaves he spoke of?” she thought. “Who called their lie a good deed? Oh, my Gerard, my poor deserted child—we are drowning in deep waters.”

The journey to Tergou had cost more than she could afford. A customer fled with unpaid debts. Again, she was forced to open Catherine’s angel—her last resort. But as she descended the stairs with it, she found loose silver on the table, along with a note:

She gasped. Then laughed—then wept with joy.

“He is alive!” she cried. “He sends this by some kind hand.”

She kissed the paper again and again, tucking it into her bosom.

Time passed. No news came. But every two months, a small sum of silver appeared—sometimes on the table, once flung through the bedroom window in a purse, once hidden in Luke’s basket after he stopped at the tavern to speak with a friend. The giver remained unknown. Catherine denied it. Margaret Van Eyck swore she had no part. Eli denied it too.

Each time, Margaret would whisper to little Gerard, “Oh, my poor deserted child, you and I are wading in deep waters.”

She spent half the money dressing the boy better than his station warranted. “If it comes from Gerard,” she said, “he must see his son neat.”

Soon, the mothers in the street began to sneer—especially those whose children wore ragged clothes. Their scorn stung.

Months stretched into years. The sharp pains of longing gave way to a dull, unrelenting ache. She returned to her first thought: *Gerard must be dead.* She would never see her husband again. Her marriage lines—her future—would remain unfulfilled.

This grief, once eased by Eli and Catherine’s acceptance of her betrothal, now returned full force. Others would not be so kind. And often, she wept over her son’s illegitimacy.

“Is it not enough that we are bereaved?” she moaned. “Must we also be dishonored? Oh, that we had never been born.”

Meanwhile, Peter Brandt changed. After nearly two years of confusion, his mind seemed to clear. Moments of lucidity returned. Then he and Margaret would talk of Gerard—until he drifted back into silence.

One day, returning after an absence, she found him talking with Catherine—something he had not done since his stroke.

“Eh, girl,” she said, “why must you be out?”

“I’ve told him all,” Catherine replied. “We’ve been crying together over your troubles.”

Margaret stood silent, watching them, her heart swelling with quiet joy.

Peter smiled at her. “Come, let me bless thee.”

She knelt. He blessed her—eloquently, tenderly.

“You have been the most loving, true, and obedient daughter Heaven ever sent to a poor widower,” he said. “May your son be to you what you have been to me.”

Then he dozed.

They whispered together. Catherine said, “We spoke just now of Gerard. It weighs heavily on his mind. His poor head must have listened to us even when it seemed dark. He’s a very understanding man. He thought of many things: ‘He may be in prison,’ says he, ‘or forced to fight for a king, or sent to Constantinople to copy books, or perhaps gone into the Church.’ He always had a bent that way.”

“Oh, mother,” Margaret whispered, “he only deceives himself—as we do.”

Before she could finish, a sudden cry rang out.

The old man’s eyes widened. He seemed to stare through the wall.

His voice dropped. “Sore disfigured—but I knew him. Gone! Gone! All dark.”

He slumped back, weakly asking, “Where is Margaret?”

“Dear father,” she said, kneeling beside him, “I am here. Oh, mother! Mother, what is this?”

“I cannot see you,” he murmured. “But a moment ago, I saw all around the world. Ay, ay. Well, I am ready. Is this your hand? Bless thee, my child, bless thee! Weep not! The tree is ripe.”

The physician understood. These were his final words.

Then, gently, peacefully, he lowered his head and slipped away—like a child sinking into sleep. The torch flared once, brightly, before going out.

She who had wept for poor old Martin could not endure this new sorrow with the quiet resignation that often marks the passing of an elder. Catherine tried, in vain, to comfort her with the usual phrases—how it was a blessed release, how the tree had ripened at last, as he himself had once said. But her most ill-timed words were those suggesting that now there were only two mouths to feed and one less burden to bear.

“Such cares are all the joys I have,” Margaret replied, her voice trembling. “They fill my hollow heart, which now feels as empty as it is wasted. Oh, empty chair—my bosom aches to see thee! Poor old man, how could I love him by halves? I used to sit and gaze at him, thinking, *But for me, thou wouldst die of hunger.* Once so wise, so learned, he grew helpless as my own child—and I loved him as if he had been my son instead of my father. Oh, empty chair! Oh, empty heart! Well-a-day! well-a-day!”

And though she tried to hold back, the tears came freely. Catherine stood silent, head bowed, knowing her words had failed.

Then, after a long pause, she spoke again—not from wisdom, but from the depths of her own feeling: “I speak to thee out of my head, not my heart. Thou dost well to be deaf to me. Were I in thy place, I should mourn him as thou dost.”

Margaret clung to her, and in that simple truth lay a small comfort. The platitudes had brought none.

Catherine’s heart softened further. “My poor girl,” she said, “you were not born to live alone. I have come to think of you as my own daughter. Waste not your youth on Gerard. He is either dead—or a traitor. It breaks my heart to say it, but how can one blind oneself to the truth? Thy father is gone, and I cannot always be beside thee. And here is a good lad—honest, steady—who has loved thee these many months. I’d take him and Comfort together. Heaven sends us creatures to torment and comfort us; without them, we are nothing.”

Seeing Margaret look bewildered, Catherine pressed on: “Why, surely you are not so blind as not to see it?”

“What?” asked Margaret. “Who?”

“Luke Peterson.”

“Our Luke? The boy who carries my basket?”

“Nay, he is over nineteen now—a strong, healthy young man. I’ve looked into his life, and they all say he is honest, hardworking, and never touches a drop. That’s no small thing in Rotterdam, where most lads are half man, half sponge.”

A faint smile touched Margaret’s lips—the first in days. “Luke loves dried puddings dearly,” she murmured. “And I make them just to his taste. That’s why he comes courting.”

Then she flushed crimson. “But if I thought he came for my son’s wife—be it past or present—I’d send him away sharp.”

“Nay, nay,” Catherine said quickly. “Let me not cause trouble. Poor lad! Fancy cannot be tamed. Bless you, I drew it out of him near a year ago.”

“Oh, mother!” Margaret exclaimed. “And you let him?”

“I thought of you,” Catherine answered. “I said to myself, *If he’s fool enough to serve her faithfully, then so much the better for her. A woman alone is lost without a man to carry her burdens.* But now I think the best thing you can do is marry him.”

“So then,” Margaret said bitterly, “even his own mother opposes him and would wed me to the first comer. An, Gerard, thou hast but me. I will not believe thee dead till I see thy tomb, nor false till I see thee holding another’s hand. Foolish boy—I shall never be kind to him again.”

Thus burdened by Catherine’s meddling kindness, Luke Peterson found the door closed to him. Where once he had been welcomed, he now met silence, and when spoken to, it was with sharp irritation. The gentle giant, unused to such coldness, began to tremble. One day he burst out, “Mistress, have I done anything to offend you?”

“Nothing,” she said softly. “It is I who am to blame. I am cursed. If you’ll listen to me, keep away for a time.”

“It’s all because of me, Mistress,” he said, turning to Catherine. “You, Mistress Catherine—what have I done to make her turn against me?”

“I meant well,” Catherine replied. “I told her I saw you looking at her through a wedding ring. But she won’t hear of it.”

“There was no need to tell her that,” Luke said. “She knows I’ve been courting her for a year.”

“No,” Margaret said firmly. “Or I should never have opened the street door to you.”

“But I come every Saturday night,” Luke insisted. “That’s how we court in Rotterdam. We sup with a lass on Saturdays—that’s wooing.”

“Oh, is it Rotterdam, is it?” Margaret said dryly. “Then next time, come on Thursday or Friday. For my part, I thought you came for my puddings, boy.”

“I like your puddings well enough,” Luke said gently. “You make them better than my mother does. But I like you more than the puddings.”

Then she rose, her voice soft yet unyielding: “You have seen the last of them. How dare you speak so to another man’s wife, especially when he is far away?”

“You need not trouble yourself to come here again, Luke,” she added. “I can carry my basket myself.”

“Oh, very well,” he said quietly. After a moment of silence, he stood up and said sadly to Catherine, “Dame, I daresay I’ve got the sack,” and left.

The next Saturday, Catherine found him sitting on the doorstep, weeping.

He confessed he had grown used to coming there—every other place felt strange.

She went in and told Margaret, who sighed and said, “Poor Luke—he might come in, if only he knew his place and treated her as a married wife.”

When this reached Luke, he hesitated.

“Pshaw!” Catherine snapped. “Promises are like pie-crusts—crumbly and useless. Promise her the world, rather than sit outside like a fool. A word will bring you inside now—when you humor her in everything. And if poor Gerard never returns to claim her, you’ll have her—eventually. A lone woman is always worn down, thou foolish boy.”

Brother Clement had spent more than a year teaching and preaching in Basel when one morning Jerome appeared before him, dust-covered and eyes alight with triumph.

“Give glory to God, Brother Clement,” he declared. “You may now accompany me to England.”

“I am ready,” replied Clement. “For months I have waited, devoting my spare moments between lessons and prayer to mastering the English tongue.”

“A wise choice,” said Jerome. He then explained that he had delayed their journey only until he could secure special authority from the Pope—powers to collect funds for the Church’s work in England and to hear confessions in all secular monasteries.

“Now, gird up your loins,” he added. “Let us go forth and strike a bold blow for the Church, and against the Franciscans.”

Together, the two friars set out down the Rhine toward England. In larger towns, they preached side by side; in smaller ones, they often split ways—one preaching on one bank of the river, the other on the opposite shore—and met again at a prearranged place. Both were gifted speakers, though their styles differed greatly. Jerome’s sermons were noble and commanding, rich in moral certainty, yet somewhat narrow in scope and slightly repetitive in delivery—though, truth be told, far less so than most preachers of the age. Clement, on the other hand, was full of variation, his speech often natural and conversational, flowing gently like a brook over stones. It wrapped around reason and emotion alike, tender and persuasive. Yet when stirred by higher thought, Clement rose with astonishing power—soaring above Jerome as surely as his quiet tone fell below. At such moments, he became something almost divine: a prophet aflame, an orator possessed. *Vehemens ut procella, excitatus ut torrens, incensus ut fulmen, tonabat, fulgurabat, et rapidis eloquentiae fiuctibus cuncta proruebat et perturbabat.*

I would offer literal excerpts, but five reasons hold me back: it is difficult; time is short; I’ve done this before; another writer has since surpassed me; and while similarity is a virtue in peas, it is a flaw in books. Still—lest I seem to dodge the matter entirely—Clement had a secret habit: before entering any town, he would quietly learn its recent troubles and its prevailing sins. Jerome, rigid and unyielding, scorned such tactics. He believed a preacher should speak not to the people’s faults, but to their souls, regardless of circumstance.

At one major town, several leagues from the Rh{EIF, they shared the same pulpit. Jerome took the first turn, preaching against vanity in dress—a theme he returned to often. He was eloquent, biting, and the crowd listened with approval. But vanity was not their vice. Clement followed, addressing drunkenness—their real scourge. Here, he struck hard. Drunkenness, he said, was not merely a sin—it was the mother of all crimes, breeding theft, violence, and murder. He reminded them of a parricide committed recently by a decent man under the influence of drink. He spoke of a group of drunkards who had roasted one of their own alive in a nearby village.

“Your last prince,” he continued, “was said to have died of apoplexy—but you know well he died of drink. One of your aldermen perished last month, dead drunk, drowned in a puddle. Your children go barefoot while you fill your bellies with poison that turns you into beasts—foolish as calves, cruel as boars. It drives your families into poverty and your souls into hell. I tell you: if your women drank as you do, your entire town—and your nation—would sink beneath the very bottom of humanity. How long will they remain temperate? How long will they resist the example of their husbands and fathers? Vice never stands still. You must change—or watch them follow in your footsteps. Already in Bohemia, women drink alongside men. What does a drunken woman look like? Would you wish to see your wife drunk, your mother degraded?”

The audience gasped. Medieval listeners did not sit in silence when moved. A cry of horror rose from the crowd.

“Ah,” said Clement, “that strikes home.”
“Madmen!” he thundered. “Do you think it shocks God less to see His noblest creation turned into a beast of drink than it shocks you—sinful creatures—to see a woman reduced to no better than yourselves?”

He closed with two vivid pictures: one of a drunkard’s home—chaotic, broken, filled with weeping children and empty bottles; the other of a sober man’s household—peaceful, orderly, blessed. The details were so true, so dramatic, that the women began murmuring, “Oh,” and “Ah,” and “Eh, but that’s a true word!”

The sermon caused a storm. People gathered in groups, arguing fiercely. Men grew angry; wives defended them, openly siding against the preacher. A married man, they insisted, deserved a drink—he labored for the whole family. And besides, they didn’t want their husbands replaced by weaklings. They laughed, but beneath it, unease stirred.

That very evening, a hundred men surrounded Brother Clement near the quay. They pressed coins into his wallet, offered him flowers, kissed his habit, and blessed him for daring to confront their weakness.

Jerome frowned. “Too earthly,” he muttered. “Drunkenness is not heresy, Clement. It does not warrant a full sermon.”

Yet as they traveled onward, Jerome found himself surprised. Clement’s words seemed to take root deeper than his own. They made people listen, reflect, weep—even change.

“He knows how to reach their level,” Jerome mused. “And yet, when he rises, he can soar.”

Still, the contrast troubled him. Though he secretly felt superior, he struggled to admit it. He tried to suppress the feeling as petty, unworthy of a servant of God.

“Souls are like locks,” he told himself. “Preachers must be like keys. If they do not differ, the door remains shut. And truly, this novice holds the key to these northern hearts—perhaps because he is himself a northern man.”

So they journeyed slowly down the Rhine, sometimes drifting with the current, more often walking along the banks, preaching, teaching, hearing confessions in villages and towns. Finally, they reached Düsseldorf.

There stood the small quay where Gerard and Denys had once boarded a boat to travel upstream. The friars stepped ashore. The streets lay before them, familiar and unchanged. There was “The Silver Lion,” the inn where so many paths had crossed. Nothing had altered—except him.

He walked barefoot through the town, hands folded across his chest, eyes cast humbly downward, heart calm and cold. A true son of Dominic, a faithful servant of Holy Church.

“Eli,” Catherine said, her voice steady yet soft, “answer me one question like a man, and I’ll ask no more this day. What is wormwood?”

Eli blinked, caught off guard by the suddenness of it. For a moment he looked as though he’d been asked to solve a riddle in Latin. Then he rallied: “It’s something that tastes mighty bitter.”

“That’s fair enough,” she replied, “but not what I mean.”

“Then let me have the answer myself,” he muttered.

“And I shall give it,” she said. “Wormwood is—having two idle souls under your roof, doing nothing but waiting for your shoes and mine.”

The words struck him like a stone. He sank back into his chair, eyes downcast. “Aye,” he murmured, “and worse than that—waiting for their best friend’s coffin, with nothing to do but mourn. Is it not enough to drive them mad? Why not set them up somewhere? Give them a chance?”

“I’m willing,” Eli answered slowly, “but I fear they’d drink and gamble away every shelf in the shop.”

“Nay,” Catherine said firmly, “do you take me for a fool? Of course I mean to watch them at first—keep a loose rein upon them, as the saying goes.”

“And where would you send them?” he asked.

“Not here,” she said quickly. “That would divide our own trade. No—Rotterdam against the world. There I could start them.”

Ah, self-deception! The real reason behind all this was not ambition or charity, but love—the longing to be near little Gerard.

After much talk and many promises from Cornelis and Sybrandt—promises made with fervor, if not full sincerity—Catherine set out for Rotterdam, taking Kate with her for company and change. They searched the streets until they found a shop in a good quarter, though it was in poor repair. But its disrepair worked in their favor; they secured it at a bargain price and began at once to clean, rebuild, and make it fit for business. Shelves were fitted, the living quarters tidied, and hope stirred anew.

Meanwhile, Luke Peterson never ceased asking Margaret what he might do for her. Her reply, always the same, came in a quiet, weary tone: “Nothing, Luke. Nothing.”

“What?” he would protest. “You who are so clever—can you truly think of nothing I might do for you?”

“Nothing, Luke,” she would repeat. “Nothing.”

But one evening, she changed her tune. “If only,” she said softly, “you could make something to help my sweet sister Kate.”

Luke, ever the slave to love, leapt at the chance. In short order, he built a small cart, lined it with cushions, and yoked himself to it. At dusk, he drew Kate through the town, along the broad, shaded boulevard, while Margaret and Catherine walked beside. It was a scene of gentle joy—but appearances deceived.

Kate, for her part, cherished every moment. Little Gerard sat nestled in her lap, his tiny hands clutching her dress, and she adored him with all her heart. To see him there was like watching a cherub borne by an angel, or a rosebud cradled in the cup of a lily. Such beauty drew the scorn of the vulgar. They jeered, calling Luke a thistle, mocking his lack of four legs, asking if his mistress couldn’t afford better.

Luke paid them no mind. But Kate did. “Thou hast made the cart for me, good Luke,” she said, her voice low. “That was kind. But I did wrong to let thee draw me too. We can afford to pay someone else. I love these rides, and carrying little Gerard—I do. But I’d rather not ride again than see thee mocked.”

“Much I care for their tongues,” Luke replied. “If I cared, I’d break their heads together. I’ll draw you till my mistress says stop.”

“Luke,” Catherine said gently, “if you obey Kate, you will please me.”

“And so I shall,” Luke answered. “I will obey Kate.”

One woman stood apart from the laughter—Jorian Ketel’s wife. She watched the procession and said quietly, “That is strength well used—to bear the weak. And her prayers will be your reward. She is not long for this world; she smiles even in pain.”

Joan spoke true. But Luke, simple-hearted, shook his head. “I want no prayers from the poor lass,” he said. “I do it for my mistress, Margaret.”

From then on, Luke pressed Margaret often for some task, any task. But she refused each time. Until one day, worn down by his persistence, she turned to him suddenly, her face pale, her voice sharp with meaning she could not hide:

“Find me my boy’s father.”

“Mistress,” said the servant, “they all say he is dead.”

"Not so," she replied, her voice steady despite the tremor in her hands. "They still feed me with hope."

"Ay, to your face," he murmured, "but behind your back—every tongue whispers it. He’s gone."

At that, Margaret’s eyes filled with tears. Luke, standing beside her, whimpered softly, as though the sorrow of another were his own. He had the strength of a man but the heart of a child.

"Prithee, do not weep so, sweet mistress," he said gently. "I would bring him back from the grave itself, rather than see you suffer thus."

She wiped her cheeks and drew a shaky breath. "I think I weep because they are so cruel—so double-tongued. They speak kindly to my face, yet betray me behind my back."

Then, placing her hand on his shoulder, she spoke with quiet intensity: "Luke, he is not dead. Dying men have strange visions. Listen—my father, when he lay dying, was sitting in that very chair where you sit now. Mother stood near, and I was busy at my sleeve. And suddenly, he turned his head and said—'I see him! I see him!' Not weak or fading, but blazing with fire. 'Sore disfigured—on a great river—coming this way.'"

Luke fell silent, absorbing her words.

"Ah, Luke," she whispered, "if you were a woman—if you felt for me even half what you pretend to feel—you would pity me, and go find him. Think of it—the father of my child!"

"I would, mistress," he said, "if I knew how. But how can I?"

"Nay, of course you cannot," she sighed. "I am mad to ask it. Yet—oh, if any one truly cared for me, they would. That is all I know."

Luke sat in thought for long moments, his brow furrowed. "The old folk say dying men see more than living men. Let me ponder—my mind does not race like yours. A great river... Well, the Maas is a great river."

He paused.

"Coming this way? Then if it were the Maas, he would be here by now. So it cannot be the Maas. The Rhine is greater, longer. I believe it must be the Rhine."

"And so do I," she said, her voice rising slightly. "Denys told him to come down the Rhine. But even if it is, he may turn aside before reaching home. He does not pine for me as I pine for him—that is clear. Luke, do you not think he has abandoned me?"

She wanted him to deny it. But he said, quietly, "It looks very much like it. What a fool he must be!"

"What do we know?" she pleaded, her voice breaking. "Let me think again."

"Indeed," Luke said, "I cannot gallop. Let me gather my thoughts."

After a time, he spoke. "There is a station sixty miles up the Rhine where all the public boats stop. I will go there and try to intercept him. True, I do not know him by sight—but I shall mingle with the passengers as each boat arrives and ask if Gerard Eliassoen is among them."

"And mistress," he added, "if you could give me a letter to him—since we are strangers, he might not believe a word I say."

"Good, kind, thoughtful Luke," she said, her voice thick with emotion. "I will—I will write it. Give me until supper-time."

At supper, she handed him a sealed letter, tied with silk in the fashion of the day. It was long, and written with trembling hands.

Luke held it in his palm, weighing it carefully. A shadow crossed his face.

"Say your father was not dreaming," he said slowly, "and say I find this man—and say he proves better than I expect, and returns to you at once—what then becomes of me?"

Margaret flushed deeply. "Oh, Luke, Heaven will reward you. I shall fall on my knees and bless you. I shall love you all my days, as a mother loves her son. I am so old compared to you—sorrow ages the heart. You must not go. It is not fair. Love makes us selfless."

"Humph," he muttered.

"And if," he continued, in the same grave tone, "this runaway should read your letter, and hear me tell him how you pine for him—and yet, being a traitor or a fool, refuse to return—what then becomes of me? Must I die a bachelor, and you go alone to your grave—neither maid, nor wife, nor widow?"

Margaret gasped, her chest tight with fear and emotion. She stammered, "If—oh, if God spare me from such a fate—then—then he would read it, and hear your words. And you, sweet Luke, must tell him—tell him how lovely his son is—fatherless, fatherless. Oh, Luke, can he be so cruel?"

"I doubt it," Luke said. "But I cannot be sure."

"Then," she said, "he will give up my marriage lines. I shall be an honest woman—even if wretched. My boy will no longer be a bastard. And of course, then we could both go into any honest man's house who would take us in. And for your kindness today, I swear—I will never be so ungrateful as to pass your door and enter another man's."

"Ay," he said, "but will you come *in* at mine? Answer me that."

"Oh, do not ask!" she cried. "Some day, perhaps—when the wounds cease to bleed. Alas, I’ll try. If I don’t throw myself and my child into the Maas. Do not go, Luke! Do not even think of going! This is madness from beginning to end."

But Luke moved slowly, as he always did—once a thought took root, it grew firm. His reply showed how love was shaping him into a true man.

"Well," he said, "madness is something, after all. And I am tired of doing nothing for you. I am no great talker. Tomorrow, at first light, I start. But hold—where is my money? My mother keeps it all. I never see it again."

Then Margaret reached into her dress and pulled out Catherine’s gold angel—the coin that had escaped so many times. She gave it to Luke.

And so, with a heart full of fear and hope, he set out on his journey—his mission reckless, perhaps, but not without purpose.

To us, it seems madness. But in those days, faith shaped action. Luke followed a dream—not as fantasy, but as truth. And when Catherine heard of it, she stormed:

"To send the poor lad on such a wild-goose chase! But you are like so many girls. Mark my words—by the time you’ve worn Luke clean out, made him sick of you as a dog is of its master, you’ll turn as fond of him as a cow is of her calf. And then—too late!"

The two friars arrived in Holland from the south just twelve hours after Luke began his journey up the Rhine. Thus, though neither knew it, they were drawing closer—rapidly.

Jerome, unable to preach in Dutch, pressed forward toward the coast, eager to reach England. With the current aiding their progress, the friars would have passed Luke entirely—had it not been for what happened next.

About twenty miles above the station Luke aimed for, Clement landed to preach in a large village. Near the end of his sermon, he noticed a grey nun weeping silently in the back row.

He approached her gently. "My sister, what troubles you?"

"Nay," she replied, "it is not for myself these tears flow. It is for my lost friend. Your words reminded me of who she once was—and who she is now. Poor wretch."

"You are a Franciscan," Clement observed. "I am a Dominican."

"It matters little," she said. "We are both Christians. And if you can help, I will tell you our grief."

She confessed that a young nun—beloved of the convent, her closest friend—had been lured away from her vows. After a slow descent into sin, she now lived in a small inn as chambermaid, in truth a decoy, known to sell herself to wealthy travelers.

"Elsewhere," she said, "we might take her by force. But this innkeeper serves the fierce baron on the hill above. He holds the baron’s ear. Were we to seize her, he would burn our convent to the ground."

"Nor," said Clement, "are souls saved by brute force."

As they spoke, Jerome arrived. Clement urged him to stay the night at the convent. When morning came, Clement told him of the abbess’s sorrow and his promise to try to save the fallen nun.

Jerome objected. "It is not our concern. A waste of time."

But Clement was no longer a mere pupil. He stood firm. At last, they agreed: Jerome would continue onward to secure passage to England, while Clement remained to make his attempt.

By ten o’clock that morning, a figure in a horseman’s cloak, wide boots, and a flapping felt hat stood motionless near the inn where Mary, the fallen nun, lived.

Clement, disguised, was truly wretched. Such hearts, ardent and pure, undertake miracles—but crumble when faced with the raw reality of sin. Yet they do not retreat. They pant, falter, but press on.

He hesitated at the door, prayed, then stepped inside—faint-hearted, sweating cold. But within, he became another man.

He called loudly for wine. It was brought by the landlord. Clement paid with coins from the convent, pretending to drink.

"Landlord," he said, "I hear you have a fair chambermaid."

"Ay, stranger," the man replied. "The buxomest in Holland. But she gives herself only to good customers."

Clement dangled a massive gold chain before the man’s eyes.

The landlord laughed. "Here, Janet! Here is a lover who would bind you in chains of gold—a tall lad, too!"

"Then I am doubly lucky," came a voice. "Send him hither."

Clement rose, shuddered, and followed her into the room. There sat Janet, playing with embroidery, pausing every moment to sing a broken tune. In her life, she had no patience for completion.

After polite greetings, the visitor asked if they could be more private.

"Why not?" she said, smiling. And she led him forward.

He followed, groaning inwardly.

"There," she said. "No one comes here unless they pay."

Clement closed the shutters carefully.

"What is that for?" she asked, uneasy.

"Sweetheart," he whispered, "so that God may not see us."

"Madman!" she laughed. "Do you think a wooden shutter can hide us from His eye?"

"No," he admitted. "But perhaps He has too much to do to notice us. Still, I would not have the saints and angels see us. Would you?"

"My poor soul," she said, "do not hope to escape their gaze. The only way is not to think of them. For if you do, it poisons your joy. For two pins, I’d run and leave you. Are you pleasant company, truly?"

"After all," he said, "so long as men do not see us, what matter if God and the saints do? Feel this chain—it is virgin gold. I shall cut two heavy links off for you."

"Ah!" she exclaimed, greedily touching it. "Why, it is as heavy as the chain around the Virgin’s neck at the conv—"

She stopped short.

"Whisht! Whisht! Whisht!" he hissed. "It is that chain. And you shall have your share. But betray me not."

"Monster!" she shrieked, recoiling. "To rob the Blessed Virgin of her chain—and give it to an—"

"You are none," he declared triumphantly, "or you would not care for that—Mary!"

"Ah! Ah! Ah!"

"Your patron saint—whose chain this is—sends me to greet you."

She ran to the window, trembling, and began to open the shutters.

But Clement had already removed his boots and hat. As the light flooded in, he let his cloak fall, revealing himself—a Dominican friar, calm and majestic as a statue.

He held aloft his crucifix, gazing at her with a look both loving and solemn—one that eased her physical fear, yet crushed her with spiritual terror.

She crouched against the wall.

"Mary," he said gently, "one word: are you happy?"

"As happy as I shall be in hell."

"And they are not happy at the convent. They weep for you."

"For me?"

"Day and night. Especially Sister Ursula."

"Poor Ursula!" she whispered—and wept.

"The angels weep more still. Will you not dry all their tears—here and in heaven—and save yourself?"

"Aye," she sobbed, "if I could. But it is too late."

"Satan avaunt!" he thundered. "That is your favourite lie. Listen not to the enemy, who whispers despair. I, who come to save you, have been a greater sinner than you. See—sin is not so sweet, even in this world, as holiness. Eternity stands at the door."

"How can they ever receive me again?"

"You doubt their worthiness. But in truth, they pine for you. It was their tears that moved me—a Dominican—to break my order’s rule, to wear these clothes, to enter this place. All is forgiven, if you let us rescue your soul from this den of wolves and return you to your vows."

She looked at him, tears in her eyes.

"And you—a Dominican—have done this for a daughter of St. Francis? Why, the orders hate each other!"

"Ay," he said, "but Francis and Dominic love one another."

She seemed struck.

He reminded her how shocked she had been at the thought of stealing the Virgin’s chain.

"But see," he said, "the convent, and the Virgin herself, value their lost nun far more than golden chains. They trusted me, a stranger, with this chain—hoping its sight might remind you of their love."

At last, with terrible simplicity, he showed her the end of her path—and stirred her forgotten memories.

She knelt sobbing at his feet. "I have never known peace since I broke my vows. I will go back—if you go with me. Alone, I dare not. Even if I reach the gate, I cannot enter. How could I face the abbess, the sisters?"

He promised to go with her—as joyfully as a shepherd carries a stray lamb to the fold.

But when he urged her to go at once, petty fears sprang up—like silken nets.

He swept them aside.

"And how can I walk beside you in this habit?"

"I have brought your gown and cowl. Hide your finery. Leave your shoes as I leave mine."

She gathered her jewels.

"What are these for?" Clement asked.

"To give to the convent, father."

"Their source is impure."

"But," she insisted, "to leave them here would be a sin. They can be sold to feed the poor."

"Mary," he said, "fix your eyes on this crucifix. Trample those devilish baubles beneath your feet."

She hesitated—then threw them down and crushed them.

"Now," he said, "open the window and fling them onto that dunghill. Well done. So pass the wages of sin from your hands, the glittering yoke from your neck, the pollution from your soul. Away, daughter of St.6 Francis—we linger too long in this vile place."

She followed.

But danger still waited.

The landlord stared, stunned, as a black friar and a grey nun passed through his kitchen.

"Mummery?" he muttered.

Then he understood.

"Hey! Reuben! Carl! Gavin! A false friar stealing our Janet!"

Men rushed in, threatening.

Clement charged forward, crucifix raised.

"Forbear!" he roared. "She is a holy nun returning to her vows. Any hand that touches her cowl shall wither. His body shall lie unburied. His soul shall burn in eternal fire!"

They recoiled as if struck by flame.

"And thou—miserable pander!" he shouted.

He seized the man by the neck and hurled him across the room—headfirst onto the stone floor.

Then he tore open the door and carried the screaming nun into the road.

"Hush, poor trembler," he gasped. "They dare not molest you on the highroad. Away!"

The landlord lay stunned, bleeding.

Mary glanced back—then fled.

On the road, Clement warned her: "Observe my temper. Hitherto, we have spoken of your faults. Now—mine. My anger is fierce, uncontrollable. By God’s grace, I am not a murderer. I repent—but too late. Had those men touched you, I would have shattered their skulls with this crucifix. I know myself. And I tremble at myself. Beneath this black robe, there lurks a wild beast."

"Alas, father," she said, "had you been otherwise, I would have been lost. To free me from that place required a man both bold as a lion and wary as a fox."

Clement reflected. "This is certain: God chooses well His instruments. With imperfect hearts, He works His perfect will. Glory be to God!"

Near the convent, Mary stopped abruptly, clutching his arm, weeping.

He comforted her. "You have nothing to fear. This will be the happiest day of your life."

He sent her to sit and compose herself while he entered the convent.

"Mother," he said, "give glory to God. Mary is at the gate."

The abbess was overcome with joy. She agreed to soften the path for the penitent.

Clement returned, soothed Mary, and heard her confession.

"The abbess grants you to choose your own penance."

"None the lighter," she vowed.

"Perhaps not," he said. "But today is for joy alone."

He led her to the abbess’s postern. As they walked, music and singing drifted from within.

"It is a feastday," Mary said. "And I come to mar it."

"Hardly," he smiled. "For you are the queen of the festival."

"Me? Father, what mean you?"

"Have you never heard that there is more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous who need no repentance? This convent is not heaven—nor the nuns angels. Yet some among them are angelic. And they sing for your return."

A hand trembled at the keyhole.

The postern flew open.

Sister Ursula rushed forward, weeping, clinging to her friend.

The abbess followed, moved beyond words.

Clement bid them farewell. They begged him to stay. But he declined, regretful.

"I have already tried Brother Jerome’s patience. I must hasten to the river. Perhaps sail tomorrow."

So Mary returned to the fold. And Clement strode onward—toward the Rhine, and England.

This was the man for whom Margaret’s boy waited—with her letter.

That letter was simple, tender—written only by a woman’s heart, to one who had wronged her.

She began by telling him of the birth of their son, and how the child had comforted her through the agony of his silence.

She described little Gerard in detail—the mole on his little finger.

"Know anyone with the same? If you saw him, you could not help but be proud. All the mothers envy me. But I envy no one—except the wives whose husbands come home. You come not to us."

"My own Gerard," she wrote, "some say you are dead. But if you were dead, how could I live? Others say you, whom I love so truly, are false. But I will believe that only from your own lips."

"My father loved you well. As he died, he said he saw you on a great river—your face turned toward me, but terribly disfigured. Is it so? Have cruel men scarred your face? Or lost a limb? Then you have greater need of me. And I shall love you not less—alas, do you think a woman’s love is as light as a man’s? No. Better, even than when I shed those few drops from my arm—worthless tears, you said—yet you wept for them. Remember? It was not so long ago, dear Gerard."
