She continued in this gentle tone, ending without reproach—without doubt of his love.

Not that she was free from doubt. But she dared not show it. To do so might frighten him away.

And so she entrusted the letter to Luke—her soft, loyal servant.

And so she was not an angel, after all.

Luke mingled with the passengers of two boats—heard nothing of Gerard Eliassoen. Not surprising.

But at the third boat, a black friar stopped him.

"And what would you with this man you call Gerard Eliassoen?"

"Why, father," Luke replied, "if he lives, I have a letter for him."

"Humph," said Jerome. "I am sorry for it. Yet the flesh is weak. Well, my son, he you seek will be here by the next boat—or the one after. And if he answers to that name—well, I am not the keeper of his conscience."

"Good father," Luke said, "one plain word—Heaven’s sake. Is Gerard Eliassoen of Tergou alive?"

"Humph," Jerome mused. "Well, certes—he who went by that name is alive."

"Then it is settled," Luke said, dryly.

But the next moment, he fled from sight—weeping.

"Oh, why did the Lord make women?" he muttered. "I was content with the world till I fell in love. Her little finger means more to her than my whole body. And he is not dead. And now I must deliver this."

He looked at the letter—then flung it to the ground.

But he picked it up again, snatching it with fury, and went to the landlord, tears in his eyes.

"Please," he begged, "give me work. I must keep from breaking my heart over another man’s love."

The landlord refused. "I have my own people."

"Oh, I do not want your money," Luke said. "I only want work—anything—to keep from despair."

"Good lad!" the landlord exclaimed. "Good lad!" And he gave him barrels to mend—on those terms.

And Luke worked with fury—between the boats, as they drifted down the Rhine.

Waiting for a letter from one you love can twist the heart into strange shapes. Margaret, writing to her dying father, poured out all her hope and belief—whether in vision or illusion, she could not say. When the words were written, and Luke had gone on his journey, she stood back from herself, startled by how easily she had let faith carry her away. A pang of guilt followed—what had she done? Had she given false comfort? And then Catherine came, sharp as ever, to scold her for clinging to dreams that might never come true. The rebuke was just, but it left Margaret broken. She had soared too high, only to crash down into deeper sorrow.

It was then that Joan Ketel, a woman of quiet strength and kind heart, found her sitting alone, wrapped in silence and despair. Joan came radiant with an idea. “Margaret,” she said, “I know what will heal thee. There’s a holy hermit in Gouda—a man who sees things others cannot. When he’s in the mood, he knows what lies ahead.”

“Aye,” Margaret replied, weary and doubtful. “I’ve heard of him.”

Joan, though gentle, would not be denied. With some coaxing, she persuaded Margaret to walk to Gouda, bringing with them a basket of butter and eggs as a gift. It was a long way, but they went, side by side, talking little, each lost in their own thoughts.

They reached the hermit’s cave at dusk. It was carved into the rock, dark and silent, with a small opening where offerings were placed. They set down their basket, and Margaret stepped forward, placing her lips to the aperture.

“Holy hermit,” she whispered, “we bring thee butter and eggs, the best we have. I am a poor girl, deserted, wife yet not wife, mother to the sweetest babe. I come to ask—alive or dead? True to his vows, or false?”

A faint voice answered, thin and weak: “Trouble me not with matters of earth. Send me a holy friar—I am dying.”

“Oh, no!” Margaret cried, her heart sinking. “Poor soul! Then let us come in, to help thee.”

“Saints forbid!” came the reply. “Thine is a woman’s voice. Send me a holy friar.”

They turned and walked back, silent, the wind tugging at their cloaks. Joan could not hold her tongue. “Are women so evil, then, that even a dying man must not see them?”

But Margaret did not answer. She was too far gone in grief.

Joan tried to console her, gently at first, then more firmly. “And Jorian—he’ll speak soon. He’s close to bursting. He’s grateful, truly. You saved him when no doctor could.”

“Seeing is believing,” Margaret said quietly, almost bitterly.

“I know,” Joan pressed on. “He says he’d have thought feverfew a sorry herb if it hadn’t been for you. ‘Why,’ he said, ‘if there’s a poor thing like that, I’d pull mine up.’ But then I told him remedies aren’t better for being rare. You and your herb cured him when grand medicines failed. So I said, ‘You may go down on your knees to feverfew.’ But yes—he’s grateful. All he talks about is you. Only last night—”

“What?” Margaret asked, her voice softening.

“He made me swear not to tell you.”

“Then tell me now.”

“Well,” Joan hesitated, “he said: ‘If I speak, it won’t bring him back—but it will stir up trouble. I wish I had more sense. I’m sorely troubled. But least said is soonest mended.’ That’s his favourite saying. He comes back to it from a mile off.”

Margaret shook her head. “We are wading through deep waters, my child and I.”

It was Saturday night. Still no word from Luke.

“Poor Luke,” she murmured. “It was kind of him to go on such a journey.”

“He is one in a hundred,” Catherine said warmly.

“Mother,” Margaret asked softly, “do you think he would be kind to little Gerard?”

“I am sure he would. So be kinder to him when he returns. Will you?”

“Aye.”

---

Brother Clement, guided by the nuns, took a shortcut along the riverbank, avoiding a bend, and marched swiftly toward the coast. He reached a point closer to Rotterdam than where Luke waited for Gerard Eliassoen. The next morning, he rose early and arrived in the city by noon.

Without delay, he made for the port, eager not to keep Jerome waiting. He saw several monks of his order standing on the quay. He approached them.

“Have you seen Brother Jerome?” he asked.

“Surely, brother,” came the reply. “Prithee, where is he?”

“Where? Why, there!” one monk pointed, gesturing toward a ship already under full sail.

Clement looked up—and saw it. A vessel cutting through the water, sails billowing, leaving the shore behind.

“What? Gone without me? Oh, Jerome! Jerome!” he called out, his voice cracking with pain.

The friars turned, surprised. One stepped forward. “You must be Brother Clement,” he said. Then they greeted him warmly, kissed his hand, and handed him a letter Jerome had entrusted them to deliver.

It was hastily written, cold, and distant.

*“A ship sails for England. I do not wish to waste time. You may follow if you choose, but you would serve God better here. Preach to your own people. You have a gift—Dutch hearts respond to you. But the English are haughty. You are too tender for them.*

*I met one on the road who sought you by the name you bore in the world. Be wary. Let not the world ensnare you again with its silken nets.*

Clement read it twice. His face grew pale. He felt betrayed—not merely by a friend, but by a spiritual brother. Here was Jerome, whom he had loved and admired, whom he had shared hardship with, who had once been his pupil, his penitent, his son in Christ—now casting him aside with indifference.

Had he done something wrong? Was he unworthy? Or had Jerome forgotten the very love that should bind brothers?

“You have no heart,” Clement whispered to himself. “You fly from me, man without mercy. I will not follow. I will go to Sevenbergen and pray over a grave.”

Three hours later, he passed Peter’s cottage. Children laughed and ran around it; the house had been repaired, a new shed built. He turned his head away quickly, not wanting to disturb the memory of what once was.

He walked instead to the churchyard. Among the stones, he searched for Margaret’s tomb. He could not find it. He searched again, every corner, every row.

“Ah, poverty,” he sighed. “Stern poverty. Poor soul—you were like me. No one remained to love you when Gerard was gone.”

He entered the church, knelt before the altar, and kissed the steps. Then he prayed long and deeply for the soul of the woman whose resting place he could not locate.

As he stepped out, he saw an old man leaning over the churchyard gate, peering in.

“Do you live here?” Clement asked.

“Four score and twelve years, man and boy,” the old man replied. “And I come here every day lately. This is where I expect to rest myself soon.”

“My son,” Clement said gently, “can you tell me where Margaret Brandt lies?”

“Margaret? There are many Margarets here.”

“Margaret Brandト. Daughter of a learned physician.”

“As if I didn’t know,” the old man snapped, then softened. “But she doesn’t lie here. Bless you, they left this place long ago. Gone in a moment. House empty. What? Is she dead? Margaret, Peter’s daughter, dead? Now, think on it. Likely enough. These great towns—they don’t suit country folk.”

“What great towns?” Clement asked.

“Rotterdam, they said. Or Amsterdam? I think it was Rotterdam. And gone there to die!”

Clement sighed.

“It wasn’t in her face when I saw her. I can usually tell. Alas, she was a blooming flower—cut down too soon. And here I stand, old weed like me, still breathing.”

“She was a May rose,” Clement said softly.

“Dear heart,” the old man added, “what a smile she had—”

“God bless you, my son,” Clement said, turning away. “Farewell.”

He walked on, reaching the convent at sunset. He stayed in the chapel, watching and praying—for Jerome, for Margaret—until long after midnight, until his soul had cooled, and the fire of grief had settled into quiet ash.

The day following, a Sunday, dawned bright and clear over the Hoog Straet, where Catherine’s house hummed with quiet excitement. Mass had just ended, and now the air was thick with the promise of new beginnings. The shop stood ready—clean, orderly, and proudly displaying the names of its new masters: Cornelis and Sybrandt. Above the door hung their sign: a white lamb suckling a gilded sheep, a symbol both humble and hopeful. Eli had arrived earlier, bringing goods from his own store to help them begin on solid ground. Their parents watched with swelling hearts, proud not only of their children’s venture but of the change it marked—a turning away from the toil of the fields toward the steady rhythm of trade.

Cornelis and Sybrandt walked together in the garden, hands clasped, eyes bright. “I’m sick of that old life,” said one. “It wore us down like dry reeds.” “Aye,” replied the other, “and this—making money instead of spending it—feels like breathing clean air.” They vowed then and there to stand firm in their calling, as steadfast as wax set in the sun.

Catherine, ever alert, heard their words through an open window. She turned to Eli and smiled. “They mean well. Let us bless their efforts.”

That evening, the family would gather for supper—a celebration of sorts. Margaret and her young son were invited, and the meal would be more than mere food; it would be a feast of counsel, of encouragement, of shared wisdom. Wine would flow freely, and the elders would speak plainly of trade, of diligence, of the rewards that come to those who work with purpose. It was a toast to commerce, a farewell to the unyielding land—wild oats, they called it, sown without return.

Margaret had come early, eager to help Catherine in the kitchen and to shake off the heaviness that had settled upon her lately. Both women moved about with quiet energy, their cheeks flushed as if warmed by the hearth’s fire. Then Joan arrived, bearing a fresh salad from Jorian’s garden.

“He cut it for you, Margaret,” she said, grinning. “You’re all he talks of these days. I’ll be jealous. I told him you’d be feasting today. But oh, lass—what a sermon in the new kerk! Preaching? I never knew what it meant until today.”

“Would that I had been there,” sighed Margaret. “My soul feels parched, starved for the dew of heaven.”

“Why, he preaches again this afternoon,” Joan replied. “But perhaps you’re needed here?”

“No,” said Catherine firmly. “Come, go if you wish. You’ve no call to stay.”

“I think,” Margaret mused, “I should not dull the mood at table if I came straight from a good sermon.”

“Then you must hurry,” Joan urged. “See how the folk are moving that way—and look! There goes the holy friar. Oh, mercy! The hermit himself! We forgot!”

And with that, Joan darted out of the house, crossed the street, and stopped the friar in his path. A moment later, she returned, breathless.

“There—he spoke to me,” she declared. “He said, ‘My daughter, I will go to him ere sunset, God willing.’ Such a gentle voice. And oh, my mistresses—such thin cheeks for a young man, and such great eyes—almost your colour, Margaret.”

“I have a strong desire to go,” Margaret confessed. “But my cap is not clean, and everyone else will be in their snowy mutches.”

“Take mine,” Catherine said, pointing to the basket. “But you cannot take the child—I need him for poor Kate. She has one of her bad days.”

Margaret nodded, understanding, and carried the boy upstairs. In the bedroom, Kate lay in bed, pale but smiling faintly.

“How art thou, sweetheart?” Margaret asked softly.

“Nay,” Kate whispered, “you need not ask. I am in pain—but I smile because I know you care.” She held up a small hand. “See—I brought thee one thou lovest.”

“Two, by my reckoning,” Kate replied with an angelic smile. At that moment, a spasm gripped her, fierce and sudden—enough to make any woman cry out. But she bore it silently.

“What, in your lap?” Margaret asked, interpreting the gesture.

“Nay,” Kate murmured. “He is too heavy, and I am in such pain.”

“But I love him so dear,” she added, “that I feel no weight at all.”

Margaret took the chance to prepare herself. She washed her face, brushed her hair, and tied on a clean cap.

“I am going to the kerk,” she announced. “To hear that beautiful preacher.”

Kate sighed. “And just now, I longed to go myself. That’s how it’s been this month—up and down, like the waves of the Zuyder Zee. I’d rather stay with you. Say the word.”

“Nay,” Kate said gently. “Go. And bring me back every word. Alas, I cannot go myself.”

Tears gathered in her eyes.

That settled it. Margaret kissed her sister-in-law, looked tenderly at the sleeping child, and let out a soft sigh.

“I trow I must not,” she said. “I never could kiss him lightly. And my father always said: *Never wake a child by day or night unless it is thy pleasure.*”

She paused. “Speak to Aunt Kate the two new words you’ve learned.”

And then she left, glancing back once with deep affection, closing the door softly behind her.

Downstairs, Catherine turned to Joan. “Will you help me peel these?”

“Aye, mistress,” Joan replied. “With pleasure.”

And so they worked in silence, swift and sure, the kitchen alive with the scent of herbs and roasting meat.

“Now, Joan,” Catherine said, “those who help me cook and serve the meat—they help me eat it. That’s my rule.”

“There are worse laws in Holland,” Joan chuckled. “Your will is my pleasure, mistress. My Luke has his supper already—digging in the fields today, thank God.”

Margaret descended the stairs.

“Eh, woman,” Catherine said, “that’s a hard trade. But look at her—just washed her face, turned her hair, and now who is like her? Rotterdam itself couldn’t match her!” She snapped her fingers. “Give us a kiss, hussy!”

“And mind,” she added, “Eli won’t wait for the duke. So don’t linger after church.”

Joan and Catherine followed her to the door, standing there watching as she walked down the street—her figure small but resolute against the golden light.

For among plain housewives, stepping out into the world is half an event.

Catherine murmured, “There, Joan—it feels almost as though I’ve just sent my own daughter to church, and am standing here, watching her go. I’ve done it many times. And yet… this time, it stirs something deeper. Joan, she’ll never speak ill of Gerard—even though he treated her cruelly while he lived. That’s why my heart aches for her. I’m older, wiser. I’ll see her wed to that simple Luke. And there—an end. What’s one grandchild?”

The sermon had already begun when Margaret stepped into the vast church of St. Laurens. It was a monument still in the making—no church rose in a single year. The side aisles were roofed, but the central nave and chancel remained open to the sky. Pillars stood tall and firm, some freshly whitewashed, arches bold and strong, yet only one window bore glass; the rest were jagged gaps in the stone walls, like wounds left by time. But on this radiant summer afternoon, those imperfections transformed the space into something sublime.

Sunlight poured through the broken openings, fractured into dazzling patterns that danced across the uneven surfaces. Beams sliced through the darkened side aisles like rivers of molten gold, illuminating the white columns with a glow that seemed almost divine. The central aisle shimmered with shifting squares of light and shadow, each patch cooler than any shade had ever been, each gleam like amber fire alive with heaven’s breath. Above, the blue vault of the sky stretched from west to east, so close it felt as if one could reach out and touch it. The women’s sunlit caps formed a sea of white beneath that azure dome, a striking contrast against the boundless sky.

Though the nave was packed, silence reigned. Every soul was held fast by the preacher’s voice—soft, steady, earnest—as he spoke words that carried both weight and grace. Margaret stood transfixed, her heart stirred by the beauty of the place and the solemnity of the moment. She slipped behind a pillar in the north aisle, where she could scarcely catch the words, yet found herself wrapped in a gentle devotional hush. A calmness spread through her like oil smoothing waves—a peace so deep it made her lean back, eyes half-closed, lost in reverie. To be here, in this sacred hush, felt right, even holy.

Then she saw a woman rise from a seat directly opposite, stepping aside to escape the harsh sunlight streaming through the lone glazed window. Without hesitation, Margaret moved swiftly and quietly around the aisle, claiming the spot. Now she stood near a pillar in the south aisle, less than fifty feet from the pulpit. At last, she could hear every word clearly. Her attention, however, was soon caught by something strange: the shadow of a man’s head and shoulders bobbing up and down in a most comical fashion. She fought to suppress a smile—until she turned and saw through the window the source: the sexton, Jorian Ketel, digging in the churchyard.

She watched him for a moment, then suddenly—without warning—the preacher’s voice struck her. Not just a tone, but a *sound*—a particular inflection—that pierced her soul. It resonated within her like a bell rung in an empty hall, shaking her from the inside out. Her hand flew to her chest, startled by the intensity of the sensation. Then, slowly, she turned her gaze toward the pulpit.

The preacher’s back was to her. All she saw was his tonsure, bare and round atop his skull. She sighed—a quiet, defeated sigh. That bald crown contradicted everything her heart had just heard. Yet she leaned forward slightly, eyes lowered, hoping the voice might carry that same note again. It did not come. But the voice itself began to grow upon her. As the preacher warmed, his tones swelled and softened, rising and falling with a rhythm that stirred faint echoes in her memory—echoes of laughter, love, and long-forgotten joy. She would not look up. To do so might shatter the melancholy sweetness filling her.

Then, mid-sentence, the preacher stopped. The silence that followed was sudden, profound. Margaret nearly sighed—had the sermon ended? No. She glanced around. The congregation remained still. But now, many faces turned toward her. She looked sharply behind her—nothing there. Then she noticed the others watching the pulpit. She followed their gazes.

There, in the pulpit, sat the friar—his face frozen in horror. His eyes, naturally large, now bulged unnaturally wide, staring straight at her from a pallid, bloodless face. He looked like a corpse woken from death. Margaret recoiled, cringing, certain something terrible lurked near her. But there was nothing—she was simply at the edge of the crowd.

At once, the church erupted. Figures rose from their seats, leaning forward. Hundreds of agitated faces darted between the friar and Margaret, then back again. The rustling of sunbonnets created a loud whispering sound. Women shrieked, men muttered. And Margaret, seeing all those eyes fixed on her, fled behind the pillar, trembling, casting one terrified glance at the preacher.

That glance—though fleeting—caught the expression on his face: a look carved in stone, etched with recognition. It passed through her like ice water. She gasped, sank onto a pile of wood chips left by the workmen, and buried her face in her hands.

The sermon resumed. She heard the sounds—words, cadence, passion—but they meant nothing. Her mind spun, refusing to settle. Only one thought took root: *He knew me.* That look—the look of recognition—was burning in her memory, sending shivers through her limbs.

The sermon ended at last, not with silence, but with a crescendo of fervent eloquence that lifted the crowd’s spirits, distracting them from the earlier pause, the ghastly stare, the unspoken dread.

Margaret slipped away with the others, joining the flow of people leaving the church. But at the door, she hesitated. Instead of going home, she turned and walked into the churchyard—toward Peter’s grave.

Though poor, she had given her father a slab and a headstone. She knelt beside it, kissed the cold stone, then draped her apron over her head so no one could see her hair. “Father,” she whispered, “you often said I was wading in deep waters. But now I think only God knows how deep they are. I’ll follow that friar to the ends of the earth—but I’ll keep my distance. I’ll make him tell me why he stared at me like a dead man roused from the grave, with no one behind me. Oh, father—you always praised me here. Speak for me there. For I am truly wading in deep waters.”

She sat upon the tombstone, facing the church door, her face hidden. There, in silence, she waited—for the holy man to return.

The church stood hushed and still, its stone floor patterned with shafts of golden light that pierced through the stained glass. Above, the vaulted ceiling seemed to glow with a soft, celestial purple, as though the heavens themselves had drawn near. Father Clement felt his soul stirred by the quiet beauty—just as Margaret had once done. This sacred space did not merely please the eye; it lifted the spirit toward the source of all goodness and purity.

His gaze swept across the nave, filled with villagers gathered for worship. A thousand white caps, each delicately edged with gold thread, shimmered like frost on a winter field. He had wandered far in his years—through cities, forests, and foreign lands—but never had he seen anything so strikingly pure and peaceful as this sea of heads bowed in reverence. Earlier that day, he had thundered from the pulpit with fire and judgment, but now, beneath the gentle afternoon sun, his heart softened. The harshness of his words seemed out of place. Instead, compassion surged within him. These were souls who rarely heard of mercy, whose ears were deafened by law and fear rather than love.

He began to speak—not with anger, but with tenderness, pouring forth the message of salvation. His voice was calm, yet deeply felt, carrying the weight of truth without the showiness of those preachers who spun endlessly like weathercocks in the wind. He moved not just their minds, but their hearts. Yet he did not forget those burdened by sin or sorrow. As he spoke of Christ’s boundless grace, he turned toward the southern aisle—where sunlight streamed through a high window, casting a radiant pool upon the floor.

And there she stood.

Margaret Brandt.

Her face glowed in the light, her auburn hair catching the sun like molten fire, framing a countenance both familiar and transformed. She leaned lightly against a marble column, her lashes lowered in quiet attention. Her expression was one he knew well—soft, listening, open-hearted. It was the same Margaret he had left behind: only more mature, more radiant, as if time had polished her instead of fading her.

Clement froze.

No emotion at first—only a sudden numbness, as if the world had stopped breathing. Then, slowly, his throat tightened. Words failed him. He trembled, staring at her as though seeing a vision from beyond death. There she was—his lost love, returned. Her presence stole every other thought. The congregation faded into silence, their forms blurring into shadows. All he could hear was a distant rustle, a low murmur of movement, like a dream half-remembered.

She looked up.

Full into his eyes.

Violet eyes—her own—staring back at him with a look neither recognition nor ignorance, but something deeper: a fleeting moment of startled wonder, the instant before understanding dawns.

In that breath, Clement lost himself. His lips parted, ready to cry her name—then she turned away, swift as a bird, vanishing into the crowd. But not before giving him one last glance—quick, sharp, electric. That look struck him like lightning. It left her trembling, her mind reeling, and him gasping, clutching the pulpit as if to anchor himself to reality.

He forced himself to speak again, muttering words no one could grasp. Then, haltingly, he resumed his sermon, stammering at first, then gathering strength. As she disappeared from sight, he convinced himself it had been a vision—a glimpse sent from heaven. And in that delusion, his voice rose, swelling with fervor, nearly slipping into rhapsody. The people listened, stunned, as if touched by divine fire.

When the service ended, he sat down heavily on the pulpit stool, drained and shaken. But soon, a notion took hold—one common enough in those times: if he had found no grave for her in Sevenbergen, perhaps God had brought her back to him here, in this very church. She must be buried nearby—perhaps right beside that pillar where she had appeared.

The idea settled in his mind like truth itself.

He would ask the sexton.

The church was empty now. Clement stepped through an opening in the south wall onto the grassy ground beyond. There, digging a grave, was the man he once knew as Jorian—the lad whose life he had saved long ago. But Jorian did not recognize him. Without his beard, the friar’s face was unrecognizable—tonsure, grey-streaked hair, pale cheeks hollowed by fasting.

“Son,” Clement said softly, “if you remember those you have laid to rest, tell me—has any Christian been buried inside the church, near a pillar?”

Jorian paused, wiping sweat from his brow. “No, father. All burials are in the churchyard. Why?”

“Never mind. Tell me—where lies Margaret Brandt?”

Jorian blinked. “Margaret Brandt? She died three years past. Buried here.”

“Oh,” Clement whispered. “Then I must know—was it near this pillar?”

“No,” Jorian replied, frowning. “That was before my time. The vicar might know. If she was noble—or rich enough to pay him.”

Clement sighed. “Alas, son, she was poor. And paid dearly for it. Her father, Peter, was a learned physician. She came from Sevenbergen—to die.”

As he spoke, his head drooped. He seemed no longer aware of where he stood, or whom he addressed. His mind had slipped back into memory, into grief.

Jorian stared, then spat into the dirt. “Are you making sport of me, holy sir? Or has some fool played a trick on you?”

He resumed digging with sudden force, clearly annoyed. Clement watched him, puzzled, but with a quiet sorrow in his eyes.

But Jorian, though gruff, was not cruel. After three shovels of earth, he stopped. “By the saints,” he muttered, “what a boor I am, speaking so to a holy man. You stand there like a lamb, and I growl like a dog.” He set down his spade, pulled on his doublet, and said, “Wait—I’ve it now. You’re not looking for Margaret. You want Peter Brandt’s grave. He does lie here—near the west door. Come, I’ll show you.”

He didn’t know that someone waited on the tombstone—someone who had been watching, hoping, for this very moment.

Pietro Vanucci and Andrea did not recognize the friar without his beard. For indeed, a man’s beard—especially one grown wild and untouched—can become part of his face, shaping it, defining it. Remove it, and he may vanish from memory entirely.

And so, as the sexton led the way, the friar walked forward, unaware that the past was waiting just ahead—waiting to reclaim what had been lost.

As Jorian pulled on his doublet and jerkin, preparing to leave for Peter’s tomb, he spoke without pause. “They called him a magician back in Sevenbergen. And it’s said he gave them a taste of his craft when he left—claimed he saw Margaret’s boy coming down the Rhine, dressed fine and rich, but with a scarred face from some foreign blade, and not all the limbs he’d had when he set out. But nothing came of it. Margaret still waits for her son. And Peter lies as still as any of his neighbors—though she did put a stone slab over him, to keep him where he is. You’ll see.”

He placed both hands on the edge of the grave, ready to climb out, when the friar laid a trembling hand upon his shoulder and whispered, breathless, “How long since did Peter Brandt die?”

“About two months,” Jorian replied. “Why?”

“And you say his daughter buried him?”

“No, I buried him. She paid the fee and raised the stone.”

“Then… if he had only one daughter—Margaret?”

“No more, at least not that he ever acknowledged.”

“So you believe Margaret is—alive?”

“Believe? Why, I’d be dead myself otherwise. Riddle me that.”

“I cannot, sir. You love her.”

“Not more than reason, being married and father to four sturdy lads like myself. The truth is, she saved my life barely six weeks ago. Had she been dead, she couldn’t have done it. I could not keep food down; doctors could do nothing. My Joan said, ‘It’s time to buy you a shroud.’ ‘I dare say,’ I told her, ‘but let’s borrow one first.’ Then in comes my lady—this very Margaret, who, by your reckoning, died three years past—opens the windows, shifts me where I lay, and cures me in the blink of an eye. With what? That’s the puzzle. With the most despised herb in the garden—sweet feverfew. A weed, they call it. But now, every time I pass my patch, I tip my hat and say, ‘Fly service to thee!’”

Jorian paused, then noticed the friar’s pallor. “Why, father, you look ill—pale, then red, then white again. What ails you?”

“The surprise—the joy—the wonder—the fear,” Clement gasped.

“What has it to do with you? Are you kin to Margaret Brandt?”

“No,” he said, voice low. “But I knew one who loved her so deeply, her death nearly killed him—body and soul. Yet you say she lives. And I believe you.”

Jorian stared, then after a long silence, spoke solemnly. “Father, you’ve asked many questions, and I’ve answered truthfully. Now, for Our Lady’s sake, answer me two: Did you truly know someone who loved this girl? Where?”

Clement hesitated, close to revealing himself—but recalled Jerome’s letter, and the name he had once borne in the world. “I knew him in Italy,” he said at last.

“If you knew him, you can tell me his name,” Jorian said cautiously.

“His name was Gerard Eliassoen.”

“Oh,” Jorian breathed. “This is strange. Wait—why did you say Margaret Brandt was dead?”

“I was with Gerard when a letter arrived from Margaret Van Eyck. It told him she was dead and buried. Let me sit—my strength fails me. Foul play! Foul play!”

“Father,” Jorian said, “I thank Heaven for bringing you to me. Sit down—you look like a ghost. You fast too much to be strong. My mind misgives me—I think I hold the clue to this riddle. And if I do, there are two villains in this town whose heads I would gladly smash as I do this earth.” He clenched his teeth, lifted his long spade high, and brought it crashing down upon the mound again and again.

“Foul play?” he roared. “You never said a truer word. If you know where Gerard is now, waste no time—go to him, show him the trap they’ve laid. My wits may be dull, but while the slow hound puzzles over the scent—go to it. And I think you and I have grasped two ends of the same stick—and a very foul one.”

Then, after the usual prelude men of his sort always make, Jorian came to the heart of the matter. He had been hired by the burgomaster of Tergou to repair the floor of an upper room in his house. Nearly finished, he returned suddenly to collect his tools—and heard loud voices below. Curiosity took hold. He lay flat on his stomach and listened.

The burgomaster was speaking of a letter—how Cornelis and Sybrandt were to replace one meant for Hans Memling, with another addressed to Gerard. “Their will was good,” the burgomaster said, “but their courage small. So to give them heart, he showed them a drawer full of silver. If they did the trick, each could take as much as their hands could hold.”

Jorian remembered it well—especially that night, when he could not sleep for thinking of the bargain. Next morning, at dawn, he saw Cornelis and Sybrandt emerge from their house—each with a black eye.

“Oho!” Jorian muttered. “Hans has marked you well. I hope that’s all you got for your pains.”

Sure enough, they hurried toward the burgomaster’s house. Jorian slipped into hiding.

At this point, the monk’s nostrils flared, his eyes restless with tension.

“Well, father,” Jorian continued, “the burgomaster led them into that very room. He held a letter in his hand. I’m no scholar, but I’ve as many eyes as the Pope. I saw the drawer open—those two knaves plunged their hands in and pulled them out full. Saints in glory, how they strained to hold more and more! Sybrandt had smeared his hand with something sticky—glue, I think—and managed to carry off a few pieces clinging to the back. Ha! ha! ha! ’Tis a sin to laugh.”

So luck was on the wrong side, as ever. They’d done the deed—but how, no man would know till Judgment Day. And they left their mortal jewels behind in that drawer.

They got their handful of silver. But the devil had the better of the bargain.

“There, father,” Jorian concluded. “That’s off my chest. I often wanted to tell someone—but dared not. Not to the women. For if I had, Margaret would have had no friend left in the world. Those two black-hearted scoundrels are the favorites—always are. Have you not seen the old folk just opened a new shop for them here, in the Hoog Straet? Look—there’s their sign: a gilt sheep and lambkin. A pair of wolves suckling their dam would be nearer the truth. And today—today they feast the whole family. Oh, what a fine world it is.”

He turned to the friar. “Say something, holy father. You sit like stone. Not even a curse for them—those heartless rogues?”

“Was it not enough that the poor lad was alone in a strange land?” Jorian thundered. “Must his own flesh and blood steal away the one blessing his enemies left him? And think of her—waiting, waiting these years, sitting by the window, watching the street for Gerard! So constant, so tender, so true. My wife says no woman ever loved a man more faithfully than she loves that boy those villains tore from her. And every day, she weeps salt tears. And I think—had it not been for those greedy, lying knaves, that winsome lad—whose life I saved—might be beside her now, the happiest man in Holland. And that sweet girl—she who saved my life—might sit with her cheek on her lover’s shoulder, the happiest woman in Holland instead of the saddest. Oh, I thirst for their blood—those sneaking, lying, cheating, cowardly, heartless, bowelless—what now?”

The monk leapt up, livid with rage and despair, and fled, fists clenched and raised high. The fury was so terrible, so wordless, that Jorian’s own anger vanished at the sight. He stood stunned, watching the storm he had unleashed.

Just then, a small, trembling hand gripped his arm. It was Margaret Brandt.

He started. Her sudden appearance seemed impossible. She had waited long at Peter’s tombstone, but the friar had not come. So she went into the church to search for him. She found no trace. Then, walking up the south aisle, she saw the shadow of a giant friar racing across the floor and part of a pillar—passing through her very form. She nearly screamed—but remembered Jorian’s shadow had entered from the yard. She tried to climb out the nearest way. She succeeded, though with difficulty. By then, Clement was vanishing down the street. But even from afar, she saw his agitation—his body spoke of torment.

Jorian and Margaret looked at each other, then at the distant figure of the fleeing friar.

“Well?” she asked, trembling.

“Well,” he replied, “you startled me. How come you here?”

“This is no time for idle talk,” she said sharply. “What did he say to you? He spoke to you—don’t deny it.”

“Girl,” he said, “he asked me where you were buried in this churchyard.”

“Ah!”

“I told him—nowhere, thank God. You’re alive. Saving others from the churchyard.”

“Well?”

“The long and short of it is—he knew your Gerard in Italy. A letter came saying you were dead—and it broke your boy’s heart. Who wrote it? Ah—by the demoiselle van Eyck. That was how he put it. But I told him no—it wasn’t the demoiselle nor any noblewoman who penned that lie. It was Ghysbrecht Van Swieten—and those foul knaves, Cornelis and Sybrandt. They swapped the real letter for one of their own. I told him I saw the whole villainy through a crack. And now—if I haven’t told you!”

“Oh, cruel! Cruel! But he lives. The worst fear is gone. Thank God!”

“Aye, lass,” Jorian said. “And as for your enemies—I’ve given them a dig. That friar is friendly to Gerard. He’s gone to Eli’s house, I think. I told him where to find Gerard’s foes—and yours. And wow—when he’s angry, he’s a force of nature. He turned black and white, flew apart like a stone from a sling. Girl, there was thunder in his eyes and silence on his lips. Made me cold.”

“Oh, Jorian, what have you done?” she cried. “Quick! Quick! Help me there—the power has left my body. You don’t know him as I do. Oh, if you had seen the blow he gave Ghysbrecht! And heard the crash! Come—save him from worse harm. The water is deep enough—but not bloody yet. Come!”

Her voice was filled with agony. Jorian sprang from the grave, pulling on his jerkin as he ran.

But as they hurried, he asked, “What on earth do you mean? You speak of the friar—and I of Gerard.”

“Man, can’t you see?” she said. “That friar is my boy’s father. I’ve waited for him long, Javax. Well—he’s come to me at last. Thank God for it. Oh, my poor child! Quicker, Jorian, quicker!”

“Why, you’re mad as he,” Jorian said. “Wait! By St. Bavon—that was Gerard’s face—no, not like it—yet somehow… it was. Come on! Come on! Let me see the end of this.”

“The end?” she whispered. “How many of us will live to see it?”

They ran in breathless silence until they reached Hoog Straet. Then Jorian tried to calm her.

“You’re making trouble for yourself,” he said. “Who says he went there? More likely to the convent—to pray and weep, poor soul. Oh, cursed, cursed villains!”

“Didn’t you tell him where those villains lived?”

“Aye, I did.”

“Then quicker, oh, Jorian, quicker! I see the house. Thank God and all the saints—I shall be in time to calm him. I know what I’ll say. Heaven forgive me! Poor Catherine—’tis of her I think. She has been a mother to me.”

The shop was a corner building, with two doors—one for customers in the main street, another round the corner. They were twenty yards from it when they heard a roar inside—like a wild beast. Then the friar burst out, white and raging, tearing down the street.

Margaret screamed and fainted into Jorian’s arms.

“Stay, madman, know thy friends!” Jorian shouted after him.

But he was deaf, charging ahead, fists shaking high above his head.

“Help me in, good Jorian,” she moaned, suddenly calm. “Let me know the worst—and die.”

He supported her trembling frame into the house. It was unnaturally silent—not a sound. Jorian’s heart pounded. A door stood before them, unlatched. He pushed it gently with his left hand.

And there, on the threshold, stood Margaret and Jorian.

What they saw within—you shall soon know.

Supper-time had come, and Eli’s household gathered round the table, all save Margaret. Catherine, surprised, looked to her husband, expecting him to insist on beginning without her. But Eli shook his head. “We’ll wait a moment,” he said quietly.

“Why, I told her plainly you would not wait for the duke,” Catherine murmured.

“She is no duke,” Eli replied, his voice low but firm. “She is a poor, good girl—my own daughter—who has waited not minutes, but years, for a graceless son of mine. You may set the meat upon the board; when she comes, we shall eat, no longer delayed.”

The scent of roasted meats and simmering stews rose warmly from the dishes, tempting even Eli, who usually held fast to his principles. He relented. “She will come if we begin,” he said. “They always do. Sit down, Mistress Joan—you are no servant here, but a guest.” With that, he motioned the covers aside and raised his knife.

Then, with a sudden crash of sound, the door burst open—not by Margaret, but by a Dominican friar, pale as death, eyes blazing with fury. In one stride he was at the table, towering over Cornelis and Sybrandt, his arms outstretched like vultures poised above prey. His voice thundered through the room, raw and terrible:

“Cursed be the lips that lied and said Margaret was dead! May they rot before the grave, and burn upon white-hot iron in hell! Cursed be the hands that forged those letters—may they be severed by the hangman’s blade and grasp eternal fire! And cursed thrice be the cruel hearts that believed the lie, that tore true love apart forever! May they waste away on earth, joyless, loveless, hopeless—may they crumble to dust before their time, and burn in flames unending!”

He cursed the very food before them, every morsel, every drop of wine, every hair upon their heads. Then, turning from the trembling pair who had nearly vanished beneath the table, he tore a letter from his breast and flung it at Eli’s feet.

“Read this, old man!” he shrieked. “You locked up your son, and now see what monsters you have bred! Let the memory of my wrongs—and hers—haunt you all for ever! I shall meet you again at judgment day. On earth, I will never see you again!”

And with that, he was gone—as swiftly as he had come—leaving behind a silence so deep it seemed the house itself had frozen. The family sat motionless, stiff and white as statues around the steaming, untouched meal.

It was then that Margaret and Jorian entered—just in time to witness the scene: figures petrified in horror, the supper forgotten, the air thick with dread. Margaret’s eyes swept the room, and she gasped.

“Oh, joy!” she breathed. “Everyone is here. No blood has been shed. Oh, you cruel, cruel men! Thank God He did not take your lives!”

At the sight of her, Catherine let out a sobbing cry, then turned her face away. But Eli, having read the false letter and finally grasping the truth, saw Margaret enter—her face pale, her eyes filled with sorrow and relief—and surged to his feet in a storm of rage.

“Stand back!” he roared. “Let me reach those traitors—I’ll hang them myself!”

In an instant, he drew his short sword and lunged toward the two cowering men. “Fly!” cried Margaret. “Fly!”

They scrambled under the table, crawled out the other side, and fled. But before they could escape the house, Eli darted around and blocked their path. Catherine wrung her hands, helpless. Blood was certain to flow—until Margaret and Jorian seized Eli’s arms, holding him fast with all their strength. Only then did the fugitives slip free.

Eli, furious and thwarted, stormed after them into the street, shouting curses into the night. They were a furlong away, running like hunted beasts.

Inside, Eli returned, shattered. He grabbed the wooden board inscribed with the names of the accused, smashed it to pieces, and hurled it into the fireplace. The flames licked greedily at the splinters.

Catherine sat rocking, her apron pulled over her face. Joan rushed to her husband’s side. Margaret knelt beside Catherine, her arms wrapped tightly around her, whispering comfort despite her own breathless exhaustion.

But Catherine could not be soothed. “Oh, my poor children!” she wept. “Miserable mother! It’s a mercy Kate was ill upstairs. Thank God for that!” She broke into fresh sobs. “It would have killed her. He should have stayed in Italy. Why come home to curse his own flesh and blood? To tear us all apart?”

“Hold your tongue, woman!” Eli snapped. “You still stand with the guilty! Your weakness made these rogues what they are. I wanted to correct them young—sharp remedies for sore ills—but you always shielded them, undermined me, weakened my hand. And you, Margaret—leave comforting her. Her pain is nothing compared to yours. Yet she has no justice in her bones, nor ever will. Come to me—now. You are my daughter from this hour.”

It was a command. Margaret kissed Catherine gently, then tottered to Eli’s side. He placed her in a chair beside him, and she laid her head upon his chest, silent—no tears, only a depth of sorrow too great for words.

“Poor lamb,” he whispered.

After a long pause, Eli spoke again, his voice cracked but steady. “Come, good folk,” he said to Jorian and Joan, “we are in trouble, as you see. But that does not mean you must go hungry. For the sake of Our Lady, eat. Do not add to my grief by making me seem a churl. What the devil!” he added with a grim attempt at courage, “the more knaves I rid myself of, the greater my need of honest men and women—those who can clear the dish and bring light to my eyes. Eat, I beg you.”

Catherine, still weeping, nodded weakly. Such simple souls—so noble, so old-fashioned in their hospitality.

Jorian, whose appetite had grown sharp since his illness, was ready to obey. But Joan leaned close and whispered something. Instantly, he stepped back.

“No,” he said firmly. “I will not touch food cursed by Holy Church.”

“Indeed,” Eli murmured, abashed. “My son, raised at my table, has cursed my own victuals. That is strange. Well—what God wills, man must endure.”

The supper was carried out into the yard and cast aside.

Jorian took Joan home. That night, sorrow settled heavily over Eli’s house.

Meanwhile, where was Clement?

He lay full-length upon the cold stone floor of the convent church, his lips pressed against the lowest step of the altar, consumed by terror, guilt, and shame. Through the storm of his penitence, however, flickered a fragile joy—Margaret was alive.

Night fell, and he remained there, weeping and praying. Dawn would have found him still, but then a thought struck him like lightning: in his obsession with his own sins and Margaret’s suffering, he had neglected another duty—one far more urgent. A man was dying, and he had failed to tend him.

He rose, groaning under the weight of his many failings, and set out into the rain. The sky darkened; wolves howled in the distance, closing in. But Clement cared little. He was himself again, or nearly so—his soul reborn in contrition. Danger meant nothing now. Duty called.

Through the storm and the darkness, he walked steadily, beating his breast and crying out in Latin, over and over:

What a soul must endure—sensitive, tender, loving, devout—when suddenly thrust into a crisis of such magnitude and urgency, no words can fully convey. To imagine it is one thing; to live it, quite another. Were I to write a whole book on the inner struggle that unfolded within him during those few hours, we would still fall short of capturing its depth. Yet let me tell you two acts he performed afterward—acts that reveal the quiet strength and resolution that followed the storm of his emotions.

After spending the night with the dying hermit, exchanging prayers and spiritual comfort, Clement did not journey toward Rotterdam as he had planned. Instead, he turned his steps toward Tergou. His purpose was clear: to face his most formidable enemy—the burgomaster Ghysbrecht—and reclaim what was rightfully Margaret’s. In his hand he carried the parchment, a document whose own history could have been a tale in itself. He traveled weary and dust-covered, stopping at a fountain to eat his simple meal of black bread and drink water from the stream. But just as he raised the bread to his lips, a servant woman rushed up, breathless, begging him to come quickly and administer last rites to her dying master.

Without hesitation, Clement returned the bread to his wallet and followed her silently. She led him to the Stadthouse. As they approached the door, he hesitated, a faint shiver passing through him. Then, composed once more, he stepped inside and climbed the stairs. There, propped on pillows, lay Ghysbrecht—pale, weak, already resembling death. Clement stood in the doorway for a moment, recalling the tower, the forest, the letter, and all that had brought them to this point. Then, softly, he said, “Pax vobiscum.”

His voice trembled slightly. The sick man welcomed him with trembling joy. “Thank God, you’ve come in time! Absolve me, father, pray for my soul—you and your brethren!”

“My son,” replied Clement, “absolution comes only after confession. And confession must be full, without reservation, if you would save your soul. Reflect now—what sin weighs heaviest upon your conscience?” He knelt and offered a prayer for wisdom, then rose and said, “Confess your sins.”

“Oh, father,” whispered Ghysbrecht, “they are many and great.”

“Then let your penitence be equal to their weight,” said Clement gently. “Only so may you find mercy.”

The burgomaster clasped his hands and began, with outward sorrow, to list his transgressions. He confessed to eating meat during Lent, missing mass on Sundays and holy days, neglecting other duties of faith—each detail spoken with careful precision. When he finished, Clement spoke again, calmly: “These are faults. Now speak of your crimes. You should have begun with them.”

“But father,” stammered Ghysbrecht, “if these are not crimes, what else could be?”

“Are you confessing to me—or am I confessing to you?” asked Clement, his tone sharpening.

“Forgive me, father! I meant to confess to you. But I do not know what you mean by crimes.”

“The seven deadly sins—have you escaped them all?”

“Heaven forbid! I know none of them by name.”

“Many commit them daily without knowing their names,” said Clement. “Begin with the one that leads to lying, theft, and murder.”

“I am free of that one,” insisted Ghysbrecht. “How do you call it?”

“Avarice,” said Clement.

“Avarice? Ah, yes—I’ve always been thrifty, but I’ve kept a good table, and never neglected the poor. Alas, I am a sinner, perhaps the next will catch me. What is the next?”

“We are not done with this one,” replied Clement firmly. “Remember, the Church is not to be mocked.”

“Am I in a state to mock her now?” cried Ghysbrecht, bewildered. “Avarice? Avarice?”

“Have you ever robbed the fatherless?” asked the friar.

“Me? Robbed the fatherless?” gasped Ghysbrecht. “Not that I recall.”

“Once more,” said Clement, “I warn you: you are trifling with the Church. Miserable man! Another evasion, and I leave you. The devils will gather round your bed and drag you into hell.”

“Oh, do not leave me!” shrieked the old man, terrified. “I beg you—stay!”

“The Church knows all,” said Clement coldly. “You have robbed the fatherless. I will not ask again.”

“Floris Brandt?” whispered Ghysbrecht, recoiling in horror.

Clement stared at him, unyielding. “Yes. Floris Brandt.”

The burgomaster lifted himself up in bed, eyes wide with dread. “How did you know?”

“The Church knows many things,” replied Clement. “By ways hidden from you. You thought to deceive her, calling a friar you believed ignorant of your sins. ‘I’ll confess only to someone who doesn’t know my past,’ you said. ‘So I shall cheat the Church on my deathbed.’ But God, more merciful than you are to yourself, sent one who could not be deceived. I have tested you. I have warned you. But you cannot confess—because you are not truly repentant. Die as you have lived. I see the fiends already gathering. They wait only for me to turn away. And now I go.”

He turned to leave. But Ghysbrecht clutched at his robe, desperate. “Mercy! Holy man, stay! I will confess everything! Everything! I stole from my friend Floris. Alas, it should have ended there—he lost little—but I kept the land from Peter, his son, and from Margaret, Peter’s daughter. I meant to give it back… but I couldn’t. I couldn’t.”

“Avarice, my son,” said Clement, “avarice. Blessed be you—there is yet time.”

“No,” moaned Ghysbrecht, “I will leave it to her in my will. She won’t wait long—only a month or two at most.”

“For which month’s possession,” said Clement, “you would damn your soul forever. Fool!”

The sick man groaned, pleading for reason. But Clement, firm yet gentle, persisted. With infinite patience, he drew the dying man away from his grasp on another’s inheritance. At times, the temptation to produce the deed—brought expressly for this purpose—was strong. Once, he almost reached into his breast, but remembered yesterday’s rage and held back. He mastered his anger. He overcame his deep disgust for the man, whose presence made his flesh crawl. And finally, without a word of the parchment, he guided Ghysbrecht to full restitution.

How that restitution was carried out, and what effects it had upon the burgomaster, will be told elsewhere. So too will the terms of their parting. But I promised to record two acts that revealed Clement’s inner state. This was the first.

The second is brief—just two words:

As soon as he knew beyond doubt that Margaret had her inheritance, that she was secure and rich—

He vanished.

The day after the terrible scene, the little house on the Hoog Straet lay heavy with silence, like a tomb. Catherine, usually so brisk and full of life, moved through it as though her spirit had been drained away. Her eyes were red from weeping when, after dinner, she set out for the convent, hoping to find Gerard and begin the slow work of mending what had been broken. She meant to soften his heart, if only by a single word.

It took some time before the porter could understand whom she sought. When he finally did, he told her that Gerard had left late the previous night and was not expected back. Disheartened, Catherine returned home and broke the news to Margaret.

She found her sitting still, motionless, as if all joy had fled from the world. The child clutched tightly in her arms seemed to be all that remained—her last anchor. She held him close, afraid someone might take even this small comfort from her.

“Come to the Hoog Straet,” Catherine urged gently.

“For what?” Margaret whispered, her voice thin and weary. “You must think I am the cause of all this sorrow.”

“No, no,” Catherine said quickly. “We are not so cruel. And Eli loves you—he may yet be won over.”

“If I can help,” Margaret murmured, “then I will go.”

They arrived to find Eli and a carpenter replacing the old sign—once bearing the names Cornelis and Sybrandt—with a new one: *Margaret Brandt*. Catherine’s heart sank. Though she loved Margaret deeply, this act pierced her like a knife.

“The bane of one is another’s meat,” she muttered.

“You cannot make me spend money unjustly,” Margaret replied coldly.

“You are a good soul,” Catherine said, trying to keep her voice steady.

“Aye,” Margaret answered, “but best, since he is the strongest.”

The next day, Giles dropped in. Catherine told him the tale, painting the brothers as victims—outcast by their father, abandoned by their kin. She pleaded for pity, for justice, for mercy.

But Giles saw things differently. He listened patiently, then spoke plainly: “Those rogues got off too lightly. They deserve to hang at Margaret’s door. And now—hurrah!—my favourite returns.” He smiled broadly, his pride restored. “I’ll show him,” he declared, “what it means to have a brother at court who knows how to serve a friend and guide him right.”

“Bless you, Giles,” Margaret whispered softly.

“You’ve always stood by him, dear Giles,” little Kate added. “But alas, I know not what you can do now.”

Giles left, and silence settled once more—until a quiet knock at the door.

A well-dressed man stepped inside, asking if Margaret Brandt was there.

“Hear this, lass!” Catherine called cheerfully. “You’re wanted!”

“Well, mother,” Margaret said dully, “here I am.”

Then came the shuffle of feet. A frail, pale old man was helped into the room—Ghysbrecht Van Swieten.

At the sight of him, Catherine gasped and threw her apron over her face. Margaret shuddered violently, turning her head sharply away, refusing to look.

A weak voice trembled from the visitor’s lips: “Good people, a dying man has come to beg your forgiveness.”

“Come to see the ruin you made,” Catherine snapped, pulling down her apron and breaking into sobs.

“There, there—she faints! Eli, quick, help her!”

“No,” Margaret said faintly. “It’s just the shock. Let him speak. But he is the murderer of me and mine.”

“Alas,” Ghysbrecht whispered, “I am too weak to stand. No one offers me a seat.”

Eli, who had followed him in, stepped forward, half angry, half ashamed. “Well, burgomaster,” he said stiffly, “it is not our custom to leave guests standing while we sit. But mark this—your actions have done us great harm.”

His voice shook, but he held himself in check—for this was his own home.

Then, unexpectedly, a soft voice broke the tension.

“Father, mother,” little Kate said gently, “I owe you my duty—but this is not right. Death settles all accounts. See how death stares from his face? I shall not live long. His time is shorter than mine.”

Eli hesitated, then hurried to bring a chair. With careful hands, he placed it before the dying man. Ghysbrecht’s attendants helped him sit.

“Fetch the boxes,” he said.

They brought two wooden chests and withdrew, leaving the old man alone among those he had wronged.

All eyes turned to him—except Margaret’s.

With trembling fingers, Ghysbrecht opened the first box and pulled out deeds. “This land and these houses belonged to Floris Brandt,” he said. “They belong to you, his granddaughter, by right. I took them once, for a debt long paid with interest. Now I return them—tears in my heart, and shame in my soul.”

He opened the second box. “Three hundred forty golden angels—the rent and fines I collected beyond what was owed. I kept them… thinking I would give them back one day. But greed held me fast. I was not born dishonest—but I became so. Forgive me, please, against temptation.”

“Indeed!” Catherine exclaimed. “And you, burgomaster—the man who punished thieves all your life! But better late than never. Margaret, can you hear? He’s given you back your own. You’re rich now. Alack, what a mountain of gold!”

“Let him keep land and gold,” Margaret said, her head still turned away. “Give me back my Gerard—the one you stole from me with your treachery.”

“Alas,” Ghysbrecht said, “I wish I could. But what I can do, I have done. It cost me much. I rose from my deathbed to do it myself, lest misfortune prevent you from claiming what is yours.”

“Old man,” Margaret said quietly, “you, whose god is gold, have done this. God and the saints may forgive you, I hope. As for me—I am no saint. I am only a woman, broken-hearted. Speak to him, Kate. I am already dead.”

Kate paused, then spoke in a voice like music, gentle and clear: “My sister carries a grief no riches can heal. Give her time, Ghysbrecht. It is not natural she should forgive you all at once. Her son is fatherless. She is neither maid nor wife nor widow. The blow fell only two days ago—and it laid her heart open, bleeding.”

A deep, silent sob escaped Margaret.

“Therefore, give her time,” Kate continued. “And before you die, she may forgive you—even to please me, who may soon follow you, Ghysbrecht. In the meantime, we—whose wounds are deep, but not as deep as hers—forgive you. You are penitent, and dying. And I, for one, will pray for you from this hour. Go in peace.”

Her words fell like a blessing. Even Eli offered the old man bread and wine, but Ghysbrecht declined.

“What I have done,” he said, “is enough to strengthen me. Man sees only a little way ahead. That land I clung to so tightly—it was a bed of nettles all along. Now it is gone—and I feel lighter, freer, as though I have shed a burden.”

He called for his men. They lifted him into a litter and carried him away.

When he was gone, Catherine lingered over the gold, dazzled by its weight and glow. She had never seen such wealth gathered in one place. She nearly scolded Margaret for staying behind like a statue.

“Oh, come and see!” she insisted, teasing her. “Think of the possibilities!”

“Leave her be, mother,” Kate said softly. “How can she enjoy gold when her heart is heavier than lead?”

But Catherine pressed on. At last, Margaret relented.

She stood before the treasure, staring, wide-eyed. Then suddenly, she wrung her hands and screamed: “TOO LATE! TOO LATE!”

She collapsed into sobs, overwhelmed—not by riches, but by the agony of what might have been. If only a fraction of this wealth, a piece of this land, had come to her a year or two ago—when it was truly hers—Gerard would never have left. He would never have gone to Italy, never have chosen another path.

“Too late! Too late!” she cried again, her voice breaking with sorrow.

Not long after, word reached Rotterdam that Margaret Van Eyck had died and been buried. By a will made the year before, she had bequeathed all her possessions—after funeral costs and small gifts to Reicht Heynes—to her beloved daughter, Margaret Brandt, with a heartfelt request that Reicht remain in her service until she married.

Through this legacy, Margaret inherited a well-furnished house, along with paintings and sketches that would today be considered priceless. Among them was one she cherished above all others: a painting titled *A Betrothal*. The solemnity of the ceremony was captured in the man’s grave expression and the woman’s quiet contentment. Though nearly the entire composition was painted by Margaret Van Eyck, Jan van Eyck had completed the rest. The details were so finely rendered they still astonish viewers today. Margaret sent word to Reicht to stay in the house until she could summon the courage to return there—until she could bear to face the silence where her mother’s voice once rang out—and to guard especially the picture “in the little cubboord,” meaning the diptych.

Soon after, Luke Peterson returned home and learned that Gerard had become a monk.

He nearly lost his mind with joy. He rushed to Margaret and said, “Heed, mistress. If he cannot marry you, I can.”

“You?” Margaret replied. “Why, I have seen him.”

“But he is a friar now.”

“He was my husband, and my son’s father long before he ever took vows. And I have seen him—I’ve seen him.”

Luke was utterly bewildered. “I’ll tell you what,” he said. “I have a cousin who is a lawyer. I’ll go ask him whether you are legally married or free.”

“Nay,” Margaret answered firmly. “I shall ask my own heart, not a lawyer. Is this how you regard me? To go making me the talk of the town? Oh, fie!”

“That’s already done, without a word from me.”

“But not by those who hold me in respect. And if you do it, never come near me again.”

“Ay,” Luke sighed, “you’re like a dove to everyone else—but to me, you’re a hard-hearted tyrant.”

“It’s your own fault, dear Luke, for loving me. That’s what keeps me from being as kind to you as I wish. Listen, Luke, my bonny lad. I am rich now. I can make my friends happy—even if not myself. Look around the street, look through the parish. There are many women fairer than I, and none so worn down by sorrow. Look high, and choose your own. Speak to the girl yourself, and I’ll speak to her mother; they shall not refuse you. Take my word for it.”

“I see what you mean,” Luke said, turning red. “But if I can’t have your love, I want none of your money. I was your servant when you were poorer than I—much poorer. No. If you’d rather be a friar’s leman than an honest man’s wife, you’re not the woman I thought you were. So let us part, without malice. Seek your comfort on that road—where no woman has ever found it. As for me, I’ll live and die a bachelor. Good evening, mistress.”

“Farewell, dear Luke,” she said softly. “And God forgive you for speaking thus to me.”

For days, Margaret dreaded—and yet longed for—the moment she might meet Gerard again. She told herself, “I wonder not that he stays away. I would too.” Yet he must know he was a father. The desire to see their child would surely overcome everything. “And,” she whispered to herself, “if meeting him does not kill me, I feel I shall be better afterward than I am now.”

But day after day passed, and no word came. A cold dread began to seep into her soul. What if his absence was deliberate? What if he had gone to other monks, men of colder hearts, who had told him never to return? The cloister had already shown itself as merciless to true lovers as death itself.

At that thought, life seemed to drain from her.

Now, for the first time, deep anger mingled with her grief and fear. “Could he ever have loved me? To flee from me and our child without a word? Why, even poor Luke thinks more of me than he does.”

While her heart wrestled with these thoughts, Giles burst in, roaring with excitement. “I’ve hit the mark! Our Gerard is Vicar of Gouda!”

To understand this triumph, a brief glimpse of Giles’s life at court is needed. Some months before, his mind had suddenly awakened. He himself marked the change on June 8th, when, swinging by one hand along a rope strung with washing in the drying yard, something cracked inside his head—and lo! his intellect was unleashed. At court, his sharp wit, blunt speech, booming voice, and tiny frame made him a force to be reckoned with. Without the last, he might have ended up at the gallows. The young Duchess of Burgundy and Marie, the heir apparent, both doted on him, as noblewomen have always doted on dwarfs. The court poet wrote verses in his honor, buttering his back enough to stew Goliath. Even Giles’s own rough sayings were turned into elaborate poetry by the poet.

The result was a letter sent to Eli, titled:

*“The High and Puissant Princess Marie of Bourgogne Her Lytel Jantilman Hys Complaynt of Y’ Coort, and Praise of a Rusticall Lyfe, Versificated, and Empapyred by Me the Lytel Jantilman’s Right Lovynge and Obsequious Servitor, etc.”*

But Giles reached his peak with a clever mix of brains and brawn. On the eve of a grand joust, he challenged the Duke’s giant to a strength contest. The challenge sparked laughter and anticipation.

Giles had a tall pole planted ready. At the appointed hour, he climbed it like a squirrel, then bent his body at a right angle and held it—before sliding down so fast the princess shrieked and hid her face, fearing her little Hercules had perished.

The giant managed only ten feet, then looked up and down in despair, sweating profusely, before descending to argue.

“It wasn’t greater strength,” he claimed. “It was smaller size.”

The crowd laughed loudly. The truth was clear: Giles excelled at climbing poles; the giant excelled only at excuses. In short, Giles had measured their minds—with his own body.

“Come,” said Giles, “if you insist, I’ll wrestle you, my lad—if you’ll let me blindfold your eyes.”

The giant, stung by defeat and confident he could win this way, agreed.

“Madam,” said Giles, “see yon blind Samson? At my signal, he shall bow low and remove his hat to me.”

“How may that be, if he’s blind?” asked a maid of honour.

“I’ll wager on Giles for one,” said the princess.

“That’s my affair.”

When several wagers were placed, Giles struck the giant in the groin. He doubled over (the bow), and his hat fell off.

The company roared with delight at this clever jest. Giles fled. The giant pursued, but too late—Giles had prepared a hidden door in the wall, just wide enough for him, not a giant, and painted it to blend perfectly. He tore it open and vanished, leaving behind a message written large on the back of the door:

> *Long limbs, big body, panting wit,*
> *By wee and wise is bet and bit.*

After this, Giles became a power.

Now, let him speak.

Finding Margaret skeptical about the news and doubtful that a dwarf could influence Church affairs, he recounted:

“When the princess summoned me to her bedroom, as usual, I did not come full of mirth or country sayings, as I often do, but dull as lead.

‘What ails you?’ she asked. ‘Are you sick?’
‘In heart,’ I replied.
‘Alas,’ she said, ‘he is in love.’
Five brazen maids of honour giggled.
‘Not so mad as that,’ I said, ‘seeing what I see at court of women folk.’

‘There, ladies,’ she said, ‘let him be. He’s a liberal mannikin, and still gives more than he takes in saucy words.’

‘In all seriousness,’ she said, ‘what troubles you?’

I told her I was thinking, and what troubled me was that common folk sometimes kept their word—but princes never.

‘Heyday!’ she said. ‘Your shafts fly high this morning.’
I said, ‘Ay, because they hit the truth.’

She said I was as keen as keen, but it became neither me nor her to play riddles. ‘Stand aside, mesdames,’ she said, ‘and speak freely.’ For she saw I was in earnest.

I began to tremble—mind you, she could shed freedom and don dignity faster than slipping from dressing gown to kirtle of state. But I softened my voice like honey (why do you smile?), and said: ‘Madam, one evening five years ago, as you sat with your mother, the Countess of Charolois—now in heaven, worse luck—you with your lute, she with her tapestry—do you remember a fair youth entering with a letter from a painter named Margaret Van Eyck?’

She said she thought she did. ‘Was it not a tall youth, exceeding comely?’

‘Ay, madam,’ I said. ‘He was my brother.’

‘Your brother?’ she said, staring at me.
(What are you smiling at?)

So I told her all that passed between her and Gerard—how she wished to give him a bishopric, but the good countess said, ‘Gently, Marie—he is too young.’ Then both promised him a living. ‘Yet,’ I said, ‘he has been a priest for years, and no living. Hence my bile.’

‘Alas!’ she said. ‘It is not my doing. All you’ve said is true—and more. I remember my dear mother saying to me, “See thou to it if I be not here.”’ Then she cried, ‘Ay, dear mother, no word of thine shall fall to the ground.’

Seeing her moved, I said quickly, ‘Madam, the Vicar of Gouda died last week.’ (For when you seek favors from the great, you must know exactly what you aim at.)

‘Then thy brother is vicar of Gouda,’ she said, ‘as sure as I am heiress of Burgundy and the Netherlands. Nay, thank me not, good Giles,’ she added, ‘but my good mother. And I thank thee for giving me something to do for her memory. And doesn’t she weep for her mother? And doesn’t that make me weep for my dear brother whom I love so much? To think that a poor little elf like me could speak in the ear of princes and make my beautiful brother vicar of Gouda—eh, lass, it is a bonny place, and a bonny manse, and hawthorn in every bush at spring-tide, and dog-roses and eglantine in every summer hedge. I know what the poor fool loves—leave that to me.’

Giles began his tale strutting before Margaret, but ended it in her arms. She could not contain herself, and embraced him tightly. “Oh, Giles,” she said, blushing, kissing him, “I cannot keep my hands off you—your body is so small, and your heart so great. You are his true friend. Bless you! Bless you! Now we shall see him again. We haven’t seen him since that terrible day.”

“Gramercy, but that is strange,” said Giles. “Perhaps he’s ashamed of having cursed those two vagabonds—our own flesh and blood, worse luck.”

“Do you think that’s why he hides?” asked Margaret eagerly.

“Ay, if he hides at all. But I’ll have him announced by the bellman.”

“No,” she said. “That might offend him.”

“What care I? Shall Gouda go without a vicar, and the manse grow wild with nettles?”

To Margaret’s secret satisfaction, Giles had the new vicar proclaimed in Rotterdam and nearby towns. He easily convinced her that Gerard would hear of it soon and come to his post. She visited his manse and imagined how comfortable it could be made—how dearly she would love to do it.

But days passed. Gerard came neither to Rotterdam nor Gouda. Giles was mortified. Margaret was furious and heartbroken. She said to herself, “He thought me dead, so he came home. Now that I’m alive, he’s gone back to Italy—that’s where he’s gone.”

Joan advised her to consult the hermit of Gouda.

“Oh, he’s surely dead by now.”

“Yon one, perhaps. But the cave is never empty long—Goudا never lacks a hermit.”

But Margaret refused to go again to Gouda for such a purpose. “What can he know, shut up in a cave? Less than I, likely. Gerard has gone back to Italy. He hates me for not being dead.”

Soon, a man from Tergou arrived with news from Catherine: Ghysbrecht Van Swieten had seen Gerard later than anyone else. Margaret decided to visit the property left to her and bring Reicht Heynes back to Rotterdam. Naturally, her first step was Ghysbrecht’s house.

She found him in his garden, seated in a wheeled chair. He greeted her weakly but warmly. When she asked if it was true he had seen Gerard after August fifth, he replied, “Gerard no more—but Friar Clement. Ay, I saw him—and blessed be the day he entered my house.”

Then he told her, in his own words, of his meeting with Clement.

He also revealed that the friar had confessed he came to Tergou with the missing deed in his bosom, intending to force Ghysbrecht to surrender the land. But finding him repentant, he changed course.

“Was not this a saint—come to right you, yet must save your soul in the doing?”

When she asked if he recognized him, he said, “I never suspected it. It was only after three days that he revealed himself. Listen while I speak my shame and his praise.

I said to him, ‘The land is restored, and my stomach feels lighter—but another fault clings to me.’ Then I told him of the letter I wrote at the request of his brethren, whose duty it was to restrain them. I said, ‘That letter was meant to separate two lovers—and with the devil’s help, it did the foul work. Land and houses I can return, but that mischief is done forever.’

‘Nay,’ he said, ‘not forever—but for life. Repent it while you live.’

‘I shall,’ I said, ‘but how can God forgive it? I would not,’ I added, ‘were I He.’

‘Yet He will forgive it,’ he replied, ‘for He is ten times more forgiving than I am—and I forgive you.’

I stared. Then he said softly, quavering, ‘Ghysbrecht, look closer at me. I am Gerard, son of Eli.’

I looked—and looked—and at last, lo! it was Gerard. Verily, I would have fallen at his feet in shame and contrition—but he would not allow it. ‘That becomes not mine years and his, for a particular fault. I say not I forgive you without struggle—not being a saint. But these three days you have spent in penitence, I have spent under your roof in prayer. I do forgive you.’ Those were his very words.”

Margaret wept. The old man spoke with brokenness, and the story touched her deeply. He continued: “And even then, he bid me farewell.

‘My work here is done,’ he said. I could not stop him. For though he forgave me, the sight of me must be wormwood to him. He left me in peace—and may a dying man’s blessing follow him wherever he goes. Oh, girl, when I think of his wrongs, and yours, and how he avenged himself by saving this stained soul of mine, my heart is broken with remorse, and these old eyes weep night and day.”

“Ghysbrecht,” said Margaret, weeping, “since he forgave you, I forgive you too. What is done, is done. And you have let me hear what I would have walked the world to learn. But oh, burgomaster, you are a wise man—help a poor woman who has forgiven you her misery.”

She then told him all that had happened. “And,” she said, “they won’t keep the living for him forever. He may lose it—as well as break all our hearts.”

“Call my servant!” the burgomaster cried, suddenly energized.

He sent for a table and writing materials, dictated letters to the burgomasters of all major towns in Holland, and one to a Prussian official, his friend. His clerk and Margaret copied them, and he signed them. “There,” he said, “the matter shall be dispatched throughout Holland by trusted couriers—and as far as Basel in Switzerland. Fear not—we shall soon have the vicar of Gouda in his village.”

She returned home filled with renewed hope, blaming herself for ingratitude toward Gerard. “I value my wealth now,” she said.

She also resolved never to judge his actions until she heard his own explanation.

Not long after, disaster struck again. Catherine, as it happened, had secretly met the brothers the very day after their expulsion. Cornelis followed her to Tergou, living on secret funds, while Sybrandt chose to stay in Rotterdam. Before leaving, Catherine asked Margaret to lend her two gold angels. “For,” she said, “all mine are spent.” Margaret was eager to give them. But the moment the words left her lips, she saw a look of regret on Catherine’s face—and instantly understood where the money would go. It was meant to sustain Sybrandt until Catherine could find a reason to visit Rotterdam again—and then bring him some of her own savings.

But Sybrandt, now with gold in his pocket, believed it endless. Free from restraint, he lived like a complete drunkard—until one afternoon, in a drunken spree, he climbed onto the roof of the stable at the inn where he was carousing and began walking along it—a trick he had done many times sober. But now, his unsteady mind made his legs fail. He rolled down the roof and crashed onto a horizontal paling, hanging there for a moment in a semicircle—then toppled and lay silent on the ground, amid roars of laughter from his companions.

When they tried to lift him, he couldn’t stand—only fell giggling each time.

They staggered down the street with him, carrying him to the shop in the Hoog Straet. He had babbled his disgrace everywhere.

As soon as he saw Margaret, he hiccupped, “Here’s the doctor who cures all hurts—a bonny lass.” He also declared he bore her no malice, for he was visiting against his will. “Wherefore, prithee send away these drunkards, and let you and me have t’other glass, to drown all unkindness.”

All the while, Margaret flushed pale and red at seeing her enemy—and his insolence. But one man whispered what had happened, and a strange mark on Sybrandt’s face caught her eye.

“And he cannot stand up, you say?”

“He couldn’t just now. Try, comrade! Be a man now!”

“I am a better man than you!” Sybrandt roared. “I’ll stand and fight you all for a crown!”

He rose—and instantly collapsed into his attendant’s arms with a piteous groan. Then he began cursing his companions, claiming they had stolen his legs. “I can feel nothing below the waist.”

“Alas, poor wretch,” said Margaret. She turned gravely to the men and said, “Leave him here. And if you brought him to this, go on your knees—for you have ruined him for life. He will never walk again. His back is broken.”

The drunken man heard these words. The foolish look of intoxication vanished, replaced by agony. “The curse,” he groaned. “The curse!”

Margaret and Reicht carried him gently and laid him on the softest bed.

“I must do as he would do,” she whispered. “He was kind to Ghysbrecht.”

Her fears were confirmed: Sybrandt’s spine was fatally injured. He lay helpless, fed and cared for by the man who had once deeply harmed him.
