The news reached Tergou. Catherine came over.

It shattered her. She blamed herself. “Oh, false wife—oh, weak mother,” she cried. “I am rightly punished for my treason to my poor Eli.”

She sat by his bedside for hours, rocking silently. She never recovered fully. From that day, the first grey hairs appeared in her hair.

As for Sybrandt, all he begged for was Gerard. He whined to Margaret like a wounded hound: “Oh, sweet Margaret, oh, bonny Margaret, for our Lady’s sake, find Gerard and bid him take his curse off me. Thou art gentle, thou art good—thou wilt entreat for me, and he will refuse thee nought.”

Catherine shared his belief that Gerard could heal him—and joined his pleas. Margaret hardly needed urging. After the burgomaster’s efforts failed, she sent her own agents—and spent money lavishly. Among them, poor Luke enrolled himself.

She met him one day, looking thin and weary. She spoke kindly. He broke down, sobbing, saying he was more miserable than ever, and would gladly be friends again—on almost any terms.

“Dear heart,” she said sadly, “why can’t you say to yourself, now I am your little sister, and you are my older brother, worn down by care? Say so, and I will indulge you, pet you, make you happier than a prince.”

“Well, I will,” Luke said fiercely, “sooner than stay away altogether. But above all, give me something to do. Perhaps I may have better luck this time.”

“Get me my marriage lines,” said Margaret, suddenly somber.

“That’s as much as to say, get me him! For where they are, he is.”

“Not necessarily. He may refuse to come near me—but he will not deny a poor woman, who once loved him, her lines of betrothal. How can she enter any honest man’s house without them?”

“I’ll get them for you—if they’re in Holland,” said Luke.

“They’re as likely to be in Rome,” Margaret replied.

“Let us begin with Holland,” Luke suggested wisely.

The slave of love was given money by his tender tyrant and wandered far and wide—coopering, carpentering, searching for Gerard. “I can’t be worse if I find the vagabond,” he muttered, “and I may be a hantle better.”

Months passed. Sybrandt improved in spirit, but not in body. He became Margaret’s lifelong charge. Another sorrow fell upon Catherine, bending her further. She lost her lively nature, no longer singing in the house. Her nerves were frayed, and she lived in terror of misfortune befalling Cornelis. The curse weighed on him too. She prayed Eli, if she had been a faithful partner all these years, to take Cornelis back into his house and let her live in Rotterdam awhile.

“I have good daughters here,” she said, “but Margaret is so tender, so thoughtful. And the little Gerard—he is my joy. He grows more like his father every day, and his chatter cheers my heavy heart. I do love children.”

Eli, strong but kind, consented reluctantly.

And the people of Gouda petitioned the duke for a real vicar. “Ours never comes near us,” they said, “these six months past. Our children die unchristened, our folk unburied—except by chance visitors.” Giles’s influence blocked the complaint once—but a second petition was drawn up, and he gave Margaret little hope the current situation could last another day.

Yes, the hermit of Gouda was in truth the vicar of Goudー—though he knew it not, so complete was his retreat from the world. My reader will recall that as soon as the fire of passion within him began to fade, a wave of remorse crashed over him. He had been undone by love, and now he trembled at himself. Only those who have climbed high in spiritual devotion, only those who have fallen from such heights, can grasp the horror he felt. It was as if he stood on the edge of a chasm, betrayed by his own confidence.

“Ah, good Jerome,” he cried aloud, “you knew me better than I knew myself! How bitter yet how healing your warning was!”

He had long been accustomed to examining his soul, and now he saw plainly what had stirred his fury: Margaret. She was the root of it all.

“I love her more than God,” he whispered, broken with despair. “More than the Church. What can come of such love—for me? For her?”

The thought sent a chill through him. “Let the strong fight temptation,” he said. “It is for the weak to flee. And who is weaker than I have shown myself? My religion, my penance—what are they but a house of cards, built slowly, carefully, only to collapse at the breath of earthly desire? I must begin again. On a firmer foundation.”

And so he resolved: he would leave Holland at once, spend years in some distant monastery far from her, where time and solitude might harden him against the lure of the flesh. By then, perhaps, the flame would be quenched. Perhaps, older and stronger, he could return—not as a man, but as a monk. And Margaret—she would forget him. She would marry another, and love him. The very pain this thought caused him proved that he was walking the path of duty.

Yet even as he turned away from her, he did not abandon her entirely. Her well-being still mattered. In fact, the thought that he could provide for her, make her secure and rich in this world—though she was not bound to despise wealth—gave him strength. It sustained him in the agony of silence, of leaving without a word, without a glance.

“Oh, what will she think of me?” he groaned. “Will I seem the most cruel, the most heartless creature alive? But so it must be. Better she hate me—wretched though I am—than that I fail in my purpose. Heaven is merciful. It gives me this comfort: I can force that villain to restore her fortune. She shall never lose another true lover because of poverty. Another? Ah, me! Ah, me! God and the saints, help me!”

Thus he set forth on his mission. But first, as you may remember, he went at night to hear the confession of the dying hermit of Gouda.

He found the old man near death, and stayed by his side until his eyes closed and he was buried beneath the floor of the small oratory attached to his cell. The end was peaceful—a quiet close to a stormy life. Once a soldier, the hermit still wore a steel corselet beneath his skin, saying he was now Christ’s warrior, just as he had once been Satan’s.

Clement confessed him, prayed beside him, and then, in turn, sought counsel from one who was dying in such holy calm. The hermit advised him to take up his own place in this secluded retreat.

“It has been a hard battle against the world, the flesh, and the devil,” he said. “I never truly won until I withdrew into the fortress of solitude.”

These words, and the serene passing of the hermit, left a deep mark upon Clement. There was no resistance in him to such a calling. The solitary life was still revered in the Church—whether in anchorites sealed in cells, or in independent hermits living apart in wild places. And Clement knew much about them. At the monastery near Tergou, he had studied their lives; in the Vatican manuscripts, he had devoured their stories with awe. He had talked earnestly with mendicant friars of various orders, who, before the invention of printing, were the keepers and carriers of these sacred annals.

His teacher, Jerome, had spent three years as an anchorite on the heights of Camaldoli—a place where for over four centuries the ancient Thebaid had lived again. Though Jerome was cold and reserved on most matters of faith, he spoke passionately of the hermits. He had pored over the records of St. John Baptist’s abbey, where caves dotted the mountainside, and told Clement of nobles and warriors who had ended their days there—of bishops and archbishops who had passed from sees to hermitages, or from hermitages to sees.

Among them: the Archbishop of Ravenna, and Pope Victor the Ninth. He described their severe disciplines—the way each hermit sought out his weakest point and attacked it relentlessly until he became strongest there. He spoke of the seven daily prayers, held every day regardless of weather or season—matins, prime, tierce, sext, none, vespers, compline—when the solitaries would climb from distant peaks, over treacherous paths, to worship together.

He even named some of the anchorites he had known: Moncata, Duke of Moncata and Cordova; Hidalgo of Spain, who left worldly splendor in his youth; Father John Baptist of Novara, once a general, now a private soldier of Christ; Cornelius, Samuel, and Sylvanus.

Of Sylvanus, Jerome told a tale with grim pride: when the great Duchess de’ Medici obtained papal permission to visit Camaldoli—something long denied—he met her at the first wooden cross. Surrounded by courtiers and flatterers, he rebuked her, warned her, pleaded with her not to profane the holy mountain, where no woman had set foot in centuries. And she, struck by the place and the man, turned back—her entire retinue following her—before a single word was spoken.

In Basel, Clement had gathered more tales, especially of German and English anchorites. He had even compiled a *Catena Eremitarum*, a chain of hermits, beginning with Paul of Thebes in 250 AD, who lived ninety years in solitude, down to 1470. He called them *Angelorum amici et animalium*—friends of angels and animals.

So, though he had never imagined becoming a recluse, the path was already laid. When the dying hermit blessed the citadel of solitude—where he had fought and won—and offered Clement his breastplate of faith, Clement whispered: “Heaven itself led my foot here.”

It struck him too as a sign that his patron saint, St. Bavon, had been a hermit—a stern one, a knight of the solitary cell.

Once reconciled with Ghysbrecht Van Swieten, Clement hurried to the hermit’s dwelling, hoping it had not already been claimed. Such places rarely remained empty long.

He found the rough stone door slightly ajar. For a moment, he feared it was too late. Then he stepped inside—softly, reverently.

No. The cell was empty. And there, untouched, lay the hermit’s possessions: a large ivory crucifix, pens and ink, seeds, a skull—memento mori—his cilice of hair and bristles, a worn sheepskin cloak and hood, his hammer, chisel, and psaltery.

People had passed by, but no one had dared enter. No one had stolen. Faith and simplicity guarded the door more fiercely than iron bars or moats ever could.

As Clement settled into the cell, a sudden flutter broke the silence. A great brown owl dropped from a corner and flew out the window, its wings brushing cold air against his face.

He started. Was this a demon, trying to deter him from his soul’s salvation?

Then he reconsidered: could it be a spirit, a guardian left by the hermit? Or simply an owl?

Finally, he decided: it was just an owl. And he would try to befriend it.

He knelt and began his new life with prayer.

But Clement had not only a passion to subdue—one whose power made him fear for his eternal fate—but also a penance to fulfill. He had yielded to anger, his greatest failing, and cursed his brothers. Now he must atone.

He looked around the modest cell—furnished with comfort—and compared it to the images in his mind: the terrible desert of holy Jerome, who wrestled with sickness and despair for four years; the thorny niche where young Benedict hid, surviving on scraps shared with a raven; the hollow tree of St. Bavon; the cavern at Fribourg where a nameless saint lived, eyes chilled by perpetual darkness, ears deafened by endless waterfalls; the pillar of St. Simeon Stylita, where he stood forty-five years; the stone box of St. Dunstan, barely room to sit or lie; the sealed tombs of Thais and Christina; the damp dungeon of St. Alred.

All these places—dozens more—came to mind. And he said to himself: “This sweet refuge is for the safety of the soul. But what of penance? Jesu, aid me against future faults. And for this fault, I vow: I will see no human face for a year and a day.”

He had precedents. The original occupant of this very cell had likely taken the same vow—hence the two narrow openings, through which he could speak and be answered without being seen.

Adopting the ancient rule of hermits, Clement divided his day into the seven canonical hours, ignoring the shifting light. He memorized the Psalter. In every gap between prayer and sleep, he worked with his hands.

But this self-imposed vow created a problem: what labor could he do unseen, that would benefit others?

For the hermit was to work only when necessity demanded it. Yet Clement’s needs were met by the villagers.

So on moonlit nights, he crept out like a thief and dug gardens for the poor. He wove baskets and slipped them quietly into humble homes.

And since he could not serve travelers during the day, he went out at midnight with hammer and chisel, carving moral and religious sayings into the sandstone along the road.

“Who knows?” he mused. “A chance word may strike deep.”

Oh, sore heart, comfort the poor and bereaved with holy words in their own tongue. For he said: “Well, ‘tis *clavis ad corda plebis*”—the key to the people’s hearts.

He remembered Colonna telling him of Eastern kings who inscribed their victories on mountains. “What,” Clement asked, “if those monarchs are wise to carve their glory on rock, making blood-bubbles endure as long as earth? Shall I let the stones around me remain silent to the King of Glory, whose word made them, and whose breath will reduce them to dust? No. These stones shall speak of eternal peace, of the Lamb—whose frail, afflicted, yet happy servant carves them.”

At that time, the inspired words that had comforted generations were not yet printed in Dutch. So these carved sentences—gold from the Gospel—seemed fresh oracles from heaven, like dew on parched flowers. They softened hearts, lifted spirits, and sent weary travelers singing.

These holy messages, appearing as if by magic; his wise answers given through the window to those seeking counsel; above all, his invisibility—soon brought him a great reputation.

It grew stronger still when, under tears and pleading, he gave medical advice—though always reluctantly. If patients recovered, they credited the holy hermit. If not, they blamed the devil.

“I think he killed nobody,” someone said, “for his remedies were weak and womanish.”

Sage, wormwood, sion, hyssop, borage, spikenard, dog’s-tongue, our Lady’s mantle, feverfew—and faith, above all. And only in small doses—except faith.

When villagers brought him eggs and milk, he refused them with horror.

“Do you not know the hermit’s rule? Bread, herbs, water. Eggs are birds in disguise. When the bird dies, the egg rots. Milk is little better than white blood.”

When they brought too much bread, he refused it.

“You who go among the poor can give it to them.”

“But, holy father, we want you to give it.”

“No. To live on charity and pretend to be generous is to lie with the right hand. Giving what belongs to others to the poor, I would steal their thanks and cheat you, the true giver. That is what thieves do—they boast of bleeding the rich into the lap of the poor. *Occasio avaritiae nomen pauperum.*”

When nothing else convinced them, this Latin phrase always turned them around. So did a line from Virgil’s *Aeneid*.

Thus, his fame grew—yet within, he was deeply critical of himself.

“I cannot deceive myself,” he said. “I cannot deceive God’s creatures. See the birds—how shy they are. I feed them, I long for their trust, yet they never come near. Why? Because no Paul, no Benedict, no Hugh of Lincoln, no Columba, no Guthlac dwells here. The hunted deer does not come. No Fructuosus, no Aventine, no Albert of Suabia. Not even a squirrel dares approach for the acorns I’ve stored. No Columban. Even the owl has fled. They are not deceived. I have a Pope’s word for that. May Heaven rest his soul.”

Clement had one advantage over the image of Margaret he carried in his heart: he had suffered loss, and survived. The mind cannot fully repeat such pain. He had learned to regard her as dead. After that scene in the churchyard of St. Laurens, that habit had been shattered—but enough remained to rebuild it. He saw her as dead to him.

Through strict division of time, constant prayer, and hard labor, he managed, in about three months, to numb the earthly part of his heart.

But then—within days of this fragile peace—there came a crushing despair. Words cannot describe it. Despair has no likeness.

Voices whispered in his ear: “Kill yourself! Kill! Kill! Kill!”

And he longed to obey. Life was unbearable.

He wrestled with the darkness—praying, weeping. “Oh, Lord,” he begged, “let my enemy scourge me with red-hot whips, drag me across rocks by the hair, attack me like a lion, gnaw me with serpent fangs—any pain, any terror—but not this soul-deep gloom that shuts me from Your light and the saints.”

Then a chilling thought struck him: what if the triumphs of darkness in deserts had been hidden, while only the defeats were recorded? Ancient writings hinted at such things—now they seemed to grin with terrifying meaning.

“THEY WANDERED IN THE DESERT AND PERISHED BY SERPENTS,” wrote an early father of hermits. “And were seen no more.”

Another, later, wrote: *Vertuntur ad melancholiam*—they turn to gloomy madness.

Were these not the same? The fathers never mourned bodily death. No—the lost hermits were lost souls. The serpents were diabolical thoughts, born of solitude.

St. Jerome entered the desert with three companions. One fled in the first year. Two died—how? The only one who endured was a giant soul with an iron body.

The chronicler made no comment. No wonder.

So what if this was the truth? That for every mighty soul who survived, many others perished in silence?

Now, the darkened recluse searched history for weapons against despair. The greatest was prayer.

Alas—he could not pray with true fervor. His mechanical routine had dulled his heart. He prayed louder than ever, but his soul remained cold. The words rose alone.

“Poor wingless prayers,” he cried, “you’ll never reach halfway to heaven.”

Once, a fiend of this sort had been driven from King Saul by music.

Clement picked up the hermit’s psaltery. With effort, he mended the strings, tuned it.

But he could not play. His soul was out of tune. The sounds jarred him, nearly drove him mad.

“Ah, wretched me!” he cried. “Saul had a saint to play for him. He was not alone with darkness. But here—no sweet bard of Israel plays for me. I, alone, crushed, with a black fiend sitting mountain-high upon my heart, must make music to lift it to heaven. It cannot be.”

And he fell to the earth, weeping, tearing his hair.

One day, as Clement lay in his cave, consumed by sorrow and silence—no prayers, no songs, only a soul weighed down by despair—a sudden thought pierced through the darkness. If he had once given comfort to the poor and the weary, why should he not now offer himself the same solace? He would fill this prison of stone with the words of God, with sacred texts, with the gentle consolations of faith. Like Christian at the feet of Apollyon, he reached out—not for a sword, for he had none—but for his chisel, that humble tool of quiet labor, and began to carve as if his very soul depended on the strength of his arm.

They say Michaelangelo, in the centuries to come, did not model his statues in clay and hand them over to artisans to chisel. No—he seized the marble block, envisioned the form within, and struck it with mallet and steel until chips flew like sparks from a forge, and the shape burst forth. So too did Clement work: without plan or sketch, he drew upon memory, summoning holy phrases, then dashed into his task, carving them deep into the soft rock between moments of struggle and sleep.

He begged travelers for candle stubs and foul oil. “Anything will burn,” he said, “if only it gives light.” And so, at night, his cave glowed faintly, like a blacksmith’s hearth seen through cracks in the door and window. The villagers passing by crossed themselves, whispering of witchcraft. But inside, one sacred phrase after another emerged from the stone:
*O God, who in wondrous order appointest the ministries of angels…* (the full collect).

Beneath the great crucifix fastened to the wall, he carved these words from Augustine:
*O Christian soul, look upon the wounds of the suffering One, the blood of the dying One, the price paid for our redemption! Reflect on how great these things are, and weigh them in the balance of your mind—so that He may be fully fixed in your heart, who for you was wholly nailed to the cross. For when the sufferings of Christ are recalled, nothing on earth is too hard to endure with calmness.*

Soothed by the presence of these sacred words, and worn down by ceaseless labor and prayer, Clement one morning collapsed from exhaustion. A deep sleep overtook him, lasting many hours. When he awoke, quiet and still, he heard a tiny chirp. He opened his eyes—and there, perched on his breviary resting on a low stool, was a robin redbreast. The bird fluffed its feathers, smoothed them again, cocked its head with feigned wisdom, and preened itself with all the dignity of a courtier.

Clement held his breath. He half-closed his eyes, afraid to startle the fragile visitor. The robin hopped down to the floor, went through its little show of cunning, then with three stiff hops—like a ball of wool on wires—landed on the hermit’s bare foot. There it swelled and contracted, puffing its chest like a proud lord. But Clement closed his eyes completely, barely breathing, content only to feel the tiny claws upon his skin.

Then came a flutter of wings—the bird was back on the breviary. Clement decided to try feeding it. But how? He had bread nearby, yet dared not move. Slowly, slowly, he crept his hand toward the bread, froze, then slipped a crumb between thumb and forefinger. With a flick of the wrist—like a boy shooting marbles—he sent it flying, keeping his arm perfectly still.

The robin saw it fall, pretended to ponder, then remained still. Another crumb followed. Then another. Finally, it darted forward and snatched one, but seemed uncertain—then fled, carrying the prize to a higher perch: the hermit’s knee.

Thus the game continued, until a larger piece rolled along. This was a treasure. The robin pounced, lifted it high, and vanished into the night, the air humming with its swift flight.

“Bless you, sweet bird,” whispered Clement, “your wings are music, and you are a feathered ray that has come to brighten my darkened soul.”

And so, renewed, he returned to prayer and to his tools, his courage stirred. That day’s work read:
*Come, Creator Spirit, visit the minds You have made. Fill them with Your divine grace. Ignite the senses with light, strengthen our weak bodies with perpetual power.*

Days passed. The weather turned colder. But Clement’s heart grew warmer. Despair, like a cloud, had drifted in and now drifted out. It had come unbidden, and now left without warning. Soon, everything reversed: his cell shimmered with joy. His work pleased him; his prayers were rich with devotion; his psalms rang with praise.

Birds flocked to him, drawn by their crimson leader. They flew from snow and frost, from villages where men were Cain to each other, and found peace in the company of Abel—friends, true and fast.

One sharp, frosty night, as Clement sang praises on his psaltery, the hollow cave echoed with sacred song, as if it were Tubal’s shell or David’s own harp. Then he heard a clear, mournful whine—not discordant, but strangely melodic. It grew louder, less tuned. Peering through the cracks in his door, he saw a great red wolf sitting outside, nose raised, moaning softly into the night.

Clement smiled. “My sins are leaving,” he murmured, “and the creatures of God are accepting me, one by one.”

In a surge of joy, he broke into song:

And all the while, the wolf bayed in reply.

But greater still was the sense that he was drawing near to the celestial communion—the true mark of the hermit. He began to dream of saints and angels, visions so vivid they felt real. He saw figures clad in woven snow, eyes more beautiful than those of the antelopes he’d seen in Rome. Broad wings, colored like the rainbow, fanned him gently. Soft voices urged him onward.

Yet soon, his dreams took a strange turn. He wandered with Fra Colonna among ancient ruins. The friar was lame, leaning on a staff, which he waved over temples and palaces—Egyptian, Greek, Roman—and instantly they rose again, whole and grand. Musicians sang songs that might have outshone Apollo. Women, divine in form, danced in marble courts. Sculptors shaped beauty from Parian marble in minutes. Philosophers debated profound truths, while youth listened in reverence.

Yet beneath it all, a shadow lingered: *This is only a prologue. Something lies behind—something ominous, something hidden.*

One night, Colonna pointed. Cities vanished. They stood on a vast desert plain beneath a crimson sun sinking to rest. Palm trees stood tall; reed huts dotted the horizon. “These are the anchorites of the Theban desert,” Colonna said calmly, “followers not of Christ, nor His apostles, nor the great fathers—but of Greek disciples of Egyptian pupils of the Brahmins and Gymnosophists.”

Clement longed to rush forward, to embrace these holy men, to confess his troubles. But he was bound—his feet rooted to the ground. The sun sank. Darkness fell. Colonna’s figure blurred, yet his eyes blazed tenfold. From them came a voice:
“No, let them be. A pack of fools. I see how dismal it all is.”

Then, suddenly cheerful:
“But I hear one has a manuscript of Petronius, on papyrus. I go to buy it. Farewell—for ever, for ever, for ever.”

And it was pitch black. Then, behind him, a gentle glow—roseate, warm, radiant. It lifted his feet from the earth. He turned—and there stood Margaret Brandt, her face glowing with sunlight, her hair shimmering like a saint’s halo.

She blushed, smiled, and looked at him with ineffable tenderness.
“Gerard,” she whispered, “be whose thou wilt by day—but at night, be mine.”

At that moment, the shock of seeing her awakened him. He lay trembling, drenched in cold sweat. That vision—her radiant face, her voice—had become his nightly keynote. Awake, he could pray, worship, and master his thoughts. But asleep, she came—Margaret, or Satan in her likeness—an angel of light.

He knew it was a fiend. Not because it was ugly, but because angels cannot blush. And so he understood: the enemy had grown subtle.

He had read of such tricks—from Saint Anthony to Nicholas of the Rock—hermits beset by visions, sometimes of pleasure, sometimes of love, always of warmth and touch, yet always deceitful. He remembered the tale of Saint Macarius, visited by a lovely spirit who wept and wept, feigning sorrow, stealing his tears and half his virtue.

But alongside these warnings, he knew the hermits’ weapons: discipline. *Domandum est Corpus*—the body must be tamed. For twelve hundred years, this had been their creed. They crushed the heart through pain, mortified the flesh, silenced the passions.

So Clement resolved: the enemy had retreated only to return stronger. He had allowed him days of purity and joy—to lull him into carelessness. Now, the soft seductions began.

He tightened his rule. He shortened his sleep, lengthened his prayers, increased his fasting to abstinence. Once, he ate only at sunset. Now, he ate once every two days, drinking only water.

The visions grew clearer.

Then he turned to the hermits’ greatest remedy—the cold bath. He found the deepest part of the stream near his cell, fed by a holy well. He cleared stones, dug a hole where he could stand waist-deep in icy water. On the next diabolical attack, he leapt from his bed and plunged in.

The cold stole his breath. It froze his marrow.
“I shall die,” he gasped, “but better this than eternal fire.”

The next day, he was stiff, aching, bones like teeth gnawing at him. And even in sleep, he felt the pain—until the phantom appeared, smiled pityingly, and the ache vanished.

Now, he feared returning to the water, weakened by fasting. So instead, he scourged himself until blood ran. He lay down, smarting, exhausted. As the pain dulled to a throb, the past rushed back.

He sat with Margaret at the duke’s feast—music divine, purple fountains gushing. Youth and love filled the air. Then they stood at the altar, man and wife. No interruption. They walked hand in hand, sharing their nightmares.

He confessed: “I dreamed you were dead, and I was a monk. The dream was so real—so full of detail—that only my eyes prove it was not truth. Yet now, I know we are one.”

That key struck—every dream thereafter ran upon it. Awake, he was Clement, the hermit, risen from night’s visions. Asleep, he was Gerard Eliassoen, the happy husband, reunited with his beloved.

His constant fasts, combined with other austerities, had reduced him nearly to a skeleton. Yet flesh still clung—unsubdued, quivering with earthly desire. “Or why else would evil spirits hold such power?” he asked.

His certainty grew when one day he caught himself slipping into sleep, feeling *relief*—because now Margaret would come, and he would feel no pain. The unreal would become real, the real unreal—for an hour.

He rose with a cry of horror. Stripping to the skin, he climbed to the brambles above his cave and threw himself onto them, rolling and writhing in agony. He came back a mass of blood, moaning for hours—until exhaustion brought a deep, dreamless sleep.

He awoke in pain—but with joy in his soul. He had broken the spell.

Yes, it was broken. Day after day passed. Her image no longer haunted him. He sighed at his victory.

The birds grew bolder. They perched on his hand. Two let him gild their claws. With food scarce, he had more to give.

But peace did not last.

A woman’s voice came from outside. She told him his story in a few words, then asked: “Where can I find Gerard?”

He was stunned. Instinctively, he replied: “Pray for the soul of Gerard, son of Eli!”—meaning he was dead to the world.

He sat, bewildered. When she was gone, he decided to risk being seen. He peered after her—but she ran quickly, and the road was clear.

“Satan!” he muttered.

That night, the visions returned—more vivid than ever. He could count every auburn hair in Margaret’s head, see the pupils of her eyes.

Despair set in. “I must leave this land,” he said. “Here I am chained to memory. A breath from hell has infected this place—even these holy words lose their power.”

Unconsciously imitating St. Jerome, he took his warmest cloak and laid it out in the woods, beneath a tree. He lay down—bare, broken, like a sculpture of bone and leather that might once have served as Apollo.

Whether imagination ebbed, as modern minds suggest all things do—or whether this act severed some unseen bond—I know not. But his sleep was dreamless.

He awoke nearly frozen—but warm within, joyful.
“I shall yet be a true hermit, by God’s grace,” he declared.

The next day, someone left on his platform a new lambswool pelisse and cape—soft, warm, ample. He hesitated—its comfort was tempting. But then he smiled. It was the right skin. A sign from Heaven.

It warmed his bones after his brief rest.

Now, at one moment he saw victory ahead—if he could survive. At another, he warned himself: “It is only a pause. Be on guard, Clement.”

He was like a soldier deep in enemy territory.

One clear, frosty night, he returned to his cell. The stars shone brilliantly—sky seemed vaster, brighter, watching with a thousand eyes.
“Oh, wonderful,” he breathed, “that men should commit crimes by night, and others live only for this small world, ignoring that glorious one which reveals its wonders every night to any eye not blinded by habit. Thank God I am a hermit.”

He paused at his door. It was shut.
“Why, I thought I left it open,” he said. “The wind? There is no wind. What does this mean?”

He placed a hand on the rough stone. Through a crack, he saw the oil wick burning exactly where he had left it.
“What is happening to me?” he sighed. “I tremble at nothing. Either I closed it myself—or the fiend shut it behind me to disturb my peace. Back, Satan!”

He entered swiftly, lit a large taper. As he did, a soft sigh echoed in the cave. He started—dropped the candle. It went out. He bent, relit it, listening. When it burned steady, he shaded it with his hand and cast the light around.

In the farthest corner, the wall seemed broken. He stepped forward, heart pounding. The flame brightened—and he saw the outline of a woman.

Another step. Knees knocking.

Her manner was one that stirred compassion rather than fear in any heart not hardened by prejudice. Her chest rose and fell like a bird’s, her cheeks flushed with shifting hues of red and pale white, and she pressed her hand against the wall instinctively, as timid creatures do when trembling. The look in her eyes—deep purple and full of love, reverence, sorrow, and tender remembrance—was fixed upon the thin, gaunt figure of the hermit, and it was a moment rare in nature.

“Aha!” he exclaimed. “At last thou comest—flesh and blood! As thou camest to holy Anthony. But I know thee. I suspected thy schemes were not yet spent. I am prepared.”

With these words, he snatched up his small crucifix and held it out before her, his hand shaking violently, while in the other he clutched a candle. “I exorcise thee!”

“Oh, no!” she pleaded, holding out both hands gently. “Do not harm me! It is Margaret.”

“Liar!” he shouted. “Margaret was fair, but not so surpassingly fair as thou. Thou flinched at that sacred name—thou cunning deceiver! In the name of God, I exorcise thee!”

“Oh, Jesus!” she gasped, overwhelmed with dread. “Do not curse me! I will go back. I thought I might come. For mercy’s sake, do not turn me away! Oh, Gerard—is this how we meet after all? After all?”

She sank almost to her knees, sobbing from deep distress and wounded affection. Though steeped in fear of evil spirits, he might still have doubted whether this gentle creature, so clearly human and real, was not a mere illusion or a trick of the dark. Yet her heartfelt cry to the divine name broke through his delusion, letting him see and hear with clear senses. He gave a cry of regret and reached for her—but weakened by fasting and emotion, he could not lift her.

“What?” he panted, bending over her. “Is it truly you? And did I greet you with harsh words? Alas!”

They stood silent for a time, choked by feeling, unable to speak.

“I care little,” said Margaret bravely, struggling against tears. “You took me for another—for something terrible. Oh, oh, oh!”

“Forgive me, sweet soul,” he whispered. “Since I came here, I have been sorely tempted by darkness.”

She looked around with a shudder. “Then take my hand, and let me lead you from this place.”

He stared at her in astonishment. “Leave my cell? Return to the world? Is that why you came?”

“Yes, Gerard,” she said softly. “I have come to bring you home—to your vicarage in Gouda. You are now the priest there, thanks to Heaven and your brother Giles. Your mother and I have made it warm and welcoming. It is comfortable enough in winter, I promise. But wait till spring comes—the hawthorn blooms, and the walls grow bright with roses and sweet woodbine. Have we forgotten you? Or the things you loved? And dear Gerard, your mother waits—she should not be out of bed so late. Please, please, come with me. And once we leave this place, I’ll show you a treasure you’ve gained without knowing it. Oh, what have I said to cause such pain?”

He had drawn himself into a tight, fearful posture, watching her with a gaze half filled with suspicion, half with dread.

“Poor child,” he said solemnly, though deeply troubled. “Would you have me risk both our souls for a quiet house and its flowers? This is not your doing—some cruel force sends you, poor innocent, with this lure. But I shall unmask it even through you, and you shall see it and loathe it as I do. Margaret, my lost love—why am I here? Because I love you.”

“No, Gerard,” she replied, “you do not love me—or you would not have hidden from me. There was no need.”

“Let there be no falsehood between us,” he said, “who once loved so faithfully—and who may never meet again on earth.”

“God forbid!” she answered. “I love you. And if you had forgotten me, you would have married long ago. You are the one who found me—buried here, unseen by men. You are a priest, a monk. What good can come from our living near each other, nurturing a passion once pure, but now—by Heaven’s will—unholy? No, though my heart breaks, I must stand firm. I am the man now; I am the priest. We must not meet again—until I am taught by solitude, and you are joined to another.”

“I accept my fate, but not yours,” she said. “I would rather die ten times than let you stay in this lonely place, when a kind home awaits you.”

Clement groaned. With every word she spoke, two truths grew clearer: his duty, and the agony it would cost.

“My beloved,” he said, voice thick with tenderness and resolve, “I bless you for giving me one more glimpse of your face. May God forgive you and bless you for breaking in a moment the peace I built over six months of silence. Still, a year of penance shall restore me to calm. My poor Margaret, I seem cruel—but I am kind. It is best we part—now.”

“Part, Gerard? Never. We have seen what parting brings. Part? You haven’t heard half my tale—not even a tenth. I do not bring you here merely for comfort. Listen!”

“I cannot,” he said. “Even your voice is a temptation—its music, its memories.”

“But I say you must listen,” she insisted. “For I leave this place unheard.”

“Then we must part by other means,” he said sadly.

“What other way? Would you shut me out, being stronger?”

“No, Margaret,” he said, “I know well I would endure many deaths before laying a hand upon you. Your body is dearer to me than my own. But a thousand times dearer are our immortal souls—both yours and mine. I have resisted this trial long enough. Now I must flee it. Farewell. Farewell.”

He moved toward the door, opened it, and stepped halfway out—when she darted after him and seized his arm.

“No,” she said. “Another must speak for me. I meant to reward you for yielding to me—but since you are unkind, I need help. Turn this way for a moment.”

“No,” he said.

“But I say yes. Then turn your back on us—if you can.”

She loosened her grip slightly, thinking he would not refuse such a small request. But at that moment, he saw his chance and grasped it.

“Run, Clement, run!” he cried, and in a burst of strength born of devotion, he tore himself from her grasp and fled. A few steps later, he leapt across the narrow stream and ran beside it. When he realized she did not follow, he stopped and turned back.

She lay face down, arms stretched out. He had knocked her down, perhaps hurt her.

When he saw this, he groaned and took a step forward—then suddenly threw himself into the icy water.

“There,” he cried, “destroy my body—but save my soul!”

Standing waist-deep in cold water, he watched as Margaret rose slowly to her knees. She was pale, her eyes glistening in the night. Then, in a voice broken by grief, she called:

“Oh, God! You who know all—You see how I am treated. Forgive me. For I will not live another day.”

She sprang to her feet and ran past him, close to where he hid, screaming:

In one cry, so much anguish poured forth—wounded love, wounded pride, despair, and the edge of madness.

Clement heard it—and his heart froze with terror and remorse, worse than the cold water numbing his bones. He knew he had driven her away forever. In the midst of his grim triumph, a fierce impulse rose within him—to curse the Church, to curse faith itself, for demanding such cruelty from a mortal soul.

At last, half-drowned, he crawled from the water and staggered back to his cave.

“I am safe here,” he groaned. “She will never come near me again. Unworthy, ungrateful wretch that I am.”

He collapsed onto the floor, not without a secret hope that he might never rise again.

But soon he noticed the hourglass—midnight had passed. Slowly, he removed his wet clothes, moaning at the pain he had caused the one he loved. Then he put on the old hermit’s cilice—a rough garment of bristles—and over it, a breastplate. He had never worn either before, doubting himself worthy of such armor. But now he needed all aid. The bristles might distract his sorrow with bodily pain; the breastplate might carry some holy virtue.

He knelt and prayed humbly, asking God to free him that very night from the burden of flesh. Then he lit all his candles and recited his psalter, each word falling like lead from a heavy heart. Through it all, he moaned quietly.

Suddenly, he noticed a small bundle in the corner, unnoticed before. At one end, something glimmered—like gold woven into silk. He approached, and as he looked closer, he raised his hands in joy.

“It is a seraph,” he whispered. “A lovely seraph. Heaven has witnessed my trial and approved my sacrifice. This heavenly flower is sent to comfort me, fainting under my burden.”

He knelt, gazing at the golden hair, the soft skin, the cheeks like peach blossoms.

“Let me feast my eyes on you before you leave for your blessed home—and my cave grows dark once more, as it did when she left.”

But the hermit startled the child. The boy opened wide eyes—blue as the sky—and seeing a strange figure kneeling over him, cried:

Tears streamed down his tiny cheeks.

Perhaps, after months without seeing a human face, Clement judged childhood beauty more truly than others could. This northern child, with his long golden hair, seemed far more angelic than any imagined figure of heaven.

Yet the spell was broken—not unhappily. Clement, who had always loved children, found his heart touched by the child’s innocence, his sorrow, his tearful plea for his mother.

He used all his gentleness to soothe him. The boy, though young, was remarkably perceptive. Soon, the cries ceased, replaced by wonder. Quietly, he studied the wild-looking figure before him—strange, yet kind; armored, yet harmless.

Clement wondered how the child had come to lie there, glowing in his dark cave. Then he remembered—he had left the door open. He concluded that someone, perhaps in desperation, had placed the child there, seeking to rid themselves of him.

At this, his heart ached for the abandoned child. Tears welled in his eyes—pure tenderness. Even beneath the mother’s fault, he saw divine mercy guiding her act to ease his own sorrow.

“Now bless you, bless you, bless you, sweet innocent,” he said. “I would not trade you for an angel in heaven.”

“'Tis pooty,” the child replied, dismissing the praise with childish indifference.

“What is pretty here, besides you?” Clement asked.

“Ookum-gars,” the boy said, pointing to the breastplate.

“Quot liberi, tot sententiunculae!” Hector’s child once screamed at his father’s shining helmet. Here, a medieval boy was enchanted by polished armor, and his sadness eased.

“There are prettier things,” Clement said. “There are little birds. Do you love birds?”

“Nay. Ay. En um ittle, ery ittle? Not ike torks. Hate torks um bigger an baby.”

He confessed, in broken speech, that storks frightened him—great wings flapping, darkening his days.

“Ay, but my birds are small and good—oh, so pretty!”

“Den I ikes 'm,” the child declared. “I ont my mammy.”

“Oh, sweet dove,” Clement sighed. “I fear I must take your place. Do you have a daddy as well as a mommy?”

The conversation, considering their ages and circumstances, was unlike any ever held between mortals. And just as he asked, an unseen listener heard every word—with tenfold intensity.

So now, you must see through her eyes, hear through her ears.

Margaret, running past him, was nearly undone. She was in the state where mothers have killed their children—sometimes themselves too. She rushed to Reicht Heynes, pale and trembling, and clung to her neck.

“Oh, Reicht! Oh, Reicht!” she gasped, unable to speak further.

Reicht kissed her and began to weep. Even the great mastiff whined—a sign of sorrow.

“Oh, Reicht!” Margaret moaned. “See how he has treated me!” She showed her bleeding hands from falling on the stones.

“He threw me down—so eager to escape. He took me for a devil. Said I came to tempt him. Am I the woman to tempt a man? You know me, Reicht.”

“Nay, indeed, sweet Mistress Margaret—the last person in the world.”

“And he would not look at my child. I’ll throw myself and him into the river tonight.”

“Oh, fie! Fie! Sweet woman, don’t speak so. Is any man worth your child’s life?”

“My child! Where is he? Why, Reicht—I left him behind. Oh, shame! Can I love him so much as to forget my own child? Ah, I am rightly punished.”

She sat down, and Reicht joined her. They wept together.

After a while, Margaret stopped crying and said firmly, “Let us go home.”

“But the bairn?” Reicht asked.

“Oh, he is well where he is. My heart turns against my own child. He cares nothing for him—wouldn’t see him, wouldnere speak of him. I brought him proudly, dressed him nicely, combed his hair. Nay, turn about—it’s his child as well. Let him keep it awhile. Perhaps that will teach him to care for its mother—and for himself.”

“High words on an empty stomach,” Reicht said. “Time will tell. Come home.”

They started off, but at the second step, Margaret stopped—unable to move.

“Reicht,” she whispered, “what else have I left? I cannot.”

“Who said you could? Think you I paid attention? Words are breath. Go back for him. Time to rest.”

Reicht led the way. Margaret followed—then stopped again as they neared the cave.

“Reicht,” she said, “go ask him—will he give me back my boy? I cannot bear to see him.”

“Alas, mistress,” Reicht sighed, “this seems a sorry end to all that has passed between you. Does your heart whisper no excuse for him? Do you truly hate him, whom you waited so long for? Oh, weary world!”

“Hate him, Reicht? I would not harm a hair of his head. But I cannot look at him. I have grown afraid of him. Oh, when I think of all I suffered for him, and what I came here to do—bringing my darling to call him father. Ah, Luke, my poor chap—your wound shows mine. I thought too little of your pain, whose true love I scorned. And now mine is scorned. If the poor lad were here now, he’d have a fair chance.”

“Well, he is not far off,” Reicht said—though not with cheer.

“Speak not of men to me,” Margaret said bitterly. “I hate them all.”

“For the sake of one?”

“Flout me not. Prithee, go forward and get me what is mine—my only joy.”

Reicht went ahead. Margaret sat by the roadside, covering her face with her apron, rocking herself as women of her land did, her soul full of bitterness.

So great was her inner struggle, she did not hear Reicht return—nor feel her hand on her shoulder.

“Mistress Margaret!” Reicht said quietly. “Take a fool’s advice—go softly to that cave, with all the ears and eyes your mother gave you.”

“Why, Reicht?” she stammered. “I thought the cave was burning—it was so bright inside. And I heard voices.”

“Voices?”

“Ay, not one, but two—unlike—one man’s, one child’s—talking as pleasant as you and I.”

“I’m no expert at peeping,” Reicht admitted. “But if voices are speaking in that cave, and they’re near as those are to you, I’d crawl on my belly like a serpent before I missed a word.”

“Whisht, Reicht! Bless thee! Stay here. Kiss me! Pray for me!”

And before the words faded, Margaret was flying toward the hermitage, silent as a lapwing.

Near the cave, she crouched—her movements smooth, quiet, almost snake-like. She reached the door and found a crack. She listened.

She fought hard not to rush in. Warned by failure, she was cautious.

After a while, she slowly lifted her head—like a serpent raising its crest—and looked through the widest gap.

The boy, asked if he had a father, first shook his head. But when pressed, he remembered:

“Dad-da ill man; run away and left poor mum-ma.”

She who heard winced. It was news to both.

Some careless woman had told the child this—and now it came out, right before Gerard.

His reply surprised her. He cried:

“The villain! The monster! To abandon you, sweet one. He knows not the joy he turned his back on. Well, my little dove, I must be father and mother to you—since one ran away, and the other left you to me. Tomorrow, I shall ask those who bring my food to bring milk and eggs. Bread is good for old me—but not for you. And I shall teach you to read.”

“I can yead, I can yead.”

“Ay, so young? All the better. We shall read good books. I shall show you the way to heaven. Heaven is beautiful—far fairer than earth. There are little cherubs like you, in white, glad to welcome you. Would you like to go to heaven one day?”

“Ay, along wi'-my-mammy.”

“Not without her?”

“Nay. I ont my mammy. Where is my mammy?”

(Oh, what it cost poor Margaret not to rush in and hold him!)

“Well, fret not, sweetheart. Perhaps she will come when you sleep. Will you be good and sleep now?”

“I not eepy. Ikes to talk.”

“Then let us talk. Tell me your name.”

“Baby.”

He blinked at the giant’s ignorance.

“Hast none other?”

“Nay.”

“What shall I do to please you, baby? Shall I tell you a story?”

“I ikes tories,” he clapped.

“Or sing you a song?”

“I ikes tongs,” he said, growing excited.

“Choose—song or story.”

“Ting I a tong. Nay, tell I a tory. Nay, ting I a tong. Nay—”

His mouth drooped—he couldn’t choose.

Then his face cleared.

“Ting I a tory.”

“Sing you a story, baby? Well, why not? Sit on my knee?”

“Yea.”

“Then I must remove this breastplate—it’s too hard for your cheek. So. And now this bristly cilice—these might prick you. So. And now my best pelisse, in honor of your visit. See—soft and warm. Bless the kind soul who sent it. Now I sit. And you on my knee. And my arm under your head. So. And now the psaltery—play a tune. Not too loud.”

“I ikes dat.”

“I’m glad. Now listen to the story.”

He chanted a child’s tale, singing a moral refrain now and then. The boy listened rapt.

“I ikes oo,” he said. “Ot is oo? Is oo a man?”

“Ay, little heart. And a great sinner.”

“I ikes great tingers. Ting one other tory.”

Story No. 2 was sung.

“I ubbs oo,” the child cried. “Ot caft is oo?”

“I am a hermit, love.”

“I ubbs vermins. Ting other one.”

But during the final tale, Nature claimed her due. The child’s eyelids drooped.

“I is not eepy,” he murmured faintly—and slept.

Clement laid down the psaltery gently and rocked the child in his arms, humming a lullaby from Tergou—once sung by his own mother.

The child slipped into deep sleep.

He stopped humming and gazed at him with infinite tenderness—and sorrow. For in that moment, he could not help thinking of what might have been—had not a single sheet of paper carried a lie.

He sighed deeply.

Then the moonlight flooded the cave—and with it, Margaret Brandt knelt at his side, hand trembling on his shoulder.

The hermit stared—wide-eyed, breathless—at the child cradled in his arms and then at Margaret kneeling beside him. His astonishment was matched only by the storm of emotion that surged within him at her unexpected return. The girl who had once trembled beneath his grasp now glowed with a radiant beauty: cheeks flushed, eyes bright as stars, lips parted in quiet triumph. Her face bore a look he had never seen before—a mother’s pride.

He blinked. He stared again. From the sleeping child to Margaret, back to the child—his mind reeled. “Us?” he whispered, voice cracking.

Margaret smiled, not unkindly. “What? Does a father not know his own child? And you—a man of God too? Fie, Gerard! You pretend too well. You’re too wise, too good, not to have known all along. I watched you. Look at you both now—this little one is your flesh and blood, held close to your heart.”

Clement trembled. “These words… this angel—mine?”

“Whose else? Since she is mine.”

He turned fully toward the child, and the expression on his face defied description—awe, tenderness, wonder—all wrapped into one. His hands shook as he gazed upon the infant, absorbing every feature as if reading a sacred text.

Margaret followed his gaze. “He does not take after me,” she said proudly. “But sometimes—he is your very image, tiny though he is. See this golden hair? It was your colour at his age; ask your mother. And this mole on his little finger—look at yours! There it is. Your mother told me long ago you bore this mark. And oh, Gerard—it was this very sign that led our child to find you for me. When I watched from above your window and saw you feeding the birds, I recognized you by that mark on your hand. I knew then—you were his father.”

She seized the child’s hand, kissed it fiercely, and pressed half of it into her mouth. “Ah, bless you! You found your poor daddy for me—and now you’ve brought us back together after our little quarrel. The first, and the last. You were cruel to me, my poor Gerard—but I forgive you. For loving your child.”

“Ahhhh!” Clement sobbed, choked with emotion. Weak from fasting, broken by solitude, the strong man collapsed into sobs, nearly fainting.

Margaret, alarmed but composed, laid a gentle hand on his brow. “Do not take on so,” she murmured. “Be brave. So, so. Dear heart, you are not the first man who has gone out into the world and returned richer by a little soul than when he left. Being a man of God, take courage. Say He sends you this child to comfort you for what you lost in me. And truly, it is not so much, my lamb. The better part of love will never cool here—though perhaps it may in yours. And rightly so, being a priest, parson of Gouda.”

“I? Priest of Gouda? Never!” he breathed weakly. “I am a friar of St. Dominic. Yet speak on, sweet music—tell me all that has befallen you, before we are parted again.”

Some might have protested such a parting, raised the true question of their bond. But Margaret was no ordinary woman. She did not repeat her mistakes. Once defeated, she would not be undone twice. She nodded, turned her back on the manse as if it were a dream not meant to be revisited, and began to tell her tale—especially dwelling on the kindness shown her by his parents.

As she spoke of her trials, his hand crept into hers. She felt him flinch, tremble with anger at the injustice done to her, then squeeze her hand tightly, sharing her sorrow through every nerve.

“Oh, piteous tale,” he sighed. “A true heart fighting alone against bitter odds. It seems small now—seeing you here, nursing my son. We have had a warning, Gerard. True friends like you and I are rare. To part before death divides us is madness.”

“And that is true,” Clement murmured, off guard.

Then she asked him to tell her of his suffering for her sake. He begged her to spare him. She consented—but with quiet questions soon drew out every detail. Each time, she sighed deeply, hid her face in her hands, trembling at the perils he had endured—even though they were past.

To console him, she knelt and lifted the child gently. “Kiss him softly,” she whispered. “Again, again—if you can. He sleeps sound. This is all I can do to comfort you until you leave this foul den and reach your sweet manse beyond.”

Clement shook his head.

“Well,” she said, “let that pass. Know this: I have been sore affronted for lack of my lines.”

“Who dared affront you?”

“No matter. Those who would do it again if you’d lost them. Which God forbid.”

“I lose them? No—they lie near your hand.”

“Where? Oh, where?”

Clement hung his head. “Look in the Vulgate. Heaven forgive me—I thought you were dead, a saint in heaven.”

She looked. On the blank pages of the poor soul’s Bible, she found her marriage lines. “Thank God!” she cried. “Thank God! Bless you, Gerard, bless you!”

But then she gasped. “What is this, Gerard?”

On the same pages were pinned every scrap of paper she had ever sent him—their names written together in jest, a lock of her hair, half a silver coin they had once shared, a straw she had sucked her soup with on the day he first saw her.

When Margaret saw these tokens—proofs of love, signs of a gentle heart bereaved—her joy at recovering her lines was eclipsed by overwhelming tenderness. She swayed, touched her chest, leaned her forehead against the stone wall, and wept silently—so quietly he did not see. She would not let him see her weakness. Not now. For to help him, she must be stronger. Emotion weakens.

“Gerard,” she said softly, “I know you are wise and good. You must have reason for what you do, however strange it seems. Speak as old friends. Why are you buried alive?”

“To escape temptation,” he replied. “My rage against those two sprang from the heart. That heart I must deaden. Dei gratia, I shall. Shall I, a servant of Christ and Church, court temptation? Pray daily to be led into it, and walk into it with open eyes?”

“That is good sense,” she said, with perfect candour. “Unanswerable.”

“Perhaps,” he sighed. “Yet tell me—have you escaped temptation here? I ask because when I am alone, my thoughts grow wilder than in company. Speak plainly—come!”

“I must confess,” he said, “I have been more tempted here by evil imaginings than in the world.”

“There now.”

“Yes—but so were Anthony and Jerome, Macarius and Hilarion, Benedict, Bernard, and all the saints. It will wear off.”

“How do you know?”

“I feel sure it will.”

“Guessing against knowledge. Here, men are sillier than women. Proud in their own conceits, they refuse to see. Their stomachs are too high to be taught by their eyes. A woman, if she went into a hole to escape temptation and found it there, would simply lift her farthingale and step out—without knowing how wise she was, until she watched a man in the same plight.”

“Nay,” he said, “I grant humility and teachability lead to wisdom. But still—here I wrestle only with imagination. At Gouda, she I love as no priest or monk should love any but angels—she would tempt a weak soul, unwilling yet not loth to be tempted.”

“And that is another matter,” she said sharply. “Would I tempt you? To what, in God’s name?”

“Who knows? The flesh is weak.”

“Speak for yourself, my lad. You are thinking of some other Margaret—not Margaret van Peter. Was ever my mind turned to folly and frailty? Wait—is it because you were once my husband, as these lines prove? Do you think the road to sin is easier for you than for others? How shallow are the wise! And how little you can read me—when I can read you from head to toe. Come, learn your ABC. If a stranger offered me unchaste love, I might shrink, feel hurt—but I’d defend myself without fuss. Men, I know, are so—sometimes even the best. But if *you*, who have been my husband, and are my child’s father, were to humiliate me in my own eyes, in yours, in his—either I would spit in your face, Gerard, or, since I’m not vulgar, I would snatch the first weapon and strike you dead.”

Her eyes flashed fire. Her nostrils flared. It was glorious to behold. No one could doubt her sincerity.

“You had no sense to see that,” Gerard said quietly. And he pondered.

Margaret watched him in silence, then regained her composure. “Let us not dispute,” she said gently. “Tell me of your folk.”

“My father?”

“Well—he warms to you and me. Poor soul—he drew his sword on those two that day. But Jorian Ketel and I mastered him. He drove them from his house forever.”

“That cannot be. He must take them back.”

“He will never do it for us. You know the man—hard as iron. Yet he would for one word from one who refuses to speak it.”

“Who?”

“The vicar of Gouda. He will be at the manse tomorrow, I hear.”

“How you come back to that.”

“Forgive me. I am but a woman. We nag. You should keep me from it with questioning.”

“My sister Kate?”

“Alas.”

“What? Has ill befallen even that sweet lily? Out and alas!”

“Be calm, sweetheart. No harm has come to her. Oh, no—far from it.”

She forced herself to be still, then murmured in a low, gentle voice:

“My poor Gerard—Kate has left her troubles behind. It was like the rest. Ah, such as she saw never thirty, nor ever shall while earth endures. She smiled in pain. Well—thus it was: she took a languor, a loss of all her pains.”

“A loss of her pains? I do not understand.”

“Ay, you are not experienced. Even your mother almost blinded herself, saying, ‘It may be a change for the better.’ But Joan Ketel—wise woman—looked at her and said, ‘Down sun, down wind!’ The gossips agreed: ‘Be brave, you who are her mother—she is half-way to the saints.’ Your mother wept, but Kate would not let her. One ancient woman said, ‘She will die as easy as she lived hard.’ She lay painless most of three days—tasting heaven ahead. And when she was just leaving, she asked for ‘Gerard’s little boy.’ I brought him and set him on the bed. The child behaved as peacefully as he does now. By then she could not speak—but she pointed to a drawer. Her mother knew what to seek: two gold angels you gave her years ago. Poor soul—she kept them till you came home. She nodded toward the child, anxious. We understood. We placed the coins in his little hands. When his fingers closed around them, she smiled content. She gave her earthly treasures to her favourite’s child—for you were her favourite—and her immortal jewel to God. And passed so sweetly, none of us knew exactly when she left us. Well-a-day, well-a-day!”

Gerard wept.

“She has not left her likeness on earth,” he sobbed. “Oh, how the affections of earth curl softly round my heart! I cannot help it. God made them after all. Speak on, sweet Margaret—your voice rolls the tides of the past back upon me. Youth’s loves and hopes glide into my dark cell, my darker bosom, on waves of memory and music.”

“Gerard,” she said, “I am loth to grieve you—but Kate wept a little when she first fell ill, because you were not there to close her eyes.”

He sighed.

“You were within a league, yet hid your face from her.”

He groaned.

“There—forgive me for nagging. I am but a woman. You would not have been so cruel to your own flesh and blood knowingly, would you?”

“Oh, no.”

“Well, then—know that your brother Sybrandt lies in my care, with a broken back—fruit of your curse.”

“Mea culpa! Mea culpa!”

“He is very penitent. Be yourself and forgive him this night.”

“I have forgiven him long ago.”

“But can he believe it from any mouth but yours? Come! He is but two butts’ length away.”

“So near? Where?”

“At Gouda manse. I took him there yesterday. For I know you—the curse was scarce cold on your lips when you repented.” (Gerard nodded.)

“And I said to myself: Gerard will thank me for taking Sybrandt to die under his roof. He will not beat his breast and cry *mea culpa*, yet grudge three footsteps to quiet a withered brother on his last bed. He may have a bee in his bonnet—but he is not a hypocrite. Not all pious words and uncharitable deeds.”

Gerard literally staggered where he sat.

“Forgive me for nagging,” she said.

“Your mother waits for you. Is it right to keep her on thorns so long? She will not sleep tonight. Bethink thee, Gerard—she is all to you that I am to this sweet child. Ah, I think more of mothers since I had my little Gerard. She suffered for you, nursed you, tended you from boy to man. Priest, monk, hermit—call yourself what you will—to her you are only one thing: her child.”

“Where is she?” he murmured, voice quavering.

“At Gouda manse—wearing the night in prayer and care.”

Now was the moment. Margaret had waited. She showed him, in plain Dutch, that his life was not piety—but spiritual selfishness. A priest had no right to care only for his own soul, as he would not for his own body. That was not the path to heaven.

“But,” she said, “who ever lost his soul by saving others? The Almighty loves him who thinks of others. When He sees you caring for the souls the duke has put in your charge, He will care ten times more for your soul than He does now.”

Gerard was struck.

“You are shrewd in debate,” he said.

“Far from it,” she replied. “Only my eyes are not blindfolded by conceit.”

So long as Satan walks the earth, tempting men—and so long as the sons of Belial do not lock themselves in caves but run like ants, corrupting others—the good man who hides apart plays the devil’s game—or gives him the advantage. You, a soldier of Christ? Ask your comrade Denys, a soldier of the duke—has he ever skulked in a hole, shunning battle because danger lurks there as well as glory and duty? Your sole excuse is fear. You make no secret of it. Go to—no king nor duke has such cowardly soldiers as Christ. What did you say in Rotterdam church about the man who buried his talent in the earth? Offended the giver? Your gift for preaching—is it not a talent? A gift from your Creator?”

“Certes—such as it is.”

“And have you used it? Or buried it? To whom have you preached these seven months? To bats and owls? Have you buried it in one hole with yourself and your once-good wits?”

“The Dominicans are preachers. They were founded for preaching. You are false to Dominic—and to His Master.”

“Remember, Gerard, when we walked young together—now old before our time—did you not see a sheep cast, three fields off? You left your sweetheart (by her good will) and ran to lift it for charity? Well—then, at Gouda is not one sheep in trouble—but a whole flock. Some cast, some strayed, some sick, some tainted, some devoured. All for want of a shepherd. Where is the shepherd? Lurking in a den like a wolf—in his own parish? Out fie! Out fie!”

“I scented you out, partly, by your kindness to the birds. Note this: you, Gerard Eliassoen, must love something. It is in your blood. Born to it. Shunning man, you only seek earthly affection—one peg lower.”

Gerard interrupted. “The birds are God’s creatures—His innocent ones. I do well to love them.”

“Are they creatures of the same God as we? As he who lies on your knee?”

“You know they are.”

“Then what excuse for shunning us and being kind to them? Since man is an animal, why pick him out to shun? Because he is the paragon? You court the young of birds—and abandon your own young? Birds need only food—and wings. They deserve no pity if they cannot fly. But this sweet dove on your knee needs not only bodily food—but spiritual. He is yours as well as mine. I have done my share. Soon he will be too much for me. I look to Gouda’s parson to teach him piety and lore. Is he not worth more than many sparrows?”

Gerard started, stammered an affirmation.

“You wonder,” she continued, “to hear me quote Scripture so fluently. I have studied it four years. Not because God wrote it—but because I saw it often in your hands before you left me. Heaven forgive me—I am but a woman. What do you think of this verse? ‘Let your light so shine before men that they may see your good works and glorify your Father which is in heaven.’ What is a saint in a sink better than a light under a bushel?”

Therefore—since the sheep entrusted to you bleat for you, cry, “Oh, desert us no longer—come to Gouda manse!”—since I, who know you ten times better than you know yourself, pledge my soul it is for your soul’s good to go to Gouda manse—since duty to your child, long abandoned, calls you there—since your sovereign, whom Scripture bids you honour, sends you there—since the Pope, whom the Church teaches you to revere, has absolved you of your vows and orders you to Gouda manse—

“Since your grey-haired mother watches for you in grief, turns the hourglass, sighs that you come so slowly to her at Gouda manse—

“Since your brother, broken by your curse, awaits your forgiveness and prayers for his soul, lingering in his body at Gouda manse—

Take in your arms the sweet bird with crest of gold who nestles to your bosom. Give me your hand—your sweetheart, your wife, your friend, the truest friend you ever had—and come with me to Gouda manse!”

“It is the voice of an angel!” cried Clement.

“Then heed it—and come forth to Gouda manse!”

The battle was won.

Margaret lingered, glanced swiftly around the room, selected the Vulgate and psaltery. The rest she sighed over and left. She picked up the breastplate and cilice of bristles, dashed them to the floor with feeble fury.

Seeing Gerard watch her in surprise, she blushed. “I am but a woman—‘little’ will still be ‘spiteful.’”

“Why carry those? They are safe.”

“Oh, she had a reason.”

And so they set out for Gouda parsonage. The moon and stars shone so brightly it seemed almost daylight.

Suddenly, Gerard stopped. “My poor little birds!”

“What of them?”

“They will miss their food. I feed them every day.”

“The child has a piece of bread in his cowl. Take it—feed them now, against the morn.”

“I will. Nay—I will not. He is as innocent, and nearer to me and to you.”

Margaret drew a long breath. “'Tis well. Had you taken it, I might have hated you. I am but a woman.”

After a quarter-mile, Gerard sighed. “Margaret—must I rest? He is too heavy.”

“Then give him to me. Take these.” She carried the child. “Alas, alas! I remember when you would have run with the child on one shoulder, and the mother on the other.”

“I trow,” said Gerard, looking down, “overmuch fasting is not good for a man.”

“A many die of it each year, winter time,” she replied.

Gerard pondered. Watched her carry the child with ease.

Near a mile, he said, surprised: “You said it was but two butts’ length.”

“Not I.”

“You said so.”

“That is another matter.”

She turned to him, face like a Madonna. “I lied,” she said sweetly. “And to save your soul and body, I’d tell a worse lie than that, if need be. I am but a woman. Ah, well—it is but two butts’ length from here, at any rate.”

“Without a lie?”

“Humph! Three, without a lie.”

And indeed, in moments they reached the manse. A candle burned in the vicar’s parlour.

“She is still awake,” whispered Margaret.

“Beautiful! Beautiful!” said Clement, stopping to gaze.

“What, in Heaven’s name?”

“That little candle—seen through the window at night. Look—does it not resemble some fair star of prodigious size? It delights the eye, warms the heart of those outside.”

“Come—let me show you something better,” said Margaret, leading him tiptoe to the window.

They looked in. Catherine knelt on the hassock, her “hours” open before her.

“Folk can pray out of a cave,” whispered Margaret.

“Ay—and hit heaven with their prayers. For it is for a sight of you she prays—and you are here.”

“Now, Gerard—be prepared. She is not the woman you knew. Her children’s troubles have broken the brisk, light-hearted soul. I see she has been weeping. She likely gave you up, being so late.”

“Let me reach her,” said Clement, trembling. “That door! I will wait here.”

When Gerard approached the door, Margaret, fearing sudden shock, tapped sharply at the window and called, “Mother!” in a loud, expressive voice.

Catherine clasped her hands, rose halfway—then the door burst open, and Clement threw himself wildly on his knees, arms outstretched.

She uttered a cry only a mother could—“Ah! My darling, my darling!”—and clung sobbing to his neck.

Truly, she saw neither hermit, priest, nor monk—but her child, lost, despaired of, and now in her arms.

After a while, Margaret entered, eyes wet, cheeks flushed, a holy calm settling over the troubled hearts.

They sat together—three—hand in hand, murmuring soft, loving words. The one in the middle drank in their affection, their humble wisdom. He was forced to eat a nourishing meal. At dawn, he was tucked into a snowy bed.

And by morning, he awoke—as from a hideous dream—no longer friar, no longer hermit, no longer Clement. But Gerard Eliassoen, parson of Gouda.

Margaret returned to Rotterdam long before Gerard stirred from his sleep, leaving her son behind. She sent Reicht—faithful, sturdy Reicht—off to Gouda at once, carrying the vicar’s grey frock and large felt hat, along with detailed instructions on how to care for her new master.

Then she went to Jorian Ketel. “He is the closest I’ve ever known,” she told herself, “so he is the one for me.” Together, they undertook two secretive acts—acts so clever, yet not cruel, in my view, though Margaret believed them to be bold. But if you ask what these deeds were, I must say: since she, a woman, kept them hidden until her death, and I, a man, am bound by silence—*Verbum non amplius addam.*

She stayed away from the Gouda parsonage.

Sometimes, small things unnoticed during passion grow sharp in memory later. When Margaret reflected on what had passed, she was wounded by Gerard’s assumption that she could forget the priest who had once been her lover. “What did he take me for?” she asked aloud. That thought sparked a quiet shyness she wouldn’t have felt otherwise—she was innocent, after all—but pride joined modesty, whispering, “Do not go back to Gouda.”

So she left little Gerard there, trusting him to complete the work her mother’s heart claimed as his own—not hers, nor her wit or wisdom—but to bind his father forever to humanity.

Yet this act of grace cost her deeply. She had never been parted from her boy even for an hour. Without him, she felt strange, desolate. After the first day, it became unbearable. What did she do? At dusk, she crept up to the parsonage, lurking like a thief until she saw Reicht Heynes alone in the kitchen. Then, softly tapping at the window, she whispered, “Reicht, for pity’s sake, bring him out to me—unseen.” With Margaret, whoever occupied her thoughts lost their name and became only “him.”

Reicht soon found a reason to bring the child out. There followed a scene of joy, then tears when mother and son parted again.

They arranged that Reicht would take the boy halfway to Rotterdam each day at a fixed hour, where Margaret would meet them. At these meetings, after the laughter and play—mother and child tumbling together like a young cat and her kitten—the boy sometimes played quietly at their feet, while the two women seized the moment to talk seriously about Luke Peterson.

“Reicht,” said Margaret, “I nearly promised him to marry Luke Peterson. ‘Say the word,’ I told him, ‘and I’ll wed him.’”

“Poor Luke!”

“Why poor Luke?”

“To be tossed between yes and no.”

“But Reicht, you haven’t ever looked at him with affection, so why side with him?”

“Me?” she replied, tossing her head.

“Oh, forgive me. Well then, you can do me a favor.”

“Whisht! Whisper! That little darling is listening—eyes like saucers.”

At that, both women ducked their heads under one cap.

Two women plotting against one boy? Oh, you great cowardly serpents!

But after five days of these secret meetings, Margaret began to feel the injustice of it—irritated, unhappy.

She was weeping when a cart arrived at her door. In it sat the Vicar of Gouda, clean as a new coin, beard freshly shaved, hands white as snow, a faint blush in his pale face—dressed in the grey frock and broad hat she had sent him.

She rushed upstairs, washed away her tears, put on a cleaner cap (theoretically), and came down.

He took both her hands, kissed them, and a tear fell upon them. She turned her head to hide her own.

“My sweet Margaret,” he said, “why this distance? Why keep aloof from your own good deed? We’ve waited for you every day—and no Margaret.”

“You said things.”

“What? When I was a hermit, a donkey?”

“Aye. No matter—you said things. And without cause.”

“Forget what I said. Who listens to a madman’s ravings? For now I see I’d have become a gibbering fool within months. No one could have saved me but you. Oh, what wisdom and kindness you showed! But I cannot thank you here—I must do so in the home you gave me, among the sheep you made my flock. Already I love them dearly. There, I shall bless ‘the truest friend a man ever had.’ So now I say to you, as you once said to me—come to Gouda manse.”

“Humph. We’ll see.”

“Margaret, think you I’d have kept your dear child so long unless I knew you’d return daily? He curls around my very heartstrings. But what right have I to him compared to yours? Confess—you’ve had hard thoughts of me.”

“No, no. Ah! You’re yourself again—always thinking of others. I’m half tempted to go to Gouda manse just for that.”

“Then come with half your mind—it’s worth more than most people’s whole.”

“Well, perhaps I will—but no rush,” she said coolly (though she burned to go). “Tell me first how you get along with your people.”

“Oh, already the poor are rooted in my heart.”

“I knew it.”

“And there are such good souls among them—simple, rough, superstitious, yet wonderfully kind.”

“Oh, I leave you to find good in a bushel of bad.”

“Whisht! Whisht! And Margaret—two men had been enemies for four years. Each came to the manse to win my favor. But give glory to God—I won their hearts, made them friends, and made them laugh at their folly.”

“But are you truly their vicar? Answer me.”

“Certainly. I’ve gone to the bishop, taken the oath, rung the church bell, touched the altar, missal, and holy cup before the wardens. They handed me the parish seal—here it is. Yes, a real vicar invites a true friend to Gouda manse.”

“Then my mind is eased. Tell me more.”

“Well, sweet one, nearest to me is a poor cripple—my guardian angel and his (you know her name by the way you turn your head)—placed beneath my roof. Sybrandt and I are brothers now—closer than ever before. It would gladden and sadden you to hear how we kissed and forgave each other. He speaks of you in praise, lives in piety. He says he’s happier now than he ever was in his strength. Out of my house, he shall never go—only to heaven.”

“Now tell me something that happened to you, poor soul! All this is good, but not news to me. Do I not know you well?”

“Well… at first, I was dazzled by sunlight and couldn’t go out—like an owl—but that’s past. And good Reicht Heynes—humph!”

“What of her?”

“This to your ear only—she is a diamond. Her voice cuts through me like a knife, and all voices seem loud except yours—so mellow, so sweet. Wait—now I’ll give you tidings. Yesterday I spoke with an old man who thinks himself ill-tempered, tries to appear so, but oh—so threadbare, yet the best heart beneath.”

“Why, it’s a parish of angels,” said Margaret, ironically.

“Then why do you stay out?” retorted Gerard. “Well, he said no parish in Holland has such power of the devil as Gouda. Among his examples: ‘We had a hermit—the holiest in Holland. But being Gouda, the devil came this week and took him—bag and baggage. Not a ha’porth left, save a piece of skin—just like a hedgehog’s—and a bit of old iron, polished up.’”

Margaret smiled.

“But,” continued Gerard, “the strangest thing is—the cave has truly collapsed. Had I resisted you, it would have buried me where I buried myself alive. Therefore, I see the hand of Providence—condemning my past, blessing my present life. What say you?”

“Can I understand such mysteries? I am but a woman.”

“Somewhat more, I think. This very tale proves you my guardian angel. All else confirms it. Come to Gouda manse.”

“Well, go on—I’ll follow.”

“No—ride with me.”

“Not so.”

“Why?”

“Can I say why? Being a woman, I only know I seem—to feel—to wish—to come alone.”

“So be it. I leave the cart to you, as you say, a woman. I’ll walk, as a man again—with joyful news of your coming.”

When Margaret reached the manse, the first sight was the two Gerards together—the son playing freely on the lawn, the father slumped in a chair, hat pulled low, pencil in hand, trying patiently to sketch him.

After a warm greeting, he showed her his drawings. “But I fail to fix him,” he said. “He is incarnate quicksilver. Yet note his changes—infinite, yet none ungracious. All is supple, easy. How he melts from one pose to another!” He paused. “Woe to illuminators! Looking at you, sir baby, I see how awkward, lopsided, ugly toads I and my fellows painted in missals—calling them cherubs and seraphs.” Finally, he threw the paper aside in despair. Margaret slipped it into her bosom.

That night, by the peat fire, he pointed to the brass candlesticks and other gleaming metal. “See how beautiful they glow,” he said.
