Catherine’s eyes sparkled. “And oh, the sheets I lie in here,” he added. “Often my conscience pricks me: ‘Who art thou to lie in linen like snow?’ Dives was never so flaxen as I. And to think there are people in the world who possess all these fine things—and still are not content. Let them spend six months in a hermit’s cell, seeing no human face—then they’ll find how lovely and pleasant this wicked world is. And that men and women are God’s fairest creatures. Margaret was always fair—but never so bright as now.” Margaret shook her head, doubtful.

Gerard continued, “My mother was ever kind and good—but I did not notice her beauty till now.”

“Nor I,” said Catherine. “A score years ago I might pass in a crowd—but not now.”

Gerard declared each age had its own beauty. “See this mild grey eye—filled with motherly love for so many of us. All that love has left its shadow—and that shadow is a beauty beyond time. See this delicate lip, these pure white teeth. This brow—well-shaped, where comeliness turns into reverence. You are beautiful to me, mother dear.”

“And that is enough for me, my darling. Time for bed, child. You preach tomorrow.”

Reicht Heynes and Catherine exchanged a glance: *We have an amiable maniac to supervise—one who calls everything beautiful.*

The next day was Sunday. They heard him preach in his own church. The place was packed—curious at first, devout by the end. Never had his gift shown so powerfully. Deeply moved by seeing his people, his heart swelled over the flock he had long neglected. In a sermon lasting two hours—yet seeming but twenty minutes—he unveiled the whole scripture: he terrified the careless, strengthened the wavering, comforted the afflicted, uplifted the poor. When he finished, the congregation stood rapt, unwilling to believe the divine music of his voice had ceased.

Need I say two poor women in a corner sat entranced, tears streaming?

“Where did he learn all this?” whispered Catherine, her apron to her eyes. “By our Lady, not from me.”

As soon as they were alone, Margaret threw her arms around Catherine’s neck and kissed her.

“Mother, mother—I am not quite happy—but oh, I am proud.”

And she vowed on her knees never, by word or deed, to let her love stand between this young saint and Heaven.

Reader, have you ever stood by the sea after a storm, when the wind suddenly dies? The waves do not stop with the cause—they lash harder at first. Yet we know calm has begun, gently rocking them to sleep. So it was with these lovers, from that night when they walked hand in hand beneath the stars—from hermitage to manse.

At times, a wave would roar—but it was only memory’s echo of the tempest. The storm itself was over. The boiling waters began to fall—down, down, gently, but surely.

This image takes the place of endless details that would bore. What matters now is the general state, and the strange tangle of feeling that arose. History, bolder than romance, offers few things stranger than the footing on which Gerard and Margaret now lived—for many years.

United by love, familiarity, and a marriage irregular yet legal. Separated by Holy Church and their own consciences, which sided wholly with the Church. Yet bound by a living pledge—lawful at its birth.

Living near each other, she calling his mother “mother.” For years, she brought her boy to Gouda every Sunday, returning at dark. Wherever she went, it was a festival at the manse. She was received like a queen. Catherine was often with her, Eli frequently. Tergou held little charm compared to Rotterdam—and eventually, they left it altogether, settling in the capital.

Years passed—quiet, uneventful, free from great hopes or fears, so alike that without dates I could scarcely mark their passage.

But early in 1471, the Duchess of Burgundy—openly opposed, yet secretly aided by the Duke—raised troops to help her deposed brother, Edward IV of England, invade the realm. Our old friend Denys enlisted. Passing through Rotterdam to the ships, he learned that Gerard was a priest and Margaret alone. He told her that marriage was not his habit—but since his comrade had broken his vow, he felt bound to honor it for him. “A comrade’s honor is as dear to us as our own,” he said.

She stared—then smiled. “I prefer to remain your she-comrade,” she said. “Closer, we might not agree so well.” As her she-comrade, she equipped him with a new sword from Antwerp and a double handful of silver. “I give no gold,” she said, “for it vanishes as fast as silver—and harder to reclaim. May Heaven keep you safe from peril. There are famous fair women there to beguile you with their faces—and men to strike you with axes.”

He was hurried aboard at La Vere and never saw Gerard at that time.

In 1473, Sybrandt began to decline. His fragile life had been sweetened by his brother’s tender care and his own rare contentment—remarkable given his past. Gerard spent two hours daily with him—reading, singing, praying, drawing him in a soft carriage they had built together. When death drew near, Sybrandt begged Margaret be summoned. She came at once. With his last breath, he sought forgiveness—again—though she had granted it long ago. She stayed until the end. He died, blessed and blessing, cradled in the arms of the two true lovers who had parted him from life. *Tantum religio scit suadere boni.*

In 1474, there was a wedding in Margaret’s house—Luke Peterson and Reicht Heynes.

This may seem odd. Let me explain the interrupted conversation.

Margaret continued: “Then you can easily make him fancy you. And for my sake, you must—for my conscience pricks me. I must provide him with a wife—the best I know.” She instructed Reicht to be always kind and cheerful toward Luke, while she would be deliberately irritable. “But do not be so simple as to criticize me,” she said. “Leave that to me. Make excuses for me—I’ll make myself black enough.”

Reicht accepted the task like a command to sweep a room—and obeyed exactly.

For two years, they subjected poor Luke to this dual pressure. He came to see Margaret as fog and wind, Reicht as sunshine. Gradually, his affections shifted—without knowing how or when.

On the wedding day, Reicht embraced Margaret, nearly weeping. “He was always my fancy,” she said. “From the first moment I saw him.”

“Heyday! You never told me that. Are you as sly as the rest?”

“Nay, nay,” Reicht insisted. “But I never thought you’d really give him to me. In my country, the mistress expects service before the maid.”

Margaret settled them in her shop and gave them half the profits.

1476 and 1477 were years of deep trouble for Gerard. His conscience forced him to oppose the Pope. His Holiness, siding with the Grey Friars in blurring the distinction between Mary and Christ, offered indulgence to all who added this clause to the Ave Maria: “And blessed be thy Mother Anna, from whom, without stain of sin, proceeded thy virgin flesh.”

Gerard, like many northern clergy, called this flat heresy. He refused to utter it in church, warned his flock against using it privately, and rejected the new feast the Pope invented—the Feast of the Miraculous Conception of the Virgin.

This earned him bitter enmity from the Franciscans, who had the power to place him in serious danger and inflict many petty humiliations. In crises, he consulted Margaret. She either said, “I do not see my way,” refusing to guess—or gave advice that proved remarkably wise. He had genius; she had extraordinary tact.

When affection blinded her judgment, he stepped in. She knew she spoiled little Gerard, and Catherine ruined him—yet neither would part with him. He remained at home, talents neglected. A shrewd nine-year-old, instead of learning obedience, played and learned selfishness from their endless devotion, ruling two intelligent, spirited women with an iron rod.

Gerard saw this with pain. He intervened gently but firmly. After much struggle, he succeeded in sending the boy to the finest school in Europe—run by Haaghe in Deventer—in 1477. Many tears were shed, but the boy’s progress reconciled Margaret somewhat. Reicht, now her business partner, allowed her to visit him often.

And so the years flowed on. These two, faced with one of the strongest temptations imaginable, became each other’s guardians—not tempters.

Of course, the polished morality of the next century—teaching that vows to God are sacred only if reasonable—had not yet entered any mind. Their choice was clear: self-denial or sacrilege.

It was strange to hear them speak with open tenderness of their son—while a frozen wall stood between themselves.

Eight years had passed. Gerard, compared to most men, was happy.

But Margaret was not.

Her usual expression was gentle pensiveness—but sometimes she grew irritable, petulant. She snapped at Gerard now and then. If she visited and found a monk with him, she would turn and go home. She hated monks for separating her from Gerard—and passed that hatred to her son, whose contempt for them lasted until death.

Gerard bore it like an angel. He knew her heart was gold—and hoped the bitterness would pass.

He, now the right man in the right place, loved his parishioners and was loved in return. From dawn to dusk, he labored in good works, regaining his natural cheerfulness. To be honest, some of his humor was a mask—he was the greatest peace-maker since Mr. Harmony in the play. In ten years, he reconciled more enemies than his predecessors had in three centuries. One trick? Making quarrelers laugh at their dispute—thus undermining discord. But beyond that, he genuinely enjoyed harmless jokes.

He was also a master of animals—squirrels, bears, fawns. Once, a farmer brought him a mule believed possessed. “Tame this vagabond, parson, if you can.” Six months later, Jack not only obeyed—Jack ran to his whistle like a dog.

One day, sheltering from rain outside a tavern, he heard a drunk inside boast he could drink more at a draught than any man in Gouda. Gerard marched in: “What, lads? None take him up for Gouda’s honor? Shall a stranger claim we’re weaker than he? No—your parson takes him up. I’ll find a parishioner who drinks more.”

A bet was made. Gerard whistled—Jack clattered in, calm as ever, nose in his hand.

“A pair of buckets!” shouted Gerard. “Let’s see which of these two sons of asses drinks more!”

Another time, two farmers argued whose hay was better. “Ask the parson,” they said. By now, he was their referee.

“How lucky you thought of me!” he said. “I have a guest staying with me—the best judge of hay in Holland. Bring me a double handful each.”

They arrived. He placed the bundles on chairs. Then whistled.

Jack entered.

“Lord a mercy!” said one farmer.

“Jack,” said the parson, casually, “just tell us—which is the best hay?”

And so the years passed—peaceful, full of quiet duty, and profound, unspoken love.

A priest is never more truly a priest than in the chamber of death. Gerard performed the final rites of the Church for the departed with solemn precision, as he would have done for any humble soul in his parish. His movements were automatic, his voice steady—yet beneath the ritual lay a storm unspoken. He knelt afterward, not from duty, but from awe, and offered thanks to Heaven for her peaceful passing, her end marked by faith and grace. Then, all thought turned to one thing: to remove her from strangers’ hands and lay her to rest within the sacred ground of his own churchyard.

That very evening, a single-horse cart, draped in black cloth, set out for Gouda. Inside rested a coffin—and beside it, Gerard, broken and silent, his arms wrapped around the cold lead, his chin pressed against it as if clinging to the last trace of her presence. The energy that had carried him through the preparations had spent itself; now, he was crushed, immobile, bound to the casket like a man chained to sorrow.

The driver of the cart walked ahead of the horse, speaking not a word. When he stopped to feed the animal, he did so in hushed tones, mindful of the grief that hung over the mourner like a shroud. At nightfall, they reached an inn, where landlord and driver, moved by compassion, tried gently to coax Gerard inside for food and rest. But he resisted fiercely—his eyes wild, his voice low and fierce, like a dog guarding its master’s grave. They gave up, drew a cloak over him, and left him alone in the darkness, still clutching the coffin as if life itself depended on it.

At noon, the cart arrived at the manse. A dozen parishioners stood gathered, each bearing their own small sorrows, but all already feeling the absence of their parson. When they saw the cart and recognized Gerard—so pale, so shattered—they let out a collective cry of grief. It stirred him from his numbness. He looked up, saw their faces, and tried to speak.

“Oh, my children… my children!” he gasped, but the words choked in his throat, and no more came.

Yet the next day, despite warnings and pleas, he insisted on conducting the burial himself. Standing at her grave, he read the service with voice only faintly trembling. Tears fell freely upon the earth, some from him, many from those who loved her. When the prayers ended, he remained motionless, rooted to the spot like a statue carved from sorrow. The people stepped back, respectful, leaving him to his solitude.

Then, without warning, the sexton—simple-minded, thoughtless—began filling the grave, the clods of earth falling softly but steadily onto the coffin. At the first sound, Gerard screamed—a raw, piercing cry that tore through the quiet air.

The sexton froze. Gerard staggered, hand flying to his chest. “Something snapped,” he whispered, breathless. “I felt it… I heard it… here…” And he pointed, trembling, to his heart.

Jorian Ketel, standing nearby, mourning the woman who had been kind to him, rushed forward. Together, he and the sexton supported Gerard, guiding him slowly into the manse. There, half-swooning, he leaned against the wall, eyes wide, whispering once more: “Ah, Jorian… good Jorian… something broke inside me… I felt it… here…”

Two weeks later, a frail and hunched figure approached the Dominican convent on the outskirts of Gouda, seeking an audience with Brother Ambrose, who now governed the monastery in the absence of the prior—deceased recently—and before the arrival of his successor. The man was Gerard, returning to the cloister not as a man of faith renewed, but as one whose life had grown too heavy to bear. He came not to serve, but to rest.

He entered as a novice, though only in name. In truth, he was broken—body and spirit—and knew it well. This place, quiet and sacred, was where he wished to lay down his burdens, near Ambrose, his trusted friend, and among the monks whose company had always been a solace. His home, once full of warmth and purpose, now echoed with memories of her—the woman whose absence left a void no sermon or sacrament could fill. The weight of those memories pressed upon him like a physical pain; the house was no longer a refuge, but a prison of longing.

Ambrose, who understood both Gerard’s worth and the depth of his sorrow, harbored a quiet hope that healing might yet be possible. Perhaps with time, care, and gentle guidance, the vicar could recover and return to his parish. With this intention, he assigned Gerard a modest but comfortable cell above the main gate, where the air was fresh and the light soft. He strictly forbade fasting or any harsh penance, insisting that the body must be preserved if the soul were to find peace.

But within days, the new prior arrived—an austere man, stern in manner and uncompromising in rule. At first, he devoted himself entirely to reforming lax customs and restoring order. Yet when he learned that the vicar of Gouda had taken up residence as a novice, he reacted with sharp disapproval. “It is well,” he declared, “but let him first surrender his vicarage—or leave. I will have no fat parsons under my roof.”

The prior summoned Gerard immediately. The latter obeyed, stepping into the chamber with slow, measured steps. The moment their eyes met, both men froze. Recognition flashed between them—sudden, startling, almost unbearable.

“Clement!” one breathed.

“Jerome!” the other replied.

The world seemed to pause. A past long buried stirred anew.

Jerome remained as stern and reserved in temperament as ever, yet his heart had softened toward Gerard. During the time he had spent in England, he had missed him more than he dared admit, and since then, the thought of his younger brother’s fate had haunted him. What Jerome heard in Gouda—especially that Gerard had stood firm against the Pope and the Minorites over what he called “the infernal heresy of the immaculate conception”—only elevated him in Jerome’s eyes. But when a young monk, weeping, revealed the true cause of Gerard’s illness, Jerome’s disdain flared anew.

“Dying for a woman?” he muttered, shaken by the idea. He resolved to prevent this disgrace. Twice each day he visited Clement in his cell, wielding all the authority and eloquence of his years in an effort to rouse him from his spiritual despair. He urged him not to abandon the Church, not to let worldly sorrow rob it of one of its most gifted and devout sons at such a pivotal moment.

Gerard listened with quiet reverence. He agreed with Jerome’s logic, admired his strength, confessed his own frailty—but still, he grew weaker, inching closer to the threshold of eternity.

One day, Jerome told him he had learned the full story—and done so with pride. “But now,” he said, “you undo it all. This is the triumph of earthly love. Better to have yielded, repented, and lived; than to resist while she lived, and surrender now, body and soul.”

“Dear Jerome,” replied Clement gently, his voice soft and free of reproach, “you do me injustice. There is no passion here—only deep affection, and I will not be ashamed of it, neither here nor in heaven. Think: is the dog who dies grieving at his master’s grave guilty of passion? Neither am I. Passion might have saved my life—but destroyed my soul. She was my guardian angel. She upheld me in duty, in charity. Her face gave me courage in the pulpit; her voice comforted me in times of ingratitude. She wove herself into every good thing I did. After leaning on her so long, I could not go on alone. And know this, Jerome—I am no rebel against God. It is His will that I depart. When they covered her coffin with earth, something within me broke—a bond too sacred to mend. I heard it, felt it. From that moment, no food tasted like anything. If I were blind, I could not tell bread from flesh by taste.”

“Holy saints!” murmured Jerome.

“And yet,” continued Gerard, “from that same hour, my sorrow lifted. I smile again—often. Why? Because I believe God, who holds life and death in His hands, gave me that moment—the great summons. A cord of life snapped within me. He is merciful. I would have lived in pain; but He said, ‘Enough has been done, enough suffered. Poor, weak, loving servant, your failings are forgiven. Your sorrows lead you to rest. Come to Me.’ I come, Lord. I come.”

Jerome groaned. “The Church has always known holy men of fragile hearts,” he said. “I would give ten years of my life to save yours. But I see it cannot be. Die in peace.”

And so, within days, Gerard lay dying—not in torment, but in serene joy, so radiant that even seasoned monks gathered to hear his final words.

That evening, he saw Giles and begged him to care for poor Jack, to ensure little Gerard’s trustees fulfilled their duties, to kiss his parents for him, and to send Denys to his friends in Burgundy. “Poor boy,” he whispered, “he’ll feel lost without his comrade.”

Then came a private meeting with Jerome. What passed between them was never fully known, but it must have been profound—so deeply moved was Jerome that he left the chamber with hands crossed over his chest, head bowed, and breath drawn in quiet sighs.

Two monks stayed through the night, watching vigil. All through the hours, Gerard spoke softly—prayers, praises, thanksgivings. Once, he wandered, seeing her walking in green meadows, surrounded by spirits in white robes, beckoning him forward. They smiled and gestured. The monks smiled too, touched by the vision.

And just before dawn, three slow, light taps sounded against the wall—one after another. Gerard heard them, and whispered, “I come, love, I6 I come.”

This much is certain: those words were spoken, and then he prepared to leave.

He summoned all the monks keeping watch. They came, hovering like gentle angels, whispering holy prayers. Some knelt with faces to the ground, others cradled his head with tender hands. When one began praising his life of self-denial and charity, Gerard interrupted.

“My dear brothers,” he said, “take note: he who dies here in such peace does not hold these modern notions of human merit. Oh, how terrible it would be if I did! No—like the Apostles, like the early Church fathers, I believe we are justified not by our wisdom, piety, or good works, but by faith.”(1)

Silence fell. The monks exchanged glances.

“Please sweep the floor,” he said, his voice clear and strong, as if restored by divine power.

They obeyed, awed and curious.

“Make me a great cross with wood ashes,” he added.

They formed a large cross upon the floor with ashes.

“Now lay me down upon it,” he said. “So shall I die.”

They lifted him gently from the bed and placed him upon the ash-cross.

“Shall we stretch out your arms, dear brother?” one asked.

“God forbid!” he replied. “Am I worthy of that?”

He lay silent, eyes raised upward in rapture.

Then, half to them, half to himself, he whispered, “Oh—how buoyant it feels. It lifts me floating in the sky, where my merits once dragged me down like lead.”

Daylight broke. His face was turned upward, hands clasped—just as Margaret’s had been. And near the hour she died, he spoke his last word.

“Jesu!”

With that, he fell asleep.

They dressed him for burial. Beneath his linen, they found a horsehair shirt.

“Ah!” cried the young monks. “Behold a saint!”

But beneath the hair cloth, they discovered a thick, long tress of auburn hair.

They recoiled. Horror seized them. Voices rose in protest and defense.

Just then, Jerome entered. Hearing the commotion, he turned to Basil, a zealous young monk shouting about scandal.

“Basil,” he said, “is the woman who owned this hair alive or dead?”

“How can I know, father?”

“Then for all you know, it may be the relic of a saint.”

“Perhaps,” Basil replied skeptically.

“You have broken our rule,” Jerome declared. “It says: 'Do not interpret any brother’s act with evil intent when it may be understood innocently.' Who are you to judge such a man? Go to your cell. Stay there a week in penance.”

He took the lock of hair and carried it away.

When the coffin was ready to close, Jerome cleared the room and laid the tress upon the dead man’s chest.

“There, Clement,” he whispered to the still face.

Then he fastened the coffin shut himself, performing a penance for the act.

The next day, Gerard was buried in the churchyard of Gouda. The monks followed in solemn procession from the convent. Jerome led the service, clearly acting on the deceased’s wishes.

The grave was deep. At its bottom rested a lead coffin. Gerard’s own, light as a feather from his wasting, was lowered beside it.

After the rites, Jerome addressed the crowd of mourners. As he spoke of the departed’s virtues, loud sobs and tears erupted—tears falling upon the coffin like rain.

The monks returned to the cloister. Jerome gathered them in the refectory.

“We have laid a saint in the earth today,” he said. “The convent will keep his trentals—but we shall feast, not fast. For our beloved brother is freed from the burden of flesh. His labors are ended. He has entered into joyful rest. I alone shall fast and do penance—for I confess, to my shame, I judged him unfairly, and only knew his worth when it was too late.

“And you, young monks—do not speculate whether that lock of hair was a token of love or a relic of sanctity. Instead, look to the heart he wore beneath it. Above all, study his life, his words, his deeds. Follow them if you can—for he was a holy man.”

Thus, after the fever of mortal life, these true lovers found peace.

The grave, kinder than the Church, united them forever.

And now, a man of another age and land, stirred by their story, has sought to build their tombstone, to rescue them from unjust oblivion.

He asks not your pity, but your sympathy—for their rare constancy, their pure devotion, and the cruel separation imposed by a vile heresy(2) within the Church itself.

No, do not mourn their early deaths. Their end was happy. Let their lives teach you: on earth, obstacles often stand between us and perfect joy. Let their passing strengthen your reason and your faith—preparing you for the inevitable.

For if you cannot bear the thought that these two died young, remember: had they lived a hundred years, they would still be dead. How then shall you endure when those you love most—gentle, true, faithful—slip from your arms into the grave, and fly from your home to heaven?

Such is the lot of all.

In every age, the Master of life and death—kinder, wiser than we—has taken the sweetest flowers of earth and transplanted them to heaven.

Let their story stir your heart, not your grief.

Beati sunt qui in Domino moriuntur.

(1) He quoted Clement of Rome: “Not by our own wisdom, nor by our piety, nor by our works done in holiness of heart, but by faith.” —Epistle to the Corinthians, i. 32.

(2) Celibacy of the clergy—an invention truly fiendish.

In accordance with a custom I loathe yet cannot bring myself to defy, I pause here at the end of my tale to gather up the scattered threads of lives that once wove through its fabric—those who, though minor in the grand design, lent truth and breath to the journey. Not every figure deserves an epitaph; those fleeting souls served their purpose if they made Gerard’s path from Holland to Rome feel lived, not imagined—a world peopled by flesh and blood, not mere puppets.

Eli and Catherine outlived the ages, their names fading into memory as Gerard and Margaret became shadows in the minds of others. Giles, too, endured long years; he reached the court of Bavaria, still standing at ninety, though now little more than sinew and bone, his voice like a trumpet grown thin with time. Cornelis, unchallenged and long forgiven by his mother—who clung to him ever more tightly as her children drifted apart—waited patiently for the death of his parents. But Catherine’s sharp words had foretold the truth: before either she or her husband passed, Cornelis had already worn out. At sixty-five, he lay dying in his mother’s arms, a woman of eighty-six whose strength had not failed. He had lain unconscious for hours, but just as death approached, he stirred, opened his eyes, and spoke plainly of how he would rebuild the shop and premises once they were his own. “Yes, my darling,” she murmured softly, smoothing his brow. And then, in silence, he was gone—turned to dust, carried to the grave by every foot he had once waited to mend.

Denys, shattered by the loss of his comrade, found solace in returning to Burgundy. There, a modest pension from the court sustained him until, unexpectedly, he inherited a fortune from a distant relative. For many years, he was known in his homeland as a gruff old soldier—grumbling about women, yes, but capable of telling vivid tales of war when the mood struck him.

Jerome, disillusioned by the laxity of northern ways, withdrew to Italy. Through noble connections, he rose to become a mitred abbot at seventy. He enforced strict discipline, ruling his monks with iron resolve. They feared him, respected him, hated him—yet none truly loved him. For ten years he governed without warmth, without trust. Then one night, alone in his chamber, he died. The Vulgate lay on his pillow, the crucifix in his hand, and upon his lips—a faint smile, softer than any seen in life. Perhaps, in that final hour, he was not quite alone. Requiescat in pace. The Master he served has many servants, and among them, minds of every kind—sometimes stern, sometimes faithful, always human.

And so, the golden-haired boy, Gerard Gerardson, does not belong solely to fiction. He belongs to history. She has recorded his birth in different words than mine. Above the tailor’s house in Brede Kirk Straet, she has inscribed: *“HAEC EST PARVA DOMUS NATUS QUA MAGNUS ERASMUS.”* She has written half a dozen biographies of him. Yet there remains a task for her still. No small mind, no partisan eye, can fully grasp the greatness of Erasmus—just as no dwarf can comprehend a giant. He was not only the foremost scholar and theologian of his age, but also the natural-born dramatist of his century. Some of the finest scenes in this book spring from his own medieval pen, lighting up these pages with brilliance. For genius such as his does not speak to die. Its work may seem dormant after the first impact—yet each new wave of understanding brings it back to life. From the dust of ancient libraries, it rises again—budding, blooming, bearing fruit, seeding wisdom across generations, through centuries.

Thus ends the tale.
